Flagrat enim et interno aestu delectabiliter exardescit, et ad ea quae foris sunt, non videtur incandescere, sed frigescit, dum quidquid est hujus vitae, tanquam sterile gelicidium jam non curat, et seraphin ardentibus interno se desiderio configurat. Verumtamen ut eamdem lampadem constet inutiliter non accendi, nec conqueratur proximus ex ea sibi quidquam utile non impendi, quae prius lampas ignis, consequenter et flammarum dicitur lampas esse, ut non solum sibi, sed et proximus diligenter perpendentibus appareat non deesse. Nam qui amat, et amoris incendio fortiter concrematur, non languore torpet, non otio, sed vigilantius operatur: oculisque non lippientibus [0482A] gratam largo munere fundit lucem, et se formam operantibus, ambulantibus praebet ducem. Quem ardentem et lucentem non exstinguit aquarum multitudo, non minis, non blanditiis cedit amans, vel ejus fortitudo; non denique flumina, non majorum inundatio pressurarum, non fames, non gladius obruent ignis exuberantiam vel flammarum. Charitas enim tanta viget violentia vel vigore, ut non possit obrui parvo tribulationum impetu vel majore, ut aquarum multitudinem, et roris guttulas pluvialis, et incursus majores fluminum amore sufferat praemii spiritalis. Huic igitur charitati recte quidquam perfunctorium non confertur, imo quidquid potest hic haberi, ei digne charitas antefertur: cuicunque caput sanum et judicii veritas non aufertur, [0482B] hanc eligit et diligit super omne quod transitorium hic offertur. Unde subdit: *Si dederit,* etc.



## CAPUT XLIII.

*Si dederit homo omnem substantiam domus suae pro dilectione, quasi nihil despiciet eam.* Quisquis non gaudet sola insensibilium vel irrationabilium portione, sed humanam figuram obtinens, praepollenti *281* fungitur ratione; si dederit quidquid habet acquirendae intuitu charitatis, nil dedisse videbitur, si compos hujus factus fuerit voluntatis. Substantia nominatur quidquid in praesenti nostra vel necessitas, vel cupiditas coacervat, et in usus temporales vel expendit procuratio, vel conservat; substantia, inquam, non qua subsistimus essentialiter ad vivendum, sed quae nobis viventibus substare vel subsistere [0482C] dicitur ad utendum. Quae ob hoc non incongrue substantia domus hominis appellatur, quia ejus necessitas talibus adminiculis sustentatur, eisque domum suam ditat quisquis sollicitus, et honorat, qui tamen vel arcere pauperiem providus, vel augere divitias cupidus elaborat. Cujusmodi substantiam profligat largius et dispergit, qui profundo acquirendae dilectionis desiderio se immergit, qui cum illam dederit, et istam se persenserit accepisse, datum conferens et acceptum, sibi diligentius intuenti videbitur nil dedisse. Tanta enim aviditate diligit et amplectitur hoc acceptum, ut ducens pro nihilo quidquid dederat sic despectum, et ejus quod praeterit, ad id quod non interit, nulla comparatio [0482D] videatur, sed ut nihil illud, occiduum, istud vero manens, ut magnum quid et praecipuum habeatur. Nec est abs re, si corpus hominis hoc loco substantia nominetur, cum in eo vel ex eo homo subsistere comprobetur; et ob hoc *domus suae* addit Scriptura facere mentionem, quia illic thesaurus animae habet tanquam in vase fertili mansionem. Si igitur corpus istud, cui constat animam tam tenaciter admisceri, ut ab affectu ejus non possit facile cohiberi (non est enim invenire, qui velit ab hac domo sive corpore spoliari, cum Paulus quoque optet supervestiri potius quam nudari; et Petrum ter amantem ab ista lege carnis amor penitus non reduxit, sed Christo praedicente, quo non vellet, alius illum duxit): si corpus, inquam, istud, cui [0483A] gunfis tam tenacibus anima colligatur, homo cordatus dederit, nihil dedisse congruum arbitratur [n: (Rom. VIII)]. Non sunt enim condignae passiones hujus temporis. Quam dilectionem ob hoc attollit Sponsus tam multipliciter et commendat, ut tantopere commendatam Virgo diligens magnipendat; et cum perpenderit commendatae culmen non modicum Sponsi munere se adeptam, intelligat se in hujus oculis non despectam. De qua sodales subjungunt: *Soror nostra,* etc.

## CAPUT XLIV.

*Soror nostra parvula est, et ubera non habet. Quid faciemus sorori nostrae in die quando alloquenda est?* Videmus, inquiunt, Virginem in amoris gratia non mediocriter profecisse, sed tamen ad optatum necdum [0483B] plenius pervenisse, quia, etsi amoris intuitu ad contemptum praedictae substantiae jam pervenit, adhuc tamen, quem sic amat, in decore proprio non invenit. Et quia soror nostra est praecelsis quidem meritis, non natura, unius Dei Patris haereditatem nobiscum postmodum perceptura, loquentes ad invicem de illa paululum conferamus, et, si forte nostri quid indiget, non jam singulariter, sed omnes pariter afferamus. Quantum nobis visum est, quod ista soror nostra, quae, ut supra dictum est, in cubiculum meruit jam induci, adhuc tamen non se gaudet de cubiculo in cubiculum introduci; ista quidem causa est, quod necdum satis est sufficiens, nec adulta, sed laborans parvitate, et ad annos quasi [0483C] nubiles non perducta. Solet amor inhonestus quem praevenit intemperantia vel libido, quem usurpat et deturpat Venus male suasoria vel cupido; solet, inquam, praeripere aetate Virginem immatura, voluptati magis obtemperans, quam parans Virgini profutura. Sed quoniam amor iste quem habemus in manibus, etsi vehementior, tamen prudentior amat esse, et amator, hunc amorem non tam sibi quam Virgini vult prodesse; exspectat, reexspectat idem Sponsus, et habet patientiam in amore, quandiu Virgo meritis et gratia proficit ampliore. Adhuc ergo parva est, et videmus eam ubera non habere, quamvis supra fuit ostensum eamdem uberibus non carere, sed quia necdum plenam videntur sufficientiam obtinere, ea dicimur non habere, quae sponso volunt [0483D] quidem, sed nondum satis praevalent apparere. Non sunt aptae nuptiis virgines, dum adhuc puerascunt, dum aetas est parvula, dum adhuc ubera non turgescunt, quae, etsi parum prominent, et aetatis proferunt specimen profuturae, adhuc tamen retinent priscam teneritudinem immaturae. Quia igitur sic parva est, et sic eam constat ubera non habere, quid faciemus ei? quid ultra jam poterimus adhibere; quid quod ad nos pertineat ultra poterit jam conferri, ut diem nuptiarum tandem gaudeat non differri? *282* Alloquenda quidem est, et in secretiorem thalamum inducenda, sed ante de praesentibus, et necdum sufficientibus educenda, et ut possit hinc educi, quid ultra nobis est faciendum, quod scilicet proficiat ad diem tam desiderabilem obtinendum? In die illo hoc [0484A] est, in respectu et profectu diei illius, quid conferre possumus huic sorori, quo nostro vel studio, vel amore eam praeparabimus ampliori, ut ad diem perveniat, pro quo velut impatiens et tam sollicita nunc habetur, quando eam amator nobilis, consummata lege sponsalium, alloquetur? Etsi enim superius cum ea, vel de ea, multifariam modisque plurimis est locutus, non tamen munus completorium, sed studium est meritorium prosecutus; nunc restat ut haec illum intra cubiculum cubiculi prosequatur, prosecutam eo quo novit modo ille ineffabiliter alloquatur. Alloquendi vocabulo mysterium tegitur spiritale, quia figuris familiariter utitur hoc epithalamium nuptiale, et haec allocutio qua sponsum sponsam optamus et praedicimus convenire, ipsa est [0484B] conjunctio, qua quaerentis facies datur quaesiti faciem invenire. Allocutio est, cum praesentatae praesens quidquam dici congruum non celabit, sed carenti corruptela suam illi faciem revelabit, nullisque mediantibus alter alteri sociabitur in secreto; et Virgo videns Verbum, amore satiabitur jam completo.



## CAPUT XLV.

*Si murus est, aedificemus super eum propugnacula argentea. Si ostium est, conpingamus illud tabulis cedrinis.* Quaerentibus sodalibus quid faciant quod illi congruum sit diei, quo Virgo visura est optatam diu gloriam divinae speciei, ipsi tanquam sermone vicario non differunt respondere, decernuntque Virgini [0484C] sollicita benevolentia providere. *Si murus est,* inquiunt, compactus lapidibus et caemento, imo virtutibus copulatis charitatis mediae ligamento, restat ut super eum argentea propugnacula fabricemus, murique fortitudinem defensione superaddita confirmemus. Est Hierusalem civitas Sancti, collectio fidelium numerosa, addicta in praesenti fructuosis laboribus, spe inconfusibili gloriosa, quam in unum velut manipulum unus Dominus, una fides copulat et constringit, et eamdem Virgo sancta exemplo et doctrina, meritis et intercessionibus circumcingit. Si ergo murus est, imo quia est, gaudens civibus circumponi, expedit circumposito defensionem aliquam superponi, ut scilicet nostra sollicitudo, nostra cohortatio desuper vigilet et intendat, ne ad [0484D] illum penetrandum hostis vel ad modicum se extendat. Etsi enim laborantem Virginem, necdum, sicut desiderat, possumus hinc transferre, hoc saltem laboranti debemus et volumus jam conferre, ut eam et nostra defensio reddat contra quaevis occurrentia praemunitam, et frequens allocutio, ut patienter sufferat, eruditam. Sic muro propugnacula non lapidea, sed argentea praeparamus, cum virginem sollicitis defensaculis, et alloquiis confortamus, cum hostium incursantium malitiam prohibemus fortiter ab accessu, et illis inclamamus, securam esse virginem de successu. Ne autem civitas haec muro videatur circumposito sic inclusa, ut per eum, ab eis quae non a se, sed quasi deforis habet beneficiis, sit exclusa; ipsa, quae murus est, ostium nihilominus [0485A] appellatur, per quod quidquid civitati est necessarium ministratur. Per Virginem enim Sponsus ad collectionem fidelium diligit introire, per eam quoque omnibus in ea confidentibus subvenire; ipsa omni clausa viro, soli Deo fidei clavicula reseratur, ut per ipsam ad homines Verbum caro visibiliter inferatur. Si igitur ostium est, cedrinis illud tabulis compingamus, hoc est praedictae hujus gratiae invictam fortitudinem adjungamus, ut cuivis detrahenti occurrat odorifera latitudo, et forte durius insistenti resistat indeficiens fortitudo. Haec interim dum laborat, et sudat Virgo nobilis in agone, praeparemus et confortemus ejus patientiam spe coronae; et revera non longe est quod sperat et postulat sibi dari, ut sentimus, jam videbit et gaudebit Sponsum nuda [0485B] facie revelari.

## CAPUT XLVI.

*Ego murus, et ubera mea sicut turris, ex quo facta sum coram eo, quasi pacem reperiens.* Audiens Virgo angelos erga ipsam negligentes et desides non haberi, sed sui sollicitos, suum patrocinium, vel ministerium polliceri; brevi sermone monstrat quae sibi gaudeat jam conferri, sperans mora longiore, quae sunt reliqua, non differri. Ego, inquit, donante gratia et operante manus industria jam sum murus congeriem vivorum lapidum charitate ligante media non casurus, *283* cui mea supereminent ubera, sicut turris, honorem praestans muro, terrorem inferens hostibus accessuris. Sicut murus virtutum congeriem et internae vinculum charitatis, sic ubera vitae formam [0485C] et doctrinam designant veritatis, quae prodeunt et festinant foris omnibus apparere, ut diligentes instruant, cogant adversarios abhorrere. In quibus, etsi nondum ad complendum praesentes nuptias, est perfecta, ea tamen annis retro plurimis est adepta, ex quo scilicet coram eo quasi pacem meruit reperire, cujus pacem alteram affectat, et in proximo exspectat invenire. Ex quo enim ad concipiendum sanctus ei Spiritus obumbravit, non pacem, sed quasi pacem nasciturus ei Filius apportavit, quia pacem a vitiis, pacem in gratia, a strepitu carnalis geniturae, non pacem visionis, non pacem mansionis in aeterna gloria permansurae. Neque de suo solius profectu ostendit se gaudere, sed monstrat et caeteros profectum non mediocrem obtinere, qui [0485D] per eam donante gratia adeo profecerunt, quod vinea non palmitibus, sed dives populis fieri meruerunt. De qua subjungit: *Vinea fuit,* etc.

## CAPUT XLVII.

*Vinea fuit pacifico, in ea quae habet populos. Tradidit eam custodibus, vir affert pro fructu ejus mille argenteos.* Ex quo operante Spiritu, coram eo reperi quasi pacem, vinea Domini Sabaoth profectum habuit efficacem; et quae prius angustis Judaeae finibus est detenta, nunc in ea quae habet populos latius et feracius est inventa. Ea quae habet populos, fides, vel unitas, vel dilectio potest dici, cui constat diversos populos unanimo spiritu sic addici, ut apostolis praedicantibus non solum multa crediderint [0486A] millia Judaeorum, sed et in omnem terram sonus exierit, et audita praedicatio sit eorum. Cujusmodi vineam ad custodiendum, apostolis virisque apostolicis commendavit, quorum praedicatio eam non solum in Judaea, sed et in nationibus propagavit; et Paulus cum Judaeam indurescere conspicit et perverti, extunc et deinceps ad gentes asserit se converti. Quae prosperante gratia, parvo tempore sic excrevit, sic infantiae novitatem et teneram inefficaciam abolevit, ut vir, id est potens non tam viribus quam virtute, pro fructu ejus mille argenteos, id est sua donet omnia pro salute. Flos vineae, vitae est conversio; fructus, est perfectio secutura, pro cujus centenario quisquis cupit esse vir, projicit transitura: fructus denique ipsa est retributio praemii [0486B] spiritalis, quod vir sibi comparat contemptu pretii temporalis. Qui enim non muliebriter, sed viriliter agere comperitur, pro fructu ejus vineae dare quidquid poterit non metitur, sed avidus praemii spiritalis, ut illud recipiat cum usura, pretii temporalis prodigus, affert illud sine pondere, numero vel mensura. Nam mille argenteos, id est quidquid vel infinitum numero, vel magnum pretio possidebat, quod ejus oculis arridebat fallaciter, favorabiliter in auribus tinniebat, ad pedes apostolicos afferens, projicit, et habet vice stercoris in contemptu, ut aeternum fructum recipiat, spretorum temporalium interventu. Enarratis autem Virgo tam suis quam profectibus aliorum, commendata vinea quae magis viget populis quam multitudine pampinorum; non [0486C] jam angelos respondentes, sed arrectis auribus sponsum audit, qui et Virginis et vineae favet laudibus, et applaudit.

## CAPUT XLVIII.

*Vinea mea coram me est: mille tui pacifici: et ducenti qui custodiunt fructus ejus.* Ostendit Sponsus quod vinea quae sequitur, et temporalia dat pro ipso, non ambulat in tenebris, sed est in lumine coram ipso, cui favens et approbans, quod datis propriis maneat jam in ipso, non par pari retribuit, sed duplum, sive centuplum cum seipso. Ille, ait, qui propter me temporalem habet substantiam in despectu, ut confortetur amplius, meo se esse noverit in conspectu; et legenti vel audienti notum fiat cuivis inexperto, quod diligentem diligens, inde [0486D] gratam faciem non averto. Illi quippe mille argentei quos, juxta verbum tuum, diligit vir afferre, qui secundum formam tuam amat invisibilia visibilibus anteferre, erunt pacifici, id est pacis praemia merebuntur, pacem illis conferet, qui pro aeternis propria largiuntur. Nec pacifici solum dici poterunt, sed ducenti, id est pacem duplicem conferent largienti, quia pax sive perfectio, quam rerum distributio promeretur, et in praesenti magna est, in futuro maxima prosequetur. Sicut in mille perfectio, sic intelligitur et in centum, qui profecto duplicantur, cum vinea tam efficacem ducitur ad proventum, ut abjectis superfluis, pacem mereatur duplicem *284* invenire, quisquis illius fructus amat cura vigili custodire. Qui enim praeesse forma, doctrina [0487A] commendabili vult prodesse, et supradicti fructus custos sollicitus amat esse: hic per mille argenteos pacem primam, sed non praecipuam introducit, et centum in ducentos commutans, secundam meliorem postmodum superducit. Ostenso autem breviter quod omnibus perfectis competit gratia generali, statim redit ad virginem amore et sollicitudine speciali; et cujus, supra omnes praedictae vineae palmites, habet curam, eam de pace transitoria vult transire citius ad mansuram.



## CAPUT XLIX.

*Quae habitas in hortis, amici auscultant, fac me audire vocem tuam.* Etsi, ait, tam eos qui afferunt, quam qui afferre differunt mille argenteos pro ducentis, ego adhuc differo, nec induci suffero ad optatum [0487B] praemii consequentis; te, quam prae cunctis diligo, nolo diutius a desiderio cohibere, sed optione data, volo te, quidquid elegeris, mox habere. Tu ergo quam eduxi de habitaculo tenebrarum, de umbraculo durae mortis, et excellenti gratia habitas non in arido, sed in hortis; elige verbum gratum, vocem tuam exere, dic tu ipsa, stant sodales, amici auscultant, audire cupiunt a te ipsa. Ego ipse qui novi melius, quidquid dicere jam disponis, audire volo vocem, et internae beneplacitum optionis, ut dicendi modus non mihi sed caeteris innotescat, quos tua latet optio, si non vocibus elucescat. Apud te amor vane praetereuntium et timor supervenientium non arescunt, sed fides, spes, dilectio, tanquam [0487C] horti rore florido dilucescunt; et tam mira istorum gratia tuum desiderium sic delectat, ut ad ea quae infra sunt, nulla concussio te inflectat. Optas quidem egredi, seu transire protinus ad superna, fastidiens quidquid est temporis, apprehendere citius vis aeterna, quidquid ad praesens contuli, futurorum desiderio vis mutare, rejecto carnis pallio meam dilecti faciem praesentialiter salutare. Et illa: *Fuge,* etc,

## CAPUT L.

*Fuge, dilecte mi, assimilare capreae, hinnuloque cervorum super montes aromatum.* Multis supra locis aut vicibus dilectum Virgo diligens invitavit, eumque advenire modis pluribus postulavit; et in ipso Cantici capite ejus osculum diligentius praeoptavit, [0487D] et per totum hoc epithalamium id se velle et expetere demonstravit. Quid ergo sibi vult, quod nunc repellit eum, cujus se languere desiderio supra clamat, quid causae esse dicimus, quod monet fugere eum, quem sic amat, nisi forte quod amantes habent iras spe concordiae gratioris, quia, ut quidam praedicat: *Irae amantium, redintegratio est amoris?*
Sed, ut videre videor, amor Virginis iras nescit, sed eum quem sic amat, videre citius inardescit: et quia novit eum hoc in loco vel corpore non videri, optat illo secum ire, ubi eum valeat intueri. *Fuge,* ait, *mi dilecte,* ad secretum Patris sanctuarium, [0488A] cito redi, illuc tecum me advoca, ubi nullis ultra molestiis possim laedi; exue me citius ab hujus corporis corruptela, et ubi licet, quantum licet, mihi visibilem te revela. Et quia capreae hinnuloque cervorum similari supra fueras assuetus, esto et nunc in hoc negotio velox, agilis, et discretus, quid deceat sponsam matrem digne consideratio tua cernat, et a cunctis pure hominibus excellentiori privilegio me discernat. Montes aromatici, supernae sunt et angelicae potestates, quae nobis laborantibus varias et necessarias afferunt sanitates, quorum ministerio utilia nobis aromata comparantur, eo tamen disponente, cujus arte pigmentaria temperantur. Infra istos montes angelicos nolo mihi ulterius colloquaris, sed fuge supra eos, ut longe excellentior habearis: [0488B] tene sedem in Patris dextera, tam angelis quam hominibus inaccessam, mihi tecum, ut video, matri cum filio jam concessam. Tene ergo manum dexteram meam, et me deduc in tua voluntate, sequar Agnum quocunque ierit [n: (Apoc. XIV)], nulla claudicans tarditate; fuge cito, ut fugiam, quia et ego fugere sum parata, te praevium videbo fugiens super angelos exaltata. Postquam autem virgo Sponsa, mater a Filio gloriosius est suscepta, et sedem gloriosam cum Sponso super angelos est adepta, quo honore gaudeat, quo se gaudio videat honorari, silendum magis censeo, quam de talibus audeam verbosari. Quod enim meus vel mei similis non capit intellectus, quis modus proferendi esse poterit [0488C] vel effectus, cum etiam quod utcunque intellectus aestimat contemplari, non tamen possit facile verbis congruentibus explicari? Illud sane dici potest, quod ubi est Filius qui sumptam carnem ad Patris dexteram collocavit (quidquid illud vere est quod Scriptura dexteram appellavit); illic est mater ejus quae illi carnem propriam ministravit, quae ex suo utero integritate salva Deum hominem generavit. *285* Illic, inquam est, et honore glorioso vel gloria honorabili coronatur, et de illo, et in illo, et cum illo quem genuit, compos desiderii gloriatur; eique Sponso Sponsa veris et sinceris complexibus sic inhaeret, ut amore satiato, irremissum amoris desiderium perseveret. Est igitur mater cum Filio non solum spiritu, de quo vel tenuis dubitatio non habetur, [0488D] sed etiam corpore, quod nimirum incredibile non videtur, quia etsi hoc Scriptura canonica non clamat evidentibus documentis, ad hoc tamen pia fides adducitur verisimilibus argumentis, quod, etsi non satis probat quis in verbo et scientia repentinus, illud tamen dignum credi noster ille asserit Augustinus. Nec est molestum angelis si cum Sponso Sponsam, matrem cum Filio thronum vident regium obtinere, et quem prius in gremio, in coelesti solio nunc tenere; si humanam carnem vident supra se in matre et Filio gloriosus honorari, et apud nos inchoatas feliciter, illic felicius nuptias consummari.

De quibus quia, ut valui, etsi non ut volui, sum [0489A] locutus, et pede satis lento loquendi terminum assecutus: quaeso te, Virgo sancta, ut, cum tuo in coelestibus Filio nunc assistas, ab ejus, qui tuus est, cura et sollicitudine non desistas. Tuus quidem ego sum, si non satis condigno merito, affectu saltem paululum promptiore, tuus, tibi serviens, quamvis adhuc nesciens utrum dignus odio vel amore [n: (Eccle. IX)]; tuus, tibi desiderans obsequiis et muneribus complacere, si tamen in proposito mihi dederis efficaciter praevalere. Tu igitur, Virgo sancta, de manu mea suscipe parvum munus, non est aurum, non argentum, non lapis regum donariis opportunus; sed inculta verborum libatio, sensu prodita grossiore, parva satis oblatio, sed plena vigiliis et labore. Cujus exercitio tanquam rudi gymnasio postquam me [0489B] contuli, multis molestiis sum percussus, et occursu malignantium velut a fronte graviter repercussus, opusque inchoatum multoties pressuris durioribus [0490A] intermisi, sed revocante et juvante tua gratiore memoria non dimisi. Tu igitur cujus ope, in camino pressurarum sub gravi malleo non defeci, sed utcunque respirando, opus coeptum in tuo nomine jam perfeci, nunc oblatum suscipe, offerentem corripe misericorditer, et emenda, emendatum dilige, dilectum tuo Filio me commenda. Scio enim quia si fuero tua illi benevolentia commendatus, vel me prorsus non mordebit, vel morsu non nocebit coluber venenatus; et vel linguas detrahentium ad modestum silentium ille tuus Filius revocabit, vel rumores eorum veneficos in antidotum salutiferum commutabit. Sic nimirum a cunctis nocentibus, tuo spero interventu, tua gratia liberari, liberatus per gratiam donis potioribus cumulari: cumulato jam [0490B] concedes per te in Filio gratulari, et ut finem ponam libro, mihi tandem a malis libero vobiscum in coelestibus gloriari.

*Joannes GALLEMART S. Theol. Doctor, et catecheseos professor in Universitate Duacensi, hac 7 Febr. 1618.*

## *101* HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF THE SAME.

[0181A]You demand a work heavy and arduous, and unequal to my strength; not sufficiently attending to what you so insistently, so anxiously ask for, and from whom, since — to confess the truth — I in no way know or feel within myself an understanding so subtle that I might be able to bring to effect what you desire. And indeed the poet is found to have admonished his hearers rather carefully — among whom I sometimes recall that I sat, a boy — that those who write should not be headlong, rashly presuming upon any great matters whatever, but rather circumspect, taking up a matter equal to their own strength: *Take up,* he says, *you who write, a matter equal to your*
*Strength; and turn over long what your shoulders refuse to bear,*
*What they are able to carry.*
[0181B] But if the weighing of one's strength is a narratorial thing in the songs of the heathen, much more is it so in the nuptial and spiritual Song of Songs, which surpasses not only the dirges of the Muses and the empty fables of the poets, but even the hymns of our own men and the songs of the prophets. Furthermore, so many treaters of this work, as many modern as ancient, are to be found, that I do not know whether those who come later could add anything beyond; and since there are very many commentaries of theirs upon this Song, anyone coming later [0182A] would seem; not so much to strike out new things as rather to steal what was found before. Nevertheless, whatever I object does not appear to satisfy you, but you wish me to attempt what is not to be had in my knowledge or in my eloquence. And assuredly a spiritual matter weighs down and overweighs heavier shoulders, since spiritual things, according to Paul: « The animal man does not perceive [n: (I Cor. II)]. » And so, like a man prudent and aware, I put my hand into the fire, or commit myself in a fragile skiff through the deep perils of the sea, trusting in him alone who wills that his own be worn down by labour not in vain, who, being good and merciful, says to those who speak of him and labour for him: « I am here. » With him, I beg, do you also commend me by your prayers, and obtain for me his grace, that I may be able to do what I wish — which, as one just and [0182B] truthful, he will not grant to my merits, and, as one compassionate and merciful, he will not deny to your prayers. *102* You men of old know only one moon;
In our times another and greater is at hand.
The sun, long alone, is amazed at a greater newness,
For a new moon brings forth a new sun.
If you wish to know better which, or who, I shall unfold it:
Christ the sun rises, the moon Mary bears him.



## PROEM ON THE SONGS.

[0181]

[0181C]A certain king of kings and lord of things (and if anything worthier or more excellent can be named, whereby his power and powerful excellence may be commended) obtained a region of wondrous and unheard-of greatness, in which he decreed to make no portion divided off for another. It seemed indeed agreeable to his good pleasure that his kingdom should remain undivided to himself; and that none there should be reckoned greater than he, or even his equal, who by an equal power, rebellious and insolent, might be hurried away into an affront. A certain part of that region is held to be loftier, brighter, more honourable, which seems the worthier for his more frequent presence; the other part far lower, more rugged, dark, to its own Lord perhaps not gracious by an equal merit. But in that part over which [0182C] he presided above, a great order of many princes attended upon him, who had received a command to serve their lord with bowed neck, and with unwearied zeal to modulate praises consonant with him. Wherefore he also made them chief and conspicuous by a wondrous and admirable dignity, and, as it were, by a certain secondary power upon the throne of the kingdom; so that they might preside in excellence over all who lived in the whole kingdom, and might themselves lie subject to their own Lord with worthy reverence. One of them, who seemed to himself not inferior to the rest, who rejoiced in the benefit of comeliness and honour he had found, conceived something lofty and rash against his lord; and seeking greater things, judged that he would be like him. And in this very many out of so great a number of great ones consented with him, who [0183A] presumed to think themselves equal to the highest of all; and he at once despoiled them all of the glory conferred upon them, and, despoiled, destined them for the lowest part of that kingdom. For in the highest part he suffered nothing repugnant, nothing unfitting, nothing troublesome, nothing at all dishonourable to linger; but the evil once arisen he presently cast down by a severe judgment, and set the evil ones far from the serene glory of his countenance. But they, being set far off, did not even so cease from malice [n: (Sap. XII)], but infected the dwellers of that outermost part with the venom of their own wickedness, and forced them to become rebels against the lord of them all, and drove them by threats and by force, by wiles and by blandishments, into a like injury. For there that highest king, by a counsel which he himself knows, suffered the evil to run wild and grow strong, nor did he at once restrain each evil man with the hastened sickle of punishments; [0183B] but, though he could either by a nod alone forbid that they should be done, or presently avenge each hurtful deed once done, he seemed wondrously patient to forget them as they went on to worse. So in a short time, as much by the prompting of the greater as by the consent of the lesser, that whole lower part of the kingdom is depraved, and all flesh corrupted venerates its king and lord neither out of fear nor out of love; but him whom, being present, it both does not see with the eye and, with a malevolent heart, now does not feel, to his commands (if perchance it sometimes hears them) it does not consent. Sometimes indeed, looking down upon them from on high, he destined his messengers for them, and speaking in many parts and in many ways, called back those who had gone astray through error to better things and to things next to salvation; but very many of them, entangled in the hard and long-lasting bonds of the vices, [0183C] were softened neither by his warnings nor by his promises. Only a very few, to whom the spiritual teaching was made brighter and more pleasing, or whom perhaps natural reason and understanding admonished, had by a sounder counsel a humble regard toward that their King, and, good men among the evil, worshipped the Lord according to place and time. Yet in so many spaces both of places and of times men of this kind were found so rarely that, since — as was said before — all flesh had been corrupted, that king could easily know his own by name everywhere among the nations, whereas the multiplicity of the evil could now be comprehended by no number of men. And this endured not only for many years, but for many ages of years, in which against their king and against his law the [0183D] people hardened their neck. All of them guilty, and by the merit of their guilt *103* introduced at the last into the eternal darknesses of the prison, save for the fewer who had before been brought back into his grace. But throughout the whole series of times in which the people was found to be held in the aforesaid error, that king had purposed to have mercy on them at the end of times; in the last age to impart his grace more abundantly to the wretched, whom he saw perishing as much through ignorance as through malice. He chose a wondrous and sufficiently marvellous manner of showing mercy; but the reason why he should choose this rather than another cannot be clearly comprehended, save that he saw it more pleasing to his own good pleasure, and for this reason no one rightly wise doubts that it is better. But this mercy which he was to show to the erring people in the last days, and the manner of showing it whereby he was to fulfil it, he willed to be revealed in [0184A] diverse nations as well as places and times to very few, whom by an ampler grace he willed to be called *seers* or prophets. And they, with the eye of the mind unveiled, willing to open the mystery to the rest who did not know it, nevertheless took pains to open it in figures and riddles; and preaching to the peoples the benefits of the aforesaid king that were to come after, they brought forth many things indeed by tongue or by pen, but obscure ones, so that they might neither, after the manner of the envious, wholly conceal the king's grace, and yet might not divulge the holy mystery to the unbelieving who were unworthy of it. But some of them committed these things, understood and foreseen, to a remembering writing, and so transmitted them to those who were to come long after in the succession; that not only those then present, but rather those coming after, might read true things in the Scriptures, which the [0184B] understanding of those who went before foresaw and did not begrudge to those who should come after. And among those who wrote one after another, a certain man puts himself in the middle, whose knowledge and teaching ecclesiastical authority does not set behind the rest; who, perceiving by a prophetic spirit the secrets of things to come, brought them forth by a wondrous kind of writing to the knowledge of the rest. That highest king of whom we speak, having no end nor beginning of existing, having not by grace but by nature to persist unchangeably; whose strong power it is given to none to have leave to resist, but to whom he wills, and how he wills, a welcome possibility of standing by: he had a Son of the same nature, substance, majesty, coeternal, coequal, of one power through all things. Him he had appointed to send to that depraved and pestilential nation of men, that among them and in the midst of them he might make a lingering dwelling, [0184C] and might take from them a certain virgin to himself by a nuptial covenant, whom nevertheless, above the law of marriages, he would keep entire in mind and body as a virgin. For he saw that by the benefit of marriage anger, brawling, hatred, and rivalry are called away far off, and joy, fairness, welcome fellowship, peace, and love are called back; and that to this not two alone, but many thousands together are called together; and that men who are diverse and (what is more wicked) adverse are effectually drawn on to will the same thing and to be unwilling for the same thing. He saw that nations diverse in tongue and in manners, regions sundered from one another by land, by sea, by much distance between, are alike allied by the reconciled marriage of one bridegroom and bride, and that from then on and thereafter they obey, cultivate, love, and venerate one another. Finally, by the benefit [0184D] of marriage the longed-for offspring of sons is acquired, and among them a welcome brotherhood of minds thrives; and as both brothers and cousins are multiplied, natural love and affection grows beyond measure, and thus the primal usefulness of the nuptial bond is extended to more. In this way, then, or rather in a far more excellent way, he purposed to call back his enemies, and, taking a bride from among them, willed to turn them into friends; so that when men should render the right of brotherhood to the bridegroom of their sister, they might, having found a fitting degree, advance in loving toward the eternal. For the Father, who was appointing to send the Son to this, and the Son, who loved to obey the sender in all things, is God immortal, impassible, invisible by nature, whom no visible creature could either see or hold visibly; and for this reason, among men, the very Son of God [0185A] willed to be received into the virginal bridal chamber of the bride, so that, proceeding thence as a bridegroom, he might be seen and held in nuptial form and habit. And before this should really come to pass, some, as has already been said, foresaw it in the spirit, and left it set down in their writings, some obscurely, some more obscurely. One of them is found to have described the mutual affections of the Bridegroom and the Bride more expressly, and to have woven, as it were, a tale subtle and honourable, spiritual and modest. That man knew that singers, men and women, are employed at temporal marriages, and that by them measures of song and various praises are set forth; that they touch with a taught hand the lyre, the cithara, the symphony, and weave a concordant melody with sackbut, pipe, and psaltery, so that in all these they are found becomingly to rejoice with the nuptial [0186A] chamber, and to admonish the other guests to rejoice together. Formed wondrously by that form or example, our scribe followed up this notable bridal chamber with epithalamic praise: he composed a new and unheard-of drama after the likeness of the comic poets, who, as they speak, bring on the various persons of the stage. This kind of writing antiquity before him certainly did not know, but from him, as it seems, posterity took it up far below: while the schools of the Greeks that followed after, because they could not sufficiently grasp what he wrote mystically and of what, at least transferred that same manner of writing to their own vanities and follies.



## EXPLANATION OF THE TITLE OF THE SONG OF SONGS. Now the title of this work is: *Songs of songs of Solomon.*

[0185]

[0185B] *104* Since in this little work he wrote nothing but praises of the Bridegroom and the Bride in concert, he superscribed in the very title Song, or Songs, so that at the very forefront the prudent reader might by that reminder be prepared for the praises of the bridal chamber, and, loving them, might modulate them not by the [sic: *molodia*] of the voice, but by the concert of manners. But because many both before and afterwards are found to have brought forth Songs in their writings, yet not to have described the praises of this bridal chamber in them so excellently; for the commendation of these and for their distinction from the unequal rest, he set down here not only Songs, but Songs of songs. For just as both the Holy of holies and the Sabbath of Sabbaths are more eminently exalted above holy things and Sabbaths, and ages of ages are preferred in dignity and glory to ages; so, since in the writings of the ancients [0185C] there is much commendation of Songs, something ampler and far more sacred is promised and contained by the Songs of songs. And lest the writer of this work be unknown to its readers, and, the writer being unknown, the authority of the writing be lessened, he pointedly set himself to make mention of its author, plainly naming Solomon in that same title. *Songs,* he says, *of songs of Solomon.* [var: Vulg. *Canticum canticorum Salomonis*, singular] This Solomon was held to be a king and a king's son, and for this reason he rightly venerates the highest King, the King's Son; describing with how great a grace of peace his marriage shines out, and with what quiet and glory the noble Bride lies hidden in his bosom. Furthermore, as the Interpreters say, by the name of Solomon *peace* is signified, and his peaceful kingdom is designated by the testimony of Scripture; whose warfare an Egyptian hand did not succour as though he were weak, [0185D] but rather from Dan even to Beersheba Satan, that is the *adversary*, did not meet him. « He had, he says, peace on every side round about, from Dan even to Beersheba [0186B] [n: (III Reg. IV)]. » And below: « Rest, he says, my God has given me round about, and there is no Satan nor evil encounter [n: (III Reg. V)]. » [var: Vulg. 3 Kings 5:4 *requiem dedit Dominus Deus meus mihi per circuitum* — Migne omits *Dominus*] By whom is signified he who by his own power made both one, who set himself as a corner-stone to the Jews and to the Gentiles coming from opposite sides [n: (Ephes. V)], who, coming from the bosom of the Father, nevertheless did not cast off heavenly things, who coming to the unjust made salvation and justice near to them. He who gathered into one, as by a bond of concord, the earthly and the heavenly, whom not so much the quality of their place as the inequality of their merits had long sundered from one another; when in the bridal chamber of the Bride he celebrated a spiritual marriage, by which he wondrously joined the divine and the human nature in a unity of person. Rightly, therefore, is the describer of this work called Solomon, that is, *the peaceable* [0186C], hinting that a song of this kind is not worthily sung by anyone unquiet, lest anyone think that he has attained the contemplative or theoretic summit of knowledge who has not first been carefully instructed in the moral and the natural. For the more effectual teaching of which, he, being about to write this book, is found to have sent two others before it, and in each to have described each matter with vigilant care; having in the first that which they call ethics or the moral, in the second physics, which they assert is called natural. In the first he teaches the untaught, and composes us to elegance of manners, and while composing them he frequently interposes the Father and the Son; moreover, in the [sic: *tilulo*] also he calls himself a king, a king's son, so that both the dignity of a father and a royal fear may compel us. *The proverbs,* he says, *of Solomon the son of David, [0186D] king of Israel.* In this book he implants a fatherly discipline in the untaught and the little ones, asserting that he who does not hear falls the more heavily into ruin; but that he who understands [0187A] possesses his own helm, because an obedient man ought rather to speak victories than to be silent [n: (Prov. XXI)]. But in the second he teaches a man well composed and endowed with an age now mature, that every creature under the sun lies subject to vanity; and that in the same state no begotten thing abides, but everything that is begotten tends by nature to perishing. *105* And since those things which are of the world are not going to remain in a stable degree, but by an inevitable law their appearance and figure passes away, he probably hints that such things are not to be clung to, but that something else ampler and nearer to salvation is to be sought. But because it is a rare and arduous thing in some manner not to see visible things — that is, to cling to visible things by no affection of the mind — in the title of this book also he called himself a king, a king's son, [0187B] and, as though by right of command, addressed the assembly, that is, the Church. *The words,* he says, *of the Preacher, the son of David, king of Jerusalem.* He willed indeed that those whom the timely sweetness of teaching does not sufficiently allure should be shaken and driven by the untimely authority of a king, and that it should promote them to a more advanced place of natural knowledge, so that they might judge contemptible whatever they know to be unstable by the privilege of a temporal course. In the third volume he makes no mention of royal power, but, that being now buried, he names Solomon simply; showing that they who worthily come to this reading, lulled in the peace that is due, seek the vision of the Bridegroom alone. This reader indeed, having utterly despised what he understands to be transitory, and having learned by every diligent care what is oppressive, now with a freer spirit obtains the contemplative place, [0187C] from which the presence of the Bridegroom shuts out whatever unfitting and harmful thing comes upon him. In these volumes, then, he comprehends moral, natural, and contemplative knowledge; in the first of which the son lays hold of a father's discipline, not of money; in the second he grasps that all things passing under the sun are vain; in the third, having forgotten what is below, he stretches himself wholly into the divine and the heavenly. In the first every untaught man is formed in good manners by a father's watchfulness; in the second the visible world is disfigured for him by the desert of its mutability; in the third that lower man is reformed with a wiped face, and, brought into the sanctuary, is conformed by a welcome likeness to him whom he sees. In the first Abraham hears him commanding, hastens to go out, is prepared for moral [0188A] obedience [n: (Gen. XII)]; in the second Isaac digs wells, seeks waters, searches out natural things [n: (Gen. XXVI)]; in the third Jacob sleeps upon a stone, is present among angels, contemplates divine things [n: (Gen. XXVIII)]; he sees God himself, as he says, face to face, and is saved. In the first he feeds the future bride, still untaught and a little one, with moral precepts, with the rules of discipline, with a saving binding, and shuts her in more strictly and wraps her about; in the second, now grown up, he frees and looses her from the frauds of suitors and from the bonds of deceivers; in the third, now marriageable, the Bridegroom claims her alone for himself alone and joins her to himself, to whose chaste commerce no unchaste person joins himself. Rightly, then, is that first book, the executor of precepts, called ethical or moral; the second, the pursuer of visible things, physical, [0188B] natural; the third, the attainer of invisible things, contemplative, theological, spiritual — the later it is in order, the more principal in a worthier excellence. In it Solomon saw and foresaw that a certain virgin was to be born of the royal stock, one who would please the highest King and his Son far beyond all others; in whom the Son of God would dedicate to himself a temple, a tabernacle, a bridal chamber, that in it he might celebrate a marriage certain to some beforehand, but utterly untried by all. And lest anything honourable or fitting should seem to be lacking to that marriage, he says that with the Bridegroom the friends of the Bridegroom, and with the Bride maidens, are at hand; and so, with four persons as it were speaking to one another, he orders a spiritual epithalamium, by whose frequent approach and withdrawal the nuptial drama is woven. And the virgin whom Solomon sees thus to be loved by the Son [0188C] of God, and to be specially chosen for this ministry, or (if it please better) mystery, is she who is noble in birth, notable in manners, beautiful beyond the daughters of men, wise in letters, humble in spirit, glorious in merits; she, I say — that I may at last name her — is Mary, sprung after Solomon from his posterity, who joyfully occupies the first part of this drama. For whereas many before the virgin spoke very many things here and there about a marriage of this kind, and followed out its heraldings and its prior approaches, Solomon in this book brings forward nothing of theirs into the middle, but suddenly brings on the aforesaid virgin speaking.

## BOOK ONE.



## CHAPTER THE FIRST.

[0187D]



## CHAPTER THE FIRST. (cont.)

[CANT. I.] *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.* Here first there occurs a question to be asked: since in this drama four persons, as it were, are brought on addressing one another — the Bridegroom and the companions of the Bridegroom, the Bride and the maidens who accompany her — why at the beginning the Bride more hastily leaps forth to speak, when that office would seem to be granted to the worthier Bridegroom. But by this it is hinted that the virgin is not darkened by ignorance, but with a learned spirit searches out the words of the preceding prophets; [0188D] and just as it is agreed that Solomon as well as the rest foreknew things to come, so did she know the things that had been foretold of her. She knew therefore that in many parts and in many ways God had of old spoken beforehand in the prophets [n: (Hebr. I)], and *106* had followed out whatever was necessary for the making of the marriage — he who from the days of Moses and far beyond had foresignified by many figures of things and riddles of words that this was to be, namely, that for the grace of the marriage he would come into the bosom of a virgin. But the virgin wills that all things that foresignify should [0189A] now be silent, that figures and riddles should not have place as before, that he who is promised should at last show forth his own presence, and should not any longer hold back the desire of her who awaits him from the sight of him. Because, she says, things promissory do not suffice for a tender love, but the languor grows heavy if things fulfilling are deferred longer than is right; since for obtaining what I love I neither ought nor am able to bring to bear things coercive, I judge it worthy simply to offer words of entreaty. *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.* I have learned, she says, from the report of the Scriptures, that it was once said to Abraham that the nations would rejoice that they were blessed in his seed [n: (Gen. XII)]; and that this is not held worthy of belief in Isaac his son [n: (Gen. XXI, XXII)], but is more effectually fulfilled at the fitting time in mine. Isaac too, begotten of a father now aged, ready, obedient, prepared [0189B] for the victim at a boyish age — what did he designate but this joy of mine, which my God assigned to me before I came to be? But as the world grows old I grieve that he whom I desire does not draw nearer, that he who is to be sent does not more quickly obey him who is to send him, that to me who love and long my joy is not conferred, which I desire the more in that it is not taken away from him who possesses it. I have learned that Jacob, about to sleep, did not put a pillow under his head, but with a stone set beneath slept far sweet [n: (Gen. XXVIII)], in which I have no doubt that he is figuratively foresignified who, when the kiss has been given me, shall be cut from the mountain without hands. In Judah the son of Leah, whom the aged father wills to be praised by his brothers [n: (Gen. XLIX)], from whom it is certain enough that the Jews are derived both in race and in name, no other seems to me [0189C] more fittingly signified by him than he who confesses God the Father to be Lord of heaven and earth [n: (Luc. X)]. I have learned of Joseph, whose death is found more pleasing to his brothers than his life [n: (Gen. XXXVII)], from the time that, having become a dreamer, he was clothed with a coat of many colours [n: (Gen. XXXIX)], whose chastity is read to have been assailed by the threats or the blandishments of a shameless mistress, but the young man leapt over the snares set before him with an unencumbered mind. He it is, as I see, who, when the kiss has been given me, shall be clothed with a new garment varied with virtues, and, proceeding as Bridegroom from the bridal chamber, shall suffer many envious men; who shall flee the malice of the present life as an unchaste harlot, having the cleanness of the highest chastity and of chaste goodness as his handmaid. He it is to whom, as Lord of things, the rest shall bow with bended knee, whom the stars, the sun and the moon, whom kings and [0189D] princes shall adore; who shall sustain with wondrous prudence Egypt labouring more with death than with famine [n: (Gen. XLI)], and shall minister the nourishment of life to all who worthily ask. Why should I unfold Moses, Aaron, Joshua, why the order of the judges, why should I name David, why the other kings, why each of the prophets, in whose catalogue not one at all is set down who does not by word or by deed speak beforehand of him whom I desire? But because he sent all these before as certain heralds and timbrel-players, in whose preludes he did not yet give his presence but promised it, now, impatient of delay, I do not accept their heraldings; I weigh all at a low price, since he is not received in presence. My understanding has indeed [0190A] now perceived that he is to come, since they promise it, but so great a love of him who is to come has intercepted the desire of me who wait, that whatever promissory thing now creeps up to the understanding or to the memory — as trumpets and flutes, sistra and psalteries, and whatever clatters outside at the door — I now, as it were, loathe, while I wish him alone to be led into the midst, and to be brought into my bridal chamber more sweetly and more laboriously. Let him therefore who is to come not stretch out the delay longer, let him not hold the desire of me who wait in suspense by an intolerable postponement, but let him who was promised of old at last descend as dew upon the fleece, and let him not salute from afar, but show himself nearer to her who longs [n: (Judic. VI)]. For I wish that he hide himself no longer in the bosom of the Father, that he not from thence dull my ears with a wordy frequency of messengers, but that he flood me — who have long borne it and can bear it [0190B] no longer — with an ampler grace, and pour himself wholly into my lap by a full inflowing. For to what does it profit that a soul held in suspense be soothed by so great promises, and that what is promised be experienced with no effect at all, since languor rather leads to death if health be always absent, and the beloved be not at last presented to her who loves by a welcome commerce? *Let him therefore kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.* He, moved by the heat and the desire of her who asks, although he does not at once fulfil the impatient soul of her who waits, still goes on to send to the virgin a more pleasing messenger, who in private speech should tell that the Lord is nearer. And whereas in many of those who went before there was much holiness, in this one much fortitude was found, in fact as well as in name, who, telling that the most mighty defender of Israel was at hand, [0190C] worthily deserved to be reckoned specially by the name of Gabriel. He, sent to the virgin, not forgetful of the excellence of him who sent him, does not stand outside at the door as one hindered by servile chains; but with greater confidence he entered a certain vestibule of the inner bridal chamber, having already professed both by word and by countenance who he is and why he comes. « Hail, he says, full of grace [n: (Luc. I)]. » The angel marvels that the virgin's secret place is unapproachable even to himself, carefully perceiving that it is not granted save to her Lord alone; and he rejoices to find the place of the bridal chamber so serene that, lying open to God alone, it rejects every stranger. *107* Hail, he says, virgin worthily glad beyond all virgins, now filled with the worthy gifts of all grace: to whom my Lord and the Lord of all has sent me before; nay, I see that he who sent me [0190D] is already with thee. « Hail, he says, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. » I thought that I came as a forerunner by the command of him who sends, but the commander has seemed to me to come before his messenger: perhaps because he willed first to find the virgin alone, lest I should seem to approach her, untaught and timid, without him. I judge that the angel, whom the Lord who sent him had already come before, did not find the aforesaid virgin in the forum or in the street, in tumult or in dance; nor did he find her held at last by spindle, needle, comb, wool, flax, nor by servile work, nor at the loom, but at leisure, or rather at a spiritual business, clinging to the Scriptures with an understanding or an affection wholly holy, not carnal. The angel himself therefore reveres her, found thus, and thus intent upon a divine [0191A] study, all witnesses removed; and marvelling at a youth robust not in years but in advances, he gives with much reverence the greeting entrusted for the virgin. « Hail, he says, full of grace, the Lord is with thee, blessed art thou among women [n: (Luc. I)]. » Thou, he says, so given over to a leisure or a business so honourable, so modest, oughtest worthily to be declared blessed among all women, or beyond all women; and so great a blessing shall attend thee, full of grace, that neither a first like thee nor a second following shall be made equal to thee. « And when she had heard, he says, she was troubled at his word, and thought what manner of salutation this should be [n: (ibid.)]. » The virgin, seeing an unwonted appearance of a man, is greatly afraid; and hearing something new, troubled none the less, she shudders, both because a man was not accustomed to be present at her spiritual leisure, and because she had not yet [0191B] perceived that she was worthy of so great an excellence. She turns therefore and turns over again what a salutation of this kind portends, what the angel standing by, or the Lord who sends him in, intends, since she does not yet manifestly comprehend the secret of the mystery, and it seems worthy that the virgin fear in all things, lest she offend. And the angel said: « Fear not, Mary, for thou hast found grace with God [n: (ibid.)]. » Let not a sudden fear, he says, trouble thy girlish mind, since with God thou hast found a saving grace; refuse not with a fearful heart his holy purpose and his good pleasure in thee, since that Lord gives thee the greetings which I, a messenger, bring. And he adds: « Behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and shalt bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name Jesus [n: (ibid.)]. » In thy womb, he says, the Son of God shall celebrate a wondrous marriage, and [0191C] thy very womb shall beget [sic: *eumdum*] Bridegroom as man, whom thou shalt call Jesus, by the desert of his own goodness; for he shall save his people from sins. And Mary said: « How shall this be done, since I know not a man? » [n: (ibid.)] Since I, she says, have decreed that I shall not marry in a carnal wedlock, and thou truly assertest that I shall shortly bring forth a son, by thy leave let me say it, I wish without doubt to know the manner whereby this, as being unfitting, can fittingly come together. I had indeed read, Isaiah writing it, that this marvel was to be; but neither he nor another had said that this was to be in Mary; and because this shoe seems wrapped about with a tangled latchet, thou, to whom perhaps it has been given, I wish that thou make it loosed for me. And the angel [0191D] answering said to her: « The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee [n: (ibid.)]. » Know, he says, that thou shalt experience no commerce of a manly coupling, but shalt conceive, by the working of the Holy Spirit, possibly indeed, yet ineffably; because he shall utterly remove from thee whatever unseemly thing is either said or felt, and shall forbid every heat of foulness by interposing himself as a kind of shade. And since the Spirit of God works this begetting holily and wondrously, without doubt that which shall be born shall be holy; and of God there shall arise no other than the Son of God, since in thee God and man are personally made one. And Mary said: « Behold the handmaid of the Lord, be it done to me according to thy word [n: (ibid.)]. » Having heard the manner in which a marvellous begetting may come to pass, in which God may be born of a [0192A] virgin who shall know no commerce with a man, the humble virgin is ready to obey the Lord, and now hopes and loves that what she understands to be holy should come to pass the sooner. Because, she says, it is the Lord whom thou preachest, and I know myself the handmaid of the Lord, I now ask that thy word be fulfilled, and that it be done to me according to it: rejoicing that he, good and merciful, has not despised me, undeserving, but, clement and most high, has looked upon me, cast down and humble. And so, the ministry which thou hast faithfully fulfilled being accomplished, and the mystery which thou hast spoken being understood with a faith sufficiently certain, this thy forannouncing has left me rather in suspense and, as it were, unquiet, nor is anything enough for me if I do not feel him present who sent thee. Let him therefore now send no other in his own stead, and let no messenger promise things to come to a hastening mind, [0192B] but rather let him now at a fitting time present himself to me, let him, present, presently kiss me who am present. *Let him kiss me,* I say, *with the kiss of his mouth.* Let this joining, I say, be made in me not by lips, but by two natures coming together, so that both natures may wondrously be of one person; and those whom until now both fault and natural diversity had set far from one another, let an undivided unity of person now league together in firm peace. For I understand that the fulness of the Godhead shall come into my womb, keeping unharmed my seal of virginal chastity; and that in this bridal chamber the Son of God himself, by the sweet kiss of the marriage, shall join in the unity of person two unlike things of natures. God shall indeed become man, the excellence of his own nature *108* not contaminating, not consuming, but powerfully purifying [0192C] and assuming the nature of man; and the assumer shall give to the assumed a marvellous and incomparable gift, namely, that the assumed and the assumer may become one by a wondrous conjunction. One, I say, not either God only, or only man, but one God-man; one Christ. Not indeed so that the substance of God be confounded, but so that humanity be assumed into God. This assumption, this joining, whereby God willed to unite man to himself personally, and to strike or to unite a covenant of peace between nature and nature in the womb of the virgin, is in the present passage called by an honourable word a kiss, because peace returned among those at discord is confirmed by a kiss. The virgin therefore wills that in her womb the concord of God and of man be repaired, and that the repaired concord be strengthened by an unshaken covenant, so that he who was God and Son of none but God the Father [0192D] may in a new and wondrous manner become the bridegroom and the son of a mother. Let him become the bridegroom, joining the virgin to himself by a certain conjugal covenant, resting in her bridal chamber, peace having been made by the nuptial kiss; in her, or through her, begetting spiritual sons by a spiritual efficacy, so that both he and she may rejoice in the fruit and offspring of sons. Let him become the son, taking true flesh in her womb, yet keeping her wholly entire, a virgin and unstained; and in her, as God, consecrating all the saints as sons and heirs of God, and, born of her as man, making them his co-heirs. At this benefit, ancient indeed in its promises, modern in fact, the virgin rejoices and exults, and asks that it remain for ever; and considering that by that good an evil both following and long-standing can be destroyed, [0193A] she wills that, when the kiss has been given her, he strike an everlasting pact with her. For she sees that he judges it wholly unfitting and unworthy that peace should not be unshaken when someone has given the sign of peace; and for this reason she wills him to be wrapped in that binding, as it were, which, once confirmed, ought not and cannot be further loosed.



## CHAPTER II.

*Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.* The mouth of the Lord — so is every holy man or prophet called, through whom he unfolds to men his own thoughts and secrets; through whom he both reveals to us things past and foretells things to come, more sweetly commands good things, more severely forbids evil ones. It is agreed that Moses was of old the mouth of the Lord, to whom God seems to have granted so great a grace that he was held privy to this secret long [0193B] beforehand, and that as a faithful messenger he should speak it as a thing that was to come after. « A prophet, he says, shall God raise up to you from among your brethren, like unto me; him shall you hear [n: (Deut. XVIII)]. » [var: Vulg. Deut. 18:15 reads *Prophetam de gente tua et de fratribus tuis sicut me suscitabit tibi Dominus Deus tuus: ipsum audies* — singular "thy brethren," "thou shalt hear"; the printed plural form is that of Act. 3:22] That David was the mouth of the Lord is doubted by none of the faithful — he who venerates this mystery foreknown by a prophetic spirit; and lest perchance he seem to begrudge to others what he foresees, taking up the psaltery, he modulates praises and Songs to him. « He himself, he says, as a Bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber, hath rejoiced as a giant [n: (Psal. XVIII)]. » That Isaiah's word may be commended with worthy reverence, and that the speech may not be judged contemptible on account of the speaker, in speaking to a people of hard neck, which is not easily moved to faith, in order to allure them or perhaps to terrify them, he sometimes declares himself the mouth of the Lord. « The mouth, he says, of the Lord [0193C] hath spoken these things [n: (Isa. I)]; » [var: Vulg. Isa. 1:20 *quia os Domini locutum est*, without *haec*, "these things"] and as Isaiah declares himself to be the mouth of the Lord, so too Jeremiah ought to be believed, and can none the less be said, to be so — men who, at the Spirit's teaching, spoke beforehand of the virgin's childbearing, and followed out the mysteries to come with a foreannouncing word. Isaiah: « Behold, he says, a virgin shall conceive and shall bring forth a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel [n: (Isa. VII)]. » [var: Vulg. *et vocabitur nomen ejus Emmanuel*, "and his name shall be called"; Migne prints the second person plural *vocabitis*] Jeremiah: « The Lord, he says, shall make a new thing upon the earth, and a woman shall compass a man [n: (Jer. XXXI)]. » [var: Vulg. Jer. 31:22 *creavit Dominus novum super terram*, "the Lord hath created," a past tense] Finally the angel Gabriel himself is found to be the mouth of the Lord, by whom the virgin, now grown up and marriageable, is approached in person concerning so great a mystery; and lest even a slight darkness of not knowing leave her in suspense, he unfolds both that she is to bring forth and the manner of the bringing forth. Whence the virgin, sufficiently certain, wills now no longer to hear the mouth of the Lord, but, burning [0193D] with love, wills to feel the kiss of the mouth — namely, that she may be cherished by the gracious coming of the Bridegroom, by a firm peace, by an unremoved presence, according to what is announced by the prophet or by the angel, as by the mouth of the Lord. « Be it done to me, she says, according to thy word [n: (Luc. I)]. » Be it done, that the fulness of grace may render me blessed among women; that the royal beauty of the bridegroom coming may adorn my bridal chamber; that the holiness of the Spirit alone may make my womb fruitful; that he may be mine, the Son of God, salvation, justice, wisdom, fortitude. By this kiss let that bridegroom, well-disposed, incline himself to me; by this let him lay me back — bride, mother, Virgin — in a peaceful bosom, in a gracious embrace; let this soothe me, refresh me, make me serene; let this, claiming me for himself, estrange me from all who come against me. But [0194A] let this be done according to thy word, which thou hast brought forth not with thy own mouth but rather with the mouth of the Lord, since thou hast been not thy own mouth but rather the mouth of the Lord; because thou art not reckoned thine own angel, thine own herald, thine own messenger, but his who speaks to me through thee, who makes thee wholly his own, that thou mayest speak. Wherefore I do not say to thee: Kiss me with the kiss of thy mouth, but rather of him: *Let him kiss me,* I say, *with the kiss of his mouth,* that he may at last deign to bless me with his own kiss, which to thee, his mouth, it was granted to proclaim with an announcing word. *109*

## CHAPTER III.

*Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.* The Virgin, hearing that, betrothed to the Son of God, she should bring forth God and man, and that in conceiving she should not at all feel a man, her purpose being kept, but that the Holy Spirit, [0194B] overshadowing her, should come upon her with an effectual power, with a certain faith and a robust hope, fervent in Spirit or in love, rejoices indeed in the hearing, but wills to rejoice more fully in a more pleasing effect. That spirit therefore of so great grace, of so great peace, so sweet, so kindly, of a power so wondrously effectual; who, warding off far away the injuries of the flesh, strengthens the purpose of chastity, who gives fruitfulness while saving the seal of virginal honour — that Spirit, I say, the virgin longs to be given to her more fully, and by him, as by a kiss, that the gifts promised her be confirmed. Let the voice of the angel cease, she says, who answers me with such great benefits, and let the Son of God himself come nearer, who betroths me, a virgin, to himself alone: let him touch me with his mouth, whose touch shall flood me with much grace; let him deign me with his kiss, let him make me fruitful with his spirit. In a kiss [0194C] of the mouth there is not only an outward joining of lips, but a certain breathing forth of what is within is also perceived and felt; and if these be clean and filled with a sweetened savour, the one who kisses pours as it were a sweet spirit into the one kissed. Since therefore the Spirit is belched forth, as it were, from the heart and mouth of the Son (for as the Spirit is preached to proceed from the Father, so also from the Son) — than which secret place none is truly esteemed cleaner and sweeter — rightly does the virgin ask to be kissed by the Bridegroom, that is, by the Son of God, so that she may taste the inward good, the saving Spirit being drawn in and perceived. I long, she says, that he come and stand nearer, in whom I have believed, whom I have loved, that that bridegroom, familiarly admitted into my chamber, may purify me, magnify me, gladden me with a sweet kiss: not that there be, as [0194D] is wont, an outward conjunction as of lips, but a certain welcome and sweet inpouring into me of the Spirit of his mouth. Finally, after God had first formed man from the slime of the earth, he breathed, as we read, the breath of life into his face [n: (Gen. II)]; and just as he is understood to have been made or fashioned as though by the hands of God, so was he animated to live in time by the breath of his mouth. Far below, Elisha, when he wished to raise a dead man, bending himself over him as he lay, willed to apply not only hands to hands but also mouth to mouth, so that, touched by the breath of the living, he might receive a living soul, and that, as the other lay upon him, the dead man might receive not a loss but rather a gain [n: (IV Reg. IV)]. But far more loftily and much more sacredly does the virgin will the Son of God to be at hand to her; much more sweetly, far [0195A] more laboriously does she will him to be present in a kiss — namely, that he impart a kiss, that is, that he make the Spirit of his mouth to be felt, that he touch her with a spirit of fuller grace and efficacy. Thou, she says, my Bridegroom, my God, deign to impart thy presence to me; give the kiss to her who asks, that is, give me to feel thy Spirit; let thy breathing upon me be so useful, so fruitful, and so pleasant, that I may both remain a virgin according to my vow, and yet, conceiving, be fruitful. Breathe upon me, I say, not only that with the rest I may be able to shape labour into a precept, but kiss the virgin, that by a kiss thou mayest give to the virgin, beyond all others, a conception: let thy kiss work wondrous things in me, and work them wondrously, so that both fruitfulness may be preserved to the Bride and virginity to the Mother by a singular privilege. You therefore in this audience, all [0195B] and each of you who stand by, if you think anything worthily and reverently of the word you have heard: attend to and love both the kiss which the Son of God the Father holds out, and the singular merit and solemn miracle of so great a mother. She, knowing and feeling the sacraments of the nuptial kiss, seeking nothing else, nor content with any other whatever, is bent as it were principally upon obtaining it; and for this reason at the beginning of her speech she asks especially that it be imparted to her, loving to experience its sweetness and its efficacy.



## CHAPTER IV.

*Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.* Let him, she says, whom I love, whom I choose before all, be wondrously joined to me; let an inward sweetness be poured out upon me by his kiss, by his Spirit; by whose help and working let the integrity of my [0195C] flesh be fortified, and let the Word be personally united in me to flesh, God to man. See the miracle of the Mother of the Lord. The virgin receives the Bridegroom's kiss, perceives the Spirit of him who kisses; and in the kiss she now conceives as a mother, while by the working of the Spirit she receives what is conceived. And this indeed the angel Gabriel had also preached beforehand, when he announced that the overshadowing Spirit would come upon her [n: (Luc. I)]; the evangelist Matthew [n: (cap. I)] afterwards confirmed it, when, recalling the deed, he commended the virgin mother. « She was found, he says, having in her womb of the Holy Spirit. » And below: « For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit [n: (ibid.)]. » This grace, this efficacy the virgin desires to be given her, when she so pointedly asks to be kissed by the bridegroom: longing in the [0195D] kiss not to feel the outward kisses of the Bridegroom, but that his inward Spirit pour forth an effectual grace upon her. In which type, as you know, when we are presented at the altar, and, consecrating the sacred mysteries, are ourselves also consecrated to the Lord — because by the desert of so great *110* an office we are now filled with the Holy Spirit — religion judges it worthy that we who stand by should kiss one another alike. Let us kiss, I say, not that we may mingle lips with lips, but that we may pour back upon others the grace of the Spirit we have received; and let those who stand by that same sacred mystery, humble and intent, become partakers of the sacrament by the working of the Spirit and the designation of the kiss. The virgin therefore wills that the earnest of the nuptial kiss be given her by the Bridegroom; she wills to receive by the Spirit of his mouth a certain [0196A] commerce of spiritual efficacy, namely, that both the integrity of her modesty and of her special purpose may remain unviolated, and that her virginal womb may conceive in a new manner and bring forth what it has conceived. This gift, this benefit, this grace that virgin alone deserved to find: that, when she was to conceive, not the knowledge of a man but the inpouring of the Spirit was found to come before her; that by a kiss alone, a virgin alone, alone might bring forth God and man, and that in her childbearing things so diverse, so discordant, should come together in a sounding miracle. But that Bridegroom, feeling the devout impatience of her who burns, does not turn away his ear from the desire and the prayers of her who calls upon him; and that mercy, which is his own, and his ancient counsel he does not hold back with himself any longer, but drawing nearer he presents himself more sweetly to her who loves. He presents himself, I say, and gives the vehemently [0196B] longed-for kiss to her who asks; and, the kiss being given, he gives a greater confidence to her who speaks, namely, that she should not at once withdraw as though the business were finished, but that, having once begun to speak, she should now go on confidently. So indeed you also, brethren, know that it sometimes happens when two are seen to come together alike from opposite sides: if the lesser earns to find the favour of the greater, the greater at the beginning deigns to impart a kiss to the lesser. And having received it, the lesser is strengthened with a longer confidence, so that thereafter he may speak out boldly whatever he judges worthy; and he who has felt the other's goodwill in holding out a kiss is rendered now more confident and more ready to speak. And so the virgin, having received the Bridegroom's presence, comforted by the nuptial kiss, knowing that she was to be a mother [0196C] by the inpouring of the Spirit in a virginal womb, somewhat more confident, turns herself as it were away from prayers, and turns herself with worthy praises to the Bridegroom now present.



## CHAPTER V.

*For his breasts are better than wine.* [var: Vulg. *ubera tua*, "thy breasts" — the second person, which the commentary at once expounds and which the lemma is re-printed with later in this same chapter] Rightly, she says, did I long for thy coming far beyond the time promised; rightly did I ask that the kiss of thy coming be given me, because I knew and perceived — not led by the sense of the flesh, not taught by my own spirit but by the divine — that thy breasts are far better than wine. Since in the Bridegroom's kiss she had felt not the breasts but, as it seems, the lips, and for that reason ought consequently to have commended the lips and not the breasts, what does it mean that here, making no memorial of the lips, no word of them, she makes mention, as though by an erring simplicity, of the breasts? For indeed it is not [0196D] bridegrooms' breasts but brides' that are wont to be commended, since it stands fast that children are not suckled at the breasts of men; and as we count worthy of praise those things which we have known to be fruitful, so those same things rightly go without it which remain idle and without fruit. But it is in some manner naturally implanted in every one, that setting aside what is wholly untried by him he turns himself to that which is more familiarly known to him, and takes for his example that which is not uncertain to his art or office. So the sailor, when he speaks, calls all prosperous things gentle breezes, a level sea, a strong sail, oarsmen and a keel; but adverse things, rushing winds, a swelling strait, waters running down into the bilge. The soldier [0197A] too, wordy in almost everything he loves, draws his examples from what belongs to the soldier's office, and scarcely anything sounds in his mouth but lance, sword, shield, helmet or breastplate; and though a degenerate fear sometimes renders these things hostile to him for fighting, yet for speaking they are friendly by familiar use. What, again, do the scholarly clerics speak of but books, or the authors of secular letters? What do the more religious sort bring forward but the testimonies of the divine letters? What, in fine, do we poor men speak of, but the things that have been impressed upon us by poor authors or poor guardians — we, I say, to whom both the dignity of nobles and the abundance of the rich is inaccessible? Therefore, because the things of women are familiarly known to the Virgin, at whose breasts little infants grow to boyhood: [0197B] speaking to the Bridegroom, she assigned to him simply what belongs to women — nay rather, she compared his fruitful grace to breasts. And in this she withdraws us also from the literal sense of the words, hinting that they are big with a spiritual understanding, when she attributes to the Bridegroom what is the easier to find in the bride the closer it lies, and which she knows perfectly well belongs to him only for the sake of the comparison. *For thy breasts are better than wine.* The Virgin knew indeed, and had read in the books of the ancients, that righteous Job, stripped of his substance, bereft of the offspring of his sons [n: (Job I)], wounded with a hard scourge from the sole of the foot to the crown *(Job II)*, and moreover wearied by his wife's most grievous reproach, at last complains, sorely enough and wretchedly enough, and turns it over again, that death coming beforehand at the opportune [0197C] time did not release him from such great evils. Why, says Job, did not I, wretched, die and breathe out my life in the womb; when I came forth from the belly, why did I not at once end my life by a worthy peril; why, to the increase of misery, was I strengthened by the placing of knees under me, why, to the heaping up of the same, was I at last ( *111* ) suckled at breasts [n: (Job III)]? » I judge that the breasts at which Job grieves and complains that he was suckled — counting it far better that he should first have been weaned from his mother — poured into him no health-bearing milk, no life-giving nourishment, but the venom of the asp, or the wine wherein is luxury. Of which you have read: « The wine of them is the gall of dragons, and the venom of asps, which is incurable [n: (Deut. XXXII)]. » That wine, or that venom, is the very persuasion and teaching which the serpentine depravity of the perverse sows abroad and spreads, [0197D] which makes its hearers drunken and seduces them, and turns them aside and leads them from faith into error, from justice into injustice.
