Wherefore in Egypt, as the psalm bears witness [n: (Psal. LXXVII)], the Lord smote the vines of the wicked, and in his canticle Moses arraigns the vine of the Sodomites [n: (Deut. XXXII)]; because Egypt and Sodom mix for those who recline at their table a poisonous wine — a form of perversity, a doctrine of malice, the crooked road of injustice. On the other side, in Jeremiah the sons of Jonadab earned praise [n: (Jer. XXXV)], who, having heard their father's precept, did not drink wine of this kind, while their minds, not made mad by the sense of seducers nor by a ruinous consent, kept the rule of truth according to their father's mandate as well as [0198A] his example. Heretics have, and false Catholics have, a wicked wine, by which, their mind lost and their foot broken, they fall into diverse errors either of faith or of morals; and in like fashion they corrupt and lead away their little hearers. The Jewish people also has, and the Gentile has, a wine by which each of them, wickedly made drunk, is held fast and darkened in wretched error; and now and then the one drags and goads the other into headlong ruin. Of which sort a certain poet says beautifully: . . . . *there met me a procession worth*
*the telling; a drunken old woman was dragging along a drunken old man*.


Judaea and the Gentile world are not undeservedly said to have grown old, since it is agreed that each was a people from ancient time, [0198B] and each of them is found not to have been content with its own ceremonies, but often to have strayed aside into the other's error. Did not the Gentile world, ill drunken, seem to you to be dragging the Jewish people along, when in whatever ways it could it urged them to worship the gods; and that most wretched people was held by a like drunkenness, and followed the leader who went before like an ox led to the slaughter? Elias, seeing a procession of this kind coming to meet him, could not bear it, but either laughing was kindled with anger, or being kindled hastened to deride the same as it met him, so that he might strike the erring leaders with a mocking chastisement that they should not go before, and the straying hearers with a chastising word, that they should not follow after. « Elias, says Scripture, coming to all the people, said: How long do ye halt between two sides? If [0198C] the Lord be God, follow him; but if Baal, follow him [n: (III Reg. XVIII)]. » And below: « Elias, he says, mocked the prophets of Baal, saying: Cry with a louder voice, for he is a god, and perhaps he is talking, or is in an inn, or on a journey, or at least he sleepeth, that he may be awaked [n: (ibid.)]. » [var: Vulg. "he mocked *them* (illis)"; the naming of the prophets of Baal is not in the received text] Nor are the Jews only seduced by the pestilent persuasion and error of the Gentiles, but the Gentiles too are sometimes drawn into the superstitions and follies of the Jews; and Judaea, grown old in evils, does not allow the wretched Gentile to be loosed from his chain, but, herself ill drunken, goes before him who is drunken, blind before blind, even to the last ditch. Their procession the Lord execrates in the Gospel, not so much in derision as in censure, and threatens them with a woe to come, as terribly as he does truly, so that when they have heard his hard and [0198D] truthful warnings, both the leaders who go before and the followers may be either amended or left without excuse. « Woe to you, he says, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who go about the sea and the dry land to make one proselyte; and when he is made, you make him the son of hell twofold more than yourselves [n: (Matth. XXIII)]. » [var: Vulg. *quia circuitis*, "because you go about"] Paul too, beholding a procession of this kind, seemed not to laugh, but, burning with zeal, tenacious of the right, impatient of harm, to shrink from it, so that with a free voice he did not spare even Peter, who seemed the first and the worthier among the apostles, because in this procession he was held to be the one going before in a timid error. For this man was unwilling that that man should be given the turbid wine to drink, and that a crowd equally turbid should follow him ill drunken, lest from this procession not only [0199A] laughter, or derision, should be begotten, but the truth of the Gospel too (which is not lawful) should suffer an unworthy peril. « When Cephas was come, he says, to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed [n: (Gal. II)]. » And below: « When I saw, he says, that they walked not uprightly unto the truth of the Gospel, I said to Cephas before them all: If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of the Gentiles and not as do the Jews, how dost thou compel the Gentiles to live as do the Jews [n: (ibid.)]. » Paul, noting that both the leader and those who came at his heels were made drunk with the cloud of error, and that among them the evangelical truth was not kept purely enough, counting it a grave offence and not bearing that it should go unpunished, broke forth at once into the midst, and with the rod of correction stretched out interrupted that blameworthy procession. And this the same Apostle judged worthy of the telling, [0199B] and speaking to the Galatians he set it forth again among other matters pleasantly and from memory — perhaps so that not only the Galatians but we too, by his teaching, might know both what the greater owe to us and what we owe to the greater. For the lesser owes no consent to the vices and errors of the greater; but if something grave and intolerable be detected in him, he must needs reprove it out of hatred of the fault, out of zeal for a more gracious justice, taking the more diligent heed that he insert nothing of swelling insolence or rancour. And the greater ought not to disdain the lesser's admonition with a swelling brow, nor to strike back at one who worthily corrects him as though by the privilege of authority; but with a kindly ear to obey the monitor, or rather *112* his admonitions, if only it be clear that they truly [0199C] and humbly serve charity. It is beyond doubt over against this wine — by which either Cephas or anyone else goes astray wandering, and in the procession either goes before or follows after, tottering with a lame step — that the Virgin says and asserts the Bridegroom's breasts are better, knowing by experience that they are more pleasing not only to outward hearing but to inward taste as well. The breasts of the Bridegroom are his form and his doctrine, his example and his word, his life and his speech, with which he cherished and nourished his little hearers as with milk, and fed and strengthened the greater as with bread and solid food. For this indeed he was born a child, that he might show himself suited to little ones, and he advanced in age, that he might show himself a man to those further advanced, in all that he did and said leading and teaching the little ones or the greater, according as they made themselves the readier to take in small things or great. « For coming forth from his [0199D] chamber, beautiful in form above the sons of men [n: (Psal. XLIV)], » [var: Vulg. Ps. 18:6 *tanquam sponsus procedens de thalamo suo* is here fused with Ps. 44:3 *speciosus forma prae filiis hominum*, whose word order is inverted] rich in the incomparable fullness of saving doctrine, he willed first by the merit of his form to please not only the Virgin but us also, and afterward by word and doctrine to teach all who should prove docile. For because we are unwilling to show his word an obedience worthy enough of it — whose face at first we are deservedly compelled to shrink from — Jesus began, as you have read [n: (Act. I)], to do and to teach, so that by the enticing appearance, as it were, of his deeds he might call and lead us on attentive and well-disposed, and having sweetly allured us might strongly bring us into his lecture-hall. With the right breast, as it were, in doing great things, he showed himself worthy of commendation, and caught in the snare of his form those who looked [0200A] the more diligently; with the left, in saying great things, he makes those whom he already holds learned and blessed hearers, but those who despise him he by no means leaves unpunished, though he teach them. Who would not call these breasts of the Bridegroom better than ruinous wine? Who, unless he be drunk with wine, would contradict the Virgin who asserts it? — since those who are drunk with the wine of the damned, and those who pour it out with them, do not so much run as fall blinded; but those who are drunk with the Bridegroom's breasts, are blessed? « Blessed is he, he says, whom thou shalt instruct, O Lord, and shalt teach him out of thy law [n: (Psal. XCIII)]. » [var: Vulg. *Beatus homo quem tu erudieris*, "Blessed is the man whom thou shalt instruct"]



## CHAPTER VI.

*For thy breasts are better than wine.* In the Bridegroom's breast, indeed, the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are laid up, which are utterly hidden from the prudent and the wise of this world; and he who conceals their secrets from so [0200B] many who are somewhat grown, and for so long a time, now reveals them to little ones, coming forth from his chamber by the goodness which is his own. For through the ages that ran their course behind us those incomparable treasures lay hid in him, but when the flesh of the Virgin had been assumed they burst forth marvellously, like swelling nipples out of his breast, and poured forth not dry drops but streams and rivers, and shed themselves with full horn upon all who worthily drew near. Wherefore the Virgin too, after she has received the kiss, does not straightway turn aside from the Bridegroom as though bidding farewell, but leans back upon his breast for the sake of profiting; and applying the drawing-vessel of a pure mind the more capaciously the more greedily, she is given drink, she is filled full with the welcome abundance of the breasts and their flowings. There she thirsts with a deep longing for knowledge, there for wisdom, hidden by a profound counsel [0200C] from very many, and feels it revealed to her more openly; and now, as she consulted not the angel, so neither the prophets who went before, but leaning alone upon him alone she draws, as Job has it [n: (cap. XXVIII)], and draws to herself wisdom out of hidden places. I am deceived, if that disciple of the Bridegroom also, whom he loved, did not understand that wisdom and knowledge flow from his breast, when, placed at the Supper, he acquiesced not so much in the wine and the material feast as he rested with a welcome reclining upon the breast of Jesus, between those very breasts. There he saw the Word abiding in the most secret bosom of God the Father [n: (Joan. I)], he saw the Word made flesh in the virginal chamber of the Bride his mother; he saw the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, luminous with a brightness plain to him, dark to the prudent and wise of this world under a certain veil spread over them. [0200D] He saw, I say, and did not begrudge to reveal them, not to all but to the faithful, and to commit them to a remembering script with the swift pen of a scribe, so that the understanding hearer might love to aspire to the secrets of that same breast, and from his own poverty of merits to breathe again in the presence of those treasures. To this there came not Porphyry, nor Aristotle, nor Socrates, nor Plato, nor the first, nor the second, nor that third Cato falling from heaven; nor in fine anyone who, blinded by malice, shrank from the newness of grace, holding and retaining the oldness of his own knowledge or wisdom. Whose knowledge is proclaimed by a truthful judgment not to heal but to puff up [n: (I Cor. II)], and whose wisdom is judged to be gross foolishness with God; [0201A] in which nevertheless they remain fixed, by I know not what sense of the truth, seducing themselves by a certain privilege of antiquity. One of whom says: *Let those who make haste* — so he says — *drink the new must; let the jar pour out for me the*
*ancestral unmixed wine.*


Not the must of the new grace from the Bridegroom's shining breast, but choosing rather that the old wine of error be poured out for him from a muddy vessel, whose sweetness seems to him the more acceptable and the more perfect for himself, the more both use has confirmed it and ancestral antiquity has sanctioned it. But that new must, which cannot be borne by old vessels, let those drink who make haste, who love to gaze upon the Bridegroom coming forth from his chamber; who, warned by angels after the manner of the shepherds, come hastening, and him whom they see, [0201B] whom they love *113* they do not press down with silence, but announce with a hasty proclamation [n: (Luc. II)]. To whom none was found to hasten sooner, none more perfectly, than she who deserved to prepare for him at his coming the chamber of her own womb, who reclining upon his breast drew and felt his knowledge and wisdom to be more gracious, better in sense, in judgment, than the error of the philosophers.

## CHAPTER VII.

*For thy breasts are better than wine.* The Bridegroom's breasts may also be called his mercy and his truth, which it is agreed work in a more special way in the Bride and mother virgin; with which the law given through Moses can neither be nor ought to be made equal, though it may be judged good and, in its own time, necessary. [0201C] « For the law is good, if a man use it lawfully [n: (I Tim. I)]. » [var: Vulg. *Scimus autem quia bona est lex*, "But we know that the law is good"] Yet in the law there is found a certain harshness of wine, which works wrath and does not bestow grace, which will have a tooth taken for a tooth, an eye for an eye [n: (Exod. XXI)], the striker struck back and the other cheek not offered [n: (Matth. V, Luc. VI)]. The law indeed commands many things, commands great things, but it does not bring the obscure into the light; if it brings forth anything vital, it draws a clinging chaff over it, it burdens blind minds, it weighs down hard necks and blunts them, it does not pour in the mildness of grace, the sweetness of the Spirit. The law duly gives or promises temporal things according to desert, it torments the offender, it does not remit the penalties deserved; it works a severe judgment, a heavy justice, it knows not mercy, it is not appeased freely and without price. Who would suck such [0201D] a grape, and his teeth not be set on edge the harder? Whose taste and palate would not turn the more bitter at such a draught? — where wrath reigns without mercy, and judgment is exercised, whereas mercy is worthily exalted above wrath and judgment? [n: (Jacob. II.)] And so the Virgin, marking the commandments of the law which in a manner deceived the people, since without the spirit of grace they laid down hard and unbearable things, praises the Bridegroom's breasts, which received her more graciously and more sweetly: « Me, she says, O Lord, according to the Psalm, me thy mercy and thy truth have upheld [n: (Psal. XXXIX)]. » [var: Vulg. *misericordia tua et veritas tua semper susceperunt me*, "thy mercy and thy truth have always upheld me"] Mercy it is by which the Lord of the heavens willed to enter the nuptial chamber, having an unbegotten Father, and willing to have a virginal [0202A] mother. Truth it is by which he consummated that will in a happy work, when « the Word was made flesh [n: (Joan. I)], » and God as man dwelt marvellously in the virgin. Mercy it is by which he did not compel the world to undergo the penalties it deserved, but for the blotting out of them chose this time, these nuptials, this virgin. Truth it is by which he happily made bright the chosen time by his coming, and by which, the Spirit working, he made the chosen virgin fruitful. « Mercy, he says, and truth have met each other [n: (Psal. LXXXIV)]. » That the virgin might be made worthy, mercy ran before; that she might become a mother, truth straightway ran to meet her; and there is not, as with us by the desert of guilt, a parting or a running away of the virtues, but in her there is their welcome coming-together, their meeting. Running before, mercy prepared a place for the Bridegroom who was to come, [0202B] and fencing harmful things far off, adorned the chamber with the flowers of virtues; and when it was adorned, truth likewise presented itself, which ineffably made God man in the virgin according to his purpose. God's mercy, therefore, toward the Virgin is his readier will and affection; and truth is the fulfilling or effecting of that will; since not merits but mercy makes the virgin gracious, and truth renders her, already full of grace, glorious. For you have read what is written and foretold: « For God loveth mercy and truth, the Lord will give grace and glory [n: (Psal. LXXXIII)]. » In the Virgin God loves to work mercy and truth, when he wills that she who is freely chosen should truly glory of grace, when he purifies her with the incomparable gift of spiritual [0202C] grace, and gladdens her with the singular privilege of a special glory. « He hath regarded, she says, the humility of his handmaid; and from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed [n: (Luc. I)]. » [var: Vulg. *ecce enim ex hoc*, "for behold, from henceforth"] In the regard of humility she would have merciful grace commended; in the proclaiming of blessedness she would have true glory signified, because both the humble handmaid becomes rich in the gifts of grace, and, city of the great King, we worthily say of thee, glorious. Rightly, therefore, the Virgin says the Bridegroom's breasts are better than wine, because no antiquity whatever ever conferred on any, nor did the censorious harshness of the law bring this with it, that mercy should come into a virgin, that truth should be born so that she might be made full of grace, and might rejoice in an incomparable glory.



## CHAPTER VIII.

*For thy breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the best [0202D] ointments.* The Virgin, reclining in the bosom of the Bridegroom, leaning back upon his breast, resting between the breasts, set apart from things outward, acquiescing in things inward and more secret, feels wonders, tastes sweet things — not with the palate but with the experience of a rejoicing heart — and rejoices in her sense to be flooded with the sweet fragrance of sweet things. For the breasts of the Bridegroom hold not a simple drink of milk, but ointments, wondrous confections, the seasonings of medicinal things, which, gathered and compounded *114* of exceedingly precious spices, were foreknown to few and fully shown to none in all the ages or days behind us. The inward abundance of them is not drawn by any little ones and sucklings; but the Bride, [0203A] a virgin fuller of grace, greater in advancement, experiences it in his very presence, in whose chamber that compounding or mixture of ointments was itself made — a mixture that would profit her first, far and more amply, but us little ones less and later. For when mercy and truth, as has been said above, had run to meet each other, they prudently and carefully gathered certain spices, as it were, which, brought from opposite quarters, they drove together into one little bundle, and by the perfumer's art reduced them into most sweet ointments. For between God and man an ancient discord was in play, in that the injustice of man was joined by no agreement to the justice of God: and the Bridegroom coming brought justice, gave peace, and made her that went before and her that followed to be joined in a welcome kiss: « Justice, he says, and peace have kissed *(Psal. [0203B] LXXXIV)*. » For when, by the justice conferred, he made him just who had been unjust, the discord gave way which had long grown old between the just and the unjust, and at once peace succeeding — because in the justified it perceived nothing but what was just — gave and received the kiss of the long-desired justice now found. To God therefore, who is just, the just man had peace, and by a marvellous assumption God was made man: God, I say, assuming, giving his own justice to the assumed, yet with the vigour of his own justice as the assumer not consumed. Further, as mercy and truth meeting each other make a confection or an ointment, so justice and peace kissing each other make none the less a certain seasoning, whereby health, or beyond doubt a healing salve, is given to him whom the Samaritan shall have mercifully lifted [0203C] onto his beast [n: (Luc. X)]. In short, in the chamber of the Virgin they came together as in a little mortar, and in a most welcome coming-together compounded an ointment, or ointments useful enough: the Father's precept, the Word's presence, the overshadowing of the Spirit; an obedient ear, a firmer faith, and the flesh of the Virgin. Of these spices in an earthen vessel there is made no rustic confusion, but by a learned hand and the physician's art a certain contusion, and when they have been distributed in fitting number and measure and weight, there are precious ointments, both mitigating pains and restorative of health. The compounding of which is of so great a fragrance, doubtless, or scent, that the Bride, to whom the benefit of a fuller grace is given, is delighted and marvels at the odour-bearing sweetness of the ointments, which are not only [0203D] good, but beyond doubt the best of better ones. For although before the law, and under the law, very many things were found which by the merits of a devout faith are medicinally turned into ointments, which God, ever loving honours, is read to have smelled, and is believed to have been many times delighted with a most welcome odour of sweetness, yet these of which we speak are found by experience to be the best of all that went before, being nearest the chamber, or rather being found to be the chamber itself. Into the earth of that chamber God sent spittle from his own mouth [n: (Joan. IX)], and in a manner wonderful enough made clay like none above or below, whose touch and anointing restores the light denied from the ancient time of birth, and whose sweet fragrance ineffably soothes the sense of smell. This sweet fragrance Isaac is believed to have felt beforehand from far off, [0204A] and, taught through the Spirit, to have foretold of it in a mystery, when his son Jacob presented himself to him in very good garments, and a most sweet odour of the garments breathed upon his father's nostrils: « Behold, he says, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field, which the Lord hath blessed [n: (Gen. XVII)]. » To this field is given the incomparable sanctity of a new blessing, and for this reason, consequently, an unfailing fullness of flowers, and fruits, and odours, which Isaac, perceiving from afar, marvels at exulting; the Virgin, feeling it near at hand and experiencing it in the thing itself, gives thanks ineffably. And from her and through her the sense of that same fragrance, however thin, comes to us, scarcely at last arriving, because it finds us set far off, and having found us has made us as happy as we are glad at its coming — not, however, by our own [0204B] merit, but by the intervention of that same Virgin. For although ointments of this sort were compounded in the virgin, yet they were not held with her within narrow bounds, but with abounding grace they came down to those further off, and anointed us both with an odour-bearing touch and with a health-bearing odour. And in that she says ointments in the plural, not ointment, she hints that in us not one kind of evil singly has been found, but our misery has procured for itself many languors, many infirmities, which the physician at his coming has carried away with medicinal ointments. « Truly, says Isaias, he hath borne our languors, and he hath carried our infirmities [n: (Isa. LIII)]. » [var: Vulg. *dolores nostros*, "our sorrows"] Truly he bore and bore away, carried and carried off our languors, our infirmities, which, being many and various, demanded the touch or [0204C] fragrance of no single ointment; but different ones needed different remedies of ointments. But we who, labouring under much sickness, have no leisure for learning what is healthful, whom either dullness of wit or the torpor of loathing presses down, so that we bring little diligence to them; we, I say, know not what infirmity needs what ointment: and having experienced manifold diseases, we are darkened in the knowledge of curing. But that physician of ours, alone presiding within his own workshop, prepares for each sickness a fitting medicine, and by his craftsmanship he does not wish the sick to be present everywhere, nor that the art or the knowledge should pass over to them, but that it should profit them. Nevertheless, so far as anyone may experience in himself *115*, for whose healing the physician [0204D] loves to impart his care, he seems to have brought forth to us three ointments one after another, and by them to have conferred on us who are sick an opportune remedy.

The first, biting and rough, shook us the more harshly, and, anointing as it were from without, straightway struck a certain heaviness into the inward parts, and troubling and dislodging the disease long grown in, increased it, and presented it, as it were, all at once to sense and to knowledge. And when it was presented, the wicked mind raged and groaned, scarcely bearing itself, while it turns over the newest things and the old, and, pricked and stung, wrapped itself round with hard recollections of iniquities, and rolled itself down among the thorns and briars of thoughts accusing, or even defending, it. Thus the troubled mind began at once to abhor thy foulness, and by the desert of its own vileness [0205A] to be the more vehemently displeasing to itself; by the hatred of its own self to bear witness to certain new things and contrary to the old, and by a changed judgment to detest what had pleased it before. This fragrance of the ointment, after the manner of a draught, brought in a shuddering fear, by which, when the passages of the veins had been purged, it led us on to a healthful vomiting, so that, spitting out with free disdain or loathing the former blandishments of the vices, we might truly reckon as losses what before were falsely thought gains. That penitent showed himself touched by this odour, who, labouring in his groaning, washed his bed with tears, whose eye was troubled at the regard of his faults by the Judge's fury, and who confessed by a healthful vomiting that he had grown old among his enemies [n: (Psal. VI)]. For odour and stench do not agree well together, nor do they abide in one seat, but when, the nostrils being loosed by grace, the odour of the precious [0205B] ointment is let in, the stench of the vices, impatient of its company, is sent out; and with the greater vehemence this healthful potion is poured in, the larger the flux and the looser the outlet by which the worthless filth goes forth. For that odour is « living and effectual and more piercing than any two-edged sword, and reaching unto the division of the soul and the spirit, of the joints also and the marrow, and a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart [n: (Hebr. IV)]. » And for this reason, when with the physician's devoted care it has been pressed upon anyone in season, out of season, when it has entered as powerfully as mercifully the wounded borders of the sick man: no passage of the veins, no lurking-place or recess of the marrow, no place at last from the sole of the foot to the crown is inaccessible to it. It runs therefore and runs about, and going round after the manner of the swallow [0205C] it ranges everywhere, it searches out all deep and hidden things with a censor's office and keenness, and whatever it finds contrary to life, liable to fault, given over to vanity, it sweeps together with a strong broom, and having swept it together casts it out, preparing a place for health.

The second ointment, further, breathes more healthfully, gives the odour of a gentler benefit, brings back the hope of living and brings in love as well, so that the sick man, feeling himself relieved by the laying down of a heavy burden, may now hope for better things, and in hope may love to work. At this odour the spirit that languished before revives, and with returning appetite longs for the food of life: refreshed with the food of grace, it rejoices that the necessary strength is restored, and that the hands hanging down and the feeble knees are strengthened [n: (Isa. XXXV)]. Thereupon, embracing with a ready affection the gift of strengthening grace, he goes out to his [0205D] work, holding welcome the labourer's exercise; and stretches out watchfully to labour the hands unfolded from their torpor, he hears and hearkens, that he may go and bring forth a more gracious fruit. Forgetting the things that are behind, he gives his effort the more attentively to virtue, he chastises his body and worthily brings it into subjection [n: (I Cor. IX)]; and the things which before seemed bitter or perhaps impossible are, on the contrary, reckoned as easy as they are healthful. Hence he embraces fastings, vigils, continence, patience, and judges it fitting to be ruled and made subject by the counsel of his elders; for love of the right he renounces the pleasures of the flesh — nay, even his own wills — that he may subject his body and himself to God. For God wills this order to be kept in us, that thus, within a just law and the bounds set for them, single things be restrained: [0206A] so that the spirit, commanding the flesh, may drive and bring it under itself, while itself obeying its greater is one spirit with God. Who, wretchedly set in the filthy hovel of this body, who, wrapped round with so many stains or snares of malignant spirits, could so set out, loosed from the threats or ambushes of enemies meeting him, if he had not been anointed with this ointment of strengthening grace? Who would not recoil from the entrance at the very bolt of exceeding difficulty thrust against him, or would not fail in his going forward at the manifold onset of impediments; if he were not touched by the odour of this ointment so sweetly, so effectually, that as he began, so also going forward he should not be broken? In fine, whoever rightly examines the course of those who go forward knows that whom the Father loves as a Son, he rebukes and chastises [n: (Hebr. XII)]; [0206B] nor does he wish him to glory in the obtained benefit of the promised inheritance whom he has not first suffered to be scourged with many tribulations of sufferings. But if by the impulse of vices, or of scourges, the just man gives way a little and totters, the odour of this ointment meeting him revives him the more quickly: and so great a sweetness does not endure that he should be crushed and fall into failure, but with a hand set under him it cherishes him and promotes him the more diligently to a fuller advance. Wherefore threatening evils do not draw him back utterly from what he has begun, but grace mercifully fashions his labours and struggles into a precept: and him whom it permits to be cold and to sweat, by the counsel of its own pity it strengthens after the sweat with the health it has promised again, and makes him stronger.



## CHAPTER VIII. (cont.)

*116* The third ointment, however, calms the sea, tempers [0206C] wrath, stills the winds by its majesty, with its hand makes serene the turbulent motions of the soul; it levels the road, holds the right hand, steadies the step, and, as though the harbour were already found, makes a man secure and confirms him. For within himself the strong traveller, now in a manner serene, happily estranged from the assault of vices and from any degenerate consent, united by patience, now presumes upon a sure thing, as it were, trustfully and humbly. And though whatever adversities there be murmur behind his back and press upon him, yet they do not withstand him to the face with effectual boldness, while, forgetting the things that are behind, he covets and faints for the courts of God alone [n: (Psal. LXXXIII)], and turned to him with his whole affection, longs, as it were, to join face to face. « My face hath sought thee out, he says; thy face, O Lord, will I seek [n: (Psal. XXVI)]. » [0206D] Touched by the odour of this ointment, he either does not feel adversities of any kind, or reckons them empty, counts them for nothing, does not consent to them, and burns with so great a longing for the things ahead which he already feels, that with a deaf ear he passes by whatever is discordant and dissenting. Let all things then that can hurt for a time roar and clatter with threats or with blows, let the things that can profit flatter with fraud, with lying, with entreaty, with reward: what will this man do but hold his sure road gladly and bravely, and, as from the brow of a mountain, answer those barking below with that word of the Apostle: « Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword? I am sure that neither death nor life [n: (Rom. VIII)]. » [var: Vulg. Rom. 8:35 has *an persecutio*, "or persecution", before "or the sword"] Since therefore so great a certitude of perseverance confirms him that he cares not what any adverse [0207A] strength may clamour: he now seems to obtain the reward laid up for him, which stands promised to those who persevere and abides unfailing. « I have finished, he says, my course, there is laid up for me a crown of justice [n: (II Tim. IV)]. » And again: « By hope we were saved [n: (Rom. VIII)]. » Whoever has experienced the odour-bearing sweetness of this ointment becomes not uncertain of things to come as though they were present, and so bravely and so sweetly goes forward from virtue to virtue, that he hopes, and holds the hoped-for salvation already as though given. The first ointment, therefore, purged out the wickedness of the old leaven; the second, by the new gift of a lump, prepared the unleavened of merits; the third confirmed those feasting with the sure privilege of health restored. The first, with a heavy scouring-cloth and a shrewd draught-vessel, turned the house about, and overturned the bilge as well; the second [0207B] poured a strengthening medicine into the sick mind; the third rendered hope more certain, that it should no longer fear fall and ruin. Accordingly the first may be called purgative, the second strengthening, and the third confirming, because by the first every sick man is cleansed of the dregs of his vices; by the second, with a welcome file and labour, the health he wished for is repaired; by the third, the mind is confirmed in its purpose both by a certain humble gladness at present gifts and by a sure confidence of things to come. With these ointments the holy Virgin had felt the Bridegroom's breasts to abound, and had felt that she was not to keep their grace with herself, after the manner of the envious; with the vent closed; but to offer out of doors a most sweet odour to the devout and the humble, and by its benefit to fatten with an abundance of merits minds that were dry before. But because [0207C] the benefit of so great an odour is not reached by human powers, if he that comes is not forestalled by the divine hand and help; the Virgin shows by what gift it may without doubt be reached, so that, this being shown, he who hears and does not love may be held inexcusable.



## CHAPTER IX.

*Thy name is oil poured out.* The Bridegroom's name is Jesus, which was named by the Angel before he was conceived in the womb [n: (Luc. I)]. And who either understood this name more truly, or loved it more sincerely, or preached it more fittingly, than that virgin mother herself, to whom the Angel first announced it: « Behold, he says, thou shalt conceive in thy womb and shalt bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name Jesus [0207D] [n: (ibid.)]. » Jesus, in the Latin tongue, is called *Saving*, or *Saviour.* According to his work is his name also, and he has his name from the thing itself, « for he shall save his people [n: (Matth. I)]. » Rightly therefore is he called Jesus, who shall be the salvation of the people, whose « name whosoever shall call upon, he shall be saved [n: (Joel. II)]; because both to him who calls devoutly the right hand of the Lord gives strength, and to him who confesses worthily he is become a hearer unto salvation [n: (Psal. CXVII)]. This name the Bride calls oil, and *eleos* in Greek is, in Latin, *mercy*, because that this Jesus or Saviour willed to be ours, our own justice did not give it to be so, but his mercy; for while our own merit cast us far from his face, he, calling us back, by that mercy which is his own made us safe. Whence the Apostle: Not by the works of justice [0208A] which we have done, he says, but according to his own mercy he saved us [n: (Tit. III)]. » When God appoints to save the undeserving, after wrath he remembers this mercy; through this name, or for the sake of it — this oil — he has pity on the unworthy and the wretched; by the strength of this name he drives our enemies far off, and, freeing us from vices, restores us to himself as friends. Which he who had long stood wandering in the way of sinners now hopes for, now promises himself, rejoicing at the visitation of grace, knowing that the gifts of God are not of his own repentance, that the calling is not conferred by it, but that the name and the oil of mercy is borne above all the liquors *117* of merits. « For he gave him a name which is above every name, that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow; and every tongue should confess that Jesus is Lord [n: (Philip. II)]. » [var: Vulg. *donavit illi nomen*, "he bestowed on him a name", and the confession runs *quia Dominus Iesus Christus in gloria est Dei Patris*, "that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father"] [0208B] Therefore that penitent says: « For thy name's sake, he says, thou wilt quicken me [n: (Psal. CXLII)]. » And he adds: « In thy mercy thou wilt destroy my enemies [n: (ibid.)]. » And in another psalm: « For thy name's sake, O Lord, thou wilt be merciful to my sin [n: (Psal. XXIV)]. » To which hope, to which assertion, not even the Lord himself gives the lie, but through Isaias, taught by the Spirit, he mercifully foretells it, so that the penitent, hearing this, may presume to be strengthened with a fuller confidence, and may know in what he ought to glory as healthfully as he does truly. « For all they that love thy name shall glory in thee, O Lord [n: (Psal. V)]. » Of which name, through Isaias: « For my name's sake, he says, I will remove my fury far off [n: (Isa. XLVIII)]. » For the sake of the name, or of the oil which pours out the dew of mercy, he removes far from those who had deserved it [0208C] his judgment and his fury; and if he were not held to be Saviour, if not pitying and merciful, what would every wretched man be, but justly pressed down by his intolerable justice? But what is it that the oil is called poured out? So long as oil is held in a little vessel, either it is not known, or how great its grace and usefulness may be is not felt, because, though the physician who knows all things knows it himself, yet the sick do not, to whose wounds still to be healed he has not applied it. For a time this oil was held as in a sealed vessel, when the Son of God was accounted good indeed and merciful with himself, having in very truth the purpose of pitying in his affection, but not yet fully gladdening the wretched in the effect. In a vessel, as it seems, he willed this oil [0208D] to be contained, when by a hidden judgment he would not have mercy on the angels who grew proud, when he neither turned them from their fall by grace going before, nor after their lapse converted them by mercy coming to their aid. But to those who stood he gave to feel this oil, whom he mercifully deigned to keep, lest they should fall along with the others, increasing for them and laying on so effectual a soothing of this oil that from it they received a sure and unswerving firmness for standing. Yet since this is above us, we should perhaps say that it pertained nothing to us, if we too did not feel the benefit of that same oil; nay rather, if he did not more largely and more lavishly incline the open vessel toward us, and, the oil being wholly poured out, incline as it were his whole mercy toward us. For both our necessity and his goodness seemed to require this, that [0209A] to a fuller misery a fuller mercy should be conferred; and because there is no distinction but that manifold sin gathers and confounds both Jews and Gentiles [n: (Rom. X)], the whole face of this oil should pour itself out on both, that the yoke might rot. Which the Prophet foreseeing in the Spirit and praying for: « May God, he says, have mercy on us, may he make his countenance shine upon us, and may he have mercy on us [n: (Psal. LXVI)]. » [var: Vulg. adds *et benedicat nobis*, "and bless us", between the two clauses] What does he mean by "have mercy," and "have mercy"? He adds: « That we may know thy way upon earth, thy salvation in all nations [n: (ibid.)]. » Because, he says, we have sinned, both Gentiles and Jews, and there is no distinction, it is needful that this pouring out of the oil should reach to both, that thou mayest graciously call us Jews back to him who is the way, and that we may alike know thy salvation in all nations. [0209B] Oil shut in a little vessel, or in a closet, keeps the holy angels safe; but oil poured out heaps together the scattered handfuls of elect men: and mercy, which to protect the healthy hid itself within the sanctuary of heaven, when the vessel is inclined pours itself out to heal sick men. « O Lord, he says, bow down thy heavens and descend; touch the mountains and they shall smoke [n: (Psal. CXLIII)]. » He who offers the full vessel of mercy to the angels who stand, inclines the vessel to heal sick men upon earth; and what seemed to be held in it he now pours out with a liberal, even a prodigal hand, and upon those who must be greatly pitied he pours out much mercy. At whose healing touch the harmful swellings go down, the stings are pressed back, the pains of wounds grow gentle; like smoke the vanity of proud minds [0209C] vanishes away, and, the disease being driven off, health revives and grows strong.



## CHAPTER X.

*Thy name is oil poured out.* The Bridegroom's name is Christ; and Christ is called *anointed*, because God anointed him with the oil of gladness above his fellows [n: (Psal. XLIV)]. Not only anointed, but he may also be called oil, in that by his own power he wipes us clean of the harmful phlegm, and with a sweet grace anoints us who are withered and dry. For the name of Christ, defined with a fitting understanding, teaches that God and man are united in one person, and that one Christ is effected by the wonderful and incomprehensible force of the joining, although the natures of God and of man are far unlike. For as a rational soul and corruptible flesh make one [0209D] man, so God assuming and the man assumed render Christ none the less one: and while the unconfused diversity of both natures is held, yet in Christ himself the unity of person is preached. And if the faith of this name be poured out over us by the sprinkler of him who has mercy, if the concretion of the natures, the unconfused unity of the person, be loved by us: because he flows and abounds with much chrism and wonderful charism, he makes us glad outright, while he makes us fruitful with the merits of the virtues. But this oil, or this name, is now no longer shut within the narrow *118* bounds of Judaea, but is poured out among the nations even to the ends of the world, nor does anyone among them rightly think himself to come to salvation [0210A] who does not first go forward in strength by the faith of this name. « There is not, he says, any other name under heaven whereby we must be saved [n: (Act. IV)]. » [var: Vulg. *nec enim aliud nomen est sub caelo datum hominibus*, "for there is no other name under heaven given to men"] There is none, therefore, who can hide himself from the true light of this oil, since its ray pours itself out mightily unto the ends of the earth; and it enlightens every man coming into this world [n: (Joan. I)], who has not by an obstinate malice made himself unclean. For everyone who has happily obtained by the gift of grace ears to hear knows, and everyone prudently instructed in the faith of this name knows, that Christ is the corner-stone, the coupler of Jews and Gentiles, himself the head of the Church, the one mediator of God and men; our bone and our flesh by a nuptial commerce and a natural fellowship, himself anointed and anointing those near him with spiritual power and grace. [0210B] Which oil, or name, he so poured out far and wide both among Jews and among Gentiles, when the love of him spread itself abroad in their hearts: that first among the Jews the apostles truly confessed Christ, and consequently among the Gentiles many were anointed with the same chrism. For when the apostles were asked whom men said the Son of man to be, they answered that the word or judgment of all was not one, and when at the last their own mind about this was more diligently asked, Peter, as much for himself as for the rest, reported in a learned discourse: « Thou art Christ. And he: Blessed art thou, he says, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood hath not revealed it to thee, but my Father who is in heaven [n: (Matth. XVI)]. » But after this oil, or name, had flowed mercifully in Judaea, Idumaea also received [0210C] the pouring out of the same: and into it Christ at his coming so stretched out his shoe, that he made them friends whom he found strangers by the desert of error. And when they had received so great a name with a fixed faith and a hope beyond doubt not empty, they were called generally by that same Christ Christians, and whoever was worthy to be contained in the catalogue of the faithful, as he willed to be a Christian, so he willed to be reckoned by the name. Rightly therefore is this name called not poured in but rather poured out, in that it is assigned not to the Jew only, not to the Greek in particular; but though those first glory in the faith of this name, yet neither are those further off held to be shut out from that same glory. For into all the earth the sound of this name has gone [n: (Psal. XVIII)], and its pouring out has passed to the ends of the earth, imparting to those far off as to those near [0210D] the benefit of salvation — to those, that is, who have loved to adorn their faith with works. For whoever of the faithful are spread abroad from the rising to the setting, from the north even to the south, are steeped in the Christian name or in the oil of Christ, nor is it shut off from any by land, by sea, or by any space whatever, but it is poured out upon all on whom God has willed to have mercy.

## CHAPTER XI.

*Thy name is oil poured out.* The Bridegroom's name is God. A name of this sort the Father is believed to have poured into the Son, when he is said to have begotten him coequal, coeternal with himself, when the unbegotten gave to the begotten to be naturally God, and willed that none but God should be party to this giving. [0211A] For as whatever God is, so whatever has been substantially drawn from him, is more fully poured into this one; by no beginning, no end, no place, no time is any one shut out; and from him from whom he has his being, from him it is essentially granted to him — that which to every creature is naturally inaccessible. But he himself who is God poured out his name, in a manner, like oil, when he did not confound the newly-made angels with a cloud of ignorance, but by the bounty of him who had made them they perceived from whom they had been made, and received that the Father and the Son together are inseparably one God. Nor did this pouring out instruct the angels in heavenly places only, but the same instruction passed over to men on earth as well, and the certainty of divine knowledge marked out Judaea, and in Israel there was [0211B] received the greatness of this so illustrious a name [n: (Psal. LXXV)]. « Adore him, he says, all ye his angels; Sion heard and was glad [n: (Psal. XCVI)]. » Whom the angels in heaven venerate as God and Lord, his fellow-citizens of Sion on earth also, hearing the name, give thanks; and among that people the name of God is celebrated, the oil is strong when poured, though not yet poured out among the nations with a fuller grace. But when the long-desired fullness of time came, in which the height of the divine counsel was made known to us, the Son, sent from the Father, willed to be made man in the Virgin and of the Virgin, and thus that the name which is God should be more fully published abroad both among the Gentiles and among the Jews. « Let the nations know, he says, that thy name is God [n: (Psal. LXXXII)]. » [var: Vulg. Ps. 82:19 *Et cognoscant quia nomen tibi Dominus*, "And let them know that thy name is Lord"] « And all kings shall adore [0211C] him, he says; all nations shall serve him [n: (Psal. LXXI)]. » [var: Vulg. *omnes reges terrae*, "all the kings of the earth"] Whom him? He adds: « His name continueth before the sun [n: (ibid.)]. » What profit is there in this name? « And in him shall all the tribes of the earth be blessed [n: (ibid.)]. » What is that name? « Blessed be the Lord God of Israel [n: (Luc. I)]; and blessed be the name of his majesty. The name of his humility is Man; but the name of his majesty is God [n: (ibid.)]. » Of which the Apostle: « Who is over all things, God blessed for ever [n: (Rom. IX)]. » This God, abiding in the bosom of the Father and dwelling in light inaccessible, having from him, or with him, an equality ungranted to angels as to men, willed that before the *119* Virgin's bringing forth his name should be poured among a few, but after the bringing forth should now be poured out with a fuller rush [0211D] upon all everywhere. For him whom the nations of the Gentiles knew not, being hidden, and whom few of the Jews, taught by the Spirit, in some fashion perceived, after he had been poured into the womb of the Virgin at the end of the times, he was poured out through the streets and squares after the likeness of water. « I am poured out, he says, like water; and all my bones are scattered [n: (Psal. XXI)]. » After the manner of water he poured himself out to the common knowledge of all, when his charity spread itself abroad in our hearts, when he scattered abroad the gifts of his graces, gave to the poor, when he gave to men him who strengthens, the bread of angels. Whom therefore Isaias far above calls hidden, we now see, as with the oil poured out, set forth to all: set forth indeed that he may pour the healing oil over the sick, hidden that he may hide us who are healed in the hiding-place [0212A] of his face. « Truly, he says, thou art a hidden God [n: (Isa. XLV)]. The God of Israel, the Saviour. He is hidden, when in the bosom of the Father he hides himself far from human gaze; but set forth, when out of his mother's womb he pours himself out for the salvation of Israel. Hidden, when in God, as God, he veils his face from us; set forth, when he reveals himself as having come to save his people. Upon the hidden the angels ever burn to look; the poured out and set forth men now love to cherish, and those whom, weighed down by the burden of a corruptible body, the desirable hiding does not yet hold, this pouring out of the oil now renders fervent in spirit. Wherefore the Virgin, when she had said: *Thy name is oil poured out,* subjoined: *Therefore,* and the rest.



## CHAPTER XII.

[0212B] *Therefore the maidens have loved thee.* Because, he says, thou hast poured out thy name like oil, when, coming forth from the bridal chamber, thou didst truly teach that thou art not man only but God also: this teaching they that are taught of God by no means neglected, but with a spirit made new they loved thee whom before they had not known. And these he named maidens, not by error but prudently, and therein designated the affectionate tenderness of those that love, because this age both loves more tenderly, and adorns itself more curiously, and bestirs itself more often — roving in its eyes, restless in its runnings to and fro, not knowing how to stand still, while its eagerness is unfulfilled. Those therefore whom the mould of hurtful eld does not disfigure, whose inward face the wrinkle of former depravity does not furrow, whose eye grows not dim, whose tooth falls not, whose querulous voice does not [0212C] grow hoarse, whose trembling step does not give way, whose spine is not bent with age, but in whom, such things being laid aside, warmth is strong and the vigour of the mind grows young again — these assuredly kindle more vehemently to loving, bear delay more heavily, faint more sweetly, languish more graciously. And indeed maidens, while they desire to obtain the end of their vow, study more curiously to please those whom they love; and that they may render themselves more pleasing to their sight, they strive with utmost care and utmost zeal to be seen more beautiful. Giving therefore their labour either to the keeping or to the getting of beauty, with a mirror set before them they consider the state of their face, and rejoicing in the good things which they weigh to be theirs by nature, what nature has conferred less of, they supply by watchful care. And the more beautiful they [0212D] have offered themselves for pleasing, the more pleasing are they rendered for bearing children, because they who in the eyes of their bridegrooms are delighted with an ampler beauty are more graciously rewarded by those same with a kiss, and made fruitful by an embrace.

One of such women, taking the mirror anxiously in her hand and discerning in it more diligently what she is, brought forth; because the body which is corrupted discolours the beauty of the soul, and the earthly habitation labours to weigh down a mind given over to many things [n: (Sap. IX)]. And this mind, pressed but perhaps not oppressed, that she may restore it both to righteousness and to salvation, she chastises her body and worthily subjects it to servitude [n: (I Cor. IX)]; with a view to love she shrinks not from enduring peril, nor death; she wipes away whatever spotted thing she judges to displease the Bridegroom; she wills her forehead to be white, her tender cheeks to flush faintly, her lips to breathe shamefastness, [0213A] her words moderation: her whole face, in short, to shine again with a new grace, that she may worthily please him to whom she wills to show herself approved. But when with cleansed brow, with a face so glad, she has shown herself approved and lovable, by the merit of this labour and this love she has not remained unfruitful: but, the Spirit making her fruitful, conceiving in a generative womb, she has borne sons to the Bridegroom by spiritual word and work. To whom she also says: « My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you [n: (Gal. IV)]. » And that: « In Christ Jesus, by the Gospel, I have begotten you [n: (I Cor. IV)]. » A certain other maiden, when she was fervent, and in that very fervour was pledging herself to remain fixed and steadfast, being not attentive with a judgment worthy enough to her own infirmity, still raw and insufficient, was found a little over-confident: « Lord, [0213B] says Peter, I am ready to go with thee both into prison and into death [n: (Luc. XXII)]. » And he, whose part it was, as with all else, so also to know Peter himself the better, knowing that he willed indeed what he had said, but was not able: « I tell thee, he says, Peter, the cock shall not crow this day, until thou thrice deny that thou knowest me [n: (ibid.)]. » And since the denial of the diffident would have come utterly to failure, if the mighty grace of him that has mercy had not set a hand beneath; willing that Peter should not only spring back from his rash lapse, but, being afterwards confirmed, should travail with spiritual sons: « I, he says, have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and thou *120* being once converted, confirm thy brethren [n: (ibid.)]. » Visited afterward indeed by the regard of divine mercy, and strengthened by the ampler gift of the Spirit breathed upon him, that same Peter grew white-hot to love [0213C] more strongly, to persist more firmly; and by the merit of a stronger love he deserved to hear from the Bridegroom himself: « Simon son of John, lovest thou me more than these? Feed my sheep [n: (Joan. XXI)]. » [var: Vulg. John 21:15 reads *pasce agnos meos*, "feed my lambs"; *pasce oves meas* belongs to v. 17 — Migne joins the question of v. 15 to the command of v. 17] The apostles therefore, and apostolic men, are not undeservedly named maidens, who in this drama are declared to accompany the Virgin Bride; and what renders them maidens is not fewness of days, not of age, but a more fervent faith, an impatient love, the grace of the newness granted them. For when that error had been driven out which had been widely scattered abroad in Judaea, the Pharisees preaching that Galilee would not bring forth Christ, and that, according to them, it was in no wise worthy to be believed that the carpenter's son, the brother of James, should be Christ [n: (Matth. XIII; Marc. VI)] — one who rather among them earned stones [0213D] not for a good work but for blasphemy [n: (Joan X)], and because, being man, he confessed himself God by usurpation; when, I say, this error had been driven out, the newness of faith was conferred upon the maidens, and what the Bride had earlier drawn in secret was carried over to the apostles. To me, says the Bride, thy name, O God, thy oil poured itself in, when thy dew poured over my fleece, when thy divinity poured over me, when I beheld within me God entire, the Word of the Father. The Son of God, and I myself, wholly full, loved thee with a plenary affection. But when I was filled, this oil was poured back upon those that are near, and, that it might be able to be received, was poured out upon the maidens; and what was poured into me, since they could not receive it, they neglected; poured out upon themselves, with fervent spirit they loved it. For none followed that same Virgin more familiarly, [0214A] or by her mediation more fully attained the knowledge of the Bridegroom, than the apostles, who, both before and after Christ's passion having long conversed with her, heard from her more frequently the mystery of the Word incarnate. These « all, he says, were persevering with one accord in prayer with Mary the mother of Jesus [n: (Act. I)]. » [var: Vulg. Acts 1:14 *Hi omnes erant perseverantes unanimiter in oratione cum mulieribus, et Maria matre Iesu, et fratribus eius* — Migne drops "with the women" and "and his brethren"] One of whom beyond the rest took the care of that same Virgin, and at Christ's command diligently reduced himself to her service; and imparted to her, as a son to a mother, a compliant diligence, and, having received her into his own, served her with the ministry of a provider. But she, having conversed so long a time with John and with the rest, who shall weigh with what affection she embraced them, with what care she strove to teach them the things she had known earlier and more perfectly, and to recount more frequently and more insistently [0214B] the wondrous order both of her conceiving and of her bringing forth? For the things which she saw through, fulfilled in herself by a high and ineffable counsel, she grudged not to those that stood by her, nor to maidens of this sort; but she rejoiced to call them to mind often in their ears, willing that they equally should obtain a share of the grace granted her. Accordingly, when she had said: *Therefore the maidens have loved thee,* she added: *Draw me,* etc.



## CHAPTER XIII.

*Draw me; after thee we will run in the odour of thy ointments.* [var: Vulg. *in odorem unguentorum tuorum*, accusative — "toward the odour"; Migne's ablative *in odore* is the reading Philip expounds throughout] Though the Virgin is raised to so great an excellence that by the gift of grace she is advanced to the Bridegroom's kiss, from this indeed she takes to herself gladness and a spiritual confidence, yet of her own strength she presumes nothing. For as she did not conceive the willing of good by her own merit, so she did not receive the accomplishing of it save from another: [0214C] and from him from whom she has all whatsoever she knows to be useful and desirable to her, from him she asks to be drawn after him, to whose service she has devoted herself. For she neither is, nor intends so to be, nimble that she should run before, striving only for this, and judging this to suffice her, that she should run behind; and to this very thing, by her own judgment, she does not prevail unless she be drawn, unless she be not dragged back by the burden of her own infirmity; unless she be driven forward by the sweet Spirit of grace to the things that are before, and not driven back by the wicked spirit to the things that are behind. From him therefore she asks to be drawn after him, not unwilling, but hindered still by the fetter of corruptible flesh, whose fortitude, though it be already perhaps firm enough in a prompt spirit, yet the flesh by a certain natural heaviness is somewhat infirm. [0214D] Him therefore whom she loves the prompt spirit burns to follow, wishing above all that the flesh may not retard him more than is just, but that, as the virgin's spirit loves to cleave to God, so the flesh may be able to wrest nothing injurious from that same spirit. For a prompter will provokes and lifts up not a few to stronger things, but the same men a carnal infirmity calls back and softens; and by a heavy softness either casts them headlong into failure, or at the least in no wise suffers them to be advanced to perfection. And for wretches of this kind, whom their wretchedness draws back with a softer bond, what is needful but that they be drawn and attracted by a stronger spirit, so that, the softness of him that wickedly draws back being pressed and oppressed, the pitying hand of him that draws on may at length prevail? « Therefore, he says, have I drawn thee, pitying thee [n: (Jer. XXXI.)] » There is also that drawing whereby the flesh is not now compelled [0215A] to obey, but which is found rather to soothe the spirit itself; a drawing, I say, far sweeter, of a certain inward delight, when the spirit is delighted by the taste and the love of the truth it has tasted. And in place of this the Bride and Mother wills to be held by a grateful longing, and by it to be sweetly moved forward to the things that savour of the spirit; and to be frightened away from their sweetness by no disquietudes of temporal things, but to be wholly swallowed up by the serene face of him whom she loves. And if a face of this kind be shown to one that loves, even for a little, if *121* to it, once shown, an eye purified by right judgment be directed, both the shower and the beholder are bound together by the bond of so great a love that he who loves is drawn on to the beloved by an indissoluble knot. Drawn, I say, not by violence, not by molestation, not by fear, not by hatred of the drawn or of the drawer, but by love; by that drawing whereby [0215B] the nursling is drawn after the nurse, whereby a son follows his father or a daughter her mother — nay, by that drawing whereby he that loves faints away into the beloved, the more graciously as the more sweetly, while he desires to obtain, and insatiably covets to desire. Whereof by Hosea: « I will draw them, he says, in the bonds of charity [n: (Ose. II)]. » And he that is drawn answers: « My soul hath cleaved after thee [n: (Psal. LXII)]. » So our Virgin chooses and asks to be drawn after her beloved, that he, namely, may by his grace give effect to the loving and the following; and that with affectionate love the Bride after the Bridegroom, the Mother after the Son, may kindle, and that not flesh to flesh, but the soul to God may the more strongly cleave. For as she recalls that she was weighed down by the loss of a certain death, whose unhappy soul had once cleaved to the pavement, so this Virgin, because after the Bridegroom's [0215C] kiss she loves nothing but life, desires to be drawn after him through whom she may live — not unwilling, but eager in affection, fervent in spirit, unencumbered in merits. And since, being thus drawn, thus helped, it is not expedient that she tarry, assuredly she will not follow him that draws her with a limping footstep, but with prompt pace, with agile step, with hastened foot she will run, and to him for whom she sighs she will make speed by an unencumbered road. *We will run,* she says, *in the odour of thy ointments.* She says in the plural: *We will run;* though in the singular she had set before: *Draw me.* If thou shalt have drawn me to thee by a special affection and grace, that thou mayest make me pleasing and blessed by the nuptial kiss, that thou mayest both cleanse and make fruitful thy bride by a princely spirit, that by a new and untried manner I may rejoice in a virginal childbirth; if me, she says, [0215D] thou shalt have thus drawn, then not I alone by a spiritual gift, but with me the maidens shall rejoice by a certain general benefit, so that they may follow me, who run before, more devoutly according to their own measure, and may be declared to run with me together after thee, whom they love. And so give me first, give me chiefly, the kiss; draw me by the bond of charity, grant me to know, grant me to feel the ampler grace of thy goodness; and this shall not profit me only, nor shall I be found to run alone, but we shall run, and all that love shall come to thee alike, though not with equal running. By the example indeed and by the merit of the Virgin, who is found to have run first and more perfectly, the apostles and their successors believe that they have found grace: who, having put off as it were the tunic of a wrinkled eld, grow young like the eagle, not with feathers renewed, but with manners [0216A] renewed. The Virgin was drawn and attracted by a certain thong granted to none besides, whereby with a heart utterly untiring she cleaved to the Bridegroom and Author; led upward and carried up, the Holy Spirit overshadowing her so strongly, so sweetly, that she conceives God, nature setting aside the right ingrained in it. And he who is conceived is himself he whose word runs swiftly, who, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills like a giant, outruns all the rest [n: (Cant. II)]; and to the following of him the Virgin weighs that she must needs be drawn, whom she does not lay hold of save when her native slowness has been laid aside. But who is either found readier to be drawn, or is rendered nimbler for running, than the Virgin, whose flesh is wholly lightened of the load of sin, and by that lightening drawing is wondrously made one with God that draws? And so the Virgin, being thus drawn — which she knows to have been granted to no other [0216B] — now runs, now advances, now presses on the more hastily to what she has desired: teaching and leading the fervent maidens to perfection, though none, however nimble, comes to an equal advancement. Perhaps for this reason the Virgin asked in the singular that she be drawn, but affirmed her running to be not alone but together with the rest, because in choosing her especially for his Mother the Son of God drew her to himself, yet she did not draw to herself alone the fruit of this work. For from the fact that she was singularly exalted to the prerogative of motherhood, no small profit was conferred upon the maidens that follow; while they studied worthily to imitate that same Virgin, and each according to her own measure ran to love the Bridegroom. « They ran, he says, both together, but John did outrun Peter more swiftly [n: (Joan. XX)]. » [var: Vulg. John 20:4 *et ille alius discipulus praecucurrit citius Petro* — the Vulgate does not name John] And another: [0216C] « So I run, he says, not as at an uncertainty [n: (II Cor. IX)]. » *We will run,* they say, *in the odour of thy ointments.* The odour of the ointments is the sweetness of spiritual gifts, which when any of the elect have perceived by a keen scenting, not grudging it to the rest but rather rejoicing in their company, they hasten with eager course to come to it, or rather into it, bearing no delay, and scarce deferring to find what they have already sensed beforehand. You know that it belongs to dogs by nature that what they do not even see with their eyes they are granted to sense beforehand with their nostrils; and if they have been worthily trained by hunting use, they run this way and that, they hasten, they bay, they cry out, until they have overtaken it — to such as these Paul says: « So run that ye may obtain [n: (II Cor. IX)]. » But if any one, keener of nostril, has sensed some anointed thing or ointment, with such greediness [0216D] of the odour he has drunk in does he follow the allurement, that neither promises, nor threats, nor death at last, nor life, can call him back from it, and he reckons all things loss that he may gain only the thing he covets. But how great are the ointments, when weighed in their own fullness, where they are kept under key and in a chamber beneath the perfumer's hand — ointments which, before from afar they have been found present and in fullness, so hold men's hearts intent by the sweetness of their odour? How great is the fullness of them that already refreshes those present, whose odour flowing outward so works upon them that drink it in, that it makes them, with the soles of their feet made firm, not only to come but, out of hatred of heavy delay, *122* to run? Who will grant to us, set far off, to sense this odour even a little? Who will bestow a stronger step upon our weakened feet, [0217A] upon our enfeebled knees, so that by pitying grace we too may some day be found running, or at the least may step by step follow from afar the maidens that run before? Happy are they to whom the Bride and Mother signifies that she will give her fellowship, with whom she asserts that she will run in the odour of the ointments; who in truth so runs with those same maidens that she runs before them, and, while they still remain outside, herself more swiftly and more familiarly runs within — which, signifying, she subjoins:



## CHAPTER XIV.

*The king hath brought me into his storerooms.* She who a little before had asked that she be drawn by him whom she loves, now confesses herself drawn and brought into his storerooms; and the grace she has found she does not hide out of envy, nor [0217B] dishonour by obscure silence, but to the praise of the Bridegroom and to his glory she makes it manifest to the maidens. For because, burning with an ampler desire, she shone again with ampler merits, the Bridegroom brought her as it were in a snatching into his own secret chamber; and to her, thus brought in, he showed the wondrous abundance of spiritual things, the presence of the ointments, the truth of the gifts promised. Having entered thereupon and beholding the incomparable storehouses of Solomon, she was astounded, and as it were grew stiff at the grace of the new vision; and having no more spirit in her, nor able to contain herself for joy, she ran back outside, announcing the benefit she had deserved to obtain. You, she says, to whom divine grace has already granted that you should run, see that you incur not a blameworthy failure through delay or through toil, but constantly and bravely run to riches that are not uncertain, unknown [0217C] perhaps to you, but to me not wholly untried; and he who brought me into his fullness, and has not yet led you to what you have desired — by that counsel which he himself knows — wills indeed that you should rejoice at my present goods, and by my example have a surer confidence of your own. And him the Bride here willed to name not bridegroom, not beloved, but King, willing, as I judge, to designate the royal power of the Bridegroom: to commend his wealth, his riches, the fullness of all things, whereof the storerooms of kings beyond all others are found to overflow. Moreover, that he is powerful no rightly wise man can doubt, since truthful Scripture is found to affirm it by many testimonies: for both he casteth not away the mighty, since he himself also is mighty [0217D] [n: (Job XXXVI)], and: « Whatsoever he would, he hath done [n: (Psal. CXIII)], » and power is at hand to him when he shall will [n: (Sap. XII)]; and that he is rich, the Apostle says: « Who is rich, etc. [n: (Rom. X)], » and the Gospel: « There was a certain rich man who had a steward [n: (Luc. XVI)]; » without doubt signifying God. Finally, who is richer than the Lord, whose « is the earth and the fullness thereof, the world, and they that dwell therein? [n: (Psal. XXIII.)] » [var: Vulg. Ps 23:1 *et universi qui habitant in eo*, "and all they that dwell therein"] The Bridegroom of the Virgin therefore is not unfittingly called King, by which name both his power and his abundance are commended; who moreover is recorded to have not a storeroom but storerooms, that his store may be taught to be far greater — since it is certain that more things are contained in storerooms than in a storeroom, and that many things are filled up with many, and diverse with diverse abundance. Into [0218A] many, then, rather than into one, does the Virgin declare herself brought in, signifying that she has attained the hidden treasures of wisdom and of knowledge. In which she deserves to receive not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit which is of God [n: (I Cor. II)], that she may know the things that have been given her by God; and knowing, may venerate, so that when she sees in herself the Word of God, and loves him made flesh, yet having the mind of Christ, she may know him no more according to the flesh [n: (II Cor. V)]. Moreover the hidden things of the divine wisdom, uncertain to all others, are made certain to the Virgin by an incomparable gift, in an unspeakable manner; and she rejoices to be led into that sanctuary of secrets, whereto the other virgins rejoice to be brought, not with equal step alongside her, but after her. She first, she more perfectly, both received the announcing angel and, according to his word, felt [0218B] the overshadowing Spirit: she knew that in the conceiving she bore no fault, no coition, and that in the bringing forth she uttered no groan according to Eve's law. She knew that he whom she cherishes, whom she embraces according to the natural need of little ones, is the life and the vital nourishment of angels; that he whom she holds in her lap, whom she suckles at a mother's breast, is God from eternity in the hidden bosom of God the Father: she knew herself, by a wondrous newness, the mother of God and man, and herself the nurse of her own nourisher and maker, and of all things. These, perhaps, are the storerooms into which the Bridegroom brought the Virgin Mother, which none but the wise Architect built with his own hand, and which in building he filled with so great a store of spices that the odour, as of the sweetest ointments, may rouse to running all that are slow. There is as it were one storeroom [0218C] whereby the divinity came down into man unconsumed, another storeroom whereby humanity was taken up into God; which two, namely the Word and the flesh, are so joined to each other by a certain wondrous work that in Christ they are both naturally diverse and personally not disjoined. And whosoever seems to understand and take up either of them without the other, if he confesses Christ either man without God or God without man, is seen to have entered one storeroom, as it were, of the King, *123* but to have sprung back from the other either by ignorance or by contumacy. But Mary the Virgin entered not one only, but both alike, who professed him whom she bore to be at once God and man; upon whom she leaned the more devoutly as the more surely, holding in memory, and sweetly calling to mind, [0218D] what she brought forth, and whom, and in what manner. For she brought forth not man only, but God also, whose wondrous humanity and humanized divinity was indeed uncovered to the Virgin brought within, but for some time was covered to the maidens themselves — who, running in the odour after that Mother and Virgin, shall be brought forward, and into those same storerooms, when the time and their merits shall have agreed, shall be led in. And with these to be led in the Virgin declares that she will rejoice, signifying that through them she will receive an increase of joy; since she who is already secure concerning the gift received by herself, when they too shall have received it, will enjoy an ampler joy for their sakes. This is what she adds: *We will exult,* etc.



## CHAPTER XV.

[0219A]

*We will exult and be glad in thee, mindful of thy breasts above wine.* Turned, or rather turned back, to the maidens, she announced her joy to them, and by that announcement invited them to run the more constantly: and this being briefly accomplished, she straightway called back both her word and her face to the Bridegroom, because she judged it sweeter to speak to him than of him. Whoever loves the more tenderly, though he gladly converse with others about him whom he loves, holds it far more grateful to speak to him, if perchance the choice be granted; and speaking of him, he loves to commend him to his hearers, while speaking to him he rejoices to taste his grace. And so the Bride, speaking of the Bridegroom, seems to do it for the sake of the maidens themselves, that she may exhort them, namely, to love him whom she loves; [0219B] because her love of him is so great that it fears neither rival nor concubine, nor does she count it her own loss if any other be provoked to love him. Nay rather, that joy which, loving, she wills to have in her beloved, she reckons to be made greater if it befall that others also obtain a share in him: and therefore, quickly referring herself to the Bridegroom, with whom she holds it grateful to converse more often, she asserts that she rejoices not over her own advancement alone, but over theirs together with hers. *We will exult,* she says, *and be glad in thee.* It does not suffice one that loves to proclaim her joy in a single word, but she doubles it, that by doubling she may be able the more expressly to intimate its abundance; and to the intimating of it, though she seem to unfold the same or like words at some length, yet she will not be able worthily to unfold as much as she feels. Or perhaps in that she says: *We will exult,* [0219C] she signifies the joy which inwardly she does not hide, which she rather so pours forth outwardly in voice or in any work whatever, that to the eyes of beholders the kind of her love may be shown, so that whoever worthily attends may be kindled to love in like manner. « Thy justice, he says, I have not hid in my heart; thy truth and thy salvation I have declared [n: (Psal.
