XXXIX)]. » But because every dissembler sometimes does or says very many things which, though their appearance be good, yet the inner conscience gainsays them, the Virgin adds: *And we will be glad in thee;* signifying that joy which, God being witness, lies hid in the secret of the heart, when, answering to what is shown outwardly, the heart within grows cheerful. Which the prophet seems to designate in a single verse, and in it to assign, as it were, each to each more distinctly: calling that [0219D] gladness which is contained in secret, but that exultation which is exhibited by outward tokens. « For this, he says, my heart hath been glad, and I have exulted under my tongue [n: (Psal. XV)]. » [var: Vulg. Ps 15:9 *et exsultavit lingua mea*, "and my tongue hath rejoiced" — Migne gives the first person and adds *sub*, the very word the exposition turns on] And elsewhere: « Let the heart of them rejoice that seek the Lord [n: (Psal. CIV)]. » And that: « Deliver me from blood, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall exult thy justice [n: (Psal. L)]. » From these places it is gathered that between being glad and exulting there is this difference, that to be glad belongs to the heart, to exult to the work; because both by affection and by effect ought every just man to rejoice in him from whom he hopes to obtain both present grace and future glory. Although exultation is sometimes assigned to the heart also, and one is declared not only to be glad but to exult in secret, so that exultation may seem to differ little or nothing from gladness, [0220A] since, like the one, so the other is asserted to be inward. « To him, he says, I cried with my mouth: and I exulted under my tongue [n: (Psal. LXV)]. » [var: Vulg. Ps 65:17 *et exaltavi sub lingua mea*, "and I extolled him under my tongue"] Under the tongue, he says, that is, in the heart, as below in this Canticle: « Honey and milk are under thy tongue. » And Anna in her Canticle: « My heart hath exulted in the Lord [n: (I Reg. II)]. » And this same Virgin Mary in hers: « My spirit hath exulted in my [sic: *Desalutari*] [n: (Luc. I)]. » In that therefore she says: *We will exult and be glad,* by the doubled word she signifies a heaped-up joy, which she understands that both she and the maidens will receive, and that by the gift of a more bountiful grace they will rejoice as much over things to come as over things present. For to godliness, which deserves to be brought into the aforesaid storerooms, the Author of the storerooms promises the joy of the life which now is and of that which is to come [n: (I Tim. IV)]; and by the giving of the things promised [0220B] he already bestows the present in the thing, and the good things that follow in hope, whereby, the cloud of sadness being wiped away, the heart of them that seek the Lord is soothed. Moreover in the present he advances knowledge, refreshes and makes serene the conscience; in the future he wholly estranges both from all darkness and from all disquiet: and that reality, *124* and this hope, warns to love, gives to run to him, and grants that he who runs faint not, but rather advance until he come to that same. Accordingly the Bride, saying: *We will exult and be glad,* subjoins: *in thee;* so that when, whether from things present or from the good things that follow, exultation or gladness is given us, none of us may glory in himself, but in the Lord; and that, forgetting himself, who has of himself nothing but death and sadness, he may with tender affection call to mind him from whom is life, and — that I may say it better — who is life. *Mindful,* [0220C] she says, *of thy breasts above wine.* With thy breasts, she says, thou givest suck, thou nourishest, thou refreshest the thirsty, while thou givest, while thou sustainest with free gifts them that love thee: while thou grantest that they who love thee, having obtained thy grace, be made perfect by a desirable advancement. Who, having relegated their substance and cast away the purse of their own depravity, rejoice in the hundredfold recompense of voluntary poverty; and being by the present benefit and by the milk of the left breast made stronger, are by the gift of the right breast now made more certain of receiving the reward of eternal life. Breasts of this kind are above wine, that is, better than wine, because present perfection and the promise of things to come are offered to the just more profitably and more graciously than are the tribulation and anguish that are inflicted upon any of the wicked, who both in present things are tormented by a wounded conscience and in the future await an irremediable punishment. [0220D] « Tribulation, says Paul, and anguish upon every soul of man that worketh evil [n: (Rom. II)]. » And Jeremiah: « With a double destruction, he says, destroy them, O Lord [n: (Jer. XVII)]. » [var: Vulg. Jer 17:18 *et duplici contritione contere eos*, without the vocative] This wine, harder than gall, of a most bitter taste and savour, this deadly cup of the Lord's wrath or fury, all the lost drink, by the merit of a more worthless life — they who do not attain to the Bridegroom's breasts, full of grace and of a more gracious nourishment. « Thou hast drunk, says Isaiah, at the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath; even to the bottom of the cup thou hast drunk, and thou hast drunk even to the dregs [n: (Isa. LI)]. » [var: Vulg. Isa 51:17 *usque ad fundum calicis soporis bibisti*, "the cup of dead sleep"] And expounding what this cup is, he says below: « There are two things that have come upon thee, wasting and destruction, and famine and the sword [n: (ibid.)]. » [var: Vulg. Isa 51:19 inserts *quis contristabitur super te?* between *tibi* and *vastitas*] Than this wine or cup the Bridegroom's breasts are far better, which promise [0221A] or exhibit more gracious things both to the Bride and to the maidens, whom by the hand of mercy he sets far from wrath and fury, far from the heavy judgment, and whose longing both present perfection and the recompense that follows satisfies. *Or we shall be mindful above wine,* that is, we shall be more mindful of the breasts than of the wine. He calls wine, as it seems, the transitory suffering of this life, which upon them that sigh brings the injury of no slight annoyance from the eternal, while the body that is corrupted and the necessary habitation of earthly things weighs down the soul, and presses down the mind with the burden of very many thoughts. And though a weighing-down of this kind is to any just man either destructive or purgative of vices, when God burns and chastises him whom he loves with the heavy but useful cautery of scourges, yet because it pricks, and a draught of this kind grows bitter [0221B] in the palate of him that tastes, everyone who burns to draw heavenly things the more sweetly wills that it be set far from him. Whereof the royal Prophet: « Thou hast given us to drink, he says, of the wine of compunction [n: (Psal. LIX)]. » The harshness of penalties, of which neither the poor man nor the richer is found free and immune, since even an infant of one day experiences it by a heavy law, is a troublesome pricking and a potion suited to healing, bringing in the hateful but plainly fruitful bitterness of discipline; which every wise man, in respect of itself alone, diligently rejects, but in view of the fruit that follows judges must be patiently borne. And though present experience compels him to remember it, yet a more perfect fruit and a sweeter hope warn him to forget it: and he is more gratefully mindful of spiritual goods and of a salvation that will longer endure, than of the bitter potion and [0221C] of a compunction that will more quickly pass. Whose grace seems to be attributed not to all, but to very few, whose foot is found worthily set upon a rock; that an unbending uprightness may carry the firmly established man up to the things above, and that by the merit of uprightness he may receive an ampler and more perfect certainty. Therefore there follows: *The upright,* etc.



## CHAPTER XVI.

*The upright love thee.* For he who does not go down to the lowest things with bent knee and crooked ham, but hangs himself upon high and arduous things with fervent longing; who is not bowed down according to the promptings of malignant spirits, that to them the wished-for ease of passing over him may be afforded — he assuredly is upright, and is judged to hate what he rejects, and, abhorring the things forbidden, is approved as loving the forbidder. [0221D] Finally you have: « Ye that love the Lord, hate evil [n: (Psal. XCVI)]. » He hates evil who does not incline to it the drawing-vessel of his heart, who does not cast down his eyes into the deep, or into the earth [n: (Dan. XIII)]; who does not bear with an even mind him that exhales a foul smoke from the dunghill of this life, who afflicts the nostrils with its incense, blinds the eyes, discolours the inward face. But by hatred of evil — which he detects to be tending into the deep — loving better things and things agreeable to salvation, he stretches heart, hands, eyes upward; and not only, though pressed and oppressed by a wicked burden, does he not bend down to the lowest things, but, raised up to the things above, he cleaves to them inseparably with his whole longing. And because those things stand and by an unbending uprightness are directed to *125* standing, it is certain that they become upright who are raised up to them by advancing merits; [0222A] and as they that make idols or the images of the nations are made like to them [n: (Psal. CXIII)], so they are conformed to heavenly things who cleave to their uprightness. And heavenly things, which are also not unfittingly called heaven or the heavens, which are prepared for the Lord as a house or a habitation, a place, a seat, a throne, do truly embrace the Lord himself, and him that sits therein, with affectionate longings, and cannot but love him whom they contemplate ruling mightily and reigning sweetly within them. « Our Father, he says, who art in heaven [n: (Matth. VI)]. » And: « I have loved, he says, the beauty of thy house, and the place of the habitation of thy glory [n: (Psal. XXV)]. » And: « The heavens declare the glory of God [n: (Psal. XVIII)]. » And: « The Lord, in heaven is his seat [n: (Psal. X)]. » And: « Heaven is my seat [n: (Isa. LXVI)]. » And many things of this kind you will find, [0222B] which assert that God dwells in heaven or in the heavens, and presides over seat, place and house with gracious good will: and the mutual gratefulness of the seat and of him that sits is brought about no otherwise than if, grace granting it, uprightness answer to uprightness. For God, being upright, wills to have those like himself, nor to be loved save by those who love to cleave to his uprightness — whom nothing but love makes to cleave to that same uprightness, and nothing but uprightness makes truly to love. Which the Virgin Mother perceiving: *The upright,* she says, *love thee,* because they who do not pervert their intention by the desire of the flesh, but with a willing heart turn themselves to him who is supremely good, it is certain that they set out upon a straight way, upon a royal way, and, advancing rightly, obtain the Good which they desire. Finally: « God is good to Israel, to them that are of a right heart *(Psal. [0222C] LXIX)*. » [var: Vulg. Ps 72:1 *Quam bonus Israel Deus, his qui recto sunt corde* — Migne drops the exclamatory *Quam*, "How good"] For they that follow the serpentine windings and the meanders of a crooked depravity do not taste how sweet, how delightful is the rule of the divine goodness, because to that uprightness which is good, which is just, which is supremely praiseworthy, the crookedness of malice or of injustice neither agrees nor cleaves. But he who with free horror suspends himself from earth and earthly things, and, seeking the things that are above, lays hold of them rather with an upright heart than with his hands, feels indeed that great and greatly praiseworthy is the greatness, equally great and magnificently to be commended the multitude of the divine sweetness — whose sweetness, though report perceives it, yet by an inward sense no man experiences it save he who is found like to the good God by uprightness of heart. And uprightness of this kind [0222D] the Lord seems to set in order by a fitting advancement, and to invite the apostles to it in the Gospel: willing them to be made not only readier to seek after it, but also more certain of the order of that very thing which is to be sought: « Let your loins, he says, be girt about, and lamps burning in your hands: and you like to men who wait for their lord [n: (Luc. XII)]. » [var: Vulg. Luke 12:35 *praecincti*, "girded"; Migne here prints *percincti*, and prints *praecincti* himself at 0223B below] This prudent craftsman of a discriminated uprightness, setting things in order, first lays as it were a base, he casts the foundation of the work: and the base being laid, he sets up the firm shaft of the column, and places upon it the capital, the ornament of that same uprightness. By the loins indeed is understood the will or the affection of this life, the concupiscence of the flesh, the acquiring of the will's desire: and for this reason the censure of divine [0223A] justice wills the loins to be girded, since it wills us to be restrained from all things not only that are not lawful, but that are not expedient. And to set aside harmful things, and to abstain from the things of concupiscence, to forbid carnal appetites their completing effect, to restrain loose motions with the strong girdle of chastity — this is a certain solid base, and the beginning of holiness. For whosoever seeks to obtain uprightness of living must first take care to abstain from things unlawful and unprofitable, so that when he has laid the base of the continence that must needs come first, he may confidently set upon it the weight of the fabric that follows. Perhaps for this reason, to that man who laboured with a grievous feebleness of the feet, who sitting at the temple gate begged an alms of them that entered in, Peter, moved with mercy, gave no help of money, because a mighty grace, [0223B] had given the Apostle not gold, nor silver, but by a mighty word he restored soundness to the lame feet, and that man, his soles made firm, walked leaping and glad [n: (Act. III)]. And rightly did Peter first impart soundness to the feet, and that man consequently, walking with his soles made firm, leapt up; because first the infirmity must needs be brought to an end, and, this base being laid, the fabric rise the more robustly to advancement. Accordingly, when he had said in the Gospel: « Let your loins be girded [n: (Luc. XII)], » he subjoined: « And lamps burning in your hands [n: (ibid.)]. » For when a man has with due horror cast off the works of darkness, in an order just enough there follows the kindling of the lamps, namely that before men his holiness may shine, and that like a pillar of fire the uprightness of his manners and of his justice may stand forth. [0223C] The lamp in the hands signifies brightness in works, when upon the base of the continence whereby you abstain from the things that are not expedient, you apply an eminence of works, an uprightness of manners, and after the manner of an unbending column you study to remain steadfast and immovable, and to be pre-eminent in life and manners over all beneath you. But because it does not suffice that a man shine with great works, unless through them he aim to please not men but the Lord, he adds: « And you like to men who wait for their lord [n: (ibid.)]. » The intention or expectation whereby you do not court a transitory reward, but with ever-wakeful care await your Lord from above, is a certain fortification of the aforesaid uprightness, and like [0223D] the capital of the column, a commendable ornament. For a column is bare and unfitting if it be not *126* adorned by a capital set above it, and insufficient is that uprightness which is not held fast by the expectation of the Lord; whereby, as by a summit, it surpasses and transcends all the things that are of the world, and after the manner of Jacob's ladder lays hold of the heavens from above. Whence Paul: « Our conversation is in heaven, whence also we look for the Saviour [n: (Philipp. III)]. » There the Apostle asserts that he converses, whence he loves to await the Saviour of himself and of all; and whatsoever is by worthy judgment declared upright and stable, is by this awaiting, as by a certain roofing, brought to completion. Wherein the Bride and Mother, being far more fully instructed and having attained that same uprightness by an ampler advancement, loves the Bridegroom, [0224A] and is joined to him in chaste commerce, learning by experience that to her who loves rightly his embrace is not denied. For because, according to the prophet, upright is the Lord our God, and in him no iniquity is held [n: (Deut. XXXII)], with a countenance assuredly gracious he beholds the Virgin's equity; and in her the strength of his kingdom holds a realm peaceful enough, whose uprightness agrees with so great an equity of hers. To her indeed the same Prophet says: « The rod of direction, the rod of thy kingdom [n: (Psal. XLIV)]. » The Virgin herself also is in the Scriptures for this reason, as I judge, called a rod, when she is figured in them by a mystical speech, so that by the name of the rod may be understood not only the flowering beauty of the Virgin, but no less her clean and fruitful uprightness. You know that Aaron's dry rod put forth leaves on the second day [n: (Num. XVII)], and, unaided [0224B] by natural fomentations, brought forth nuts by a wondrous newness: wherein it is doubtful to none that the uprightness of the Virgin is figured, who, nature standing astonished, and knowing no man, is brought forward to the bearing of a son. Isaiah also, beholding a rod that should come forth from the root of Jesse [n: (Isai. XXI)], knew that a Virgin should be born of the stock of Isai; but him who by an incomparable process ascends from her as a flower, he did not weigh what better thing to figure than her son. In this very drama the angelic Spirits marvel, when they behold that same Virgin ascending through the desert like a wand of smoke [n: (Cant. III)]; namely for this, that the Virgin, forsaking the things that are beneath, stretches herself more freely into the things above, and, treading the earth with her purpose behind her, lays hold of heaven by her longings. But because one comes not to this uprightness [0224C] save by file and labour, nor is entrance made into the kingdom of God save through many tribulations, as Scripture testifies [n: (Act. XIV)], the Virgin wills that the maidens be not scorched by present annoyances, but in the pressure of temporal things be refreshed by the consideration of spiritual. For the maidens might be moved at this, that she who seems already to have been led to the Bridegroom's kiss, and by her own testimony to have been brought into the storerooms of the King, nevertheless still labours under pressures, is wearied with a wretched burden, and, though she boasts herself beautiful, has her face accused of foulness. Whereupon the Virgin seems anxiously to forestall them, and, that they may weigh each thing worthily, to instruct them more diligently — because both the foulness that appears is to pass away with a swift course, and a beauty unbending in its state remains to follow after.



## CHAPTER XVII.

[0224D]

*I am black, but comely, daughters of Jerusalem, as the tabernacles of Cedar, as the skin of Solomon.* [var: Vulg. Cant 1:4 *sicut pelles Salomonis*, plural, "as the curtains of Solomon"] The blackness which fouls and infects the comeliness of this Virgin is the adversity of the present life, which weighs upon her and afflicts her against her will, which does not suffer the joy of the Spirit, the grace of a peace begun, to be brought through to the harbour of a consummated beauty. For upon the Bride, fervent indeed in Spirit and sighing after continual peace, aspiring in the Bridegroom's sight to a perfect beauty, there come fear, peril, the annoyance of hurtful injury, tribulation and anguish, grief of the inward parts, the sword of passion — which upon her face, which sometimes a spiritual gladness, the light of grace, floods over, spread instead a cloud of sadness, a shadowy blackness. For neither to the Virgin herself [0225A] did the present life give continual peace and unfailing joy, but she grieved and groaned, harassed by many annoyances, and in the number of her days she brought forth white pebbles in such wise that yet among them very many blackening ones were not lacking. Indeed the heathen, since they distinctly number and weigh their sad and their prosperous days, that they may comprehend with sure knowledge which outweigh which, as with white pebbles they mark the series of prosperous days, so with the blackness of pebbles they mark the sad and adverse. Black therefore is the Virgin, when she feels herself afflicted with temporal annoyances, when she sees him whom she bore crucified by mockers; and him whom she knows to be present to the angelic spirits as their author and Lord, and in the bosom of God the Father to be God in equal glory, made flesh in her and of her, she sees now made subject [0225B] to the power of his persecutors, with many assailants and no defender of him at hand. Black is the Mother, when she beholds her own flesh, which she loves not by vice but by nature, hard pressed in her son by an untimely death, when whatever ill he suffers at the Father's bidding, by the circuit of a natural sling, redounds pitiably into the Mother's heart. Black is the Bride, when she hears the Bridegroom, even after he rose from the dead, blasphemed by his own countrymen; when she sees his preachers, the apostles, scourged; when she considers that whatever she herself knows of him, or the holy oracles declare, *127* is a sign which the rebellious and unbelieving contradict. In all which, who shall weigh with what mourning, with what sadness her mind wastes away, with what wrinkles it is drawn together, with what pallor her face withers: since the sorrow which inwardly weighs down [0225C] and afflicts the mind, the countenance for the most part displays, and the outward foulness of the flesh sets forth? Which Solomon asserting says: « A sorrowful spirit drieth up the bones [n: (Prov. XVII)]. » Sadness therefore, the bones being dried up, blackens and disfigures the Virgin, and, joy being set far off, seizes and usurps for itself the first place, nor suffers the present form to rejoice in a fairer one, since the body that is corrupted darkens it with a blacker dye. Nor is it a wonder if the Bride, made more sorrowful, confesses herself black and deformed, since in this she is not unfruitfully made like the Bridegroom whom she loves, who, for that he is weighed down with annoyances while he is held by corruptible flesh, is by the testimony of the Scriptures declared to have no comeliness and no beauty. « There is, he says, no beauty in him, nor comeliness [n: (Isa. LIII)], » and: [0226A] « We have seen him, and there was no sightliness [n: (ibid.)]. » But he who has no comeliness, no beauty, is understood to be black and deformed; so that the Virgin is not to be accused, if she be conformed to him in blackness, since blackness is to be assigned to neither's ignominy or shame, but the present state of living, given over to wretchedness and toil, renders them deformed. From the bearing of which Christ willed not to be free, but as to all others, so to the Bride and Mother he offered himself for an example, that the Virgin might not herself shrink from seeming black and deformed, but in this also might patiently show herself conformed to the Bridegroom. Finally, below in this epithalamium the Bride says of him: « His locks are black as a raven [n: (Cant. V)]. » Because therefore he is made swarthy and grows black like a raven, the Virgin in no wise blushes to confess herself black also; but lest anyone [0226B] should reckon that very blackness to be the more grievously burdensome the longer it lasts, having made mention of it the Virgin straightway asserts herself comely. *I am black,* she says, *but comely.* Though I suffer penalties, she says, by the merit of human depravity — penalties which in the present furnace are vexed and purged by the cautery of a transitory heaviness — yet beneath this burden a form lies hid, a beauty is nourished, which justice makes glad and an unfailing length makes firm. The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit liveth because of justice [n: (Rom. VIII)]. [var: Vulg. Rom 8:10 *spiritus vero vivit propter iustificationem*, "because of justification" — Philip's exposition below repeats *propter justitiam*] And though the manifold death of penalties, she says, afflicts my bodily life by the merit of the first sin, and daily fastens me, as I die, upon a heavy gibbet: yet that inner man, rich before God, is renewed from day to day, lives because of justice, is adorned with the merits of the virtues. And the more the present [0226C] wretchedness discolours the outer man, so much the more does the love of things to come advance and adorn the inner; to whom both here and now the grace of loving heavenly things gives strength, and, when strength is consummated, promises glory and salvation. « O Lord, says the Prophet, in thy good will thou hast given strength to my comeliness [n: (Psal. XXIX)]. » He who is beautiful in form above the sons of men, by the privilege of his own will, the brightness of eternal light and the mirror of the divine majesty, by his own will imparted strength also to his Mother and Bride, whose comeliness he himself, who had given it, being King and Lord, desired. To whom also, speaking below, he says: « Show me thy face; thy face is fair [n: (Cant. II)]. » And she, as she is called black and deformed by suffering temporal evils, so is she called comely or fair [0227A] by affectionately loving spiritual things, whose inestimable comeliness so affects her that loves it that it makes the blackness of her that suffers to pass over into whiteness. Therefore the Prophet: « O Lord, he says, I have loved the beauty of thy house [n: (Psal. XXV)]. » And the Lord in the Gospel to them that love him: « Your sorrow, he says, shall be turned into joy [n: (Joan. XVI)]. » As therefore affliction renders her black, so love renders the same woman comely: and the former indeed belongs to the present time and is more quickly to have an end, but the latter, though it began in time, yet in no time shall it cease. Whence also the Virgin declared herself to be, not rightly comely and black, but black and comely, because with her blackness held the first place, while it was granted to tribulation to rage against her with looser reins, and both by its coming [0227B] and by its going to come before the beauty that was to be. Of which John says: « Death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor sorrow shall be any more, which former things are passed away [n: (Apoc. XXI)]. » [var: Vulg. Apoc 21:4 *quia prima abierunt*, "for the former things are passed away"] This heap of evils therefore came first to the Virgin's heart, but found in it no dwelling or stable place; nay, as it importunately came before her beauty that was to be, so it was compelled to depart when that later beauty more fully came upon her. The Virgin's beauty is, when with fervent spirit, desiring the face of God, she anxiously wipes with her hand the stains of her inward face; when she clears her eye, cleanses her conscience, makes serene her heart, when with severe judgment she sets far off the assaults of them that clamour against her; when at last with a pure and agile mind she is caught up into ecstasy, when she comes to [0227C] the throne of majesty, unapproachable to the slow and the negligent. Whereof he that sat upon the throne subjoins: « Behold, I make all things new [n: (Apoc. XXI)]. » The Lord makes new when with the hand of mercy he wipes away the oldness of our inner man, when he knocks upon ignorance, heals the conscience, directs the will; when, the error of falsehood being wiped away, he grants us to speak truth with our neighbour, when he more gently pours in the delight of that same truth, when at last, to confirm the grace of her inward beauty, he hides us from the tumult of men in the hiding of his own face. She therefore who, exposed to threshings and sufferings, reckons herself black and deformed, the same, hidden in the hiding of the divine face, rejoices to be made conformed to it; and her whom the furnace of tribulation *128* renders shadowy, as it were, with its own soot, [0227D] the ray of contemplation by its outpouring makes bright and comely.



## CHAPTER XVIII.

*As the tabernacles of Cedar, as the skin of Solomon.* [var: Vulg. Cant 1:4 *sicut pelles Salomonis*, plural, "as the curtains of Solomon"; the whole chapter expounds the singular skin] Because she had called herself black and comely, she shows in what manner she is black and comely. *Black,* she says, *as the tabernacles of Cedar, comely as the skin of Solomon.* Cedar is interpreted *darkness.* Tabernacles are called, not stable houses, but movable huts, which are set up either by shepherds in the pasture or by soldiers on campaign, and, being placed for a time, are not made firm upon a stable foundation; but when it is convenient they are carried elsewhere without loss. The Virgin therefore not unfittingly confesses herself black as the tabernacles of Cedar, hinting that the condition of this life, by whose bonds she is still [0228A] held, grows dark indeed with much dye or cloud of annoyances, and grows bitter with many stings and prickings of sufferings; whose hateful and shadowy bitterness is nevertheless not founded in an abiding state, but passes after the manner of a tent, and, like a guest, does not linger. Affirming which, Job: « After darkness, he says, I hope for light [n: (Job XVII)]. » And the Lord in the Gospel: « Sorrow, he says, shall be turned into joy [n: (Joan. XVI)]. » For that which the Virgin grieves at, that which she groans at, that which she suffers of the annoyances of temporal life, passes away and is turned into the light of spiritual joy: nor does she complain so much of the presence of a night that will pass, as she rejoices in the sure hope of a light that will remain the longer. Strengthened by the gift of that hope, she cares little for the momentary pressure, while she conforms a pure and untroubled mind [0228B] to the glory that shall come upon her: and, the frost or old age being wiped away, as it were, by which for an hour she is drawn together and sickens, she blossoms again with a glad spirit, and grows young after the manner of an eagle. Whereof Solomon beautifully: « A rejoicing mind, he says, maketh a flourishing age [n: (Prov. XVII)]. » For whose inner man's age would not flourish, whose broken oldness would not grow young by the benefit of the rock — in whose conscience pure faith, secure hope, and abiding love come together, and all these in all things constantly obey God alone? Accordingly the Virgin is rightly called comely as the skin of Solomon, who, the sense of the flesh being cast off, as it were knows not the annoyances of a passing suffering: whose conscience continual obedience, and whose obedience a cheerful conscience, renders commendable and serene, adorns her countenance, and declares her face a stranger to the filth of dust. [0228C] A skin indeed is drawn off from a dead animal, is separated from the flesh by a scraper rather of iron than of flesh: but once separated, it knows no more the hurts or sufferings of the body; struck, it does not grieve; an annoyance being inflicted, it does not sicken. Finally it is shown pliant, tractable, and apt for various uses, if only the labour and industry of a prudent craftsman work upon it: and if a careful craftsman love to bestow his pains, it is found the readier to obey in innumerable ways. So too the Virgin is separated from the things that are of the flesh by that strong scraper which is proclaimed to be sharper than any two-edged sword [n: (Hebr. IV)] and to reach unto the dividing of the spirit and the soul; and she, drawn and drawn off by that iron, as it were knowing not the affections and afflictions of the body, [0228D] loves to forget them, and, being stretched out unto the things that are above, to remember chiefly those. Whom that highest craftsman, designated by the name of Solomon, yet of far ampler benevolence, wisdom and power, drawn off from bodily affection, so fitted to his own spiritual good pleasure, so formed, anointed with the oil of grace, unto all things that were worthy, that no rebellion, no contrariety at all was had in her, but she was rendered, after the manner of a skin, nimble to obey in all things. « Behold, she says, the handmaid of the Lord; be it done unto me according to thy word [n: (Luc. I)]. » You see that, the message being heard, according to his word the handmaid gives herself over to the Lord, and in nothing does the thing formed gainsay its former, nor the shard the potter; but the throne of Solomon is made subject to the command of him that presides over it, nay, the heaven of heaven, his seat, is stretched at the pleasure of him that sits upon it. [0229A] For to this end God stretched out the heaven like a skin, that that prophetic word might stand: « Heaven is my seat [n: (Isa. LXVI)]; » and that other: « The Lord, in heaven is his seat [n: (Psal. X)]. » But who more worthily, who can more fittingly be called heaven, than the Virgin who deserved to be adorned with so many stars of virtues, whose varied brightness mitigates the troublesome darknesses of this life, while it calls back the errors of the unskilled multitude to knowledge? She herself brought forth the moon that should shine out for those darkened in the night, when she exalted the Church, that it might show itself luminous to all: when by form and by doctrine she instructed the holy apostles, whose manner of life imparted a necessary light to the dwellings of the lands. Finally the Virgin herself, or that heaven, brought forth the greater luminary, which conferred upon a languishing world a fuller saving [0229B] remedy: which, because he is God alone, and no other can be made equal to him, has worthily been called the Sun by a certain singular privilege. So the Virgin alone and no other bore so great an offspring; that wondrous heaven in wondrous wise brought forth the sole Sun, who thus fashions day for them that watch, when by his presence he lights up and floods our air, and thus strikes night into the drowsy, when, the mass of earthly sins being set between, he hides himself. But this Sun alone among all things, and above *129* all things luminous, beautiful in the light of his countenance and in form above the sons of men, if he loves by his grace to make fruitful lands heavy with so great a weight of their own, how much rather does he make heaven abound with ampler gifts? Which heaven he is read to have stretched out like a skin, wherein he seems to have shown its nimble obedience, [0229C] because the Virgin, who is reckoned comparable to heaven, nay commendable above heaven, in nothing, not even a little, struggles against the good pleasure of him that commands. I indeed, as I see, am not a skin in the Lord's hand, who am found hard and rebellious toward him that calls and commands, who to his voices and warnings give not open ears, but stop them; and if perchance it fall out that I hear, that I may not obey what I have heard, I harden my heart. But if sometimes, being visited, penitent with a softened heart, obedient to his commandments, I promise perseverance in them; when I am now entering upon the correcting of my own manners or of my people's, behold, a wind rushes in, thunders, tempts, destroys, and I break off what I had begun. For that worst tempter heaps up many darts for himself, by whose infliction he either terrifies the mind more roughly, [0229D] or more gently soothes and unnerves it: and the flesh leads the vanquished spirit into its own right, and, that I may become wholly flesh, the love of carnal things seduces me. Who therefore shall deliver wretched me from the body of this death? [n: (Rom. VII 24.)] Who shall separate me from this flesh by the strong sword of the spirit, that, slaying the flesh and resigning it to the beasts and the birds of Babylon, I may be found skin alone, and be stretched out at the command of Solomon? But if to me, or to any like me, that gift is not yet granted, to whom the bridegroom's chamber and the sanctuary of God still seems unapproachable, yet the true Solomon did not defraud our virgin of that grace, but formed her, after the manner of a skin, to his every pleasure. For her, drawn off from the concupiscence of the flesh and from the hurtful affection of depravity, he lifted up on high by the hand of mercy unto purity: and, [0230A] the desires being scraped away, he spread over her, as it were, varied colours and a starry beauty; nay, he brought in the merits of the virtues and heavenly grace. Which truly the virgin willed should not lie hid from the daughters of Jerusalem, not knowing how to grudge to her familiars the grace she had found; so that to those whom the virgin's blackness can trouble, if it be too negligently regarded, both a worthier cause of that same blackness and a briefer duration of it might be shown.



## CHAPTER XIX.

*I am black, but comely, daughters of Jerusalem.* She names as daughters those whom a little above she named maidens, wherein she designated both their tender affection and their fervent desire; and because daughters, quickened to hear more serenely and to see more studiously, attend more subtly and love more tenderly the praises of a commended beauty: [0230B] You, she says, whom no stolid dullness holds back from understanding, attend and see how commendable is my beauty; you whom the confused blindness of Babylon does not darken, but whose eyes the grace of an inward vision enlightens and unveils. Whence also I pointedly call you daughters of Jerusalem, by which name I the more diligently compel you to see, so that when you hear and mark that you are called by such a name, you may know that a name ought not to be empty, but rather to be derived from the thing. You are therefore truly daughters of Jerusalem if you see, if what is darkly said you intelligibly grasp, if what outwardly sounds harsh you reckon as a shell or as chaff, and what within is sweet and vital you long for, as the kernel, the grain, the fine flour. Finally, know that I myself, who invite you to understanding [0230C] and suffer you neither to be darkened by ignorance nor to wander in gloom, am rightly called Jerusalem by the merit of seeing, to whom it is plain that these divine mysteries and heavenly sacraments are revealed. And when after the manner of childbearing I lead you out of the darkness of ignorance, when with study and labour I bring you through to the light of truth and knowledge, when with affectionate solicitude I form you by more perfect rules of living, what do I do but, in a mother's stead, conform you to my own bowels, or rather to my own manners? And indeed to one of you the Bridegroom says: « Behold thy mother [n: (Joan. XIX)]. » Whose daughters you are by doing well, that is, by not considering my blackness with an over-searching attention — whose cause is profitable, and whose end is already near at the door — lest perchance by too much curiosity you run into a present [0230D] stumbling-block, if you attend to this only, that I am black, more than is just. Accordingly she says: *Do not,* etc.

## CHAPTER XX.

*Consider me not, that I am black, because the sun hath discoloured me.* [var: Vulg. Cant 1:5 *Nolite me considerare quod fusca sim*, "that I am swarthy", and subjunctive; Migne prints *nigra sum*, black and indicative, which is the reading the chapter expounds] See, she says, that you fix not carnal eyes upon my burdens, that the adversity of a shattered will beget no stumbling-block for you, that your consideration be not childishly astounded at my annoyances, as though it were not fitting that my manner of life should grow bitter with tribulations. Have, I pray, as befits daughters of Jerusalem, understanding, and weigh the cause of this thing rather than the effect; what is seen by all, I will to be as though not seen at all by you, and what lies hid from the unwise, I will that you the more wisely *130* behold. That I am black, that I am sorrowful, [0231A] that a cloud of momentary hurt flies about me, that the waters enter even unto my soul and the sword of passion passes through: this the true Sun has done, he by his own counsel has brought me to this, he has spread over my face a dye or blackness of this kind. That Sun, in whose absence a fouler and misshapen night presses in, and all the variety of things is found discoloured and formless; but in whose presence the sky shines, the earth rejoices, its surface is rendered manifold, and the very face of things is made in some sort conformed to what is comely: that Sun, I say, who by the regard of his countenance refreshes and adorns all things, by a certain absence of his own discolours me for a little. For from those who weigh me down he absents himself by a strict judgment, but to me who endure he does not yet present himself for a kiss — perchance that they may advance to the worse by wickedly inflicting [0231B] evils, and I on the contrary to the better, by patiently bearing annoyances. Finally, a prudent virgin, in the letter, greedy of preserving or increasing her beauty, sometimes lays a fillet manifoldly upon her face, that under the veil the beauty desired may advance, and may appear of greater grace when it has been nourished under a medicinal covering. And truly her lover (if only his uprightness be not inexperienced in such things) does not despise a virgin whose face is covered, knowing that whence her comeliness for an hour grows dark by the veil drawn over it, thence, when it is afterwards taken away, it shines out the more pleasingly. So I too am black, wrapped in the dye of a certain veil, and while I live in the flesh not yet wholly loosed from annoyances; because that Sun of mine, who [0231C] wills me to be still in the hovel of this night, wills me not to be altogether free from its injuries. For the place and the time in the midst of which you still see me are not, by a certain implanted law, of full peace or of rest — which peace not even my Bridegroom himself chose to obtain in them by the privilege of his power, but, as is known to you, willed rather to fear and to be weary [n: (Marc. XIV)]. And he who, pressed by many discomforts, willed at the last to undergo death, wills that I too, set here, should not lack the same sufferings, which I bear patiently in his memory and love, being sure indeed that he not only wills but consequently also does. For he who does not yet honour my face with a full colour discolours it, as I seem to see, by his delay; and he who wills me to be blackened by a burden that will the sooner [0231D] pass away — what he disposes to be done, that very thing I do not refuse to do. Since therefore in this wrestling-school my patience the more fully strives, I pray, daughters, that the consideration of these things scandalize you not, and that you attend not to what I suffer, lest your weakness so take offence, but to who it is that wills me to suffer, the knowledge whereof commends you. Nor is whatever I suffer for his sake worthy of scandal, but it is a greater suffering to lack sufferings apart from him; because he who, ill-happy, is granted to be excluded here from the scourge, grieves as a wretch hereafter not to be included in the number of the elect. But my Bridegroom, who himself also endured to be black in the present, wills that same blackness to be in me as in all his own; who, when the fitting time shall have come, will take away this colour, and will change mourning into joy, the dye into whiteness. Whence [0232A] what was said, *The sun hath discoloured me,* can be taken for this, which is (he shall discolour) — the past, namely, for the future; because he who made the things that are to come was indeed about to do that in the Virgin which the virgin, being the more sure, asserts him already to have done: for what the Virgin already foreknows to be future concerning her glory, taught by that Spirit whereof she is full, she does not foretell, does not demand, but, secure of its fulfilling, rejoices and affirms it already fulfilled — which faith and hope possess, and only the fact murmurs back as unfulfilled. Do not, she says, judge my blackness worthy of consideration, as though either it hurt while present or could linger longer, because « I passed by, and lo, it was not [n: (Psal. XXXVI)], » nor is a trace of it to be found; and for you too it shall now be no more, if you will, to pass by in like manner. For that true Sun who bestowed his light [0232B] upon this world, who is risen for us to this end, that he may draw his own out of the deep, will the sooner abolish my dye or blackness with a gracious hand, and will utterly remove wrinkle and spot, grief and every tear. Nay, that I may seem to speak better and far more surely, he has already removed them, has already cherished my sick mind with the wished-for remedy, because by his grace he has already advanced me to such certainty that I hold as done what my understanding has foreknown is to be done next. But as, when he who consoles me by his benefit is set before you, your consideration is not worthily weighed down by the presenting of my blackness, so it is expedient that they who press me hard with their malice should know that their way also shall perish, and that they themselves shall not rise again in the counsel of the just [n: (Psal. I)]. And who that is rightly wise would weigh or [0232C] consider with heavy care whatever they inflict, whose power is quickly to pass away? and would not rather make little both of them and of the annoyances inflicted by them, when he detects in them nothing firm, nothing stable? *131*



## CHAPTER XXI.

*The sons of my mother have fought against me, they have set me a keeper in the vineyards: my own vineyard I have not kept.* They who ought to have spared her, and to have defended the Virgin from the injuries of others, to run against them that laid hands upon her, to fight back against her assailants, to give their life for her, by their own death to preserve their sister, on the contrary assail her, and rejoice to harass her with persecutions. And, affection being shattered, the law wounded, that right utterly broken which the law of nature has appointed to be kept even among brute beasts, the mother fears not to persecute the daughter, [0232D] the sons the sister: they molest, tear, torture, disembowel; in nothing do they show mercy. Judaea, or the Synagogue, I judge to have stood as the Virgin's mother, who according to the law of the flesh is believed to have borne her, and whom with maternal solicitude she cherished in a tender bosom until the years of advanced youth, and imbued with legal ordinances. But the sons of the mother, in flesh as in manners, are the Jews, blind leaders of the blind, Pharisees more by malice than by knowledge, who, forgetful of the brotherly covenant, the more grievously afflicted their sister when they fastened her son to the cross rather with viperous tongues than with iron nails. Of whom the prophet Amos: « They have not, he says, remembered the covenant of brethren *(Amos I)*. » For of this covenant, whereby brothers ought to be the more affectionately bound to a sister, they, sick with a venomous [0233A] perfidy, would not more soundly be mindful; but as though strangers to the stock, set far from nature, they render her rights neither to a sister nor indeed to a human being. And who of sound head would think soundly of Judaea, who is a mother and yet loves not, even as the fables report of Medea, to which mother there was no love of her sons, no care, but, kindled with hatred, she took them out of the way by an untimely death? As Medea, so Judaea strives to render false that argument which nature has woven for the safeguard of a debt of love — an argument which not only the modern loquacity of disputing clerics winnows and affirms, but also the sagacity of the heathen, tried from of old. If she is a mother, they say, she also loves. But because Medea was a mother and yet loved not, she put off, as they say, the nature of a mother rather than neglected it; and since [0233B] even a brute beast is held by a natural affection toward its own young, she is convicted not to be a mother who is not softened even by a beast's feeling. For the rest, Solomon, upon whom God bestowed wisdom, the assessor of his own throne, by this argument proves that harlot to be the mother who chose that her own infant be given alive to the lying woman rather than, at the king's word, be cut asunder by the sword that was brought. « She said, he says, whose son was alive, to the king (for her bowels were moved over her son): I beseech thee, my lord, give her the living child, and do not kill it. On the contrary the other said: Let it be neither mine nor thine, but let it be divided. The king answering said: Give this woman the living child, and let it not be slain; for she is its mother [n: (III Reg. III)]. » And elsewhere it is written: « No man hath hated his own [0233C] flesh [n: (Ephes. III)]. » But Judaea loves to obey neither the testimonies of Scripture nor the commands of nature, but to rage against her daughter with an incredible hardness; and, overstepping the rights of the laws, she spreads abroad and practises a most evil fury of mind, whose sons likewise no more considerate regard restrains from malice. For they are those who, like their mother, neither fear God nor reverence man, who with obstinate malice deny that God is man, and think it does not befit his majesty and deep counsel that he should will and be able to come down to bear our miseries. They indeed assert that the mother of Christ conceived of Joseph, and that she remained a virgin neither in conception nor after childbirth; and whatever is venerably preached either of her integrity [0233D] or of her son's majesty is by their testimonies disowned as feigned and frivolous. If a virgin, they say, has borne, she first lay with a man. Whence also they persecute her son not for a good, as they say, work, but for blasphemy [n: (Joan. X)], and endeavour to scrape his memory from off the earth: namely because, among those who are mere men, he takes to himself something more, and, being man, himself presumes to make himself God. At the last, malice pressing on, they adjudge the innocent to death, they accuse him as one not paying due reverence to the law and to the king: they shut him in with bonds, smear him with spittle, heap buffets upon him, hand him over to the judge, and the judge to the soldier; an unlovely clamour resounds; and they crucify him, these with clattering tongues, those with nails. And what do all these things do but rave [0234A] against the Virgin, sound the trumpet furiously, wrestle against the walls of her patience? They assail and storm the tower of her constancy with a heavy ram, they shake it unmoved, but by the interposing of grace they do not take it. And it is to be noted that, although both Gentiles and Jews rage against the Virgin, though Pilate and the soldiers do what the Pharisees demand in words, yet here, where the battle is recounted in a prophetic spirit and in a nuptial song, the Virgin makes mention of her own only, and no mention is made of outsiders. *The sons,* she says, *of my mother.* Why this, save because, as you know, by right judgment he troubles the more who dishonours when he ought to have shown deference, who (when in his bosom, as a friend's, rest was to have been hoped for) hands over to the hands of an enemy the one he ought to have cherished? For when an enemy curses, the cursing is *132* borne the more patiently; [0234B] when foe rages against foe, he deserves either not to be blamed, or not to be blamed harshly; when a stranger does not succour a stranger with generous good will, as he wins no praise, so neither does he incur much reproach. But the man of peace, the man of one mind, the man familiarly known [n: (Psal. LIV)] speaks the more unjustly, so that he offends, when a friend or a neighbour draws near against me more harshly, when, instead of loving me, he venomously detracts and assails, when he shows evil for good, hatred for love: whence have I to bear it, whence to be able to act patiently, and not rather to complain that the faithless man rages fraudulently? Being silent therefore about the Gentiles, the Virgin complains of the Jews, and their malice is for the present brought into the midst — who, being the sons of her mother, so grievously offended the Virgin, and repaid her with battle for defence, [0234C] with hindrance for help. But that we may know that the evils which they the more studiously accomplished profited us who are set far off, by the disposing of God's wisdom, and that their malignity and the damage inflicted upon the Virgin was our profit and the increase of a desirable grace, the Virgin adds:



## CHAPTER XXII.

*They have set me a keeper in the vineyards, my own vineyard I have not kept.* Any soul whatever may rightly be called a vineyard, of which the one seems to be compared to the other by a certain likeness; because as a vineyard or vine is found to consist of many things — of the tendril, the cluster, the shoot — so also the soul is marked out with many powers or virtues. Let not the sons of my mother glory, says the Virgin, that [0234D] they have fulfilled their wickedness upon me, that raging against me they have filled my soul with heavy bitterness, that my vigilance did not keep it against their violences, but that their sword passed through it. For whence they the more violently took away my own soul, thence, not knowing what they did, they transferred me to the keeping of many; and when they brought the graver loss upon my vineyard, they conferred a useful benefit upon you, daughters of Jerusalem. The abandonment or failure of my vineyard is without doubt your advancement in spiritual things; and in that they hurt me for a time, as they reckon, they set for you, to whom I pass over, a necessary keeper. And not unfittingly may there be signified by the name of vineyards not only souls one by one, but by flocks the assemblies [0235A] of souls; because as many shoots obtain the name and the yield of the vine, so many souls together make a flock or an assembly, to which the Lord, speaking: « Fear not, he says, little flock [n: (Luc. XII)]. » And the Prophet: « Thou hast brought a vineyard out of Egypt [n: (Psal. LXXIX)]. » And elsewhere: « The vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth is the house of Israel [n: (Isa. V)]. » [var: Vulg. Isa 5:7 *vinea enim Domini exercituum*, "of the Lord of hosts"; Migne prints the Hebraism *Sabaoth*] The sons therefore of the mother, who brought the aforesaid annoyances upon the Virgin, transferred her, driven from her own vineyard, to many others; because she who was wickedly despised by her brethren and fellow tribesmen was received by many vineyards or assemblies of the Church. But the Virgin did not fortify her own vineyard by her keeping, because that wicked people obeyed neither her warnings nor her examples, but, rejoicing to be left to its own will by a judgment hidden from it, with a hardened neck [0235B] ran into that curse of Isaiah: « Woe to the sinful nation, to a people heavy with iniquity, to a wicked seed, to wicked sons! » [n: (Isa. I.)] Whom perchance both the prophet and the Virgin therefore named sons, and not daughters, because by the masculine name she designated their perverse strength — men mighty and strong against the Virgin's soul, drunk with the wine of the damned, in whose merits they rejoice, and whose penalties also they shall bear: « Woe to you that are mighty, he says, to drink wine, and strong to mingle drunkenness [n: (Isa. V)]. » And that other: « The strong have sought after my soul [n: (Psal. LIII)]. » These strong and mighty men, when they drove the Virgin back from the keeping of their own selves, compelled her to pass over to the keeping of our vineyards; and what was worthily taken from them that were nearer, according to their merits, was conferred upon us [0235C] that are further off by the grace of a divine gift. How many assemblies throughout the whole world rejoice today to be fortified by this Virgin's patronage, and their churches to be guarded by her welcome solicitude, who, though they execrate, as is right, the malice of the lost sons, yet give thanks that it was useful and necessary to themselves? But to say nothing of others, brethren, is not this assembly of yours gathered in honour of this Virgin, and are not this place and church dedicated in her name; and do you not rejoice in her keeping and her special patronage, embracing your keeper with a certain affection and spiritual tenderness? Which of you, when he calls her memory to mind, or even when he hears her name, does not rejoice with devotion, does not applaud with devout [0235D] obedience, hoping to find her Son placable and propitious if he can come before the mother with due reverence? Happy fault, useful battle, fruitful perversity, whereby a hateful brotherhood rages against our Virgin, whereby, the ragers being left behind, a gracious blessing passes over to us, whereby the Virgin disowns her brothers, reproves her own household, hates her own; sets our vines in order, hedges them with a wall, prunes, digs, and (that I may conclude briefly) keeps us with all diligence. Nevertheless, because in these vineyards too there may sometimes *133* be found men who presume by their evil manners to pull down those same vineyards, the virgin, turned toward the Bridegroom, wills to be more fully taught [sic: *a beo*] who are his, that she may beware of those whom she has known not to be reckoned in the number of his own. And so she says: *Show me,* etc.



## CHAPTER XXIII.

[0236A]

*Show me, O thou whom my soul loveth, where thou feedest, where thou liest in the midday, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of thy companions.* Thou, she says, whom I love not in word, not in tongue, not in the mere noise of the lips, but with heart and mind and with all the strength of the inward parts: show where thou feedest, where a welcome refreshment is prepared for thee, where thou findest the food wherewith thy hunger may be filled. « For I was hungry [n: (Matth. XXV)], » he says. I know that a prudent shepherd does not tarry in all places, not in all pastures, but prudently searches out which they are, and in which a profit is to be had; and shrinking from and passing by those which he has known not to have the sap of life, he feeds and refreshes in those which he has perceived not to shrink from life. And beautifully she inquires so anxiously not about the food but about the place, [0236B] because perchance she knows well enough with what fodder he is delighted, holding it certain that his food is cleanness, justice, truth, and other such things as effectually work true holiness. But who knows where this holiness is truly and firmly to be had, unless he be taught by him who teacheth man knowledge, since man knows not what is in man, nor is judgment worthily made concerning another [n: (I Cor. II)] — whose face, though it appear, yet whose conscience is not seen? The Virgin therefore wills not to be seduced by the outward face of men, but to be led into the very chamber, as it were, of truth; and to come to the place where the Bridegroom rejoices to find pasture and rest, not by a material foot but by a spiritual eye. Finally Joseph too is sent by his father's solicitude to visit again his brothers in the pastures, [0236C] and coming into Sichem, a man being found, most diligently asks where they feed — the boy not understanding that he would be a burden to his elders, and that he would not rejoice, as he had hoped, in the finding he desired. « I seek my brethren, he says; show me where they feed. And the man said to him: They are departed from this place; and I heard them saying: Let us go into Dothaim. Joseph therefore went forward after his brethren, and found them in Dothaim [n: (Gen. XXXVII)]. » Rightly is Joseph read to have found his envious brothers in Dothaim, to which place they are reported to have come not by chance but of set purpose, knowing perchance that they would there not so much find a life-giving pasture as fulfil a wicked will and a decree of crime. Dothaim is interpreted *their green [0236D] fodder,* or *sufficient failing.* Their green fodder, that is, the envious men's, is envy itself, which they taste, which they chew over, which grows strong in their minds, which with a pestilent savour grows sweet inwardly in their throats; which is not trodden down by a censor's foot, does not wither by a swift repentance, but with untiring rancour grows green even to the height of crime. For nothing is more welcome to the faithless than to envy their betters, to disparage the absent, sometimes to fawn upon the present; with a feigning countenance (when the power of hurting is not at hand) to smile, and, when the time for hurting has shone out, to hurl the poisoned dart. As therefore in Osee Ephraim feeds on wind, when he vainly desires what he hopes for to come to pass *(Osee XII)*, so every envious man is not [0237A] unfittingly recorded to have come into Dothaim, when he is delighted with the poison of spite as with a green fodder. But because Dothaim is also interpreted *sufficient failing,* whence that wicked man tends the more vehemently toward the effecting of his malice, thence, guilty of the crime, he falls into an ampler failing of conscience; and that damage alone which he loves to inflict upon another plainly suffices for a torment to the man who labours under envy. Which a certain heathen beautifully hints: *Than envy,* he says, *the Sicilian tyrants have found no*
*greater torment.*
But whoever is agreed to bear in his mind that venomous spite, than which the Sicilians found no heavier torment, he assuredly is convicted of failing from the quiet state of the mind, and a failing of this kind suffices for the death of him that fails. For he who envies is found to hurt himself more [0237B] than his neighbour, and what he attempts to inflict upon another he is found to suffer first; and his own envy, which for the most part is not felt by the other, pulls down the man from whom it proceeds, as the moth a garment. Joseph's brothers therefore, who, as you have read, were found in Dothaim, that is, already forestalled by a certain inward failing and by envy, seeing Joseph and speaking beforehand one with another, run to meet him as he comes, offering to him who knew nothing not a greeting, not a kiss, but hatred. « Behold, they say, the dreamer cometh; come, let us kill him [n: (Gen. XXXVII)]. » A wicked place, a place execrable and unspeakable, a place to be detested in the judgment of all (of those, at least, who are soundly wise); a place worthily to be named not refreshment but failing, where charity perishes, brotherhood fails, and an accursed spite prevails. [0237C] Because therefore many are known to feed in Dothaim and in other places of this kind, and whoever have followed them are struck with some penalty or other, the Virgin, anxious not about the general breadth of the many, asks in what *134* place and in what special solitude the Bridegroom feeds. For she knows that his place is not possessed by many, she knows that in his pastures there are not many lords; she knows likewise that not every pasture is the Bridegroom's, and therefore she desires the more diligently to know which is his.



## CHAPTER XXIV.

*Show me where thou feedest, where thou liest.* I know, she says, that thou feedest not in the covert of the reed, that thy cleanness does not rest in moist places, wherein that Behemoth lies hid in a rest that is welcome to him [n: (Job XL)]; wherein he cherishes [0237D] and promotes his wicked depravities, and by a pestilent feeding brings evil wills into effect. In these indeed thy soul takes no pleasure, thou hast no will in them, as by Isaiah's oracle thou truly assertest concerning the Jews, who, not being subject to thy will, to thy good pleasure, are cast forth from thy refectory, far from thy face. For how dost thou feed where thou dost not yet choose to dwell, where, straitness compelling, thou lovest not to walk more freely, where the appetite of feeding is beaten back by a certain bitterness set against it, when a wicked seed, when a provoking house is found? I am sure that mount Gelboe is not held pleasing to thy pasture, wherein Saul, David's adversary [n: (I Reg. XXXI)], fears not to enter [0238A] battle, wherein the strong fall and death adjudges Saul and Jonathan to its own laws, upon which no dew, no rain comes, as David complaining curses it. I know likewise that the plain of Sennaar is not offered to thy pasture [n: (Gen. XI)], wherein, pride reigning, no reverence is paid to thee, wherein the presumption of an unskilled multitude is struck by the diversity of tongues, and, they being divided one from another, a tower of infinite greatness is not completed. The plain of Mageddo also I judge does not please thee for feeding [n: (II Paral. III)], wherein the archers struck the just Josiah unto death: from which that justice which was already glad in the hope of victory, the fortune of the battle being turned, is carried back utterly dead. But hast thou perchance chosen the valley of Tophet as suited to thy pasture [n: (IV Reg. XXIII)], which thou hast known to be most delightful in situation, [0238B] foul in sacrilege; wherein the children of Israel paid honour not to thee, their God, but to Moloch, in a wretched superstition, and by a blind rite carried over to him their sons and daughters through the fire? Not thine is the pleasantness of this valley, which pleases not Josiah either, whose pestilent rite that same king's sagacity took away, when those whom the very face of the place and its most delightful beauty invited to sacrilege, the scattered bones of the dead and the heaped foulness of corpses drove back. Because therefore thou feedest not in mountains, plains and valleys of this kind, I ask that thou teach and more diligently show where thou dost feed, if perchance thou art foretold to have other mountains, plains and valleys, in whose lap thou art delighted, feeding or lying down.

The Virgin indeed knows that other mountains are commended in the Scriptures, in which no one is read to perish [0238C] but to be saved, which the Bridegroom himself, loving them and visiting them with a friendly affection, makes worthy of himself and fit for a special pasture. Joel the prophet: « In mount Sion, he says, shall be salvation [n: (Joel. II)]. » And David: « He chose mount Sion, which he loved [n: (Psal. LXXVII)]; » and again: « Mount Sion, the city of the great King [n: (Psal. XLVII)]; » and that other: « The Lord loveth the gates of Sion [n: (Psal. LXXXVI)]. » And what wonder if that mountain, which the Lord embraces with a benevolent affection, is asserted to offer welcome fodder to him that embraces it, so that the lover is not denied to feed in that which he loves — to whom there is no refreshment at all save where his love is? Therefore perchance John: « I saw, he says, upon mount Sion a Lamb standing [n: (Apoc. XIV)]. » [var: Vulg. Apoc 14:1 *et ecce Agnus stabat supra montem Sion*, a finite verb, "the Lamb was standing"; the exposition immediately following turns on the participle *stantem*] But standing to what end, unless [0238D] for feeding? For the lamb stands while he feeds; but while he rests, he lies down. But the Virgin, anxious not about one only but about both, asks where the Bridegroom feeds and where he lies down, as though one place were for feeding and another none the less for resting. For the Bridegroom is the Lamb. For of him of whom John elsewhere says: « He that hath the bride is the bridegroom [n: (Joan. III)], » of the same he said: « Behold the Lamb of God [n: (Joan. I)]. » The Bridegroom therefore, or the Lamb, feeds upon a mountain — not upon that which Isaiah names dark [n: (Cap. XIII)], nor upon that which Zacharias asserts to be great and to be brought down into a plain before Zorobabel [n: (Cap. IV)]; but upon mount Sion, which is commended by the merit of seeing, which, having its name from the thing, [0239A] past the objects set close at hand, descries things more remotely placed. Of which mountain Isaiah prophesying: « Send forth, he says, the Lamb, O Lord, from the rock of the desert to the mount of the daughter of Sion [n: (Isa. XVI)]. » [var: Vulg. Isa 16:1 *Emitte agnum, Domine, dominatorem terrae, de petra deserti*; the title "the ruler of the earth" is not printed here] Finally through Ezechiel the Lord promises: « Behold I, he says, will feed my sheep [n: (Ezech. XXXIV)], » and, determining where he will feed them: « In the mountains, he says, of Israel will I feed them [n: (ibid.)]. » Israel is interpreted *seeing God.* Good therefore and rich would I call those mountains to which it is granted to behold God, whose pasture the good Shepherd is found to promise to his sheep; because the saints who are pre-eminent in virtues are lifted up by their merits, who, dwelling in the heavens, are flooded with the light of contemplation: they assuredly refresh God's good pleasure, God's desire, God's will; they offer to his commandment the richness of a manifold [0239B] spiritual obedience. « To the saints, he says, who are in his land, he hath made wonderful all my wills in them [n: (Psal. XV)]. » He hath made wonderful, he says, that is, he fed, cherished, and wonderfully brought through to effect, that I might do in them all things whatsoever I willed, and that their works might be great and wonderful, sought out unto all my wills [n: (Psal. CX)]. Finally *135* in the Gospel the disciples: « Whither wilt thou, they say, that we go and prepare for thee that thou mayest eat the pasch? » [n: (Marc. XIV.)] And he: « The master, he says, of the house will show you a large upper room furnished; there make ready [n: (ibid.)]. » In that he says an upper room, it is high and eminent; in that it is large, it is broad and sufficient; in that it is furnished, it is fair and alluring. The upper room in which the Bridegroom's refreshment is, is commended by the height of its dignity, [0239C] because the heaven of heaven is assigned to the Lord, and the earth to the sons of men [n: (Psal. CXIII)]; and, that it may suffice the more, it is enlarged with a great space, because he is not gladdened by a scanty seat and a niggardly tripod; and, that it may ever allure him, it is spread and fitted with wrought carpets and sweet-smelling flowers, because he that is beautiful above the sons of men spurns things unclean, unseemly and foul. The Bridegroom feeds also in a plain — in that plain, namely, which is levelled by the tearing out of masses of rubble, which, rooting up thorns and briers, is beautified with a pleasant surface; which, the barren frost being wiped away, is made fruitful by a spring-like mildness, laughs with green herbs, and is varied with the manifold colour of flowers. Of which the first and chief says: « I am the flower of the field [n: (Cant. II)]. » Rich is that plain, nor is it to be negligently passed over in silence; upon whose [0239D] face Ezechiel sees many bones [n: (Ezech. XXXVII)], and exceedingly dry, which by an ineffable hearing perceived the word of the Lord, and received sinews, flesh and skin by a wonderful joining, and at last, the spirit coming from the four winds, lived again. Finally in the Gospel [n: (Luc. VI)] the Bridegroom, coming down from the mountain, stood in a plain place, wherein, because the power of healing and the fullness of grace shone forth, a copious multitude of peoples flowed together to him from every side; and the good Shepherd, marking that it was eager to hear and to be healed, refreshes it with a generous hand with the word of life, with saving fodder. The Bridegroom feeds also in the valleys, which David asserts to abound with corn [n: (Psal. LXIV)], and in the valley of Josaphat, which seems to glitter with the grace of humility, while the greater each man is, the more he makes himself less in all things, and he whom his neighbour worthily [0240A] commends and lifts up, discolours himself by his own judgment. « When you have done, he says, all good things; say that we are unprofitable servants [n: (Luc. XVII)]. » [var: Vulg. Luke 17:10 *cum feceritis omnia quae praecepta sunt vobis*, "all things that are commanded you"] And that other: « If we judged ourselves, we should not be judged [n: (I Cor. II)]. » In mountains, plains and valleys of this kind the Bridegroom feeds, because loftiness of life, evenness of manners, and humility of judgment is the Bridegroom's welcome refreshment; which as a prudent craftsman he himself works in his own faithful ones, while he rejoices to bring his wills through to effect in them. « My meat is, he says, to do the will of him that sent me [n: (Joan. IV)]. »



## CHAPTER XXV.

*Show me where thou feedest, where thou liest down in the midday.* Having asked where the Bridegroom feeds, the Bride adds the asking where [0240B] he also lies down in the midday; touching upon the custom of shepherds, who, when they have given their labour to the pasture in the first part of the day, at midday turn aside and lie down for the sake of rest. Since therefore foxes are known to have dens, and the birds of heaven nests [n: (Luc. IX)], into which very many wretched men, with blind brow and erring foot, tumble down: the Virgin wills to know more surely whither the Son of man chooses to turn aside, and where he would lay back his own head for the sake of quiet. For the season admonishes, when the world is sultry and burns, when with a keener sun the midday sky glows white, that the provident Shepherd should turn aside into the shade and rest, and that the little flock, fleeing to him, should lie hid at ease. The sun is sultry, the heat falls upon the minds of the wicked, when the wicked heap of vices flows together upon them: when avarice, when lust, when [0240C] ambition lords it over them, when with the burning of such things their inward face is blackened. In this midday therefore, whose heat that world cannot bear to endure, that Holy One to whom nothing unclean pertains, whither he turns aside, where he pauses, where he finds it welcome to find a chamber, I myself, if it might be done, would wish to know, not so much by knowledge as by experience. For when pride lifts us up in the goods either of nature or of grace, when a clinging anger inflames us, envy torments us, lust makes us soft; when prayer is heavy, divine reading is loathed, when the word of the preacher, the ear being closed after the manner of the asp, is not heard: it is to be feared lest, weighed down by this heat and unseasonable distemper, that shepherd, forsaking us, flee away beneath a convenient shade. With a heavy and parching sun the world set in [0240D] wickedness was sultry, and with the midday burning Egypt or Ethiopia laboured, when that Holy Spirit overshadowed the incorrupt Virgin, and prepared in her for God the Son of God a welcome covert of shade [n: (Luc. I)]. The same burning, or distemper, had lain hard enough upon the Pharisees, and with a looser rein had been spread abroad among the Jews, when Christ, forsaking them, turned aside to a few apostles, and gathered them like a hen under the shadow and covering of her wings. But when even unto the cross the Jews and the Gentiles raged against him at midday, and some with the tongue and others with the hand poured forth the venom of a boiling wrath, he himself, not so much with the foot as with the affection, more with the mind than with the eye forsaking those whom he despised, saw standing beside the cross his Mother and the disciple whom he loved [n: (Joan. XIX)]. And *136* when he had received the vinegar, [0241A] which being tasted rather than drunk he thus fulfilled the mystery, upon these, whom the Spirit overshadowed, he rested the more graciously as he rested the more sweetly; and while the sun was sultry without, whose rage filled him full, bowing his head toward these, and delivering up his spirit, he fell asleep. Thus, no longer bearing the midday and the raging heats of the Crab or of the Lion, at the sixth hour consummating the agony, or the mystery, of the Passion, he turned aside and loved the shade of the Spirit, the serene lying-down of the tomb, to which the stone set against it was no hindrance for one that should rise again. « For he lay down as a lion [n: (Gen. XLIX)]. » [var: Vulg. Gen 49:9 *requiescens accubuisti ut leo*, second person, "resting, thou hast lain down as a lion"] Whom indeed the tomb was able to hold as long as he willed, but, his will fulfilled, he was not held back by the barrier of the stone; nay rather, for rising in the morning the divine power rendered him strong as a lion, and equally for rendering requital at midday to them that raged. [0241B] Nor do I judge it unworthy if we reckon that the same Bridegroom lies down in you also, if we declare that he finds even in us some little rest: since both to serve him and to soothe him is our will, by the gift of his grace, although for them that will the power is not yet wholly free. But if we ourselves, or perchance any others, should judge that it does not sufficiently befit us to ascribe to ourselves that whereto all our betters scarcely avail to come: it is to be feared lest on the contrary we distrust more than is just, and by a degenerate distrust incur an equal peril. Between the two therefore let not Daedalus, but the Father of spirits teach us to fly; let him rule the unknown way, let him be willing to give the grace of journeying, lest we be plunged in mud and dregs while, after the likeness of the earth, we keep to the things nearer to carnal men, [0241C] or lest we be pressed down from glory while after the fashion of [sic: *lchari*] we foolishly assail the higher things. For the Bridegroom lies down in us, if we are proved to love him, if with diligent zeal we make ourselves ready for his service: if whatever clamours against him and gives offence we hasten to wipe away with broom or with razor, if the secret of our heart, for love's sake, we adorn with the flowers of love. For nothing does he desire more gladly, nothing more eagerly, than to be loved, namely when we truly embrace him with a singular love, when whatever the world offers we cast far away as refuse for his sake, when in the world or in ourselves we love nothing beside himself. Finally John [n: (Cap. XIII)] declared that he reclined upon the breast of that same Bridegroom, because he, above the rest, loved him as he reclined: nor is any other, as you know, said to recline [0241D] in that same place, save he whom Jesus, by frequent testimony, is not silent that he loves.
