And rightly it is read that not Jesus lay down in John's bosom, but John in Jesus' bosom, because it is believed that we did not love him first, but that he first loved us: and where a man truly understands that he is loved, there he rejoices to recline, and to be delighted with a sweet reclining. For Christ before his passion understood that John was weak, as the rest also were, and that he himself was loved less than sufficiently by the disciple whom he loved, because throughout that time neither John nor Peter either willed or was able to undergo death for him — which, before his Spirit was received after the resurrection, none of them deserved to obtain. But for the rest, Christ was found so to love those whom he chose, and his charity toward them so constrained him as he loved, that for them [0242A] he willingly gave his soul unto death, and those whom he held in his bosom he defended from death by dying. But after his resurrection, appearing to the same disciples, he breathed upon them [n: (Joan. XX)], and by a most serene breath assigned to them the pontifical office of binding and loosing, when a little after the vehement Spirit inflamed them with fiery tongues [n: (Act. II)], and unbendingly strengthened them against the threats, the entreaties and the bribes of the world; and that death's turn which he first willed to undergo for them, they themselves, not wrapped about with the ropes of avarice but with a prodigal bounty, rendered back. In these, and in such as they, the Bridegroom must not undeservedly be believed to lie down, with whom he finds nothing whereby his rest can be hurt: in whom devotion is vigorous, discipline glows the more devoutly, where the furnace does not smoke, but the whole workshop of love utterly burns. For because the Bridegroom, [0242B] as has been said before, desires to be loved, and love is a fire, those whom he beholds to be kindled and to burn with love, in these, as upon a little bed, he wills to lie for the sake of quiet. And on this account he is said not to lie down save at midday, when the sun, nearer to heaven, is removed farther from the earth, when hotter than its wont it sends forth purer rays, when with a greater burning it affrights the broader fields of the aether. And perhaps he feeds in the morning, when the troublesome mist of the nights now withdraws, when the sun, necessary to one that rises to his works, goes before him; when its rolling wheel strains upward with labouring horses, and, knowing not how to stand in one place, does not aim to journey and to advance for itself. Through which space of time the sun affords the day a useful nourishment, whereby the day, cherished and promoted, gradually receives [0242C] increase, until the sun, hastening and arriving at mid-heaven, is fixed, where, now higher in degree, it is compelled either to stand or to descend. So indeed, when to you, brethren, sitting in darkness, the Sun of grace brought the morning light, the night's error being laid aside you hastened to lay hold of discipline; and the more fully he spread out for you his brighter rays, the more gladly you labour and take to yourselves the ampler advances. While therefore with watchings, fasting, sweat and cold you chastise the contrary body, while, devout and humble, you bind your patience with the ropes of obedience, and in regard of the commandments banish your own will; while you labour to work the food which perishes not, but which abides, and with untiring zeal eat the labours of your own hands: assuredly with you the Bridegroom feeds along with you [0242D] *137* and labours, even as the devout lover and getter of wisdom indeed prays: « Give me, he says, wisdom, that she may be with me and may labour with me [n: (Sap. IX)]. » For in feeding there is indeed a life-giving fruit, but beyond doubt with labour; the labour is a little thing, made bearable by the more welcome fruit: and for this cause, when the just man invites patience along with himself to labour, he loves not so much the labour itself as its better fruit. Accordingly the Virgin desires the more anxiously to know not only where the Bridegroom feeds, but also where he lies down, that she may avail to come to his more welcome state; because, although while he feeds he gives us no middling advance, yet while he lies down and rests he carries us forward to perfection more graciously and more surely. When therefore, the body being chastised, the murmur of the passions lulled asleep, the labour of temporal actions not wholly laid down but for an hour [0243A] set aside; when prayer, devotion, the rumination of the reading you have heard makes you serene within, and the grace of the divine vision snatches you up, hung from the earth, as it were on high; when (though hurriedly and for a little) you seem to be present among the angelic spirits, and, beholding after some fashion the glory of the Lord, you say with Peter: « It is good for us to be here [n: (Matth. XVII)]; » when with the love of such things you are sweetly sultry as with a fire, and a Sun brighter than the sun floods you with the ray of his own brightness: then indeed in you the Bridegroom feeds, and is delighted with a friendly rest, rejoices in such a midday, and day is glad in day, light in light. For as the wicked enemy, the author of evil, the prince of ruined Babylon, loves the deep darkness of night and the cold of the north wind, so the Bridegroom who is God, unfailing light, burning fire, putting the welcome presence of himself [0243B] far from the unlike and the unworthy, lies down and reposes in those whom he perceives to be burned with the fiery torch of divine love, whom, snatched into ecstasy, he beholds to shine with the midday light, and not to be burned up. Who, forgetful of things present, are intent upon heavenly things alone, not content with the dawn or the morning sun and the works of them that are beginning, but are carried up to the perfect day and the fervent midday, one spirit with God, not made perfect only by reason of the flesh's fellowship as yet. Happy is he who, forgetful of the things behind, deserved to be thus stretched out to the things before, and, loathing the morning's mildness, to be thus kindled with the midday's advance and an exceeding fervour; to hold the bridegroom in his bosom, to embrace him with affection as with an arm, to fasten his eyes upon the sun, and not to be turned aside to the carcases of this flesh. Happy, I say, if yet [0243C] he fears not the fall of this benefit, if the midday of this heat and of this splendour alike inclines not to its setting; if the flesh draws him not back, and the still weaker law of nature, which cannot yet bear the glory of a happiness that shall abide. Happy therefore is that day whose midday goes not down, in whose fiery light the Bridegroom ever abides and reclines: to which whosoever shall have come, he perseveres in it with steadfast step, and, its good being found, affirms that nothing is better, nothing more delightful. In which the holy angels ever behold the face both of the Father and of the Son, and the souls of the saints are not held estranged from the sight of him; which souls, snatched away already from the wicked world and from the prison-house of the flesh, are received with the angels into the quiet chamber of that same Bridegroom. There a fuller and more perfect midday is found, where the day declines not, and [0243D] is not ended by the oncoming of evening; and there dawns not save one only day, neither advancing nor failing, whose splendour is not made swarthy, whose splendid heat does not grow lukewarm. Accordingly no man in this life fully receives such a midday, but foretastes it; there he is fully satisfied, where delay, being shorter, does not straiten, where the love of all men toward God burns continual and unremitting, and he himself who is loved gratefully lies down in all and rests. And so upon earth he feeds — in him alone, being accepted, to whose account he sets down justice, he pours in the bounty of grace; with whose good works, as with herbs and flowers, he refreshes his own will; whose manners he accepts, whose equity he loves to see; in whose merits he rejoices, whose virtues he embraces, whose holiness he receives; for whom the morning day and the sun shine with an imperfect light, while he labours and advances, [0244A] because labour is fashioned in a precept [n: (Psal. XCIII)]. But in the heavens the Bridegroom lies down, where the day rises not with a dim light, but as at midday the sun glows red with an advance already ripe, whose warm splendour, and heat equally splendid, have nothing imperfect, but with unmoving pole, as in a kind of solstice, they stand perfect. In the day therefore the day, light in light, in the sun the sun lies down sweetly and rests, because the just man in the kingdom of his Father shines bright as the sun [n: (Matth. XIII)]; and the Bridegroom, the sun of justice, receives in him a chamber and a rest welcome to him in this, that it is not straitened in space, not troubled by the assault of annoyance. Accordingly the anxious Virgin not undeservedly asks that it be shown her where he feeds, where he lies down whom she loves with a singular love, that when it has been shown, she may safely and gladly follow thither, lest (if it be shut) [0244B] she be borne wandering after the flocks of the companions.



## CHAPTER XXVI.

*Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of thy companions.* He is Christ's companion who wills to be reckoned by his name, who says that he is his, who chooses to profess his faith; who announces his word, who preaches the way of truth; who joins himself to Christ, either in the reality or in the image of holiness. But because there are many who rejoice not in the true *138* reality, but are coloured with the image, who by affection and by work detest what they build up by word or by countenance: these the Virgin willed to call not a flock but rather flocks, knowing that the singular name is more fittingly attributed to the just. Whence below in the Song: « Thy hair as of goats, thy teeth as a flock of sheep [n: (Cant. VI)]. » [var: Vulg. Cant 6:4–5 *capilli tui sicut grex caprarum*, "thy hair as a flock of goats" — the singular *grex* Philip's argument turns on is absent from the first clause as printed] And in the Gospel: « Fear not, little flock *(Luc. [0244C] XII)*. » The flocks therefore of the companions are the multitude of them that believe falsely, in whom there is a show of piety, but no virtue, no strength of works; in whom the ostentation of the Christian religion is apparent, in whom the preaching or the doctrine of Scripture sometimes sounds forth, but the life savours not rightly, the discipline of their manners is not fragrant enough. Who for the most part wound and seduce the consciences of the weak, and, turning aside from the path of justice, lead them into the broad room of error, and by open converse or by hidden counsels or by worse examples corrupt good manners, and either take away from them the narrow way of religion utterly, or at the least break it off for a little. After seducers of this sort the most prudent Virgin wills not to be borne, but to discern wisely who [0244D] ought to be preferred to whom, lest, if she take Nicolas for Stephen and Judas for John, she be held like to them, or be twofold a daughter of hell. Which evil the Virgin knows to be wrought at the instigation of the malignant spirits, whom iniquity set and removed far from the seat of the heavenly ones, while they beheld not the divine excellence with an eye humble enough, but, affecting an unapproachable likeness, fell from heaven after the manner of lightning. Who, knowing that they shall never return thither whence they had fallen, but that men made of clay shall ascend by the working of grace and by merits, corrupted with malice, envy and are tormented with a wondrous grief, and with utmost straining do hurt to those to whom they behold this grace to be given; since therefore they have an untiring mind for envying, and, according to a certain heathen, a thousand arts of hurting are theirs, as much at midnight [0245A] as at midday they stretch out their nets, and either by an arrow in the darkness, or by a midday assault, they seize the incautious and the wretched [n: (Psal. XC)]. The arrow flying in the darkness, which strikes grievously while it is unknown, is the hidden suggestion whereby our mind is soothed, when, a kind of veil being spread over it, it promises itself either no wound or a venial one, and, as with a little wound, lets in a deadly poison to the wretched heart. But the midday assault is the open malice of the assailant, when the vehement shamelessness of the malignant one pours out all its strength, when it grievously casts us down from the throne of patience, of obedience, of continence, or perchance, when we resist, threatens and sets before us losses, perils and martyrdoms more evidently. But if perchance the malignant spirit find any man stronger, so that he fears not its terrible threats, [0245B] nor its keener onset, it lays aside its threats, is silent about perils, brings nothing in violently, but turns itself fraudulently to a certain show of religion: for perceiving that watchings, prayers, abstinence, fasting, the labour of the hands are pleasing to some, it does not resist but presses on, and exhorts them first to abide more strongly in these things; and, lest they be outstripped in them, to guard themselves the more anxiously each against the other; and then, not content with the due time, not to keep the measure regularly appointed. While therefore anyone, fervent in spirit, attempts to be no less than the rest, and does not hold back with the bridle of moderation the loosened horse of desire; while he forestalls the solemn vigils, that he may pray more devoutly or ruminate somewhat more sweetly out of the Scriptures; while he fasts and abstains, lest he should as it were burden his belly with meats that will more quickly pass away; [0245C] while, being still vigorous in body, he strains beyond the labour of the hands that is due; while for these things, or for the like of these, he stretches himself out with looser reins: there meet him on this side and on that the blasts of vainglory, the love of praise, a presumptuous self-esteem, contempt of others, rash judgment, a harsher and hurtful reproof. For condemning the rest, whom he beholds to keep a looser measure as though they were lukewarm, he now reckons himself, as being more strongly fervent, better than all men; and the more inconsiderately he burns for greater things, the more, hurt by the wind of pride, he withers the more wickedly and is the more foully emptied out. For him whom fervour drives headlong, a vanity brought in beneath receives, and a certain show introduced deceives his conscience, which, feigning a good thing by a false light, blunts and darkens his eyes, while he works the more subtly who transfigures himself into an angel of light. [0246A] By whose work this wretched man in no wise reckons himself deluded, but rather as flooded with a kind of ray of the midday sun, in which, while he attends only to the surface as to a conspicuous flower, he hopes for a surer fruit, and does not detect the flaw in the root. Seduced therefore by him, he now wanders after the flocks of the companions, while, as though working well, he is defrauded by the craft of the malignant spirits, whom in some sort he finds to be Christ's companions and fellows, while he reckons that he pleases Christ, and is nevertheless found to please them. After companions of this sort the more prudent Virgin wills not to stray, nor to be defrauded by their midday show of good, but to detect their cunning with a keen-sighted eye, and to find Christ in his own light and in a midday that does not deceive. I will, she says, to find thy light, a true light, [0246B] useful and serene, lest, deceived by error, I run after another's light; lest the falling Lucifer falsely take to himself the likeness of Michael, lest Satan offer himself to me in the form and appearance of Gabriel. I will, she says, not to be seduced by the midday assault and demon, not to be led away by their blandishments and deceiving pretence, who lie in calling themselves thy companions, who, rejoicing in the name of angels, enjoy not the angelic blessedness. *139* Lest therefore the aforesaid light and day of these men should flatter me guilefully, show in what man or in what angel a rest welcome to thee is had, which with thyself glows red and flames, not only in the day, but in the midday, being perfect, neither begun in the morning nor growing toward evening by a downward course.

[0246C] Hitherto the Bride, the Virgin, has spoken of him and to him whom she more tenderly loves, and has followed out her love and desire in continuous speech: now she takes up silence, yet not omitting speech altogether, but breaking off a little for the sake of hearing. And so let us too in this place take up silence and rest awhile, and at last set an end to this first book, since it also asks that a limit be set to its own length, and our weakness asks that the labour begun be now, at least for a little, laid aside. But to the setting forth of that which the Bridegroom vouchsafed to answer the Virgin, if the day shall have dawned, I will take care to turn back my resting pen; if that Holy Spirit shall vouchsafe to come and teach me in silence what may please him that I should speak rather than be silent.

## BOOK TWO.




## CHAPTER THE FIRST.

[0245D]

*If thou know not thyself, O fairest among women, go forth, and go thy way after the footsteps of the flocks.* After the Virgin's many words, wherein she showed the heats of her own mind, wherein she asked that the longed-for kiss be given her and the Bridegroom's chamber be shown her: not hardness, not contempt, nor at length any further bar of silence holds the Bridegroom, but, having diligently heard her vows and prayers, he gives an answer. [0246D] And assuredly the Virgin, who so anxiously wills to be taught where the Bridegroom lies down, he admonishes first that she neglect not to gaze upon herself the more studiously, that, turning to her own things, she be not ignorant of her own beauty, lest perchance, being unknown, it be discoloured by mould or by negligence. For not warily enough does he kindle himself to acquire the rest, who does not attend with the eye of worthy consideration to the things first acquired, and who heaps up with rash labour the riches he has coveted, while he [0247A] does not watch over with diligent care the things laid up long since. As the Poet describes, the hunter errs not a little and offends, who chases what flees and, spurning what is taken, leaves it behind; and the prophet Aggeus showed that he also is none the less to be reproved who put the wages he had gathered into a bag with holes [n: (Agg. I)]. Accordingly the Bridegroom sends the Virgin first to consider her own beauty, and does not permit her to give the things past over to oblivion: putting her in mind of this very thing, which he counsels her to remember, that she may the more easily be able to incline her ear to his admonitions. *O fair one,* he says, *among women.* That that Virgin whom the Son of God chose beforehand for himself from eternity for a mother, in whom, taking flesh at the fitting time, he gathered himself into narrower limbs, of whom he willed to be born, the hedge of her flesh not being broken [0247B] by a new manner of birth, whose son he was made, being before the birth and after the birth utterly uncorrupted in chastity: that that Virgin, I say, was beautiful among the rest, that is, before the rest of women — this I judge worthy to be believed, nor is a faith of this sort faulty. For neither is it credible that God, the Son of God, should have chosen a mother swarthy, one-eyed, marked with a scrofulous swelling, or hunchbacked: and not rather one beautiful with a snowy countenance, a rosy colour, pleasing eyes and a full body — so that she who was chosen before the rest of women for a worthier office should not only be uninfected with any foulness, but also, in bodily appearance, fairer than all and perfect. Although the fact that she is called fair among women befits not so much the grace of her countenance and the comeliness of her body, as her perfect manners and that admirable [0247C] holiness of hers, by which, full of grace by the angel's witness — which is nowhere attested of any other woman — she alone deserved to be made the mother of Christ alone. Regarding a beauty of this sort, the angel says: « Blessed art thou among women [n: (Luc. I)]. » For she herself is blessed among women, that is, in the midst of women, upon whom by Eve's desert a harsher curse is inflicted, to whom, as to her that first offended, they are by a wretched law conformed, and, being liable to sins, are deformed by their motherly likeness to her. Among whom, wretched and deformed, an ampler beauty was granted to this Virgin, who, having overpassed the old curse and the hereditary law, the Spirit overshadowing her, put far from herself every heat of malice and every stain of sin, and by the merits of innocence and by the beauty of her mind [0247D] set herself before all women. And to the increase of her beauty, rejoicing in the wholeness of her body, she is made fruitful in a new kind untried by all; and by an unspeakable birth the virgin brought forth such a son that no other bore, either before or afterward, one mightier or one equal. Accordingly so great and so incomparable a loftiness — what is it but the wondrous and eminent beauty of this Virgin, wherein she was not only not forestalled by the rest of women, but was herself found far fairer and more excellent among them all? To the considering of which the Bridegroom calls her back *140* and leads her again, and does not yet more fully bring her into the longed-for chamber, that she may first know with how great a grace she is adorned, and whence and whither she has come may be recalled by a mindful humility. Thou, he says, who hast now obtained a greater grace than all women, [0248A] and, remaining a virgin, art wondrously made the mother of God, while thou findest not what remains and dost not yet come to the thing longed for, attend more diligently to what has already been conferred upon thee by my gift. For since, greedy of things to come, thou dost not yet prevail to obtain them, if thou take care humbly to remember the grace already received, the perception of things present will more solidly confirm thy faith, and faith confirmed will await things to come both the more sweetly and the more securely. But if thou set aside and know not the things which thou already provest as though present, and, while thou graspest at things untried, art found neglectful of the things proved: *Go forth* — which indeed I say to thee neither counselling nor commanding, but striking fear with threats, and, foreknowing what is to come, foretelling these things. Go forth, he says, that is, thou shalt go forth, and shalt deserve to be flung back from the secret place, thou shalt be made far [0248B] from the sanctuary into which thou askest to enter, thou shalt be driven from that very welcome chamber which thou willest to be shown thee, and thou shalt seem to go forth when thou art not permitted to go in. So indeed they are said to be blotted out of the book of the living who deserve not to be written with the just in the eternal volume; and by common speech we say that these things are taken away from us which, being hoped or longed for, we know are at last not conferred upon us. And so the Virgin also will complain that she goes forth outside, when by the desert of her ignorance she shall suffer repulse from the entrance, when, forgetful of her own beauty, she shall appear foul and discoloured, when out of the remembrance of things present she shall not have a sure confidence of things to come. But if, O Virgin, thou shalt mindfully consider that thou hast the pledge and earnest of the Spirit, which none of the elect deserved to obtain in that manner at all; thou shalt assuredly know that whatsoever [0248C] thou worthily askest is not taken away, nor is the just desire of her that is aflame defrauded, but deferred. For thou who hast received so many and so great things above all women, who without a father didst conceive a Son by the working of the Holy Spirit, who, according to Gabriel, didst find a wondrous and unspeakable grace with God, while thou didst bear him whom thou hadst conceived without coupling and without groaning — what dost thou henceforth by right reckon to be denied thee, if only the time shall come when it shall be worthy to be given? He therefore who has conferred so much, from him await what remains; and if, as for the most part appears, he shall make a delay to thy longing mind, await it again; and lest perchance the delay weigh upon thee, remember what thou hast already received, and by the memory of the things received strengthen thyself unto faith and patience. For in that which thou already holdest thou hast surpassed all the beauty of women, [0248D] and with the fair face of thy mind thou hast gone before all the daughters of Eve; and if thou shalt know this, and shalt render worthy thanks to the giver, then, sighing after what remains, thou wilt not give an undue murmur to him that defers. For to this end he defers, that the desire deferred may groan more fervently and more constantly, not that, faith being shaken, it may faint away through impatience; that in the time of delay thou mayest cultivate and adorn thy fair face the more amply, and not more negligently discolour it with the dust of forgetfulness and with a degenerate ignorance. *If therefore thou know not thyself,* go forth from my company, from my bosom, from me, from the very face at last of him whom thou hast loved: *And go thy way after the footsteps of the flocks,* which a little before thou didst dread. *Go forth,* he says, *and go thy way.* For whoever has gone forth from the sanctuary which he ought to have entered, going on to worse, is now not permitted [0249A] to stand, but to go away; and because he feared not to forget himself and the counsel of the one admonishing him, he is compelled to journey far from himself and farther from the one admonishing. And he goes away after the footsteps of the flocks who follows their depravity going before him, who, being lovers of errors and of sects, know not the unity of the faith; or who, living after the manner of beasts, entice and deceive those who follow them, and grievously persecute with their own depraved manners those whom they go before.



## CHAPTER II.

*And feed thy kids beside the tents of the shepherds.* When anyone has gone forth and gone away, having his understanding already darkened, he is said to feed kids, while he brings depraved affections through to their effect, while he cherishes and furthers inconstancy of mind, wantonness of manners, bodily uncleanness, and loves to lead an animal [0249B] life. He perhaps feeds lambs who, strengthened by the spirit of pitying grace, has harmless acts, clean and simple thoughts, whose fruit and whose whiteness that highest Shepherd approves and loves, and to the feeding of them he admonishes his lover: « If thou lovest me, he says, feed my lambs [n: (Joan. XXI)]. » [var: Vulg. John 21:15 *Simon Ioannis, diligis me plus his? … Pasce agnos meos* — a question in the received text, printed here as a condition; Migne gives the interrogative form of the same verse at 0254B] But he feeds kids who, with corrupted mind, with seduced spirit, with lost will, does evil things, rejoices in malice, is weighed down by equity; and follows after those things which the just judge judges to be set on the left hand [n: (Matth. XXV)], that upon them the avenging angel with his ministers may harshly rage. Kids of this sort he is said to feed, not in the tents of the shepherds, from whose fellowship he is barred by his own urgent malice, whom their life does not entice, whose works do not delight but offend him, nor [0249C] does he love to imitate what they set forth in doctrine and in manners. And because he is not found to dwell in the tents of the shepherds, in which the voice of exultation and of salvation alike is heard, he at least remains near, nor are pastures found farther off, while *141* he holds the name of Christ, no other baptism, the sacraments in common. And so, shrinking from virtue, he glories in the show of piety, and, not holding the reality, is visibly overshadowed by the sacrament of faith; and on this account he is recorded to feed, not within, but beside the tents of the shepherds, because, although he be in some sort without, yet the appearance of the thing is neighbour to it. Shepherds are all the perfect, who follow out the right faith not so much in name as in works, who, washed once in the laver of regeneration, [0249D] are often washed again with devout tears, who devoutly celebrate the sacraments of the Church unto their own salvation, since they obtain not so much the outward form of them as the power. In which tents they correct their own depravities into straightness, they subject their own wills to the divine good pleasure; and with discreet governance they rule their affections as they do their works, and day by day pass on to ampler advances. But in these men do not dwell, though they draw somewhat near to them, they who destroy the faith by their works, while they do not forsake the sacraments of the faith, who, not having the power, are adorned with its outward title; and they imitate as shepherds those whom they shall have seen to be good, not in the reality, but in name. But perhaps to some it will seem hard and austere that the Bridegroom addresses the Virgin Mother thus, that to her who has spoken beforehand of sweet things and loves him tenderly he thus threatens at the very beginning [0250A] of his answer; since it is certain that after the aforesaid kiss she does not thus go forth from him or go away, and accordingly that things so heavy and so superfluous do not befit one that kisses or loves. For although it can more fittingly be assigned to any soul, or even to the Church, to whom, when she offends, Christ judges it useful now to promise and now to threaten: yet the beauty of this one is believed to be especially the more constant, in whom God is made man, and the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily. I judge it worthy therefore that we should see a little more attentively how the Bridegroom loves to answer like for like to the Virgin who has spoken beforehand in the language of love; and how, having already perceived beforehand her prayers, her vows, her untiring desire, he, returning praises for praises, has not dissented from her desire.



## CHAPTER III.

[0250B]

*If thou know not thyself, O fair one among women, go forth and go thy way after the footsteps of the flocks.* [var: Vulg. Cant 1:7 *o pulcherrima inter mulieres*, superlative, "O fairest among women" — the same head lemma is printed *pulcherrima* at 0245D] The Bridegroom, not willing to promote the Virgin by degrees to advances, teaches her how she may deserve to obtain the grace of advancing: namely, if the things she has so obtained she so lay up with herself, as in a hidden place, that the guileful enemy may not lay his pitchy hand upon them even for a little. For he often lays a hurtful touch upon the better goods of a greater grace of holiness, when he pours over them a ruin, the wicked mist of a darkening vanity; when either with the heavy blast of pride he overwhelms and hardens a mind endowed with gifts, or at the least with a light breeze he somewhat darkens the beauty of a tender face. For it is difficult for any Virgin to behold herself endowed with the better gifts, and either not to be shaken by the battering-ram of proud [0250C] vanity, or not to be moved by a blast however slight: to feel herself excellent in form and praiseworthy in countenance, and never with a bent mind to consent to one that praises her the more often. Whence it is necessary that she who wills not to be touched by pride should not set a mirror before herself, lest, when she has seen herself fair, she should perhaps set herself before the rest: nay rather, that she may not consent even for a little to the flattering deceiver, she should offer her face, unknown to herself, to be known by her chaste lover only. And so the chaste lover, willing that the Virgin should please none but himself, wills that she should not have knowledge of her own face; he wills that the Virgin should not know herself, should not marvel at her own beauty, lest, marvelling or praising, she should glory in herself rather than in the Lord. That angel would have been held happy, if [0250D] in some sort he had not known himself, when in the delights of paradise he outstripped Lucifer in splendour; happy, I say, if he had not been proud of the things he had received, and, being founded by God, had not thought himself God's equal. Far better, far more happily, Abraham knew not himself, when, as though not knowing himself, he sought divine converse, when, forgetful that he was held great in merits and more illustrious in life, by a prudent counsel he confessed himself to be nothing but dust and ashes. « I will speak, he says, to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes [n: (Gen. XVIII)]. » Happy also king David, who, because he wills not to know the letter of the law which he had learned, setting little by his own, deserves to enter into the power of the Lord; and, not establishing his own, serves God's justice with bowed neck, and, forgetful of his own things, remembers only the things that are the Lord's. [0251A] « Because I have not known letters, he says, I will enter into the powers of the Lord; O Lord, I will be mindful of thy justice only [n: (Psal. LXX)]. » On the contrary, that wretched Nabuchodonosor, who put not the knowledge of himself away from himself, who knew himself rich, most powerful, endowed with various successes, who attended more to himself commanding than to him through whom kings command, and, beholding himself great, set little by the author of his own greatness. « Is not this, he says, the great Babylon, which I have built in the strength of my might, and in the glory of my beauty? » [n: (Dan. IV.)] But if anyone shall object that some are found to have gone over their own illustrious works, in which nevertheless Scripture does not judge that they were reprehensible: let him attend to the time, let him discern the cause *142* and in whom this is found to be done; and let him know when [0251B] and why it is found to be as lawful as it is necessary. For when anyone perceives that he is the more grievously constrained to suffer or to do evils, if he wills to be plucked out of them by prudent counsel, as feet out of a snare, he can, nay he ought, lovingly to recount the goods which he has already obtained, that by the memory of better things he may be able to remove the evils that press upon him. Hence it is that Job, when he was shaken with so great a weight of evils and with their number at once, and was urged by his wife's insistence to curse God at last, calls back to memory and goes over the goods which he had already received; and the heap of evils did not wrap him, who was mindful of good things, in the stains of impatience. « The heart of the widow, he says, I comforted, and I was clad with justice: and I clothed myself with it as with a garment. I was an eye to the blind, and a foot to the lame; I was the father of the poor. And when I sat [0251C] as a king with his army standing about him, yet I was a comforter of them that mourned [n: (Job XXIX)]. But now the younger in time deride me [n: (Job. XXX)]. » And above: « If we have received good things at the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evils? » [n: (Job. II.)] [var: Vulg. Job 2:10 *si bona suscepimus de manu Dei, mala quare non suscipiamus?* — *Dei* becomes *Domini*, and "receive" becomes "endure"] The good man did not think his own good things worthy to be pressed down in silence, when so great a manifoldness of evils straitened him on every side, so that the sweet remembrance of good things might render light the burden of the pressure that lay upon him — as long afterward the Scripture of a certain Wise Man admonished: « In the day of evils, he says, be not unmindful of good things [n: (Eccli. XI)]. » To this end avails, as I judge, that saying which the letters of the Gentiles so favourably extolled, and, as worthy of memory, handed on in writing to posterity, which [0251D] some assert that one of the seven wise men of Greece uttered, while others rather affirm that Apollo answered it in an elegant oracle: « Know, he says, thyself, O man. » Because the wise men of the world knew that man consists of a rational soul and a body, of which they asserted that he has the one in common with the gods and the other in common with the beasts, those of them whose doctrine was sounder preferred reason to the body, and by that judgment, detracting from the beasts, they deferred (as was more fitting) to the gods. And so they willed that man should be ruled by reason going before, and that the bestial flesh should be subjected to the rational spirit; and, the spirit being carried up, that man should be taken away from among the beasts, and, if not in place, at least in merit, be transferred into the fellowship of the gods. [0252A] For to this end, and on this account, they reckoned man to have been made, and that this difference lies naturally between man and beast: that the beast freely gapes after earthly things, while man is bidden to aspire to heavenly things — which the uplifted face given to man also seems to indicate. Of this thing Apollo wills that man should prudently be mindful: to know whence he comes, and whither by reason's desert he ought to journey; to forget what is beneath and behind him, as though given over to sleep; to wake up, by the nimbleness of his powers, to that which is before. But because very many turn aside and stray from the path of reason, who after the manner of beasts are plunged in the filth of earthly action, who entangle and wrap their hands in grievous offences, who cast their feet into voluntary sins and do not absolve themselves from the crimes laid against them, of whom scarcely any is found who lives according to man, [0252B] nay, according to the philosopher, is found to live as a swine or an ass: therefore the seer cries out, does not permit the tripod to be silent, the oracle sounds, a censorial voice sends forth its doctrine: Great Apollo thunders, and, the lightning being loosed, wills to be feared; he wills that horse and mule, swine and ass be frightened away from error and ignorance; he wills that all the better sort be admonished to honest knowledge, and that his own hearers be advanced to the understanding of reason's excellence. « Know, he says, thyself, O man. » Of which sentence Paul was not unaware, when he was constrained to suffer grievous things, when, tenderly compassionating the weakness and the scandal of the Corinthians, he was set afire, lest he should be weighed down more than is just with another's load, or perhaps that he might seem worthier to be heard by them that were weighed down: he has recourse to knowledge, professes that he knows himself a man — one who serves not [0252C] the flesh, but who glories to be grafted into heaven. « I know, he says, a man in Christ caught up even to the third heaven; and I know such a man, whether in the body or out of the body, I know not, God knoweth, that he was caught up into paradise, and heard secret words which it is not lawful for a man to utter [n: (II Cor. XII)]. » And he added: « For such a one will I glory [n: (ibid.)]. » Do you see that Paul knows himself to be a man lifted up to the third heaven, to visit paradise, and to glory for so great a grace? To this end, namely, that the Corinthians should not defer more to false apostles, and prefer guileful teachers to his doctrine and his merits. Otherwise, if this cause or necessity, or one like to it, had not been, which forced a wise man to this as it were unwisdom, [0252D] assuredly he would have remembered that saying of the Gospel spoken to his fellow-apostles, and would have held it, as worthy of memory, in speech as in conscience: « When you shall have done all good things, say that we are unprofitable servants [n: (Luc. XVII)]. » [var: Vulg. Luke 17:10 *cum feceritis omnia quae praecepta sunt vobis*, "all things that are commanded you" — Philip's gloss immediately below expounds *omnia bona*] In which saying it is given to be understood that no one is proved to do all good things, unless the saying of this be added to the rest of his good things: and he does not colour the heap of his good things with a surface worthy enough, who is not ignorant of it for the sake of avoiding vanity. That therefore you may know the Bride to be perfectly holy and humble, the Bridegroom teaches that this ignorance is in her, who, while she hastens to the rest which the son does not yet give but promises, does not commit the things which she already obtains to a boastful [0253A] memory. *If thou know not,* he says, *thyself, O fair one.* For in that he says Si, it is not a dubitative but an affirmative conjunction; as that poet: « Ye gods, if there be any piety in heaven. » And so the Bridegroom says: *If thou know not thyself, O fair one* — which indeed is difficult, but yet *143* is a man — *Go forth.* But go forth whence and whither, save from thy contemplation to thy work? Go forth from the consideration of thy own beauty to the forming of the beauty of others; as though neglectful of thyself, be anxious for very many: form the disciples, teach the apostles the things which thou hast more perfectly known of me; stoop to John, whom as a son thou, a mother, hast received. *Go forth,* I say, *and go thy way after the footsteps of the flocks.* They who preside over flocks walk after their footsteps, and are known to have the care of them before [0253B] their eyes; lest any should stray, lest any should sit down weary, they lead their watchful eyes about, they rejoice with the healthier, and every weak one they carry back upon their shoulders or lead home. It is therefore a mark of power to preside over flocks, and the apostles are admonished to sit beside the Virgin as she presides, that the Virgin may command them, and as a mother may bear the care of all, and that they may hear their mother, as the Gospel affirms. « Woman, he says, behold thy son [n: (Joan. XIX)]; » and to the disciple: « Behold thy mother [n: (ibid.)]. » For when the care of John is delegated to the Virgin Mother, the care of the rest is not, as I judge, banished from her; but what is more specially assigned to one for the sake of a certain mystery is designated as generally necessary for all. For neither does John alone receive Mary and venerate her whom he has received, nor does the Virgin [0253C] embrace John alone with the affection of a devout care, but, loving all, she is zealous to show herself useful to all, to show herself pre-eminent in doctrine and imitable by all. « All, he says, were with one mind continuing in prayer with Mary the mother of Jesus [n: (Act. I)]. » [var: Vulg. Acts 1:14 *hi omnes erant perseverantes unanimiter in oratione cum mulieribus, et Maria matre Iesu, et fratribus eius* — "with the women" and "and his brethren" are absent] And so the Virgin is admonished to go away after their footsteps, that she may search out their goings with a diligent eye, that she may investigate the more anxiously what they do, whither they tend, by what way they pass; that she may advance what is worthy of praise, and may not pass over the wanderer either, but chastise him. The flocks are the apostles, and they who are gathered to them by faith and by works, who, imbued with the evangelical sacraments, are separated from the error of the ignorant, who, venerating the Virgin and believing her word, sighing after the eternal pasture, hold in contempt the things that are of the world. [0253D] To whom it is said through Ezechiel: « And you, my flocks, saith the Lord [n: (Ezech. XXXIV)]. » Whom perhaps he therefore willed to call flocks in the plural number, because the apostles, being bidden to preach the word of the Gospel to the nations that should believe, being divided one from another under the Spirit's leading, chose diverse parts of the world, in which by their zeal in preaching they gathered many flocks and assemblies of men, and many churches. Who, although they are diverse in place, in time, and in the merit of their virtues, yet, while they all come to the catholic faith and the evangelical doctrine, many flocks are brought back into one, and very many into one Church: and all are united in the undivided sacrament of faith and of baptism.



## CHAPTER IV.

*And feed thy kids beside the tents of the shepherds.* He calls the apostles kids, who, although it is not denied that by the Virgin's word and [0254A] example they advance to a great holiness, yet, while they live a mortal life and are held in the prison-house of the flesh, according to the Bridegroom's counsel confess themselves unprofitable servants, and, being ignorant of their own justice, confess their sins with a humble voice [n: (Luc. XVII)]. One of whom: « If we shall say, he says, that we have no sin, we seduce ourselves, and the truth is not in us [n: (I Joan. I)]. » And another: « In many things, he says, we all offend [n: (Jac. III)]. » Those therefore whom the whiteness of conscience, the beauty of innocence, the simplicity of manners, the eminent holiness of merits render lambs, the same the confession of sin with fear makes kids, while as yet a man knows not whether he be worthy of hatred or of love. Accordingly, when any just men are called lambs, and innocence merits their praises, [0254B] which are not held worthy to be commended save by Christ's gift: he says « my », as he pointed out long afterward to Peter, when to him that loved he assigned the care of them that love. « Simon son of John, lovest thou me? feed my lambs [n: (Joan. XXI)]. » But when he wills them, by the desert of sin, to be reckoned by the name of kids — whom James and John assert are not held to be without sin — he says « thy », that he may lay upon the Virgin an ampler care of them, whereby she may keep watch over the healing of them, and the Virgin may carry them forward to a better state. As it was said to Moses: « Go down, thy people hath sinned [n: (Exod. XXXII)]. » Or because, as the lambs by the Gospel's testimony obtain the right hand, so the kids are known to be set at the Bridegroom's left [n: (Matth. XXV)]: by the kids he wills, not unfittingly, all the Virgin's acts to be signified, that is, whatever [0254C] in this life the Virgin is bidden to work in time. For the chastising of herself, care for others, preaching or doctrine, sweats and colds, watchings, fasting, discipline are indeed Christ's gifts, but they seem to pertain to his left hand, because, not fixed with a steadfast step, they quickly deserve to obtain an end. Yet if they be fed, they also make an increase; not as it is in Osee: « Foolish Ephraim feedeth the wind [n: (Ose. XII)], » [var: Vulg. Hos 12:1 *Ephraim pascit ventum*, with no *stultus*, "foolish"] but let the Bride take care to feed beside the tents of the shepherds, that is, that she conform herself to the precepts of the Scriptures and to their authors. The shepherds are Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Moses and David, the patriarchs and the prophets, of whom some are found to have laboured, in the letter, in the feeding of flocks, and all of them to have kept watch far more anxiously in ruling and correcting [0254D] manners. And *144* perhaps such shepherds therefore choose to dwell in tents, because they teach and love to hasten from virtue to virtue; and nothing present suffices them as they stretch toward a greater advance, until, that which is in part being done away, they come at last to the perfect. Beside whose tents, and according to whose doctrine and example, the Virgin is bidden to rule and direct her own acts, that she may follow the rule of the Scriptures, which the long series of the prophets long ago set forth as a thing to be known and held. For although the Virgin Mother by a certain special grace already goes before those same authors, yet in time their authority goes before her, nor is it an injury if she be invited to their form and commendable doctrine, that [sic: *vidilicet*] she may follow by [0255A] example those whom she now seems to excel in merits. But whence the Virgin has this, that she may prevail to do what she is admonished, that, not knowing herself, she may go forth, and, going away, may rejoice to feed the kids — this the Bridegroom shows her, that she may glory in the Lord alone, and, knowing not her own face, may marvel at his face alone. Therefore he adds: *To my cavalry,* etc.

## CHAPTER V.

*To my cavalry in the chariots of Pharaoh have I likened thee, my friend.* He calls her friend, whose mind accords utterly with what it hears, whose converse now disagrees from the commandments not even a little, who is so zealous to do and to accomplish all things that are commanded, that, loving him who commanded, she may deserve to be loved by him. As it is written in the Gospel: « You are my friends, if you do [0255B] the things that I command you [n: (Joan. XV)]. » Further, that she might become a friend, he likened her to his own cavalry in the chariots of Pharaoh. He alludes to a thing done, he touches the history, which describes that the children of Israel passed over the depths of the sea with a dry footprint, but that the chariots of Pharaoh and his whole army utterly perished. But in what respect the Virgin Mother is held like to this people, it is fitting to see; for a likeness of this sort seems not to have a fitness worthy enough, especially since in that passage the people of Israel is not found to have had horses, and there was no cavalry, seeing that it is agreed that horses and horsemen were lacking to it. For of Pharaoh it is written: « The horse and the rider he hath cast into the sea [n: (Exod. XV)], » [var: Vulg. Exod 15:1 *equum et ascensorem deiecit in mare*, "he hath thrown down"; the verb printed here is that of Exod 15:4, quoted two lines below] and below: « Pharaoh's chariots and his army [0255C] he hath cast into the sea [n: (ibid.)]. » But when the children of Israel passed over, no mention is made of horses or of chariots, nor do they escape Pharaoh's threats by such a defence, lest anyone should reckon that what the hand of God alone willed wondrously to work was worthily to be assigned to horses or to chariots. Finally the sea, though perhaps by a ship, yet is not crossed by a horse or by a rolling wheel; and in that passage the people experienced neither a ship nor a vehicle, but, the waves being divided and standing on this side and on that after the manner of a wall, they pass over with dry foot, not about to feel the onset of the Egyptians any more. And so for no other cause is it rightly called a cavalry, save that God sat upon it spiritually, and as ruler mercifully presided over the subject people; and that people was the chariot, or the four-horse car, of him that presided, and he willed to be the leader and charioteer of the car [0255D] that bore him beneath. To whom Moses says: « Thou hast been a leader, he says, in thy mercy to the people which thou hast redeemed [n: (Exod. XV)]. » And Habacuc: « Thou who ridest upon thy horses, and thy chariots are salvation [n: (Habac. III)]. » Such a cavalry, he says, as I made my own in the chariots of Pharaoh, that is, above all the chariots of Pharaoh, and made over to my own service, when I set it free, being led out of Egypt, from among the hands of its pursuers: so by a deep mystery I bound thee to a certain wondrous ministry, when I blessed thee, my chosen mother and Bride, among women, that is, above all women. For all the motions, all the onsets which the flesh suggests, which the enervated mind heaps up, all the crowds of vices which Egypt, ruinously depraved, sends forth and sends in, I drowned and quenched with the flood of the water that bore them down, and I wiped away thy stains by the benefit of the grace [0256A] that washed them clean. And, the enemies being quenched, thee, assigned the more freely to my service, made over with a willing neck to a light and sweet yoke, I, a mighty horseman, a skilled charioteer, lead through the midst of the sea, and, the waves being removed on this side and on that, I bring thee through to the solid land of the living. There stands on the right hand and on the left the overhanging height of the waters, which an invisible strength holds fixed after the manner of a wall; they are astounded and marvel that they are held by a new and unwonted kind of thing, that a way is given to the four-horse car, and that the slipping waves are not feared. For so, turning and dwelling in the midst of sinners, attending on this side to the foolishness of the Gentiles, on that to the scandals of the Jews [n: (I Cor. I)], thou drawest upon thyself from their malice no fault, no sin; thou art not broken by reproaches, thou dost not forsake the way shown thee beforehand. And not only does the heap of the overhanging wave [0256B] not press or oppress thy head, but neither does a passing stream so much as touch the feet of thee that walkest; nay rather, with dry foot, with clean footprint, with unspotted life, thou passest by the way of this world, unassailed by any touch of the vices. But endowed with so great a gift, how art thou not a friend — thou whose converse in a world so unclean is so chaste, who wast made the keeper of my mind, the sharer of a spiritual secret, a true mother, knowing nothing of the marriage bed? But that in conceiving she knew not the marriage bed, nay rather that from that time and thenceforward no touch of Venus *145* hurt her virgin mind, the Bridegroom seems to intimate in the words that follow, whereby he willed the more evidently to commend her chastity.



## CHAPTER VI.

*Thy cheeks are beautiful as the turtledove's.* In the cheeks [0256C] it is agreed that the Virgin's beauty appears the more, in which a snowy colour is found to blush faintly beneath; nay, whiteness and redness seem to envy one another, while each strives to hold alone the surface of the cheeks. Or, if it please better — nay, because it does please — when whiteness pours itself over the whole face with a large bounty, and redness overspreads itself upon the cheeks with a thin sprinkling: they smile upon one another, and there comes to be a certain friendly fellowship of colours, while out of the snowy the rosy, and out of the rosy the snowy, is made the more pleasing. And so the cheeks are coloured with the Virgin's commendable comeliness, which are adorned by a grace in them not confounded but diffused; in which the ruddy colour, or the sanguine redness, is joined to whiteness, and the one does not disdain the other, but with a throat ever greedy is satisfied. The Virgin's whiteness [0256D] is the cleanness of her flesh and her virginal integrity, which no stain, no bodily corruption harms; which, being the more safely fortified, grows not foul at the robber's violent onset, being the more diligently shut in, grows not pale when the blast blows more harshly. But the redness which is becomingly coupled to the snowy colour is the fervour or the heat wherewith the inward mind rejoices to burn; which, since as in a furnace it can scarcely contain itself within, seems to appear without in works as upon the cheeks. For how greatly the Virgin burns inwardly with spiritual love, she cannot fully express without by bodily work; but out of the abundance which her inward conscience comprehends, a kind of ruddy spark shows itself without upon her face. By this redness and whiteness I judge the Virgin's cheeks to be called beautiful, whose beauty her lover [0257A] delights to gaze upon; and the beauty which, by the grace of humility, he wills to be unknown by the Virgin, as was said before, he himself, not grudging, loves to impart to her in fitting praises.

Nor is it to be thought that he brings any hurt to that beauty in that he makes mention of the turtledove among her praises, because the turtledove, though it be believed to be of no merit and of no holiness, yet affords a type of modesty and a pattern of a modest chastity. For having obtained one mate it knows no other thereafter, and keeping faith to that one alone it blushes to know another: and if perchance that one be lost, not even so does it wish to have another; it grieves as a widower, nor will it sit upon a green branch. How great a love, how great a faith, how great a desire of chastity, how holy and imitable an appearance of chaste honesty does it set forth, in that as one present so one absent it loves [0257B] singularly whom it has chosen, into whose fellowship it once brought itself back with faith for a go-between? To which turtledove can she better, can she more worthily be compared than that Virgin of virgins in whom God willed to be made flesh, when already she was caught up with her whole desire to love him singularly, so that, abhorring every man, she was troubled even at an angel's entering? And when her son was born, no concupiscence of man harmed the mother none the more, but the bearer clave to him she bore, the Bride to the Bridegroom, with a love not to be loosed, in such wise that no carnal onset should thereafter bring loss to her chaste spirit, nor should she thereafter feel any blandishment of another love; cleaving to heaven alone, she knew not the frail pavement, and so loved the flesh in her son as the sacrament in the Bridegroom. To the Bridegroom indeed with firm faith [0257C] she loves to cleave, and to show herself to him as a chaste virgin to her one husband, in whose bodily presence for some time she rejoices, and in whose spiritual love and commerce she is proclaimed blessed. « Blessed art thou that hast believed, » says Elisabeth [n: (Luc. I)]! But when he was as it were lost — that is, when, dying and rising again, he disdained human fellowship, and returned thither whence he had come, that is, to the Father's right hand — she, abhorring the public gaze, with chaste heart and modest face, remains a widow, groaning after the manner of the turtledove. And because she had not the Bridegroom, whose presence had been green and delightful, keeping faith to him absent she now sat upon no wood but a dry one; nor did another Bridegroom preside over her with a like privilege, though another perhaps stood by her as a son by the grace of ministering. Wherefore, as I judge, [0257D] when Christ, set upon the cross, commended his mother the Virgin to John who stood by, and carefully made over the disciple to her service, he expressly did not say: Woman, behold thy bridegroom; and to the disciple: behold thy bride, but he said: « Woman, behold thy son; and to the disciple: behold thy mother [n: (Joan. XIX)]. » For in many sons a mother's fruitfulness, with wedded faith unharmed, is commended, but in many bridegrooms chastity is accused of intemperance: and therefore, that the Virgin might be kept for one husband even in his absence, no other Bridegroom, but another son, stood by her in the present. Finally the other John, greater than whom there hath not risen among them that are born of women, understood this mystery, as he plainly shows to all; who, though he might be believed to be the Christ, who was the Virgin's own Bridegroom, yet the more evidently declares that he is not the Christ, is not [0258A] the Bridegroom. « You yourselves, he says, bear me witness, that I said, I am not the Christ. He that hath the Bride is the Bridegroom. But the friend of the Bridegroom, who standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth with joy because of the Bridegroom's voice [n: (Joan. III)]. » You see that John, loving *146* to measure himself with a worthy eye of consideration, while others lied concerning him, himself prudently chose not to lie; and knowing his own bounds, does not assert himself to be the Bridegroom but the friend, lest by usurping a falsehood he should rather make himself an enemy. And so to the Virgin there is no Bridegroom but Christ, who in her womb celebrated wondrous and incomparable nuptials, and made her fruitful not by male coition but by the divine Spirit, by whose presence the same Virgin ever grows green, and at his greenness the loving virgin grows glad. [0258B] For so long as the bridegroom is with her, she cannot but rejoice, in whom she sees that her own flesh has no stain of flesh; who in the bridal chamber of her womb was made one flesh with her, in a union having indeed no vice, but opportune for the salvation of all. And because such, so spiritual a commerce felt nothing contrary in the joining, assuredly it brought no vice into what was conceived; and Christ was born not, like the rest, a son of wrath also by nature, but he lived with clean flesh, to die by an impulse not necessary but voluntary. Finally, about to die: « If in the green wood, he says, they do these things, what shall be done in the dry? » [n: (Luc. XXIII.)] The Bridegroom calls himself the green wood, whose root in the conceiving is not gnawed by a hidden little worm, whose stem, that is, his life, is not held by rottenness, however slight; the spreading of his words [0258C] as of branches withers not at a hurtful blast, but, to conclude briefly, the whole substance grows green with an inborn vigour. To whom that better applies which Paul says: « And if the root be holy, so are the branches [n: (Rom. XIII)]. » Rightly then is any other man called dry wood, whose conceiving is not sufficiently purified, and whose conversation is assailed by vices; who of himself or by himself germinates not, is not made fruitful with a just germ, unless, by the Bridegroom's bounty, the dew of divine grace be poured upon him from above. Therefore the Virgin, so long as the Bridegroom is with her, rejoices in green wood, but when he is absent she reckons every wood dry; nor does she find another wherein the turtledove's foot may rest even a little, which withers not at the touch, whether original or actual, of vices. [0258D] Showing therefore that she grieves for the Bridegroom's absence, while she neither has him whom she loves nor wishes to have another in a like place, she sits in the dry, and groaning she shows herself a widow, and both by her posture and by her groaning represents the form of the turtledove. Nor is it to be thought that from this her beauty is deprived of its grace, in that a widow's sadness compels her to sit and to groan, because as worthily in the Bridegroom's presence the Bride's face grows glad, so it is not foreign to grace if in his absence it wastes away. And so he rightly commended the Virgin's cheeks as beautiful like the turtledove's, to whom, both present and absent, the Virgin kept the faith she owed, who, knowing him alone to be a man endowed with a deity united to him, gave herself wholly and devoutly to him with modest chastity. To whom the Bridegroom subjoins:



## CHAPTER VII.

[0259A]

*Thy neck, as necklaces.* The Bridegroom, praising the Virgin, uses comparisons unheard of, and, as the first face of them pretends, not sufficiently choice for expressing the likeness, since neither cheeks seem to suit a turtledove nor a neck a necklace, unless a careful reader take pains to find the hidden fitness. A band is knotted to the neck, that he who has been bound may be held, and, being held, may be led away hence thither, thence elsewhere, otherwise, at the pleasure of him that holds him; and if the leader-away be malevolent, he that is led away is wretchedly taken captive, and, his liberty lost, is made bondsman to the rule of the stronger. Whereby the pitying Lord once perceived a certain Virgin pressed and oppressed, who, deceived and enticed, at the first despised not fraudulent blandishments; [0259B] but afterwards, offering her neck to the bands, she took no care that she was led to ignominy, and, forgetting her inborn liberty, turned herself aside to a hurtful servitude. Seeing her and pitying her, the Lord invites her back to that which was lost, warns her not to suffer herself to be held any longer by another band, and, that she who with the loose bar of shamefastness let the corrupter in may be loosed from his band, bids her hear a chaste and saving monitor. « Loose, he says, the bands of thy neck, O captive daughter of Sion [n: (Isa. LII)]. » Thou, he says, who once wast worthily called daughter of Sion, when, seeing God with the mind, thou wast seen of him with a kindly return; from thy neck, whereon no precious stone, no gold now glitters, no necklace, but a corrupt mind, the heat of the flesh, a youthful desire has defiled it; loose, I pray, the bands, that what is foul, prostituted to an unpermitted baseness, [0259C] may be wiped clean with a strong hand and be restored, set free, to honesty. With that filth the neck of this our Virgin, whom we have in hand, was not fouled, nor grew hard with a stubborn neck, with an untamed heart; but the Bridegroom rubbed it clean with a soothing voice and a soft hand, and upon it, rubbed clean and made smooth, laid a light burden and a sweet yoke. Whereof also you have received a commandment: « Take up my yoke upon you, and learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart [n: (Matth. XI)]. » The Virgin's neck therefore is her meek humility, a humble meekness accustomed to the laws of obedience; whose form or example the Bridegroom himself willed to afford, when, obedient to the Father, God willed to appear as man in a virgin's womb. Whose obedience the Virgin understood to be worthy enough and to be imitated, and, a lover of this pattern, [0259D] lifted not up her neck swellingly, but hearing with the hearing she bore the yoke — not that which Adam laid heavy upon his sons, but that which, being light and sweet, more graciously eased the neck of her that bore it. *147* For as, according to the heathen, that appearance is no honour but a burden which will hurt the wearer, so on the other side that appearance is no burden but an honour which will adorn; and assuredly Christ's yoke burdens not him that loves it, but honours him, dishonours not the neck of him that obeys, but adorns it. How great a comeliness of mind seems to you to shine out in the Virgin's words, how great necklaces — not dewlaps — to hang from her neck; who, at the angel's word whereby she is forewarned that she shall bear God, confesses herself not a noblewoman of royal stock but a lowly handmaid? Nor indeed was it new and sudden for her to obey [0260A] the divine warnings, who for very many days before had been accustomed to serve God; so that with faithful purpose she vowed herself to remain a Virgin also, for which nevertheless she had neither a commandment in the Scriptures nor a pattern among her forerunners. By the teaching of his Spirit alone, who graciously presided within, she was disposing to keep her chastity unviolated; and she deserved not to be cheated of her hope and desire, nay — what is greater and more wonderful — to be made fruitful, such a purpose abiding. But by a new kind she both remained Virgin and was fruitful, whereas before and after neither has she who was Virgin been fruitful, nor has she who was fruitful remained Virgin: of so great a prerogative she willed to speak or to think nothing lofty, nothing unseemly, nor to dissent from him whom she knew as a Master meek and humble of heart. And so no man so bore the light burden and the sweet yoke, [0260B] no other so conformed himself to the obedient Bridegroom, as she who furnished him with the garment of her own flesh, whose obedient neck seems, to them that consider worthily, an ornament.

Finally it is she who is found so to be beneath Christ the head, that there is no doubt she is above the rest of the body; and she seems to hold the middle place between the head and the body, nor can the Bridegroom's sons reach to the Bridegroom save with the Mother between. When she, the Bride, is present to us, it is good to cleave to him, but when she is absent the members cannot cohere with the head; to us set far below, the Son of God has come down through her, to whom our infirmity ascends not save through her. She first, she more blessed, receives a great gift, whereby many and diverse are made as it were one; whereby the two [0260C] walls have been united by one faith, by one baptism, and, running together to Christ, have leaned upon him personally. Finally she commends us to the Bridegroom and Son by her intercession between, invites us to pray, admonishes him to attend; the Bridegroom's mother and handmaid, the empress of us all, she joins the disjoined, holds fast the joined, a mighty and effectual mediatrix. For seeing us dry, and that we have no wine at the wedding, and knowing that without wine the wedding pleases not worthily enough; pitying them that were to perish of thirst, she hastens anxiously to come before them, and confidently to approach the Son for the failing of the wine. The Mother of Jesus, he says, saith to him: « They have no wine [n: (Joan. II)]. » And perceiving that the humble intercession of a loving prayer is not made void, but comes to profit for us, nay for all that sat at meat, she says to the servants: [0260D] « Whatsoever he shall say to you, do *(ibid)*. » And when they, according to the Virgin's word, inclined their ear to the command, the waterpots are filled with water, and clarified wine is rendered: by a thing worthy of a miracle our tastelessness is turned into savour, torpid cold into fire, a more negligent contempt into love. A good neck, a good intercession, a good mediatrix at last, who joins those whom Eve, the hurtful separatrix, had disjoined; who invites the Son to bounty and us to obedience, and brings it about that we omit not to render service, nor he to confer benefit. Nor is it beside the point that the Bridegroom praises that same neck as necklaces, which bear the ensigns of matronly wealth and of honourable chastity; which, made of gold and stones with learned art, [0261A] with a preeminent appearance adorn the neck, cover the breast, and close the double hem of the garment. You know that by gold understanding and wisdom are for the most part signified, and by stones virtues and works are figured; and the craftsman sets the stones in the gold and orders them diligently, when he works strong things and disposes his works wisely. And rightly did the Bridegroom mark out the Virgin's neck by the comparison of necklaces, because the humble meekness wherewith the Virgin obeyed to bear the yoke the more sweetly the longer she bore it, or the prerogative of merit whereby, being nearer to the head, she went before the remaining members of the body, whereby she interceded with the Bridegroom as an effectual mediatrix for his sons; glitters with the gold of wisdom, is made solid with the stones of works, and is adorned by the craftsman's hand with a worthy coupling of virtues. For who more strongly, who more wisely bore the yoke that is sweet to him that loves it, who loved [0261B] more fervently, who obeyed more graciously him that sweetly disposes all things, than the Virgin in whom the Word coeternal with the Father, the Wisdom of God, willed so to be clothed with flesh that, remaining what he was, he vouchsafed to be found in habit as a man? [n: (Philip. II.)] But the Virgin's prerogative, strengthened by the gift of this mystery, closed like a golden necklace the hem of her garment from above; since it confers upon the Virgin not only comeliness but also defence, that within the bosom of the flesh she may not feel the fraudulent robber. For as from the mind, so also from the flesh the Virgin drove back everything hurtful; nay, the shameless robber knocked not at the bosom of her rest, seeing and envying that it was fortified from above with wondrous grace, so that no entrance could anywhere be found for any malevolent one. And for this cause perhaps the Bridegroom named not a necklace but necklaces, [0261C] wherein he signified a manifold, or at least a twofold, prerogative of grace: namely that whereby the Virgin's Spirit faints with tender love toward her salvation, and that whereby the flesh, now tamed, lusts nothing against the spirit. In *148* Paul, as he says [n: (Rom. VII)], two laws struggle against one another, whose spirit as well as flesh work not more fully the things that they will; serving the law of God with the mind, he is believed already to have one necklace, but with the flesh serving the law of sin he prevails not yet to obtain the other. By how much therefore Paul is the more wretched, who is still snatched into diverse things, whose Spirit wills the things that are above, and whose insolent flesh wills the contrary; by so much is the Virgin the more blessed, to whom a twin necklace is already given, whose Spirit cleaves to God, whose flesh wrestles not [0261D] against the Spirit. Blessed, I say, is she who, fortified with necklaces, admits no unchaste robber, who keeps the enemy far from the doors of her virginal modesty, who suffers not even the shameless dogs, the vices of the flesh, so much as to bark at her gate, from which the loving Bridegroom willed to make her chamber serene. Nevertheless he did not so utterly banish the other assaults from that same chamber, nor deny some kind of access to them that rushed in harshly; wherein, although the cruel malignity of him that brings them deserves to be reproved, yet the humility of her that suffers them contracts not guilt to itself in like measure. Wherefore the Bridegroom says:



## CHAPTER VIII.

*We will make thee muraenulae of gold, vermiculated with silver.* The *muraenula* is a fish which, nourished in the waters, bears many times to be beaten and driven on by their billowy flood, [0262A] yet rejoices not to be driven to death by the impulse of the water; shaken by the tempest it fears not to be swallowed into the deep, and, putting its tail (as is said) in its mouth, it folds itself into a round; taken by the fisherman's art it enriches the tables of them that feast, and by a pleasing savour invites us to the desire of it. Such a fish the Bridegroom perhaps seems to promise to the Virgin, were it not more manifestly shown in the promising; for he utterly forbids us the understanding according to the letter, when he says that this same fish is of gold or of silver. Finally he does not say: We will give thee — which could be understood of eating — but: *We will make for thee,* which is understood of having; because the fisherman indeed gives *muraenulae* but does not make them, whereas the Bridegroom not only gives his own gifts but also makes them. For his are the [0262B] gifts, whose author makes them precious.

And so in the estate of this life, not stable but billowy, in this sea exceeding horrible, and, when faith is lost, full of shipwreck, the Virgin feels herself beaten with many annoyances and tribulations, but not weighed down unto failing and impatience. For the Bridegroom works in her a certain fortitude as it were of fishes, whereby, standing in the midst of the waters, she is not loosened by the manifold inundation; and, having called upon him for whose love she burns, by whose inextinguishable heat she is held, she dreads not the flood, is not swallowed up by the deeper waters. « Save me, O God, he says, for the waters are come in even unto my soul [n: (Psal. LXVIII)]. » And worthily thereafter: « Let not the deep swallow me up [n: (ibid.)]. » The restless depth of the waves, the flowing manifoldness of tribulations, cannot wonder enough [0262C] that they hasten to be gathered against the Virgin as with a battle-line drawn up; and yet by no assault, by no onset do they prevail to break her that resists, that persists unharmed among the waves after the manner of fishes. They drive, they drive not out; they wrench, they wrench not away; they shake, they shake her not out of the state of solid firmness; they are astonished, beholding the Virgin of so great a weight; whom, as a new grace, an incomparable beauty, an unheard-of prosperity does not lift up, so a hard tribulation, the persecution of the malignant, the flowing heap of waters does not soften. For abiding in the flesh, she was in spirit not carnal but golden, that is, rich with the gold and treasure of spiritual wisdom; retaining in herself nothing soft, nothing fluid, nothing of unskilled dullness, but solid and shining, of grave understanding, [0262D] of an exquisite treasure of fortitude. For in the furnace of tribulations, at the smell of the fire, she was not caught beforehand after the manner of chaff, nor was she found like hay, nor like stubble, but like the finest gold [n: (I Cor. III)]; and her, being prudent, whom the inundation of waters sank not into the depth of the sea, the furnace of fire befouled not with soot but wiped clean. For the greatness of tribulations found in her no scruple, no stumbling-block whereto any hurtful or unseemly baseness might cleave, but when floods and fires passed in emulation through her or over her, the floods assuredly found her a *muraenula*, and the fire found her golden.

But in that the Bridegroom declared that he would make not a *muraenula* but *muraenulae*, he signified, as I judge, not one virtue but very many, which the good [0263A] craftsman forged with the learned hand of his power, and, compacted with wondrous workmanship, prepared for the Virgin's adornment and defence. Further, the *muraenula*, bringing its tail back to its mouth, is then seen to make of itself a circle or a ring, when the end of a virtue begun with good intent is bent back to its beginning; when the Virgin's patience, for the sake of him whom she loves, chooses to bear whatsoever grievous things, and no adversity prevails to remove [sic: *cam*] from her purpose. But another *muraenula* may be called her obedience, whereby, from the time that she was saluted by the angel, she is found so given over to the heavenly commands that, according to Gabriel's word, the Spirit working, being faithfully joined to one Bridegroom and rejecting every other, she was intending to please him alone who sees in secret. And who can speak or think of that *muraenula* anything that shall seem to you sufficiently to befit her praises, [0263B] when, namely, with no man for a go-between, the angel's word is made to her — he calling her blessed among women, *149* she declaring herself a handmaid; he pledging that she, unknown of man, shall now be the mother of the Lord who is present [n: (Luc. I)], she, yielding faith, yet answering herself humble; bearing a new man who with God in the beginning was God [n: (Joan. I)], she, uttering nothing lofty, nothing swollen, remains abject and humble? There is also a greater and a more excellent one: that *muraenula* which is named love, or charity, which, sitting upon a throne, holds princedom over the rest with a kind of royal sceptre; which, preeminent above the dignity of faith and hope, brought over them with a noble sovereignty, proceeds the more effectually, rejoices the more securely, being led into the Bridegroom's very chamber.
