Out of *muraenulae* of this kind, as out of certain meshes, a cord [0263C] or a chain is woven together, more solid indeed than gold and a stranger to the filth of the dust; forged in the furnace of tribulation by the learned hand of the goldsmith, reduced neither by the waters into softness nor by the smoky fire into ashes. Does it not seem to you that Paul compacted diverse *muraenulae*, and wove them, being compacted, into one cord or little chain, to which the pressure of tribulation stood as furnace and anvil, out of which by a wondrous workmanship came forth the golden graciousness of the *muraenulae*? « Knowing, he says, that tribulation worketh patience, and patience trial, and trial hope, and hope confoundeth not, because the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts [n: (Rom. V)]. » You see therefore that out of the furnace and the anvil of tribulation the bronze of patience is brought forth, which constitutes the root [0263D] and immovable foundation of the cord or chain; whereupon leans the loftiness of the virtues that follow, which the beauty preeminent in the gold of charity consummates. And this is charity unfeigned, and a worthily commendable connexion of virtues, which the pleasing mingling of silver vermiculates and adorns; when the cord of *muraenulae* is so laboriously knit together that a vermiculation of silver is found inwoven in it. Vermilion, which is a red colour, or the little worm which is of one colour with vermilion, signifies Christ's passion, whereof mention must needs be made in all things that we do, so that when we think that we serve him, obey him, love him, we may diligently call to mind those things which he unworthily suffered for us. His garment indeed grew red for us, as Isaias testifies [n: (Isa. LXIII)], and his raiment was fouled as of them that tread in the winepress; [0264A] in whose type you know that a commandment was of old promulgated, that a red heifer should be sacrificed for sins [n: (Num. XIX)]. The red heifer is he who says in the Psalm: « But I am a worm and no man; the reproach of men, and the outcast of the people [n: (Psal. XXI)]. » Of this worm and this outcast, of this reproach, he ought the more diligently to be mindful who desires the more perfectly to obtain the *muraenulae* promised to the Virgin, because the golden connexion of virtues gives not sufficient adornment if the red little worm and the silver be not inwoven. Finally the little worm is bent back into a ring and a manifold circle, that in it the worthy perfection of the aforesaid remembrance may be figured; and being cut off and divided into two separate parts it still lives, signifying him who, being struck upon the wood of the cross, slept a little while, but straightway waking [0264B] « now dieth no more, death shall no more have dominion over him [n: (Rom. VI)]. » In whose faith and love and rightly to be loved remembrance the Virgin lived, when the persecutor harshly fixed the sword not so much in his body as in her soul; and when the Son's death came even unto the Mother's tender heart, yet the Mother's faith and love found not death. Was not he dead who escaped death by a timid denial [n: (Marc. XIV)], and he who, shaken with fear, leaving the linen cloth, fled naked; and they who, all forsaking him, entered the more hastily upon flight, and held the signification neither of the little worm nor of the silver. For silver, being bright and sonorous, is said to hold the form of speech, whose chastity in the furnace, whose testing in the fire, fears not to render a voice; which, having nothing of lead, nothing of tin, grows not dark [0264C] in the burning, but, passing through unharmed, grows glad more brightly and more sonorously. You have it that the word of the Lord is a chaste word, silver tried by the fire, proved of the earth, purified seven times [n: (Psal. XI)]. [var: Vulg. Ps 11:7 *Eloquia Domini, eloquia casta*, plural, "The words of the Lord are pure words"; the singular *eloquium* is the word Philip goes on to expound of Peter and of John] And by Isaias; « If thou pass through the fire, he says, thou shalt not be burnt; and the flame shall not hurt thee [n: (Isa. XLIII)]. » [var: Vulg. Isa 43:2 *cum ambulaveris in igne, non combureris, et flamma non ardebit in te*, "when thou shalt walk in the fire, thou shalt not be burnt, and the flame shall not burn in thee"] Peter's speech in the fire is found not sonorous, but sordid after the manner of lead [n: (Marc. XIV)]; and John's speech is found not bright enough, since the one answered not a good word, a truthful word, to them that upbraided him; the other, taking to flight, hid himself under silence; having read, but neglected, that which is written: « Take not the word of truth utterly out of my mouth [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]. » And again: « And I shall answer a word to them that upbraid [0264D] me [n: (ibid.)]. » But the Virgin, embracing Christ's passion diligently with the arms of faith, presses not down her love of him negligently under silence; but what she, believing, loves, she evidently preaches when the time requires, as truly loving, so confidently bringing forth the word of faith. Worthily therefore is she given the special adornment of *muraenulae*, which are vermiculated and adorned with approved silver, since to her perfected virtues the Bridegroom interposes a diligent remembrance of his own passion; which the Virgin puts not off, both to carry through in her manners and to bring forth in her words. Such an adornment the Bridegroom asserts that he has not made for the Virgin but will make, showing that in this life that gift is not present to her but future, because while the Virgin labours and sweats and strives strongly in the contest, not [0265A] the completing of the wayfaring, not joy, the receiving of it for her, but the promise gives of the crown. For here, as upon an anvil, the mesh is beaten, a promissory perfection is drawn out, and, grace prospering, it is bent back that it may become completive, that the tail *150* may cleave to the head, that the end may be conformed to the beginning, and that the perfective conforming may be made firm with a stable rivet. In type of this Moses commands the head and the tail of the animal to be offered, hinting that a spiritual conversation should bend back the end to the beginning, that the mesh may be made whole, that the ring be made, that the *muraenula* be rounded again, that an action well begun be consummated with a like ending. Which, because while the Virgin lives here she obtains it not yet more fully but awaits it, to her that awaits the Bridegroom casts up no fear or distrust; but rather comforts her expectant mind with hope, cherishes it with a promise, makes it secure; asserting that he will do whatsoever [0265B] befits her perfection. Nor let it move any that he says not: *Muraenulae of gold* I will make *for thee,* but *we will make.* For although here the Son alone seems to speak or to promise, yet he alone works not the effect of the promised gift, but it is agreed that the Father works with the son, and the holy Spirit equally, whom it is certain are separated from one another neither in nature nor in work. « My Father, he says, worketh, and I work [n: (Joan. V)]. » And again: « Whatsoever things the Father doth, these the Son also doth in like manner [n: (ibid.)], » and there is no doubt but that the Holy Spirit doth them also. Of whom the Son says in the Gospel: « We will come, he says, and will make our abode with him [n: (Joan. XIV)]. » The same, speaking to his virgin Bride: *Muraenulae,* he says, *of gold we will make thee, vermiculated with silver.* And she:



## CHAPTER IX.

[0265C]

*While the king was in his repose, my nard gave forth its odour.* The praises being uttered wherewith the Bridegroom commended the Virgin's cheeks and neck, the promise of the *muraenulae* being made whereby he comforted her girlish mind, he now seems as it were to give place and to withdraw from the Virgin's sight; but not going far from her mouth and her love, he is held fast by her grateful remembrance. For the Virgin, turning to those maidens who tarry with her, who with anxious hearing await their mutual discourses, rejoices to speak of the Bridegroom and to commend his excellence, and to proclaim what his excellent benevolence has conferred upon her. *While the King was,* she says, *in his repose.* My Bridegroom, she says, is not base-born, not [0265D] plebeian, not of a viler impotence, but the son of the highest king, and himself a king of no lesser excellence; from the Father's session, from the royal seat, from the hiding of an unapproachable greatness, where the angels see his face and unwearied desire it; he willed to come hither to the earth for the salvation of perishing souls, and rested in my bridal chamber with the delightful love of the nuptials: in my womb, I say, that King gladly reposed, and such a repose pleased him well enough that reposed therein; and whereas in the foxes' holes and in the birds' nests he had no pleasing rest for himself, he complained not that he had found anything in me that should displease his repose. But reposing there he filled me wondrously with his grace, while, keeping me a virgin, he abolished the Virgin's barrenness; and his effectual fire burned me up for a holocaust, and not the reek of flesh but a most sweet odour of ointments filled the whole [0266A] house. For when in this his repose that majesty more sweetly leaned back its head, and God the Son of God inclined himself into my womb to take flesh; my virtue received no mean increase, a larger advance of grace, and was made as nard, fragrant within with vigour, giving without a fitting odour.

Nard, according to the letter, is a lowly herb, of a hot nature, of a richer juice, thick with leaves, mighty in odour, fit for the compounding of spices. By which not unfitly is figured the virtue of the virgin Mother, which before the Bridegroom's coming seemed small and known to God alone; but when he was present it gave the sweetness of its odour far and wide, pouring out to them that were without the benefit of an ampler knowledge. While the Bridegroom reposed in [0266B] the Virgin's womb, the just Joseph wonders at an unknown mystery, but, the Angel revealing it, he smells the magnificence of the sacrament [n: (Matth. I)]; understanding that the Virgin was not corrupted, nor had conceived of another womb, but had received a wondrous conception by the gift of the Holy Spirit. This odour Elisabeth seems none the less to have perceived with a prophetic nostril, when the Virgin, already great with child, is read to have gone up into the hill country, at whose saluting voice the little John leaped in the womb [n: (Luc. I)]; and with great dancing the whole dwelling of the mountain resounded like a ringing echo. For Elisabeth felt, and the infant in her womb felt, the repose of the incarnate Word, and smelled the sweet fragrance of this precious nard; the priest with his voice, the infant with his motion, applaud the Virgin as she comes, they extol her as she salutes them, they render worthy service [0266C] to her that goes before them: « Whence is this to me, says the priest, that the mother of my Lord should come to me [n: (ibid.)]. » And he adds concerning the Son: « For behold, as soon as the voice of thy salutation was made in mine ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy [n: (ibid.)]. » With whom rejoicing the Virgin great with child so loves to rejoice together, that yet, like nard, she is found to remain humble, and, being fuller in grace and richer in an ampler merit, the young woman ministers with dutiful diligence to the elder. For she willed to tarry three months with the priest, holding it fitting to converse for that time with the aged matron, to take care of her, to bring *151* help, to sit the more anxiously by her as she travailed, to have compassion on her pains, to still her groans, to show a pleasing solace. Nor did the Virgin afford to the woman in childbed only the solace [0266D] of an attendant, but, as some think, she performed as it were the office of a midwife; not that the Virgin, being unskilled, had been accustomed to such a ministry, but that, being meek, she might show a ready mind toward the woman in childbed; and that, first holding and beholding the child as he was born, she might render him better, whom she knew to be the prophet of the Most High, the forerunner of Christ who was to be born [n: (ibid.)]. Elisabeth sees the Virgin's humility, and considering it she marvels; with the Spirit of prophecy she smells the humble excellence of this nard: she sees that wondrous bush, to be proclaimed to all ages, burn unharmed [n: (Exod. III)], and the nard, hot by nature, nay fervent in spirit, not consumed; she feels that a richer juice is in the humble nard, that in the Virgin's womb a purer fount of mercy gushes up; she sees the humble nard [0267A] made thick with leaves, and the Virgin abound in words of modesty, in saving doctrine. Of all which, although the Virgin's nard shows not yet a fuller effect, yet little by little it gives an odour to some that have sound nostrils, so that even with a slight perception they may perceive how great a virtue is in the Virgin, how great a grace of virtue, and how great a hope of health there is for the sick in the aromatic nard. For whoever shall have felt in himself a disease or a languor, if with greedy nostril, if with due love he shall have perceived this odour; not only shall he not grieve to be weighed down, nor to fall away into failing, but he shall rather rejoice to be assuaged and to pass over into advancement.

Finally the very odour of the nard is found to receive an advance, when with the process of time the Virgin imparts a greater knowledge of herself; when, after the birth of the Son, who advanced in wisdom [0267B] and in age, she is known to be his mother with the incorrupt chastity of a Virgin [n: (Luc. II)]. For when the Word in flesh, God in man, was conversant among men, and by many was called man only, whether out of ignorance or out of malice; yet very many knew him with a truthful judgment to be God and man, and believed that as before the birth so after the birth his Mother was a Virgin. *While* therefore *the king was in his repose,* that is, when God, being great in man, showed himself as lowly, and, hidden from the unbelieving, lying secret from them that were without, appeared only to his own chamber-servants, *my nard gave forth its odour,* that is, my light under the bushel, my virtue in the dark, lay not hid, but became known to Peter as well as to the rest that had a true faith. Whence to him asking: « Whom do men say that the Son of man is *(Matth. [0267C] XVI)*; » and again: « But whom do you say that I am [n: (ibid.)]. » Peter answered: « Thou art Christ the Son of the living God [n: (ibid.)]. » He, asking concerning himself, called himself my Son of man. Peter, having drawn in the odour of the nard, affirmed him the Son of the living God; understanding that my Christ is so held to be a virgin's son, that rightly he is proclaimed the Son not also of a man, but of God. This odour the Gentiles perceive not with sound nostril, nor the Jews, who, not knowing me a virgin, deny him to be the Son of God; and derogating from the Mother, to whom a Father was altogether wanting for the joining, they weigh not the unspeakable begetting both of the begetter and of the begotten. Therefore with stopped nostrils, with blind sight, with deaf hearing, with impious hands they afflict me, who, the odour not being perceived, [0267D] crucify Christ as a mere man; whose unsound judgment the centurion rightly contradicts, when, having seen the earthquake, he says that Christ is the Son of God: « Indeed, he says, this was the Son of God [n: (Matth. XXVII)]. »

But much more amply did my nard smell sweet, my virtue shine out, when the King reposed upon the royal throne and upon the seat of rest; wherein, removed from earthly things, he found a more pleasing place, and, far from the envious, suffered neither injury nor labour. For dwelling in this world and set in a life subject to death, wherein he seemed as it were forsaken by the divine protection, he suffered so many and so great things, walking through the straits of a harder path, that this is rightly judged a dwelling not of rest but of labour. Wherein: « God, my God, he says, why hast thou forsaken me? [n: (Matth. XXVII.)] » And whereof: « I have laboured, he says, with bearing [0268A] [n: (Isa. I)]. » And Jeremias: « O Lord, he says, thou hast given them a shield of heart, thy labour [n: (Thren. III)]. » [var: Vulg. Lam 3:65 *Dabis eis scutum cordis, laborem tuum*, "Thou wilt give them a shield of heart" — future, and with no vocative] But when, dying, he had fulfilled the laborious journey, death being triumphed over, and rising again immortal had ascended to the heavens whence he had come: he sat at the right hand of majesty on high, being made now so much better than the angels, by how much he obtained above them a hereditary name [n: (Hebr. I)]. When upon this seat or royal throne that King possessed the peace that was owing to him, and, reposing in the Father's session, rejoiced with a coeternal glory; the virgin's nard was found to smell more copiously and more fruitfully, and virginal fruitfulness to shine out the more graciously the more richly. For when the Spirit was sent and came down in fiery tongues, when suddenly a vehement sound came from heaven upon the disciples [n: (Act. II)], the blindness of ignorance and the strait [0268B] of fear are driven far from them, and they utter as prudently as confidently the things they had known of Christ. For assuredly the Virgin had recounted to them in a long series from of old concerning the Bridegroom's kiss and the nuptial covenant, and, the law of the body not being observed, concerning the bodily conceiving and birth; and how he that assumed and he that was assumed had been united personally, the one not degenerating in what he assumed, the other not consumed by the glory of him that assumed: God and true man, Christ had advanced in wisdom and in age, and at last both laid down and took up his own soul with a free power. These things and much more, which it is not easy to recount in the present place (especially since they are so many that they can scarcely be contained in a book), the virgin through many years before took pains many times to explain to many, whom the same Bridegroom willed *152* to attach the more familiarly to himself. All which, [0268C] because when the Spirit was sent from the heavens they were more fully understood, were with a fuller understanding the more gratefully received; and the things which, while the Bridegroom was labouring and mortal, had pleased less being covered, now that he is immortal and reposing in rest, please more amply being uncovered. The virgin's nard therefore gives to the faithful its own odour, that is, the odour fitting to it, when her virtue and holiness show a fuller knowledge of themselves; when, the Bridegroom reposing at the right hand of the divine majesty, the knowledge of the aforesaid truth becomes more fully known and grows the more sweetly sweet. I wonder whether that woman was not seen to signify this very thing, who willed to present a pound of ointment of precious spikenard to Christ as he reclined [n: (Joan. XII)], which with due reverence she poured upon his feet, and with a larger bounty upon his head, [0268D] and that happy house of Simon was wholly filled with the odour. Whereof Jesus himself, bearing witness: « She hath wrought, he says, a good work upon me [n: (Matth. XXI)]. » Truly a good work, nor can a better easily be found, when Jesus, reclining among his guests, rejoices that his feet and his head are anointed with spikenard; that his humanity is not pressed down under the silence of ignorance, that the summit of his divinity is lifted up by the proclaiming of a fuller knowledge. Which our virgin took pains to commend not so much by her words as by her manners, to proclaim it commendable as much by living as by speaking, lest she should seem, like a wordy soldier, to dispute of war and victory, who, being delicate, willed not to bear the burdens of the camp, the encounters of such things. Therefore she subjoins:



## CHAPTER X.

[0269A]

*A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; he shall abide between my breasts.* Myrrh is a bitter spice, according to the judgment of physicians, wherewith, if a man diligently anoint the bodies of the dead, its bitterness gives to the corpses so effectual a remedy that for length of days they feel no corruption of worm or of rottenness. By the name of myrrh therefore the virgin's Bridegroom is rightly figured, with whose bitter bundle her conscience is not weighed down; but what is reckoned heavy and most bitter by another that loves not, is judged by her that is greedy of salvation to be by so much the sweetest as it is the more saving. The bitterness of myrrh is the Bridegroom's word or commandment, whose first taste, as it were, some are found so to abhor, and its first face, its very hearing, so to displease them, [0269B] that with hardened heart they not only choose not to consent, but hasten to spring back further from it as from a thing hurtful and contrary to themselves. You know that when Christ in the Gospel was speaking of perfection to a certain young man, and was exhorting him to the contempt of riches and to a voluntary poverty; he spat out the savour offered him as sad and bitter, and held not what he heard, proclaiming himself covetous more by deed than by word: « When the young man, he says, had heard the word, he went away sad; for he had great possessions [n: (Matth. XIX)]. » Elsewhere, when Jesus had said: « He that eateth my flesh and drinketh my blood, abideth in me and I in him: many, he says, of his disciples, hearing it, said: This saying is hard, who can hear it? From that time many of his disciples went, he says, [0269C] back: and walked no more with him [n: (Joan. VI)]. » You see that these give not faith to what they hear, that they bear not a hard word as it were the bitterness of myrrh; that they have no profitable consent with such an adversary, but with a lost mind abhor that saving commandment. « Be, he says, at agreement with thy adversary, whilst thou art in the way with him [n: (Matth. V)]. » But the Virgin whom we have in hand spat not out such a commandment, but bore the bitterness of myrrh with a willing mind; and what the ill-delicate reckon the sharper with a hurt palate, she with a better counsel and a concordant Spirit loves to hold the more pleasing. Wherefore also she named of that same myrrh not a bundle but a little bundle, wherein she signified the sweet, if I may so say, [0269D] bitterness of the divine commandment; which presses not, weighs not down the neck or the shoulders of her that bears it, but increases love in her, and love makes light the yoke of him that lays it on. For whatsoever she judges necessary for herself in this life, she rejoices to accomplish and to carry through not as Simon under compulsion, but for the bridegroom's love; and with that little bundle she embalms her own flesh, and takes pains to make it firm with an abiding estate, while whatever she bears in the flesh she loves to commend wholly to her beloved. Our labour indeed, the labour of us wretched ones, or our wretched action, rots away as often as Christ's love grows cold in us; and if perchance the ready Spirit burns with love of him, myrrh is a bitter bundle to us, when either the flesh grows weak or waxes insolent against the Spirit. For neither can we utterly break our own wills, nor wholly banish [0270A] the pleasures of the world or of the body; and we unhappy ones bear such a burden with much labour, while by turns fear is overcome by hope, and hope again by fear. But the virgin embraces her beloved so tenderly, so sweetly, and her conscience is so delighted with the love of him that is sweet, that whatever of bitterness she is compelled to bear in the present, she counts it light and very little for the love of him whom she already tastes, and shall taste more fully hereafter. Therefore she says: *To me the beloved,* she says, *my own to me;* though others, she says, seem *153* to bear a hard bundle, who have not yet deserved to obtain a concord of the flesh and of the Spirit: to me nevertheless my beloved has willed already to show himself a little bundle, to me who, the wrestling of the flesh being lulled to sleep, have been granted to cleave to his continual embraces. For the Virgin, considering that he whom she loves [0270B] is a King, and therefore that he is powerful, rich, noble; cares not if at any time hard things clamour without, since within, in his embrace, she rejoices already secure. For him whom a little before she calls a King: « While he was, she says, King in his repose [n: (Cant. I)], » she now loves to name her beloved, that she may show that she loves one not weak, not poor, not base-born; upon whose embrace she hangs herself with fervent affection, and whatever is beneath or behind she little esteems with a worthy disdain. Wherefore, when she had said: *A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me,* she adds: *Between my breasts,* etc.

## CHAPTER XI.

*He shall abide between my breasts.* Good is this Bundle, and to be desired not moderately by her that loves, which [0270C] bows not the back or the shoulder, nor brings disgust upon her that bears it; but with a pleasing sweetness abides between her breasts, where we discern that what is loved is not so much borne up as held and pressed close. Not so is he of whom it is written: « He turned his back away from the burdens [n: (Psal. LXXX)]. » And you have read that the shepherd carries the lost and found sheep back to the flock upon his shoulders [n: (Luc. XV)]. Of which the same, complaining, says: « I have laboured with bearing [n: (Isa. I)]. » But the Virgin, bearing the aforesaid little bundle of myrrh, thinks not that she labours, nor says that she carries that little bundle upon her back or her shoulder, but, by a new manner of speaking, that he gladly abides between her breasts, where the seat of the heart is said to be and love to hold princedom. And the Virgin's breasts seem [0270D] to figure her twofold love, whereby, namely, the Virgin loves to love the Bridegroom as God and man: God as Creator and Lord of the whole creation, man as her son by the grace of a wonderful and unspeakable begetting. To whom that rightly applies which was said by the Prophet: « The God of my heart, and God is my portion [n: (Psal. LXXII)]. » Finally there is none who knows not that a mother embraces her son between her breasts, whom, from the very fact that she is a mother, she is proved by a certain law of nature to love: and the Virgin, for love's sake, compared her Son to a little bundle, whom the prophetic word, by the merit of his humility, named a boy or a little one. « A little one, he says, is born to us [n: (Isa. IX)]. » That little one sweetly abides between his mother's breasts, whom, not by nature but by a prevailing grace, [0271A] the mother strongly embraces: and with unremitted love she holds the more firmly, on this side God, on that man, nay her son wholly and at once, and lets him not go; she loves, and by no impulse of bitterness leaves off loving. Of whom she says below: « I held him, and I will not let him go [n: (Cant. III)]. » Nor does the mother embrace only her son, but the Bride embraces the Bridegroom the more tenderly, and as she, so he rejoices in a mutual embrace; who, when he kisses her, as was said in the beginning of the drama, assuredly abides the more sweetly between her breasts. For in a kiss (if indeed it be consummated the more greedily and the more sincerely), as mouth is said to be joined to mouth, so breast to breast; nor is the love of them that kiss proved to advance to a nicety, if the kiss given with the mouth be not made firm with a pleasing embrace. Rightly therefore does the Virgin assert that the Bridegroom abides between her breasts, [0271B] that is, that a tender love is confirmed with the glue of an embrace; which, lest after the manner of others it be reckoned brief and perfunctory, the Bridegroom is said never to be disgusted with, but to make a tarrying therein. *Between my breasts,* she says, *he shall abide.* Whereof she subjoins: *A cluster,* etc.



## CHAPTER XII.

*A cluster of Cyprus is my Beloved to me, in the vineyards of Engaddi.* Wonderful and much to be loved is this beloved, whose excellence my understanding, or the understanding of one like me, does not grasp; yet, that it may in some way grasp him, I hear him named now myrrh, now a cluster, knowing nevertheless that he is none of these things, but that he is figured by these names. A cluster is a fruit which, with the process of time and ripeness obtained, is fit for eating, and afterwards, being pressed in the press, strains out the liquor of wine for drinking. By which [0271C] name the Virgin's Bridegroom is not undeservedly called, whose knowledge is ripened in the heart of them that rightly believe by a fitting advance; and, being ripened, he himself is eaten with the greedy affection of them that love him, and by that spiritual food the life of them that eat is spiritually quickened. Asserting which in the Gospel: « He that eateth me, he says, he also shall live by me [n: (Joan. VI)]. » Happy is he who both wills and is able to purchase this food, his substance being sold, and to prepare the greedy jaws of his heart for such a viand: to repair with its so sweet taste the withered strength within, and, the care of the flesh being cast off, to strengthen the Spirit with diligent zeal. Happy, I say, is he in whose conscience the knowledge of this cluster grows ripe, whose appetite burns for it, in whose jaws it grows sweet, who, loving to anoint his palate [0271D] with a pleasing savour, feels its vital juice *154* pass through to his inward vitals. Which having passed through, the flesh withers, the spirit is made fat, the outward man faints away, the inward is renewed: the sense of the flesh subsides, the spirit receives increase, and when the one is as it were dead the other stretches the more hastily toward its issue. For being no longer content to eat the cluster with famished jaws, after the vital food he desires to drink off a fruitful cup; nor does the eating he has desired seem sufficient enough for him, if it be not seasoned with a sweeter wine and a more pleasing draught. And so with the roasting press of devotion and of love he presses strongly the cluster now ripe, throws out the grape-stones, and strains the wine that shall please the more graciously: and he who until then had as it were eaten with some labour, drinks the more sweetly and grows the more fully glad, while he feels nothing contrary in love. For food seems in a manner to be changed into [0272A] drink, and the cluster into wine, while a man is found so sweetly to be made drunken with divine love that, forgetting things present, he is held by the desire of things to come alone, and, knowing no sadness, seems already to enjoy that joy of his Lord.

Whose sweetness the most blessed Virgin foretasted more fully than all, and with whose wine or love she burned far more vehemently; especially when, after the Son's death (which, being seen, the Mother could not but grieve at), his flesh was found to flower again by the benefit of the resurrection. For she who, while he was dying, tasted the sad bitterness of a certain myrrh, when the same rose again exulted the more sweetly, as one that had drunk wine; and that her joy may be clearly known to be more excellent than the rest. The cluster whereof the discourse is, is not unfittingly commended from its place: *A cluster,* she says, *of Cyprus [0272B] is my beloved to me.* Cyprus is an island, before the rest that lie about it, rather first than second, as they say. who have seen it, so fruitful of the very best wine that not only is its fruitfulness held pleasing and sufficient for itself, but from thence also wine is carried over into other regions by the merit of its own. Whose cluster is found fairer to look upon, more pleasing to eat, sweeter to drink, when at the ripe season it makes trial of the winepress of them that tread; and as it seems to smile upon the sight, so also upon the taste, and the mind of him that loves it rejoices to answer it as it plays before him. Rightly therefore did the virgin will to call her beloved a cluster of Cyprus, who vouchsafed to present so great a joy to her that loved him, that, the mourning being wiped away which the passion of him that died had brought, she was rendered as it were drunken with the most sweet taste of him that rose again. Who, although to many others he was a cluster [0272C] that they might rejoice, and that by the grace of him that rose again they might have hope of rising again in flesh and in spirit, yet the virgin asserts that to her he was nothing but a cluster of Cyprus, to whom the Bridegroom is believed to have afforded an ampler and a more perfect joy. For the virgin had known both that the Son's death would profit for the blotting out of vices, and that his resurrection would bestow the merit of justification; and in both, while others variously distrusted, she distrusted not, and by how much the more firmly she believed and the more robustly she loved, by so much the more amply did she rejoice. Worthily therefore did she understand him in whom she believed, whom she loved, to be in a manner comparable to a cluster of Cyprus, whose love grows ripe with her by an incomparable advance, and, being tasted the more fully and the more sweetly, makes her grow glad the more strongly and the more joyfully. But that this cluster may be commended with a yet ampler grace, mention of the vineyards of Engaddi [0272D] is not kept silent; and although Cyprus once named seemed sufficient and enough, Engaddus is added, that nothing may be able to be lacking to the commendation.

*A cluster,* she says, *of Cyprus is my beloved to me, in the vineyards of Engaddi.* As it seems, she says that a cluster of Cyprus is in the vineyards of Engaddi, which saying the truth of the matter contradicts according to the letter; because Engaddus is known to be far more remote from Cyprus, and neither custom nor necessity is found for clusters to be carried over from vineyards into vineyards. For if a man should labour to carry clusters from vineyards into vineyards, he is accused of a certain ineptitude in the judgment of the prudent; as if, his senses being lost, he should carry wood into the wood, or pour waters into the fullest sea, when that ought rather to be carried thither where most certainly it does not abound. Finally [0273A] Engaddus is said not to have vineyards, but certain little trees, which it is agreed are better than vines; which, if they be pricked with a learned hand at the opportune season, are known to sweat oil, nay the liquor of balsam. And because their owners till such little trees with much diligence, that like vines they may be made readier to produce liquor; [sic: *idco*] perhaps the divine word called them vineyards, whereby it signified them both as subject to tillage and as rich in a precious liquor. Because therefore a cluster of Cyprus is not to be found in these vineyards or little trees, nor can what has been said fit according to the letter, it is necessary that in this word a spiritual understanding be sought, which, as you have already received, holds the greater princedom in this drama. In the tree or the little tree the virgin's Bridegroom is not unfittingly figured, who, if [0273B] he be pricked by the touch and love of them that worthily believe, sweats oil, gives the liquor of a precious balsam, brings forth much grace to her that loves, and pours back a more pleasing spirit. « Therefore, he says, I love them that love me [n: (Prov. VIII)]. » [var: Vulg. Prov 8:17 *Ego diligentes me diligo* — the emphatic pronoun "I", not the connective "therefore"] And in the Gospel: « Somebody, he says, hath touched me: for I have felt power going forth from me [n: (Luc. VIII)]. » [var: Vulg. Luke 8:46 *nam ego novi virtutem de me exiisse*, "for I know that virtue is gone out from me"] This Bridegroom, when he is touched with the pleasing affection of one that loves, pours back the sacred balsam, the power of an overflowing spirit; he brings forth that which stills diseases and by its presence keeps off all hurt, he brings forth that unction which, error as well as ignorance being driven out, teaches concerning all things. And this benefit seems to be intimated by the very name of the place, if any man shall have turned it over or been able to search it out more expressly, because Engaddus is interpreted *the fount of the kid,* or *to the eyes of temptation,* whose [0273C] *155* interpretation serves the mystery of so great a matter. The kid is reprobated in the law, which is sent out into the desert by the ministers [n: (Levit. XVI)], and in the Gospel the same is set on the left hand by the merit of sin [n: (Matth. XXV)]; and for this cause, by him, sin or the sinner is not unfittingly figured, who by his own merit is reprobated by him who loves nothing but justices. But the fount of the kid is the Spirit himself, whose infusion washes sin, cleanses the sinner, renders the flesh of Naaman the leper purer than a boy's [n: (IV Reg. V)], changes the kid into a lamb, giving the merit of an innocent life [n: (Joan. IV)], and becomes in him that has drunk a rich fount, a fount of water springing up. The same Spirit is also not undeservedly called the eye of temptation, by whose light and grace temptation is foreseen [0273D] far off; who, teaching man knowledge, forming wisdom, directing the understanding, the darkness of night being wiped away, leads him on to the perfect day. The cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi therefore is this our virgin's beloved, because the love and joy wherewith her mind is affected is made solid in Christ himself, worthily in his own Spirit; and loving him in him, she rejoices of him and not of another. To her indeed he is a fruit-bearing tree, a medicinal balsam, a vital fount, a laver of injustice, the light of knowledge, a spiritual eye; and whatever is judged necessary either for the driving off of evils or for the obtaining of goods, is truly proclaimed to be had in him and from him. And lest we be judged wholly strangers to that benefit, although we are in no wise made equal to so great a merit of this virgin, with the sacrament of holy [0274A] baptism we have received certain visible things in token of things invisible. For we are anointed with oil in figure of the heavenly medicine, whereby, torpor being driven far off, we are prepared for an agile discipline, that our spirit, anointed with the divine spirit, may be held the stronger in the wrestling, and may the more readily slip out of the adversary's hand or snare. Afterwards we are washed throughout with the clean fount of visible water, that we may be spiritually cleansed from the filth not so much of the flesh as of the soul; and that we may exchange the rough motions of the kid for all meekness, and reserve in ourselves nothing on the left hand, nothing worthy of judgment. Thirdly a light is kindled for us, that our eye may not grow dim, that when it has foreseen whatever things are hurtful it may either forbid or chastise them; that, not being ignorant of Satan's cunning devices — what, namely, they feign, what they intend — it may walk honestly as in the day, [0274B] and darkness may not overtake it. So his own baptizer instructs the strenuous athlete, when he is newly girded for the contest, more by significations than by speech; that when he has received a lively understanding of the things which have been said, he may with the utmost effort, with grace, take pains to come through to their effect. In all which the virgin is believed to be equal to none, not second, but far before the rest she enjoys, rejoicing, the Bridegroom's love; and to her by a special privilege that saying worthily belongs which we know to be as yet forbidden to us, our merits requiring it. *A cluster,* she says, *of Cyprus is my beloved to me, in the vineyards of Engaddi.* After the virgin had spoken these things of her beloved to the maidens, and had mystically set forth what of patience, what of joy she has in him; he, as it were turning himself back to her, delays not to answer the more graciously, [0274C] praising and commending what he understands, and loves, to be preeminent in her.



## CHAPTER XIII.

*Behold thou art fair, my friend, behold thou art fair: thine eyes are of doves.* Thou, he says, who before all women art a friend to me, an enemy of all malice, of all foulness. Behold, that is, not only with all the just in the life that follows, but far more praiseworthily than all the rest in the present: *Behold,* I say, *thou art fair,* strong with a certain singular beauty, wherewith none of women, neither earlier nor later, can be compared. For it is fitting that he who is beautiful in form above the sons of men should have to himself such a one as by a singular grace displays a special beauty, whose face no unworthy and degenerate foulness may darken, but [0274D] love may conform her, the beloved, to him by whom she is loved. But when he had said: *Behold thou art fair, my friend;* what is it that he repeated: *Behold thou art fair?* What means this, fair and fair? Perhaps he repeated it to this end, that none should doubt of the aforesaid beauty, but that the assertion following might confirm the testimony set before; because it is both proclaimed that every word stands in the mouth of two witnesses [n: (II Cor. XIII)], and it is recorded that the authority of the law and of the prophets hangs upon two precepts [n: (Matth. XX)]. Some say that he therefore called the virgin fair twice, that he might mark her as having had a double beauty; who, conceiving and bearing, wondrously continues a Virgin, and in so great a prerogative truly avers herself humble, whereas for the most part [0275A] any woman is found either humble, but corrupted, or somewhat prouder, if perchance she has been uncorrupted. Worthily therefore fair, whom no hurt of integrity has disfigured, and again fair, whom an incomparable humility has adorned; so that the little flower of virginity renders her that is humble in spirit the brighter, and one humble in spirit renders her that is bright with the virginal flower the fairer. But I (not prejudging those who, it is agreed, have irreproachably thought this) judge that the Bridegroom, by repeating, expressed something proper to a lover, who, tenderly loving him by whom he rejoices to be loved, says pleasing things, and it does not suffice him to say once *156* what is loved. For the force of love has this familiar and proper to itself, that when it has enticed a man with the bond of a dearer affection, it stirs him up to speak gracious things of that which he loves, and, [0275B] unless they be repeated, the same things do not seem to him fruitful enough. Love admonishes the lover to speak the more willingly, and, that he may express his affection, to repeat the word the more often; nor does this reading seem to the lover to be required more than is right, even if, according to the poet, it has been ten times repeated. Whence David also, when he would markedly express the love which he had had toward his son, and could not press down with silence the grief of his death, went mourning and with covered head, forgetful of the royal dignity, and speaking of his son repeated the same speech the more often: « Absalom my son, my son Absalom [n: (II Reg. XVIII)]. » The same in the Psalm: « God, my God [n: (Psal. XCII)]. » And elsewhere: « May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us [n: (Psal. LXVI)]. » You see that to speak once what pleases [0275C] a lover is not thought sufficient, but the tenderer affection rejoices to repeat what it had said; because whatever can be said, he that is given over to love does not yet esteem it enough, in comparison with that which he grasps in his mind, inexpressible in words. For this cause the Bridegroom, setting himself to address the Virgin with soothing words — in that, as you have heard, he willed to call her fair a second time — strove by the repetition not so much to commend her beauty (which is great) as to intimate to his hearers the affection wherewith he is held toward her. But because very much beauty shines out in the eyes of girls, in her praise he asserts that she has the eyes of doves, which he wills to be understood, as I judge, not those of this head, not carnal, but the spiritual ones of that inner man. [0275D] Doves have certain properties implanted in them from nature, which generation transfers by an unspeakable law from the former to those that follow; wherein they are reported to differ far from the other birds, upon whom these gifts of nature are not all of them bestowed upon all. For they are said to have seven natures, or powers of nature, whereby they both seek what is useful and are kept back from what is hurtful; which to set forth by name and to compare with the virtues of holiness (being perhaps about to speak of them at another time) I now defer for brevity's sake. Finally the Holy Spirit was seen to appear in a dove [n: (Luc. III)], intimating to us that he has no small likeness with her, since he himself is found marked with seven principal gifts, and she is marked, as has been said before, with the pleasing sevenfold of nature. When therefore the Bridegroom declares the Virgin's eyes to be [0276A] of doves, he commends in her the seven gifts of graces; not the perishing light of the head, but the beholding powers of the mind, discerning of just and unjust rather than of days and nights. And rightly does he praise her whom he considers, thus conformed to his own Spirit, to have the sevenfold grace of virtues; from whom driving far off the drowsiness of the flesh and womanish torpors, he bestowed on her spiritual watchfulness and dove-like eyes. Indeed the Spirit himself rested more abundantly upon none of women than upon that same Virgin, in whom he rested sevenfold, since what bodily doves obtain figuratively from nature, he gave the whole of it to her in spirit, in truth rather than in figure. Whence rejoicing, and not ungrateful for the Bridegroom's praises received, she calls him also fair, with a praise nonetheless [0276B] doubled; and she rejoices to render the like to her praiser, and thus by an answering praise their mutual love is strengthened.

## CHAPTER XIV.

*Behold thou art fair, my beloved, and comely.* Because thy holiness has bestowed beauty upon me, my heart being cleansed, from this I have known that in thee also there is much beauty; for if deformity held me while my eye was not yet wiped clean, thy bright form would in no wise appear to me. But now, marked after the manner of doves with spiritual eyes, I attend more keenly how polished thy face is: and I see that there is in thee a form fairer than the sons of men, whom very many see only as not having beauty or comeliness. For the raven-like sight, which is pressed hard with a foul blackness, [0276C] beholds thee only as deformed, only as a man; and, held by error, it assigns thee to a judgment unworthy enough, while it says that thou art John, or Elias, or one of them of former times [n: (Matth. XVI)]. But to me, whose faith is not shattered, whose sight is not raven-like, but to whom the sevenfold grace and the dove-like form are at hand: far off is thy mortality of infirmity, far off is foulness, and the incomparable beauty of both natures shines sweetly forth. Thou assuredly art fair with a wonderful and singular Godhead, endowed with a substantial unity together with the Father and the Spirit: having with them the same natural excellence, a coeternal greatness, a coequal kingdom and power. Wherein none of the gods is found like to thee, nor is any other God marked with so great a prerogative [0276D] of beauty; because, although the personal distinction gives to understand that the Father is one and the Holy Spirit another, yet the natural substance renders him one God, and not another. Whatever therefore of beauty the Father and the Spirit are known to have, my beloved, I perceive with sure faith to shine back in thee: and this it is that entices me to love thee and to choose thee as my beloved, to follow thee, and not to desist, until I attain and come through to what is perfect; and because the loftiness of thy divine beauty is not hidden from me in the *157* present, the wonderful beauty of thy humanity also pleases me not slightly: whereby thou art so held a man among men, mortal among them that are dead in sin, that although thou sufferest the penalty, yet thou art not burdened with the guilt of mortals. Which comeliness none of the sons of Adam has deserved to obtain from [0277A] nature, because no man's conception, no man's begetting lacked a fault; but a singular cleanness, a special excellence, adorned thee alone, whom alone, conceived of the divine Spirit, a virginal womb brought forth. But this thou dost not manifest sooner, nor more fully, to any of men than to me, my beloved; whom thou dost so honour with a singular merit that I bring thee forth, God and man, in sure truth: mother of the Bridegroom, Bride of the son, with a wondrous and incomparable chastity. To me therefore thou art fair, to me especially thou shinest forth comely, who art made known both as God in man, and as a man Holy above men; whom, as Son, the equality of nature conforms to God the Father, and whom, as man, the law of sin and the general conception of men does not darken. Fair, I say, thou art, because thou art the brightness of eternal light, the mirror without spot of the divine majesty, the splendour of the Father's [0277B] glory, the figure of his substance, the image of truth [n: (Hebr. I)]; light of light, the rising sun, bringing to the world the morning day, day of day, lying down at noon, knowing no evening setting. When, caught up in ecstasy and lifted in the Spirit above visible things, I consider thee so fair with the cleared edge of my mind, then, as if forgetful of myself, I cannot not love thee, whom I behold to be such; I burn to commend thee, my beloved, and thy beauty.



## CHAPTER XV.

*Behold thou art fair, my beloved.* Nor does the wonderful beauty of thy Godhead alone please me, which thy loftiness, coequal with the Father and the Spirit, obtains; but thou hast also kindled me not slightly with that comeliness wherewith, abounding in grace, thou, the lofty one, didst descend to lowly things. [0277C] For no small comeliness is that wherewith, girding thyself, thou art strongly clothed, when by the Father thou wast set over Sion his holy mount [n: (Psal. II)]; when, taking flesh in me and personally made one with it, thou didst come forth as a Bridegroom out of the chamber [n: (Psal. XVIII)], marked with humility in power. In which flesh, above the law of the flesh, thou didst not feel the vices of the flesh, but, conceived of the Spirit, didst flower with an inborn vigour; and, suffering the penalty of the flesh, thou didst fail in the sight of them that persecuted thee, but in the sight of the faithful thou didst perfect the saving mystery for the world. For it was needful that, living in the flesh under penalty, thou shouldest teach us, shouldest show thyself a master of living as much by thy manners as by thy words; that with anvil and hammer thou shouldest forge the rule of the Gospel, and, suffering death in [0277D] the flesh, shouldest triumph over the devil, the author of death. But being given over to death, thou didst rise on the third day, and, made immortal, strengthening faith, didst give hope: to the heavens whence thou hadst come thou didst carry up the substance of our flesh, and, the Spirit being given to thine own, thou didst raise their minds thither. Who, worthily considering that thou wast able so to be born and to live, to die and to rise again, and that thou didst will by a deep counsel, as man, to do these things for men, would not be amazed, would not wonder, would not love this comeliness, would not greedily embrace so mighty, so kindly a giver? Which, although it be hidden from others, from whom, their guilt requiring it, grace of this kind is either taken away, or, being to be given hereafter, is now deferred by a hidden judgment; yet to me in the present the order of this matter is declared, to me it is open, to me it is pleasing, what thy Godhead [0278A] works in man. *Behold,* I say, *thou art fair, my beloved, and comely.* Behold, that is, in evidence to me is the beauty of thy majesty; to the opened eye of faith the excellence of the Godhead presents itself, which by its bounteous gift floods the understanding of my mind, and, the understanding being made clear, gives the effect of an indissoluble love. Behold again, the saving dispensation of thy humanity is not hidden from me: the conception, the nativity, the converse of a singular merit; the power, the cleanness, the patience, the praise of the doctrine, the flashing of miracles, the integrity of manners, the perfection of discipline. In all which thou, a man, art adorned above men, and with a singular comeliness art compared neither to a prophet nor to an apostle: and therefore I love thee before all, thee alone I choose, my beloved, although as yet, while life is lived here, imperfectly (as I seem to see). But [0278B] that imperfection may not trouble me more than is right, I desire that thy presence may manifest itself to me more nearly; and lest I should seem to invite the fair and comely one to foul things, I have taken pains to prepare a place fitting for a lover.

## CHAPTER XVI.

*Our little bed is flowering; the beams of our houses are of cedar, our panelled ceilings of cypress.* Because the noble Virgin has found a fair and comely lover, she does not after a rustic fashion call him forth to labour, for delicate love knows not to be worn down by degenerate toil or torment, but loves quiet and leisure, and rejoices in a kiss or in a joining. As yet unversed in this, that *158* lover, a rude one, seems to have stood forth, nor did his love afford him rest worthy enough: who asks that she whom he loves be given him for this, that they may be able to labour together, [0278C] but not yet rejoice to keep holiday. « Her have I loved, and have sought her out, he says, and have sought to take her to me for a spouse; and I became a lover of her beauty [n: (Sap. VIII)]. » And below: « Send her out of the seat of thy greatness, that she may be with me and may labour with me; and that I may know what is acceptable with thee, for she knoweth all things and understandeth [n: (Sap. IX)]. » This man saw that it was as yet fitting for him to labour, and that Wisdom, whom he loves, should labour together with him, that by the common toil the lover, as yet less wise, might be taught, and, when he had been taught, might be carried forward to the rest of the little bed. Finally that woman whose praiseworthy fortitude is commended is recorded to put her hand to the neck, and to take hold of the spindle with her fingers; and she seems to be made gracious to her husband, in that she has not eaten [0278D] her bread idle [n: (Prov. XXXI)]. But our Virgin, far surpassing both this woman and that lover, obtains now quiet, not tumult; leisure now, not labour; and offers not a wrestling-school to a contender, but a little bed to a lover, which she has taken pains to adorn and to make ready with a more cultivated ornament. The Virgin's little bed is the secret place of her heart, which she tills and cleanses with a diligent hand and care, lest anything unseemly and unbecoming should appear to the Bridegroom at his coming; and, that she may afford a sweet repose to his so great dignity, she props it and fills it with the pleasing softness of a careful workmanship. And because, besides the softness laid beneath, a noble lover rejoices also in comeliness, the Virgin, not unskilled in the matter, adorns the little bed with a pleasing flower; and, the flower of a wondrous chastity being scattered with much diligence, she renders that same little bed as it were a little garden of delight. [0279A] For lest any man, hearing of the Virgin's little bed and taking it ill, should doubt of the profit, and should stray from the path of holiness by a gross and carnal understanding, the Virgin declares it adorned with gathered flowers; and the flowers are chastity, and the repute of that same chastity. For virginal chastity adorns her secret knowledge after the manner of a flower, and renders the little bed pleasing, pouring out the grace of comeliness and of odour; because it is that which is preeminent by an excellent virtue and merit, and which, that it may offer itself as a pattern, shines out with an eminent fame or name. Wherein nothing bodily, nothing bestial is understood, nothing given over to sin, but the whole utterly spiritual; because the drama, or the song, or the nuptial epithalamium flowers with mystical words, having nothing of hay or of flesh. But although that thing thus flowers and avails which love has more diligently prepared, [0279B] yet the Virgin named it not a bed, but rather a little bed; by which name she fulfilled that law well enough known to her, whereby she was wont to hold to lowly things as much in word as in deed. Wherefore also, she says, I call that same little bed not properly mine, but in common ours, and (which is worthy of praise) I do not presumptuously assign it to myself; because, although I was found obediently to consent to him that called and helped me, yet both his preventing grace and his following mercy willed to impart the efficacy. Not mine therefore, but ours ought the little bed rightly to be called, which it is agreed is prepared by the work and diligence of both of us; which thou with the hand of grace, and I with that of labour and industry, have made serene — thou by benefit, I by exercise; thou with the flowers of virtues, I with the flowers of manners, have adorned it. Whereof I willed to make [0279C] so marked a mention to this end, that, called forth by its beauty, thou mayest vouchsafe to come to its dwelling; and that, far from the tumult wherein I know thou art not often present, I may rejoice — than which is nothing better — to be with thee in the flowering secret place. For although for the sake of the brethren and of neighbours it is needful to speak and to go out, yet, that I may behold thee, it is much more pleasing to enter into silence, and in the leisure of quiet to be soothed by thy presence, to enjoy a mutual embrace, to experience the fruit of love, the joy of the Spirit. To the deserving whereof our houses also seem to emulate my zeal, and with however slow a foot to follow me as I rest in the little bed; which, although they are not yet able to be advanced to this, that they should become a little bed, yet are already found to deserve no slight grace. And in this I rejoice, yea [0279D] and I shall rejoice, because thou pleasest not only when thy presence is now held in the little bed, but when, according to the Prophet [n: (Psal. XLVII)], it shall be known to be in the houses; to which, namely, in beams of cedar thou givest an incorruptible firmness, in panelled ceilings of cypress a lasting ornament nonetheless.



## CHAPTER XVII.

*The beams of our houses are of cedar; our panelled ceilings of cypress.* By houses he means the churches of the faithful, the congregations of the just, the assemblies of the cloister, in which all the simpler sort can be reckoned stones, but the greater and more prudent are more fittingly called beams and panelled ceilings. The beams, set in order over the building after the manner of a vault, and distributed from either side of it one against another, below indeed [0280A] embrace the breadth of the building with arms as it were outstretched; but above, with heads as it were joined, they are knit together with a solid nail. But the panelled ceilings are laid beneath the height of the beams, and are stretched out from one wall to the other in a spread length; and they confine and bind those same walls with a certain binding as it were, lest by a hurtful shock they should decline from their straightness or *159* stature. By the name of beams the order of prelates is not unfittingly figured, whom, hung up from earthly things, the loftiness of their merits commends; who, bearing the troubles of showers and of winds, that is, the hard assaults of the lost, cover and protect from these the tender manners of their subjects. Who, raised toward the things above, all narrow themselves to the beholding of that one thing necessary, and, bound the more strongly by the nail of love, [0280B] while they see, cleave the more augustly, and taste the more sweetly; judging it better to be with Christ [n: (Philip. I)], while they contemplate his excellence, but yet deeming it needful to live in the flesh for the brethren's sake. Who therefore lift themselves up with a subtle desire to relish the things that are above, and condescend with kindly care to visit their neighbours; and, gathering them under their wings, they cherish and protect them as a hen, and, having quickened them to the virtues, fortify them by examples and by doctrine. And these indeed, that they may be commended by a worthier merit of virtues, are declared beams of Cedar, whose part they bear; because Cedars, as they say, incorruptible and tall by nature, are strong with so great an odour that serpents are said to shrink from it. Those therefore are worthily found to be advanced to the height of prelacy [0280C] who, lofty in merits, love to behold heaven with desire; whose works are ever strong with a steadfast virtue, that they may not rot; whose repute is so great that all the malevolent shudder at it. Nor is it far from prelates that the Cedar is said not to be burned up by fire, bearing the figure of those who are not to perish in the burning of the passions; whose wonderful fortitude knows not to be broken by the concupiscence of the flesh, nor does their most sweet odour turn to ashes at the odour of fires. But the panelled ceilings, which are also said to be of cypress, signify those whose discipline is strong and preeminent among the rest; by whose strong work and obedience of a perfect will a pattern of persevering is given to the lesser ones gathered in the Church. The Cypress too is itself declared incorruptible and odour-bearing, [0280D] and moreover it is without knots, and no scruple is found in it; rightly signifying him who, readier and smoother by a divine gift rather than by nature, obeying without delay, never kicks back at the joining. For in some men the virtue of obedience is so knotty, so teeming with murmuring, so scrupulous with so many complainings, that a command as it comes does not walk before it upon a smoother way, but for the most part stumbles into contempt or into a graver wrath. But those to whom it is given to be strong with the smoothness of the cypress, being without knots and polished, rejoice in the discipline of obedience; they love whatever the discretion or doctrine of prelates shall command, nor does a sudden fall of impatience set itself against the command. By these as beams and panelled ceilings spiritual houses go forward, are covered, are fortified, and avoid ruinous [0281A] and carnal falls; their holy and wonderful beauty is strong, because, according to that which was said, holiness becometh the house of the Lord [n: (Psal. XCII)]. But the Virgin willed to declare these houses ours to this end, that she might show that she has fellowship with the Bridegroom before the rest; because what is the Bridegroom's, the Bride reckons ours by nuptial right, and as Christ, so also the Virgin is careful for the spiritual profit of us all. Marking therefore that not only she herself but her own also have profited spiritually, and that prelates and subjects have come to the likeness of the cedar and the cypress, she exults and invites the Bridegroom to rejoice in these also, and, leaving the restless, to be delighted with the pleasing rest of the houses. And he:

## CHAPTER XVIII.

[0281B][CAP. II.] *I am the flower of the field, and the lily of the valleys.* If the Bride's little bed, he says, is green with flower, glows with a virginal comeliness; if it shines and is fragrant with spiritual adornment and beauty; if, rich with a royal culture, it seems to smile upon them that worthily consider it — what has it that it may truly assert it has not from another? For neither has it of itself that it should be glowing with a flowering comeliness, nor does he flower whom the Bride declares flowering, save by a flower; and for this cause let him that flowers not glory in himself, but in the flower, since assuredly he has not of himself that he should flower, but of the flower. But if whosoever flowers desires to know more attentively whence he flowers, lest a foul ignorance should discolour the comely and flowering one: I am God, the Son in the Father, the light dwelling in light inaccessible. *I,* I say, have been made *the flower of the field,* having an unwearied beauty. The root of Jesse has budded, and [0281C] a flower has come forth from the root, nor did it will to lie hid in a chamber under a bushel, or in a bed under a coverlet; but it was made the flower of the field, that it might be made known more plainly to all, and that whosoever knows not one so conspicuous might not be worthy to be excused. For I who from eternity was God hidden, that I might not be seen, coming down from this mountain, the field received me that I might be held; nor did I enter the gates and walls of cities, nor again did I climb a steep mountain, lest either I might be unknown, or might not be the more easily laid hold of by him that knows. For if the strong man went up to the mountain, the weak would remain excused; but in a city the citizen would keep off the stranger; *160* and thus, injury prevailing, the one would plead that the other was the readier, and Habacuc [n: (cap. I)] would accuse me of silence, the wicked devouring one juster than himself. I [0281D] therefore willed to be a flower in the field and not in a farm, which assuredly the countryman claims for himself by hereditary right; which he breaks up with the plough, furrows with the share, digs zealously with the hoe, because it answers fruitfully to nothing but the work of hands. But the field is properly assigned to no man, it knows not the tiller's hand, it is sown without its surface being broken; but quickened by the sun, drenched with heavenly rain or dew, it grows warm and buds, and with the process of a fitting time it laughs with flower. Nor is it unfitting if the Virgin of Virgins be asserted to be signified by this field, in whom no man, no carnal commerce, works anything; but, her flesh being whole, a spiritual rain coming down as upon a fleece, she is made fruitful and buds, and rejoices in a flowering or snowy comeliness. For this field, which no greedy workman has hurt, no rustic hand has ploughed; [0282A] no hurtful swelling has raised it up, but a diffused humility has levelled it; I am the flower, coming forth assuredly not by human zeal, not by tillage, but brought forth by a heavenly gift, endowed with an incomparable birth. I am the flower wherewith the pleasing levelness of this field is adorned, nor does it flower of itself, but by my gift is thus blessed; and therefore, although the Virgin worthily rejoices at so great a benefit, yet let her glory in me and not in herself, in the flower and not in her that flowers. For although the flower does not send forth fruit as soon as it is born, yet, being about to give it at the opportune season, it already promises it; and as no other flower is found mightier than mine, or than me, so neither does any man make trial of a better fruit in another. But lest I should seem to have mercifully provided for the Virgin alone, and to have grudged my mercy to any lesser ones, I who was made the flower of the field, [0282B] endowing the Bride with a special privilege, have flowered in the valleys also — with much indeed, but not with an equal benefit.



## CHAPTER XIX.

*And the lily of the valleys.* Valleys, nay deep valleys, which on this side and on that are overshadowed by neighbouring mountains, and, lest they wither with thirst, are watered by waters flowing down on either hand, seem to me to signify the humble and the lowly, whom the love of discipline keeps unwearied under the laws of their elders. Who, since they bring back nothing lofty or swollen from an indolent Maecenas, judge themselves unprofitable servants with a humble holiness, and bow their ear the more diligently to the admonitions of the Scriptures and to either Testament, desiring to abound rather in plenty of merits than of corn. Christ confesses himself the lily of deep valleys of this kind, [0282C] because, though he is the more exalted, yet he is declared to look upon lowly things [n: (Psal. CXII)]; nor does his Spirit rest save upon the humble and the meek, whose conscience shines again with a clean humility and a humble cleanness [n: (Isa. LXVI)]. And worthily enough did he will to be named a lily, signifying thereby what he came to work among the valleys and for the valleys' sake; that he might not darken the cause of his coming to them that rightly attend, whom, when he has rendered them taught, he may the more effectually conform to himself. The lily is girt about in a round with whiter leaves, after the likeness of a valley, having within it something red in the depth: in its leaves indeed showing itself seemly and bright, but in the red representing the appearance of blood. The whiteness of the lily figured the cleanness of the flesh assumed, which neither [0282D] the conception before nor the converse after blackened; but, though begotten of flesh, it knew not the flesh's own poison, and by the merit of virtues, as with a snowy splendour, it shone. But that red thing bears before it the pleasing memory of the passion, whereby, his blood being shed, he washed away the handwriting of the covenant formerly entered into, which our first parents wretchedly made with the author of sin, when at his will they touched the forbidden tree. Christ therefore is a lily, when he glows with the merit of an innocent life, when in the flesh he is not held by the stain or the glue of a cleaving vice; when the malice of men assails and accuses him as man, and he as man refuses not to suffer hard and bitter things for men. He is the lily of the valleys, when to the abject and the humble he gives an example and a grace of living, commends innocence, [0283A] implants a love of continence; when, having first suffered grievous things, he calls them forth to the virtue of suffering, teaching great things, doing greater, and proclaiming the time of doing. But if it be said that what is red within the lily holds the appearance of fire, « and God is a fire, » as it is certain that Scripture declares [n: (Deut. IV)]; that redness, as I see, hedged about with a snowy splendour, is God in man, covered [sic: *ooopertus*] with the robe of clean flesh. In whose wrapping he hid himself from the wise and the prudent, but revealed himself to the little ones and the humble that behold with faith [n: (Luc. X)]; who so look upon the covering or whiteness of the assumed flesh without, that they look within upon the fiery redness also of the hidden Godhead. Of whom Peter: « Thou art, he says, Christ the Son of the living God [n: (Matth. XVI)]. » And Nathanael: « Rabbi, thou art the Son of God, thou art the king [0283B] of Israel [n: (Joan. I)]. » And the centurion: « Indeed this was the Son of God [n: (Marc. XV)]. » Christ so made himself the lily of these valleys, when he disclosed himself to his humble ones not only as man, but as God within man; to whom his innocent humanity was so shown with a clean whiteness, that they discerned also the hidden Godhead with an unoffended faith. Whom, after he had taught them what they must faithfully think concerning himself, repeating the Virgin's praises, he invites the more diligently *161* to see how she imitates the Bridegroom amid the troubles of this life, while rest is not yet full, nor unfailing peace obtained.



## CHAPTER XX.

*As the lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters.* Although, as you have heard, I said that I am the lily of the valleys, [0283C] yet know further that I am among more grievous thorns; by which I suffer myself to be touched the more often, to be pricked the more troublesomely; but, touched and pricked, I lose not my due state or whiteness. After this pattern my friend has her converse among the evils of this world, and by a wonderful power the light is proved to shine in the darkness; and the darkness poured about her does not darken her flowering light, nor do threatening thistles thresh out her unbroken beauty. She rises like a lily among thorns, and grows; among dark things she shines, among rough things she grows meek; driven by the blowing wind she seems to feel some workings, but she sustains no hurts of whiteness or of odour. I deem the grievous thorns to be the cares and anxieties of this life, wherewith the minds of the just (while life is lived here) are harassed; they groan and [0283D] long that, being more fully freed from them, they may at last with Christ rejoice in the fruit of peace obtained. Thorns are nonetheless the Jews and the Gentiles alike, who, aged in malice, childish in lost sense, execrating the faith, wrapped in grosser darkness, persecuted Christ and his Mother with a grievous hatred. Among whom the Son and the Mother flowered after the likeness of a lily, and alike kept their whiteness unhurt and their own odour, while, contracting to themselves nothing of guilt from their malice, with unconquered patience they spurn the detracting tongues. Nay, by how much the more the life of the malignant grows dark with a foul soot, by so much the more does the holiness of these, worthily considered, shine forth; nor has the undefiled beauty of the lily less of comeliness and grace, if beside it be seen the rough foulness [0284A] of the thorns. The lily among thorns therefore has an ampler title of praise, since, while those grow dark, this retains a more pleasing form; because while both Gentiles and Jews rage with serpentine tongue against the Lord and against his Christ [n: (Psal. II)], Christ, the flower and the lily, grows meek in manners, and shines with miracles and doctrine. To which flower and lily the virgin takes pains the more diligently to be made like, loving and desiring to glory in so great a likeness; and as among thorns the lily is made beautiful with a splendid comeliness, so the Bride among the daughters is adorned by the merit of virtues. By daughters he means those who, lacking manly rigour and a masculine spirit, are torpid with a womanish softness, sleep with a feminine drowsiness; feeble for honest work, effectual for what is soft and hurtful, crafty in flattering, treacherous [0284B] or shameless in detracting. Who, seeing or hearing of the Mother rejoicing in her son, clothed with a lost sense deny her to be either a virgin or fruitful; and, endowed as she is with a singular gift, they measure her carnally according to the common law of all, while they lie that she brought forth in no other way than the manner made trial of by other women. But him whom she bore they deem the son of Joseph, and testify that he has very many brethren (though he is an only one); they know not that he is man begotten of a human being without a Father, shrinking from what they hear, that he is God, the Son of God, without a mother. Among these and their blasphemies the virgin is not broken, does not wither, but her mind is strengthened by faith, and, flowering, grows young with the joy of the Spirit; she embraces that tender and unfading flower of the root, and imitates its comeliness with a zeal not so much of steps as of advances [0284C]. Finally, according to Solomon: « A joyful mind maketh a flowering age [n: (Prov. XVII)]. » As therefore the son, a flower and a lily rising among thorns, yet feels not the thorns, since he consents not to their malice by a like affection; so the mother and friend, having her converse among the daughters, knows not the darkness of the daughters, but, a daughter of light, shines, not having the works of darkness. Nay, that more may be said, not only do the thorns bring no harm to the lily, but the lily confers very much ornament upon the thorns; and the singular whiteness which in the lily, by a natural benefit, spreads itself abroad, pours over no small grace upon the nearer thorns. Did not the lily pour out an incomparable benefit on every side, when Christ poured forth devout prayers for them that persecuted him? when with the hand of mercy he scraped away the foulness [0284D] of the thorns, and turned the buckthorn into a flower, and the prickles into fruit? « Father, he says, pardon them, for they know not what they do [n: (Luc. XXIII)]. » [var: Vulg. Luke 23:34 *Pater, dimitte illis: non enim sciunt quid faciunt* — Migne prints *ignosce* for *dimitte*, and *quia nesciunt* for *non enim sciunt*] Drenched as with dew by this prayer, the roughness of the thorns grows meek, the inward dryness yields, benevolence grows green; after a new manner the little branch buds and puts forth leaves and flowers, and the little flower grows glad to imitate the lily, if but with a slight whiteness. Who knows not that thorns once dry sometimes flower out by the gift of the summer season, and that in them not so much the old prickles as fresh little flowers stand out; which, standing by the lily, though far unequal in greatness or comeliness, yet rejoice in a whiteness in some sort like, and in a nearer neighbourhood? To us therefore drawing near to Christ the beauty of the lily [0285A] contracts to itself nothing of foulness, but our foulness acquires from it no small grace for itself; and while the pleasantness of the lily thus admits us, *162* as the fulness of a planted garden, our solitude, once dry, now at last flowering, rejoices exceedingly. Foreseeing which, Isaias: « The desert and the pathless land shall be glad, he says, and the solitude shall exult; and it shall bud as the lily [n: (Isa. XXXV)]. » [var: Vulg. Isa. 35:1 *florebit quasi lilium*, "shall blossom as the lily"] Our mind is not undeservedly called a desert and a pathless land, when, forsaken by God, it is not inhabited by citizens of virtues or of works, when the kindly author walks not in it, loves not to behold it, marking that solitude to be beset by the prickles of vices as by thorns. But when divine grace as a spring mildness shall visit it, and shall call the white lily within the garden's plantings, assuredly it shall be glad, it shall exult with the gift of a new bounty [0285B], because, joined to the lily, it shall bud as a lily. For shrinking from the buckthorn, which the roughness of thorns was to bring forth — because a punishment fiercely raging awaits thorny manners — it shall bring forth sweet little flowers rivalling the lily in whiteness, and shall exult in the hope of fruit, having the first-fruits budding.
