Among thorns of this kind that white lily — nay, the brightness of eternal light — works wondrously, and rejoices to turn rough things into a plain, and the prickle into a flower; being about, by that goodness which is his own, one day to bring the matter to this, that the flower may bring forth fruit, and that he may rejoice in the fruit he shall enjoy. So also the friend is rightly believed to have her converse among the daughters, to bear care of them, to work their salvation the more anxiously; and those who were once wandering in mind, lifted up in eyes, shameless in tongue, barren of works, vouchsafing them at length her fellowship, she renders agile and fruitful. [0285C] For those whom she admits within the noble council-chamber of her hearing, she suffers not to remain barren as they stand by her; but instructing them with a word, fortifying them beforehand with a pattern, helping them with her intercession, she invites them to love, urges them to work, and gladdens them concerning the outcome. And thus those who once by the merit of their life had been daughters of Babylon, having entered into Jerusalem she renders daughters of vision; among whom, rejoicing, she sees the Bridegroom, loves to embrace him, and, as he the Bride, so she loves to venerate him with worthy praises. Whence she says: *As,* etc.



## CHAPTER XXI.

*As the apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons.* The Bride, hearing herself praised with the Bridegroom's worthy praises — from whom she has it that she is worthy to be honoured [0285D] with the heraldings of praise — lest she should seem ungrateful, hastens to render the like to her praiser, not being ignorant that reciprocal praises are pleasing to a lover. Whom she rightly enough willed to compare to an apple tree, which it is agreed shines out among the trees of the wood not so much more loftily as more excellently; for since the trees of the woods bring forth no fruit that can be suited to human eating, in the apple tree there is good fruit to be found, the best refreshment. For Christ is a tree whose strength sustains no harm, whose leaf yields not to a wind raging the more harshly [n: (Psal. I)]; whose all things prosper, and in its time it shall give fruit, wherewith it now invites those that hunger, and hereafter shall satisfy them. Christ is the tree of life to all who strongly lay hold on him, who hang themselves up with a strong desire to take his fruit; who strive not to lay hold with a wandering sense on whatever other things [0286A] shall meet them, since they mark not that from these hang the fruit of life, the health-bearing apples. I believe all men can be named trees of the wood, who, though they have the leaves of words, lack without doubt the saving fruit; because in them there is not salvation, there is not life, there is not an unfailing force of nature, but a certain barrenness of virtues, a guilt of the flesh by the fault of their begetting. For there is not so anything in them, as also from them, that is vital, commendable, gracious; there is not anything in one man that is saving to himself, fruitful to the rest; because whatever is in any man — if yet anything worthy and necessary be found in any man — whosoever truly makes trial knows it to be not of his own, but of Christ's. But Christ, a man among men, is not unfittingly compared to an apple tree, who, conceived [0286B] of the Spirit, is not accused of a barren nature; whose root is harmless, whose thicker shade hides us from the hurtful heat, whose fruit is more wholesome, whose most sweet odour spreads itself far abroad. Finally these three things can alike be found in the apple tree, nor is there another in the woods that rejoices to mark itself in like manner with these three; but in the apple tree especially shade, fruit, and odour are coupled by a natural binding, and from him who is God and man they proceed with a spiritual abundance. With which he refreshes, feeds, and soothes those who received him, who, piety being received, deserved to be called and to be sons; who, because they betook themselves from darkness to the light of faith, by a happy change passed over from trees of the wood into sons of God. Whom Christ marking, sons of God and heirs, is not confounded to call them brethren, to love them as coheirs [0286C] [n: (Matth. XXV)], that among many brethren he himself, the firstborn, may stand out with a princely honour, and that he who was once the only son may rejoice in a number of sons now plural. For he himself, God of God, was born the Father's only-begotten; but born man of a virgin, likewise his Mother's only-begotten; but, taking counsel for the elect, he opened the bosom of grace more bountifully, and those whom nature had denied him he made brethren by the benefit of adoption. Such brethren or sons the Son of God and of man himself so excels, as the fruit-bearing apple tree surpasses the trees of the woods; because both the fruitfulness of the apple tree *163* is set before their unfruitfulness, and no man whatsoever (however just he may have been) is compared to Christ. Understanding which, Peter, when the centurion deferred to him more than was right, and gave to a mere man what religious devotion owes to Christ [0286D], did not rashly usurp to himself what he knew was not his own, but declared who he was, how barren, how unlike the apple tree. « Cornelius, he says, falling down at his feet, adored him. But Peter lifted him up, saying: Rise, I myself also am a man, even as thou art [n: (Act. X)]. » [var: Vulg. Acts 10:26 reads *Petrus vero elevavit eum*, and the verse ends "I myself also am a man"; the added clause "even as thou art" is not in the received text] And below: « Announcing, he says, peace by Jesus Christ; he is the Lord of all [n: (ibid.)]. » You see that Peter neither wills nor endures to be adored by Cornelius, showing that a mere man ought not to be so honoured; giving to understand that this privilege is owed to Jesus Christ, that he alone, a man among men, should be venerated with divine obeisance. I deem that neither does an angel will such obeisance to be shown to himself, and, though greater than man, yet he is found to reverence man; in whom he now perceives [0287A] something new and untried by all generations past, hidden from the ages, uncovered in the fulness of our time. Whence, when John, rejoicing that very many things were shown him by the angel, and willing to venerate the shower of them with a worthy obeisance of humility, as he thought, fell at his feet, willing to show him the honour owed to greater ones, the angel, measuring himself worthily, was seen to shrink from it. « After I had heard, he says, and seen, I fell down to adore at the feet of the angel who showed me these things, and he said to me: See thou do it not [n: (Apoc. XXII)]. » And above: « I fell down, he says, before his feet, to adore him, and he said to me: See thou do it not, for I am thy fellow-servant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus. Adore God [n: (Apoc. XIX)]. » The angel wills not [0287B] to be made equal to Christ, the servant to the Lord, nor the unfruitfulness of the woods to be compared to the fruitful tree; but as the apple tree is agreed to be preeminent among the trees of the wood, so the angel knows Christ to be preeminent among the sons. Finally the angels too are sometimes named sons in the Scriptures, who are proclaimed always to see the face of God the Father; and according to Job the sons of God are read to have come to stand before the Lord, among whom that wicked angel Satan also is read to have been present [n: (Job I)]. Moses also: « He appointed, he says, the bounds of the peoples, according to the number of the children of Israel [n: (Deut. XXXII)]. » calling the children of Israel angels. Which another translation more evidently intimates, saying: « He set the bounds of the nations, according to the number of the angels of God. » For by some it is believed that God chose out of the nations as many to be saved [0287C] as there are found angels to have remained when the others fell; so that as many sons out of men may be prepared for him to see him, as are contained equally as sons among the angels that already see. But among these sons the Bride's Beloved is preeminent as an apple tree, because as in a mere man, so also in an angel there is no salvation; but in Christ, who, though less than the angels by reason indeed of the suffering of death, yet is far more exalted by reason of the union of God and man. Therefore when the angel had said to John. « See thou do it not, » he adds the cause, saying: « Thy fellow-servant his own, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus, adore God. » I, he says, am worthily the servant not only of God, but of God made man; the fellow-servant of thee and of them who by faith and by work bear testimony to Jesus; nor does it befit a servant to take away from his Lord his own [0287D] rights, since rather every creature ought to defer to the Creator. Do thou therefore adore not an angel, but God — God, who took not hold of an angel that he might save an angel, but took hold of the seed of Abraham that he might make him safe; God, who, emptying himself and taking the form of a servant [n: (Philip. II)], was found in habit as a man; according to which manhood, although he was found less than the angels, yet he is reckoned not much less, but a little less, if what Scripture declares be taken with an undeviating sense. « Thou hast made him a little less than the angels, says David [n: (Psal. VIII)]. » And Paul: « Him, he says, who was made a little lower than the angels by reason of the suffering of death [n: (Hebr. II)]. » Christ assuredly consists of God and man, but man of soul and [0288A] body; and the soul is the greater part of man — greater, I say, not in bulk, but in dignity and excellence, in that man was made in the soul to the image and likeness of God. But the body is the lesser, that is, the inferior part of man, according to which part Christ is found less than the angels, in that the angel's nature is not clothed with the wrapping of flesh that must die; but that immortal Spirit, strong in understanding, endowed with reason, may remain in that which it was made without the hurt of death. The spirit of man also is declared to be of the same or of a like nature, itself also endowed with reason, having a beginning, and not held by the narrowness of an end; but, poured into a body which is begotten corrupted with an original fault, by a wondrous and pitiable enough law it is weighed down by that body's deserts. Whence you have read: [0288B] « The body that is corrupted weigheth down the soul; and the earthly habitation presseth down the sense that museth upon many things [n: (Sap. IX)]. » The soul therefore, which is of the same or of a like nature with the angel (for creatures of this kind are as it were of one genus by the merit of reason), first indeed discolours its native beauty from the fellowship of the flesh, but afterwards, by the assent of the will, slips into the ruin of vices. But because the flesh of Christ, conceived of the Spirit, contracted no original fault to itself, it drew not the soul poured into it to a guilt which it had not known; but as both the conception and the converse kept the one unpolluted, so creation and the Creator's condescension rendered the other free from every *164* stain. But the soul, whose nature immortality, understanding, and reason so ennoble, and which neither [0288C] a prevailing incorporation nor any defilement dishonours — such a soul as Christ is to be believed to have assumed into a personal unity with himself, nor is he that assumed believed to have consumed the dignity of that which was assumed — than such a soul, I say, neither an angel nor any creature whatsoever is greater; he alone is greater, to whom, as Creator, no creature can be made equal. According to which soul Christ ought not to be esteemed less than the angels, which soul, strong with an inborn dignity, could be depraved by no vice; and although the maker did not confer this not-being-able upon the thing made in the making, yet in assuming he conferred it upon this soul by assuming. For what neither an angel nor a soul obtains by the privilege of its condition, by force of nature, the Creator conferred upon the creature to whom he willed, when he willed; and he who had first conferred upon the angels that none could fall further, or fear it, [0288D] afterwards gave to the soul which he assumed, that a holy confirmation should equally remain in its footing. It remains therefore that Christ be asserted less than the angels according to the flesh only, which, as was said before, is judged the other, the lesser or inferior part of man; and therefore he is rightly read to be made less, not much less than the angels, lest it should seem to be according to the whole man, but a little less, that mention may be known to be made of the flesh alone. But guilt has made us wretches much less than the angels, whose flesh conception and whose soul incorporation has so infected, that, guilty on both sides, we deservedly accuse our begetting, held by a hard law, in that the fault has been turned into nature. Whence Paul: « We are, he says, by nature children of wrath [n: (Ephes. II)]. » [var: Vulg. Eph. 2:3 *et eramus natura filii irae*, past tense: "and we were by nature children of wrath"] And [0289A] although the burden of guilt did not weigh down the good angels, but grace better confirmed them who were well created, yet among them, as also among men, Christ is to be believed to be preeminent, and, as the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so to obtain the primacy among sons of this kind. The angels indeed venerate Christ not as God only, but as God made man, in whom they contemplate the fruit of salvation and the protecting shade; through whom they see, and do not envy, that men pressed and oppressed by the heavy bundle of damnable offences are converted and return to the saving excellence of merits. Which neither crops, nor a ram, nor a calf, nor finally man or angel could work, nor was there another name given wherein we should be saved; but life so complains of faintness, and health of loss, that for [0289B] fruit or for healing every creature is ineffectual. Because therefore the barren wood did not give life, fruit, the efficacy of a mighty medicine, nor the craft of any workshop; and to a sick world they that promise are already hateful by the merit of their delay: there arose the tree of life, a fruit-bearing apple tree, in the midst of paradise. Whose sweeter shade, driving far off incitements, whose fruit freely refreshing those whom oppressive hunger had hurt, not only brought man back to the fellowship of the angel once lost, but also raised human nature above the angelic dignity. For the angel beholds our nature now made one with God in Christ, and, considering its fruit, worthily confesses himself barren; because he who was not able to restore either a falling fellow-angel or a lost man ought not to have compared himself to Christ, who was able [0289C] to do all things that he willed. Marking which, the Virgin rightly: *As the apple tree,* she says, *among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons.* Whereof she subjoins:



## CHAPTER XXII.

*Under the shadow of him whom I had desired, I sat; and his fruit was sweet to my throat.* If, she says, I have wished to commend my beloved, as you have heard, if I have wished to compare him with a fruitful apple tree among barren trees, do not think me uncertain of the things I set before you, and abounding in words but untried in things worthy of praise: by experiment I have learned that this apple tree is useful, that it is good; I have felt how great a refuge is in it, how great a refreshment, how great a salvation; because under its shadow it has been granted me not [0289D] only to be, but to sit, to flee the harmful heats, to obtain the grace of quiet. A good quiet, which the hand not of wrath pursuing but of grace loving has fashioned; over which not dark death, but the spreading apple tree has cast the shade of its boughs and leaves; in which the sinner is not buried in the tomb of despair or of ignorance, but the just mind is soothed with a sweet refreshment by the benefit of advancement. Wretched is that people which long willed to sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, forgetful of heavenly things, to cleave carnally to earthly; which, not knowing the living life, grew dark with the dim death of crimes, of which shadow the body is the death without end that is to follow. For sin, whereby the soul is pierced through as by a sword, and is found to be made further off from him who is life, is the first death of the soul, sadder in the time to come, [0290A] pleasant now; but the eternal damnation which justly follows is the second death. And that indeed is a death, and the shadow going before of the death that follows; but this is both a death and the truth of the shadow that went before. Although it may befall us to be in the first of them, it is not of counsel that we should sit, that is, that we should obtain a lost quiet with no regard to repenting. For he who sits in the shadow, and does not fear to forestall the death that is to come, when she coming hastens to find him *165* torpid, and whom she has found in the dark and as it were in her own right, she binds, and holds him, cast into prison, by the unloosable force of her binding. Yet nevertheless the vehement spirit, having pity on some, terrifies them and shakes them with a sudden sound; and the Dayspring, visiting from on high, floods them with the morning light; and when they have been led forth out of sleep and out of the shadow, harsh and nightlong, of a hard peril, a glad day receives them, [0290B] and a shadow sweeter and of the daytime. Now the day is faith enlightening: the virtue of hope is the sweeter shadow, in the foreknowing of the vision; in which, though it be good to be, and better to live, it is best to sit, until at last it be granted to obtain the full light more fully. He is in the shadow of the daytime who knows that not only present things but also things that follow have being; who sees through a glass that which it is agreed is not yet visibly at hand; who with undoubting faith understands that the invisible God is; who believes him to be a rewarder of them that hope in him. Paul: « It behoveth, he says, him that cometh to God to believe that he is; and that to them that seek him he be a rewarder [n: (Hebr. XI)]. » Without this faith no one shall please God, nor is that conscience worthy whose knowledge shall not hold God; because he also that is ignorant, as you have read, is read to be ignored, and in truth [0290C] he who is not known cannot be accepted by one who does not know him [n: (I Cor. XIV)]. Therefore the Prophet: « He believed, for which cause he also spoke [n: (Psal. CXV)]. » [var: Vulg. Ps. 115:1 *Credidi propter quod locutus sum*, first person — "I have believed, therefore have I spoken"] Thou art thyself my God. Without faith, therefore, no one can be just; nay, that I may say more, he who has not believed ought not even to be said to be; and he who is not, consequently is not in the shadow either. Of such it is written: « Deliver not thy kingdom to them that are not [n: (Esther. XIV)]. » [var: Vulg. *sceptrum tuum*, "thy sceptre," and with the vocative *Domine*] He is rightly said not to be, who knows not that God is, to whom, though he has been made, he by whom he was made is not yet known; who with blinded mind is driven far from the desert of existing, not having yet attained that faith which is the shadow, or the beginning, of subsisting. Of which Paul: « If only, he says, we hold the beginning of his substance firm unto the end [0290D] [n: (Hebr. III)]. » He therefore who has faith, holding firmly that God is, both is, and is in the shadow; but it is not enough to be there. Nay, he must labour, who is already agreed to be by the merit of faith, that living in it he may deserve also to be just. For to be in faith is not yet to be just; but to live by faith, or to live in faith, is reckoned for justice, since a dead faith, even though it does not love, does work. For love is the life of faith, and therefore not he who believes, but he who loving believes, is proved to live; and living in faith he is worthily praised, and is proclaimed commendable for justice. Whence by Habacuc: « My just man, he says, liveth by his own faith [n: (Habac. II)]. » [var: Vulg. Hab. 2:4 *iustus autem in fide sua vivet*, "the just man shall live in his faith," without *meus*; the possessive with *ex* is the wording of Heb. 10:38] Even one that is not just will be in faith, but none save the just shall live in faith; because he too is in faith who says: « Lord, Lord [n: (Matth. VII)], » and yet it is not [0291A] opened to him; and he lives in faith who, doing the will of the Lord, is heard. And because faith is not the presence of the thing wished for, but the substance of the thing to be hoped for and, as was said before, the shadow of the vision [n: (Hebr. II)], the just, whom their own merits do not yet admit to that same vision, promise themselves meanwhile not so much to be as to live in its shadow. « In his shadow, they say, we shall live among the Gentiles [n: (Thren. IV)]. » [var: Vulg. *umbra tua*, "in thy shadow," second person] In the shadow the just shall live, when in faith they shall love to work, when justly, piously, holily they shall give diligence to their converse; when it shall be given them with a living faith to rejoice among the Gentiles, that is, among men, to whom it is not yet given to glory in the vision found among the angels. They shall live indeed in the shadow, when him whom it is agreed was made flesh in the womb of the Virgin they shall hold with firm faith to have been born God before the ages; [0291B] when him who was found a man to suffer hard things for men they shall love as being God, coeternal with and altogether like to the majesty of the Father. Lastly they shall live, when, as though the things which that man willed to endure unworthily among men were put behind them, they shall understand and shall love God blessed unto the ages to be pre-eminent above all things; when, leaving behind what any animal men can see and hold, they shall have before their eyes chiefly that which none but the spiritual deserve to have [n: (ibid.)]. Therefore they set this first: The Spirit before our face, Christ the Lord. Christ the Lord is held to be a spirit before our face then, when our faith beholds him now not according to the flesh but according to the spirit; when, understanding that his flesh alone [0291C] profits nothing, it knows him who quickeneth to be God, a spirit [n: (Joan. VI)]. For the very many things that are preached of him according to the flesh, they who still savour the flesh embrace too childishly; and the hinder parts of Christ they do not put last, but with faith injured, not knowing the order, they put them first. When Peter heard the nearness of his Passion preached, he was found to embrace the flesh a little more tenderly than the spirit; and before his face he had Christ indeed, but a man about to die, not a spirit raising up, not the God of life about to give the dead back again. « Far be it, he says, from thee [n: (Matth. XVI)], » this shall not be, thou shalt not die. And he: « Go, he says, behind; thou savourest not the things that are of God [n: (ibid.)]. » [var: Vulg. Matt. 16:23 *Vade post me, Satana*, and the name is not omitted; *retro* is the word of Mark 8:33] Therefore Paul, removing his hearers from the things that are man's, wishes them to be made readier for the things that are [0291D] God's, understanding that the things of the flesh are by right judgment to be set behind, and that God and the things that are his are to be set before the face. « That you may walk, he says, worthily of God [n: (I Thess. II)]. » And elsewhere: « And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer [n: (II Cor. V)]. » In this shadow, or faith, in which it is granted even to the unjust to be, but to live, as was said before, to none save the just, there is indeed much labour, while it is lived in with fear; for wretched man knows not whether he be worthy of hatred or of love [n: (Eccle. IX)]. But the virgin Mother, who before all found grace with God, keeps sabbath in it, obtains a happy jubilee; and not only lives (which is common to all that labour) but, as one secure, *166* sits, which she obtains as her own by resting. For she it [0292A] is upon whom that Holy Spirit came, in whom the power of the Most High found out for itself a pleasing rest; and setting her far from fault or from fear by the veiling of the shadow, he conferred upon her, in love alone, a peaceful sitting. *Under the shadow,* she says, *of him whom I had desired, I sat.* With desire she had desired that God the Son of God should come unto her, that a grace untried by all should come before her childbearing as it came before the conception; that kissing her, whom he had kissed, he should fortify her with the seal of chastity, and should keep, as her mind, so also her flesh, with the virgin flower unhurt. Which being received, the Virgin, now knowing neither fault nor fear, sits as it were upon a throne under the shadow of a more gracious refreshing; and while the rest labour below, whom the want of merits still cramps, she in the great furnished upper room already tastes an unspeakable sweetness. *And his fruit,* she says, *[0292B] was sweet to my throat.* The fruit of the shadow, or of the overshadowing Spirit, is the eternal sweetness, which the Virgin's palate already feels and her inward mind more sweetly tastes; but that savour is still held as it were in the throat, while the belly gapes for it, and its greed is not filled. In this life assuredly whatever of the sweetness from above is foretasted, whatever of the divine and incorporeal the mind beset with flesh experiences, is still as it were in the tasting, whereby the desire of the taster is soothed; it has not yet come to the belly, where perfect satiety is found. Therefore rightly the Virgin, to show that she has attained no little sweetness, and that so long as we live here every sweetness is unfinished, *his fruit,* she says, *was sweet to my throat;* not yet [0292C] to my belly, because both for the present she rejoices to be delighted with a most sweet tasting, and looks to be satisfied unto perfection, when his glory shall have appeared. And whoever tries the office of eating a little more attentively knows that food in the throat is indeed not yet swallowed, but is being swallowed; and that the swallowing is so near that it cannot, or scarcely can, be called back outward to the mouth, so that the eater reckons as eaten what he has felt to be already turning in his throat. So too the Virgin, while she is still engaged in this life under the law of mortals, is kindled with a love so sweet beyond other mortals, that the fruit of love, or of the beloved, already grows sweet in her throat, and, confidence prevailing, no threatening fear grows bitter there. For she has already so experienced that highest thing, that desirable good of the world to come, that, reaching out to what is perfect, [0292D] she is not uncertain of the remainder of that same good; and she already holds in her throat what we, still far unequal, hunger after; what we, still needy, scarcely foretaste on the tip of the tongue or on the lips. For neither we nor the like of us have yet been brought so far as to rejoice more fully, being led into that sanctuary of God; whereof the virgin, still living in the flesh, takes to herself no small confidence, and what is to be more fully hereafter she already confidently presumes as though it were done.



## CHAPTER XXIII.

*The king brought me into the wine storeroom: he set charity in order in me.* [var: Vulg. Cant. 2:4 *introduxit me in cellam vinariam*: no *rex*, and *cellam*, "wine cellar," for the printed *cellariam*] Whom he names king, and why, I recall that I said above, when the Virgin remembered that she had been brought into the king's storerooms; which, though they are worthily reckoned filled with many riches, are nevertheless not [0293A] recorded to be storerooms of wine. But now the Virgin declares that she is brought into the wine cellar, hinting that with the passing of time she is led on to an advancement of conscience; wherein she not only rejoices already over the gift of grace received, but is made drunk with an incomparable gladness as with abundance of wine. For if that most excellent cup of which you have read [n: (Psal. XXII)] makes drunk any just men you please, so that, the Spirit falling from heaven, it makes them talkative as men wet with new wine [n: (Act. II)] — of what merit do we judge the virgin to be, in whose womb God hid himself, and to whom, brought in, the whole wine cellar pours itself out more graciously? How could she who was brought in fail to have a mind made drunken, for whom no narrower cup, no wisdom mingled wine in a bowl, but an overflowing cellar, a house of wine, put forth a spreading richness and flooded her more richly [0293B] as the rush of a river floods a city? For the Most High, willing that his own proper tabernacle should be adorned, that a holy place holier than the rest should be graced with worthy virtues, did not bring out little gifts to her with a grudging hand from his inner sanctuary, but more graciously brought her in within the secret places of his sanctuary. Where the one beloved is joined to the one lover alone, and out of that fountain, or in it, draws waters with a fuller joy [n: (Isa. XII)]; by which, washed, she is made white; by which, drinking, she more sweetly grows glad, is made drunk with joy, and warms mightily as with wine. But this drunkenness does not disturb the mind, does not confound the virgin soul, does not darken the memory, does not take away knowledge but pours it in; it thinks no evil, deals not perversely, loves equity, stirs up no anger, brings in no hatred, nourishes love, [0293C] sets charity in order [n: (I Cor. XIII)]: *He set,* she says, *charity in order in me.* Of no small merit is she, of no small holiness in fine, in whom not only charity but also the order of charity is pre-eminent; and while in very many others love is diffused, in her especially the diffusion abides unconfused. For most men, though they love, yet do not keep order in loving, but either darkened by ignorance or weighed down by a heavier negligence, *167* love more what should have been loved less, or less what should have been loved more, or set in the last place what was worthily to be set first. But the Virgin, prudently taught in all these things, and hindered by no stains of negligence from fulfilling what she knew, loves herself, as is worthy, in the Lord, [0293D] loves, as it is written, every neighbour as herself [n: (Matth. XXII)]. And among those whom faith or nature makes neighbours, whom the authority of the written law commands to be loved with measure, the prudent Virgin knows how to discern whom she should embrace with less and whom with more love, to whom she should defer less, whom she should reverence with greater diligence. And lastly, in Christ also, whom she conceived of the Holy Spirit and brought forth, in whom a personal unity coupled God and man, the true Mother so loved both with a discerning judgment that charity did not err, which that same Son set in order in her. For first she loved God, whom she knew to be the Creator of things heavenly and earthly, and the most orderly lover of the things he had created, united to true flesh and in a wondrous manner made man — she loved him with her whole heart, [0294A] with all her strength, without measure. For in this love no measure whatever is bidden to be kept, and no bound; and how much God is to be loved, no writer has taught, nor Holy Scripture; but whoever is found to have expressed the manner of loving more subtly is seen to have taught not how much, but out of how much, he ought to be loved. « Out of thy whole, he says, heart, and out of thy whole soul, and out of all thy strength [n: (Luc. X)]. » This is the measure — if measure it be — wherewith the Virgin mother rejoices to love God in Christ; the depth whereof human speech cannot clearly express; the sweetness whereof, though a more fervent soul may somehow experience it, yet one who may unfold it in words is not easily to be found. Out of all therefore that she had, that she could, she loved in her Son; to the incarnate deity she applied [0294B] her mightier power, her readier affection; to every creature whatsoever she preferred the Creator with worthy reverence, and held God united to man more pleasing than all things. But the man, whom she knew to be her own virgin flesh, conceived without man, born without any groan of his mother, and by nature and natural binding to be her own neighbour, she loved as herself, as she had read it worthy to do. For since no man hates his own flesh [n: (Ephes. V)], as you recollect that you have read, although he may know that some fault or other has been present to that same flesh — how greatly must we believe that the Virgin mother loved the Son, in whom fault had nothing, and nature was astonished to have lost its ingrown right? For the Virgin in conceiving bore no embrace, no coupling; in bearing she felt no pain of body, no wounding; [0294C] the original guilt, which of old had been turned as it were into nature, being driven far off grieved, and could by no means take hold of such a begetting. Of old the law of sin was wont to come before every woman about to bear, and drove both mother and son like tributaries to the usury; upon all alike that were born it stamped the striking of its own coinage, nor was there any so happy as to escape this pressure. The Virgin alone, bringing forth in wondrous manner a singular firstborn, in conceiving and in bearing did not undergo the general sentence; she rejoiced to have such a neighbour, nay, such a Son, in whom the injury of the origin could obtain nothing of its own. This neighbour therefore the Virgin [sic: *reete*] loves as herself, and, if it be lawful to believe it, she must be said [0294D] to love him more than herself, because she judges that so great a man, above every man, is to be loved, and to be embraced more tenderly and more eagerly than herself as well as than all others. And what by the Spirit's teaching she understands, and understanding loves, must be done, by the working of that same Spirit she is not powerless or ineffectual to fulfil; and therefore the Son, the man whom in a manner unspeakable she brought forth out of herself, as she understands that he is to be loved, so she can love, and does love, more than herself. We wretched ones assuredly either cannot grasp with the understanding the things that are perfect and highest, or, for fulfilling them, have not a perfect and effectual grace; and therefore perhaps God, pitying our infirmities and ourselves, commands us for the time to love any man as ourselves. But the Virgin, full of God, rich with the gift of a fuller grace, [0295A] is carried up into the hill country and to a step of loftier merit; and the man whom she knew to be born of her materially, hindered by no stains of origin, clean in flesh and by the Spirit united in kind to God who is inaccessible to all, she loves above all whom she understands to be endowed with sparer merits and grace, holding it worthy not only not to prefer herself to him, but not even to compare herself with him in love. This order of loving he who is loved himself inspired, and in the loving Mother he set a chief charity in order, so that her whom in his own birth the Son had wondrously granted to be both a virgin and fruitful, he might in a manner no less wondrous render, if not equal in merits, at least second. For inferior to Christ alone, she is pre-eminent above all the rest in the light of holiness; but holiness is made bright by nothing save the excellence [0295B] of charity, which, the more subtly and expressly it grasps the necessary order, the more perfectly and effectually it shows itself Christ's neighbour. This benefit Christ works in the wine cellar, into which the Virgin, being brought, rejoices to burn with the fire of charity; judging nothing more gracious, nothing more delightful, than to be aflame; nothing in the present more wholesome than to be smitten, or to languish, with the heat of charity. Whereof she adds: *Stay me up,* etc. *168*



## CHAPTER XXIV.

*Stay me up with flowers, compass me about with apples, for I languish with love.* They who love unlawful things, and are not yet reckoned to have possession of them, are declared to sicken and to pine away by the putting off of their desire; and their [0295C] ruined mind runs into the troubles of languishing, if the fulfilment of their vow does not come to the aid of their wretched will. Whence Ammon, who greatly loved Thamar the sister of Absalon, when he could not yet fulfil what he had evilly coveted, fell sick; and despairing that the wickedness he sought after could be brought to effect, he went day by day, wasted with leanness, toward his failing. « It came to pass, he says, that Ammon the son of David greatly loved Thamar the sister of Absalon, and pined away for her exceedingly, so that he fell sick for the love of her. To whom Jonadab: Why, said he, art thou thus wasted with leanness, O son of the king, day by day? And Ammon said: « I love Thamar the sister of Absalon [n: (II Reg. XIII)]. » If he sickens and pines away who is weighed down by an unlawful love, if he who is pressed by the desire of Venus is wasted day by day, how are we to believe that the Virgin mother, loving [0295D] the Bridegroom, sickens, she who fails toward her salvation not by the incest of Venus but by the heat of a chaste wound? For she loves, and in loving, as by a wound, she slips into a kind of failing, while she does not yet lay hold, and yet so strains the edge of her mind toward what is perfect that, not content with what she has, she pours out her whole desire upon what is to be had, and as though she obtained nothing, so she burns to cleave to the things to be obtained. Reaching therefore toward what she wishes for, and not yet feeling it consummated, she languishes and fails, and cannot obtain what she desires; she seeks after it and awaits it, and still complains that she has not the effect of it. What is healthier than this languishing, what more languid than this health, could the Virgin experience, at least in this life, who, unwilling that anything savouring of earth should be found within her mind, wished to cleave with unbending embraces to God alone, [0296A] and was still constrained, perhaps for the sake of others, to remain here? She wished, and was not able, unbreakably to enjoy God, to be loosed from the heavy body, not to be worn down by labour, to rejoice in jubilee; judging it good to enjoy invisible goods, when as yet, so it seems, she must needs be held by things visible. And so to one thus willing and not able, her converse in the flesh is somewhat burdensome, yet assuredly to the maidens who are to be nourished it is not a little fruitful; because the example and teaching of the Virgin profited the holy apostles, while through her among them the order of life and the discipline of manners flourished. And she, marking that she is put off from that which she loves the more, wishes some consolations to be brought to her waiting; and the maidens who live with her she invites to advancement, that seeing it she may bear her own unfinished state, as it were, more patiently. [0296B] If, she says, the presence of a perfect rest does not yet receive me, if faith cannot yet pass over into the rule of vision; if impossibility languishes, because possibility is not yet consummated; if I am afflicted with groaning so long as imperfection is not healed by perfection; I wish at least that you meanwhile be advanced to fitting profits, and by my word as well as by my example deserve the same blessedness along with me. If that highest and discerning provider of things wills me to be here longer, if by a deep counsel he wills my presence to profit you; if he puts me off from glory, I do not accuse the good pleasure of him who puts me off, and so long as it shall please him I do not refuse the labour laid upon me. Do you meanwhile, while there is time, come together to the bed, as it were, of my sickness, and stay me up with spring flowers, [0296C] that is, with your good affections, as I labour under a desire deferred; put far from you the old dryness, the harshness of winter; and with a flowering diversion and a springtime solace warm again one who is languid with the heat of love. For it will be no small consolation, no slight refreshment, to one who burns; it will be reckoned a poultice, or oil, or a binding, to one who is sick, if, the winter frost being driven far off, you flower with the beauty of spring; if after the flowers of affections you bring forth the riper fruits of works. A good tree indeed is graced in the welcome season of spring with the flowers of its beauty, and not content with that grace is afterwards laden with the fruit of works; wherewith the country husbandman, who had laboured in it, seeing himself compassed about, rejoices that the labour he bestowed is repaid with a fruitful gift. So [0296D] the Virgin also wills that the maidens who are with her hold the place of a good tree, and, set in the garden of the Bridegroom, wills them to flower with faith and desire; and with the passing of time to abound in good works, stayed up and compassed about wherewith she may await the Bridegroom the more richly, the longer she awaits him. For the more shall deserve to profit by her word and example, and shall be held in her company when the Bridegroom shall have come, the richer and the more festive shall she herself appear to him at his coming; and not only for her own merits, but for theirs also, shall she obtain a greater glory. Rightly therefore she desires and demands to be stayed up with flowers and compassed about with apples, since she does not yet know God face to face; that meanwhile she may rejoice over the advancement of those whom she instructs, and, when the time shall have come, may glory the more over them and with them. And she asks not only to be stayed up [0297A] with flowers, but also to be compassed about with apples, because with a flower and no fruit no hungry man can be filled; and although the latter of these necessarily comes after the former, yet the flower is a pleasant plaything to the sight, but assuredly is found not sufficient for the eating. And indeed, *169* as without virtue the appearance of piety is not fruitful, so faith without work is read and understood to be idle *(Jacob II)*; and affection does not suffice, which, if it have time and place, is not brought through to effect; and a good understanding is to all, not to them that have understanding, but to them that do it [n: (Psal. CX)]. *Stay* therefore *me,* she says, *up with flowers, compass me about with apples,* that I may rejoice when I have heard you say: « We ought to obey God rather than men [n: (Act. V)]. » And this: « We cannot but speak the things which we have heard and seen [n: (Act. IV)]. » Let me rejoice too when I have felt [0297B] you going rejoicing from the presence of the council [n: (Act. V)], because you were accounted worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus. *Stay me up,* I say, *for I languish with love,* not with an injury of the head, not with a palsy of the limbs, but with love; not with the straitness of a fever, not with any trouble of the body, but with love; than which nothing more burning, nothing more vehement, can anyone experience, while what is loved is tasted, and is seen and not held, is believed to be present and is ardently sought, and cannot be found. But wherein both his presence may be felt and his absence grieved over, she straightway subjoins; and the good will of him who is present, and the delay of him who is absent, she thus sets forth in a single little verse:



## CHAPTER XXV.

*His left hand is under my head; and his right hand shall embrace [0297C] me.* The left hand of the Bridegroom under the head of the Bride shows him present, but the right hand that shall embrace rather than embraces hints that he is absent; so that while a sad complaint is drawn out over his absence, there is good cause to rejoice over his presence, such as it is. For when he had said, *His left hand is under my head,* he subjoined, *and his right hand shall embrace me,* not: embraces me: hinting thereby that the benefit of the left hand is already held in present possession, but that the present embrace of the right hand is not yet had. And because the Virgin had said that she languished with the burning of love, that it may agree with her languishing she hints by the words that follow that she is lying down, since she declares the left hand not to be laid upon her head but placed under it; and it is certain that a comforting hand is placed under one who lies, not under one who stands. And so in the Gospel the servant of the Centurion [0297D] is declared to lie; and if you ask the cause, it is that he is palsied and tormented. For whom that same Centurion hastens by a messenger sent to come before the Lord, praying that he would deign with his most mighty word to help him as he lay. « Lord, he says, my servant lieth at home [n: (Matth. VIII)]. » Why does he lie? Palsied, he says, and grievously tormented. What wilt thou have done for thee? « I am not, he says, worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed [n: (ibid.)]. » Elsewhere too we read that a very great multitude lay in five porches, and no cause is put in but the various sickness of their bodies; who wait for an angel to come down into the pool after the accustomed manner to move the water, so that he who has come down first after the moving of the water may, his body being washed, feel the healing. [0298A] « In these, » he says, porches, « there lay a great multitude. » Why it lay, he sets forth: « Of them that languished. » Why in the porches, he adds: « Of them that waited for the moving of the water [n: (Joan. V)]. » If therefore the multitude, if the Centurion's servant are declared to lie, in that they are held by languishing or by palsy, it is not out of tune that of the Virgin, who declares that she languishes by the violence of love, it should be understood also that she lies, which belongs to one who languishes. And to her languishing and lying the Bridegroom does not absent himself longer, but the beloved presents himself to his beloved with a welcome kindness; and lest love should languish too hardly, and languishing bear a harder delay, he puts his left hand under her head, softer than a pillow or any couch. The left hand of the Bridegroom (as some assert) is temporal prosperity, strength, riches, beauty, birth, learning in letters; and whatever [0298B] in this world seems for a time to smile upon us, which no man can obtain unless God give it. Which things are for that reason quite fitly called the left hand, because in this present life such things are not denied to the evil as well as to the good; and those things above all are sought after with all their striving, which are set at the left hand of the strict Judge in that true and severe judgment. All which things the Bridegroom, being present, puts under the head of the Bride, when he sets her holy mind above all things transitory; and what every perverse man with corrupt judgment reckons the highest allurements, the Virgin presses down and despises, judging them loss for Christ. For as the man who craves such things exults and dances in the getting of them, so — nay, far otherwise — the wise Virgin rejoices in the despising of them; and whereby she pleases the Bridegroom, in that at his regard, as at a head [0298C] set over her, she spurns all the rest, thereby the other displeases him, while he lays himself down under those same transitory things. But the right hand of the Bridegroom is that more fruitful and living sweetness of grace which the animal man, blinded in heart, does not perceive; but he alone knows it, nay the Spirit of him, immortal, to whom the spiritual unction gives the understanding which it teaches for knowledge. This therefore the Virgin, set as yet in this body, already tastes; but lest she take it in with a widened bosom, the presence of the flesh cramps it for her; this she perceives, and having perceived it rejoices to be greatly delighted; she is delighted and hungers, and hungering is not yet able to be filled. This delight assuredly has here a beginning but not an end; it pours itself into them that love, to them that desire it it *170* promises an end; but to them that worthily persevere it gives that [0298D] end whose beginning knows no trouble, whose consummation knows no end. Beholding which the Prophet: « Delights, he says, at thy right hand even to the end [n: (Psal. LI)]. » Which right hand, since to one who loves and waits it is not yet more fully conferred, but the present life, as it were the left hand, the more troublesome as it is the longer, is set before it: this she feels and does not consent to, but by the excellence of her mind rises above the enjoyment of it; that other she hopes for, and affirms as to come, which, though not in time, yet by its own worth is already preferred. *His right hand,* she says, *shall embrace me.* He who has not wholly denied me his presence or his coming, while he has brought into contempt those temporal things which are given by him, shall be seen to present himself to me far more fully and far more delightfully, when his right hand and unfailing life shall deign to embrace me.

[0299A]There are those who would have another sense found in the left hand set beneath: namely that there are signified the spiritual things which divine grace wills to bestow upon the Bride; wherewith, while she lives here, the Bridegroom loves to mark her out, and to soothe with their sweet refreshment one who labours under the sun. For because she confessed that she languished with the heat of love, and, held by languishing, seemed, as was said above, to lie; and that the languor of one lying down should not, with the delay pressing, sink into weariness, the Bridegroom puts his left hand under her head, that upon it she may lay herself down in her languor. The Virgin grieves indeed that the sight of her Maker is not yet more fully granted her; she wishes to be dissolved, for that sight is inaccessible to all mortals; under the heavy delay her inner mind languishes and lies down as though wearied; and firm faith, a surer hope, an unwearied charity put themselves beneath her. The welcome fellowship of these virtues, [0299B] or their fellowly grace, their present carefulness, their faithful keeping, their spiritual consolation, when it does not suffice that the Virgin be compassed about with flowers or apples, fulfil for her languid mind, for her head as if wearied, the office of a bolster. While the time weighs upon me, she says, while the days are evil, let me here rest a little; while I languish with love, while I lie in languor, let me lie hid in your lap. Here is my rest, here my dwelling, until at last I grow old in a hundredfold, not of years but of merits; and when that is fulfilled, let the long languor give way — I shall be made young as the eagle. For from that time and thenceforth, after the poet's manner, I shall count my years like Nestor upon my right hand; nay, passing over from the left to the right, after the Prophet, I shall watch from the morning; in the morning I shall stand watching, and shall contemplate him whom I have desired, or rather my own desire; and under his right hand, [0299C] when his own glory appears, I shall be satisfied [n: (Psal. XVI)]. Then no longer shall the left hand, that is, the consolation of present virtues, be put under my languid head, but the right hand and the eternal sight of God shall be conferred in fulness; which shall embrace me standing and seeing with dearer arms, shall surround me wholly, and nothing anywhere shall be left languid. But meanwhile, while I await the coming glory of that right hand, I will not despise the grace already present, nor the solace of the left; but lying hid in it I shall be glad according to the place and the time; and when faith shall have passed into vision, and hope into the thing itself, I shall glory. And the Bridegroom, considering the Virgin so provoked with love, and lulled asleep in the soft lap of the left hand under the hope of the right, speaks thus: *I adjure,* etc.



## CHAPTER XXVI.

[0299D]

*I adjure you, O daughters of Hierusalem, that you stir not up, nor make the beloved to awake, till she herself will.* The Bridegroom, speaking to the maidens, shapes himself to our manners, and after the manner of men calls them to witness rather hardly, and adjures them; knowing that negligence or forgetfulness sometimes shuts and stops the ears of the weak, and that the transgression of commandments does not go long unpunished. Warning them therefore lest he be thought to command negligently, and lest they should not take diligent care to keep a commandment as though it were a very light one, he binds them more hardly and puts in an oath, that upon those in whom infirmity works sloth the sacrament may strike fear. I will not, he says, that the beloved, under whose head I have put the spiritual left hand, to whom, resting in grace, I have given to look for the eternal glory; I will not, he says, that you call her back [0300A] to business or to temporal care, until she herself shall have seen that the same care is made wholesome for you. For she knows better when she ought to be free for spiritual leisure or for spiritual business, when she should take counsel for you by word and by temporal foresight; when she should read more devoutly, pray more urgently, meditate more closely, when she should turn herself back to you, of whom she is not held forgetful. And when she shall have seen her return and her presence to be needful for you, she who assuredly loves not so much to be set forth to you as to profit you, she will do a kind of injury to her spiritual leisure, and will change necessary acts into voluntary ones. I will therefore that you bear evenly with her return to you until she will it; for she will will it when she shall have seen a fitting time to press upon you: knowing that your business must not be utterly let go, and that her own leisure [0300B] must indeed be held to chiefly, yet must sometimes be broken off. They who in the Church are set over the rest in care and office are instructed by this teaching, if they will attend to it more diligently: namely that with the highest zeal they should give diligence to spiritual leisure, and should not leap back from it at the blandishments and enticements of things temporal. For the most part we are so hindered toward spiritual things by such cords of *171* negligence, and are found so lukewarm, or rather so cold, toward them, that we make more haste to run about, to hear, to see, to be full of words, judging nothing more grievous, nothing more troublesome, than to sit, to read, to write, to meditate. And, to heap up the evil, if we have seen any unwilling to cleave to worldly business, spurning running about, speaking more sparingly, abhorring rumours; giving their labour to reading, sweating more gladly at meditation, and, if they have understood anything, committing it to a remembering writing: [0300C] these, with drawn-in lip, hooked nostril, and lifted brow, we mock at; and, since stones are lacking, with a slanderous tongue we stone them. Why is this? unless because we do not hear the warnings of the Bridegroom wherewith he adjures the daughters of Hierusalem, or rather, hearing them, with malice running to meet us we in no wise obey; doubtless drawing upon ourselves the wrath of him who, a Judge more severe, hates and pursues them that detract! « The man that detracted, he says, against his neighbour, him did I persecute [n: (Psal. C)]. » Yet nevertheless it is proper to those who are seen to preside over the rest in the Church, not to lord it over the clergy, but to show themselves a pattern to their subjects; not to entangle the mind with outward cares or with worldly business, but with a mind bent down to serve spiritual studies; not to be present willingly at the causes of men of the courts, nor at the [0300D] contentions of worldly men, but to be at hand with a fitting purpose for the study of letters and for spiritual leisure. Let their whole will betake itself to those better things; let necessity, not pleasure, bring them back to these lower ones: in the former let them be hidden, that they may diligently draw the hidden things of wisdom; to the latter let them be brought back, patiently, for the sake of their brethren and neighbours. But they who wish to detract from such men, and to draw them back from their spiritual purpose, let them fear the warnings of the Bridegroom, whereby both the Bride is helped and the daughters of Hierusalem are adjured; because their studies will not be hurt by our envious murmuring, and the indignation and the animadversion of the strict Judge will pursue the wicked detractors. But what is this, that the daughters of Hierusalem are adjured by the roes and the harts of the fields, as though such animals were known [0301A] to be feared or loved, so that by a mention made of them more diligently those women might be more attentively moved to hold the bidding they have heard? And who would believe that the commandment of one so adjuring should be kept the more carefully, and not rather be reckoned useless and altogether frivolous, since the reverence of any oath scarcely holds a man, if that by which he is adjured is reckoned of no weight or moment? But in this play, although carnal and contemptible things seem to be named, yet in them a sounder understanding loves to search out spiritual things; and abhorring what the literal surface sounds and clamours, it holds great only that which the spiritual content shows to them that seek it. To the roe, then, as men say, this is implanted by nature, that she is not content with plains and valleys for her pasture; but she seeks the lofty tops of the mountains [0301B] with the utmost care, as though nowhere else she would find a sufficiency to please her. The wide breadth of the fields, the low and sunken valleys, granted from the beginning by the laws of nature to all cattle everywhere, she passes by with a kind of disdain; she goes to rocks inaccessible to the rest, and there she loves to feed delightfully, to take leaps confidently, to make unwearied stay. Whereby, not unfittingly, that virtue can be figuratively signified which, not content with transitory goods, is zealous to gaze upon the highest and heavenly things; which, going beyond those things in which the common infirmity of many is seen to linger, both wills and is able more graciously to embrace certain steep places inaccessible to lesser men. Which, forgetting the troubles of the present life as things put behind it, engrafted among the companies of the angels, nay, going forth in desire beyond the angels, [0301C] having climbed above the flatness of things below, is caught up by the love of things above, and hanging from the highest peaks is fed with the sweetness of things eternal. But the hart, which with hunger and a fitting greed devours serpents and venom, which the other animals abhor and judge alien from their food, signifies that virtue of the mind which loves to swallow up deadly sins, and to bring an eating diligence to the destroying of them. For there are some who do not indeed reach the excellence of contemplating, but who gird themselves with a strong sword to destroy vices; who, as it were the food of bread, devour the people of the lost, and by a wholesome eating bring to nothing the force of offences. And when the fraud of them that assail has stuck in these men like an arrow, they compel it by an art quickly sought out to leap back; and they do not suffer the hurtful iron long to have mastery in the wound, [0301D] but when it is drawn out they grow strong again by a saving medicine. But because it is agreed that this virtue belongs to men that are humble, whom it is agreed to be not rough with wickedness but smooth with the good will of their manners; who, though they have done great things, yet say that they are unprofitable servants: therefore he says harts of the fields, namely such as strongly embrace the broad commandment of the twofold love, and run the way of the commandments when they are enlarged in heart and mind. And lastly, when harts set themselves to pass through [0302A] the deeps of waters, in that very passage they so set themselves before one another in order that the head of the one that follows is laid upon the haunches of the one that goes before, and that same one in like manner puts itself under another that follows. But he who has set himself before them all, and is stayed up by no forerunner, when he is hindered by weariness from bearing the labour of swimming and of carrying, leaving him who is placed beneath, hastens to betake himself to the last place, whom he knows to be still free and not bearing another that follows. So, bearing one another's burdens in turn, they busy themselves to fulfil the law of Christ [n: (Galat. VI)]; imitating a building in which stone loves to hold up stone; whose holding up the affection of charity works, *172* by whose strong ship they are drawn out of shipwreck and led to the harbour of their will. *I adjure you,* he says, *daughters of Jerusalem, [0302B] by the roes and the harts of the fields.* You, he says, whom it beseems to be daughters of Hierusalem, that is of peace, without which the sight of God can in no wise be present to you, by those virtues whereby you both tread down vices and love rewards, I will adjure you, that you presume not, by a counsel led astray, to go against the sounder desire of the Virgin. By those virtues, I say, which are lifted higher in searching out and contemplating God, and by those likewise which are stretched more widely into the love of a neighbour, I adjure you, lest you be found to assail with troubles a neighbour who is at rest, and to fight against God, in whose left hand she reclines. For this rest of hers is useful and welcome to her who rests, and not unwelcome to me who know more fully what is expedient for whom; and therefore I will both that she, while it is time, give diligence to quiet, and that you who are weaker be kept from [0302C] murmuring or from judging. Who will grant me not only that I stir not up nor make to awake any that sleep, nor be found guilty of the commandment by rashly judging them that rest; but that I too may rest in the left hand of the Bridegroom which gives its grace, and may lie hid from the heat and the whirlwind and the rain in the hiding place of his tabernacle? For happy am I if I may so deserve to die, so to sleep; if the Bridegroom deign to soothe me with the benefit of this death, with the grace of this sleep; if the daughters of Hierusalem be forbidden to hinder this, so that I be not compelled to leap back either to the troubles of life or to the watchings of guilt [n: (Num. XXIII)]. Happy am I, I say, if my soul, dying the death of the just and fainting, may long for the courts of the Lord [n: (Psal. LXXXIII)]; if it may fall asleep either in the left hand of the Bridegroom or at least on the knees of the Bride; if it may learn by experiment how sweet [0302D] that sleep was to the Virgin, how delightful — she from whose kiss the first book took its beginning, and in whose sleep let this second receive its end. For I judge it worthy that for the present my pen should not hasten to pursue the rest, but that, while the Bride sleeps, it too should lay itself down a little; and when she shall have willed to awake, and charity shall constrain her, watchful, to speak, my pen shall gird itself again, so far as its strength allows, to a labour interrupted rather than laid down.



## BOOK THREE.



## CHAPTER THE FIRST.

[0303A]

*The voice of my beloved.* Rightly did the Bridegroom will to warn the daughters of Hierusalem under an oath, that they should not presume to remove the beloved from her sleep or her leisure until she willed it, knowing that she, when the fitting time should come, would more suitably wake up and betake herself to those whom charity compels her to remember. And she, having tasted the slumber wherein she deserved to fall asleep in his left hand, does not wish to pass over in silence the savour she drank there; but for the sake of her neighbours, breaking off a little what she had begun, she is roused, she wakes, she reports to us what she has perceived. But first she shows that she has heard the Bridegroom speaking, and has caught the voice of the speaker as one well known; who, careful for her sleep, not only puts his left hand under the head of her that sleeps, but also with a terrible oath [0303B] sets himself against the troubles that come.

## CHAPTER II.

*The voice of my beloved.* This voice, I say, which in leisure and sweet silence makes me serene; which keeps outward troubles away from the calm chamber of her that rests; which thunders and adjures, and drives far off importunate assaults; which satisfies in part, though not wholly, the desire of her that sleeps: this voice, I say, is beyond doubt his whom I have loved, whom in cherishing me, in defending me, I have already often known to be gracious to me. I recognize him whom I love, I feel his voice now present, I perceive by the hearing that he loves and does not neglect one who loves; his voice sounds for me, speaks of me, and favouring me grants me a defence, and to you who are set beneath grants a teaching neither useless nor contemptible. His voice declares [0303C] me his beloved, plainly hints that my will pleases him, teaches you discipline, teaches also knowledge, teaches goodness too [n: (Psal. CXII)]; it admits me into the chamber, or rather into a kind of porch, of a welcome peace, and suffers me to sleep a little; to you who wait it *173* is not silent as to what it inwardly judges to be expedient. I therefore, the friend of the Bridegroom, stand and rejoice because of the voice of the Bridegroom [n: (Joan. III)], and shall rejoice the more when he shall have appeared who is heard; and would that, until I see him, I might not see death. But when will he come? Why does he weave delays? Thinkest thou, shall I see him? Would that he might rend the heavens and come [n: (Isa. LXIV)]. I wish indeed that the herald should no longer speak before him, that the forerunner should no longer go before; but that he himself who speaks should come nearer, that my heart may see [0303D] and rejoice that the word of that prophecy is fulfilled, which with a truthful heralding he uttered by the mouth of Isaias: « I myself, he says, that spoke, behold I am here [n: (Isa. LII)]. » Yet nevertheless, so far as I seem to myself to forebode, nay so far as I seem already to feel, behold he comes; he has found out the way of prudence, the manner of journeying, the fitting time; and he whom I desire, for whom I sigh, whom I embrace with unceasing vows, behold he comes with a rush, and is already nearer, at the doors.



## CHAPTER III.

[0304A]

*Behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills.* The Virgin burns to look more nearly upon him whom she loves, seeing and not envying that his presence is not held unprofitable; and him whom she first perceives to be coming she announces to any that will hear, that at the word of her who announces the hearer may run up and run to meet him that comes. For neither is she moved with envy if abundance of him be given to others also, if the beloved in his coming offer himself to be seen by the rest also, that he may be loved; whose love reconciles lovers and puts into them a spiritual consent, so that if any [sic: *signa*] burn the sooner, she may not fear to have an emulator, not a rival. Therefore here too the virgin hides not the presence or the coming of her beloved, but announces it to the daughters, wishing that it may come to the profit of all — him whom for this cause she proclaimed a little above to be gracious in beauty, [0304B] that she might consequently show him fruitful not to herself alone but to the rest also. She says above: « Behold thou art fair, my beloved, and comely [n: (Can. I)]. » And a little after: « As the apple tree among the trees of the woods; so is my beloved [n: (Can. II)]. » But whom there, announcing him fair, she plainly intimates to be not absent, why here does she proclaim him coming as though he were not present, since there she did not say that after his presence was granted he had withdrawn, so that she must needs say that he had drawn near again? But, as is known to one that has experience, it is a property of lovers or of love, that he who loves and desires to be held by the bond of a straiter affection should sometimes withdraw himself, that he may draw his beloved after him and be anxiously sought; and sometimes return, that he may caress her and be the more eagerly held. Now he both goes and returns, and is said to be to us now absent, now present, [0304C] he whom a sounder faith believes never, nowhere not to be at hand; because he who is always and everywhere present by the privilege of an uncircumscribed majesty is yet called absent when he withholds, and present when he bestows upon us the grace of his goodness. Now therefore the Virgin rejoices and announces that he is coming, marking that in his coming there is no delay, that he finds no obstacle; but that, leaping upon the mountains, he passes over the hills that meet him, that so he may be seen to reach the appointed place by a swift advance. But the Virgin, speaking mystically, willed to call the good angels mountains, who, it is certain, shine with the excellence of a primal holiness; who, created sublime, fell not by the blast of pride nor by the impulse of avarice, but by the merit of persevering, or by grace alone, [0304D] advanced to an unswerving firmness. In whom God leaps, when he keeps not the hidden things of his counsel with himself alone, but shows himself to them wonderful in his counsels over the sons of men; when what he purposes to work among men in the process of time he vouchsafes upon his heavenly throne to reveal all at once to the angels. For the salvation of men, which God willed to work in the midst of the earth, distributing it through diverse places and times by a saving dispensation and providence, he willed that the angels in heaven should [0305A] first know all at once, that by their ministry he might afterward impart his benefits to the earth. « Are they not all, he says, ministering spirits, sent to minister for them who receive the inheritance of salvation? [n: (Hebr. I.)] » God therefore, coming to the Virgin, in whom he works a wonderful mystery, leaps first in the angels, to whom a swift and full knowledge is presented; he makes known to Gabriel the things which he, being instructed, may afterward carry to Mary: God wove the prophecy for the angel all at once, but the angel for the Virgin in order: « Hail, he says, full of grace; behold thou shalt conceive and bring forth a son [n: (Luc. I)], » etc. God leaps also in the angels, when not by himself but through them he undertakes to instruct us, to give warnings of salvation, to impart any benefit whatsoever; and when, to teach us or to rule us, [0305B] they are found to go forth suddenly or to leap, he may be said to do this, whom, it is agreed, they that do it obey. « I heard, saith Daniel, the voice of a man between Ulai; and he cried and said: Gabriel, make this man to understand the vision [n: (Dan. VIII)]. » And to Mary asking: « How shall this be done, because I know not man [n: (Luc. I)]? » the angel says: « The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee [n: (ibid.)]. » But whether God be asserted to leap in the angels, that is, to the angels, or perchance to men through the angels, that he may bestow upon them with an abundant gift his own presence and the presence of his own; yet he skips over the hills, when he baulks them of the grace of that same gift and enlightens them not with the knowledge of himself by a like benefit. But the hills are the demons, *174* who, it is agreed, are borne above earthly men [0305C] by the privilege of nature, yet by the desert of their fault are not to be reckoned with the spirits above; who, having fallen from among them, grow great no more upon an equal summit, and having slipped down to men, swell against them the more wickedly. From whom God hides the mystery hidden from the ages; he reveals not the grace of his coming, the mystery of great godliness; but passing them by, whose good nature the depravity of pride dishonours, he manifests himself and his own wisdom to better ones, whether angels or men: « Wisdom, saith Paul, we speak among the perfect; which none of the princes of this world knew [n: (I Cor. II)]. » And to Micheas, prophesying more truly, Sedecias the son of Chanaan said: « Hath then the Spirit of the Lord left me, and spoken to thee? [n: (III Reg. XXII.)] » Plainly it is so. The Spirit of truth leaves and skips over [0305D] the proud and the lying, but the humble in spirit he saves, and teaches them by the gift and presence of his goodness; to these he hastens as a giant rejoicing and suffers himself to be felt more present; those, given over to forgetfulness, he flies past with a light bound and admits them not to the knowledge of himself. Nor is it repugnant to a fitting sense if the Virgin also be said to have mountains and hills in herself, that her loftiness may be commended in spiritual goods and in temporal; of which the spiritual are rightly compared to mountains, and the temporal to hills, which, though great, are yet not equal to the spiritual. The mountains indeed in the Virgin are chiefly the gifts of those virtues by which, or for which, we know it to have been granted to the same Virgin that she should worthily be pre-eminent above the rest in the Church upon a lofty height, and worthily [0306A] please him who is truly called the mountain of mountains. Her love is a mountain, her humility a mountain, the integrity of her chaste purity is a mountain, in which the Bridegroom leaps, that is, shows himself present by the magnificence of his divine majesty; into which, according to the angel's word, the fulness of grace [n: (Luc. I)] wholly pours itself, that in these the incomparable loftiness of the Bride may stand out and rejoice. But that her love was much — not one to whom, offending, indulgence forgave more, but one to whom, loving, the grace of the beloved committed more — she herself intimated a little above in this drama, saying: « His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me [n: (Can. II)]. » And she set the merit before it: « Because I languish with love [n: (ibid.)] » But her humility, of what excellence, of what merit it is to be believed, she herself also shows, and no doubt at all is to be had, that that regard of God [0306B] chose her that he might look upon her, or that the Virgin believed herself chosen, so that she answered concerning it the more confidently: « Because he hath regarded the humility of his handmaid [n: (Luc. II)]. » Lastly, the integrity of her purity, as in the flesh so also in the heart, was not hidden from Isaias, and an angel long after confirmed the old prophecy; and since nothing like it was heard before nor after, it is agreed that it was fortified beforehand by the excellence of a singular holiness: « Behold, they say, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son [n: (Isa. VII; Luc. X)]. » Mountains of this kind he, coming and leaping, willed to take away from the virgin and to bestow, and the same the Virgin took pains to render back and to offer to the bestower: in these he rendered himself present to her with a bounteous hand, with full grace; in the same she rendered herself pleasing to him beyond all women [n: (Psal. XLIV)]. Lastly, [0306C] the daughters of Tyre are read to entreat the King's countenance with gifts, and here he is presented in the mountains, that is, in most lofty [sic: *vul*] gifts; and seeing these his own gifts and his own presents, by which as by singular things he exalted the Virgin, rendered back to himself, he gave himself wholly to them, as it were, with a gracious leap. But the hills which he, leaping, is said to skip over are those gifts of the Bridegroom which, though great, he willed to impart to the Virgin; yet in these the sum of religion, the perfection of life, does not consist, but a comeliness shines forth which, being fitting to the person, does not attend religion as an inseparable companion. For beauty, birth, knowledge, which flourished in the Virgin with a certain excellence, were suitable to comeliness, but were not so necessary to salvation that without them it is not sometimes found among some that the supper is led, nor does any man's holiness, in their absence, [0306D] despair of being brought into the joy of its Lord. But the Bridegroom, willing that nothing comely, as nothing necessary, should be lacking to the Virgin, granted her to be holy in inward goods and elegant in outward: to those bringing himself wholly, nor forsaking them, since they were to abide with a stable footing; these regarding in passing, inasmuch as by the privilege of nature they were to pass away. Passing these by, or skipping over them, he despised them not with disdain or hatred; but, them, shining with a transitory bloom, he beheld not with a fixed gaze; comparing with better things those which present grace exalted and the end has injured, he rather transferred himself to those, and clave not to these that have an end. The elegance of the countenance has an end, the beauty of the body is not held by a stable thong, the glory of parents passes, the line of descent is not long held for a great thing; prophecy shall cease, as you have read [n: (I Cor. VIII)], knowledge [0307A] shall be destroyed; these things and the like of them he who gives them abhors not, but beholds as one passing by. For not chiefly for these is the Virgin proclaimed commendable, but rather for those things which an incomparable holiness works; in which, as upon mountains, he in his coming wills to leap, and these, of unequal merit, to skip over as hills. He indeed is the highest bestower of goods and the lover of all that he bestows, in whom all equity and no iniquity is found; distributing many things to his own, he measures not all by one measure or weight, but discerns each severally and imparts to each a worthy diligence. Wherefore also the Virgin subjoins concerning him: *He is like,* etc. *175*



## CHAPTER IV.
