*My beloved is like to a roe and to the fawn of harts.* [0307B]Very many are not led with a fitting subtlety to that which must be done, but are either held by negligence or seduced by ignorance; and when the foot cleaves too slow, or the understanding that goes before is darkened, they do not desire what is worthy, or do not lead it to prosperous outcomes. Which kind of pestilence I judge untried by none among men, but from the first parent it has been inevitably implanted in all his posterity, so that for the most part they either see not, or are not able to go thither where they might rejoice to find life and light, both their own and their people's. For what befell the first parent, first offending, by vice alone and not by nature, is in us that come after, far more wretched, both by vice and by nature; and by a law wretched enough we now either will not, or cannot, deliver ourselves from stains of this sort; and Paul is all too [0307C] truthful: « By nature, » saith he, « we are children of wrath [n: (Ephes. II)]. » [var: Vulg. Eph. 2:3 *et eramus natura filii irae*, past tense — "and we WERE by nature children of wrath"] Would that thou wert, Paul, a man not having a spirit, and wert rather speaking a lie [n: (Michae. II)]; would that thou wert not led by another law of the flesh against the law of the spirit; although thou, now rightly willing but not yet more fully able, reckonest that there is no condemnation to thee, because whatsoever thou so willest and canst not yet fully do, God accounts as done! But I, wretched, far inferior to Paul, whose eye grows dark, whose spirit languishes and with languor bends toward its end — a vicious nature working, a natural vice prevailing — bound by the law of the flesh, obey not the spiritual law. When therefore someone reads me the new Gospel, presses upon me the old prophecy; when upon the ten-stringed psaltery David more often sounds his psalmody; when [0307D] Paul goads me, urging me with harder warnings to go forward, that worthily following those set over me I may likewise go before those set under me: I, of a hard neck, what am I but an ass at the lyre, and, the goad availing nothing, an ox heavy with natural weight standing toward wrath? For taking up the psalm and the harmony of Holy Scripture, the new as well as the old, and being bidden to give the timbrel, to render a concordant symphony, I know not how but to bray, to make an ill-sweet melody sound harshly; I will not follow Debbora [n: (Judic. V)], nor imitate Moses or Mary [n: (Exod. XV)]. Unhappy man that I am, upon whose soul the body that is corrupted has pressed this brand, whose sense, intent upon many things, the earthly habitation has so weighed down [n: (Sap. IX)]; whom an asinine dullness makes blunt [0308A] and stolid, and a sluggish sickness like a good man's makes slow and going backward. Over against him, happy is that man, conceived of the Spirit, whose mind the burden of the flesh blunts not, whose willing — never anything but good — no impossibility beats back; who with a sagacious understanding contemplates things uncertain and hidden from the rest, and with an effectual power works whatsoever he will. A happy man, I say, who knows not the dullness of the ass nor the sloth of the ox, who alone by an inborn power grows effectually strong both toward subtle things and toward remote; who prevails for both, having a sight likened to the roe's, and like also to the fawn who with swift course passes more speedily to what he desires — as they report who have known the various natures of beasts. For there is in diverse creatures much diversity of natures: the roe, though slower than the hart, [0308B] yet sees more sharply, and what may suit or perchance may not suit her as she feeds, she beholds and discerns more subtly. Lastly, she is said to have within her a certain humour, wherewith if a man prudently anoint the eye, it shall be sharpened to see the better; and so not only does she prevail by the sharpness of a readier sight, but the anointing of this inward humour gives to us also the grace of seeing. Who is worthily like to her, save he to whom every will speaks and the hidden thing of the heart lies open, that Bridegroom and beloved of the Virgin, from whom nothing is hid; who with a strict and sharp scrutiny judges and discerns the causes of all, and far removes and severs the evil from the best, the good from the worst? He indeed, alone a man among men, beholds the eastern regions and the western at once, and from beholding them is hindered neither by distance nor by obstacle; [0308C] whom in the searching of things a false appearance seduces not, and whom neither error nor forgetfulness draws away from a true judgment. Lastly, in him is found that humour fitted for medicine, as he knows far better who makes trial of it not so much by knowing as by feeling; which if any man, more greedy of seeing, pour diligently upon his eye, blindness is removed, and blearedness spreads no cloud over the sight. The humour is the Spirit of Christ, the water of wisdom, the fountain of water springing up, the virtue going out from him for the healing of the poor woman that besought it [n: (Luc. VIII)]; his is that water of Siloe, wherein he who had not sinned that he should be made blind washed, not without fruit, his own eyes first smeared with spittle [n: (Joan. IX)]. But the fawn of harts is borne over the level of the fields with a rapid course, and is preferred not only to roes but to harts riper in age; and while a fitting [0308D] strength is at hand for him, an agile body, an age still younger, he spurns barriers, overtops the thickets, leaps the hedges, knows no bounds. So indeed he cares not, fears not the bite of dogs, the snares of them that lie in wait, the traps that meet him, but outflies whatsoever pursuers; and when he is believed present, sooner than one can say it he absents himself; when he is reckoned absent, by a sudden coming he presents himself. To him this beloved of the Virgin is not unfittingly likened, who, being God, is not weighed down by the burden of the flesh he has taken, but wills and is able to leap over all things that displease *176*, and to come to whatsoever he will, straightway when he will. He runs past the cords stretched for a snare [n: (Psal. CXXXIX)], he past the stumbling-block set beside him; he ran not, with slipping or slippery foot, upon the snare hidden [0309A] in the way wherein he walked [n: (Psal. CXLI)]; he outruns with far mightier merits the fathers of whom he was born according to the flesh; from us that are slower he is now withdrawn according to his own will, now runs to meet us. But he is withdrawn when with a sight like the roe's he regards us not so much in the face as in the secret of the conscience, and detects hearts ill-wounded and reins hardly framed; when he considers us empty of merits, heavy with vices, ungracious in manners, and for this cause judges us unworthy of his presence, that is, of his grace; whose present grace when we feel not within us, and, while he watches, sleep heavily under the shadow of vices; when we reckon that he the more negligently forgets our excesses, that, being intent elsewhere, he journeys further off — [0309B] then, we not foreseeing it, sudden as a fawn he presently runs upon us, punishes vices, condemns the vicious, if yet mercy run not before judgment. Very often too, when, our vices being cast off, as we think, we sweat at better pursuits, and for these rightly look for the blessed hope and the propitious coming of the Lord, our understanding growing dark we set bitter for sweet and darkness for light, and cleaving to the goods we know more than is just, we chastise not worthily enough the evils we know not. And so, when offending in many things we feel not our own ignorance, being beyond doubt uncertain whether we be worthy of love or of hatred [n: (Eccle. IX)], suddenly this fawn rushes swift and flies down from on high, and the subtle eye of the roe searches our Jerusalem with lamps [0309C] [n: (Soph. I)]. He searches, I say, the hidden things of a mind darkened by certain ignorances; bringing in light, he scatters the heavy darkness of her that is whitewashed; and seeing clearly whatever unseemly thing is pressed down by our blindness, he accounts the justices which we think ours as the cloth of a menstruous woman [n: (Isa. LXIV)]. He strikes therefore, and striking that which was thought worthy of reward — what is it but that this fawn is suddenly presented to us, who was as it were absent and set far off while he spared, while he deferred the reward falsely hoped for? Who sometimes, pitying our error, draws back the avenging sword into the scabbard, and godly admonishes us to lay hold of saving discipline [n: (Psal. II)], that we, foolish and seduced, may not look for a reward in place of punishment, but, according to Jeremias, may search out our ways [0309D] with an anxious inquiry [n: (Thren. III)]. But because searching is torpid in the dark and more effectual with lamps, he himself is at hand as a roe, enlightening wonderfully from the everlasting mountains; and he pours that humour of his Spirit upon our inward eyes, that they may see made plain whatever hurtful thing hides itself in our conscience. Which being overturned and wiped away, when we now rejoice in our own cleanness, him by whose gift and grace we work in us so magnificent a work we love to love, and will thenceforth to have him more gracious, to mingle discourse with him, to deserve him propitious, to feel him nearer. Who, feeling us to love and consenting to the vows of lovers, affords us a certain abundance of himself, caresses us with gifts, assails us not with strokes; and, whatever heavy thing out of the past troubles us being put far away, that we may taste how [0310A] sweet he is, he manifests his sweetness to them that desire him. And while he is thought to be as it were at hand before the eyes and now to be felt in the hands, he withdraws himself like a fawn and wills to be sought the more ardently; he absents himself without forsaking, not as inflicting a penalty, but he marks whether an intemperate love hangs itself upon desire of the absent. Who, if he shall have seen us held by a tender love, burning toward the absent, refreshed by nothing present; burning with desire, nothing held more pleasing to us than himself: suffers not that we be tormented longer by his absence. For him whom, not seeing, we believe to have gone away into a far country, suddenly coming he again shows himself near; and those whose desire, now sound, he beholds from on high as a roe, he guards us, humbled as we are, by his sudden coming, after the manner of a fawn. Therefore perhaps he deserved to be called here not a hart but [0310B] the fawn of harts, who also willed by Isaias to be proclaimed a child and a little man [n: (Isa. IX)]; because he who, high above all gods, containing all things in himself, hides himself, by a humble condescension pours himself into the humble in spirit [n: (Psal. XCV)]. Which, because it is known to none better than to the Virgin (for every unworthy man grieves that he has not had trial enough of this gift), therefore the Virgin rightly and confidently testifies this, and bears witness that he is that one like to a roe or to a fawn. But if any of the hearers desires more curiously to know whither he — who, like to a roe and to a fawn, is said to come leaping and skipping — hastens so, and where at last he has fixed his step, let him hear that he is there where the Virgin said that he stayed his step.



## CHAPTER V.

[0310C] *Lo, he himself standeth behind our wall, looking in through the windows, looking forth through the lattices.* He, more sweetly desired, longer awaited, though he has come, has not yet, as I seem to see, arrived; but drawing near to the Bride, whose love he knew was cherished by no other remedy, he stands behind the wall, willing rather to be known than to be seen. The wall in this place is not undeservedly named the present life *177*, which is built of hours and days, of months and years, as of stones set beside or above one another; within whose straits, while we are for a time confined, we either know not God, or do not yet contemplate his face. Whence to Moses: « Man shall not see me and live [n: (Exod. XXXIII)]. » That is: no man set within the prison of this time, [0310D] within the enclosures of this life (though he be of great merit, of a mind more diligently polished), shall see me in my nature, in the glory of my nature — which glory shall appear beyond this wall to them that go forth to be satisfied. The obscurity of the present life therefore admits not the vision of so great a glory; within its darkness that face permits not itself to be seen: no man bearing flesh wrapped in the prison-house of time sees the brightness of God, freed from temporal mists. Which John beholding says: « No man hath seen God at any time [n: (I Joan. IV)]. » At any time, that is, in time; while, that is to say, the creature is subject to vanity, that is, to transitory time, it sees not God himself in his own form or nature; although sometimes it knows, yea and feels, him to be near, to stir it up to pray, [0311A] to be at hand for prayers to be heard And notably the Virgin says not: *Lo, he himself standeth within the wall,* but *behind our wall.* This wall of ours indeed belongs to time, ever tending toward its setting and oppressive likewise of them that tend with it; it grows dark within with certain darknesses of its own, as being of the evening: no dawn rising, no morning sun receives it. Set within its bounds we see not the Bridegroom's face, the glory of Christ, but beyond it, that is, after we shall have passed its bounds; when, its threshold crossed, we shall know nothing transitory any more, then shall we come to the morning after the evening, to the light after the darkness. Whence David also: « In the morning I will stand before thee and will see [n: (Psal. V)]. » And Job: « After darkness, he says, I hope for light [n: (Job. XVII)]. » Fairly again the Virgin said behind the wall, not mine, but ours. For although [0311B] the Virgin, fuller of an ampler grace, is now free of our guilts, yet this wall of the present life is common to us all; wherein it is not now fault, nor flesh heavy with fault, that withdraws the Virgin (as it seems) from the truth that is to be seen, but that the creature itself is still subject to the aforesaid vanity. We indeed, far beneath the Virgin, weighed down with the burden of faults, darkened with carnal allurements and with thicker darkness: as many motions, as many affections as we bear in us that oppress the inward spirit, so many dividing ramparts do we set between ourselves and God. But the Virgin, who, full of grace, is no longer pressed by the urgency of such things, but is held still under time by the present life alone, unwilling indeed and against her will, asserts that not many walls now, but rather one, stands between; and this one she says is not her own but common [0311C] to all. For she who by the excellence of grace has put many ramparts or walls far from herself has not at once cast off, according to her will and desire, the one that is as much hers as all men's; and she who, living with us, yet consented not to have our faults any longer, felt life itself, as a wall, heavy and set against her. For willingly she wished to see face to face him whom she loved, but that law written with an iron pen held her back from her desire, which, promulgated by God to Moses, and to men through Moses many ages before, then and now and henceforth remains confirmed by an indelible writing: « Man, he says, shall not see me, and live [n: (Exod. XXXIII)]. »

Lo, says the Virgin, I understand that the Bridegroom [0311D] stands behind our wall, who, however near he draw, wills not to show himself clearly to them that live here; and though he be far perchance from any others, between whom it is agreed that many walls are interposed, lo — that is, hard by — he stands to me, who feel that nothing but one is set against me. But he stands that he may attend me with diligent solicitude, and show himself a ready helper to me that desire to go forth; that he may comfort me while I tarry, reach a hand to me as I strive, console me with things present, and promise better things to me as I follow after. Lastly, when Stephen endures the stones and the reproaches of the Jews, grieving not so much for himself as suffering with the malice of the lost [n: (Act. VII)], urgent in prayer he was rapt into a sweet ecstasy, and sees Jesus standing — not granted to the wretched stoners. Jesus indeed was standing, that he might give strength to him that wrestled, hope [0312A] of victory to him that was to die; reaching a hand to him that trusted, that he might loose the wall for him that was to go forth, receive him going forth, and snatch him received from the turbulent conversation of the world, he thenceforth sitting down in the beauty of peace, to sit in an opulent rest. So, while the Virgin is held by the wall of the present life alone, the Bridegroom is said to stand as it were outside, behind that wall, that he may exhort her who is to go forth to stand meanwhile upon her own watch, and that she, standing and constant with manly fortitude, may await him as the keeper of her going forth. But meanwhile, while the Virgin endures delay, set within this wall, desiring indeed to be dissolved but not yet more fully loosed, the Bridegroom is recorded to look in through the windows and to look forth through the lattices; bearing care of the Virgin, he consoles her by the regard of his grace. Lest the house [0312B] be ill-blind and its inward part dark, through the windows and lattices a gracious light is poured within. And windows and lattices seem to me to differ from one another in this, that windows are stretched out lengthwise, while lattices show a round form like an eye. Through the oblong windows therefore the Bridegroom is then seen to look within, when the Bride's sojourning, wherein she is somewhat long detained within the wall, he renders luminous by a long-suffering hope and a constant *178* patience, without the grace of which light nothing is more worthy of hatred, nothing more wearisome. David, oppressed with weariness: « Alas, he says, that my sojourning is prolonged [n: (Psal. CXIX)]. » Filled with joyful light: « Thou art, he says, my patience, O Lord; my hope from my youth [0312C] [n: (Psal. LXX)]. » But through the lattices the Bridegroom looks within, when by his unconfused grace the Virgin more subtly looks about upon her own acts; and finding not among things transitory where she may suffer her foot to rest [n: (Gen. VIII)], she fixes the eyes of her mind upon him whom with a sounder desire she awaits. He looks forth through the lattices, when, putting far from the Bride the affections and motions of the animal soul, he pours into her — or, pouring in, enlightens — spiritual eyes, with which the Virgin, made circumspect, not only cleaves not to things present, regards not greedily the things that shall pass away, but with her pupils made clear sees and loves the more eagerly the things that shall abide without end. Into which eyes the vision of God pours itself, not only cleansing but also preserving cleanness, and through them consequently diffuses itself through the whole building, as it were; whose smooth and round perfection, opened outward with a more august [0312D] bosom and wider within, renders all things uncovered by the light poured in [n: (Ezech. XL et XLI)]. I wonder if the prudent builder of the Church did not look upon this very thing, who that part of her which he understood to be worthier in merits, building it round, willed to name a lattice, wherein he willed the Holy of holies and the altar to be more significantly placed. Which part deserves first to receive the grace of the divine regard, and being first sanctified is not held by the disease of avarice; but with bosom open and filled with the surpassing light of the mysteries, it pours back upon the whole Church everywhere, like an eye, the benefit of the sacrament. Whence there especially tapers or lamps are kindled, which are shown more expressly to signify the grace of the aforesaid light; from which that vision of God is understood to be presented there first, and from them to be spread abroad to the rest, [0313A] as by a scattered light. So he who, standing behind the wall, suffers not himself yet to be seen, loves to behold his beloved through the windows and the lattices; and seeing and not seen, that yet he may not be unknown, he wills his own voice as he speaks to be heard as from an oracle.



## CHAPTER VI.

*And my beloved speaketh to me.* To me, I say, who am still held within the wall, even against my will, and, if now not by other things, yet hindered by the stains of the present life; he who, standing behind the wall, awaits me willing and not yet able to go forth, and meanwhile looks within through the windows and the lattices with eyes of mercy, adds also, to the heaping up of the benefit, that he should speak, and with gracious discourse pursue the sweet lines of love. And rightly is speech said to follow sight consequently; [0313B] for her whom we have chanced to see as beloved we straightway wish also to address, and, as the trumpet exhorts them that fight, and the goad or spur the horse let go, so to exhort her by a pleasing word to a greater vigilance of love. The Bridegroom therefore speaks, and rejoices to soothe her with his address; he insinuates his own will to her, and teaches the humble one to obey, to confess herself a handmaid — most of all after hearing Gabriel's salutation — and to hold in memory that saying of Samuel which she knew to have been written long before: « Speak, he says, Lord, for thy servant heareth [n: (I Reg. III)]. » To this handmaid therefore the Lord, nay rather the beloved, speaks, to the Bride that hears; and the Bride, loving and watchful, gives an open ear to him that speaks; he by speaking gives joy and gladness to her hearing [n: (Psal. L)], she is humbled by hearing the Bridegroom's voice the more gratefully. And worthily the more gratefully, because he will not, like an adversary, speak hurtful [0313C] or sad things, but his benevolence will pursue sweet things and useful; because he who loves and is loved rages not, is not angry against his beloved, but reaches out peace to her — though not yet a perfect peace, the wall being as it were interposed. But what peace he reaches out, or what peaceable thing he speaks to her, lest it be long hidden from you, is declared in the following verse.

## CHAPTER VII.

*Arise, make haste, my friend, my dove, my comely one, and come.* Here first it may be objected, why he who a little above warned the maidens not to trouble her, not to raise her up, until she would, as she rested between the left hand and the right, now, as though forgetful of what he had warned, provokes her to rise, and urges also [0313D] that she make haste, as though it were no longer to be deferred. But he who, restraining the daughters of Jerusalem, whose eyes are not opened to this, yet left the Virgin's rising (as you know) to her own will, himself knows far more amply what and when is fitting or expedient for holiness; from whom the Virgin also has it that she prudently spends either leisure or business upon the truth. To whom, when the Bridegroom breathes in, after the quiet of leisure, the will for business; when he stirs up and rouses her charity to the care of her neighbours, he urges her slowness with a sweet goad to a work now necessary, namely that « hearing, she may say: Come [n: (Apoc. VI)], » and, being taught, may teach the truth. What does he say or enjoin to her but, Arise and make haste? That is: as in *179* leisure, so in business obey me speedily? [0314A] Thou, he says, who liest hidden sweetly above the left hand and beneath the right, who within the wall growest glad not vainly at my regard: arise, break off for a little the unfruitful embraces of sweet leisure; go out quickly into the streets and lanes, and admit hither the lame and the weak [n: (Luc. XIV)]. And because thou willest this when I will, and willest not when I will not, I may rightly have called thee my friend, marking thee an enemy to all wills that displease me. With which saying not only the present truth of the Canticles, but also the truthful maxim of the heathen worthily accords: To will the same thing, he says, and not to will the same thing, that at last is firm friendship. And thou art a friend, since thou willest to feel with me in all things, privy to my secrets, and to keep the will of my mind; thou art none the less a dove, since thou aspirest not to the things of the world [0314B] that are present, but for the absence of things eternal groanest inconsolably and sighest. For although thou sometimes willingly exposest thyself to the instructing of thy neighbours, yet thou puttest not after it that desire wherewith thou burnest toward me [n: (Luc. XI)]; and coming to these many things, thou lettest not go that one thing necessary, but only for a little breakest off the leisure of being free and of contemplating. And because thou excellest with a fitting discretion, in both thou drawest to thyself from both praise or merit in all things, and in none of them showest thyself unshapely, but comely — and by the desert of this comeliness mine, that is, not moderately pleasing to me. Thou therefore, *my friend, dove, my comely one; arise, make haste, and come.* Arise from leisure, gird thyself bravely to labour; make haste, obey without delay, lest the neediness of thy neighbours [0314C] find thee too slow; and come — not to go far from me after the footsteps of the flocks, after the flocks of the companions, but labouring with me standing by, without any loss or damage. For lest, when thou hast risen and made haste, thou desist as it were impatient from what thou hast begun, I will be at hand, comforting thee and framing labour in commandment [n: (Psal. XCIII)]; nor will I forsake thee, when thy strength shall have failed, as one set far off: to me, when thou shalt come to me labouring, thou shalt find thyself near [n: (Rom. XIII)]. *Arise,* because it is now the hour for thee to rise from sleep; *make haste,* because God loveth a cheerful giver [n: (II Cor. IX)]; *and come,* because I am with thee, saith the Lord. But that it is the hour, he consequently declares, saying: *Now the winter,* etc.



## CHAPTER VIII

[0314D]

*For now the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; the flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning is come.* While it is winter and the earth is hard-bound with cold frost, while its surface is pressed by the snow poured over it and its face is not truly coloured; while with looser reins the north wind rejoices to rage through the fields of this air, and the south wind appears not, and Favonius defers to come: assuredly the husbandman hastens not to go out to his work and to set forth the plough; he sits at home, is at leisure for himself, rejoices in the fire, and fattens himself with richer feasts. Likewise, while it is rain, the showers flowing down long and unseasonably, and pools or standing waters now occupy the fields lately dry; while from the high mountains [0315A] the torrents cast themselves down with fury, and the rivers exceed their channels and wander far this way and that; while the crops are overwhelmed, houses float, trees are torn up, and the waters of the flood, unchecked, are driven back by no command and by no obstacle: what ploughman would go out to move the oxen to the yoke? What husbandman would set to the vine the hook that shall cut away things hurtful or superfluous? But when a mightier hand harshly rebukes these things and beats them back, and, the air being made clear, a vernal sweetness pours itself upon the lands; when the more grievous importunity of rain and winter is now wiped away, and, the cloud wiped away, their own face has returned to things: then at last the ploughman grows glad, and the mind for working returns; a man goes out to the vineyard, because it is the fitting time of pruning. That is our winter, when we are held by a hard coldness of mind, when [0315B] by ignorance or negligence we are hindered from loving God; when the wicked spirit like the north wind hardens us with a continual blast, and the world set in wickedness conforms us to its own malice. But our rain is when the flux of carnal affections pours itself into our minds, and their nerveless softness diffuses itself everywhere with a billowy onset, and a great inundation is found to exceed measure and to overstep the mark, while it is neither restrained by the channel of discipline nor forestalled by the opposing hand of justice. For then, after the manner of a torrent, passion rages, the filth of vices roars, it drowns and suffocates the mind and renders it ignorant of the commandments; and if any good thing had been sown and conceived in hope or in the blade, the water of the flood snatches it away, the Egyptian river carries it off, a bitter death overwhelms it. Lastly the mind, now lost, stretches itself out [0315C] *180* to the seeking of unlawful things abroad, and draws to its own uses whatever it finds softer and sweeter; it is soothed with the sweetness of foods, with the soft touch of women, and savours nothing but flesh, and whatever thus flatters the wretched flesh. But if the divine grace vouchsafe at some time to have pity on calamities so great, to look with eyes of mercy upon the aforesaid hardness of mind, so that it will that the mind, long pressed by a hurtful frost, be loosed at last by the warmth of the Spirit, and that we be absolved from the desert of death by the benefit of indulgence: then the tenacious and harder winter, oppressive to the wretched until then, its estate being shaken and lost, is now made a thing that passes. It passes, I say, and in its passing greenness and a revived temperateness return; the south wind comes, Favonius breathes, a vernal sweetness follows, and a summer one; there laughs [0315D] the beauty of flowers, promising the fruits that follow; the vine rejoices in the hook that prunes away useless shoots. The same grace blowing, the air is made clear, the great inundation of rains is thinned; the flood is dried up, the river is called back within its bounds; discipline not vainly enjoins frugality upon them that exult and continence upon them that run riot; and, the rheum of vices being dried up, the inward workshop of the mind is graced with virtues. Which being cleansed and made fruitful by an inward gift, not only does the down-flowing rain go away and depart, but a new comeliness of the earth, a certain new face, now comes on; and where the winter has passed and the rain has gone and appears not, there the flower of good works — that is, the hope of a reward to come — now appears. And because the Bridegroom willed to impart such grace to the daughters of Jerusalem, namely that, the rubble [0316A] of a perverse will being torn out, they should now desire to come to an ampler advance, he exhorts the Virgin, rejoicing in leisure, to go to meet them and to succour them, showing at what time and with what preceding fitness this may be worthily and profitably done. Arise, he says, *for now the winter is past* — that hardness, namely, which could for a while hinder the minds of hearers, that they should neither hear the word of God nor, having heard it, love to obey; which cast itself upon them with a heavy hand and a hard command, and made the down-flowing waters, hardened with cold, to stand still; which cast over the earth cold snows as a heavy cloak, and, the burden pressing long, slew the tender sheep. This hardness assuredly was found to have held Peter with a heavy hoof, when he answered that he knew not the man whom he had known [n: (Marc. XIV)]; and a servant or a maid dealt him a buffet of fear, that he might not even [0316B] be able to speak the truth; and lest the disciple should help his master, the slothful man held his hand under his armpit [n: (Prov. XIX)]. You remember, as I think, what the truth of the Gospel affirms: that when Peter was denying and warming himself, it was cold [n: (Joan. XVII)]; and therefore at that time the Virgin is not commanded to rise to speak, but by pitying grace he that denied is first looked upon, that he may weep. For he wept bitterly, feeling himself held by a hard cold [n: (Luc. XXIII)], and that the fire at which he stood was not held fit enough to drive it away; but that same winter having passed by the regard of pitying grace, Mary is sent to Peter to announce the power of him that rose again [n: (Marc. XVI)]. Lastly, do not a great rain, many waters, the malice of the time or of the day, seem to you to have held John [0316C] the son of Zebedee, so that, his spirit as it were suffocated and the rigour of chastity bent, he was hastening to embrace the soft coupling of the flesh, the nuptials of a pleasure that must perish? But most of all a great rain, a great cleanness suffocated him, when Peter, the more confident, thrice denied his master as the passion drew near [n: (Marc. XIV)]; and he none the less, terrified by love of this life at the passion aforesaid, hurried headlong, fled naked, the linen cloth left behind. And truly he is of no slight fault, and swerves and offends not a little, who in the flood of the passions leaves behind the love of heavenly things, cleaner than a linen cloth; wherewith no man can be more honourably, none more usefully clothed, if only Christ, after his own pattern, shall have granted us to be buried in it. « He wrapped him, he says, in a clean [0316D] linen cloth, and laid him in the sepulchre [n: (Matth. XXVII)]. » But love of self and contempt of the linen cloth stripped John as he fled; hatred of the Master, the disease of avarice, the guilt of crime unnerved Judas; all at last the water bore away, the flood injured, guilt drowned — but while the rest escaped by grace, Judas, being lost, emerged not. For he, suffocated by distrust, hanged himself with a noosed throat; John laid hold of the citadel of grace, the summit of seeing, because Christ, suffering on the cross, banished the care of Judas far from his benevolence, but loving John committed the care of him to his mother the Virgin: « Woman, he says, behold thy son [n: (Joan. XIX)]. » After therefore he willed by faith in the rising Christ to remove far off the troubles of winter and of rain, and that a liberating grace should appear more eminently in those whom he had chosen, [0317A] he anxiously invited the Virgin not to be slothful to rise, to make haste, to come, because it is now the time of speaking, when the earth, that is, is not held by the aforesaid rain or winter. Nor only has so great an inclemency gone and departed, but a vernal sweetness, a flowery beauty, a hope of fruits has come on; in our land the flowers of obedience, of patience, of continence now shine forth; yet a little while, and they shall bring forth the desired fruit. It is not therefore to be deferred but that meanwhile the hook and a purging admonition be brought forth, to cut back diligently the springing shoots of negligence [n: (Sap. IV)]; let it scrape away ignorance, instruct faith, prune manners, that with worthy solicitude it may render them readier to bring forth fruit. For when the time of vintage, the day of fruits, shall dawn, there shall be no more pruning; [0317B] both the basket and the mattock shall rest — which, the winter being run out, now more fittingly present themselves, when a new greenness springs. flowers of many kinds show themselves in the earth. *181* *The flowers,* he says, *have appeared in our land, the time of pruning is come.* And he adds: the voice, etc.



## CHAPTER IX

*The voice of the turtle is heard in our land, the fig tree hath put forth her green figs: the vineyards in flower have yielded their sweet smell.* The voice of the turtle is not raised, according to musicians, among the high notes, nor is it pleasant to their ears; it sings not over-sweetly, as, according to a certain heathen, the nightingale does; but it dwells among the low notes, mournful with a certain suppressed groan, unwelcome to them that rejoice, [0317C] gracious to them that would mourn. Such a voice that querulous man seems to imitate who harshly complains that his sojourning on earth is prolonged; who, cleaving not to things present and refusing to be consoled in them, groaning for the absence of things to come, ceases not to lament. « Woe is me, he says, that my sojourning is prolonged [n: (Psal. CXIX)]. » And that other: « Weeping she hath wept in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks: there is none to comfort her [n: (Thren. I)]. » If you remember, this voice was heard in the disciples, when — their tender love, their hope provoked by a deferred desire — they dispute among themselves, and sigh, and complain after the manner of a turtle, and among the complainers much doubt and various discourses are exchanged. « What are these discourses, says he, that you hold one with another as you walk, and are sad? *(Luc. [0317D] XXIV.)* » And they: « We hoped, they say, that it was he that should have redeemed Israel [n: (ibid.)]. » When therefore the voice of this turtle is now heard in the land, rightly is the virgin's solicitude summoned to the advancing of the faith, that she may know that her preaching is not found empty nor ineffectual, which is thus forerun by so devout a groan, by so groaning a spirit. Lastly, the turtle loves to dwell in the mountains and in the more secret places; it rejoices not in the assembly of birds, nor in the public place, nor in the throng of the people; holding the form of that spiritual wisdom which neither the wandering multitude of the market-place nor the animal man perceives. Of which Job: « Wisdom, he says, is drawn out of secret places [n: (Job XXVIII)]. » And David: « The uncertain and hidden things of thy wisdom, he says, thou hast made manifest to me [n: (Psal. L)]. » And Paul: « We speak, he says, the wisdom of God [0318A] in a mystery, which is hidden [n: (I Cor. II)]. » Paul, who knew himself a debtor to the wise as also to the foolish, speaking among the perfect draws wisdom out of secret places; and he whom the dullness of the men of the market-place, or a dull ignorance, troubles not, manifests the uncertain and hidden things of wisdom to them that likewise have ears. It is therefore the voice of the turtle which, hiding from the darkened crowds the hidden or uncertain things of wisdom, renders them uncovered to the eyes or ears of very few indeed; which, veiling the secret from the multitude — the secret of Isaias, the prophecy of Elisabeth, the oracle of Zachary — whispers sweetly to those only who, having received the Spirit, hasten to the hill country, whose ears of hearing the crafty asp stops not. Lastly, that woman seemed to utter the voice of the turtle who rejoiced that she had seen the Lord [0318B] when he rose from the dead; and him whom she alone had alone seen, her desire now fulfilled, she announced not to the crowds in the street but to the apostles in secret: « Mary Magdalen came, he says, telling the disciples: I have seen the Lord, and these things he said to me [n: (Joan. XX)]. » But Mark: « Jesus rising, he says, early the first day of the week, appeared first to Mary Magdalen; and she going told them that had been with him [n: (Marc. XVI)]. » Those disciples also tarry in the secret of excellence after the manner of a turtle, who in the absence of Thomas Didymus rejoiced to see the Lord; and when they tell it to him on his return, thinking that he would likewise rejoice at such news, he, distrusting, asserts that he will not believe unless he shall have seen. Nor is it repugnant if you will to declare the same Lord also a turtle, [0318C] who, rising from the dead, willed to appear both to the women and to the disciples; whom, wholly hidden from the crowds that rejoice in the forum or the street, Galilee offered in secret to be seen by none but his own. Whose turtle's voice I deem beyond doubt to be that whereby he made himself known to his own as being at hand, that they might believe; which, removed further from the hardened hearing of the malignant, he brought only to those whom he found held by the begun affection of them that love. « Peace be to you, he says, it is I [n: (Luc. XXIV)]. » Good is that voice of the turtle, a voice from the high mountains, a secret voice, which the roaring crowd, accustomed to the suits and tumults of the forum, does not grasp; which none know but a few, whose ear worthily hears, whose eye is not darkened by obstinacy, whose vigorous understanding [0318D] more anxiously searches out the secrets of wisdom. Of which voice it is written: « His voice shall not be heard in the streets [n: (Isa. XLII)]. » [var: Vulg. Isa. 42:2 *nec audietur vox ejus foris*, "neither shall his voice be heard abroad"; *in plateis* is the wording of Matt. 12:19] Which voice assuredly, after it sounded to the [sic: *torrae*] and was heard by the disciples, the earth, hindered before by a hard cold, opened glad bosoms, growing green with a new temperateness, so that it is now worthy to be called ours — which, cursed in the first man, deserved to be blessed when the second rose again. For her whom of old the Lord strictly forbade to sin, and whom, having transgressed the prohibition, he more harshly cursed in wrath and fury: the same, rising from the dead, he blessed with his own regard, with his own grace, and, renewed by his gifts, called ours by the desert of newness. *182*



## CHAPTER X.

*The voice of the turtle is heard in our land.* She who once, [0319A] when she sinned, made herself over to another's dominion and usurped for herself a new God and another possessor, after she has been breathed upon by a new spirit and is made free of the wanderings aforesaid, is rightly called ours — the common possession, that is, of them both. For those whose spirit is one, whose flesh is one, must be said to have nothing thenceforth that is not common; but what is the bride's the bridegroom claims to himself fittingly enough, since he wills to hold even what is his own not as proper to himself but to share it with her, that they may rejoice to have all things together in common. « Our Father who is in heaven [n: (Matth. VI)]. » [var: Vulg. *qui es in caelis*, second person, "who art in heaven"] If, I say, I call the Father who is in heaven not properly mine but in common ours, rightly, O bride, do I call the land also not thine but rather ours; because, as by gift [0319B] I gave thee to be made partaker of my things, so by the giver's bounty — mine rather than thine — am I partaker of thine. Otherwise, if the land were held to be thine only and not rather ours, perhaps the voice of the turtle aforesaid would not be heard in it, and the fig tree would not put forth those green figs of hers which she put forth when the turtle was heard; and, these not being put forth, she would not bring on after them the other fruits of the later season. Almost all trees, of whatever differing kind or shape, have this as it were proper to themselves, have this implanted in them by nature: that a tree which is to put forth its fruits in the ripe season rejoices first in a certain passing offspring of blossoms. Whereof it is written: « In the morning let it flourish and pass away [n: (Psal. LXXXIX)]. » But when the tree has been widowed of its passing flower, by nature's working it is made fruitful by the access of fruits that follows; and whatever it grieved for before, [0319C] whatever loss it bore when stripped by the falling of the flower, it makes good with a new joy and exchanges for a better abundance. But the fig tree is found unlike the rest in this, nor is the plenty of fruits in her forerun by the grace of a flower; but while others are in blossom she is said to put forth her first fruits, transitory ones, as others succeed them in the course of time. So indeed the fig tree becomes fruitful by a manner unusual to all, rich with no foregoing flower in a first plenty of fruits and in a second; of which the green figs that come first are not of that grace, not of that savour, which those have that follow — the later they are in season, the better beyond doubt in juice. Yet sometimes among those green figs which are said to forerun the rest it is possible to find some, though very few, [0319D] which both go before and yet yield not place or time to those that are to succeed, but, while the others fall, stand longer and remain with those that are to come. For a green fig is sometimes found to be born between two little branches, and is guarded as it were by the careful standing-about of its neighbours; and, resting in the angle and drawing juice and nourishment to itself from this side and that, not only does it not fall, but is brought to a fuller yield than the rest. For neither are its coevals that fall accounted its equals in grace, nor do the last that come after deserve beyond doubt to be matched with it; but it deserves to be set before both these and those in scent and in savour, fit for the food of nobles, worthy to be set on no table unless a king's. Not unfittingly can the fig tree be named the Jewish people, which, when it heard Christ commend [0320A] heavenly things and teach that earthly things are not to be loved, being steeped in the sacred letters straightway put forth men that would believe, but that would not abide in the word of faith with any steadfastness of works. Who, brought forth in haste and taking on an appearance of godliness, but denying the power of it and lacking the weight of truth, fell before their time at the first blast of the wind, or, while the wind was not yet blowing, dropped off heavy with their own weight. And perhaps such men are not undeservedly called green figs, who by a sense grosser than their body wickedly despise things hidden and subtle; who, according to Paul's [n: (Ephes. IV)] word, having their understanding darkened by grossness, do indeed believe for a time, but in the time of temptation fall away into failure. Gross enough — nay, more than enough — I judge those to have been who are read to have stood by [0320B] Christ as he spoke in the Gospel; and when he discoursed mystically of the eating of his flesh and the drinking of his blood, and affirmed that none had eternal life in themselves save those who should eat, they, from whose sides an over-gross fat seemed to hang, not taking in the mystery, were found to shrink from the mystic word. « This is a hard saying, say they, who can hear it? » [n: (Joan. VI.)] When by the hardness of this saying those rude ones are wretchedly shaken, and, not solid in the truth, endure the blast of the north wind, bearing ill a plain stumbling-block in a somewhat obscure word, they plainly fall, like green figs, before their time. « From this time, he says, many went back; and now they walked not with him [n: (Joan. VI)]. » But when these had withdrawn, do not think that of that same people [0320C] there were thereafter none who would hear Christ. and be present among his hearers; for he sent before him afterwards seventy-two others into every place whither he knew he was himself to come, and by taking these out of that people he did not permit the fig tree to remain wholly barren. Lastly Judas the traitor, who for a while followed the Master among the apostles and at the last pursued him even to betrayal and to an incurable hatred, when he found himself fallen into the deep like a green fig by his own weight, bearing himself back on high far worse, hanged himself with a noose. But lest the Apostle's place should long *183* be held empty, and by one man's fall the due perfection of the consecrated number be defrauded, Matthias, as you have read, was chosen an apostle by the casting of the lot, and so neither [0320D] did the fig tree stand empty nor the number of twelve imperfect. But if this seems to any hearers small and insufficient, if a careful reader thinks that something here holds a scruple in it, let him betake himself to those of that people who afterwards believed at Peter's word, and who, now three thousand and now five thousand, filled up the number of them that fell away. Of whom there is no doubt but that, the later they are in time, the more worthily they ought to be called better than Judas and the apostates aforesaid; and that their evening succession and conversion pleased Christ far more than the morning withdrawal and headlong fall of the others. But those green figs which, when the rest were falling, remained — very few indeed — and, not slipping away with them that slipped, endured even with them that followed after, may rightly be understood of the apostles, who are chosen by Christ among [0321A] the first and perhaps first of all, and are driven from him neither by entreaty, nor by price, nor by the violence of threats. And when the good Master set himself to question them more closely, whether they too would go when the others were going back, Peter, the readier to speak, hid not what he purposed, but before the rest (as their first and chief) answered thus: « Lord, to whom shall we go? Thou hast the words of eternal life: and we have believed and have known that thou art Christ the Son of God [n: (Joan. VI)]. » Peter therefore lies hid between two little branches, that is, between the Law and the Gospel, and, taking nourishment to himself from this side and that, grows strong to persevere bravely; resting on the border of both, he leans sweetly upon either, and, carefully supported by the one, turns not away at all from the other. For he understands [0321B] that the old law prefigures the new by signs and riddles; that the new makes the old understood and does not darken it; that the old does not prejudge the new but runs before it; that the new is not against the old but runs to meet it. The lawgiver and the giver of the Gospel seem to Peter not to be at odds one with the other, since the law foretells Christ, and Christ wills not to destroy the law but to fulfil it; and in him, as in a corner, the old is joined to the new law by a certain fitness, upon which Peter, firmly leaning, is guarded by a double defence. Whereof he himself says: « We have the more firm prophetical word, whereunto you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark [ *alias* caliginoso] place [n: (II Petr. I)]. » This of the old. What of the new? « Do penance, says he, and be every one of you baptized in the name of Jesus Christ [n: (Act. II)]. » [0321C] To Peter therefore and to his fellow-apostles, who first believed in Christ, and who, when some withdrew, remained with him in his temptations, that same Christ willed to impart so great a ripeness of manners and so great a sweetness of grace that it is certain they go before both their coevals and those that came after in the merit of their living. To this order no order, to an apostle no other man could compare himself, nor — as some judge — could any, earlier or later, set himself before them in life and merits; but they become so sweet in scent, and by the ripeness of their works so ripe, that both present and future men might worthily enough yield to them. And since the fig tree has put forth such as these — not so much to be preferred to the evil as assuredly better than the good, greater after the manner of mountains, grosser in the abundance of their merits — rightly is the Bride [0321D] invited not to put off the visiting of such any longer, but sometimes to set the business of her neighbours before her own special leisure. The Bridegroom wills that the Virgin, absent too long, be not burdensome to the apostles who are as yet maidens, but that, graciously speaking to them, she confer manifest things upon their hidden ones; that she strengthen their faith, instruct their rude understanding, advance their beginning affections and lead them to perfection. He wills, I say, that the Virgin labour with watchful solicitude, that the rude apostles may be able to lay their head each under his own vine and under his own fig tree; and that, while the present iniquity passes by and the day dawns more fully upon them, each may rest meanwhile under the mighty [0322A] hand of Christ, under the shadow of the Holy Spirit. And that the Virgin's care may labour patiently upon those same maidens and may hope for fruit near at hand if she persevere diligently: the flowering vineyards, he says, have already yielded their scent; they that have already flowered in the first season will give autumn grapes. By the vineyards I judge are meant the souls of individual men now converted to the faith, in whom the calling of God who has mercy works the grace of merits, and which, growing green by an infused mildness, now plainly put forth their flower. The flower, not yet rich in fruit, gives meanwhile its scent. And as the flower by its presence renders the vineyard's place pleasant, so the flower's scent makes that same place cleaner and serene, while it suffers neither serpent nor creeping thing to remain in it, nor venom, but by a certain undivided force renders it [0322B] a stranger to all these. A good flower, I would say, and a good scent that, wherewith a recent conversion so adorns the soul that first it drives far off whatever inwardly dishonours her; so that at her first fruits the beholder's eye worthily grows glad [sic: *hila rescat*], and venomous envy, not enduring her good scent, takes fright. The wicked will not, or cannot, look with an even mind upon the good, and a juster place cannot be possessed by two masters; but when the fresh flower and the comely scent pour themselves out with a large bounty, guilt flees, the poison is shut out, iniquity hides itself afar off. Lastly, scent and stench are harshly opposed one to the other, and agree not well, nor do they abide in one lodging; but when virtue worthily flowers and the report of it sweetly grows strong, vice is brought to nothing, and whatever is evilly foul vanishes away. When Simon [0322C] Peter, flowering with a summer *184* grace, gave forth his scent far and wide, and with a large munificence published the new rule of having nothing of one's own, some who wished to be fed with that good scent in a clean conscience sold their possessions and laid the prices of them at the apostle's feet [n: (Act. V)]. But Ananias and Sapphira, who laboured with a venomous fraud and a lost mind, who burned with the disease of avarice as with inward fevers, being unwilling to aspire freely to the height of apostolic poverty, were forced at the scent of this word wretchedly to expire. So Peter, so the brethren who had come together, shine forth with a new flower, that, shining before men, they may fill the whole house with the scent; and so great a strictness is found to prevail in the Church that neither [0322D] will nor can Simon Magus endure Peter, nor Nicolas Stephen. Good vineyards indeed, which flowered so at that time; very happy souls, which put forth so prevailing a scent, in whose fellowship the serpent of envy and a poisoning fraud abide not, and the stinking malignity of the lost withstands not the health-bearing scent. « They were not able, he says, to resist the wisdom and the Spirit that spoke [n: (Act. VI)]. » But our vineyards now, since the days are evil, grow dull in no small measure; virtue is darker, love feeble, merits languish the more negligently; within the cloisters of our [0323A] conscience a disease creeps on that thrives to our hurt, and it discolours the flowers above while it plucks us at the tender root. For us therefore the holy Virgin tarries all too long, as I see; for us she sleeps, is at leisure for herself, delights in her own rest; lying upon the Bridegroom's left hand she gazes upon his right, forgetting us perhaps, and rejoices to take care of herself alone. Who shall rouse her? Who shall say to her: « Arise, why sleepest thou? » [n: (Psal. XLIII.)] For because languor and sloth have loosed us from labour and watching, and the enemy, beholding us, has now mocked our torpor and our sabbaths, the Virgin has not revisited us who are full of leaves but thin in flower and scent, and long since, our faults requiring it, she has ceased to revisit us. But if she shall see our flower flower again, and shall perceive the scent, she will not refuse to rise and to spend a more gracious diligence upon us; [0323B] and she who was found mercifully to succour her own maidens will deign to impart a fuller mercy to us who are far more wretched. For she is not wanting to those to whom she shall see that her Bridegroom also is not wanting, to whom she shall know his present grace so to be at hand that they both lack not the scent and will not deny that same scent to their neighbours, but give freely to the rest what was freely given to themselves. For those who, not having virtue, take to themselves the appearance of virtue, who study not to obtain the grace of living well but presume upon it, bestow a scent not their own but rather another's, while they contrive to give to others the form of a virtue presumed rather than received. But those souls that rejoice that they truly have the gift of some virtue, and will not have it hidden under a bushel but appear to their neighbours' eyes, [0323C] if from it they hunt after their own glory as displayers rather than the glory of the beholders, are more truly said not to give their scent but to sell it. Passing over in silence, therefore, those who are convicted of giving another's scent or of selling their own, and making mention of those who are known to give their own scent like flowering vineyards, he admonishes the Virgin to rise to them and to hasten with a watchful care; and lest, being admonished, she delay, he loves to repeat this very thing.



## CHAPTER XI.

*Arise,* he says, *my friend, my Bride, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollows of the dry-stone wall.* [var: Vulg. *speciosa mea*, "my beautiful one", in the slot that here names the Bride] [var: Vulg. *in caverna maceriae*, singular] It suffices not for a lover to admonish once her whom he loves, but he repeats it and presses it home, willing that she be not sluggish to fulfil what he admonishes; and, that he may the more move to willingness her who knows nothing of the body, he studies to soothe her [0323D] with caresses and with caressing names. Her, therefore, whom he named friend, dove, comely one when he said *Arise* the first time, he named none the less friend and dove when he said *arise* a second time — inserting the name of Bride, which I do not recall that he named anywhere above, though he is found to have called her otherwise often enough. Because to the Bride, who loves leisure and to cleave to the Bridegroom's embraces, nothing is harder than to turn the mind's edge back from him to public acts, therefore, when the Bridegroom admonishes her, and repeats it, that she be drawn a little away from what she loves the more, he casts upon her that name by which he knows her to be the more held to obedience. For the Bridegroom and the Bride seem to be bound by a certain sacred or consecrated mystery in such a way, and he to set her a bound which it is not lawful to pass, [0324A] namely that the Bridegroom shall bear the care, shall command as the powerful one, shall write the law; and the bride shall lend her ear, shall be obedient [sic: *oltemperet*] to his words, shall love his command and subscribe to it. When therefore the Virgin hears herself called bride the more insistently, remembering not so much the burden as the honour by which she loves to be bound to him that calls her, she understands that she ought not to withstand the Bridegroom even in a little thing, but always to reckon his good pleasure the merit of her own salvation. For he does not desert her when he invites her to give an example abroad to others, when he suggests that she interrupt for an hour her pleasant leisure of contemplating; he does not envy her advancement when he wills her work to be seen by those who stand about, but he wills them to profit who shall have loved to behold her good works. *185* For he wills her holiness to be so set forth to them that behold [0324B] that she may rejoice, being set forth, not to be exposed to winds and whirlwinds; he wills her so to go forth into public and to be shown to the rest, even against her will, that she may nevertheless feel herself fortified by the watchful care of him that commands. This perhaps is what he says: *My dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollows of the dry-stone wall.* I will, he says, that the Bride be sometimes shown to the maidens, that they may be able and may rejoice to be strengthened by a needful example; but that she be none the less kept within the clefts of the rock, and that the hawk's onset and hostile ambushes be barred far away. The rock (it is well enough known) is called Christ in figure, which at the touch of Moses, at the striking of the mystic rod, yields a fountain, pours out water, and gives streams with a large bounty: the people, ill parched with thirst, drink, and their beasts. The clefts of which rock are called Christ's [0324C] wounds, his passion, his death; faith in these and love of these bestow a health-bearing defence, and in the mindful diligence of them, or the diligent memory of them, whosoever shall lie hid in hope and in silence shall neither be crushed by things present nor dread the troubles to come. Nor do I think it absurd if the law and grace, mercy and truth, justice and peace, and any like things be named Christ's clefts, which, opened and found out, guard us from the onset of them that work malice: in which, that is, if any man shall have lain hid in a worthy understanding of them, they both carry him up to profit and free him from hurtful failing. But a dry-stone wall is called a plain heap of stones which, stretched out after the manner of a hedge, is not bound with mortar between, but, compacted by a slight work for the keeping [0324D] of vineyards, hedges them in and frees them from the harmful onset of beasts. And this wall may be called that fellowship of angels which was long ago ordained by the Creator's command for the keeping of the elect; which, to stand the more firmly, needs no binding of law nor of Gospel, and for which the squaring of its first condition, confirmed by grace, suffices. Whose hollows and inward little dwellings, as it were, or recesses — which whosoever has worthily entered the vineyards finds standing open — are the care and the love which the angels are seen to show to men, whom, being like doves, they will to keep from malignant onsets. To the Virgin therefore, who is invited to revisit the flowering vineyards, that, putting off her leisure for an hour, she may bestow the form of manners upon them that behold her, he himself who invites promises the clefts of life and [0325A] the hollows of the wall, that the dove, relying on such a defence, may with confidence fulfil what is commanded. Thou, he says, whose devotion of mind burns to be at leisure and to see, arise and hasten, and let no fear hold thee back; because, although thy mind, gaping after secrecy, as it were hates the public, yet there is no cause for thee to fear, whom the rock now guards in its own clefts. A good rock, which is opened by the careful hand of them that dig, which when opened imparts a health-bearing defence to the digger, which the Bride too deserved to open, not with a mattock but with desire, and to find in it not a deceitful confidence but a faithful keeping. She indeed, impatient of degenerate labour, disdained to dig the earth, and, strong in a praiseworthy pride, sought not to be plunged in muddy desires, as did that wicked servant who, having received his Lord's talent and being over-anxious [0325B] about the loss of it, dug the ground and covered it over, and would not return it with usury. « He went his way, he says, and digged in the earth, and hid his lord's money [n: (Matth. XXV)]; » and below: « Being afraid, he says, I went and hid thy talent in the earth: behold, thou hast that which is thine [n: (ibid.)]. » Far happier had this man been if he had not given his pains to this labour, if he had not with soft negligence dug the muddy earth, if he had answered his greedy lord more graciously with a doubled interest, and had so deserved to be hidden in the rock and not to be cast into the exterior darkness: « The unprofitable servant, he says, cast ye out into the exterior darkness [n: (Matth. XXV)]. » Lastly, they who digged the hands and feet of Christ and pierced his side with a lance, given over to nothing but the earth, came not to the solid rock; cleaving to softer things, plunged the more negligently into the deep, not knowing the first [0325C] commandment, they held not the second that is like it. The Virgin therefore, although she knew most perfectly the Word made flesh from the womb, yet knows his excellence no longer according to the flesh; but she is exalted upon the rock, sets her foot upon the solid rock, and, a dove nesting in the clefts of the rock, orders and disposes her young. Set upon the rock, or rather in the clefts of the rock, she avoids the ravening onsets and remains safe from ambushes; standing in the mouth of the cleft she rejoices to behold the flowering vineyards, and, that they may profit the more, she endures to be seen by them. Worthily therefore are the hollows of the dry-stone wall not closed to that same Virgin, but are spread the wider with an open recess to receive her; and they suffer her not, while she provides for the vineyards, to labour under the open sky in heat and rain, [0325D] but the angels standing about omit not to take care of her. Lastly, from of old there have stood open hollows in this wall, from the time when the angels fell thence in a ruinous fall; which hollows the prudent architect willed not to patch up out of those same stones, but willed that in the room of them that fell men should enter in by grace and by merits. And since the broken wall waits to be repaired by men, it loves to be opened to none more than to the Bride; and it puts forth to her all its approaches, all its openings, that the virgin may freely enter in by whichever she shall see will profit her. To her, thus having refuge in the clefts of the rock and in the hollows of the dry-stone wall, and, fortified by this defence, now fearing no onsets of them that work malice, the Bridegroom, adding to speak, [0326A] wills that her face be shown to him — curious perhaps to know whether anything reprehensible can be found in her. *186*



## CHAPTER XII.

*Show me thy face, let thy voice sound in my ears: for thy voice is sweet, and thy face comely.* After the Virgin, and dove, is said to be in the hollows of the dry-stone wall and in the clefts of the rock — not so much groaning, I judge, as glad with a safe defence — she is admonished to offer her face, nourished by so great benefits, to be seen by the Bridegroom, desired for the merit of its comeliness. For the Bridegroom judges that nothing now remains in her which, when offered, ought to displease the beholder, since with a mind secure her face grows cheerful as at a continual banquet, and her inward purity shines out the more manifestly [0326B] upon the surface of it. Whereat Solomon hints: « A joyful mind, he says, maketh a flourishing age: a sorrowful spirit drieth up the bones [n: (Prov. XVII)]. » When therefore the mind languishes with sadness and the soul sickens, the bones are consequently dried and the face wastes away; conscious of its own deformity it blushes to go out in public, and, though it perhaps desires it, dreads to be seen by him that loves it. But the Virgin — whose foulness, if any there was before; whose mind now rejoices; the beauty of whose conscience now flowers — when she has heard the Bridegroom's voice will not draw over herself the cloak of a degenerate shamefastness, but will show her form, which indeed shines out the more in the face. Adam, conscious of his sin, withdrew straightway into sad darkness, and, deformed with a sad face, came not forth to meet God who called him, knowing that the stains of filth [0326C] which sad guilt had brought upon his face would not please God, who is read to be a lover of beauty. But the Virgin's face, which the Bridegroom so anxiously wills to be shown to him, knowing that she is not foul nor to be reproved for a sordid foulness — her face is her conscience, strong with a certain singular grace, to which no woman can be preferred, nor indeed can any other be made her equal. For she both seeks leisure the more ardently, and, when it is found, knows how to rejoice in it more sweetly than the rest, and bears the business laid upon her the more soundly the more patiently she bears it; she knows not how to halt now on this path and now on that, but so walks that she runs to the commandment, not overstepping the bounds set for her. A conscience of such a kind shows itself in nothing save to the Bridegroom, and to him confidently; at the voice of him that commands it regards nothing as its own; when a difficulty [0326D] is set before it, it holds out no cloak of excuse; but whatever he commands, this conscience lays hold of with outstretched hands. And the Bridegroom expressly demands that this face be shown to him, because he recognizes neither the Virgin nor any other man save by the face; and the purer he shall see it, its soot wiped away, the more he rejoices to have a fuller knowledge of her. Because it is given thee to excel in manifold goods, I will that from the perceiving of these present things thou have such confidence that thou fear not to appear to me face to face, and to exhibit thy conscience conspicuous to my gaze. And when it shall show itself to me the more securely the more purely it does so, consequently thy voice also shall sound [0327A] in my ears; because, thy face being presented, thou dost rightly close thy mouth no longer, but thanksgiving and the voice of praise break forth confidently. For when the face has been seen, so serene by the privilege of grace, the pleasant voice no longer holds itself within the cloisters of silence; but as the face is worthily to be gazed on and comely to the sight, so the voice is rendered sweet and sonorous to the hearing. For she who by the desert of her imperfection still either fears the Bridegroom or offends him, and therefore shows not a secure face to him that asks it, or perhaps refuses it, her voice as yet breaks not forth sufficiently harmonious in his ears; and the averted face interrupts the sound of it, lest it grow sweet. The Bridegroom therefore wills the Virgin's voice to sound in his ears — a voice which an exceeding sweetness is found to commend, and which, sweet and delightful in the concord of a sweeter sound, sounds among the voices of women [0327B] as the swan's voice among the clamour of geese. No woman indeed so puts forth her hands to the commandments, nor consequently is any woman's exultation or confession so acceptable; none's face shines with so great a grace or comeliness, and therefore none's voice resounds with a sweeter melody. *Thy voice,* he says, *is sweet, and thy face comely.* Therefore, he says, my ear wills to hear thy voice with open bosom, because that voice is found to soothe this ear with a concordant sound; and of her whose seen face pleases by the merit of so great a beauty, the voice, concordant with the face already seen, heaps up grace. A good order, that first the face of the inward conscience be adorned, and so the voice, worthily sounding, be preached as commendable; because the praise or the teaching of one whose face, for its foulness, does not yet deserve to be shown, is not seen to sound sweetly enough. And perhaps anyone's [0327C] face has in silence a certain grace and is praised, when, namely, he lives justly and neither has he opportunity nor does necessity require that he speak; when he presents himself more secretly to God with a clean face of the heart, and does not display this very thing outwardly by the proclamation of a voice. But a clamorous voice never profits, and sometimes hinders, if a beautiful face has not gone before the voice; because praise in the mouth of a sinner is not, as we read, precious, and the declaring of justice, joined with a hatred of discipline, is none the less hateful [n: (Eccli. XV)]. But the Virgin, who is led to a greater advancement than the rest, whom the Bridegroom and Son willed to be led to perfection, both flowered with a comely face, advancing into a wondrous virtue, and sounded forth in teaching and in example, worthily *187* unto the salvation of them that heard. Whose inward face desires to be shown to us today also, [0327D] while she loves us, while she admonishes us by example, speaks to us, cries out to us; in both she is zealous, takes counsel for us, favours us, and, no longer anxious for herself, trembles for us, fears for us. But if our eye grows dim, and our ear (like the asps') grows deaf, and if her face is hidden from us and her voice grows hoarse, none the less is the Virgin's comeliness believed to have flowered in the Bridegroom's eyes both now and then, and her praising and exulting voice to have sounded sweetly in those same ears. Therefore perhaps he says expressly: *Show me thy face; let thy voice sound in my ears.* Though, he says, thou show not thy face to them that would see it, though thou bestow not the benefit of thy voice on them that stop their ears, to me [0328A] nevertheless thy face also is shown, who cannot but see my own gifts, and thy voice sounds in my ears, to which I judge it worthy to lend them. But that the Virgin's presence might not be idle to them that stood about, but might become fruitful to the maidens that worthily beheld her, the Bridegroom willed that whatever was hurtful be removed from them, that they might deserve to behold her more fruitfully when she revisited them. Therefore he adds: *Catch us,* etc.



## CHAPTER XIII.

*Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vines; for our vineyard hath flourished.* Whom, save his own dogs, does the Bridegroom seem to invite to catch the little foxes, lest those seducing little beasts dare to lurk within the vineyards, which in the dogs' absence they are found to gnaw, to hurt, to destroy — so that it is needful that the dogs [0328B] be found careful to catch them? Those therefore whom the Bridegroom has already set over the keeping of the vines, whom, being set over the churches, he has made skilled in hunting whatever is hurtful, he admonishes to be watchful, and with a keen search to pursue the deceitful little beasts, to press on and not to desist until they catch what they hunt. Of such by Jeremias: « I will send, he says, many hunters, and they shall hunt them [n: (Jer. XVI)]. » And in the psalm: « The tongue of thy dogs [n: (Psal. LXVII)]. » These dogs, to whom the Bridegroom willed to join the care of us, stand by us as we begin, and ward off loss or damage; they press on carefully, that the evils that threaten us may cease at their very rising, before they grow the harder [0328C] upon our negligence or our ignorance. For sometimes our present manner of life burdens us with more secret faults, whose soft seduction thrusts itself in privily after the manner of a fox; and, running craftily through blind windings, it wills to be unknown, and to destroy us, ill provided as we are, the more freely the more hiddenly. And when our elders meet us with their teaching, instruct the ignorant, reprove the wandering with discipline; when they show whence temptation comes and whither it proceeds, what destruction, or what death at last, follows upon which suggestion; when they rebuke fresh diseases with a censorious tongue: then, like provident dogs, they catch the little foxes in us. Whence they also who are bidden to do this the more carefully and do not care, who, slothful to hunt, shape their negligence to sleep, are called by Isaias — as by another dog — « dumb dogs [n: (Isa. LI)], » [0328D] sleeping and loving dreams, set in the place of watchmen. And indeed that same care lies upon us also far more heavily: that we should study to be found watchful in the same catching, and should pursue the foxes within our very selves with a careful search, until we prudently reach their lurking-places by a hunter's scent. And when we have come thither, we ought, according to the poet, to crush the evil seeds of the disease while they are new; and, according to the Prophet [n: (Psal. CXXXVI)], to dash our little ones against the rock; lest, either by ignorance drawing a veil or by negligence drawing us away, we be seduced into a byway of error, and be led into deadly falls and into the snares of temptations. For sometimes a crafty temptation feigns itself either nothing at all or a very little thing, and so flatters a negligent mind [0329A] with a fraudulent enticement that, while it annuls or makes light of what is felt beforehand in secret with concupiscence, it afterwards causes to be despised the actual consent given to it. And when the seduced mind attends not with a sufficiently diligent eye how the canker creeps, what the wickedness conceived intends, the very destruction of the vineyard plainly shows that the fox, little before, which brought itself in secretly, has done no small hurt. Such little foxes therefore, which thrust themselves fraudulently into our minds, we are bidden to watch, to hunt, to catch diligently; that what at first lay hid as in a chamber, decently under a cloak, may break out and come forth, and rejoice at last to be shown shamelessly. « Some, as it is written, are glad when they have done evil, and rejoice in most wicked things [n: (Prov. II)]. » [0329B] But some say (if indeed your diligence has committed to memory what it heard) that this present little book, which Solomon, as was said before, set in order after the manner of a drama, contains in itself the words of no more than four persons, as it were, who speak of nuptial love and of the spiritual chastity of the marriage. For the Bride and the maidens, the Bridegroom and the Bridegroom's companions are brought in as four persons, who for the weaving of the drama are led forth as from the wings into the midst, that the speech may pass from these to those in turn, *188* and that by an alternating speech the epithalamial drama may be satisfied. The Bridegroom therefore, who above spoke now to the Bride, now to the maidens, and with gracious diligence pursued what befits the Bride, seems here to turn his speech now to his companions, [0329C] that he may exhort them, as they attend the nuptials, to the catching of the foxes. And they say that the Bridegroom's companions are the holy angels, who, it is agreed, are certainly present at these nuptials — as you know that Gabriel was sent to the Virgin in the beginning, and that neither he nor the rest are wanting to the ministry of men. In these nuptials indeed no small care presses the Bridegroom, that he provide for the Virgin, and for them that attend him, things that shall profit: that the Virgin first and more excellently may rejoice in the nuptial chamber, and secondly that the maidens lack not spiritual advancement.
