It was said far above that by the name of maidens are figured the apostles and apostolic men, who are seen more especially to attend the Virgin Mother of the Bridegroom with a handmaid's affection, while they love to venerate her childbearing [0329D] with an assiduous wonder and a solid faith, and to imitate her fruitfulness by bearing sons also, not by coition but by the spirit. These shepherds and teachers the Bridegroom wills not to be burdened beyond their power by the onset of malignant spirits, but to be freed by the kindly affection and patronage of the angels, that the vineyards may not wither in the flower of their first season by the fraud of the foxes, but by the care of the good spirits may grow strong unto the late fruit. The Bridegroom therefore admonishes the good spirits, who in this epithalamium are the companions, to be careful and to strive after the nuptial advancements; to stand nearer to them, and worthily to take care of those whose destruction or hurt the careful Virgin wills not. For the Virgin has much care for the maidens [0330A] or apostles, whose manner of life will profit herself indeed most of all, and others much; from whom the angels' solicitude is bidden diligently to ward off things hurtful — a solicitude that by this zeal or ministry will please both the Bridegroom and the Bride in no small measure. To whom the Bridegroom, speaking, says: *Catch,* etc.



## CHAPTER XIV.

*Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vines.* You, he says, angels, whom flesh has not made equal to men, nor guilt to the evil spirits, whom pride or disobedience has not cast out from the Creator's face; who abide and remain with me from the beginning unto perpetuity as companions, glorious by a likeness received, not made equal by an eternal greatness: I will that you be diligently present to us, that is, [0330B] to me and to the Bride as we celebrate our nuptials, and that whatever strives to withstand be by you made ineffectual and weak. For since some no longer run with open violence upon a level path, they glide in by blind windings and whisper venomous frauds; and, detracting from the Virgin, they labour to resist her wishes, while what she asserts of Christ they discolour with a dissuading guile. They dissuade, lest either the hidden divinity of Christ be seen by the eye of faith, or, when faith has seen it, lest it be firmly loved in the mind; and they strike a hard buffet of ignorance or of fear into those who will deny, or they graft in the love of visible things into those who will neglect the faith of things invisible. Who are these but wicked demons, learned in malice, full of fraud, who love nothing holy, who seek nothing worthy of praise; who, [0330C] when violence is wanting to them, have the love and the skill of seducing, and, according to a certain heathen, have a thousand arts of hurting and more than that? These, by the cunning of a wondrous art, not by any right of power or of virtue, seduce Judas Iscariot, greedy of money rather than of salvation; and lest he love his master; they dissuade him with manifold guile, and persuade him to become a traitor guilty of hatred. « When the devil, he says, had put it into the heart that Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, should betray him [n: (Joan. XIII)]. » These shake with the thunder of fear, a little after, unto denying, that Simon Peter who a little before had promised himself a lot for standing fast; and the sudden denier would have perished within the crafty jaws of the beasts, had not the powerful prayer of his pitying Master come to his aid: « Simon, he says, behold Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you [0330D] as wheat: but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not [n: (Luc. XXII)]. » Nor only before Christ's resurrection did the cunning of them that work malice cut short the number of the apostles, but after the resurrection also it prepared a snare for the chosen deacons; into which, though it drew not Stephen, full of faith and of spirit, nor the five that remained, yet it brought in the seventh, Nicolas the newcomer, unto a new heresy. Whose fraudulent cunning the Bridegroom rightly designated by the name of foxes — creatures which nature has not armed with much strength, but has fortified with so great a craft, with so great a refuge of divers frauds, [0331A] that they are said in the Gospel to have manifold retreats of burrows among us: « The foxes, he says, have holes [n: (Luc. IX)]. » The demons have hidden retreats and dark lurking-holes; they have runs past tracking and winding footprints, so that no simple man easily sets his foot to track them out, since either he cannot see them, or, if perchance he has seen them, straightway loses them. Sometimes the fox, when the necessity of hunger seems to press her hard, running to the refuge of fraud, feigns to lie dead; and when the birds have come near, hoping to have their food in the dead carcase, *189* she seizes them unawares, rejoicing to win a victory over the living. So that wicked spirit, who is ever found to hunger after our ruin, when with open nets he cannot ensnare [0331B] any of the winged (for, as Holy Scripture recalls [n: (Prov. I)], and the truth of them that have proved it affirms, in vain is the net cast before the eyes of them that have wings), feigns himself dead and of no strength at all against the just; he yields, and as it were now grants them to prevail unto the good things they shall have willed. And they, when they judge that they stand as though they should thenceforth not fall, rejoicing together in a long advancement and now secure by much practice, come sometimes to this carrion of the world, seeking a little too immoderately after the things that pass, believing that nothing hurtful is in them, but rather things that shall profit for necessary uses. But that wicked one, holding it in memory that by the ancient law it is forbidden that carrion be touched [n: (Levit. II)], and seeing the just now held guilty of the written law, if even but a little; judging that the incautious appetites of temporal things are of his own right, wickedly [0331C] reviving on a sudden, lays a strong hand upon the birds that are to perish. So indeed they who thought that they were catching, and turning what they caught to their own uses, are found to be caught, and, being alive, to lie beneath the dead; because, while the living covet a little too incautiously the carrion of faults, that carrion, as it were dead, revives strongly and truly unto the ruin of the living. That Samson, more prudently execrating the fraudulent foxes, laid hold of them alive, and held no fewer than three hundred; and, binding them two by two, with their heads free and their tails bound, and fire set beneath their tails, he wove a mystery worthy of praise [n: (Judic. XV)]. This prudent Samson, who is also said to be strong of arm, who by a prudent fortitude is believed to have carried away the gates of death, is the beloved of this our [0331D] Virgin of whom our discourse is, whom the truthful understanding of faith preaches to be God and man. Who took not one fox, not two only, but three hundred together, because he detected all the malice of all the malignant spirits; who so is man that as God also he regards all things circumspectly, and nothing appears imperfectly to his sight. By the number of a hundred, as you know, any perfection is figured, and the hundredfold perfection is not unfittingly recorded to be tripled: since, for that which the malignant spirits have suggested to us, however slightly, unto affection, and for what by word and what by deed they have drawn to any effect whatever, this sterner judge gathers them all with a hooked hand unto perfection, and, preparing fire for them all, drags them all to a miserable failing. And indeed now, as with head unbound [0332A] and mouth free, the wicked spirits rave; but their hinder parts are bound indissolubly; and when at the end of things the possibility of raging is forbidden them, fire being rendered to their deserts, an unfailing labour of suffering presses them hard. Whereof in the Gospel: « Everlasting fire, he says, which was prepared for the devil and his angels [n: (Matth. XXV)]. » And Paul: « Whose consummation, he says, is unto burning [n: (Hebr. VI)]. » But in the meantime, while that consummation is still deferred, while the last burning is not yet brought upon the foxes bound together, the Bridegroom wills to admonish his companions, that is the good angels, the more diligently, that they be willing to apply diligence to the catching of the evil ones. For because men, assailed by demons and filled with many miseries, do not stand if the ministering spirits resist not the ambushes of the hurtful, [0332B] the good come near and detect the frauds of the evil, and, when they are detected, show them beforehand to men, that they may carefully beware. For to this end are the ministering spirits set over men, to this end appointed to their care and keeping: that what men cannot do, being slower by nature and by negligence, these — whom both nature and merit have made far keener — may foresee, may forestall, may forewarn men and help them to beware; lest at any time the enemies exult and insult and say, "We have prevailed to hurt." Man indeed, the weaker, willing to build or to rebuild the walls of an inward holiness, to restore Jerusalem, to repair the breaches of a city long since overthrown, has many who assail and hinder the unremitting labour of one so pressing on; who, when [0332C] they see, envy, and, to say the least, deride the watchful insistence of the labourer. Who, when they observe that of himself he is not strong enough for the building, and scarcely escapes with unhurt footstep the mockery or the pressure of his enemies, despise the work begun, and assert that it cannot be brought to perfection, but that the foxes will lightly pass over the unfinished work with a derisive leap. Whence in Esdras, Tobias the Ammonite: « If a fox go up, he says, he shall leap over their stone wall [n: (II Esdr. IV)]. » And it is added: « Hear, O our God, for we are made a reproach: cover not their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from before thy face, because they have mocked them that build [n: (ibid.)]. » You see the wicked rivals mocking the labour of them that build, and, while these advance, already rejoicing [0332D] in the future leap of the foxes; to whose mockery, or to whose leap already presumed upon, the weakness of those men makes no full resistance, if the skilful keeping of the angels stands not by them as they labour. Because therefore the diligence of the just labours at restoring the building of the mind, and the mockery or oppression of them that work malice sometimes discolours the work begun, the Bridegroom admonishes his companions the more insistently and urges them on, whose stronger care more fully searches out the frauds of the assailants. You, he says, who can forestall with nimble sight the cunning of the envious spirits, catch us the foxes that think to leap over the wall of them that build; lest the unseemly leap of those foxes dishonour what these men build, or lest any fraud of the enemies *190* discolour the reforming of the city. Who say says Isaias, « to my soul: [0333A] Bow down, that we may pass over [n: (Isa. LI)]. » [var: Vulg. *animae tuae*, "to thy soul" — in Isaias the words are spoken to Jerusalem, not to the speaker] Against which Nahum the prophet also: « He shall not add again, he says, that Belial pass through thee [n: (Nahum. I)]. » Who shall grant that Belial add not again to pass through us, nor that the fox, holding the work of the building in contempt, leap over it — unless the Bridegroom's companions, who are commanded to succour men in this, and to forestall with prudent watchfulness the derisive leaps or assaults? Let them therefore catch us the foxes while they are found to be little and as yet weak, lest they grow great and pass over the wall, which, being low, can easily be leapt; and if they be granted to try its lowness with a free leap, growing worse and worse they will hasten to destroy our vineyards. And since these vineyards flower and hope to be advanced to fruit by the summer's mildness, it is needful that the little foxes be removed further off, [0333B] or that their frauds be so detected by a worthy providence that (even if they will) they may not be able to have power to hurt them that advance.



## CHAPTER XV.

*For our vineyard hath flourished.* He who a little before named (vineyards) consequently names a single (vineyard), though rather in counting the passage is wont to be made from the singular number to the plural; hinting by this that the souls to which the Bridegroom willed to give a saving life he gathers, by the union of faith and of consent, into one people's assembly. « We, say they, are his people, and the sheep of his pasture [n: (Psal. XCIX)]. » And they call themselves (a people), that the singleness of faith may be commended, and they call themselves (sheep), that the diversity of the many may be shown; because a timely unity gathers many either into a bundle or into a handful, [0333C] and one Lord, one faith, makes them one people. And that a unity of this kind may be seen to be the more expressly commended, in those apostles whom Christ willed to be gathered into one [n: (Act. IV)] the love of possessing all things together so put far off whatever stood importunately in the way, that there was one soul to them all and one heart to them all [n: (Act. II)]. This vineyard perhaps is said in a special manner to have flowered, into which the Bridegroom is read to have poured his Spirit on the fiftieth day; which, rich with a new gift and burning with the love of a new holiness, put forth new and unheard-of blossoms of a voluntary poverty. Whereof it was foretold: « The vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth is the house of Israel [n: (Isa. V)]. » Rightly is the vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth, putting forth wondrous flowers and about to put forth fruits equally wondrous, called the house of Israel — a house beyond doubt not darkened [0333D] by blindness; a house seeing God in hope in the present and about to see him again hereafter; rejoicing much in that faith, and about to rejoice far more in the sight. Within the enclosures of this vineyard it is fitting that little foxes be not admitted, or, if perchance they have been admitted, that they be not suffered to remain longer; but that, when they have destroyed by a hidden avarice Ananias and Sapphira [n: (Act. V)], as yet weakly tender, they be caught the sooner, lest they go on and fulfil the coveted malice of their fraud. For the Bridegroom's companions, faithfully standing by Peter and showing the hidden bite of the little fox in the false brethren, suffer not her venomous snares to be spread everywhere among the rest; and the seducing foxes grieve that their purpose is broken and their frauds detected. For those over whose salvation [0334A] the angels have perceived themselves to be set, and of whom they have learned that the Bridegroom truly has care, these they will not, nor do they suffer them, to be given over to the earth and to be the portions of foxes [n: (Psal. LXII)], but they forewarn them and help them not to lie under their frauds. At this [sic: *tempere*] therefore the foxes are not undeservedly called little, while they are easily kept from ravening by the ministry of the angels; which foxes, when the end of the times shall have come, will grow great more maliciously, when, namely, with their strength unbridled, the more briefly they have to rage the more freely they shall grow hot for it [n: (Apoc. XX)]. Then the angelic solicitude, as though not sufficing, will call them to a greater audience, and our own Samson, setting fire beneath, will bind the tails of them all; and the loosing of the foxes will hasten to rage into the harvests of the aliens, that the works both of these and of those may deserve to perish in one [0334B] burning. For then the wicked spirits shall perish by a fire that destroys but does not consume, and evil men also shall none the less wretchedly perish by an immortal death; those, their hinder parts indissolubly bound together, shall not return to the liberty of wickedness; and of these, as of the aliens, the harvests — both their works and the hope of their works — shall perish. And because the Bridegroom in his benevolence wills this to be kept far from the vineyards, and wills the angels to be employed in keeping it off while the time is fitting, the Bride rejoices, and loves to answer her loving Bridegroom in like manner the more, the more she sees him to be the readier toward her maidens. Whereof she adds: *The beloved,* etc.



## CHAPTER XVI.

*My beloved to me, and I to him, who feedeth among the lilies, [0334C] until the day breathe, and the shadows be bowed down.* What does she mean, that when the beloved here speaks of her beloved, this utterance of hers seems somewhat unfinished; *191* nor is any fuller sense found in it, unless something be understood from without for the finding of it? But what she who speaks would more truly, what more certainly, have understood, cannot easily, as I judge, be found out to the clear — least of all by those who, it is agreed, are hindered by a fog of mind, nor do they deserve that the hidden things of Holy Scripture be opened to them. Since therefore I am slender in understanding and abound not in merits, I myself, and no other, so hide for myself the supplement of this word, that I may neither arraign her that speaks nor weaken her word with a wandering sense; so that, if I shall have said anything there, I may rather conjecture than affirm. A little above, the [0334D] Virgin, saying: *My beloved to me,* added: « speaketh, » and « My beloved, she says, speaketh to me; » nor does that construction seem beset by the cloud of a thing understood: which, being furnished with the necessary parts, was found plainly sufficient. But now, saying: *My beloved to me,* she did not add either what he does or that he speaks, so that which of these she would have understood is left doubtful; and the more uncertain that is, so much the more freely is it granted to anyone to find whatever he shall have seen fittingly to suit the present place. In short, unrestrained love, scarcely bearing its own incitements, often finds no words more fully expressive of its own affections; and therefore its utterance is sometimes found to hang in suspense, or, that I may say more, defective through a scanty furniture. For when with its whole desire it stretches itself toward that for which it burns, [0335A] gaping after him alone to hold him, it makes little of all the rest; and if perchance it make a word about him, it heeds not time, mood, or order, and while it desires the whole, it strives not to express the whole in a word. Hence that woman in the Gospel, when what she loved had been taken away, knowing nothing but to weep, holding in her mind him alone whose sepulchre she grieved to see appear empty, seeing someone on a sudden and with a straying eye reckoning him the gardener, not much mindful of grammar, fearing no Priscian: « Lord, she says if thou hast taken him away, tell me; and I will take him away [n: (Joan. XX)]. » She who had said nothing of him before sets him down all too heedlessly, and does not set out by any worthy preceding word to whom she refers him; thinking it enough for the hearer that she herself fully thinks and fully feels, even though her half-full outward utterance does [0335B] not more fully agree with the full sense of the same. Nor is it to be wondered at if hidden love, when for the showing of itself it requires another's help, thinks a half-full utterance sufficient enough for itself; which is for the most part wordy by a sigh, for the most part even by desire alone, and despairs not of being heard, though it speak not with a full noise of words. Our Virgin therefore, diligently weighing the grace of this love, and not repaying with abundant speech the abundance of it which she has received, shuts up within the hidden place of her heart wondrous motions in an unexplainable manner, and, breathing them out but thinly, so applauds him with fewer words that by speaking she both makes this love known to the hearer, and, the furniture of words being cut short, leaves the hearer in suspense. *My beloved,* she says, *to me, and I to him.* He, I say, gives me what is his, and I give him what is [0335C] mine, that both his may be mine and mine his: and thus we may have our things alike, and, as the laws of espousal require, may rejoice that all things are common to us. And if a sense of this kind can be believed to shine out more fittingly in these words, the Bride seems to answer the Bridegroom to that which he had said; who, commanding the foxes to be taken because the vineyard had flowered, called it ours, and did not show by the words that followed whence this commendable community had come to be. For he did not say: My vineyard or thine, but: « our vineyard hath flourished. » Which word the prudent Virgin, marking it diligently with a busy ear, and turning herself again — the Bridegroom as it were withdrawing — to the aforesaid maidens, rejoices to speak of him, and with fewer words to intimate whence this [0335D] community is which the Bridegroom would designate. That it might be called, she says, not his, not mine, but rather « our vineyard, » a mutual bestowal wrought it, whereby the two are alike friends: because he of his own condescension regarded me, a lowly handmaid; my lowliness despised not the grace of him that regarded me; he loved me, perchance not by my merit but by his own good pleasure; my faith, being beloved, understood that he was worthily to be loved for his merits. The Word, disposing to be made flesh, poured himself into my handmaid's womb; taking flesh in me from me, he flooded me with his grace: I offered mine own self, I bestowed my flesh, I bound myself over to obedience, I fixed beforehand no manner, no bound, no order for the good pleasure of him that commanded; with my flesh, which in assuming he so exempted from every fault, he bought or redeemed for himself that vineyard which is said to have flowered; and [0336A] she who, while yet she withered, is bought or redeemed by our flesh, is, now that she is loved in flower, expressly also said to be ours. If the patriarchs of old, who were, it is agreed, of one father one after another — although, as you remember, not all begotten of one mother [n: (Gen. XXIX, XXX)] — say of Joseph, the last but one, « For he is our brother and our flesh [n: (Gen. XXXVII)]; » how much more may the Mother of the Bridegroom, the Bride of the son, say, our flesh? and of the [sic: *vinca*] which is redeemed by this flesh, does the son likewise say « ours? » My beloved, she says, to me: he gave what was his, whose benefit, whose mercy in all things goes before me; and I to him: I offered what was mine by a worthy return, that thenceforth the community both of things and of words might be kindly toward us. He too gives me warnings, or a command, to arise, and I offer him [0336B] a ready little ear for hearing; he exhorts and diligently admonishes that I arise and make haste; I, resigning leisure to him, patiently endure labour. My beloved is to me — what? what but loving or beloved? *192* and I render to him — what? what but the gifts of a like diligence or affection? that the love of him who is first and far the chief may be the first-begun, and mine no repayment that follows save by his own bounty. My beloved gives me a commandment, gives none the less a blessing with the commandment; I to him a nimble running along the way of his commandments with an enlarged heart; he to me help, I to him compliance; he to me good will, I to him obedience; he gives to me what is of grace, what is of love, I to him what is of reverence, what is of honour. To me my beloved bestows a saving gift upon one in need; I [0336C] render to him that requires it a willing affection; and he who, being great God and mighty in power, willed to be born man of me, rejoices to be fed not so much between my breasts as among the lilies. He who of old fed the patriarch Jacob from his youth, who much more lately satisfied five thousand men out of five loaves [n: (Matth. XIV)] — whence is he so needy, or so careless of his own power, as to be fed, since to be fed seems a mark not of power but of need? In short, when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterwards he was hungry [n: (Matth. IV)]. To whom that wicked devil, setting stones before him that he might tempt him, did not suggest that he should change them by a word into lilies, thinking that he hungered after the fashion of other men, not by a voluntary but by a necessary failing, and that therefore [0336D] loaves rather than lilies suited one that hungered. Thou, he says, whose jaws, as I perceive, are empty with a wearying fast, say that these stones become loaves by an effectual power; because, while hunger fasts with the loaves withdrawn, the appearance of lilies (though perchance to the eyes) is not seasonable to the jaws. Although sometimes the eyes too seem to suffer their own hunger, when namely they itch for seeing and are not strong enough to contain themselves; and when the uncovered appearance of the thing coveted is indulged them, their curiosity is not unfittingly said to be fed. This perhaps is what the Virgin asserts, that the Bridegroom is fed among the lilies, because to his eyes the thing wished for gives its answer not so much by word as by appearance; and the gracious greediness and hotter burning of lovers is fed not by the taste, not by the savour, but by the sight or the scent of lilies. For which cause [0337A] he is expressly recorded to be fed, not with lilies, but among the lilies; among which, dwelling and conversing, he rejoices in their fragrant comeliness; and as the Virgin, languishing with love, wills to be stayed up with apples or with flowers, so does he will to be soothed among the lilies by their pleasing bounty. And what shines white more gladly or breathes more sweetly than, in the Bride the mother, virginal integrity, faith purifying the heart, the fruitfulness of matronly modesty; cleanness, innocence, spiritual love, sweetness of manners, the form of justice, the excellence of a special merit? Among which the Bridegroom walks as on a spacious path, and, seeing and smiling, is fed with a gracious sight; he is delighted with the comeliness and the scent of excellent merits, and, being himself the flower and the lily, rejoices in the likeness he has found. For he confesses himself the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys, and in the Bride [0337B] the Virgin he beholds also the burgeoning grace of the lily; and thus he shows himself fed between the two with a certain joy, while by a subtle running to and fro he now presents himself more fully to the Virgin, now, referring himself to his own, renders himself incomprehensible and absents himself: for neither in the bosom of the father, grudging us. does he continually hide himself, nor in the mother's lap does he pour himself back with a continual good will, as it were; but going forth from him, he now runs out to her with a humble condescension, and withdrawing himself from her, he now runs back to his inaccessible throne. His running out is from the father, says Ambrose; his running back is to the father. This will of the Bridegroom, whereby he is found now absent from the Virgin, now more present; whereby he is discovered to be at hand now above man, now beyond man — [0337C] the Virgin, loving and beloved, finds by experience to abide with him as his own, while the shadows still remain, and one comes not to the grace of the following day.



## CHAPTER XVII.

*Who feedeth among the lilies, until the day breathe, and the shadows be bowed down.* For when, the night being bowed down, nothing dark, nothing hurtful in us shall any longer run in upon us, and at the morning's rising a gentler breeze shall breathe and an unfailing light shall meet us; the Bridegroom perhaps will then no longer run about among the lilies for the sake of feeding, since, being once seen by us, he will not run back again to his own to be hidden. For from that time, and thenceforward, he shall not be fed between the one lily and the other, nor shall he be shown either forsaking the one or referring himself to the other; but he shall so be in the one that he is continually presented to the other — nay, so in both that [0337D] he is absent from neither even for a little. « I, he says, in the Father, and the Father in me [n: (Joan. XIV)]; » and below, of the Spirit: « He shall abide, he says, with you, and shall be in you [n: (ibid.)]. » Therefore God in God, God abiding in himself, containing all things, shall be for ever; and none the less shall God be all things in all; and he who now breathes when he wills, in what manner he wills, and where he wills, then breathes upon all, flooding them with a light of the day, or rather of long continuance. For to whom, while it is lived here, that holy spirit worthily breathes; into whom by his kindly bounty he breathes himself not only unto life but unto a living life — upon him a brighter day then breathes with an unspeakable increase, against which the ancient night, the importunity of the shadows, thenceforward [0338A] conspires not; for God is a day, a day that a setting *193* knows not, one day, whose breathing now, and whose breathing upon us then still more, is no moderately seasonable thing. A day at whose fuller breathing the shadows are bowed down, the darknesses of the night give place, wicked spirits, or spiritual wickednesses, are driven out from among those above and pressed down even to those below. Unhappy indeed are those shadows, which, when the day breathes, are compelled to be bowed down, and, their neck being shattered, to be weighed down with infernal punishments: their power of raging lost, but not the straitness of suffering, they execrate their own heavy substance, or their eternal wretchedness of existing in evil. Far happier were they, if they might deserve to be brought to nothing, if, as of a wicked power, so also they might utterly be deprived of substance; because for a wicked man, or a wicked angel, it will be better now not to be, [0338B] than always to be in so great a misery — not of doing hurt, but of suffering. But shadows of this kind, the confusion of darkness, the obscure voice, the power of malignant spirits which shall at last more fully receive what it wickedly wrought, impatient of the day that breathes, is heavily bowed down under a hard burden, and is irremediably assigned to the avenging fire and the living worm. But meanwhile, while the consummation of the world, the last end of things, is deferred, or while the term of her days is not yet at hand for the aforesaid Virgin, the bridegroom is found to go and to come again, and not to abide unmoved; and the beloved grants not to her that loves him a fuller abundance of himself. Now, drawn far nearer to heaven as it were, he wills to be sought by the Virgin; now, drawing near to earth, he suffers himself to be felt hastily and for a little: [0338C] there he seems more present, and hence to be farther off; but thence to return, when he wills to be at hand nearest to the Virgin. Therefore he is not unfittingly said to converse among the lilies, and to delight in his running out and his running back after the manner of things unstable: to be fed between two shores, and to be turned to neither of them with a fixed footprint: now absent, now present, to go away the more quickly, and straightway to return. To whom the Virgin subjoins: *Return,* etc.



## CHAPTER XVIII.

*Return, my beloved: be thou like to a roe and to the fawn of harts, upon the mountains of Bethel.* [var: Vulg. *Bether*; and Vulg. sets the vocative after the imperative] She who in the preceding chapter spoke of the Bridegroom to the maidens, or was perhaps set alone with herself in the secret chamber of her mind, did not pursue any longer the tenor of speaking she had proposed, but makes an apostrophe to him by whom she [0338D] believes herself to be forsaken. Love is found insufficient, and consequently impatient too; it wills not to be without him whom it has once found pleasing, once most sweet; and whatever is offered or bestowed upon her that greedily sighs, apart from him, she despises with a worthy disdain, nor does anything suffice her, until she refer herself to him. Since therefore she is not yet able to enjoy him by beholding his face more fully, she wills often to make an apostrophe to him in speaking; and when she speaks of him she is straightway compelled to be turned back to him with a word of entreaty, that by him whom she desires to see she may by that very desire be worthy at least to be seen. But because, her own mortality standing in the way, she feels him more often to withdraw or to turn aside, she asks him nothing more anxiously [0339A] than to return: that returning, and marking with what love the tender Virgin is held, he may bestow upon her that loves him his grace and a more bountiful abundance of himself. But that he may not set about either to go farther away or to tarry longer, the Virgin thinks it fitting to interpose a merit with her asking, so that, even if perchance he dispose not to hear her prayers the sooner, yet, compelled by his own equity, he may not put after it the merit of her that asks. *Return,* she says, *my beloved.* For if, she says, I were entreating some great thing of one whom I love not, I should not wonder to suffer a repulse and to be defrauded of my desire; but when I pour out prayers, when I spread out suppliant hands to my beloved, whence hast thou this hardness, that what I ask thou bringest not to effect? For who is so severe, so austere, that if he weigh that he is tenderly loved he would not repay like with like by a ready good will; and that, being beloved, he would not bestow upon her that loves him [0339B] the benefit she has asked, so that, being over-hard, he offend not against the rights or the laws of love? True and sincere love turns not its ear away for long; to him that gives what is pleasing and wished for it denies not the like, it deals not out the contrary: for her whom it purely loves it is held and moved with much care; it embraces her that loves, and answers a tender affection with usury. In short, by the testimony of Holy Scripture thou hast said that thou lovest him that loves thee [n: (Prov. VIII)]; nay, some also (as they that have proved it declare) thou hast loved before ever they loved [n: (I Joan. IV)]; and since thou art laudably proclaimed to love first, with no merits going before, who would not judge it hard, if thou spurnest the prayers of them that well deserve? But it is certain that she who loves deserves to be loved, and that she who is worthy to be loved consequently deserves not to be defrauded of a just desire: [0339C] especially when she goes not hunting, after the fashion of certain carnal folk, after the things that are her own, but entreats thee alone, and only for thine own sake, to become present. *Return, my beloved.* Thou, she says, by whose love I am held, in regard of whom all other things are vile to me, by whose absence I am weighed down while things present prick or bite me; thou who, when thou art believed to be at hand, suddenly turnest thyself away, inflicting [sic: *in cutiens*] to the rude and inexperienced a burden scarce to be borne: turn thyself, I beseech thee, that thou mayest show thyself well-disposed to her that calls thee back; nay (that I may say more) return, that thou mayest present thyself to her that loves thee with the sweetness she has wished. Render, I say, the more gladly what gladly and more often thou hast already given; render to her that loves thee what she has deserved, thou who lovedst her when she had not yet deserved it: repeat *194* now of debt what before thou didst bestow freely, [0339D] or rather return at last, bestowing what thou hast promised to them that love thee. For thou hast promised that, the course of life being finished, thou shouldest be seen face to face [n: (I Cor. XIII)]; that they who see should be satisfied with fulness, and, being satisfied, should not be held by loathing: that we, glad in thy presence, should not thenceforth be weighed down by absence; that, pressed by no trouble, we should always rejoice with thee in thy glory. To this therefore I will and I ask that thou return, my beloved: that what I have somewhat tasted and seen imperfectly through a glass, I may now, the barrier of the flesh being taken away and mortality utterly banished, hold and see more perfectly with unveiled face. But because a fervent desire is not filled full by the bounty of things present, and love unfilled is not held patient enough to await things absent, the Virgin asks that not only he whom she loves should return, but that returning he should be held like [0340A] to a roe and to the fawn of harts. « Be thou like, she says, to a roe and to the fawn of harts *(supra IV)*. » The roe, as you know from what was said above, has this natural power in her eyes, that she quickly discerns and distinguishes what pasture suits her, and even in her running judges what is useful to her, what fitting to be eaten, and what unfitting and therefore by its own desert to be spat out. But the fawn of harts, whom both a younger age and a stronger nature support, is borne along with a swift running and is on a sudden present where he wills; and he so rejoices that the privilege of speed is his, that among the other wild beasts he seems to have not so much feet as winged feet. When therefore the Virgin asks that the bridegroom be like to animals of this kind, she shows that a confident and secure conscience is not wanting to her — a conscience which [0340B] at the present time neither ignorance nor negligence accuses; and, willing that this be quickly repaid to her, she refuses not to be looked upon beforehand. Thou, she says, whose presence my loving mind covets, at whose return my conscience in no wise trembles: search out and look through with what desire, with what instancy I strive after thee; with what affection, with what love, putting present things after, I await thee alone as him that is to come. Be thou like to a roe, that thou mayest search my inward parts the more diligently, and mayest not be loath to sift or to discern what good, what better thing I put after or put before: and when thou shalt have known for certain what each single virtue in me deserves, let thy justice be held swift as a fawn to render what it has deserved. For receiving the benefit of the reward I am indeed so hasty that the scrutiny that goes before, and a sudden sifting, do not [0340C] affright me; and with so great a burning do I desire the nimble good will of the fawn to come, that I refuse not to feel beforehand the subtle watchfulness of the roe. For I know that the grace of the fawn comes not to me unto a fuller gladness, if the truth of the roe go not before to sift my inward conscience; nor shall the glad coming of the one fulfil my desire, if the true sifting of the other shall not first judge it worthy to be fulfilled. « Judge therefore and discern my cause » not only « from the nation that is not holy [n: (Psal. XLII)], » which is in no wise compared with me, but also from the holy nation, whose holiness, compared with mine, is not equal — which perchance, dreading the scrutiny, wills so to be clothed with the glory that is to come upon it, [0340D] that it be not first compelled to prove the winnowing-fan of sifting. For not knowing whether she be worthy of hatred or of love [n: (Eccle. IX)], she serves in fear, and exults before the Lord with trembling: now lifting herself toward him she grows glad with the hope of the gift she wishes for; now referring herself to herself, she greatly fears a scrutiny as severe as it is true. « Who knoweth, she says, if he will turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him? » [n: (Joel. II.)] But the Virgin knows beyond doubt that her beloved is turned, and confidently asks that, being turned, he return also; and she wills that her inward parts be marked by the subtle gaze of him that returns, holding it certain that the steadfast building of her mind is overthrown by no battering-ram whatever. In her therefore in whom the keen eye of the roe shall have found nothing that is not his own, in her consequently shall the good will of the fawn give his own leap; and whose [0341A] conscience the judgment that runs before shall approve, her cleanness shall the swift grace of him that repays reward. For the roe too loves to gaze more subtly and more discerningly, and the fawn wills to be seen glad and well-disposed by the nimbleness of his running; and both rejoice to be borne over the ridges of the mountains, the summits of the virtues — he to be borne after, repaying just things; she, subtly considering all things, to be borne before. *Upon the mountains,* she says, *of Bethel.* As they say who reckon that they have the knowledge of the Hebrew names — which we have either not deserved at all or have obtained but scantily — Beth is *a house*, and el is interpreted *God*; and Bethel is named in the Latin tongue *the house of God*. And the house of God is not unfittingly judged to be the inward conscience of the Virgin, namely a spiritual bride-chamber, which is made ready for God the Son of God, which the presence of the divine majesty chose to inhabit, [0341B] adorning and honouring it with the excellence of a wondrous holiness. Which house or habitation is rightly called mountainous, plentiful not in rough and unequal ridges but in the various merits of the virtues; from whose height the flatness of us that are beneath is far removed, and among men the bridegroom alone is declared worthily to overtop it. He indeed, like to a roe or to the fawn of harts, is borne above; to whose excellence the height of any mountains whatever is not compared; who upon the mountains of the Virgin and the steep places of her notable merits is both the subtle knower of them and the nimble renderer of rewards. And while the wished-for glory of rewards does not yet meet the Virgin — which she knows does not meet her, if the giver's worthy [0341C] consideration run not before — the Virgin wishes and asks that he whom she loves tarry no longer, *195* but, returning the sooner, be made like to a roe and to the fawn of harts, so that upon the mountains of the merits and the virtues of her virginal conscience the inspection may run before, and a friendly repayment follow. For that repayer is the hart of friendship and the colt of graces. Who, although he condescends to hear the Virgin's affectionate prayers, yet does not straightway hearken unto effect to her desire; and seeing the Virgin, he wills not yet to be seen face to face, but after the manner of lovers withdraws himself and is hidden, and wills to be sought — of whom she subjoins: *In the little bed,* etc.



## CHAPTER XIX.

*[CAP. III.] In my little bed through the nights I sought him whom [0341D] my soul loveth. I sought him, and found him not.* The little bed here, as I judge, may be called a certain straitness of mind, in which the will or the intention of her that loves gathers and binds itself together, when namely she wills with the highest desire to please him whom she loves, to speak with him alone, to cleave to his close embraces. Burning with which purpose, while she wills to leap back from these things of sense, to be turned away from earthly things, and to feel only him that is invisible — as it were ignorant of the flesh, drunken with the love of the Bridegroom whom she foretastes, one spirit with him — she straitens herself as in a short little bed. Against which, her who commits not herself to a like straitness, who with a loosened mind lets in lost affections, the truth-telling speech of Isaiah accuses and reproves — nay rather, through [0342A] Isaiah, the truthful spirit of prophecy. « Thou hast received, he says, an adulterer; thou hast enlarged thy couch [n: (Isa. LVII)]. » The prophetic speech, saying that the shameless woman has received an adulterer, adds to show that she is no friend to a sufficiently narrow solitude, who has not reduced the breadth of her couch to a short little bed, nor forced herself within close bounds, her little bed being shortened. For she enlarged her couch when she poured her lost mind abroad, and received another, or rather an adulterer, when she poured in the pandering of sin; when, dissolved with nerveless softness, her feet parted, she was defiled in an enlarged couch with unlawful lovers. But the Virgin, ignorant of the aforesaid breadth, shutting herself up in a certain straitness of mind, and shutting in with her none other beside him with whom she is one spirit, sought him whom [0342B] she loved in this little bed with herself, hoping him to be at hand — she who admitted no other at all. In short, she had read in the Psalm: « The Lord is nigh unto all that call upon him [n: (Psal. CXLIV)]; » the Virgin therefore seeks the bridegroom, but the night blunts the sight of her that seeks — a night which pours itself with a darkened face over her that wills to find the sought one; and, it being poured over, the light that is sought pours not out its full rays, but, its brightness being called back, hides itself as it were under a cloak. Not one voice, but very many set themselves against the Virgin that seeks, and, that the sought one may not be found, interpose a troublesome wall; and for this cause the virgin rightly makes mention not so much of a night as of nights, by whose opposing she perceives that the choice is as yet denied her. A night is the difficulty of seeking, a night the delay of finding; a night is the trouble of deferring, a night the misery [0342C] of enduring. A night is the unfulfilment of spiritual desire; a night is the flesh that is to die, even though the conversation be now not carnal; a night, in fine, is the burdensome presence of this life, however polished with labours or with the virtues of one that labours. Through these nights the Virgin asserts that she sought the bridegroom, and that, since he met her not in the first as one that would remain, she departed not from her purpose; and that although she sought again, yet she has not yet found him according to her liking — proving by experience that there has been no full agreement of light with these darknesses. *Through the nights,* she says, *I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, and found him not.* Therefore, when the Virgin sought the bridegroom, she was not strong enough to find him, because a somewhat dark night seemed to forestall her that sought — nay, a throng of nights seemed as by agreement [0342D] to come together, striving and straining to hinder the hands and the eyes of her that sought. For although the Virgin bravely restrains herself from other occupations, and, straitened in her little bed, girds herself the more anxiously for seeking, yet she reaches not to that inaccessible light of the Bridegroom, so long as the throng of the aforesaid nights thrusts itself against her endeavour. Whence the same Bridegroom: « You shall seek me, he says, and shall not find me; and where I am, you cannot come [n: (Joan. VII)]. » The Son is indeed in the bosom, in the session, at the right hand of God the Father, of co-equal glory, of one substance, of the same majesty: co-eternal with the Eternal, equal to the Invisible, inhabiting also an inaccessible light, ungranted not only to any of us, but even to his Mother [0343A] while she lived here. For to the throne of glory, in which the Son abides in the Father and the Father in the Son, neither John, nor James, nor in fine the Virgin mother came; and as to them the right hand or the left is not given for sitting together, so neither to the Mother, who by the law of mortals is the handmaid of the Son's humanity. Although therefore the Bridegroom is here sought, whether by their desire or by his Mother's, yet he is not found at the right hand, or in the glory of God the Father; and, he being not taken away but deferred, she seems to have entered upon a counsel, and, either speaking to herself alone or perhaps to the maidens, to have said: *I will arise,* etc. *196*



## CHAPTER XX.

*I will arise, and will go about the city: through the lanes and the streets I will seek him whom my soul loveth.* Because, straitened in my little bed, I cannot find him whom I love, I will arise; [0343B] and I will set about to go round the breadth of the city; I will arise from the leisure and diligence of contemplating, and will gird myself to the zeal and the business of working. Nor will I imitate Dinah [n: (Gen. XXXIV)]; I will not go forth to see the women abroad; I will not buy a farm, nor go into the country for secular business; but I will go round the fortified city within its circuit, and will enter in unto the heart of Jerusalem for the sake of calling away and of strengthening. I will not assign my nights to fault, nor to the body, nor to leisure, but for the speaking of good I will lift up my hands in the nights [n: (Psal. CXXXIII)]; and him whom I love I will seek the more diligently through the lanes and the streets — him whom I cannot find in my little bed — if perchance I may be strong enough to find him among them. For sometimes the profit which we feel not in leisure we find more bountifully in the business of speaking; [0343C] and when we impart the due care to our brethren and our neighbours, he is the more present at hand whom by this office we obey. I judge those to be called lanes whom the straightness of faith and the certainty of a long-suffering hope directs; but streets, those whom the sweeter breadth of an advanced charity receives; through whom the Virgin asserts that she will seek the Bridegroom, because, imparting care to them, she reckons that she shall please him. For because the Bridegroom had above invited her to arise, « arise, he says, make haste, my friend, » that is, that thou mayest visit thy neighbours again for teaching: the Virgin, obeying his warnings, breaks off for a little the leisure she had taken up, and promises both to arise and to seek the Bridegroom through the lanes and the streets. For the Virgin loves with a worthy care to visit again and to go round those who are contained within the religious circuit of the fortified city, who within the enclosures of the Church confess themselves fellow-citizens of the saints and [0343D] of the household of God — removing by her intervention whatever is hurtful, and bestowing by her example the things that shall profit. And she walks through the lanes and the streets in that same city when she helps and instructs those that are upright in faith, long-suffering in hope, diffused in charity, and busies herself to promote them to better things, that she may deserve more amply to please him to whom she has approved herself. For thus is he both sought by them that love him and wills to be sought, and wills that they who seek should earn the grace of him that is sought. Thus, through those that are narrow and subtle in understanding, and enlarged in knowledge, the anxiety of them that seek is exercised; and though they profit not yet enough for the finding, they are at least promoted to a greater merit. Thus, I say, through the men of the Church, as through the lanes and the streets of the city, he wills his own face to be sought, but that face, being invisible, [0344A] not yet to be found through visible men; because, although by giving the grace of seeking he wills a greater merit to be acquired, yet he wills not that they who seek should as yet prove the wished-for fulness of the thing sought. When therefore Isaiah cries: « Seek ye the Lord while he may be found [n: (Isa. LV)], » he seems not, as I judge, to mean this, that they who seek can find here to the full him whom they sought; but rather that they who study to bring a watchful diligence to the seeking can at the present time obtain, not the reward of merit, but the merit of the reward. They therefore who have as yet to live by faith, in hope of what is to come, seek the Lord God, being about to find him not at once but afterwards; through the nights they seek the day, being about to enjoy his presence not at once, nor to come to full joy until the day shall have shone forth. For through the nights, although a worthy [0344B] zeal is bestowed upon the seeking, yet not the light, but the merit of finding the light is found; and in the presence of the nights it is a fitting time for seeking, and, the merit being found, there remains the reward to be obtained. For who would reckon to find the day through the nights, since, unless the nights give place, the more welcome day refuses to come; and since the presence of the nights can be called nothing else than the absence of the sun, and since, when the sun rises, it is agreed that flight is straightway proclaimed to the nights? While the night is indeed present, the sun sends not forth his shining orb, and, the darkness remaining, he suffers not his own face to be seen; but, hastening to his rising, he sends the day-star before as a herald, by which token he promises himself not present, but coming the sooner. But that day-star (by which messenger the coming sun is preceded) [0344C] is found by them that seek while the nights are still at hand; and when it is found, the very darknesses of the nights already grow thin, but they wholly vanish not save when the sun is risen. While therefore through the nights the absent sun is sought, sometimes the day-star shows itself, which intends not to show the sun while the nights are still present, but instructs them that seek whither they should tend, whither they should direct the eye that is to find, namely from what quarter they should hope for the presence of the sun that is to come. For so long as a deep night holds and oppresses the world, and an unclean dregs presses hard upon the consciences of us wretched men, who knows (the day-star not yet seen) whence the sun has to rise, since, with no forerunner, not even the way to him can be found? But when he that seeks the sun beholds the day-star going before, taught by that foreteller he is now held by a certain assurance that [0344D] the presence of the sun is not far from him that foretells it, but that, because the night comes between, his face is not yet seen. And so he that seeks a light through the nights finds a light, but a light of the night, being about by this light to find a light afterwards, but a light of the day; and this near day, this sun that is to come, who wills his own presence to be deferred, *197* wills the day-star to be borne before, that men may come to it more surely. This does he that asks receive, this does he that seeks find, this is the door that is unbarred to him that knocks: to him that seeks the sun for a reward, the way is first shown as a day-star; first, I say, of grace is merit given to him that labours, and so, as of merit, the sun is given, nay shall be given, for a reward to him that waits. For the bridegroom does not give the reward at once, as he gives the merit, even though perchance every man set the good wine before that which is worse [0345A] [n: (Joan. II)] — but he is the true sun, who alone above all things deserves to be loved; and he wills indeed to be seen, and, unless the day-star be sent before, he is not seen. Therefore perhaps, when the Gospel had said: « Every one that asketh receiveth, and he that seeketh findeth [n: (Matth. VII)], » marking that the benefit of merit is given in the present, it showed that another thing remained to be given in what follows: « And to him that knocketh, it says, it shall be opened [n: (ibid.)]. » He who by asking, it says, and by seeking rejoices that the merit going before is imparted to him, shall by knocking — that is, by pressing on — rejoice that the door is afterwards opened to him; because he who through the nights is advanced by grace together with merit, as by a day-star, shall, the sun's palace being opened, enjoy to the full the glory of the full light. A little above, when it said, ask, seek, knock, subjoining words answering to each, it bestowed nothing in the present, but brought forth (using the future tense) [0345B] words of promise: leaving us in suspense whether they should be fulfilled within the nights, that is in this time, or should pass over all at once to the wished-for presence of the eternal sun. « Ask, it says, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you [n: (ibid.)]. » [var: Vulg. Matt. 7:7 *dabitur vobis*, "it shall be given you"; the reading printed here is the wording of John 16:24] But lest it be long doubtful that nothing is not bestowed in the nights upon the desire of us that ask, and that nothing likewise is not deferred until the day dawn and the sun rise rather than the day-star, it straightway added: « For every one that asketh receiveth, and he that seeketh findeth [n: (ibid.)]. » This is of the present time. For it says not, he shall receive and he shall find, but « He beginneth and findeth. And to him that knocketh, it says, it shall be opened. » This is of the sun that is to come. For it says not, « to him that knocketh » it is opened, but « it shall be opened, » that it may distinguish between that which is granted us to obtain in the present, and that which [0345C] is promised to be granted much better in what follows. So to Jacob, who asked and sought not Lia for a wife but Rachel [n: (Gen. XXIX)], the father, keeping the custom of the country, gave Lia before Rachel; in the marriage he set the elder-born first — not indeed of equal beauty, but fruitful — promising that entrance to the second should be given the young man afterwards. In like manner the Virgin also, seeking through the nights, through the lanes and the streets, him whom she had known to be beautiful above all, first receives, first finds the fruitful gift of merit; but because she now pants not so much after merit as after the reward, not so much after labour as after rest, she is believed to have found nothing so long as he reveals not his face. Therefore she repeats: *I sought,* etc.



## CHAPTER XXI.

[0345D]

*I sought him, and found him not.* Behold, now for the third time the Virgin asserts that she has sought him whom she loves, and complains that she has not yet found the sought one according to her liking; and, he being not found, she is not broken by labour, she despairs not of her purpose, but perseveres in the hope of finding and in the zeal of seeking. It belongs to one that loves to seek once, and again, and many times over, what is loved; if delay come between, not to desist from what is hoped for; and if she be hardly used while that which is sought comes not the sooner, yet let her not faint: to a desire too long deferred hope comes to the rescue. The Virgin therefore seeks to behold the face of him whom she loves, and nothing suffices her that seeks so long as she perceives herself hindered from her desire; and, not content with her little bed (in which a girl's modesty might worthily seem able [0346A] to be kept), she goes about the city, walks through the lanes, and now shrinks not from being found in the midst of the streets. So great a love urges her, an unrestrained burning so kindles her — a burning that is a despiser of persons and heeds not what befits whom; which, when once it has blazed up, cares no longer for the judgment of reason, and conforms to its own unrestraint those whom it has made to burn. The virgin, blazing with that unrestraint the more delightfully the more strongly, called back by no fear of the night, dreading no public place that grudges virgins their way, seeks him whom she loves; and, not content to seek once, while she repeats it and hastens hither and thither, she is found by them that meet her.

## CHAPTER XXII.

*The watchmen who keep the city found me.* While she goes about wandering and is carried anxiously round, [0346B] while she runs to and fro and keeps seeking, and the presence of the sought one is not offered; they to whom the care or the keeping of the city is committed, who keep watch upon the walls with the vigilant anxiety of charity, come and find that she grows not sluggish with a degenerate sleep — and, loving, rejoice at her watchings and at the Virgin's anxious love. For to this end the companions of the Bridegroom, lofty in angelic dignity, upheld by a wondrous grace and stable in their own holiness, are sent into ministry, and watch over our city, that they may both see the progress of them that love and may cherish it with a ready will. These therefore find her, and rejoice that the Virgin is found; *198* they consider her that loves, and marvel at the greatness of her love; and they who had known very many lovers to be commended in a long line behind, see, and grudge not, [0346C] that the bridegroom is now more loved by the Virgin. For reckoning over in order, upwards, the citizens and household of that city, to whom it was given to have loved the bestower of grace, the author of truth, they weigh that in all of them the grace of loving was less, and they rejoice that the Virgin has found none among mortals her equal in loving. And expressly the watchmen were not found by the Virgin, but the Virgin by the watchmen: because the anxiety of the watchmen is bent upon the city to this end, that it may seek out the more diligently who receives a falling away and who a progress in holiness, and that the good will of an affectionate charity may grieve with the one and rejoice with the other. But the Virgin, as she sought not men, so neither did she seek angels; but with the highest desire she busied herself to find the Lord of the angels; and therefore, if she perceives any perchance to come to meet her, [0346D] she declares rather that she is found by them than that she finds them. And when her finders would perhaps have accosted her, being found, and asked whence and whither she was going, or what she meant to find, she, forgetful of the female sex, hastens to forestall them that were about to speak, and, impatient of love, to open her desire to them

## CHAPTER XXIII.

*Have you seen him whom my soul loveth?* The Virgin should more modestly have waited in silence while those spoke first whom she knew to hold an ampler degree of dignity, until the angels that met her should set about to admonish the woman beforehand, and, they speaking first, she thus admonished should answer. But love, being more immoderate, knows not how to use measure or governance; it fears not sex, not order, not to overpass the bounds; [0347A] it seems with a certain haughtiness of mind to forget the rights of all laws, thinking it just to remember unceasingly him alone whom it loves: « Lord, she says, I will be mindful of thy justice only [n: (Psal. LXX)]. » Holding him therefore alone in an unswerving memory — him by whose grace he loves the undeserving, and by whose justice the deserving — when she feels the angels to be at hand for the keeping of the city, to admonish the imperfect and not to fail the more perfect, she reckons their presence not enough for her, until she shall have found him whom she believes to be far above the angels. For this cause, not enduring to be accosted by those same who watch zealously over the care of the citizens, she rather accosts them inquisitively; and love, stronger than fire, not knowing how to be contained under the embers of ash, breaks into flame more evidently and wills to be seen by them that stand about. And since she is held slower to be silent and readier [0347B] to speak, she fans him alone upon her lips, and is wordy about no other — him, I say, whom she loves, whom, being beloved, she seeks the more ardently to find; and since she finds him not yet, she wills at least to hear news of him the more inquisitively. You, she says, to whom it is given always to behold the face of the father, whom it is agreed are hindered from beholding neither by fault, nor by flesh, nor by any trouble whatever: him whom I love, whom I desire to find, you have not seen — have you seen in God the Father the Son who is equally God? Has that happiness been bestowed upon you his companions which to me, his betrothed, is thus far denied by a heavy law — namely, that with a keen eye you may behold my Bridegroom in his glory, who to mine, the eye of his mother and his Bride, endures not yet to be seen? Him, I beseech you, with whom you have found so happy a grace — if it please you, if it seem fitting, [0347C] say whether you have seen him; and to me that burn either show him upon whom you desire to look, or at least declare with a comforting word your own vision of him. For it will be no small comfort to me if you declare that you have seen him, the grace of seeing whom I have not yet deserved to find; because I am not one to grieve that any others, happy men, have come before, whither I, far slower, rejoice not yet to have come. Say, I say, whether you have seen him — nay, since you have seen him, declare it laudably; commend with a saving doctrine what you have more fully perceived of him; because I judge it worthy that an ear be given to you that teach, who have deserved to contemplate his face (while we are still in the dark). You indeed, with jaws that labour not with hunger, but blessed, unwearyingly desiring, [0347D] yet — loathing being driven far off — satisfied, eat in his kingdom the living bread, the incorruptible nourishment; refreshed with the fatness whereof you know no trouble at all [n: (Matth. XVIII)]. And though you are now at hand to us that labour on the earth, for the sake of comforting, yet you are always present at his table and his banquet; and while through the importunate nights a fasting hunger presses us, in the courts of that Lord there is given you a full refreshing, one day.

The angels are not brought in to answer the Virgin's questions, perhaps because the Virgin would not endure the delay of answering, whose burning mind every deferring now troubles; and for this cause she makes plain what, impatient of delay, she did. *199*



## CHAPTER XXIV.

[0348A]

*When I had a little passed by them, I found him whom my soul loveth.* She perceives that he whom she loves is not any one of the angels, nor can be shown by an angel, since he abides far above the excellence of the angels; holding it for certain that the Bridegroom and son so veils his own face, which is God's, that none sees it save he to whom the same son shall have willed to reveal it. Unwilling therefore to linger any longer among these, nor to await their answers with an anxious hearing, the Virgin hastens to pass by the more quickly to the seeking of the Bridegroom, whom she could not find save by passing by. Or perhaps, as has been said before, the watchmen, questioned concerning the Bridegroom — not torpid with ignorance, but the readier and the freer for answering — are not silent that they had seen him in his own glory, [0348B] lest they should seem to have grudged the seeker her affections or her advances. They teach the Virgin, therefore, that he whom she loves is not to be seen with them, but is to be sought far beyond with a loving vigilance, and that a passing-by must be made by her that seeks (that she may be able to see); which done, the beloved is to be shown to her that loves according to the good pleasure of him that shows. O Virgin, they say, we both rejoice in seeing him whom thou lovest, and what we have seen and heard, this we testify; and (if thou truly desirest that the sight of him should likewise strengthen thee) it behoves thee not to stand, not to cleave, but rather to pass by. Discerning that the nature of every creature is mutable — having indeed a beginning, though not likewise about to have an end — pass thou by, and thou shalt find him of another and unlike nature, which knows no change nor shadow of a vicissitude to come. [0348C] These things, or the like of them, the watchmen perhaps answered the Virgin, and promised her the finding of him whom she so loves; but the Virgin, in more haste, did not rehearse their words in order, but set forth more compendiously what she herself had done: *When I had passed by,* she says, *them, I found him whom my soul loveth.* By the words of comfort of those, she says, by whom I was found while I sought my beloved, I was for a while detained; but burning insatiably, and not content with such solace, I was stretched out with looser reins toward that which lies beyond. For seeing that the angels did not supply me my [sic: *desideriam*], and that the keepers of the city had not the effectual grace of supplying it, I passed on, considering whether the cherubim and seraphim, and the spirits of a worthier excellence, might confer [0348D] upon me in my burning the gift of a fuller sufficiency. For as there are angels who, sent for the ministry of salvation, minister to the heirs, so perhaps there are others more worthy, who, since they are not sent by the Lord, stand by him; and by however much they are set over these lower and ministering ones, by so much are they laid beneath him to whom they rejoice unceasingly to stand by. I passed the angels, therefore, when I ascended to those worthier spirits. I passed quite by when I marked that neither sort could become the fulfillers of my desire; when I understood that among the angels not the order only but the nature is unavailing, and that no creature at all suffices for my desire. I passed by when I marked that the watchmen, or the angels, had been made. I passed quite by in considering that they had been made not by themselves but by another; and that he who had made them is so the author of these and of all things that he himself has, for his own part, no creator at all — [0349A] neither himself nor any other whatsoever. I passed by when it was truly given me to know this: that the angels, being made, can do nothing at all without him who made them. I passed quite by in considering that he who is the maker can do all things through himself, who alone suffices me for all things in giving himself. But thus to pass the watchmen, or rather to pass them quite by — what is it but to find him whom my soul loveth? who cannot be more fully found unless the creature be passed over, which none but one passing quite by is worthily able to prove. So then, passing quite by the watchmen, I thus found him whom I love, and thus came to the excellence of him who is not made but maker; I found that the Creator far surpasses every creature, and that therefore nothing besides him ought to be loved. But when the Virgin says [0349B] that she has found him whom she loves, what is it that she premises — that she had a little passed by the watchmen — when she seems to have passed not a little but very much, indeed all things, she who rejoices to have found him who is far above all things? But because, while she is held by the law of mortals, by the bond of a heavier flesh, however far she advance in the ardour of a purer desire, she yet finds not the Bridegroom save only by the eye of faith or of love, she rightly says "a little," in respect of a fuller grace. For though by zeal and grace she cleanses and advances her understanding, and by a marvellous advance, going beyond the angels, comes to her beloved: yet because this coming, while life is lived here, has something imperfect in it, the eye of faith thinks itself carried over by a small passage, as it were. Great indeed might this passage rightly be called, if she now weighed [0349C] that she was gainsaid by no burden of the flesh; if she exulted greatly not in faith but in fact, not in hope but in sight; if she enjoyed the Bridegroom's face, and no disturbance called her back from that enjoying. Great would the passage be, if she saw herself despoiled of her inborn mortality, and, clothed upon with glory, worthily exalted above the angels; sitting on the Bridegroom's throne by a royal right and no wrong, and, Bride and mother, cleaving to the son by a certain singular privilege. But meanwhile, while *200* no such fact or sight is granted, she embraces in faith and hope him whom she loves; and him for the finding of whom she says that she had a little passed by the watchmen, she declares that, once found, she held with a most firm bond.



## CHAPTER XXV.

*I held him, nor will I let him go, till I bring him [0349D] into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that bore me.* The Virgin, as was said before, sought the Bridegroom with a renewed purpose, nor found him whom she sought until she had passed quite by the watchmen set between; because so long as any other seems to be interposed between the seeker and the sought, he that is sought does not sufficiently endure to expose himself to the seeker's desire. When therefore she was seen to pass the watchmen with a lynx's eye, she rejoiced to find more clear-sightedly him whom she sought — so far, at least, as it is given to a living man to prevail; nay, above the rest of men she deserved to obtain this grace of prevailing. The Virgin found that he could not be found in purity by a living man, that the invisible could not be seen, the insensible not perceived; and the more subtly she apprehended in contemplation that he [0350A] is incomprehensible, so much the more strongly she loves [sic: *ama*], and she intends not to love anything beside him. Thus him whom she judges to be tracked not by the foot but by affection, once tracked she finds not with the eye but with a keen understanding: she holds him not with bolts, not with glue, not with a chain, but with love; she binds him not with an iron fastening but with a stronger embrace. She holds him, I say, and binds him, and slackens not the hands greedy of holding; she interrupts not her love, not her affection, not the intent zeal of advancing; him long desired she lets into the chamber of her secret heart, rejoices in the presence of him let in, and, once he is present, suffers him to withdraw no further. Some indeed are found to have held him at times, and to have drawn him to their will with certain bonds; but he seems to be admitted within their holds in such wise that, as though [0350B] impatient of delay, he at last demands to be let go. « I see, he says to Moses, that this people is stiff-necked: let me alone, that my fury may be kindled against them, and that I may destroy them [n: (Exod. XXXII)]. » The just Lord, whose eye sees and approves equity, cursing the people's hardness and the perverse depravity of idolatry, purposes to be grievously kindled against that same people, to be indignant with the sinners, and to execute swift vengeance upon them. He wills to unbridle his fury more harshly against the idolaters; but Moses withstands him, and strives to bridle him in his raging [n: (Jud. X)]; he holds him whom he loves and knows to obey now and then the prayers of them that love; he curbs him in his anger, and suffers him not to rage against the guilty according to his purpose: « Either forgive them this trespass, he says, or if thou do not, blot me [0350C] out of thy book which thou hast written [n: (Exod. XXXII)]. » God does not, after our manner, often turn the stylus; he does not overturn the marks once ploughed in, as though led by repentance; him whom, enrolled among the eternal citizens, his grace has already decreed to save, he has not afterwards scraped away, nor blotted out of the book of the living. Moses therefore, asking either that he himself be blotted out of the book which God had already written, or that God himself have mercy on the people and remit the trespass, by that which he knows in no way to befit the divine equity provokes that equity to what he judges more fitly expedient; and he holds it the more firmly and as it were binds it, even against its will, lest, incontinent of the fury conceived, it put forth a hand to vengeance. But that equity, which is thus held in check, wills therefore, as it seems, to be let go unto vengeance, because its justice wills nothing [0350D] to be remitted unpunished; and Moses thinks that so great a guilt will be avenged by the just death of them all, if the avenging hand endures not to be forestalled by the softened countenance of mercy. Lest therefore he so rage against them that all be utterly blotted out, they are helped not by their own merits but by Moses's; who wills not to hear the Lord asking to be let go, but, holding him more firmly bound, compels him by his prayers mercifully to obey. Long before, a man is read to wrestle with Jacob, who is found to be called now a man, now an angel, now even the Lord; who, marking that his wrestler could not easily be overcome: « Let me go, he says, for the morning riseth [n: (Gen. XXXII)]. » And he: « I will not let thee go, he says, unless thou bless me [n: (ibid.)]. » God, with whom Jacob strongly wrestles, he wills not to let go unless [0351A] he be redeemed at a price, unless the vanquished bestow upon the victor the grace of a blessing, without which the victor himself rejoices in no victory. « And he blessed him, he says, in the same place [n: (Gen. XXXII)]. » That he may deserve to be let go, he reaches out the gift demanded, and the Lord renders him that lets him go heaped with grace; and so at last, the liberty he had demanded being received, he is let go, and he that lets him go rejoices in the newness of the wished-for gift. But the Virgin rejoices not now in the gifts given but in the giver; she wills no other benefit than to enjoy his more bountiful presence: to hold him whom she loves, not to be drawn away from his embraces, not to be induced at any price to let him go. I will not, she says, that the grace of him whom I hold come to me in such wise that, the gift once received, the giver of the gift now withdraw; nor that the beloved's blessing be so presented to her he loves, [0351B] that he whom I love absent himself when he has blessed. For I love the things that are his only for his own sake, and whatsoever he shall have given me suffices not without *201* himself; nay, if these be denied to me that love, and he give himself to the rest, content with him alone I shall sleep in peace in the selfsame. Nor do I hold, or will I hold, him of whom we speak for myself alone, but I will provide that others too may hold him with me; for I will not, by the disease of avarice, begrudge others their profit, but the more I advance, the more shall I rejoice with the rest as they advance. I will hold therefore him whom I hold, nor will I let him go, until, when I bring [him] into my mother's house, nay, and into her chamber, I let him in; that the good which the daughter has already deserved first and more fully to feel, she that bore her may thereafter rejoice to find for herself. The mother, or she that bore this Virgin, is Judaea, who her whom she had first [0351C] borne in flesh by the pain of one bringing forth; afterwards begot to the worship of the one God by the sacraments of the law. Therefore perhaps she is called mother and she that bore her alike, that by the repeated name a twofold begetting may seem to be signified; to which begetter she that is begotten promises to render a benefit. And she renders it when she lets her beloved into her house or chamber.
