Judaea's house is faith, whereby she knew the Father and the Son, and the Spirit of both, to be God; by which faith she removed herself from the deserts and the fellowship of unbelievers; lying hid and at rest under the shadow of this covering as one secure, not about to feel the sun's importunate heats, nor the whirlwind, nor the rain. With such a roofing the unbelief of the Gentiles is not defended; it is covered by no shade, no rooftree, no tiles of faith; but is found free in the fields or under the [0351D] open sky like a wild ass; it knows no house, it endures not to be applauded, it is hedged in by no wall or dike. When therefore foul weather comes, when snow, hail, ice, the spirit of storms, when at last some power of darkness comes upon her, it rejoices to snatch her at once, finding her wandering and uncovered; and she, like chaff fixed by no weight, is tossed about. But Judaea, shut in her house, fortified as by the strength of a castle, rejoicing in a lofty rooftree and marked with certain bulwarks, puts far from her the heavy threats of the air by a strong repulse, and in the hiding-place of faith, her head laid down, now makes her conscience serene. For when the winds rush down, the heaven thunders, the air rages — which is wont to rage threateningly and over-stubbornly in our parts — she thinks nothing more serene than to be covered the more constantly by the defence of faith, [0352A] if only the defence rest upon a stable foundation. For the architect, gathering a heap of timbers and stones into a structure, if he be worthily anxious or fearful of loss, digging deep, is busy to find the rock upon which he may be able to establish the building with a firm footing. Otherwise the house itself, raised aloft upon loftier columns and finished with marvellous labour and workmanship in the eyes of the beholders — by however much it be greater and more elaborate, yet because it rests not upon a firmer rock, by so much the more does it lie subject, at the beating of the floods and the driving of the winds, to a heavier ruin. That therefore Judaea's house, that is, her faith, may take a worthy support, the Virgin, providing for her mother, promises to bring in a foundation; she promises, that is, to bring in that rock which is Christ, which by its own firmness suffers not the building set upon it [0352B] to fall. God indeed, as you have read, had been known of old in Judaea [n: (Psal. LXXV)], whose stretched-out shoe Idumaea did not yet know, because in those days he imparted some sort of knowledge of himself to the hearts of believers, but did not in their eyes clothe himself personally in visible flesh. But when the new grace, when the fullness of time was at hand, when the strength of God, condescending to the weak, willed to be made weak, the Virgin, fruitful by the Spirit, bore God incarnate, and brought forth to men, shod, him who is invisible in his godhead. And she, understanding for certain that none would thenceforth come to salvation save those who should believe Christ to be the wisdom and the power of God — Christ, I say, begotten before the day-star out of the womb of God the Father, but in the end [0352C] of times made man out of the womb of his own mother — took the utmost care that this knowledge of the matter should be conferred upon Judaea, and that the building of faith should be made firm upon this as upon a foundation. Holding him therefore, the Virgin promises that she will not slacken her greedy hands until she shall make him known more firmly to her own nation to be held; until she shall present him newly born to the believing shepherds, and afterwards, as he grows, commend him to the slower apostles. For in these the faith of the Jews is instructed by Mary's words and merits; lest the deserted house fall, it is stayed up by her help and her work; she bearing him and setting forth her offspring more truly, Judaea receives and honours Christ, believes the man to be God, and loves and adores him whom she believes. This is perhaps what this Virgin's promise signifies, when mention is welcomely made [0352D] not only of the house but also of the chamber: namely, that Judaea in the apostles will rejoice both to believe in Christ and to love him, and by the Virgin's intervention will obtain this twofold benefit. The house, as being wider, receives without distinction the many that flow in; but the remote chamber more secretly admits only them that love; and therefore the house denotes the faith which we see to be common to very many, but the chamber the love which you know to be proper to the elect. It is not enough therefore for the Virgin that she so preaches Christ to Judaea that he be believed, but she takes the utmost care that he be likewise loved by her, while she declares him both God born of God before the ages without a mother, and newly made truly man of herself without a father. To which believing and loving she leads her by her own warnings as well as merits, and brings Christ [0353A] into her house and chamber; nor does she cease from her zeal until she see her own poor desire heard, and rejoice that her beloved is found in the secret place of them that love. When he is found she envies not, she pines not as a rival, but breathes again from her *202* labour and recovers from her sickness; while, burning with charity, she grows glad at the good things of them that advance, and in that reclining, as it were, rests with a glad conscience — to whose rest the Bridegroom, favouring it, says: *I adjure you,* etc.



## CHAPTER XXVI.

*I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the fields, that you stir not up, nor make the beloved to awake, till she herself will.* The Bridegroom warns the apostles, and those who are seen to have believed alike out of Judaea, and by the Virgin's word and care to have received Christ in the secret place of faith; [0353B] he warns them, I say, not to make light of the grace once received, and not, in contempt of things present, to reach out to their former things, or perhaps to things worse than the former. For if their faith, if their love be more grievously shaken, they will break in upon her sleep, striking harshly upon the Virgin's ear; and from the joy of that rest which the Virgin willed to obtain from their conduct she will be compelled unwilling to awake to troubles. The Bridegroom warns them therefore, lest among the apostles the treachery of Judas thunder harshly; lest the doctrine of Nicolas, discordant from the rest, sound ill; lest, at the hearing of the mystical discourse, many of the disciples be struck with scandal, and, going back, walk no more with him, their purpose harshly broken. And not only these apostates, or any of the like who truly cleaved not to Christ, but the fear [0353C] of the elect also wounded the Virgin's ears not slightly; Peter's denial, John's stripping, the flight of them all made a grievous din, and compelled the resting Virgin to be roused to her watches. The Bridegroom therefore, tenderly solicitous for the Virgin whom he loved, warns those whom he perceived to be troubled by fear of their persecutors, that they faint not from the form and doctrine which the Virgin had given them, or, if they faint, may perhaps the sooner come to themselves. Daughters, he says, of Jerusalem, it is not fitting that you should will what you do not yet find her to will who forewarns you; nor is it free to you to will anything hurtful or unseemly, until she also will it, who, it is agreed, [0354A] never wills at all, the apostles indeed, grace forsaking them, willed against the prohibition, when they were not able to resist to the utmost the fault that met them; but she willed nothing of the sort, who was worthily able to withstand the faults that met her, and for this cause she was found to be roused from a pleasing rest not by her own din but by her own people's. Yet afterwards, rightly mindful of him that adjures them, and visited more fully by the presence of the strengthening Spirit, they are made comely by a secret chamber, as it were, of conduct and of merits, into which they rejoice that the Bridegroom is brought by the Virgin's help and work. And when he is brought in, the Virgin herself also grows glad not slightly, and rests in the sleep she had chosen before, in their conduct; from which the Bridegroom's diligence forbids her to be roused, lest she be afflicted by a punishment whose fault she is not held to share. Above, therefore, when with these same words [0354B] the Bridegroom willed to adjure the daughters of Jerusalem, that they should not presume to rouse the Bride resting amid the Bridegroom's embraces, the Virgin is shown to rejoice in her own advances, or over her own, which she is proclaimed to have gained for herself by grace and merits. But here, when the same adjuration is found to be repeated, the Virgin is found to rejoice over the merits of others, whose solicitude is addressed by the Bridegroom's diligence, that they repel not the grace which is found so welcome to the Virgin's desire. There the Virgin is delighted with a welcome rest amid the Bridegroom's embraces; here she rejoices that the Bridegroom rests in her neighbours' chamber; there she falls asleep in her own advances, here in her neighbours'; and in either sleep, holding the Bridegroom, she longs for his courts. But because there the same verse is in some fashion expounded, I have not thought it necessary that [0354C] the same exposition be repeated here; lest, if what was said before be said again in the present place, a superfluous repetition breed weariness in the hearer. As therefore the second book of this work took its end there, where the Virgin leaned herself upon the Bridegroom's left hand for the sake of rest, so here also I deem it worthy that a close or term be set to the present book, where the Bride rejoices that the Bridegroom is brought into her mother's house or chamber; that where it is granted the Bride to be lulled asleep by delicate advances, there our stylus may rejoice to be repaired by silence as by sleep.

## BOOK FOUR.





## CHAPTER THE FIRST.

[0353D]

*Who is she that goeth up by the desert, as a little rod of smoke of spices, of [sic: *myrrhoe*], and of frankincense, and of all the powder of the perfumer?* Thus far in this drama the beloved and the Virgin have spoken to one another and of one another, and have pursued in alternating speech what belonged to love and to grace; nor do any others seem to be brought in to speak, *203* although the maidens and the companions alike have been brought in to hear. But now the Bridegroom, by a more ample benefit, gives to the companions, to whom he had given place and grace to hear, room [0354D] to speak, that the marriage-song may be made more pleasant to them, when they too shall alike have given their fellow's token in it. The companions, therefore — that is, the angels who are said to stand by the Bridegroom at such a wedding, who, though they minister to men, are not for that kept from his face — marking with what affection the Bridegroom is held toward the virgin, by what grace, by what merit the virgin is advanced above all women, are fixed fast, are astonished, and are not worthily able to wonder, nor do they find with what praises they can fitly venerate her. An affectionate devotion indeed admonishes them that they say something; [0355A] the consideration of a magnitude to be wondered at calls them back that they say nothing; for whatever they say seems to themselves little and insufficient, and yet they think themselves worthy to be reproved if they say nothing at all. A marvellous abundance of matter for speech makes them poor indeed, and the poverty by no means satisfies their great desire; yet they speak, that they may awaken [sic: *susciten*] in us the affection of hearing, and give us hearers some sort of confidence of speaking. For none of us would attempt to speak the praises of so great a Virgin, if the excellence of the angels, as not sufficiently conscious of itself, utterly refused them; but by the pattern and solicitude of those who are ministering spirits we too are admonished to venerate the Virgin with such praises as we can. For they too show themselves to do this very thing, so far as possibility avails them, not so far as the Virgin's dignity requires; [0355B] they who do not yet sufficiently apprehend how great the Virgin's merits are, and therefore intend not to express them to the utmost in words or in praises, but wonder, and, wondering, ask who she is whom they so mark as wonderful. Who, they say, is this? We turn over, they say, the roll of women present or foregoing from of old, from the time when Eve, who was made first, gave her consent to the enemy; to many of whom the gifts of divers graces have been granted; the beauty of the inner mind, by the hands of grace as well as of industry, and cultivated — none of these can we find like to her, but she is found to outgo them all by an ineffable grace. Who then is this, to whom alone a special excellence is given, that no woman before her, none after her, is her equal; that she seems now [0355C] not even to need our patronage, nay, to surpass angels as well as men, not by nature but by grace? Who is this that walks not with bended knee after the manner of a delicate woman, but with a strong and unwearied step goes manfully forward; who takes an arduous way untried by feminine paces, and, laying hold of the ladder which Jacob scarcely deserved to see, climbs bravely through the desert? The desert, as I see, is a way and a manner of life set apart, which the multitude knows not and no common hoof treads; which is not touched by mire, not besprinkled with the dust of the streets; which fault does not defile, nor any superfluity of chaff cover. Jacob, when a stone set beneath him was seen to hold up his head, lulled in a mystical sleep, scarcely deserved to see [0355D] such a ladder [n: (Gen., XXVIII)]; which, as it appeared to him, being forbidden to them that live after the manner of men, is left to angels alone, ascending and descending. For the angels descend, meeting the Virgin's advances with a favouring joy. And they ascend, running before [sic: *praeccurrentes*] with festal praises her that advances: hastening to meet the Lord who leans upon the ladder, and asking who is this that hastens to outgo in merits the angels who are her betters in nature. Who is this, they say, to whom a virginal fruitfulness, or a fruitful virginity, has been granted, unapproached in all ages past by angels as by men; who, living in a body wrapped about with the necessities of death, runs through a life liable to vices in an unpolluted course? [0356A] For she goeth up as a little rod of smoke, which, though it rise subtle and slender from below, lifting itself into the thin airs is itself made thin; so advancing on high that it commits itself to the secret of the clouds, and, as it were emptying itself, admits not the eyes of the beholders. The Virgin assuredly, though begotten of earthly parents, yet, the earthly dregs being scraped away, made thin by the zeal of discipline, has gone forward to so great a height of merits above men that she is rightly declared to have gone beyond the capacity of them that wonder at her. Advancing thus, she gives far and wide a most sweet odour, the teaching of justice, a more gracious rule of discipline; she bestows her suffrages, she rejoices to show benevolence, which things to them that worthily consider seem to smell like spices. Therefore perhaps the smoke, to whose little rod the advancing Virgin is compared [sic: *eomparatur*], [0356B] is recorded to come forth not from the pit of the abyss but from spices; for whose compounding a multiplicity of kinds has been gathered, and they have been compounded of myrrh and of frankincense and of all the powder of the perfumer, Myrrh gives a marvellous remedy to the bodies of the dead, and by a certain natural force removes corruption from flesh that is flowing and soft: frankincense burnt up with fire is offered to God in sacrifices, and by its smoky odour the devotion of them that sacrifice is commended. Myrrh therefore, as it seems, is like to that virtue whereby the Virgin worthily subjects her body to servitude, that by fastings, watchings, cleannesses vicious corruption may be put far off, and, the laws of nature being restrained, nothing in it may rot away soft or flowing. But by frankincense the Virgin's humble devotion, or devout humility, is figured; which, when in the censer of the mind it is burnt up *204* by the fire [0356C] of the holy Spirit, melted into love, is directed like smoke to things above; nay, after the manner of a little rod, drawing itself into a narrow compass, hastens the more intently to things eternal. But by the powder of the perfumer, of which a whole heap, as it were, is added on top, the whole company of the remaining virtues is expressed; which that perfumer, by whom the medicinal health of all was found out, exquisitely heaping together and prudently pounding, reduces into pigments. Of all which, agreeing to a saving medicine, heaped together and bruised in the Virgin's heart as in a little mortar of [sic: *discipliuae*], the smoke is directed in the perfumer's sight, the odour breathes forth — to the worthy wondering at which the companions' consideration scarcely aspires. Who then is this, with whom a multiplicity of ears of corn, as it were, has gathered itself into [0356D] a handful, nay, with whom the whole company of kinds has forced itself together in her little mortar, whose merits are bruised like powder by a most subtle examination, and are borne before the perfumer like smoke, nay, like a little rod of smoke, in a marvellous ascent? From these, borne and offered, that same perfumer turns not away, but in her that offers them, as upon a little bed, reclines himself with a welcome benevolence; and he encloses that same little bed with a rampart of strength, whereby he shuts out from it, and far off, whatsoever is unseemly, whatsoever is hurtful. Of which the companions subjoin: *Behold the little bed,* etc.



## CHAPTER II.

*Behold the little bed of Solomon: threescore valiant ones compass it about, [0357A] of the most valiant of Israel.* Him whom I had called the perfumer they seem to name Solomon; who, being the author and lover of peace, willed to prepare for himself a little bed in which, hidden from the tumult of men, he might lay down his head for rest's sake, and truly show himself peaceable not in name only but in fact. And his little bed, I judge, may be said to be the Virgin herself, who for love's sake is found so given over to Solomon's service that she suffers no stranger to take rest in her, and admits not the crafty enemy, even for a moment, within the containing of her narrow mind; for which cause she too deserved to be called not a bed but a little bed, that by this diminutive a certain narrowness of hers might seem to be designated — she who, not being stretched out to take another likewise, strives to please the bridegroom alone, and is content with him alone [0357B] whom she lawfully loves. To whom that prophecy of Isaias worthily agrees, and prophecies uttered at divers times agree together, showing to every one that loves that a certain narrowness of mind befits him — that a lover embraces not many, serves not two masters. « The bed is straitened, he says, so that one must fall out: and the short covering cannot cover both [n: (Isa. XXVIII.)] » The bed of the mind is assuredly straitened in commendable wise when it purposes to lie open and to please none but the lawful one; when it has not settled in itself a dwelling, a place, a space for another; when the other is compelled to fall, or perhaps, terrified, comes not near from afar. Lastly, the covering of virginal modesty, which dissoluteness has not woven, which superfluity does not warp, draws itself close about the lawful one; the other is by no means covered by it, [0357C] nor does the Bridegroom accept a portion in common with an adulterer, nor does he suffer him to make his dwelling with him under the same covering. Whence her who straitened not the little bed nor shortened the covering, but, an adulterer being invited, wickedly widened all — her the bridegroom himself is found by the same Isaias more grievously to accuse, and to refuse the unworthy fellowship both of the adulteress and of the adulterer. « Thou hast enlarged thy couch, he says, thou hast received an adulterer [n: (Isai. LVII.)] » But the Virgin, her bed being straitened, admitted the stain of no adulterer; her covering being shortened, she suffered no crafty one to be covered; but she removed from the narrow rest of her mind whatsoever is contrary to her, and, keeping faith with the bridegroom, devoted herself wholly and singularly to him. Her therefore, who by zeal with [0357D] grace both willed and was able to show herself a little bed, so that enemies and rivals are of necessity compelled to shrink away, Solomon, loving peace and yet having care of battles, fortifies with an armed soldiery, and by a strong defence makes secure. Who assuredly, girt about not with walls, not with towers, not with material bulwarks, but with certain valiant ones, threescore in mystical number, abides undaunted under the provident hand of the aforesaid Solomon, while the keepers help her and the enemies bring in nothing of hurtful injury. But the keepers, who deserve to be called nothing but valiant, are the spiritual virtues by which it is agreed the Virgin is strengthened; which stand by her not on one side only without the other; themselves prudently [0358A] disposed, they stand round about her in an ordered circuit. Whose perfection is figured in the number sixty, which is completed of six and ten multiplied one by the other; of which the six denotes the perfection of works or labours, and the ten the perfect consequence of rewards. For because God the creator of all fulfilled his works in six days, who, as you know it is written, rested on the seventh day from the works which he had wrought [n: (Gen. II)], rightly is the perfection of working designated by the six, in the fuller obtaining of which one labours through the whole space of days. There are those who hold that the six is not to be judged perfect for this reason, that God willed his works to be completed in it, but that the primordial works were once made in six days for this reason, *205* that God knew this to be the first perfect number, [0358B] so that from the perfection of the number God might commend his works, and, they being completed in a perfect number, might show them to be no less perfect. And by the ten the perfection of the reward is rightly said to be designated, because the householder bids that very sum be given to them that labour in the vineyard; and whosoever has been faithfully held by the labour enjoined, with a view to obedience, is content with this number added at the end of time. The six therefore is taken ten times, or the ten six times, and they make sixty, when the Virgin is strongly girt both with the labour of the day's burden and with the sure hope of the reward to come; when she rejoices to give her pains to perfect works in the present, and altogether fears nothing, doubts nothing concerning what follows. But why either the six or the ten ought, according to the arithmeticians, to be judged perfect, and by what perfection also the sixty [0358C] is found to be commended — because I have undertaken to set that forth more fully in the Response on Obedience, I have willed here for brevity's sake to pass it by in silence. For those seem not yet more fully to obtain the six who, working great things, cannot fulfil greater; who, if perhaps in avoiding wicked works they are circumspect providently enough, are yet in word less perfect than they ought to be. « He that sinneth not, he says, in word, the same is a perfect man [n: (Jacob. III)]. » [var: Vulg. James 3:2 *si quis in verbo non offendit*, "if any man offend not in word"] Some also, though they keep their ways that they offend not with a slippery tongue, and already hold the six, yet do not yet draw near sufficiently to the ten; because, though they hope that they will receive a reward for their labour, they do not yet fully know whether they be worthy of hatred or of love. [0358D] The merits and advances of all these, defective, so to speak (for none of the like has deserved in this life to obtain complete ones), the holy Virgin is found to pass by, nay, far to surpass, by grace as by merits; and, still dwelling with us, she is so compassed by the mystical sixty that the observance of works and labours renders her perfect, and a wholly sure expectation of things to come makes her secure. And beautifully do they that compass her about deserve to be called valiant ones of the most valiant of Israel, because among all the virtues whose merits seek to contemplate God, those are agreed to be valiant and to be commended for especial valour by which the Virgin is compassed, and, being compassed, loves to be preserved.

## CHAPTER III.

[0359A]

*All holding swords, and most expert in war.* With how great valour, with how great care these compass the Virgin about, the armour shows as well as the mystical number; lest, if they come or come together to defend her unarmed, the more numerous they are, the more blameworthy they be, and by a just judgment be made void. Each one therefore holds and draws a twice-sharpened sword, so that if perhaps some robber shall have sought to cross the appointed bound, his presumption, at once beaten back, may utterly vanish, or rather, at the sight of the sword, he may leap far back in terror. This sword is not of iron, wherewith wicked criminals are sensibly struck, but it is the sword of the spirit, which the Apostle declares to be the word of God; for the word of God is proclaimed living and effectual and more piercing than any sword, [0359B] whereby the recesses of the soul and the inward conscience are pierced [n: (Heb. IV)]. The sword is the faithful testimony, the lucid precept, the book of the law, which the priest Joiada willed to give into the hand of Joas the king [n: (II Paral. XXIII)], that he might show to all that the knowledge of the divine law befits a king; nay, that a king ought not so much to know the law as to hold it in his hand, that is, in work. They gave, he says, into the king's hand the law to be held, and made him king. Therefore the threescore are recorded not to have but to hold swords, because it is not they that have who forthwith also hold, but they that hold are not denied to have; and it profits little, or nothing, to have a sword in the sheath, if the hand — that is, the discipline of works — draw it not forth. All the valiant ones therefore who are said to compass the Virgin about hold swords, obey the word, are exercised [0359C] in worthy works, and by so great a defence render the Virgin strong and secure, so that, the enemies being beaten back afar, she suffers neither injury nor loss. And they that so defend her are assuredly most expert in war, whose learning is not new by advance rather than by time; because to know, and not yet to do, the things that are right, is a bare doctrine, rude and, as of a new time, imperfect. For understanding gives advance not to them that have understanding but to them that do it — advance not only of knowledge but of conscience; and as conscience without knowledge is not sufficiently instructed, so knowledge without conscience is found rude and more imperfect. They therefore ought to be called not only expert but most expert, who obey the word for the waging of wars, [0359D] and lend their hand to the sword; whose solicitude so goes forth to repel the enemies' assaults that it is a terror to all, while the hand withdraws not from the sword. Concerning which sword it is subjoined: *Every man's,* etc.



## CHAPTER IV.

*Every man's sword upon his thigh, because of fears in the night.* *206* The companions diligently consider and more attentively wonder in what manner or order those threescore work the protection of the Virgin; and how provident, how sagacious they are for protecting her, and how they are held effectual not by valour only but by prudence of purpose. For each one, not laying down the sword once received, but setting upon his thigh the sword he is said to hold in his hand, is so held solicitous to war down from without whatever things may hurt, that he be not [0360A] negligent of himself, but that a diligent care of himself hold him. The thigh signifies the flesh, which is propagated from the thigh; and the flesh is weak, and is proved to fail naturally; and therefore by the thigh, or the flesh, is signified the weakness or defect which our firmness or advance incurs, as it were, from nature. For a man's virtue, to however great a magnitude it be raised aloft, has not of itself that it should be strengthened in its purpose; but if, grace forsaking it, it be relaxed a little from diligence, it is not held with a steady step, as though its wings were lost. Virtue therefore is seen to set its sword upon its thigh when, by the lucid word of the Lord, which is said to be more piercing than any sword, it worthily restrains and chastises its own weakness, and by the rigour of the word makes firm what it naturally searches out to be unavailing. It holds the sword upon the thigh when it worthily watches and strains over the guard [0360B] of itself, apprehending itself not only weak, but naturally weak; and for this cause, the more solicitous, it so guards itself against defect and ruin that it presses down the very causes of defect, as it were the thigh, with the discipline of the [sic: *verb*]. Thus assuredly, watching and straining to remove whatever things are hurtful, the Virgin's virtue rejoices not to fear from fears in the night; and all that the crafty enemy or a dark temptation strives to contrive, her learned and terrible circumspection renders utterly idle. Marking which, the angels, who are called the friends and companions of the Bridegroom, as was said before, wonder ineffably at this little bed of Solomon and at the guard of it; and they go on to commend it with yet other words, esteeming as little enough whatever they utter in the Virgin's praise.



## CHAPTER V.

[0360C]

*King Solomon made him a ferculum of the wood of [sic: *Libam*], the pillars thereof he made of silver, the reclining-place of gold: the ascent of purple, the midst he strewed with charity, for the daughters of Jerusalem.* That which they had called a little bed, they call also a *ferculum*, whereon many *fercula* are borne to Solomon, and to him that feasts is set the food which perisheth not, but which endureth. The *ferculum*, then, is the Virgin, through whom the souls of the saints are found to be commended to God, and by her prayers and merits to be raised to the Bridegroom's banquet; whom for this very end the Bridegroom willed to be prepared for himself, that through her they might deserve those things which of themselves they could not be presented. For although the souls of the saints are marked with divers virtues, and, after the manner of a banquet, [0360D] are seasoned with a manifold savour of graces, yet they lie far from Solomon's banquet as though utterly forsaken, if they be not helped by the Virgin's intervention as by a table of offering. Therefore the Bride herself is rightly called the mediatrix of us all, herself the mother is not unfitly called the empress; because, entreating the bridegroom, commanding the son, she turns his fury into favour and his wrath into most sweet love, and by the little meal of her prayer converts us, bitter, into sweetness. They therefore who before were hateful with a wild bitterness, being taken up upon the *ferculum*, are made gracious by the merit of her that takes them up; nor is there any that deserves to please at Solomon's banquet, save him whom Solomon rejoices to have offered to him by the Virgin as from a table of propitiation. For of so great merit is the aforesaid *ferculum* or table, that whosoever have had its propitiation more diligently bestowed upon them [0361A] present themselves confidently at Solomon's banquet, while they that are strangers to the table absent themselves consequently from the banquet also. For it is made of the wood of Libanus. Libanus is a mountain which a conspicuous height lifts up, which its surface adorns, which the beauty of groves clothes; whose trees a tall greatness rears up, a wondrous appearance graces, an unrottable strength makes firm. And Libanus is interpreted *a whitening,* signifying Christ, who is the brightness of eternal light, and is prepared as the mountain of the house of the Lord: whose good tree is proved to bring forth no fruit but good; whose trees, planted beside the waters of Siloe, dry not up, are not stripped of their leaves in autumn, wither not in winter, but grow young again with an untiring length and an unrottable strength. Of this wood the companions assert the *ferculum* to be framed, so that [0361B] the work may rightly be seen to be commended, as it were, from its material; because the Virgin's sanctity is compacted out of Christ's virtues, and, unto the profit of us all, is brought into a table and a *ferculum*. And because mighty Solomon so compacted her of strong and unrottable material, she felt no worm, she admitted no rot, but drove it away; she was not hurt by the hammer, by the age of time not broken asunder, but the wholeness of her strength remained, and remained still, uncorrupted. But that this same table might not swerve from Solomon's presence, that it might never nor anywhere lean aside on any part, the same Solomon willed it to rest upon a noble stay, setting under it not unstable tripods, but pillars *207* immovable, of silver. For an eminent height presented the virginal table to Solomon, [0361C] and the silver and unbending straightness of the pillars held it unmoved, whose lucid manners, whose ringing repute, whose temperance of mouth, whose force of speech Solomon's benevolence accepted and made firm. Silver, making itself conspicuous by splendour, and giving a ring at a fitting touch, is wrought into pillars, and that which is laid upon it stands defended; since the Virgin, remaining a Virgin, brought forth the Word of the Father by the power of the Most High, and leaned firmly not upon her own strength but upon his. In her also a reclining-place of gold is said to be found, because nowhere did our Solomon seem to find a rest more welcome to him, where he might will or be able to lay down his head, and to bow the excellency of the Godhead to the taking of flesh. And this is not unfitly said to be, not of lead, but [0361D] rather of gold, because among all metals nothing is held better than gold; which is also dearer in price, and heavier in weight, and stronger under the hammer, so that of it the reclining-place is deservedly said to have been made. By the gold I judge the Virgin's love to be figured, which it is certain holds the first place among her other virtues; because, though faith and hope and very many others are worthy to be commended, yet none of them can deservedly be compared to love. Which love is so weighed down, balanced by its own weight, that it slips not away to the right or the left side by a swaying mobility, runs not hither and thither, wavers not, breaks not out to the loving of any other, embraces the bridegroom alone, and lets no third break off the embrace of the two. In fine, she desires to cleave to the bridegroom with a desire so strong, with a firmness so solid, that [0362A] she is not broken by adversities, nor does she give way under the hammer of tribulation; and when Peter cracked, and John sprang back, and all fled, not bearing the raging hammer, the Virgin alone stood fast, nor ceased to love the bridegroom dying under the eyes of the bride. Such a reclining-place, then, did Solomon frame for himself in the Virgin, which a love heavy and solid and to be compared with none commended, whereon the framer himself laid down his head away from the trouble of men; and, as one about to refresh them, invited us also to the same feast. But that same reclining-place is not easily found by such as we are, whereto there is no coming save with labour, save with very great effort: whereto (as is known to him that has tried it) he attains not more fully, save he that, being about to ascend, girds himself with a worthy strength. For there are steps or stairs by which the ascent is made to [0362B] the reclining-place, whereon no mean labour was bestowed by the Virgin; and because, rightly considering, she knew them to be not dark with soot but purple, by them she advanced herself, with an honourable likeness, even to the top. In the times of the ancients purple belonged to kings alone, which by its form or colour showed forth the royal dignity, so that when the common people observed that none was clothed in purple save the prince, they might be admonished to reverence him that was marked with royal signs. Because, therefore, to the reclining-place, wherein a welcome rest is granted to Solomon, one comes not by a presumptuous leap, but by an ascent of purple; the most prudent Virgin, when she desired to come to so great a merit, clothed herself in royal purple that she might be shown a queen. And she showed herself a queen by fitting tokens, [0362C] when she eagerly took upon her a discipline of a new kind, when she first dared to enter, consecrated by the chaste purpose of her mind, the path of virginal continence untried through all the ages behind her. She showed herself a queen when she put on over her the purple, that is, virtue, whereby she brought upon her most tender body a hard servitude; when she gave her blood, not poured out by the hand of the executioner, but consecrating to God alone the vessel of her virginal body, unpierced; she was zealous to distinguish herself a queen not with womanly but with purple garments, when by loftiness of mind she chose not to feel the enticements of the body, to have dominion over her own flesh — which (as I judge) is sufficiently known to none who, a runaway from the school, has shown himself untried in this exercise. The Virgin therefore, not confounded with a womanish softness, [0362D] but red and steeped in the martyrdom of a royal passion, came and attained to this, that she should be made the reclining-place of Solomon; and by an ascent that was none other than purple she advanced to so excellent a merit, that Solomon, reclining upon her, might take his food with an untiring hunger. But the midst of this *ferculum* Solomon strewed not with tapestries out of Egypt, nor with the passing newness of flowers, but by a counsel far better, with charity; that there might nowhere at all appear in it anything which the eye of him that reclined, being greedy of comeliness, would abhor. For to all the virtues whereby the Virgin is rendered chief and marked out, agreeing with the aforesaid *ferculum* by excellent and worthy merits, there is of necessity superadded the ornament of charity woven in, without which all the rest become as useless refuse. For nothing [0363A] sufficient can be laid in the aforesaid *ferculum* whereon it is not needful that a diffused charity be laid above: nay, all the things set round about are not worthily bound together, if their midst be not filled up with the cement of charity. In the midst of all things, therefore, charity is of necessity placed, that thence a kind of nourishment may be diffused to all that are set around; that all things rightly done may be held by a binding of this sort, lest they leap asunder one from another, and that, if perchance anything have settled amiss, it may have a sufficient covering. « For charity is also the bond of perfection [n: (Col. IV)]; » and it « covereth a multitude of sins [n: (I Petr. IV)]. » And this indeed I judge to have been said not so much for the Virgin's sake as for the daughters of Jerusalem, to whom it had been granted to be present *208* while the bridegroom and the bride discoursed together; lest, when they heard [0363B] pillars of silver, a reclining-place of gold, an ascent of purple proclaimed, they should not presume to think that they could reach to those things: and should seem to be driven back far off from that *ferculum*, by no likeness, not even a slight one, to be held near it. But when they hear that in the midst of those things charity is found, by whose welcome veil the manifoldness of sins is covered, they do not doubt that they too may belong to that *ferculum*, if they love, and choose to cleave more lovingly to him that loves. For although in that *ferculum* many things are recorded to be set which are not sufficiently to be matched with such as we are, but more especially with the Virgin, yet that charity is declared to be set in the midst of them is without doubt not held alien from the daughters of Jerusalem; but it profits and heals their mediocrity not mediocrely, [0363C] to whom in this both an easiness of drawing near and a not ineffectual hope of going forward is afforded. For such a *ferculum* did Solomon, the bridegroom, the bride, Christ the Virgin, will to set forth for himself, one that should deserve to be pre-eminent above all by the excellence of her virtues; and yet should not seem to forbid the daughters of Jerusalem from following after her, who, though not altogether in all things, yet at least for love's sake would cleave to her footsteps. But that they may cleave and may see in whom they ought to rejoice, the companions or angels who speak seem to admonish them: and they turn toward them, perhaps not so much their countenance as their speech, that, being thereby forewarned, they may hasten anxiously to see Solomon.



## CHAPTER VI.

[0363D] *Go forth, ye daughters of Sion, and see king Solomon in the diadem wherewith his mother crowned him, in the day of his espousal, and in the day of the gladness of his heart.* Because the companions had foretold that the Virgin was now the little bed, now the *ferculum* of Solomon, and had described the one as adorned with much strength and the other with much beauty, lest in this they should seem to have bestowed more upon the bride than upon the bridegroom, and, in commending the Virgin, to have paid Solomon less than was due, they invite the daughters of Sion to the study of a larger understanding, that they may attentively consider what of glory or of honour the things aforesaid have brought to Solomon. Wherefore they take pains expressly to forewarn them to go forth, namely lest they should be willing to remain either in their own hovels of vices or in the darknesses of ignorance; because they are not fit [0364A] for seeing whose life is entangled in vices, or whose understanding is hindered by a mist poured over it. You therefore, they say, whom we invite the more diligently to see, know that in the things which are behind you must not remain any longer; and for this cause we will that you go out from the dark, from the wicked wrapping, and that you free the feet of your going out from the spots that hinder them. Go out therefore from the hovel of a life that darkens the understanding, go out from the midst of a dim-eyed ignorance; go out from the gross and rustic understanding of dim-sighted peoples, advance into daughters, have a solicitude concerning your advance. Go forth, and by going forth be worthily made daughters that gaze; with an anxious hand cleanse your eyes that labour with bleariness: with a mirror, as it were, set before you, wipe away the spots of your face, and after the manner of girls bestow care upon the beauty that is to be obtained. [0364B] By this going forth and advance out of the inward negligence of a blameworthy workshop, by this zeal of gazing and by the mirror of discipline, you shall obtain that vision which is necessary for you, whereby it shall be given you to see Solomon in his diadem. Solomon, I say, the king, whom none can see in his own comeliness save the saints, with face indeed washed and with a cleaner eye — they who burn with a girl's solicitude to obtain beauty, who with a cleansed eye are able to gaze upon things inaccessible to the dim-sighted. Solomon's diadem is the passibility of the flesh, wherewith the undefiled virginity of his mother crowned him, when the Lord did a new thing, and a woman compassed a man, according to the prophecy of Jeremias [n: (Jer. XXXI)] — a Virgin nevertheless conceiving and bearing, by the testimony none the less of Isaias [n: (Isa. VII)]. Which flesh, or [0364C] passibility of the flesh, is not undeservedly honoured with the name of a diadem; because, although in the eyes of the dim-sighted it is reckoned a dishonour or an ignominy, yet whosoever rightly understands that base things of any kind are unworthy of Solomon, and, understanding, loves to know what end there is in a passion of this sort — how great a contest there is in the flesh, how great the profit in the contest — assuredly attributes to it a name not of ignominy but of honour, not of dishonour but of a crown. « We see, saith Paul, Jesus, for the passion of death crowned with glory and honour [n: (Hebr. II)]. » To this crown the Virgin mother ministered the material in her womb; the Spirit, the craftsman, wrought with a learned hand the material so ministered, and wove it into a round with a work so perfect that it incomparably overtops gold, stone, or amber. The Jew, beholding this, esteems it nothing but thorns and toil; [0364D] the unbeliever, considering it, thinks it to have no beauty nor comeliness: the cleansed eye beholds him beautiful in form above the sons of men, not only because he is God, but because, being man, he is not held by the debts of men. *209* To him indeed the material of flesh is naturally common with men, but that same community is free of carnal vices; and by the power of this mystery he admits us personally into the unity of himself, and, when once we are joined to him, suffers us not to be divided from him. Which the round perfection of the diadem beautifully signifies, whose wholeness no division at all breaks asunder; whence also the diadem, taking division away, is said to signify, because whosoever is contained within the compass of this crown knows not to be divided. In this crown therefore, that is, in [0365A] his flesh, he couples and joins us to himself, and, as partakers of the contest, disjoins us not from honour and glory; which glory the mother is said in a manner to have imparted to Solomon, when the Virgin is believed to have conceived God-man in her womb. Who should not render praises to the Virgin, who should not make worthy mention of her — who crowned Solomon not with gold, not with stone, but with her own flesh; who conferred upon the king that whereof he might will and be able to glory, wherein he might conquer and be worthy to be crowned by the merit of victory? Which assuredly they record to have been done in the day of his espousal, and by that deed they intimate that night or mist is far away, because the espousal there present brought no darkness into the bridal chamber, whereon a hallowed day and a hallowing light shone. For when the Bridegroom had entered, an incomparable light arose, [0365B] and no other is admitted, and the gate lies open to none without; but with equal consent they close every approach against all that come upon them, and the companions or angels dance and clap festively before the doors. In a bright day therefore the mystical espousal is celebrated, the chaste Virgin is coupled to one man by a spiritual commerce; the woman compasses the man, Solomon is crowned with a diadem, and to God, by nature immortal, the nature of mortals is personally united. But in this day, wherein the Virgin's Creator was made her Bridegroom, who shall tell what or how great was the gladness of her heart, when in her womb our humanity was taken up into God, and, the Spirit overshadowing, was not consumed by fellowship with him that took it up? How great was the gladness of her heart is not ours [0365C] to utter or to feel, who have not deserved to enter into a sanctuary so sacred and so secret; she herself, to whom God willed to open it more fully and more perfectly, could scarce blurt out even a little of the joy conceived in her heart. « My spirit hath rejoiced, she says, in God my Saviour [n: (Luc. I)]. » Whatsoever therefore is done in the Virgin without doubt knows no night; upon her, as she crowns the king, day is poured in, light grows bright, and with a splendour diurnal, or rather diuturnal, the mother's spirit is made glad — for the worthy taking whereof our eye, the eye of the weak, grows not clear. For neither is this that Bersabee whom David, Urias not knowing it, defiled by adultery, but Mary, the flower of Virgins, whom, singular as she was, the holy Spirit took upon him to make fruitful; nor is this that Solomon who is reported to have reigned from Dan even to Bersabee forty [0365D] years, but Christ, of whose kingdom the end, of whose empire the term, is not had. Whose glory of flesh, whose diadem, no Jew, no Gentile, no accursed man whatsoever can worthily weigh — who, though a Christian in name he whitens himself with the appearance of piety, yet, denying the power thereof, grows dark with a poverty of merits. Therefore the Companions or angels, to whom by the merit of felicity it had been given already to see, lest they should seem to grudge to others the benefit they had received, think it not to be hidden under a bushel, not to be covered with silence, but they invite the daughters of Sion to prepare themselves with fervour and zeal for seeing. For in this praise is rendered not only to Solomon but to the Virgin also, [0366A] and the glory conferred upon the crowned is not taken away from her that crowns: nay, whatsoever the taking of flesh seems to work in the son that is worthy of glory is poured back upon Mary, of whom the same son willed to be incarnate. For which cause the Bridegroom turns not his presence long away from her, but after the words of the companions turns himself again to her praises, that he may show himself to be so crowned with a diadem, so beautiful in glory, that it may stand plain that the beauty of the crown is not wanting to her that crowns him either.



## CHAPTER VII.

*[CAP. IV.] How fair art thou, my friend, how fair art thou, thine eyes are of doves, without that which lieth hid within.* Because these words, as you may remember, are set down further back. and in the second book of this work are in some fashion expounded; they are not to be expounded again in this place [0366B] or at this time, but the solicitude of the readers is to be sent back to the aforesaid book. Yet in these words, as I see, somewhat is found changed, and this praise of the virgin is here forestalled by another particle; because there it was said: *Behold thou art fair, behold thou art fair;* but here; *How fair art thou, how fair.* There *ecce* is said, namely the showing of one that confirms; but here *quam* is set, namely the heightening of one that wonders there is understood only a testification that shows forth beauty, here a wonder that expresses much beauty. *How fair art thou,* he says, *my friend, how fair.* How greatly, he says, art thou fair, with how great a beauty art thou adorned, thou who art my *210* friend, and art proved the sharer of my secret; who can utter it with a voluble tongue, with a passing sound, or what hearer can take it in even if it be [0366C] uttered? For the more tenacious confirming of this there avails that which is here subjoined, which had not yet been said, and therefore was not expounded above; wherein it is intimated both that the Virgin's beauty is great, and that in that same beauty there is no crafty foulness: *Without that,* he says, *which lieth hid within.* There are some who have at hand an outward beauty, a fair surface, and a sheep-like one, but within the ravening of a wolf, a serpentine guile; and what lies open without is made comely by an overlaid hypocrisy, but what lies hid within is dark with a malicious foulness. There are others who, though they be not whitened without with a fraudulent hypocrisy, though a venomous assiduity infect them not within yet, while they are held in the body, are so [0366D] penally weighed down by a certain law of sin that sometimes, will they nill they, they slip into a fault, even a slight one; and because not whatsoever of evil our thought conceives can straightway appear to others, since even from us there most often lies hid that which in us deserves by its own desert to displease; when the Bridegroom says the Virgin to be without that which lieth hid within, he proves her free not only from evident faults, but from hidden faults also. Who is he among the saints that should glory that he is without that which lieth hid, and not rather, not understanding his own offences, pray to be cleansed from his hidden ones? who is he, I say, that, not anxious about hidden things, would serve the Lord in fear, fearing because not knowing whether he be worthy of hatred [0367A] or of love? [n: (Eccle. IX.)] The Virgin therefore, who was by no means conscious to herself of offences, and yet had not been ignorant of her own hidden things, the Bridegroom rightly avers to be fair once and again — in whom, as without, so also within, there was nothing unseemly. Whose beauty he pursues part by part, subjoining *Thy hairs,* etc.



## CHAPTER VIII.

*Thy hairs are as a flock of goats, which are come up from mount Galaath. Thy teeth as a flock of the shorn which are come up from the washing.* [var: Vulg. Cant. 4:1–2 has the plural *greges* in both clauses; the singular is the Vulgate's own reading at the parallel Cant. 6:4–5] By the hairs I judge that the senses of the body may be figured, which, coming forth from within, seek to be spread abroad without, and, liberty being received, are found to wander more widely than is just, unless perchance they be called back by censure and by the governance of rule. Whence Job also: [0367B] « I made a covenant with my [sic: *occulis*] [n: (Job XXXI)]; » And David: « Turn away, he says, mine eyes that they may not see vanity [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]. » And so of the rest. But that the hairs may worthily persevere unto the adorning of the head, they are fixed by the root in that same head and cleave to it; otherwise, when they are plucked up from the root, the welcome head of hair no longer remains, and, the hair being struck off, baldness dishonours the head. So also the senses of the body, which are all placed in the head, obtain their powers in it and work chiefly in it; if, the head being troubled, they be driven back as from their own seat, not only the head itself but the remaining members also are widowed of the greatest honour. But if, the head being sound, they have stood solid and tenacious as in a root, and have been effectual enough to fulfil their natural office, [0367C] then, after the manner of hairs sometimes straying too far, they are loosened by a wandering licence, if they be not restrained by a hand laid upon them and by a law set over them. The Virgin's hairs, therefore, a certain force of nature, as it were, renders well rooted, and the regular fitness of a binding renders them chastened without; when with a subtle providence she renders her senses solid in affection, and with a mighty censure restrains them from a dissolute effect; when in her heart she sets a measure to sensual affections, and upon them as they come forth without straightway lays the fillets of discipline. Her hairs also the Virgin worthily brings under censure, when she holds the senses of the inward mind more diligently under measure; when she suffers not those senses, by which she ought to perceive the things that are spiritual and vital, to consent by a wandering licence to things transitory and deadly. Senses of this kind, [0367D] whether bodily or none the less spiritual, the Bridegroom compares — that we, little ones, we who are still animal in our senses, may the more easily grasp what is said — to goats, which are the beasts of country folk, which are fed upon crags and on the very tops of the mountains above. And rightly did the Bridegroom will to compare the Virgin's senses to goats, because the Virgin, despising the lower things, loves to aspire to the highest alone; and though with a swifter leap she apprehends, in contemplating and in loving, things inaccessible to us, yet after a rustic manner she regards herself as lowly and base-born. « He hath regarded, she says, the humility of his handmaid [n: (Luc. I)]. » And expressly he compared the Virgin's hairs not to goats but to a flock of goats, wherein he invited the diligent hearer to understand the gathering together of the senses; because no wandering running to and fro, [0368A] no stealthy loosening drove them apart one from another, but a chaste confederation so brought them into a flock, under the shepherd's care and staff, that no wild beast would dare to break in upon any one of them, but, with hunger wearying it, would stand stupefied with jaws open and untried. But that goats of this kind may be yet more commended, they are declared not to come down but to come up from mount Galaath; whereas rather, as from the plain to the heights of *211* the mountain an ascent is made, so from the mountain to the level places there is, by the proper signification of the words, a descent. « Coming down, he says, from the mountain, Jesus stood in a plain place [n: (Luc. VI)]. » [var: Vulg. Luc. 6:17 *descendens cum illis*, "coming down with them"; the received text names no mountain in this clause] And of Moses: « Moses went up into the mountain, and was there forty days [n: (Exod. XXIV)]. » And below, the Lord to Moses: « Go down, he says, thy people hath sinned [n: (Exod. XXXII)]. » Since therefore of a mountain [0368B] not an ascent but a descent may more rightly be spoken, what does it mean that the aforesaid goats are recorded not to come down but to come up from mount Galaath — unless that great advances of the hairs, that is, of the senses, are indicated, to which that literal context, being referred, to find a worthy fitness, which does not seem literally to fit material goats? For it was not the holy Spirit's care to dispute concerning the ascent of goats, but to demonstrate the Virgin's advances by likenesses of this kind to us that are weaker; who takes pains to set out from mountain to mountain, that is, into virtue from virtue, for the sake of spiritual pasture, and to obtain not the ridges of the mountains but the heights of advances. Whence also this mountain, of which the discourse is, is named Galaath, which the judgment of the Hebrews declares to be interpreted *a heap of testimony*; [0368C] because when Laban, the fury of his threats and of his stubborn anger being appeased, was disposing to enter a covenant of peace with his kinsman Jacob, they raised a heap of stones, the stones being gathered by an equal hand, which they left to the generations that should come after as a testimony of the peace entered upon. But no one's excellence seems to bear testimony to Christ more than the Virgin's love, which is found by its own merit to be pre-eminent above the rest; which is heaped up of living and chosen stones, and is raised for increase, and gives an indelible monument as well to those that are present as to those that are to come. The Virgin therefore sets out and comes up from mount Galaath, when she apprehends the summit of sanctity by virtues heaped together; and from it she does not, as one coming down, [0368D] hunt after her own glory, but with a fitting advance bears witness to Christ's mighty mercy alone. « He that is mighty, she says, hath done great things to me [n: (Luc. I)]. » Wherefore the Bridegroom also praises the Virgin's teeth consequently, that not only in the hairs may her comeliness evidently appear, but that in the teeth also no mean usefulness may be shown, if only what is said be attended to not literally but spiritually. *Thy teeth,* he says, *are as a flock of the shorn which are come up from the washing.* The Virgin's teeth root out with a strong bite the pestilence of heresies, lest the seeds of falsehood should mightily gainsay the truth; and they chew the hardest saying concerning the incarnate Word with fitting assertions, that little ones may now the more easily give themselves over to this belief. Which teeth are not unfitly compared to a flock of sheep [0369A] — not of those which are weighed down by the hard trouble of fleece and of sweat, but of those which, their fleeces being shorn, show that they have now nothing superfluous, and which reprehend by the washing of confession whatsoever they may seem to have had. The Virgin therefore, who burns with the lawful love of him that loves her, is rightly said, as a Bride, to come up from the washing as one shorn; because she was zealous to be the more cleanly freed of the superfluous burdens of faults, the more she willed to be found worthy of belief for the commending of the Bridegroom. Concerning which it is subjoined: *All with twins,* etc.

## CHAPTER IX

*All with twin young, and there is not [sic: *sternis*] among them.* All, that is to say, both the goats that came up from mount Galaath and hung with undaunted step from its highest top, and the sheep that washed themselves, their fleeces being shorn, [0369B] and, coming forth from the washing, lacked the hard weight of fleece and of sweat. All, I say, are so fruitful by an equal grace, so pleasant by the large benefit of fecundity, that among them not one is condemned of barrenness, and each rejoices with an ampler gift and at once with a twin birth. A thing worthy of wonder, that in the flock neither goat nor sheep was found barren, that none of the fruitful ones was content with a single birth; that the Virgin's virtues, which we have taken to be figured by hairs or by teeth, are both made fruitful by love, and are not held content with a single love. For they love God, they love man also, and they despise neither God for man's sake nor man for God's sake, but according to the new law and the old they venerate the first commandment and the second [0369C] like unto it; while in the same Christ they embrace with twin arms the twin substance of the giant. For in the one Christ, whom the Virgin loves to have as bridegroom and as son, she sees two substances cohere personally one to the other, whereof the nature is indeed diverse and unlike (being, as it is, of God and of man), which nevertheless constitute in their joining one Christ, one person. To love him more tenderly and to be gladdened with a tender love, this is to be not barren, and to be made fruitful with twin young; because the holy Spirit has not much care concerning goats or sheep, but rather concerning virtues and the commendable offspring of virtues. Concerning the commendation of which he yet further subjoins: *As a fillet,* etc. *212*



## CHAPTER X.

*Thy lips are as a scarlet fillet; and thy speech sweet.* The Virgin's lips, being closed, keep the knowledge of the law, [0369D] and what they have known to be kept they heap together in the secret chamber of the heart; whose closure deserves not to be accused of an unfruitful silence, since a wise man holds his peace until a time, and the heart of him that is silent meditates prudence. In fine: « Mary kept, he says, all these things, pondering them in her heart [n: (Luc. II)]. » And when she is shaken by the hand of one that knocks, that the things gathered and kept may be brought forth, and the bolt or bar is at last struck off from her closed lips, she, obedient and now receiving the time of speaking, knocks in her turn, and brings forth nothing but discipline to them that have ears of hearing. For the obtaining whereof the prophet wills to have a door, namely that he may be able to restrain his lips by a fitting law; lest either he see, and repent, that he is pressed down by an immoderate silence, or, by a fault no less, [0370A] pass over into excess by a light much-speaking. « Set, he says, O Lord, a door of enclosure about my lips [n: (Psal. CXL)]. » O Lord, he says, give a fitting closure to my lips, give none the less an opening when the time shall be, that upon the hinge of discretion they may so turn as a door, that they be neither closed for keeping silence, nor loosed for speaking save at a fitting time. « Woe is me, saith Isaias, because I have held my peace [n: (Isa. VI)]. » And another on the contrary: « A wordy man, he says, shall not be justified [n: (Job. II)]. » [var: Vulg. Job 11:2 prints the clause as a question, *aut vir verbosus iustificabitur?*, with no negative particle in it] For the avoiding of the danger on either side the Virgin's lips found an efficacy, and by a worthy guard forestalled the faults both of silence and of much-speaking; which, lest they should speak superfluous things, pressed themselves together with a laudable closure, and at an opportune time uttered [0370B] what had seemed honourable, what useful. Wherefore they are not undeservedly compared to a scarlet fillet, whereby the hairs of the head are called back lest they flow out licentiously; because a girl's hair, lest it stray by its native lightness, is bound and conquered, and is pressed down by the power of rule. For to this end the Virgin prepares for herself a fillet clean and fine, that when with the process of time she shall have felt her youthful hair grow, she may set the one upon the other with a fitting governance, lest the hair display itself either at an unlawful time or in a disordered fashion. Further, when the prudent Virgin shall have seen the time draw near wherein it is fitting that her hair appear more freely and more openly, with a diligent hand she looses the fine fillet, and for a time frees and absolves her hair from its rule, as it were. And the hair now seems the more welcome to the eyes of beholders, the longer it is held before under the fillet's [0370C] guard; and, lying hid under a seal, it is composed and cherished, and earns to obtain a welcome beauty, which shines out the more honourably when, the fillet being laid aside, it is now permitted to go forth to the sight of men, if only it never cease to remember the fillet laid aside. So assuredly, when the discretion of him that speaks shall have been instructed under silence, and polished by a long stretch of time with lips knit together, then at last, they being loosed, the utterance leaves its native workshop, and, going forth into the ears of men, resounds a fitting discipline. Whence it is well added: *And thy speech sweet.* For when the lips, after the manner of a fillet, shall have worthily pressed together the inward affections, and shall have prudently formed with the hammer and anvil of silence the things that are to be brought forth, then their loosing, like the laying aside of the fillet, is not reprehended, grows not cheap, but [0370D] the timely utterance pleases, and the speech grows sweet to them that hear. Otherwise both the word is darkened to no purpose and the speech grows bitter, which is not formed under the lips nor grows together in silence: but for that which is to be brought forth the lips do not first hold the office of a fillet; but whatsoever shall have come into the mouth they bring forth unskilfully with open mouth. But what is it that the Virgin's lips are matched with a fillet that is none other than scarlet, unless because in this also they are preferred to ours, which are far unlike them — for our lips, though they show themselves to be closed and opened at divers times, yet to them that worthily look upon them represent not scarlet but perhaps rather mire? The scarlet, bearing the appearance of fire, rightly signifies love, which, being fiery, or rather being fire, purifies gold as in a furnace; which renders the just, more precious [0371A] than gold, fervent and burning; which burns yet consumes not, but refines and makes them that love clean. To this scarlet, or to this fire, the Virgin's lips are likened, which as well by silence as by speech serve a tender love; which, knowing no mire, grow not pale like ashes, but with a scarlet redness modestly glow ruddy and take fire. Closed indeed and given to silence, they are at leisure for God, they meditate on the ineffable, they cleave to the invisible, they rejoice in him, they suspend themselves with fervent desire toward things inward and eternal, and hold with a greedy embrace him whom they apprehend to be incomprehensible. « How great, they say, is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord, which thou hast hidden for them that fear thee [n: (Psal. XXX)]. » But being loosed, and yet not dissolute, they stretch themselves out in outward things, they set about speaking, in speaking they condescend to their neighbours, [0371B] and what they had tasted beforehand within they now bestow without upon the needy, and in this none the less show themselves to burn or to be red with scarlet. « For the sake of my brethren, saith he, and of my neighbours, I spoke peace of thee [n: (Psal. CXXI)]. » Because therefore the Virgin's lips are graced with the likeness of a fillet, and are irreprehensibly commended by a red scarlet or a fiery love, then, as her silence and her meditation *213* know no shadow of bitterness, so her speech shines again with the grace of sweetness. Concerning the praise whereof it is yet further subjoined: *As,* etc.



## CHAPTER XI.

*As a fragment of a pomegranate, so are thy cheeks, without that which lieth hid within.* Because so great is the beauty of this Virgin whom we have in hand, that our dullness cannot [0371C] easily grasp it clearly, her praiser, choosing to have pity on our infirmity, sets forth divers likenesses, that by them we may in some fashion behold her. Of which, although none can be esteemed sufficient, yet some seems in part fitting, so far only as material things can be fitted to spiritual, mean things be likened to beautiful, transitory things to abiding. Hence it is that the Virgin's cheeks, which bloom with a shamefast redness, are likened to a pomegranate, which shines with a ruddy rind, which, when it is broken, shows within a gathered multitude of grains, wherein there shines also no small beauty of whiteness. In the cheeks of a young girl, as on the eminence of the face, the excellence of beauty sets its throne for itself; and sitting there [0371D] it obtains a royal princedom, one that leans upon grace, not strengthened by privilege. Purposing therefore to commend the Virgin's beauty, the Bridegroom loves to compare her cheeks to a pomegranate, nay, to a fragment of one; that the double colour of one fragment, red without, snowy within, may speak the Virgin's praises, may sound with an equal proclamation, and that neither may gainsay the other. The red colour, bearing the form of blood, is a type of the passion which the holy Virgin sustains out of desire for her Solomon; who, whatsoever the world sounds forth by promises or thunders by terrors, spurns with a strong mind, drives off with an even foot, and distinguishes not the greatest things from the least. To shearings and pressures she opposes her rind as a shield, strongly embracing that commendable ordinance of Solomon, whereby he promises him blessed [sic: *lore*] who [0372A] now dashes the little ones against the rock, and that everyone must suffer who disdains not to live godly. And so the Virgin, patient at pressures and breakings, sickens not, nay (if she be not pressed, if she be not broken) she blushes; but broken and bruised, she grows not pale with a wan failing, but is made conspicuous by an inward comeliness, and grows white with a cheerful conscience. In fine, the pomegranate not yet broken gives a redness pleasing to the sight, but broken it gives a savour agreeable to the taste; not yet broken it gives to open nostrils an odour of wondrous sweetness, but broken it lessens it not, but reaches out one far ampler. So too the Virgin, not pressed down, not shaken by hammer or by torturer, shines with a Punic colour, is red with desire or with love; whose conversation is ruddy to the eyes of beholders, flourishing with a ripe deed, with a modest look, with a shamefast face. But if [0372B] a heavy hand press her, break her, and reduce her as it were to a morsel, and if a sword or an unsweet tribulation pass through not so much her body as her soul, no blackness is foul within, but another comeliness appears, of no less grace — namely an inward purity, and the cheerful security of a cleaner conscience. Whosoever is wise, worthily considering such a fragment, takes its sweetness not with the tooth but rather with the mind, and understands it to be gracious to the eyes not only by whiteness or by redness, but fruitful by sweetness and savour to the inward palate and to a sound taste. Whose odour also, or repute, then chiefly grows fragrant, when not only her works but her conscience also, being sifted, grows clear; when her patience is beaten with pressures and breakings, her mind is shaken, and in her there is nothing but a gathering of virtues and the whiteness or cleanness [0372C] of them displayed. This beauty of the Virgin, which can in some fashion be known both by herself and by another — if indeed any man can be found to know it — the Bridegroom praises under the name of cheeks, which display themselves in the face, and represent, after the manner of the aforesaid fragment, a twin comeliness of redness and of whiteness. But that which for the present he gives not to the Virgin, but sets forth, he expounds not by praises or comparisons of this kind: rather he wills that chief thing to lie hid from us who are too weak to take it in, that he may show it to be far more excellently pre-eminent than all the things here received. *Without that,* he says, *which lieth hid within.* From that, he says, which lies open, O Virgin, thou must be proclaimed as one to be praised — from the gifts of grace which can in some fashion be compared [0372D] with temporal things. *Without that,* that is, that being left unspoken which as yet is not seen but hidden, which, being utterly incomparable, is held far from the eyes under a seal. From which a chief praise would worthily be given thee, if it either could be said, or, being said, could be taken in by men; but what the eye seeth not, the ear beareth not, what ascendeth not into the heart of man, the present speech purposes not to expound. Sparing therefore those whom I shall bring into the auditory of this drama, I will bring myself back to the setting forth of those things which shall be able to be taken in: and, that being left unspoken which the understanding of mortals is not yet able to take in, speaking after the manner of men I will discourse of thy praises and of thy advances. *214*

## CHAPTER XII.

*Thy neck is as the tower of David, which is built [0373A] with bulwarks.* Because in the cheeks, compared to a pomegranate or to a fragment of one, the Virgin's beauty has been commended, in the neck her strength is consequently commended, which bends not itself to the weak and needy and transitory things of the world, and turns not aside its own uprightness from its purpose by a nerveless softness. She indeed sustains the presence of this life, the pack of the flesh, a heavy load, as a sweet thing, by a strong patience, by the constancy of patience; and whatsoever the world strikes in — the world which buffets the necks of all that are present — shakes her not from her standing, nor scandalizes her after the manner of the weak. For she is filled with so great love, with so great fervour of spirit, that she weighs burdens at a cheap rate, as one accustomed to such things; and after the manner of a heifer that has been taught to love the yoke or the threshing, she esteems the practice of bearing heavy things a fruit, not a hurt. Wherefore [0373B] her neck is declared like to a tower, which, fixed by its own weight, is not moved by the driving of winds or the dashing of floods; which is of so great strength that it yields not its place to the power of wicked spirits, and confers an unassailable defence upon the whole city. Whence also it is called David's, which is interpreted *strong of hand,* signifying Christ, whose hand, unassailable and unconquered, the good feel ready for help, the evil for vengeance. A tower of this kind is raised in Jerusalem to this end, that with a circumspect solicitude it may be able to foresee enemies from afar; and, if perchance they presume to draw near, that it may defend itself from their inroads or assaults, and by its own strength make light of whatsoever they bring against it. Nor does its defence profit itself alone, but the whole city also, to which it gives both a necessary [0373C] strength and a not unseemly ornament; to which the weaker city runs back at once if the enemy assail, and it, being mightier, gives confidence to her that runs back, and succours her. So too the Virgin, after the manner of David's tower, descries the enemy from afar, nay looks down upon him, and cares not; at whose look he shudders and flees back, and endures not in his purpose of confidence; and whatsoever of threats or of frauds he shall have presumed to contrive is dashed out, and the malice of him that presumes is dashed back upon himself: so great a horror does the face of her that beholds strike in, so mightily does it beat back the enemy. For the tower is built with its own bulwarks. Bulwarks cleaving to a tower seem to jut out from without, to fortify the tower strongly, to hang heavily over the enemies; from which poles, darts, stones and the rest of such things [0373D] are thrown, whereby, the tower being defended, the enemies are mightily shaken. These, as I judge, are the precepts or admonitions of Holy Scripture, the utterances of the prophets, the spiritual knowledge of letters; which it is agreed cleave with a steadfast memory to the Virgin's strong mind, and, by a manifold advance of works, keep off further whatsoever things are hurtful. For the subtlety of Holy Scripture and a spiritual understanding, a tenacious memory of the commandments, a manifest literal knowledge, render the Virgin's conscience — their own jutting-forth — unshaken, and the pressing of the enemies beaten back by ready hurlings of works. With bulwarks of this kind David's tower defends itself, and stretches itself out, as with certain arms, to beat back the wicked: because the unbending strength of the Virgin (which was said to be figured by the neck) rejoices to be strengthened by the patronage of Holy Scripture set beside it. [0374A] For there she receives that whereby she may be held stronger and more secure, whereby she may repress enemies and faithfully protect friends; which seems to cleave to her the more firmly for her own defence, but for ours to hang from her by a benefit, if not an equal one, yet not a contemptible one. Whence it is subjoined: *A thousand,* etc.



## CHAPTER XIII.

*A thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the valiant.* The same Scripture which he seems to figure in the bulwarks he seems to figure also in the shields, and to commend her under various names because of her various effects; for since her efficacy in helping is found manifold, it is no wonder if she is marked with manifold words.
