From the tower, then, the Bridegroom says that shields hang down, and, lest we deem them few, he adds that he keeps not silence as to the number; so that when [0374B] the enemies do not assail, we may not only run back to the hanging shields, but may trust in the number of the shields with a hope that does not deceive. The thousand, which is held highest in the order of numbers, because it is made up of perfect ones, is called the most perfect of perfect ones; because, as the ten is filled up out of ten units, the hundred out of ten tens, so the thousand is filled up out of as many hundreds, than which no other single number is held greater among numbers. By which number is commended the strong defence of the shields, their perfect usefulness, the useful hanging up of things perfect, which are set in order not only for the adorning or the defence of David's tower, but are also set forth with ample defence for us that flee to the tower. The Virgin indeed, whose neck *215* is compared, as has already been said, to a tower, is prepared with manifold valour for [0374C] the defence of us all, who makes clear and expounds to us the sequence of the old Scripture, showing accomplished in herself in very deed what that Scripture sets down as to come in mystery. For what Jeremias long before foretold of a woman that should compass a man [n: (cap. XXXI)], what Isaias foretold of a Virgin that should conceive and bear a son [n: (cap. VII)], what Ezechiel prophesied in a riddle dark enough of the gate not opened [n: (cap. XLIV)], what Moses marvellously prefigured of the rod of Aaron [n: (Num. XVII)], what prophecy of old declared in many places and in many ways and did not exhibit — they that give heed weigh this, that it hangs for us more evidently from Mary. It hangs, I say, from her, nor is it shut up in her with bolts or bars, but by a manifest benefit it is spread abroad even to [0374D] our knowledge, so that, running back to the Virgin, we may rejoice to find more manifestly what a grudging antiquity willed to cover from us with a mystical cloud. Whose mysteries, which we say hang for us from Mary — that is, shine forth from her and through her upon us that look upward — the bridegroom in this epithalamium rightly designated by the name of shields, and, setting them forth to us that are lower, assigned them more nearly and more specially to the tower. For the Virgin herself knew first and more perfectly the mysteries of Holy Scripture, which were both said and foretold of her in the obscure soothsaying of the prophets, and, being more subtly and more excellently instructed in their riddles, she brought them forth to us and offered them to lovers as bucklers. The hollow surface of a buckler protects and hides the citizen, and holds back or beats back from over against him the malice of the assailant; [0375A] so too the deep breadth of Holy Scripture, impassable to the enemy, becomes by the ample help of the Virgin our valour who are citizens. Assuredly through her a sanctified day has now shone upon us that were once in darkness; through her our sun of understanding has shone back in the shield of Holy Scripture; through her we now see, now hold Christ, of old promised, in figures and riddles wrapped about, the promises of Holy Scripture being now discharged. Through her the lucid perfection of Holy Scripture has condescended to us that are far lower, and with open bosom has shown itself to all that advance in zeal and understanding, in which one may see the sequence of perfect commandments that shall profit them that love, the manner and order of living, and in fine all the armour of the valiant. For whosoever wills to be armed with worthy valour finds in Holy Scripture whence he may rightly [0375B] glory, in which a life-giving building lies hid under the shadow of the letter, which grows clear, by her benefit, to them that worthily seek the Virgin. But they that have no care to seek diligently and to advance valiantly are not able to find useful armour in Holy Scripture because to them that know not the Virgin the face of Holy Scripture is dark; nor is the armour of them that are ignorant, but of them that are valiant in faith. Hence it is that the gentiles, whom a foolish unbelief harshly buffets, and the Jews, whom the Virgin's childbearing scandalizes with no less ruin; find not in Holy Scripture Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God, the knowledge whereof hangs for us, not obscure, from the Virgin. For because they draw not near to the Virgin with worthy reverence, they believe not worthily the marvellous conception, nor the childbearing so unspeakable; it remains that they either see not, or, seeing, [0375C] abhor the hanging shields, and languish unarmed, and perish of their languishing, not using the armour of the valiant. But they whose left hand is not fortified with a hanging sword, whose present conversation is not wholesomely instructed by the understanding of Holy Scripture: their right hand glories not in salvation, nor in the blessedness to come; nay, their reckoning reaches not to the right hand, but is cheated. The neck of the Virgin therefore is not unfittingly likened to a tower, through which so manifold a benefit of Holy Scripture is published to us: through which the mystery of the incarnate Word is spread abroad to us, through which the word of the Father, passing through, is presented to our ears, nay, and to our eyes. For that good word which the very heart of God the Father unspeakably uttered forth, when he ordained to come to men and to be seen by men: taking as it were [0375D] the vehicle of a voice, made for itself a path of this Virgin's neck, through which, having passage, it set itself before them that sought not and that asked not. By the passing of which word that path of his is so magnificently adorned, the Virgin's neck is strengthened with so great valour, that it is held not insufficient to bear the burdens of us that are infirm, and after the manner of a strong tower guards us that are weak. Lastly *turris*, a tower, is named from *tuendo*, guarding (as some assert), because it guards both itself and whatever lies adjacent, and by its guardianship the hope of them that run back to it is made secure, especially if there hangs down a thousandfold row of shields, and all the armour of the valiant. And because the Virgin seems more abundantly to excel in these, the Bridegroom goes on still to add praises to praises; and, loving her that is lovable, [0376A] he does what is proper to a friend to do, who esteems alike whatsoever commendable thing can be said of his friend. He says therefore: *Two breasts,* etc.



## CHAPTER XIV.

*Thy two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a roe, that feed among the lilies, until the day breathe, and the shadows be bowed down.* Far above, the Virgin commended the Bridegroom's breasts, and affirmed them better than wine, fragrant with the *216* best ointments; which the Bridegroom perchance remembering, and although a delay as it were of time has come between, allowed not her breasts likewise to pass by without praises. After the neck, therefore, which he compared to a most fortified tower, passing to the breasts, he fitted to them also a wondrous likeness, bringing forward not something of the same kind according to the letter, but fawns that feed [0376B] rather in the time of shadows than of day. The breasts signify, as I seem to see, that fruitfulness of the Virgin whereby she cherishes and advances our littleness who are infirm, whereby she gives us suck and weans us not, until she make us come to advancement, until the day arrive, and the night at length, the shadows growing thin, come to its failing. But it moves me that, bringing forward the Virgin's breasts, he says *two*, whereas according to the letter any woman's breasts are not but two: and therefore, if he had said only "breasts", keeping silence as to *two,* yet no one rightly wise would understand any but two. But in this perchance he willed to signify that the fruitfulness of which I spoke is twofold, because a single one would not pour out for us a bounty full enough; whereas the double suffices to nourish us by a joined benefit, and no sound man seeks to find a third, nor anything beyond it. For the [0376C] Virgin has a certain affection of a more bountiful benevolence toward those whom she perceives to need a stronger patronage, whom, redeemed by her son, she considers to will and to strive, and yet, weighed down by their own burden, not to be permitted to accomplish. The Virgin loves therefore to milk out a tender breast for such, and by benevolent affection to advance the weak to whatsoever is valiant: the holy Mother holding it certain that it pleases not the redeeming Son that those should perish whom he willed not to hold guilty of the original debt. But since that breast and affection of benevolence would be held insufficient if to the kindly affection there were not joined a more powerful effect, the Virgin has and obtains from the Son efficacy or effect, that she may effectually lead the weak on to such advancement as she wills. For on whom she has mercy with affectionate solicitude, him she succours and heals with efficacious power; [0376D] and with one breast as it were she bends herself to have compassion on the wretched, and with the other she now proffers to the needy the necessary help. Out of these two breasts, then — namely affection and effect — the Virgin pours into us nourishing milk, and with solicitous hand hides us from the whirlwind and from the rain; and whatsoever the lion thunders she drives back and beats back with more powerful threats, and heals with healing milk whatsoever the venomous asp pours over us. Whence also the breasts are not unfittingly compared to fawns, which, spurning what is hurtful, freely betake themselves to what is useful; which from afar see and discern what is fitting with a keen eye, and pass over whatever is harmful by a leap or by efficacious power. Which assuredly they are agreed to have derived from their mother the roe, on whom mighty nature is believed to have conferred that gift, [0377A] that she may see more sharply and discern more discreetly whatsoever shall profit, and more solicitously spurn and more swiftly pass by what shall hurt. So the affection and effect of the Virgin obtain this virtue from their mother grace, that they may discreetly see through whom they are solicitously to advance to salvation; but may pass by those whom they have perceived not to pertain to grace, and may abhor the filthy, and permit the reprobate to be the more filthy. And that the fawns are asserted to be not unlike but rather twins, in that, begotten of one mother, they are alike nourished with one milk, seems to agree with the aforesaid affection and effect, which one mother, grace, willed to bring forth by a grateful benefit. Which assuredly are associated by a certain brotherhood, by a conjoining covenant, while what the first undertakes the second follows up with completing work; nor does the former aim at anything [0377B] but what the latter is able to consummate, nor does the second accomplish anything but what it sees the first more diligently to aim at. They feed among the lilies so long as they are delighted with the virtues of them that advance, who prosper by the whiteness of their manners and the odour of good testimony; who both within grow more wholesomely enkindled, not with blushing but with love, and without grow white, as with leaves, by whitened works. And these indeed cease not to prosper by the ample benefit of the virgin, and the Virgin ceases not likewise to rejoice at their advances: until, their spirits being polished to a nicety, a sweeter day shall breathe, and the darkness of the shadows, impatient of this day, shall breathe its last. For when the morning light that knows no evening draws near, the night of present ignorance and of all trouble withdraws; and the gathered lilies are offered with dancing to the highest King, in whose [0377C] sanctuary they enjoy a sevenfold and unfading comeliness. Where there is no hunger, where now the fawns feed not, where the Virgin's breasts are poured into none that advance, where the Virgin now brings up none, instructs no one, has mercy on no one, because there infancy, there ignorance, there also misery is not had. Here therefore the Virgin feeds, where she is declared still to feed us, where, the shadows still standing, the face of the day is not seen, where, the day being now bright, a man is not taught by his neighbour, where, according to the prophecy [n: (Jer. XXXI)], God shall be known from the lesser even to the greatest. But the bride's breasts being praised, the bridegroom, as it were withdrawing himself from her and giving himself back to his companions, speaks to them, but of her, because for one that loves tenderly the solicitude concerning her is so vehement [0377D] that in this song he knows not how to speak save to her or of her. *217*

## CHAPTER XV.

*I will go to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense.* It suffices not a lover to go to the mountain which he loves, but he chooses also to anticipate his journey with a word; and while he defers rather than omits to revisit it, with a word running before he promises to go afterward. If, he says, I have withdrawn myself a little from the mountain's presence, yet I have not drawn back from it my memory or my tender love: nor have I contracted for myself contempt of it, or anger, or hatred, but have thus the more strongly drawn to me its love and desire toward me. Now the mountain, is the loftiness of this our virgin, which a fixed and immovable firmness renders commendable, [0378A] against which, although the blasts of the winds, in an array as it were drawn up, strike threats from this side and that, yet they cast not the mountain down from grace, nor from its abiding state. For against this virgin the enemies frequently hurl arrows and darts, and, their malice going forward, add the assaults of battering-rams and heavy engines; all which the virgin's mountainous loftiness and unmoved firmness cast far back, and, their efforts being made void, hurl the enemies, more harshly beaten back, to the depths. For whether the adjured hand of the mighty one be reckoned present or absent, yet so great is the love toward the virgin, so great is the bridegroom's care concerning the virgin, that she, after the manner of a mountain, is secure by his patronage, and whatsoever the raging fury of the winds shall bring in is made void. For when the bridegroom seems to withdraw from her, she permits not the withdrawal; sometimes, absenting himself, he promises to return the [0378B] sooner; and by that counsel which he himself knows he declares that he goes and returns, according as he knows it to be much expedient for himself and most of all for the virgin. Withdrawing as it were from the virgin, yet he escapes not the meshes of love; absented a little, he goes thither again; and neither the approach nor the withdrawal takes service under torpor but under love, that they may be more closely bound and cleave to one another with a stronger thong. To this end the bridegroom withdraws himself, that he may not now grow cheap by the giving of abundance of himself; to this end he goes to the virgin, that love may the more tenderly break out afresh, that he who loves and wills to be more loved by the virgin may by that furnace make her to be the more vehemently inflamed. He goes therefore to the virgin, that her love may burn again more ardently, and that, she loving more, he himself may be the more gladdened; that when he shall have felt her the more scorched with heat or with love, he may love her as she advances and cherish her with a more grateful embrace.



## CHAPTER XVI.

[0378C]

Whence another translation has: *I will go for myself to the mountain of myrrh.* I will go to the Virgin, and lest I seem to go in vain, I will go for myself — seeking indeed to take counsel for her, seeking to satisfy her, but for myself also: assuredly I shall go thither not empty, not superfluous, but I shall both bestow upon her and shall bring much to myself when I return. I will go to the virgin, whose height myrrh now marvellously claims, whose unbroken flesh no native corruption disfigures: whose integrity a wondrous chastisement renders excellent above all women, and whose excellence it renders solid and not swelling. Great is this mountain, which is agreed to be so devoted to chastised acts that it may be called, not soft and flowing, but specially a mountain of myrrh: in that no [0378D] enticing softness enervated the virgin, but an untouched rigour and the myrrh of continence preserved her. Whom also the bridegroom not unfittingly names a hill of frankincense, in that she scatters a good report both to those present and to those to come: and, being kindled by coals and by the violence of heat or of love, she is lifted up into a heap and gives to God a sacrifice of odour. Whose devotion, whose fervent affection is sweeter than all frankincense, offering itself to the Creator, bearing itself above the creature; she is a mountain that knows not how to bring forth a laughing-stock, but a hill that chooses to think nothing but humble things of itself. When she restrains and extinguishes and suffers not the allurements of the flesh so much as to mutter, when she strives to forestall with most approved myrrh the affections that breed worms, when she applies a yoke to her own wills and lays down a law, when she restrains and composes with salt whatsoever the flesh savours, [0379A] then assuredly she is a mountain, to which so incomparable a height is at hand, great virtue, great constancy, great valour of wisdom. But when she looses herself from transitory pursuits and works, and turns over in mind how sweet to the inward throat are the things of heaven, when with fiery love she resolves herself into liquid frankincense, and, forgetful of earthly things, wraps herself wholly in the contemplation of things above, then assuredly she is made a hill, while the loftier she is in merits and the more devout, so much the humbler in heart and, as it were, not far removed from the rest. And when the angel found her alone in her chamber, given over to meditation, and the Lord himself who had sent him had already come before him, the messenger of the childbearing to come; she, hanging upon the word of the Angel — nay, upon the word of the Father — with most devout love, and condescending to us that are lower and not yet capable of things great enough: [0379B] « Behold, she says, the handmaid of the Lord [n: (Luc. I)]. » When by a new grace the virgin's mind surpassed our level ground, and he who came between as a messenger *218* saw himself forestalled, with how great humility did the most devout Virgin press herself down, who, being already called the mother of God, granted to herself no name but that of a little handmaid? A strong fire being applied, the frankincense melts into a cloud of smoke, the smoke is lifted on high, the sweetness of the odour now grows fragrant: far and wide the world is seen to be taken up with the excellence of this mountain, and yet the humble Virgin still constrains herself to be called a hill. To this mountain by merits, this hill by humility, the bridegroom pledges himself to go, and, present sooner than said, he now answers the Virgin as she speaks; or rather he himself comes before her as she is about to speak, and commends her, that she may kindle herself the more closely into love of him that commends her.

## CHAPTER XVII.

[0379C]

*Thou art all fair, my friend, and there is not a spot in thee.* From the time that the Angel announces to the Virgin the word enjoined him and her salutation, and the holy Spirit comes upon her and, overshadowing her, gives virtue: in her the iniquitous law obtains not its privilege, nor does any defilement of sin, recent or ancient, remain. Now one woman is foul, another all foul, another fair, and another all fair. Foul indeed is she whom the ancient wrath, the law of nature, darkens and bows down, which contracts guilt for itself from the beginning and from the vice of birth, whose difficulty is so overmastering, so inextricable, that neither virtue nor faculty suffices to be utterly without it. But she that is all foul subjects her corrupted will to the depraved law, [0379D] and by a pestilent consent fashions an execrable unity, while what the oppressive law suggests, or rather thrusts in, she follows up with her will and obeys with completing action. On the other side, she is fair who understands the written law, the sequence of the commandments, to be good, and, the spirit now granting it, loves that it has been given, and is advanced by voluntary instinct to fulfil it more diligently, but does not yet deserve to obtain the power to prevail. To will indeed lies close at hand, but she experiences a contradictory struggle, in that the door of the difficulty is not yet opened to her will; while the one knocks strongly, strives obstinately and presses on, the other beats back more strongly, struggles more stubbornly and resists. The one, tending her face with the hand of diligence, wills to strive that, every spot being wiped away, she may be let in to what she desires; the other busies herself to resist [0380A] and struggle against this purpose, and sometimes, being the more powerful, rejoices to be sent forward to victory. But she is all fair whom the vicious law, the reproach of nature, the disease of wrath, no longer press down, no longer oppress, are not able to hinder, but that the will is provoked even by desire to repel faults, and a worthy possibility supports it as it goes before. She is all fair whose keenness of mind is vigorous, whose spirit sickens not, whose flesh is quiet and grows not insolent against the spirit; whose spirit, enduring no rebellion from what is subject to it, obeys God alone and no longer halts in the precept. She is all fair who by a rare kind of example has now come to this height, upon whom so great a grace of the overshadowing spirit has come, whose every spot the powerful hand of mercy has so wiped away that not only [0380B] guilt but even the anxious fear of guilt does not remain. That any one like ourselves should be able to obtain this, while this time rolls on and he groans under it and complains that he remains — that I may confess the truth to you, I take not to myself any certain knowledge, and therefore I presume not rashly to affirm what I know not. For although the light of the new grace is poured into our eyes, at whose rising the darkness poured over us by our parents' fault has perished, yet there is a certain spot as it were imprinted upon our face, under whose urging, while we live here, we are guilty at least in some small measure. Of which it is written: « No man is clean from filth [n: (Job XV)].--There is not a man that sinneth not [n: (II Par. VI)]. » [var: Vulg. has no clause in this form; nearest are Job 14:4 *Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine?* and Job 15:14 *Quid est homo ut immaculatus sit* — the chapter Migne's own note cites] A spot of this kind the severe law seems to have imprinted upon us wretches, and with this as with a branding-iron to have stained our beauty, so that although we strive to polish it away with the hand [0380C] of solicitude, yet we cannot wholly free it from this injurious right. Now a spot is a more tenacious mole, an unseemly brand, a discordant foulness, wherewith the beauty lying next and bordering upon it grieves to be infected, or, that I may say more, to be affected; to the wiping away of which, although the hand applies much care, yet it removes not what has now grown in and turned into nature. But in this virgin, if there was in her aught of natural vice, the spiritual grace that comes upon her cleanses and unspots it; and what in us perseveres more harshly by a wretched and tenacious law, in her the hand of grace washes away with efficacious medicine. And because the general iniquity of us all darkens her not, but in the bridegroom's sight she now flashes with a special excellence of merits, rightly does the bridegroom [0380D] love her the more tenderly and invite her, that, coming to him, she may commit herself to him more devoutly and more attentively.



## CHAPTER XVIII.

*Come from Libanus, my Bride, come from Libanus, come.* Her that is all fair, so that she is not held even by a light spot — lest perchance she seem to have given her labour to beauty without fruit — the bridegroom admonishes to come: namely from great beauty to *219* greater, that with a learned foot she may pass from that which has been given to the giver. For it is not granted to any one to remain in the things he has received, and to cleave to them with all his desire and with grasping hands, but rather, not out of contempt or hatred but out of advancement and counsel, to turn back the eyes of the mind from these to him who bestowed them, and to hold more dearly not the things themselves but himself now, while the things are held for his sake. Libanus [0381A] seems to me to designate that whiteness to which the bridegroom willed to assign the virgin — nay rather, which he willed rather to assign to the virgin — the whiteness, namely, of continence and of virginal purity, which the son conferred upon his bride and mother by the gift of his own goodness. For the bridegroom willed his own mother to dwell in whiteness, that her excellence might deserve to be commended as it were from the place; that the mountain Libanus itself, that is, the whiteness of virginal excellence, might so consecrate her that was fruitful, that her fruitfulness might become spiritual. Although, if it may be said — nay perhaps because it may — not so much the place seems to consecrate the virgin as the Virgin the place, nor is the virgin held commendable from the mountain, but the mountain from the virgin; nor has this whiteness so much exalted the virgin as the virgin has exalted this whiteness and rendered it altogether more grateful in the eyes of them that worthily consider. For even before the virgin, as mount Libanus, [0381B] so also virginity can be found, but it is said to be marked with little honour or with none; nor was any one found to be commended for virginal comeliness, or by whose merit virginity itself might rejoice to be made illustrious. To our time indeed and to this our virgin we know this to have been reserved, that, being exalted by this mountain, she should rather render the mountain itself exalted, and in a wondrous manner should herself, being the whiter, whiten Libanus, and by her own merit adorn the virginal comeliness. Great therefore is the Virgin, and incomparably to be proclaimed, to be compared with no women before her, with none that come after, who brought merit to the virginal whiteness that had before no merit or honour, and conferred on it the gift of a fuller grace. That therefore which for many ages back was among women unseemly and burdensome, from that time and thenceforward is rendered pleasing [0381C] and beautifying; and that which the daughter of Jephte, slighting it, as it were devotes and bewails, the rod of Jesse, prudently choosing it, lifts up more sacredly and honours. But because the Virgin has nothing of grace, nothing of merit, that is not received, from him who gave it she hears and receives this precept: that from so great a whiteness, in the gift whereof she first rejoices, she should refer herself to him by whose authorship virginity itself is made fruitful. *Come,* he says, *from Libanus, my bride.* Thou, he says, that hast whitened mount Libanus with a new gift, that hast exalted virginal whiteness by the excellence of thy merits, come — yet not laying aside that virginal comeliness, but, not content with it, preferring the bridegroom's grace before it. Come, not that thou now desist from the purpose of virginity, but that thou be joined more nearly to me the giver and [0381D] stand by me; that thou who rejoicest above the solid ground in virginal whiteness mayest exult the more readily in the privilege of a bride by a nuptial covenant. Therefore it is said: *Come from Libanus, bride.* But when it is repeated: *Come from Libanus,* and *bride,* is not added, he willed, so far as I judge, to admonish twice concerning that to which he perceives the virgin to cleave the more tenaciously the longer she has done so; whence, when, being thus admonished, she turns herself away, not out of hatred but at the dictate of counsel, she turns herself with an easier passage to the things that are offered. But when he repeats a third time *Come,* and does not add, *from Libanus, Bride,* he exhorts her not only to be removed from the things she now holds by advancing merits, or to be presently advanced to the espousals that are set before her, but that whatsoever she shall have gained, and this too, as though she had sweated in a twofold contest, she should do it all for love of the reward, all in hope of the crown. Come therefore, he says; turn thyself away from the things [0382A] thou now holdest, for the sake of advancing; come a second time, turn thyself more familiarly to the espousal embraces. Come a third time, that thou mayest rejoice not only in virginal honour and in the espousal chamber, but that on the royal seat thou mayest, a mother with her son, be crowned in glory. Whence it is subjoined: *Thou shalt be crowned,* etc.



## CHAPTER XIX.

*Thou shalt be crowned from the head of Amana, from the top of Sanir, and Hermon, from the couches of lions, from the mountains of leopards.* To this end is the Virgin, the bridegroom's mother, so solicitously admonished to come: that she may be worthily honoured for her merits with royal insignia, that a crown be given her not compacted of gold or of silver, of electrum, or of stones, but wrought by a certain new kind out of lofty mountains. Whose most excellent smith sets mount Amana first, [0382B] sets mount Sanir and Hermon above it and joins them to it: the couches of lions, the ridges of leopards, the prudent craftsman puts between; and thus with wondrous prudence he forges and composes a marvellous work. But what is it, that out of so many mountains everywhere in the earth he chose three, which, naming them expressly, he so brought into this marvellous work as to order Amana first, Sanir second, Hermon third, and to associate in this work those that are divided from one another by place? It does not readily occur what mystery is figured in this deed, unless perchance the interpretation of the names themselves come to our aid, which, being more diligently discussed, makes clear the darkened understanding and mystically brings the Virgin's crown to perfection. Amana is interpreted *a watching tooth,* designating the wicked *220* spirit, which is agreed to envy all upright [0382C] minds, which, ever envying, loves and desires to bite us: and by a pestilent bite to drive us on to death or to vices; and sometimes it rejoices to prevail in such business. For unto so great a crime it is found not to be torpid with sluggish sleep, but to remain constant and solicitous with watchful malice; which, although it shows not itself shameless to them that watch and stand upon their guard, yet, watching, bites and infests them that are given over to sleep and less provident of themselves. From which Sanir also is not discordant, of which mention is made next, whose interpretation evidently expresses the same watchfulness; and by this name too the same wicked spirit seems to be designated, to which it is agreed that no malice is assigned but such as is ever watchful. For Sanir is interpreted [0382D] *a night bird,* or *a stench.* A bird, using the oarage of its feathers, sustains itself by the vehicle of its wings; when it is believed to be far off, it presents itself by swift flight; and if perchance the light of day is believed not to favour its purpose, the bird of spiritual malice becomes a night bird for the seducing of the wretched. It becomes a night bird when temptation fraudulently attacks the unwary and secure man, when, being perchance detected, it thrusts itself in secretly under another appearance, when it mocks and derides him that is carried off by languor and drowsiness, when the sluggard is led like an ox to the victim — nay, is seduced — and sees it not. Nor is Sanir undeservedly said to be also a stench, because temptation, although it shuns to be foreseen, yet wills to be present perceptibly; and though, like a snake creeping in silence, it strives not to be heard, yet, bringing in by its bite a poisonous stench, it wills to be felt. Temptation [0383A] unforeseen is not perceived, as though by an open nostril, when the tempted man, his mind being weighed down, experiences the heavy pack of guilt: and whithersoever he turns himself in the little bed of darkness under the coverlet, he perceives the fruit of the stench, uncertain perhaps of the root. The root full of vice is the suggestion that secretly oppresses, but the fetid fruit is the consent or the fulfilment that follows; whose stench, when it infects the nostrils and affects the inward smelling, renders the whole man enervated with poisoned inward parts. To which Hermon is rightly subjoined, which is interpreted *execration,* or *his anathema.* For from that time and thenceforward, not only does that lost man work nothing of good, but with a fuller malice he execrates the good that he perceives with his ear, because through the chinks of the nostrils there flows in so great a gathering or bilge of vices that the discipline of the word can nowhere enter [0383B] into the heart itself. But the word being shut out, that wicked one hardens the wretched heart yet more, and, it being hardened, he closes and stops the ear also after the manner of an asp, so that not only does he no longer believe right hearing, nor love to obey, but he chooses thereafter not even to hear what is set before him as right. Thus assuredly he execrates whatsoever rectitude of manners suggests, so that a dullness wickedly let in closes every approach to him, rejoicing to present open nostrils to the stenches of vices alone, and to fill up with unclean floods the pool of his inward recesses. Because therefore no admonition, no Holy Scripture is admitted to the hardened mind, it accounts in the place of an anathema whatsoever true religion or worship holds; and, loving to be detained by the softness of mire alone and by unclean dregs, it thinks nothing more execrable than to be removed [0383C] from such things. Whence it is written: « But wisdom is an execration to the sinner [n: (Eccli. I)], » who, advancing to the worse, wills to be hurtful not only to himself but to others also; and, being powerful in malice, rejoices to be a horror to his inferiors; from whom fierceness goes forth, like a lion lying in wait from his couch, and wills that all the rest should sink under a servile fear of him. For the cruelty of some is not easily held back within the narrows of the mind, but rages and boils, that it may be stretched out to the harming of others; and when the furnace or the oven has grown white-hot with the heat of malice, a lion-like fury seeks to rage abroad against all that are subject to it. Which, if perchance it consider that the force of its power is not enough for it, seeks a new fowling, namely the guile of falsehood; and now, furious, like a roaring lion he seeks [0383D] whom he may devour, now, spotted with manifold guile, he shows himself a leopard. For that wicked spirit is manifoldly warlike, using now power to subdue the wretched, now guile; now agreeing with them that will and them that will not, now rebellious, hurting with a thousand arts, and, after the leopard's fashion, a turn-skin. And notably the bridegroom assigned lions to couches and leopards to mountains, wherein he designated both the fraudulent strength of malignant spirits and their robust fraudulence; of whom sometimes a savage strength goes forth from the couch or from ambush, sometimes from the height of power a no less deadly multitude of frauds. Whether therefore the deceitful and crafty stretch themselves out more evidently to the exercising of strength, or the robust and lofty now descend to the weaving of the meshes of frauds, [0384A] they bring in a hurtful war both upon the unwary and upon the weak; and unless the Virgin come and in mercy succour, they bear back a triumphal standard. But the holy Virgin hastens to meet such wicked enemies, bearing it ill that any of the elect should turn aside from her son's purpose; and having mercy on those whom the enemy's malice has almost destroyed; she intercedes with her son and reconciles to him those whom he has redeemed. And her son being appeased, she turns herself confidently to assail the enemies, breaks their forces, strips bare their frauds and overturns them; and that mount Amana swells, that Sanir or Hermon lifts itself up with uplifted top, the Virgin strongly treads down and softens like the mire of the streets. Worthily therefore, when full victory is carried off over them, her hand is adorned with laurel, the Virgin's head is crowned with gold; and she is said to be crowned *221* from those same mountains, [0384B] since it is now fully granted her to glory in the victory over them.



## CHAPTER XX.

*From the head of Amana, from the top of Sanir and Hermon,* etc. But I deem it not unfitting if the aforesaid mountains be beautified by a favourable interpretation, and if by them not malignant demons but men converted to the faith be figured, in whose faith the Virgin rejoicing, and solicitous for their increase, cherishes them by her benevolence and advances them by her intervention. Amana, as has been said, is interpreted *a watching tooth.* And that preacher is not unfittingly named a watching tooth, to whom, as to a watchman, the keeping of us that are infirm is committed; to whom, while there is offered a linen sheet full of living creatures, or rather of men living after an animal manner [n: (Judae 19)], it is commanded to slay and to eat, not really, [0384C] but in a spiritual mystery. « Slay, he says, and eat [n: (Act. X)]. » [var: Vulg. Acts 10:13 *occide et manduca* — Migne prints *macta*, a sacrificial verb, for *occide*] For a shepherd takes not up his watches worthily over his flock who consumes not its hardness by the admonition of doctrine; to whose watchful eye, when anything worthy of reproof sets itself over against him, applies not his tooth the more bitingly to cut it away the sooner. Against which it is written of others: « They shall eat the sins of my people [n: (Ose. IV)]. » But after the mind of Amana, the Bridegroom willed to name mount Sanir, whose interpretation seems to sound *a night bird,* because, while we grow torpid with the long custom of vices, the ever-solicitous shepherd becomes without doubt a night bird. For when a blind softness invites us to sin, nay to persist in it, the good shepherd, [0384D] who sleeps not over our keeping nor slumbers, after the manner of a night bird seems to arrive importunate and sudden, and to arraign more harshly, with the sword of the word, manners that are ill secure. Lastly Judas Machabeus, when he perceived that the nights were now pressed with silence, and that the opportunity of the time agreed with his great daring, coming upon the unwary enemies valiantly wrought great slaughter, and with watchful war triumphed over them that rested in secure torpor. For that warlike man judged that it mattered very little whether he dared to hurl himself upon the enemy in the presence of night or of day, provided only that the sluggish and cowardly incircumspection of the enemy yielded to the more cautious man, and that either by guileful valour or by warlike guile the victory were given to the warrior Moreover among the ancients it was published in a famous saying, and, lest oblivion should blot it out, it was committed to letters [0385A] among the heathen, that in war the excellence of valour alone be not sought, but a fitting guile also, that the malignity of the enemy may be craftily crushed. Guile, he says, or valour — who would ask, in an enemy? [n: (Virgil. II Aeneid.)] A prudent prince therefore, when he wills to subject the enemy's malice to servitude, as necessity requires, applies his hand now to guile, now to valour; so that if the enemy resist guile, he may fall pressed by the hammer of valour, and if the sun has not scorched him by day, he may not escape the fraudulence of the night. In that fashion a good teacher, coming upon us as we grow torpid, like a bird, taking counsel for our salvation, importunate to our will, unpleasant to our manners, closes with us that are heavy with sleep and shakes off from us an execrable torpor; and now that we are watchful, he provokes us to fly, as an eagle its young. But with what confidence or efficacy [0385B] can he undertake or fulfil this, save because he first loves to hold also the things which he preaches are to be held, and embraces with no desire the darkness of the present night, but, flying across like Sanir, like Hermon, execrates the things which he beholds below? For he invites us to doctrine as effectually as confidently who commends by his manners the discipline which he preaches by word, who neglects not himself while setting medicine before others, but execrates and shuns as bilge-water whatsoever savours of the world. « The things that were gains to me, he says, these I count as dung [n: (Philip. 3)]. » But Hermon is said to be interpreted not only *execration,* but also *anathema*; and as to what is added, *his,* that is, the anathema of an anathema, so that a teacher is then deservedly called *his anathema,* that is, the separation of separation, when he himself also is separated with all diligence [0385C] from that from which he teaches men to be separated. « I consented not, says Paul, to flesh and blood [n: (Galat. I)]. Paul therefore is his anathema, that is, the anathema of an anathema, the separation of separation: separating from himself what he strives to separate from others, or separating from the rest what he first took pains to separate from himself. And a wondrous diadem of this Virgin is marvellously woven, in which a watching tooth, a night bird, the anathema of an anathema is set; although, if any one will more diligently search out the sequence of the words, the Virgin is not expressly said to be crowned from these mountains. For it is not said: Thou shalt be crowned from Amana, from Sanir, from Hermon, but *Thou shalt be crowned from the head of Amana, from the top of Sanir and Hermon.* The head, as is known to all, has the primacy over the remaining members and over the whole body, [0385D] but the top is called the summit of the head itself; and the head is not contained in the top, but the top in the head, since the head is not held to be a part of the top, but the top the upper part of the head. By the head therefore is not unfittingly figured the order of prelates, whom the prophet names chief men, heads of the peoples; but by the top the apostolic choir seems to be designated, which in the order of prelates is agreed to hold the primacy by a certain excellence. Or perchance the apostolic order itself may be named the head; *222* but the top is Peter, who is agreed to be proclaimed first and chief, who, being appointed key-bearer of heaven as among the apostles so also above the apostles, John so remaining, followed Christ in a special manner. These apostles too are figuratively the couches of lions in which kings lay themselves down; and the Lofty [0386A] princes of the regions, their fierceness being laid aside wherewith they are wont to terrify all their inferiors, bow themselves to these men and refuse not to lie beneath their merits. For when an emperor, laying aside the diadem wherewith he shines, forgets his sceptre, indulges not his royal dignity, and, humbling himself, obeys Peter and acquiesces in Paul's admonitions: what is he but a lion stretched out resting in the apostolic chamber? These same are none the less mountains Lofty in merits, solid in holiness, who are pre-eminent not by earthly height but by spiritual dignity, to whom he lifts his eyes whosoever desires to be adorned with a luminous face, who understands himself to be a leopard, varied and spotted in his skin. Who under the burden of manifold vices, not secure in his own virtue. and not trusting in victory, about to fight in the valley or in the field against the spiritual things of wickedness: passing over to [0386B] their high places, he seeks that help and doctrine may come to him, and, lest he perish, he lays hold of discipline by their learned mastership. « I have lifted up, he says, my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me [n: (Psal. CXX)]. » Thus the apostles are rightly declared to be both the couches of lions and the mountains of leopards, whom both kings and governors, and they that are held by the various multitude of vices, hear; and, having heard them, they obey by the grace of the divine gift; and, their beastly ferocity being laid aside, they follow an ordered rule of living. But when the Bridegroom orders and disposes those ordainers themselves as living stones, they being duly disposed, he encompasses the queen Virgin and crowns her; and to her honour he renders them worthier in merits, that in the choir of just men they may by a special excellence become nearer to the Bride herself. And [0386C] because he is found not to bestow this more fully at once, he bestows on her whom he loves a promissory hope, that, the promise being made, the Virgin may now be glad in the presence of hope, and, what is more truly the case, may await with sure confidence what is to come. *Thou shalt be crowned,* he says. But by what merit the Virgin is worthy to obtain the presence of hope, the Bridegroom seems to call to mind by his own grace, that it may be made known to all that a perfect reward is not conferred on any one whose merit is not found worthily to go before it.



## CHAPTER XXI.

*Thou hast wounded my heart, my sister, my spouse, thou hast wounded my heart with one of thine eyes, and with one hair of thy neck.* Enemies are wont to be frighted off by enemies through the fear of wounds, and whoever perchance hath inflicted a wound is wont to earn the greater hatred [0386D]; and as much as he rejoiceth who hath understood himself to prevail unto hurting and unto the inflicting of wounds, so much, nay more, doth he grieve who hath been compelled to endure it. But here the Virgin woundeth, and the wounded one repayeth not hatred; she as it were prevaileth, he stretcheth not out his hands unto injuries; she, mistress of the victory, groweth merry of face and clappeth her hand, he is as it were pricked, and being pricked complaineth not, but applaudeth. For the hand taught unto battle, and the arrow of one inflicting a strong wound, is not anger, is not loss, is not an injury to him that beareth it; but the wounds of one so loving are judged more welcome and better than the kisses of a deceitful man and the frauds of one wickedly kissing [n: (Prov. XXVII)]. For the Bridegroom loveth to be wounded strongly, yet by love, to be transfixed not by a sword, but by the stronger affection of them that love him; out of the depth of which wound floweth [0387A] grace, love breatheth more sweetly, and with not blood but sweetness poured forth he loveth the more livingly, and expireth not. And rightly doth he declare that not his head, not his foot, not anything of the like is wounded — a thing which, being sometimes wounded, we see a man yet reserved unto life — but he nameth the heart itself, which, wounded even but a little, admitteth not the physician's hand, but wanting alike both space and remedy, straightway sendeth forth the vital breath. When therefore he asserteth, as it were, that his heart is made weak by the Bride's wound, and by the repeated word would have the certainty of that same wound confirmed, he intimateth that such a wound is to be understood as not pestilent, not mortal, because the heart also is not corporeal nor liable to death, but vital. But because the heart of the body is the seat of the soul, the place of life, the dwelling of hatred or of love, in naming the heart he would have understood the secret [0387B] place of a more gracious affection, wherein he receiveth and accepteth her who hath deserved to come thither specially, and by a singular merit to enter the sanctuary of grace. And this entrance he expressed by the name of a wound — not bloody, violent not by fury but by love, not by anger but by good will — because thither pierceth not the man drowsy with a degenerate sloth, but he that is clean of heart, keen of mind, violent with an unremitted constancy. Further, he twisteth no effectual violence against this sanctuary who with a foot *223* less upright turneth himself back to the love of things temporal; but rather he who with a prevailing effort studieth to forget all things that pass away, and cleaving to God alone, loveth to obtain the eternal alone. Whence also in this place he nameth her at once spouse and sister, that by these names he may signify the firmer affection of a common good will; because both to a spouse [0387C] that which is the spouse's is not denied by the right of matrimony, and the divine law requireth that a sister be held partner and sharer with her brother of the paternal inheritance. Now the Virgin is Christ's sister, and Christ equally the Virgin's brother, whose kindred upon earth is one, and in heaven one Father is said to be theirs; who, though he grant not one portion for all — not according to sex, but according to merits — yet distributing justly, as he disinheriteth not the son, so neither the daughter. Of which Father the Virgin, as she is daughter, so also heir, is not undeservedly called Christ's sister and coheir; whose more gracious affection, a love both sisterly and spousal, woundeth her brother and spouse, not with the point of a dart, but of a spiritual eye.

## CHAPTER XXII.

[0387D] *With one of thine eyes.* By this saying he intimateth that the Virgin is luminous with two eyes, but with one of them more amply and more sweetly gracious; and approving the one of them, he evidently in nowise reprehendeth the other, and not accusing the other, he esteemeth that one the more excellently. The one is perchance that eye to which it is given to behold things visible — the world indeed, and all that is agreed to be contained within the world's compass — which marketh and understandeth that those things which the order of things or nature unfoldeth together, or one after another, are to pass away by a movable change or by a changeable motion. Nay, it considereth that whatsoever is founded hasteneth naturally unto some passing away or other, and that, as in bodies, so also in spirits, nothing standeth firm to itself, save that the mighty author of things and lord of the creature hath already established certain angels [0388A] by the benefit of his own will, not of nature. But the first and chief is that spiritual eye which, removing itself far from the beholding of the temporal handiwork, and transcending the angels and utterly every creature, lifteth itself up to see the face or the nature of the Creator. Which eye, because knowing not the world it laudably fainteth unto the salvation of God, and is not troubled about many things, but coveteth that one thing necessary, is rightly called one; that is, not manifold by the love of manifold things, but loving God alone uniquely, and, beholding him alone, uniform. That eye which poureth not itself forth abroad unto the living of many things, but with a gathered gaze poureth itself into Christ's secret chamber, woundeth his heart, while it hideth itself there, sharper than a sword, where Christ hideth no eye save the one and simple. Not only [0388B] in the eye, but also in the hair, doth the Bridegroom assert himself to be wounded; who, repeating the word, plainly showeth that the wound itself is repeated, because neither was it enough for the Virgin to have driven in one dart, as it were, nor again enough for the Bridegroom to have told of one, the second being passed over in silence. The Bridegroom therefore is wounded in the Virgin's eye; he is wounded also, as he asserteth, in her hair, in that the multiplicity of hairs, loving comeliness and patient of discipline, is not snatched away by the wind, is not scattered through the empty things of a hurtful liberty, but is gathered in season, and is as it were brought back to the rule of unity itself. No woman, as I judge, hath been found in all the ages past who, her hairs being cut away and one left, was singularly content therewith, nor who could so worthily be commended for the merit of one hair, save when a plurality bound up is restrained into one by the mastery of a rule. So the Virgin also, rejoicing [0388C] to be adorned with many hairs, that is, with virtues, lest that very multiplicity be driven to be fanned by the breeze of vanity, gathereth them all together and bindeth them by a certain unity, and by a wondrous mastery bringeth them under one charity. For whatsoever is acquired by a multitude or abundance of merits, if it be not bound with the bond of love, lacketh the glory of rewards; nor doth worthy praise approve whatsoever is found manifold in merits, if it be not united after the manner of hairs by the fillet of charity. Well did Paul esteem of it [n: (I Cor. XIII)], as was fitting, who, wishing to commend it, named it the bond of perfection; because although an innumerable gathering of the remaining virtues be made, not being bound with this bond it remaineth utterly imperfect. But being bound, it fortifieth the Virgin's faith and adorneth it, [0388D] and like a hair it rather adorneth the neck than loadeth it; and with such an ornament, with such a work doth faith glory — glorying worthily indeed, when through love it worketh that which the divine law commandeth. For us whom a heavy and, as it were, bodily mass removeth and disjoineth from the head, faith, like a neck, knitteth on to Christ and joineth us; without which it is impossible that even the virgin herself should please God, and by the intervention whereof Elisabeth would declare her blessed. « And blessed, saith she, art thou that hast believed, because those things shall be accomplished that were spoken to thee by the Lord [n: (Luc. I)]. » And the Apostle: « That Christ, he saith, may dwell by faith in your hearts [n: (Ephes. III)]. » In the hair of this neck, which is united by the aforesaid bond of love, and by whose not burden but honour the Virgin's faith is distinguished, the Bridegroom with a glad dancing maketh manifest his heart [0389A] wounded, intimating that the Virgin's robust love powerfully affecteth his tender affection and troubleth it not. In praise of whom he addeth: *How beautiful,* etc. *224*



## CHAPTER XXIII.

*How beautiful are thy breasts, my sister, my spouse: thy paps more beautiful than wine, and the odour of thine ointments above all spices.* He calleth breasts of the Virgin those wherewith she instructeth little ones that they may grow great, and cherisheth the somewhat grown, that in the process of time they may come to their youth; which also he declareth beautiful, that they grow not vile to the Jews that glory in the letter of the law, but may shine forth the more graciously both to them and to the rest of the hearers. And these, whether they be first named breasts, or afterward paps, being compared with the wine of the law, are declared [0389B] to be of a greater beauty; whilst the austerity of that wine maketh the Jews as it were drunken and senseless, but the sweetness of these maketh us pleasing to God and of one accord. But because you know that the Virgin's paps were set down not far above, and there expounded, according as God granted, I forbear to make a longer delay in expounding them anew, referring the diligent hearer to the things already said. Yet because here beauty is declared to be not in the paps only, but in the breasts also, whereof there, or anywhere above, no mention is made, he seemeth more subtly to intimate somewhat perhaps new, whereto I have not applied hand or study by expounding it more diligently. The breasts, as is said, send not forth milk to little ones, but rather promise themselves about to send it forth when the time shall be, lying hid meanwhile under the shadow of an unripe season, not yet with a fitting [0389C] fruit, but rather swelling with the hope of what is to come. For so long as the Virgin marketh us untaught, hardened, and — our faults so requiring — not yet born unto the living life, she keepeth within the breasts the benefit of doctrine, and bringeth it not forth, presuming not to nourish those whom a fitting birth leadeth not out unto life. For she knoweth that it belongeth to Christ to give life to us that were long since dead, to make us new out of the darkness of the womb unto the grace of the light; but to those already born it is granted to her to impart the benefit itself, and to pour out the paps more largely upon them as now capable. If, saith she, thou wouldest give thine elect to be born unto that grace of light which I greatly desire, that, thou giving life, they might be fed with any benefit whatsoever, my breasts would come to the abundance of paps, and, living in the spirit, would the more effectually nourish them with a worthy milk. [0389D] To them indeed would I little by little unfold somewhat of thy conception or thy birth, and would reveal the secret mystery to a hearing ear; and that which with an unbelieving mind neither the Gentiles nor the Jews receive, John the son of Zebedee, sucking my paps, would drink in. Such breasts and paps doth the Bridegroom praise in the Virgin mother; and that he may close their praises with a due and equally mystical end, he setteth himself to commend not the nourishment of milk, not its rivulets or streams, but the greatest odour and the ointments preferred before all spices. *And the odour,* saith he, *of thine ointments above all spices.* Out of the aforesaid paps, wherewith the Virgin, marvellous in her childbearing, is distinguished, there is found to flow not a woman's milk, but a plenty of ointments; concerning which, if the whole past succession of the perfumers be convened, all their confection [0390A] is forestalled, not in time, but by a wondrous odour. For whatsoever the subtlety of the ancients brought forth from the beginning, whatsoever the curiosity of the heathen apprehended concerning the world so wondrously founded; whatsoever the sages, or, after Pythagoras, the philosophers, compounded by a seducing subtlety, wherewith, as with a corrupting spice, the masters infected their disciples — all this doth the preaching and the doctrine of the Virgin far surpass, wherein truth hath the sovereignty and the discipline of living prevaileth. Whatsoever also the patriarchs and prophets, relying on the gift of a foreseeing understanding, wove in obscurities of words or in mysterial sacraments; whatsoever the fathers of old perceived beforehand with a prophetic nostril, who agreed to announce with a watchful heralding the coming of the true light — the Virgin, the queen of virgins, hath surpassed by a special [0390B] advance, who brought forth in a virginal womb the Man that is the salvation of men. Whose childbearing and conception, a novelty compounded, a new confection, was first in the virginal bridal chamber an effectual health, a sound re-reading; and afterwards it so cometh forth to us by the sure mastery of the Virgin, that the very things she bestoweth transcend whatsoever went before by way of promise. For none of them that went before so expressed the truth to come as did the holy Virgin, to whom the divine goodness granted this: that beyond what could be uttered by man or by angel she herself should know the mystery of the incarnate Word more expressly and more sensibly. Whose knowing, and the sweet remembrance of that knowing, is so wondrous a confection and so great an abolishing of the ancient hurt, that the Virgin, anointed therewith as with spices or ointments, knoweth no more the wound of the fault which the malice of Eve or [0390C] of the serpent brought in. Which ointments of the Virgin, wherewith she deserved to be medicinally anointed, being shut up under a certain seal cannot be fully set forth by our discourses, because the light of the ointments so deigned to arise in the Virgin that, such as it is, it cannot so much as be perceived by another man. But the odour, or the report, of the ointments breatheth upon us sweetly and healthfully, by the sweetness whereof our languishing spirit doth now breathe again; and at that little which the Virgin spake out of her sure fulness, the odour being as it were drawn in at the nostrils, our spirit hath now revived. Rightly therefore doth he set not the ointments *225* of the Virgin — which she setteth not before us that are far inferior — but rather, what is less, the odour of the ointments before all spices; because with the benefit which was given to the apostles [0390D] through the Virgin to be smelled, no knowledge of them of old, no spices can be compared. Not without cause, when Christ was returned to the Father whence he had come, and, the apostles being left behind, the Spirit was not yet granted in tongues of fire, do the apostles judge it worthy to persevere with one accord in prayer with Mary the mother of Jesus, that what they had drawn from her they might affirm both the more constantly and thereby the more surely. For upon whom the sun shone again with a more liberal plenty of understanding, upon them there so flowed in from the Virgin herself a honey-flowing odour that, if it be compared with any sense or hearing of them of old, it deserveth beyond doubt to be borne above it in sweet delight. Whereof it is added: *A honeycomb,* etc.



## CHAPTER XXIV.

*Thy lips, O Spouse, are a dropping honeycomb, honey and milk are under [0391A] thy tongue; and the odour of thy garments as the odour of frankincense.* Well ought the Virgin's lips to be named a honeycomb, because the Virgin herself is also said to be figured under the name of the bee, which by a natural privilege is fed upon flowers, liveth upon dew, and, knowing not the marriage bed, marvellously gathereth up her offspring with her mouth; she is made fruitful with a brood without groaning or grief, and, chaste in a virginal bosom, becometh a mother not by wantonness but by love. Strong in art, skilful in wit, she groweth not slothful in her care, and with study wondrous enough maketh her prudence known, while, framing for herself a honeycomb, she setteth cells distinct in order, and within their narrow spaces layeth up honey with a busy mouth. To this bee the Virgin is not unfittingly reckoned like, who delighteth to be fed spiritually upon the flowering comeliness of virtues, who liveth in the spirit, by grace divine from above as by dew, and, knowing not man, conceiveth [0391B] and beareth a son without travail. Who, heaping up spiritual riches with a busy study, and conferring and keeping in her heart words big with meaning, filleth the secret place of her conscience with a sweetness so pleasant that inwardly she may be called honeyed, after the manner of a honeycomb. But this sweetness, which she herself tasteth more perfectly and more fully, she straiteneth not by the disease of envy, not by the key of avarice; but what the divine Spirit willed to instil into her from above of dew and of sweetness, she, loosing her lips, suffereth to drop down upon us that stand by. For the Virgin, marking what is fitting for us to hear first and what afterward, doth not put forth at once all the things she judgeth worthy to be covered; nor, like a vessel turned upside down, doth she straightway pour out whatsoever she containeth, but bedeweth us, that are less fit for all things, with a thin dropping. Not so did the Old [0391C] Testament, the figured speech of the prophets, the enigmas of the ancients, the obscure surface of the Scriptures; not so, I say did they deserve to be or even to be called a dropping honeycomb, which, though they were a honeycomb, were kept shut up under a seal. For we may call the obscurity of them of old a honeycomb, which held honey within, but knew not how to drop it, because it in no wise brought the mystic senses, the inward sweetnesses, and its profits home to our darkened understandings. That honeycomb therefore, then pressed down by a certain weight of its own, lay long unpressed by the hand of them that built; nor did there come one who, pitying us, might lift it up, and, being lifted, might with a welcome hand strain it into the mouth of the hungry. But the Virgin, filled not so much with honey as with [0391D] the sweetness of mind, rich not in money but in spiritual documents, poured not out, as from an open vessel, in a sudden rush, that which she had laid up in the comb, sweeter than honey and more delightsome than all wine; but, tempering the opening of her lips by the door of enclosure, she chose rather to bring forth so much as the very capacity of her hearers was able to bear. Less therefore did her lips drop while Christ yet lived as man among men, but more amply when, death being triumphed over, he now lived again in a greater glory; because both a blindness poured over them then pressed hard upon the stubborn Jews, and now a greater knowledge is poured into the apostles by the gift of the Spirit. The Virgin's lips therefore are dropping like a honeycomb, which are not barred with a bolt, nor is a nail driven into them; but, one part of the mouth being closed, the other part is open, and rendereth uncovered to the hearers such things as suit [0392A] the time. For she doth not, like a wordy woman, straightway babble whatsoever hath come into her mouth, but moderateth the hidden things of secrets with a discreet silence, judging it worthy that certain things be more warily held back under the veil of the tongue, which, when the time presseth, she then committeth to her lips to be dropped forth. Therefore perhaps is she declared to have honey and milk under her tongue, in whose inner chamber a twofold knowledge is contained: the one which is seen to be expedient for little ones and sucklings; the other to suit them that are now advanced and grown greater. For little ones are of necessity nourished with milk, but the somewhat grown are brought forward to the eating of honey; those protesting Christ to be a man truly born of the Virgin, these venerating the same as God born of God before the ages. Milk coming forth from flesh [0392B] may be called Christ's humanity; honey coming from flower or from dew is his true divinity; the knowledge whereof the Virgin keepeth in secret under her tongue, nor doth she scatter it abroad everywhere, or at once, with an indiscreet speech. But whereas Christ, God and man, therefore *226* showeth himself first as man, that, the visible being known, the heart of the knower may ascend to the invisible, what meaneth it that he saith there is not milk and honey, but honey and milk under the Virgin's tongue — she who teacheth him to be first man and afterward God? To none is it doubtful that in Christ the Godhead goeth first in dignity, and therefore he judgeth it worthy that in speech his humanity should not go before; but that, if a speech be framed of both alike, whether open or covered with mystery, that which excelleth [0392C] in dignity be set first in the order of speaking also. Or rather, wishing to show forth the Virgin's twofold knowledge, which she willed to hide the longer in secret under her tongue, he signally expresseth which of them was not only the worthier but also the earlier, mention being made mystically of honey first and of milk after. For the angel first announced that God was present to the Virgin, and afterward declared that, he being present, she should conceive a son, that in him whom the Virgin knew to be present she might now more firmly trust, and, having already received the greater, might not mistrust concerning the lesser gift. « Hail, saith he, the angel, full of grace, the Lord is with thee [n: (Luc. I)]. » And he addeth of the other: « Behold thou shalt conceive and bring forth a son [n: (ibid.)]. » The Lord teacheth the Virgin by the angel that he is present, and poureth in a knowledge growing sweet [0392D] more pleasantly than honey; and, the knowledge or the honeyed savour which he sendeth first being tasted, he promiseth by the same messenger the conception, which is as it were milk. For she, believing enough, could not be forewarned of the conception, if she rejoiced not to be more surely taught of the divine presence, unless she knew and felt that the Holy Spirit was coming upon her from above, by whose shadow whatsoever she is said to bring forth is made holy. But this knowledge of God's presence and of the Son's conception lieth long under her tongue in the Virgin's own understanding; of which benefit, nevertheless, her virginal discretion doth not wholly deprive us, nor doth she straightway render the stored fountain open, but draweth it forth and deriveth it drop by drop. Whose so great discretion, whose discreet working, do as it were clothe her and commend her, if yet there be any who now duly weigh her merits; [0393A] who may foresee how she chooseth not so much as to mutter to the obscure and the negligent, but loveth to pour forth by dropping to the diligent, with hands not prodigal. By garments, as is known, our nakedness is covered; by the glory of garments a virginal nobility is distinguished; nor perchance doth she please the Bridegroom save such as is so clothed with fine linen and purple that not only she fear not the cold, but appear also comely in her adorning, being found decked with double garments. Although in the present place he hath not described the quality of the garments, nor expressed how to define the quantity of their very number, reserving this for that woman whom, as hath elsewhere been said, who findeth, whose price is from afar, and cometh hither from the uttermost bounds. Which woman may doubtless be called any soul that, careful for her own, is found so given to business [0393B] that, guarding beforehand against heat or cold and a sudden onset, putting out her hand to strong things, she laboureth as though she sat at the loom. But here there is in hand not any soul whatsoever, fearful with a general want, but a certain soul of special merit or excellence; whose garments do not now cover a shame, do not now shut out the cold, but show her festal in the Bridegroom's sight by their ornaments. But because how solemn, how festal she appeared in the Bridegroom's eyes the oppressing blindness of our mind suffereth us not to see, here he hath not expressed to us the number of the garments, nor their comeliness, but, lest he be altogether silent, he maketh a passage to the odour. For in that which the Virgin either inwardly feeleth of Christ within herself, or hath now consented to drop forth — how busy she hath been, rejoicing like a bee in her honey, [0393C] or how studious of a discreet governance, like a dropping honeycomb — all this pleaseth him the more, to whose eyes alone the whole lieth open, while to us the whole is brought near as the odour of frankincense with coals. For when the virginal frankincense plungeth itself into the divine fire, it inclineth wholly, in a manner unspeakable, unto a salutary consuming: yet by the command of the stronger it is not damnably consumed, but by the merit of love and of comeliness is delightfully taken up. But how much it burneth, or how much it pleaseth by that burning, we perceive not, but scarce draw in even a thin odour, as men set far off; because, the frankincense being melted, the smoke stretcheth to the Bridegroom's breadth, while the odour or report extendeth itself by breadth unto us. Those virtues therefore wherewith the noble Virgin is honoured, and by whose noble honour she is [0393D] presented to the divine sight, are certain garments, not needful for the covering of nakedness, but suitable for a comeliness to be put forward more confidently. Which comeliness is put forward and offered to the divine sight after the manner of frankincense, conspicuous not in gold, not in garments, but in manners that shall please; whose welcome sweetness so seemeth to please the Lord that it toucheth us also with its odour, while his good will hath mercy upon us. For she loveth to wander abroad to nothing else, but rather to be straitened within these two by a rampart of fortitude: to wit, that she may show herself to her bridegroom more fully commendable in comeliness, and, dropping more thinly, may fill us with her odour. Whence it is added. *A garden,* etc.



## CHAPTER XXV.

*A garden enclosed, my sister, my spouse, a garden enclosed, [0394A] a fountain sealed up.* Because in the first garden the serpent supplanted the first woman, God the Son of God then planted for himself another garden *227*, when he filled the blessed Virgin, beyond the manner allotted to other women, with his grace, with a great kind not of herbs but of virtues. For in that garden the woman's simplicity was circumvented, the man tasted the forbidden thing, and, the taste being had, nakedness was found; death came upon them that were to live for ever, by the desert of the transgression, and the curse of mortality came upon them and upon their posterity alike. But this garden, containing not shrubs, herbs, flowers, woods of thick foliage, transitory fruits and odours, hath certain other things worthy either to be compared with such, or, that I may speak more truly, to be set above all transitory things. For it hath that which a sound and wise taste [0394B] judgeth fruitful, that which the smell by a right judgment judgeth precious, that which the inward sight, its darkness being wiped away, judgeth gracious, that which by a wondrous fulness is so plentiful as to wipe away all want. For to this garden the tree of life is set in with fixed roots, whereof he that shall have eaten (as they that have made trial have found out) is not hurt by a grievous death, but liveth a life happier than can be told, and, having been able to obtain it, hath not ceased to live further. It hath also a marvellous frankincense, or a commendable spice, or an ointment, which is found not in Arabia but in a land denied to them that die; whose odour he that shall have drawn in shall not know the serpent's stenches, nor, drowsiness prevailing, shall he feel sudden bitings. It hath none the less that welcome flower of the rose or of the violet, or even of the lily, or if there be any in flowers accounted more welcome to the sight, [0394C] which he that shall have duly marked, and shall have bent himself upon it with a keen-sighted eye, shall pass over whatever sad thing the night murmureth with a joy not transitory but tenacious. For there is in the garden a tree of life, an ointment poured out, a comely flower, the very Bridegroom of the Virgin, fair in form above the sons of men, at whose presence no base want, no needy baseness besetteth him, but in him dwelleth bodily the fulness of the Godhead [n: (Coloss. II)]. For it is certain that God is in Christ, and Christ in the Virgin, not shadowily but truly; and therefore that this very garden is full of sufficient goods, which he that planted it willed with a prudent counsel so to be enclosed, that he who seeth and envieth might grieve to be shut out. And in very truth, as it is not at all barred to the faithful and to the friend, [0394D] so, being walled about with strength, it is closed to the enemy: it letteth in no Jew, no Gentile, none empty of faith, and whom it marketh as worthy of hatred it sendeth far off with a strong repulse. In it therefore, not as in the ancient garden, doth the serpent craftily creep; he poisoneth not its fruit, he defileth not its odour, he plucketh not its little flowers; a depraved softness hungereth not, hunger proceedeth not into effect, the woman obeyeth not the serpent, nor the man the woman. And yet no weariness of a desert or of a solitude hurteth it, no grief goadeth it, while its own author walketh therein festally: at whose glad countenance the things in the garden bear fruit, the kinds of things flourish, and the manifoldness of kinds smileth upon him that is fair in form above men. For while he walketh in whose countenance is comeliness, and grace is poured abroad in whose lips, the Virgin's garden answereth with a glad [0395A] spirit, with a face unconfounded: pleasing him that walketh there, all baseness being so shut out that within nothing remaineth but beauty, poured round about with a strong defence. But what meaneth it that to say "a garden enclosed" once is not enough for the bridegroom, but he doubleth this very thing with the same names repeated — unless it be, as I remember to have been said already, that this is the force of love's intemperance, that by a speech frequently repeated it may express the greatness of a more gracious affection? Or perhaps he willed for this cause to call the garden twice enclosed, that he might show a twofold evil so shut out by the same virgin, that neither doth the spirit stand by the tender flesh with a nerveless softness, nor doth the flesh stubbornly resist the stronger spirit. For we, although with the mind we serve the law of God by grace, are nevertheless in the flesh, through the law engrafted in us, somewhat [0395B] guilty; and when we seem to ourselves circumspect with a watching spirit, we are found, the flesh being loosed in sleep, not slightly imperfect. Or therefore did this garden deserve to be called twice enclosed, because the Virgin is so found to embrace a twofold study that in neither doth she show herself at all reprehensible, but with a circumspect mind defendeth herself from the onset of enemies of every sort. For so, when necessity required, she betook herself to active business, that, hands being given to this, she might not withdraw them from the spiritual; and again she so fixed a spiritual eye upon contemplation that she shrank not from the active, which God cursed unto punishment by the desert of sin. Into an excess of contemplating she hung herself up by a honeyed sweetness; to the gathering in of her neighbour she stooped down with a milky affection; on either side, or rather round about, so fortified that she gave place to none, though sought after by many [0395C] that assailed her. But because a garden hath need of watering lest it wither, and that it may rather abound with fitting plantings and grow into a wood, this garden is said not so much to be watered by a fountain as, by a more express significance, to be called a fountain. Now a fountain is named from pouring forth, as some assert, in that it is seen to pour forth living water out of hidden places, and, bubbling up with a perennial vein, to live by an abundance not outward but inward — not by torrents, like a lake, not by rains of water, like a cistern [n: (Prov. V)]. A fountain therefore ought this Virgin also fittingly enough to be called, whose understanding withereth not, whose sense hath no parching heat, but by the grace of an inward [sic: *muueris*] she is taught unspeakably and groweth rich, and with a wondrous perpetuity, beyond what can be told, groweth glad.
