Who indeed [0395D] hideth long, as under a seal, the mystery revealed to her, and revealeth not her living abundance to them that are less capable: the manner of her fruitfulness, the form of her nuptials, the excellence of her celibacy she holdeth shut up *228* in her knowledge, like a fountain sealed. For he that assigned to her such a knowledge, so singular a conscience, left her not as a vessel without a lid, but sealed her, lest they that hear and receive not, being unworthy, be troubled with a scandal, and hasten rather to stones than venerate the mystery. And so the nuptial bed of the virgin, the inner recesses of secrets, the fountain of leaping water, the wondrous knowledge of things divine, the very author of the gift shutteth with a bar, sealeth to himself with the key of David, and unsealeth it not to the blaspheming, to the darkened, to him that worthily lacketh the price. Without standeth the crowd of the people, the undiscerning multitude maketh its noise, [0396A] and, the seal not being unloosed, it perceiveth not so secret a fountain: the subtlety of the philosophers, the princes of the world are fasting; barking, they receive not; importunate, they profit nothing. Much plenty indeed, much subtlety is in the fountain; the wave leapeth, the vein coming forth from the inner parts maketh its leaping perpetual; but the key set upon it seemeth so to cover it from all that stand without, that to the unbelieving it deigneth to open nothing at all, but to the faithful somewhat little. Yet that very thing which is little so aboundeth for us, in respect of the abundance that remaineth, so surpasseth our littleness, that none but a gathered mind, none but an undivided love can take it in — because a paradise of this sort admitteth not the envious serpent. Whence it is added: *Thy emissions,* etc.



## CHAPTER XXVI.

[0396B] *Thy emissions are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of apples.* The things which this enclosed garden, or this fountain fortified with a seal, sendeth forth — which letteth in none, or very few, to the secrets of its fulness — are as it were a certain paradise or delight of pomegranates, within of a snowy colour, but without of a red. For if a garden be planted with a prudent hand or counsel, and moistened at fitting seasons with the watering of living water, what shall be said to be more fitly brought forth than that which either hunger seeketh for the eating, or which sickness judgeth healthful and effectual for the healing? The emissions therefore of the virgin, who is figured under the name of a garden or of a fountain, he that commendeth them beareth witness to be like a paradise: nay, speaking more expressly, he saith they are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of apples, and [0396C] the rest that follow, which it is certain are medicinal. Of old there was a paradise that persuaded to a serpentine depravity, that conceived a new fraud, that slew holiness, wherein the strong man yielded to the soft counsel of the woman, and the forbidden taste of the apple brought in to them that made trial of it the fruit of death. But this paradise, which is sent forth out of the garden or the fountain of the virgin, maketh recompense more mightily for the things that were in the other more curiously lost, consisting of pomegranates, which within are of a snowy and without of a red colour, and of other apples, which are of a most healthful savour to them that eat. The red colour in the pomegranates, which presenteth itself outwardly, representeth the love of suffering and the bearing of it, which he may behold in the Virgin's life and manners who by her mastery [0396D] willeth to be taught to suffer in like sort. The whiteness within is the flower of conscience, a mind secure, which, when the world rageth without or a passion about to rage threateneth, embraceth purity and forsaketh not virginal cleanness; it is not troubled by injuries, and being beaten with vexations it faileth not. But the fruits of the other apples which are sent forth together with the pomegranates are her good works, which are not only set forth as welcome to the sight, but are also not slightly fruitful to them that taste, that is, to them that imitate, and precious not by a seducing colour but by a most profitable savour. But because to an eye that gazeth more curiously one or another kind of thing is not welcome enough, he addeth, for the heaping up of praises, many sorts of spices, that emissions so manifold may make us greatly to marvel, and to venerate her as worthy of many praises in fitting ways.



## CHAPTER XXVII.

[0397A]

*Cypress with spikenard, spikenard and saffron, sweet cane and cinnamon, with all the trees of Libanus, myrrh and aloes with all the chief ointments.* Cypresses are slender shrubs which are stretched up to a great height, whose grains are boiled down in oil by the skilled care of physicians; by which manner of boiling a commendable ointment is made, whereby a desirable soothing is rendered to the pains that are anointed therewith. So also the Virgin's virtues, exceeding subtle and straight, are carried up into the height of dignity, not by branches but by merits, whose fruitful acts are boiled in a spiritual oil, when in holy love they are stripped of a hurtful or carnal humour. But spikenard, which is a very small tree, is joined to cypresses of this sort, when the excellence of virtues is pressed down [0397B] by regard of humility; and by how much the more the Virgin is exalted among women with singular titles, by so much the more doth she appear in her own eyes humble and despised. Well therefore are *cypress with spikenard* set first in this catalogue of medicinal things *229*, which after the manner of a paradise are sent forth out of the Virgin's garden; because humility, being joined to them, so commendeth the excellence of virtues that so great a confection safely extendeth itself to our knowledge. Again, *spikenard and saffron.* Out of spikenard alone, as they say, without another spice or mixture, there is made a laudable ointment and a confection that shall profit; and Mary Magdalene willed to anoint the Lord's feet with this ointment, as hath been made sufficiently known by the witness of the gospel lesson. « She took, he saith, a pound of ointment of pistic spikenard, of great price, and Jesus anointed the feet [n: (Joan. XII)]. » [var: Vulg. Jn 12:3 *Maria ergo accepit libram… et unxit pedes Jesu*, the genitive — "anointed the feet **of Jesus**." Migne's nominative makes Jesus the agent of the anointing; the genitive stands correctly five lines later, at 0397C.] Spikenard is the contrition of the heart [0397C] which the humble and devout offer, who by a broken spirit are advanced to so great a grace that they anoint the feet of Jesus, and by a fuller progress come to the head itself, and fill the nostrils of them that stand by, or rather the whole house, with the odour. « The house, saith he, was filled with the odour of the ointment [n: (ibid.)]. » And above in this epithalamium: « My spikenard, saith she, gave forth the odour thereof [n: (Cant. I)]. » To this spikenard, both as tree and as ointment, saffron sitteth by and standeth by, which putteth to flight present fevers and meeteth and withstandeth those that are coming; which upon its surface displayeth a golden grace or colour, signifying charity, which possesseth a higher throne. Which charity doubtless loveth to be at hand to a devout humility, and so to be present to a contrite spirit as an undivided companion, [0397D] that whom she hath known to be pricked and anointed with a more devout affection, him she maketh to love the more, and not to be sundered from him whom he hath loved. For if any feverish bitterness of sadness or of sloth run in between, charity, being near and not enduring that loss be brought in, straightway meeteth it; which, weakening the hurtful things, admonisheth the devout spirit to stand in what it hath begun, lest the malevolent enemy bear off a triumph from one deceived. *Sweet cane,* saith he, *and cinnamon.* Sweet cane, which is of a somewhat red colour, having a hard bark, signifieth the strength of a constancy that will not yield to assailing vexations, which loveth to show so continual a fellowship to the aforesaid virtues that for their sake it refuseth not the loss of blood, nor the torment of martyrdom. Which constancy doubtless seemeth necessarily to be joined to the aforesaid spices, lest weariness hinder [0398A] that which devotion loveth from being consummated; lest, when a violent suddenness breaketh not the good purpose, a longer and outstretched hand wear it away step by step. And because, according to the commandment, the wise man ever remembereth his last ends [n: (Eccles. VII)], straightway cinnamon is at hand, which in colour is made like to ashes; admonishing that in all things whereunto by a fitting advance the wise man deserveth to go forward, he never cease to call to mind who, and whence, and whither he cometh. « Earth thou art, saith he, and unto earth shalt thou go [n: (Gen. III)]. » [var: Vulg. Gen. 3:19 *pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris*, "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return."] And Job: « I do, saith he, penance in embers and ashes [n: (Job. XLII)]. » Lastly, when Abraham hung himself up to speak with God with a prosperous affection and effect, yet in that excellent height he marked himself to be ashes, showing that he so rejoiced in the benefit offered him that, duly remembering what was his own, he seemed as it were [0398B] to dare nothing out of his own. « I will speak, saith he, to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes [n: (Gen. XVIII)]. » These are the aromatic shrubs that avail unto a healthful medicine, more fit for the cultivating of manners, suited to a truthful discipline, together with very many others which in aspect and in effect are diverse one from another; and Libanus bringeth them all forth together unto healing. For Christ, whom very many say to be figured under the name of Libanus, willeth the series of his virtues to be derived to us through the Virgin; and that which in many ages past the prophetic promise foretold, the virginal emission hath brought to effect in our hands. *Myrrh,* saith he, *and aloes with all the chief ointments.* » The foregoing virtues being described under an enigma or figure, whereby the love of the inward mind is spiritually instructed in the things to come, [0398C] he seemeth to pass over to the kinds of other graces, which it is certain suit bodies by a medicinal mystery. For that the flesh, upon which a natural law is laid from its conceiving, so that, living more or less, it be necessarily mortal, when it hath shaken off its morning flower by an evening setting, may yet not flow away by rottenness nor by a serpentine worm — myrrh mightily commandeth, and is seen to prevail by its command; and in the presence of this the flesh feareth not to lie subject to natural things. For myrrh is an ointment wherewith dead flesh rejoiceth to be anointed; anointed wherewith, its wholeness marvelleth that it is not dissolved by the law engrafted in it — which flesh, deprived of living vigour, knowing itself now weak, now unarmed, yet by the wondrous safeguard of myrrh knoweth not the worm of the rottenness of old ingrown in it. This same thing doth aloes also work by the power [0398D] of its own strength, whence also with merit enough it is coupled to myrrh in this epithalamium, that of things diverse, whereof the working or the effect is one, a certain companionable friendship or affection may become known. But this hath aloes by a certain right and special privilege, which myrrh hath not prevailed to obtain by the general fellowship: that besides being an unction preservative of dead bodies, it be also a potion purgative of living bowels. Myrrh therefore is the assiduity of fasting, the harshness of abstaining, the restraint of continence, the exercise of labour, the frequency of meditating, the study of learning — which things at the first taste indeed bring forth a wondrous bitterness, but, use working more strongly, are expulsive of carnal rottenness. But [0399A] because this effect prevaileth to the utmost only in dead flesh, it is needful that the sweetness and affection of living be taken away; and that, to the end the affliction sought from without may profit more sufficiently, the present life be taken out of the midst for us who are flesh. For we, though sometimes we be afflicted outwardly by some grievous action, yet live ill, the root being still venomous and the passion still alive; and it is expedient that a prudent physician, the vein being felt and knowledge gained *230* of the inward motions, should make the ill-living humours to be voided by a purgative potion. But this potion is aloes, or rather it is the inmost love of virtue, which begetteth a good hatred of guilt and of a destroying servitude; which, spitting far out from the borders of the heart the base dregs of Pharaoh, rendereth the heart, well purged, unto Christ as the porch of Solomon. Which sort [0399B] of dregs and of the uncleanness of an oppressing lees, and which potion of love and efficacy of an expelling virtue, a certain heathen, not unskilled nor ignorant of the like medicine, well showed — not to the wandering and negligent, but to them that sat in the school of discipline. *They hate,* saith he, *to sin, the good, for the love of virtue.*
Good is love, and none the less good is the virtue of love, which with a perfect hatred condemneth the bilge of a baser uncleanness; and with the besom of a strict judgment it scrapeth away whatsoever it findeth miry, and for the bridegroom at his coming spreadeth a pavement of welcome marble. But after the inward parts are thoroughly cleansed by the love of virtue, as by the efficacy of a potion, from thenceforth and thereafter myrrh and aloes work alike, and will and working pass over for us into an ointment which, against everlasting [0399C] rottenness, giveth a sufficient defence to carnal men, who are such not by vice but by nature [n: (Rom. VIII; Ephes. II)]. For neither would the will without work, languishing in idleness, attain to the obtaining of merit, nor would work without will find glory with God; but the affection rejoiceth to shine forth laudably outwardly through the effect, and the effect to bear evident witness of the affection. Whereas therefore the will, or the love of virtue, is seen to hold the former place, and it is doubtful to none that work followeth the will that goeth before, what meaneth it that, speaking in this epithalamium, he set not aloes first in his speech — which, though not in the ointment, yet cometh first in the potion? For he saith not, aloes and myrrh, but *myrrh and aloes with all the chief ointments,* because [0399D] the labour of work, which we said to be figured by myrrh, as it were leadeth and leadeth forth the love of virtue (which was said to work in the stead of a potion), and presenteth it in public; for not labour through love, but love through labour showeth itself as it were visible; and therefore myrrh is named first, which willeth to be seen first as guide and forerunner, by whose gift love deserveth to be shown forth knowable. « By their fruits, saith he, you shall know them [n: (Matth. VII)]. » Rightly doth Nicodemus in the Gospel, bearing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, a hundred pounds, and compounding this ointment for himself in altogether the same order, will to anoint the flesh of the dead Christ with this mixture, showing that it should not pass to rottenness by the law of mortals. And here doubtless myrrh [0400A] is named first, and aloes afterward, for this reason, that the will is now shown forth by a visible work; and in the eyes of them that rightly believe they came together into one mixture, by which coming together they compounded an ointment profitable for our pains. « For he was offered because it was his own will [n: (Isa. LIII)]; » and « Christ, saith he, died for us [n: (Rom. V)]. » But that Nicodemus is read to have brought a hundred pounds of this mixture intimateth that Christ bestowed his benefit upon us in weight and number; and that what had before been prophesied in transitory words and significations was at last consummated in a certain weight and a perfect number. « It is consummated [n: (Joan. XIX)], » saith he. I am deceived if the Virgin compounded not a mixture of this sort, if by this confection she put not worms and rottenness [0400B] far off; if in the compounding she passed over the weight, or the number, or the very order, and did not rather send forth hither a paradise of an ointment-bearing fulness. And lest perchance this one thing should seem to any insufficient, because a manifold necessity is for the most part not supplied by one benefit, he addeth, *with all the chief ointments,* that the Virgin's opulent emission may be signified, which together with myrrh and aloes giveth us the ointments of the remaining graces. But the first and chief are the ointments of the twin charity, which this enclosed garden bringeth forth out of the storehouse of holiness; and to worthy hearers the Virgin droppeth them down with salutary admonitions and with doctrine, heaping up doctrine by example, by manners, by discipline. And because she deserved above to be called not only a garden enclosed but also a fountain sealed, [0400C] those things being now unfolded which can be more especially assigned to the garden, the Bridegroom deferreth not to pass over consequently in his speech to those things which seem more probably to suit the sealed fountain also.



## CHAPTER XXVIII.

*A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which run with a strong stream from Libanus.* Even as thy emissions are pomegranates, or the rest that follow, which are brought forth out of the garden of delight, fitting either for eating or for healing, so thy emission is not of one garden, but rather a fountain of gardens, whereby the fruit-bearing hearts of very many love to be watered. For whosoever willeth to become a garden, and to set himself before a barren field, who willeth to bring forth a flowering comeliness and a useful fruit, ought the more studiously to betake himself to [0400D] this conspicuous and unmuddied fountain, or not to bring back the reproach of a repulse where grace is perchance offered; for to this end the Virgin's benevolence (which it is agreed that much wisdom bringeth back), willed to offer herself to us that are the weaker as a fountain, lest upon them whom eagerness seemeth to persuade to the hope of drinking, *231* the difficulty of drawing should heap a harder repulse. For we, to whom the sweetness of perceiving, once found, is pleasing, but whom too great a labour of seeking shutteth out as it were from the entrance — her fullness, like unto a fountain, doth not exasperate but rather tempereth itself, and her breadth receiveth them that are already eager but as yet without strength. But because to the greater sort, who burn to be more fully heard, the level shallowness of a fountain seemeth to be the sooner drained, to these same [0401A] the Virgin's wisdom withdraweth itself into a deep mystery, and with labour leadeth them into her fullness. But they, the more they consider that the thing they desire is removed, and hope that in a well a larger abundance of waters is contained, being kindled with desire, gird themselves with a strong urgency, knowing that they reach not deep things save by a bucket. Not content therefore with that which seemeth as it were open and common to the more part, they let down a bucket into the depth of the well by a long rope; and they persist in the work, broken off by no shakings, until they draw back the full bucket by an unbroken rope. Tasting the draught of it, they are astonished at so great a sweetness, and by their own powers they are not strong enough to take it in; and full of its abundance, at the last they do [0401B] not wipe away their dry thirst, but after the manner or with the love of them that have the dropsy, they plunge themselves into the well itself. But when, according to a certain heathen, *Waters take a taint unless they be moved,*
in the bottom of the well they find waters not standing, not corruptible by a degenerate lying-still, not corruptible by the fault of standing, but in a wondrous manner; and finding, they draw living waters, showing forth as much marvellous sweetness as fullness. To these nothing dead, nothing hurtful cometh near; no serpent hisseth in, none woundeth with venomous breath; no branch fallen from above troubleth them, no inflowing mire cometh in; their keeper the Bridegroom granteth not that any turbid thing be within. He who is Libanus, ever white with snows not [0401C] melted — nay rather is the whiteness of the highest light and the mirror of the divine power — poureth forth waters out of himself, and a spiritual affluence of waters, and by a hidden channel filleth the virginal fountain or well. Whose deep pools, though we draw not with a larger abundance, we who come with a narrow vessel indeed and with a desire that cannot contain; yet whosoever is able to weigh with what richness Libanus poureth forth waters, knoweth with what a strong stream their abundance poureth itself into this well. Come together to this fountain of living waters, ye that are set afar off, and loose you from her fetters, ye whom the wisdom of the world holdeth: pour out the philosophic swelling with repeated vomits; drunken with the wine of dragons, repair the ruin of your study by the living draught of water. A good garden, which hath [0401D] obtained the name of a fountain or of a well, marked with many a kind of fruits and of medicinal spices; rich in the watering of a water that breedeth not worms with a stinking stillness, but floweth with a strong stream from Libanus and leapeth up with a living force unto life. Of which garden the bridegroom is held with so great solicitude, with so great care, heaping up its advancements, so perfectly removing the things that would hurt, that he hath not only sealed it up enclosed, lest it should lie open to a thief or a violent robber, but hath also protected it from above, lest it should be touched even for a little by a wicked wind.

## CHAPTER XXIX.

*Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind: blow through my garden, and its spices shall flow.* [var: Vulg. Cant. 4:16 *et fluant aromata illius*, "and let its spices flow" — a jussive subjunctive where Migne prints the future indicative *fluent*] A fair order. First indeed [0402A] he addresseth the north wind and removeth him far off, lest he come hastily before and seize beforehand upon the region: lest he spread himself freely through the fields of the broad air, and pour upon a garden rich in fruits heavy blasts or hail. Thou, saith he, who hast set thee a seat as it were royal toward Arcturus, purposing to bear rule and to subject the world to serve thee, arise, and let this presumption hold thee secure no longer — thee whom I will to depart afar off, and not to rage above the beauty of the garden. Thou didst think to be like unto the Most High, thou that wast called Lucifer only, whereas to the sun, who alone is, there is no giving of light by another; and it is agreed that thy wickedness is gainsaid by the very name thou bearest, for he that hath a like can no longer be called the Most High. *Arise* therefore, and now restrain the swollen bellows of this sitting; driven from thy swollen seat, [0402B] vanish into thin airs; as a thinner dust, scatter thee among thy like; or as an emptier smoke, plunge thee into the eyes of the proud. Among our serious things thy mockeries please not, the jest of them that make sport pleaseth not; in the garden of holiness, lost to thee, there is no place for thee, who didst corrupt Eve, laughing and prevailing in her in paradise: the virgin, or the virgin's garden, shutteth the door against thee, now derided. Arise therefore, thou whom the reckoning woundeth, whom the swelling emptieth the nearer, while according to a lying hope it rageth not within the bounds of this garden: the garden being strongly enclosed, care not now to go about it in vain; give place to a better, whom it is expedient should enter as he cometh. *And come,* saith he, *thou south wind.* That other being removed further off, whose presence, whose neighbourhood is rightly grievous, come [0402C] thou south wind, come most healthful and sweet to the garden, whom the meridian pole and a warmer sun send hither, whose sending admitteth not the cold north wind. Thou therefore who rejoicest not in his hurtful company, nor sufferest him to rejoice in the princedom in the garden of holiness — because, he being set afar off, the Virgin is not yet content with such a benefit, present thee to her with a calm *232* countenance, to supply what she requireth. Out of that hidden seat wherein is nothing of darkness, nothing of foulness, rich in pure light, breathing more sweetly, come, O south wind: breathe and blow, nay rather *blow through*, that is, accomplish it with a gentle breath, that this garden may be adorned and may rejoice in a fixed adorning. It seemeth to me that the south wind holdeth the type of the holy Spirit, whose sweet breath the north wind cannot bear, and when he perceiveth him coming even by a slight scent, [0402D] he shuddereth and hasteneth to give up the primacy he had presumed. For the powerful kindness of the one is so set against the malice of the other, that by its presence it destroyeth whatsoever the other wickedly worketh; and them whom the other holdeth pressed with frost and fixed, and bindeth hard into error, this one looseth, and to them that are loosed granteth to run after the manner of torrents into love. This one visiteth the enclosed garden with a fuller coming, and with a gentler breeze cherisheth and advanceth its divers fruits, that of them may be made spices fitting for medicinal disciplines, which may flow, nay rather flow in, not to the bodies of them that need healing, but to their inward loves. And rightly doth the bridegroom either command or exhort the south wind to come, because as the Father, so also the Son testifieth [0403A] that he sendeth the Spirit, which spirit, although he is believed to be present where he will and when he will, and to profit, yet is sent by him with whom he hath naturally one being. « When the Paraclete shall come, saith he, whom I will send you [n: (Joan. XV)]. » The son therefore sendeth the spirit to the garden or virginal bridal chamber, that he coming may breathe and breathe upon it, and may soothe it with a spiritual breath; and when with a sweet breathing he shall have poured into it the marvellous persuasion of virtues, the garden yielding its spices may flow, and as it were overflow to us for a remedy.



## CHAPTER XXX.

*Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind.* Or, if it please any better, in the words aforesaid the bridegroom himself doth not wholly remove the north wind, but granteth a free choice to him that willeth to arise; because, though he be full of malice, yet he prevaileth not to come unto us unless he be sent, nor to rise up to a wicked work [0403B] unless leave be given and he be permitted. The bridegroom therefore, seeing the garden strong enough with an incomparable enclosing; and that it feareth not horrible threats, the brandished sword, cruel death; that it cannot fail through the troubles of assaults or of onsets, but be proved, and by the merit of the proving be more worthily and more gloriously crowned: turneth himself to him who ever rejoiceth to become a persecutor, and, knowing no end of the matter, dareth to put forth his hands against whatsoever men are just. *Arise,* saith he, *O north wind,* break forth out of the lurking-place of depravity, put forth all thy powers and the malice of thy perverse will: thunder, lighten, make an uproar; bring in whirlwinds, hails and storms, heap up whatsoever thou canst, add new ones to the old. But think not that with unbridled malice thou shalt prevail against the virgin: the south wind cometh, giving the virgin [0403C] to bear evenly whatsoever thou bringest in; blowing through the garden within and making it drunken with a marvellous soothing, that either she may not feel it at all, or at the least may not fail in the torment. Thou north wind, arise and rise up, and sound violently without; thou south wind, breathe within, grant that what he shall have sounded be borne patiently; thou malignant one, vex the house, that the next wall may seem to burn; [0404A] thou benign one, strengthen the bridal chamber, that, it being well secured, no burning be feared. Did not the north wind seem to you to rage the more harshly, when it drove the Jews, near of kin to her, to be mad against Mary, so that by argument they should deny the virgin's integrity of childbearing, and by the law of us all should affirm that her Son, and God's Son, was begotten? Doth he not thunder harshly, when the Jews persecute the same son, when men of another nation are joined to them as partners of their malice, when the kinsmen's stubborn fury and unlovely clamour urgeth on the strangers, and both crucify the guiltless one, those by their voices, these by their nails? It is not easy to say what a buffet, nay rather what a heavy hammer, so great a force of persecutors struck upon the mother; and yet it shook not out of her garden the comeliness of her faith and of her patience, because the south wind [0404B] reigning within enclosed it about with a rampart of fortitude, and shut out from her faith and patience all oppressing force. Thus with divers affection and contrary effect are the south wind and the north wind joined in strife; thus with divers and adverse front are they dashed together after the manner of them that wage war; and against a strong foundation the heavy assaults of the flood are hurled, whence both by a victorious constancy and by the building unhurt they are beaten back. By which conflict, by which pressure the Virgin is not dried up as kindling-wood, but as a fruitful olive is medicinally made fat; out of which sweateth an oil that is more precious than any ointment, and worthy spices flow, comparable neither to gold nor to silver. Not therefore to them alone is the contention of the north wind and the south wind profitable, whose contending purpose abideth so diverse, but the profit conferred reacheth even unto us — a stretching out of the hand, rejoicing to render back [0404C] what it hath taken, not to shut all things up in silence. But since, after the praises of the Virgin which he hath vouchsafed to recount so many, the bridegroom hath willed in this present place to be silent now, I have thought it worthy that our pen also should for a little lay a finger upon its mouth, and that the fourth book of this work should now set upon itself a fitting end.

## BOOK FIVE.

[0403] *233*

## CHAPTER THE FIRST.

[0403D]

*[CAP. V.] Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his apples.* The Virgin, seeing and approving that she hath the likeness of a garden, that she is planted with virtues and floureth with meet merits, and that with a marvellous advancement she burneth for nothing but the bridegroom's face, can no longer keep her desire under silence. For the more carefully he fortifieth her that he may defend her, the more diligently he raiseth up and commendeth her when fortified and defended: so much the more doth she love, so much the more doth she will to see her beloved's face, thinking it but little if she have somewhat, so long as she grieveth that she hath not the rest. Let him, saith she, who with a hand of power, with a word not weak, willed to root his garden, and to water it, when rooted, with living waters; who willed to enclose it and to shut out from it all things that would hurt, that they might not prevail against it, nay that they might not have any right at all in it: let him, I say, come, and let him vouchsafe to look more nearly upon that which is his own, and by a kindly looking to increase and to [0404D] guard his grace. For that the north wind is bidden to arise or is granted to rage, that the south wind on the other side is charged to come with soothing; it shall come to pass, and the garden shall feel it done, and it shall be profitable to her that feeleth it, if the beloved come to show his presence to her that loveth. He being present, the malevolent north wind shall gnash his teeth, and, hurtful though he be, shall not hurt; the south wind shall appear both sweeter and more effectual: the one, by tribulating, shall work patience; patience, trial; trial, a hope that is not confounded; the other shall work the charity which showeth itself poured abroad in our hearts. And what beloved would longer deny his presence or his coming to a garden which he planted, which he watered, to which he even gave the increase: from whose enclosure the besom of judgment cast far off whatsoever was hurtful, and which, shut in with a strong defence, he made specially his own? And whom would it not move, that he is the beloved whom she that loveth entreateth to come, and that it is nothing but his own to which he is invited as Lord, seeing that it becometh a possessor to come to his possessions even unbidden, [0405A] and that love itself is a cry, so that he cannot but call one so beloved? Let the beloved therefore come into the garden — not another's, not into another's right, but into his own — and let him show himself lovely and serene to his own; and holding as welcome whatsoever he shall see in it that is useful and honest, let him pluck it with his hand, nay let him even eat it, unless perchance he shall find the season unripe. My apples, as I judge, show themselves fit for the gathering — nay rather his apples, which put forth no ripeness save by his gift; which do not, as the apples of some men do, please when seen and straightway vanish when touched, but ripen with a savoury odour and a solid taste. Let him coming eat not only the outward face of these apples, comely to the eyes, but rather their ripeness, fruitful to an eager taste — that is, let him be pleased to take them to himself, let him take them out of the midst, [0405B] and let him rejoice to lay them up in his own storehouse. For though it be needful to abide here for the gaining of merit, yet I count it far better to rejoice there in the reward: and therefore I would be, not so much in the field of labour, as in the barn of rest, and would have my husbandman fed and refreshed with his own harvest. The bridegroom heareth the words of the bride, nay rather her desire, and answereth; and he doth not promise, according to the Virgin's prayers, that he will come, or even that he will eat; but, what is far more, he showeth sooner than the saying that he hath already come, and that he hath not with a deaf ear put off the asked-for coming even for a little.



## CHAPTER II.

*I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.* Even as the Lord aforesaid is said, when he sent the angel [0405C] to the Virgin, to have come before him, and the Virgin is said to have found grace with him: so here too, being asked to come, he promiseth not his coming to her that asketh, but confesseth that he hath come and hath done what had seemed to him fitting. Thou, saith he, dost carefully ask that I would come, but I have come already: I have come before the time as it were set by thee and the hope of the gift asked for; and beyond what thou shouldest beg or ask, being well-willing I have hastened to come, and I have visited my garden not now by one that walketh before me, but by mine own presence. For it is not meet that a garden which with mine own hand I set in order when I planted it, which when planted and watered I called forth to a fitting increase, I should give up naked of my presence into the hand of them that deceive, and should weaken the former gifts [0405D] of advancement by later and worse ones. The garden therefore which I made, by grafting in it divers virtues, that same I made my own, by conferring a useful keeping; that which I enclosed and sealed, by forbidding all hurtful things, I cherished and advanced as mine own, by affording it my unbroken presence. For how should I defraud of my solicitude, of my presence, her whom as a sister the one only Father offered me to be loved with a kinsman's affection, her whom as a spouse the mysterial oneness urged me to embrace by a severe *234* and sincere commerce — how, I say, should I defraud her, and should not rather crown good beginnings with a better ending? Of which manner of names, to wit of Sister and of Spouse, because the meaning hath in some sort been set out above, I forbear to go over it again, lest so often repeated it should breed weariness; and the prudent [0406A] reader will by no means cleave perchance to the present things alone, but will more carefully turn back his mind and his eye to the things above. But what he hath wrought in the garden by his condescension he showeth, who had been asked with so great desire to come, lest he should be thought to have done nothing there through sloth and negligence, although he had not yet accomplished all things according to the Virgin's pleasure. *I have gathered,* saith he, *my myrrh with my spices.* Strict chastisement, the strong austerity of abstinence, virginal continence, integrity as well of body as of mind: these with a wondrous anointing keep the virgin's flesh from eternal hurt, and above the right of nature, above the nature of wrath, heap up a mass of merits. Such myrrh the bridegroom coming into his garden hath now gathered, because the mother's continence so perfectly pleased the Son, that when he was incarnate, [0406B] though nature marvelled at an unspeakable begetting, yet the newness of the thing brought in no rot of pride, no little worm, no hurt. For a fruitful integrity, ungranted to all virgins before and after, the bridegroom carried away from the floor as already reaped into the barn, when by his own good pleasure and keeping he willed so to fortify her, that neither the beast of the field nor the bird that is wise for high things could come in unto her. For the pleasure of the flesh, which is wont beastlike to come before fruitfulness, marvelleth to find nothing of its own in the Virgin's conceiving; and marvelleth that in an earthly field a harvest so ripe should grow, and, being taken away as it were by stealth, should suffer nothing of the spoiler. The fowls of the air, which sow nothing honest or profitable to salvation, but for the most part make away with the sowings of others by a devouring greediness: [0406C] indiscreet presumption and empty pride, which are wont to be born of the advancements of the good, and by an inborn depravity rejoice to be fed upon their failings: these grieve that the aforesaid harvest of myrrh is so withdrawn out of the midst, that neither by violence nor by fraud can they be brought in unto it even for a little. The little birds complain that they were drowsy longer than they ought, and were forestalled by the reaper's love and watchful zeal; but that now they have hands watchful and stretched out for the plunder, and are held back by the closure of the barn and by a bar that cannot be unbarred. In such a barn the bridegroom shutteth up his spices also, and, they being sealed with the key of David, he heareth not the voices of them that bark against him, because he snatcheth away the virgin's modesty as it were by a certain reaping, lest in a field exposed to the wild beasts it be hurt [0406D] by an envious whisperer. The enemy man, who for the most part soweth cockle above the wheat, who, not prevailing to hurt the life, at the least stains the good name of the good, he driveth forth from the Virgin's touch with a hand that meeteth him, and banisheth far off the enemy of chastity from the cloister of modesty. For he willeth not that her fame, more fragrant than spices or ointments, should be able to be defiled by the stronger arguments of any sophister, but that a sure faith should hold her both Virgin and fruitful, and should preach it as a true thing, though to others it be untried. Thus withdrawing the myrrh with the spices from a plucking rival's sickle, he reapeth it and delivereth it to a barn that keepeth it more faithfully, while he heapeth together her chaste purpose and the most sweet odour of her chastity, and preserveth it by the strong patronage of truth.

## CHAPTER III.

[0407A]



## CHAPTER III. (cont.)

*I have eaten [sic: *fovum*] with my honey: I have drunk my wine with my milk.* Rich by the year's increase in the reaping of myrrh or of spices, he addeth not that he was steeped in an unction according to the literal sequence, but he eateth, though myrrh seem not to be fit for eating; and he drinketh, though no man would say that he thirsteth after spices. But because the Virgin's converse is exposed to pressings and shearings, and the perfection of her merits was gotten not by soft sleep but by watchful studies; and because, in fine, whatsoever the Virgin heapeth up for herself in the present by labour bringeth in to the Bridegroom that giveth and loveth no bitterness but sweetness: therefore, the harvest being made, he now declareth that he hath eaten, showing therein that he had hungered for the Virgin's advancements. Lastly in the Gospel: *Soul,* saith that man, *thou hast much goods laid up [0407B] for many years: take thy rest, eat, drink, make good cheer [n: (Luc. XII)]*. This rich man therefore is not he whose soul must be required in the night for the things he hath committed, but rich with his barn shut upon the harvests brought in; he stretcheth out no false hope unto many days or unto a year, he applieth to those same harvests neither threshing nor winnowing-fan. For by a wondrous manner of speaking, that which he had called myrrh or spices in the reaping he now findeth to be a honeycomb, now declareth to be honey in the eating; because the taste of him that eateth findeth nothing sweeter than honey, and no integrity is found more pleasing to Christ than his mother's. Ye know that a honeycomb is called a kind of storing case, which the more sagacious bee is found to work, marked out with waxen little cells; which bee, cunning in working, hideth herself under a certain covering, [0407C] wherein she layeth up the comb, and in the comb, with wondrous diligence, the honey. Such a honeycomb he himself, whose protection loveth to cover it and with an ever-watchful care to guard it round about — he himself, *235* I say, suffereth not to be hurt, permitteth not to dry up, but with the honey set within it bringeth it in to his own table, to his own good pleasure. A tenderer comb indeed is grievously hurt and drieth up, and, the honey being denied it, is lost through dryness and becometh empty: as when the integrity of the flesh groweth not sweet by the savoury love of Christ, and to him that hateth to sin virtue groweth not bright by its own worth. For frail flesh is rightly said to be wax, which a more studious and austere converse reduceth into a comb; into which honey is put, and an incomparable sweetness lieth hid shut up, when the love of Christ, that is sweeter, is the cause of the chastity taken up. The comb therefore which an inward emptiness drieth and consumeth, [0407D] Christ taketh not for his own food, the Bridegroom taketh not into his own grace; and worthily reprobate to him is that chastisement of the flesh, or that integrity of a maiden, which is presumed to be brought forth and offered dry, without honey. But that one is confidently presented to his sight, to his eating, which is more fully fattened with copious honey, with a gracious love; with whose fat sweetness, or sweet fatness, the eater is made glad, and the more he feasteth, the richer doth the food grow strong. But because drinking is fitly joined to eating, the Bridegroom accordingly signifieth not only that he hath drunk, but also what he hath drunk, that he may show the Virgin who serveth the cup to be both learned and rich, and the draught commendable, which refresheth and fatteneth him that drinketh. *I have drunk,* saith he, *my wine with my milk.* The prudent Virgin, studious to please by a diligent ministry, [0408A] mingled wine in the bowl for her beloved when he had worthily dined, that when he was refreshed with food and likewise made glad with wine, he might be the more bountiful to give whatsoever should be asked of him. And rightly, being given over to a service not corruptible but divine, she giveth the Bridegroom to drink not with turbid waters, but better and more advisedly with wine; showing that in the embrace and ministry of the nuptials she is not cold with any lack, but burneth with a spiritual affection. For it is not that incurable wine, comparable to the venom of asps or of dragons [n: (Deut. XXXII)], wherewith the lost error of the nations rageth and goeth astray; wine, I say, signifieth a love ungranted to rustic and ragged poor men, whereby they that are rich in grace, noble in mind, are caught up into ecstasy. Lastly wisdom, calling us forth to divine love, mingleth not insipid waters but, by a prudent mystery, wine, [0408B] that our converse, which is of little ones or of babes, may grow young, and, the wine being drunk, may ripen with worthy advancements. *Drink,* saith she, *the wine which I have mingled for you: forsake childishness, and live [n: (Prov. IX)]*. You, saith she, whom a childishness holdeth that is not of years but a weakness of manners, not of age; you who labour not by a failing of strength, but after the manner of carnal men with a languid affection: drink the wine which I have mingled for you — not Falernian, but the spiritual love whereof they that are drunken deserve to live for ever. Forsake childishness, which by no means sufficeth to aspire to greater things, which loveth not, or rather knoweth not how to love save carnally; which by an ill-advised love hindereth and darkeneth them that love, and by a hurtful dullness maketh them, being darkened, conformable to him that darkeneth. Such lovers [0408C] their own love advanceth not unto the light but removeth from the light; delight maketh not serene, but rather a hard clamour estrangeth them from sweet rest; the deceitful show of love shaketh their hearts and striketh blindness into them, and, oppressive as it is, by a most evil advancement, at the last step, bringeth in death. To such a certain heathen: *What hath undone you,* saith he, *I will tell: ye know not how to love.*
These men, made drunk not with wine, or perchance with the wine of dragons and of asps, are far removed from the saving cup of wisdom; which cup she reacheth forth to her hearers with no niggard hand: them that have drunk she refresheth, and them that are refreshed she inebriateth with a right excellent sweetness. This wine of wisdom, the cup of grace and of virtue, whereby he that hath drunk obtaineth the efficacy of life and of salvation, the Virgin who beareth God drinketh more fully; and drinking, is more sweetly gladdened, who in an unvaluable manner, remaining a Virgin, [0408D] is made fruitful. She holdeth in a chaste bosom the son begotten of God and of herself, whom she conceived in a Virginal womb, whose Bridegroom's Bride she is by a deep counsel, by a nuptial mystery; she gathereth him to her with a spiritual affection, and as she loveth the son with a Bridal love, so also the Bridegroom with a filial. In such nuptials the waterpot is not drained, the royal cup knoweth no water, the prince in the banqueting-room standeth not amazed as ignorant of the mystery; no man complaineth for the fear or the presence of poverty, the Bridegroom is not charged with an unlearned or a preposterous bounty. For he who goeth forth from the height of heaven, from the hidden bosom of the Father, who entereth the nuptial bridal chamber shut with the sign of soundness unbroken, and thence, the mystery of the nuptials being celebrated, goeth forth as Bridegroom: so great he brought [sic: *attunt*] with himself; so great a fullness he willed to be present at the nuptials, that [0409A] it is agreed that nothing honest and nothing necessary is wanting to them. Because therefore nuptials ought not to be celebrated without wine, and chiefly such as are made not with regard to the flesh alone but to the divine, in these nuptials wine faileth not but aboundeth, which not only refresheth but maketh fruitful the very celebrators of the nuptials. Spiritual love indeed, which it is agreed doth seethe more strongly than wine, is found with so great a fervour of spirit to make the Virgin drunken, that, forgetting the waters by whose flood the cleanness of chastity is in danger of being worn away, with an unwearied desire she passeth wholly into the love of truth. But Truth is Christ; and Christ is God and man. The Virgin therefore loveth God Christ with a love beyond doubt not carnal; but, because God is a Spirit, she loveth him with a spiritual love: God, I say, a spirit, she loveth with a vehement spirit, that strongly and effectually weareth away whatsoever the [0409B] flesh savoureth amiss. For God, a Spirit who willeth not to be visibly seen, rejoiceth in likeness *236* and willeth to be held by an invisible glue; and he is chiefly delighted with that love, as with an ancestral unmixed wine, wherewith he that loveth him embraceth him spiritually. Such a love he conferred of old upon the angelic spirits; and if he who willed to become an enemy out of a friend had abidden therein, man would not have been deceived, nor would he grieve to have incurred the desert of death, which by that one's envy is read to have entered into the whole world [n: (Rom. V)]. But because that love was found to be lessened in the angels, God willeth it to be restored, not in them, but in men; and both before the law and under the law he requireth to be spiritually loved by the patriarchs and the prophets; and, the days of grace being risen, he acknowledgeth this love more expressly in the Virgin [0409C] mother. Perceiving that it aboundeth more fully in her by the grace of his own giving, he willed to accept it after the manner of wine, the more joyfully as it was the sweeter; and with an eager taste he drank the draught offered by the Virgin, and in the hiding-place of his good pleasure he shut it up as firmly as irrevocably. Rightly therefore doth the Bridegroom affirm that he hath drunk his wine, that is, that he hath received with a grateful draught the divine love which he conferred upon the Virgin; the love wherewith she willed to embrace God Christ with her whole heart, her whole soul, all her strength — and the same Christ is believed to accept it, and, having accepted it, to be delighted therein. But because the Word disposed to be born flesh, God man, of the Virgin, the Virgin loving God set herself as Mother to love him as man also; knowing that the commandment of the law is not profitable enough, not fruitful, [0409D] if to the first and greatest there be not added the like or the second. She loveth therefore her neighbour, satisfying the law or Holy Scripture; she loveth Christ as man, mindful of the unspeakable begetting; she persecuteth not her own flesh in her son with a stepmother's hate, but embraceth it with a mother's affection, and loveth it by a natural right. For neither is her hardness the hardness of stones, nor can her mind be called brazen [n: (Job VI)]; but the Mother is found so given over to a tender love, that, marking Christ made man out of herself, she loveth him as herself, or, if it may be said, more than herself. But this love, this affection or care of a mother, is figured under the name of milk, which the mother by nature bestoweth upon him she hath borne; because a mother holdeth or hideth her son in her bosom or her lap, and with tender love and solicitous affection poureth in the milk. Whose [0410A] milky love, flourishing with a natural sweetness, derogateth not from the divine, prejudiceth not the wine, is not always an adversary to the spiritual; but deserveth to find no mean grace with God, if it love not to bear the first rule alone, but to serve under in the coupling. Lastly the bringer of the evangelical law, saying: *He that loveth son or daughter more than me, is not worthy of me [n: (Matth. X)]*, condemned not the privilege of nature, but prudently ordered the coupling of the two affections, that the love of God, being set before, should lack manner or measure, but that natural love should hold the second place in the joining. For although some men, who are not yet fit either to understand or to love the spiritual, take in the natural the sooner as they take it the more easily, yet it is agreed that the love which is God's is the first and greatest, which willeth the second [0410B] to be present next to itself as in a joining. And the second indeed is sometimes found in some without the first, in whom it is forestalled either by ignorance or by a degenerate negligence; but the first, which flourishing in perfection knoweth not to envy, bringing in the second, willeth ever to see it with itself in the coupling. In that therefore Paul first insinuateth as it were the second, when he is constant in preaching to the Corinthians none but Christ crucified, he spareth their weakness, he consulteth their advancement, he furthereth faith; that they who could not yet take in Christ's Godhead might at the least both understand and love his charity toward themselves; and that they might, by loving at least, render a return to that so great goodness of him whom they knew to suffer freely for themselves, nay for all. *I judged not,* saith he, *myself to know anything among you, but Jesus Christ, and him crucified* [0410C] [n: (I Cor. II)]. And a little below: *As unto little ones,* saith he, *I gave you milk to drink, not meat [n: (I Cor. III)]*. But he who thus cherisheth and advanceth the imperfect with a milky feeding, knowing what he bestoweth upon whom, speaketh wisdom unto the perfect; and preacheth Christ the Son of God to be eternal God, born before the ages, begotten and coequal to him that begetteth; and so giveth milk to the little ones and wine to the greater to drink, wherein he noteth divers advancements, or degrees of advancement; having to teach both those weaker ones by whom natural love is the more easily taken in, and those greater ones to whom the spiritual is now worthily fitting. But the Virgin, from the time she was made a mother after a new kind, was borne up by the grace of the divine gift to so great a height of perfection, that she loveth Christ as truly God with the highest [0410D] desire and by a just right, and to the same as man imparteth likewise the due right of nature. She loveth in the Son the excellence of the Godhead with a pure mind; she loveth also her own flesh tenderly and sweetly by nature; to the loving of the one she is caught up and borne aloft with a stronger heat, to the other she as it were striveth back and is brought down again with a softer step. To the one she raiseth herself up more vehemently, drunken; to the other she boweth herself more gently, sober: to the one she serveth the wine of fortitude, to the other the milk of tenderness; a twofold love flourisheth in the Virgin, and the one disparageth not the other, and Christ taketh up and accepteth the concordant coupling of both. *Come,* saith Isaias, *buy without money: and without any exchange, wine and milk [n: (Isa. LV)]*. The prophet, knowing that Christ is not appeased with a solitary love, but that the giant of a twin substance is delighted with a twinned gift, willed by a prudent counsel to instruct us to buy [0411A] wine and milk, signifying that wine befitteth God, milk man, nay rather that wine and milk befit Christ, God and man. But since this wine and milk ought to be bought according to the prophet's teaching, *237* what meaneth it that to this buying no exchange is admitted, no money, save that that twofold love, wherewith Christ, God and man, willeth to be loved alike, can be purchased neither with gold nor with silver nor with any earthly price? For not by a heap of moneys, but by poverty of spirit, is that kingdom bought and gotten, in which everyone who soundly loveth Christ abideth with him for ever; whose love also in the present nonetheless knoweth no cheap price, nor willeth to be held by him that swelleth with an abundance of temporal things. Rightly therefore doth Isaias call them forth to this [0411B] buying, who in buying put forward no mention of money, but who rather offer a slender spirit, the purity of an inmost mind, continence of the flesh, and nakedness, the soft linen being left behind. Fortified with this price I believe the Virgin entered into the nuptial market, and mingled alike for the Bridegroom the wine and milk that she had found and bought, that she might serve Christ, God and man, with a twin cup, knowing that he would not thirst for the one without the other. Having drunk thereof and been refreshed, he turneth himself again to his companions, and carefully inviteth them to the nuptial feast, that they who serve as attendants in the bridal chamber that is privy to his secrets may be accounted guests also and partakers of the rich table.



## CHAPTER IV.

[0411C] *Eat, O friends, drink and be inebriated, most dearly beloved.* He calleth the angels friends, who stood fast in his friendship when Lucifer and many that agreed with him ceased to love: who stood by him as he celebrated the nuptials, they that loved not being driven far off, and who with a worthy ministry pressed the more familiarly to know the hidden mysteries. These, that stand by and press on, that they may take the fitting advancements of knowledge, the Bridegroom suffereth not to be needy, not to be fasting; but with the storeroom opened and the bounty of his gifts displayed, he calleth them as it were to a table *of fat things full of marrow, and of wine purified from the lees [n: (Isa. XXV)]*. *Eat,* saith he, *O friends.* You, saith he, whom I willed to be present as companions and friends at the nuptials, and, they that love not being removed, to be at hand for the kisses of them that love: at my table with me [0411D] eat the things that are set before you — that is, understand the things which, being understood, shall deserve to please. Understand what of grace or of savour the solemnity of the nuptials, what the depth of the mysteries hath; what of glory or of honour the Virgin's fruitfulness, what the mother's integrity hath: understand what of sacrament is contained in *The Word was made flesh [n: (Joan. I)]*, what of help things divine bring to things human, things heavenly to things earthly. But this understanding is rightly named an eating; and when an angel, or any other of this sort, is invited to eat, the divine word purposeth not to drive away a bodily want, but signifieth that a spiritual understanding is to be sought. Lastly, when the hand of the Lord was sent to Ezechiel in a vision, and in it a book was brought sealed with a seal: *Son,* saith he, *of man, eat this volume, and going [0412A] speak to the children of Israel [n: (Ezech. III)]*. Because it profiteth nothing, or little, that the hand sent brought a sealed book, if it lie hid from the prophet what that same book containeth written out, he is of necessity admonished to eat the volume, that is, that not with the tooth but with the mind he may take what is contained in the volume. For he that eateth, not content with the mere show or comeliness of the food, burneth the more and desireth to be refreshed with the taste or the savour; and whosoever is rightly wise is fed, not with the tinkling sound of Holy Scripture, nor with a feeling, but rather with an understanding worthy unto profit. And because he cannot be fed therewith by the powers of his own will alone, but by being endowed with grace and by the benefit of the divine bounty, the prophet, after he had heard the voice or the commandment of the Lord, sufficeth not yet to himself, but declareth that he was fed by him. *And I opened,* saith he, *my mouth, and he fed me with that [0412B] volume [n: (ibid.)]*. To him that called me forth to eat I strove to open my mouth; to him that admonished me to understand I applied a zeal to obey; and he, having already come before me with the admonitions he offered, fed me, intent as I was, with the volume spread open — that is, endowed me with a large knowledge and a lettered understanding. *He spread it open,* saith he, *before me: and said, eat this volume [n: (ibid.)]*. The book indeed which the hand sent brought me rolled up, by no zeal of mine, by no powers of mine did I render unrolled; but she that brought it took away the veil that hung over it or was spread upon it, and made that which was shut up in the volume evident and spread open. For although it be mine to obey him that admonisheth, to give as it were consenting hands unto advancement, yet it is of his grace to give to me, or to any man, a nimble understanding: it is mine to open my mouth, that I be [0412C] not altogether worthy to be driven from the feeding; it is his to fill it, that is, to give it to be prudently understood. *Open wide,* saith he, *thy mouth, and I will fill it up [n: (Psal. LXXX)]*. And elsewhere: *Give me understanding, that I may learn thy commandments [n: (Psal. CXVIII.)]* And he: *Understanding,* saith he, *I will give thee, and I will instruct thee [n: (ibid.)]*. Speaking therefore to the companions whom the Bridegroom willed to be present at his mysterial secrets, he willed not that they should be as rustics fasting among the nuptials, but, a table being set forth of a deep greatness and an exquisite fullness, he set his friends far from the hunger of the unskilled multitude. *Eat,* saith he, *O friends* — that is, understand the marvellous mystery, the unspeakable sacrament, which to the rest, that are not friends, openeth the veil of ignorance: but to you *238* that minister and [0412D] stand by me I have given to know those things whereto nature attaineth not, and whereunto my grace alone supplieth the power. For neither, as some say, did the angels from the beginning naturally obtain to know the sacraments which remained more fully hidden in God; which, when the fullness of time came, that God the Son of God willed to celebrate the nuptials, he willed to reveal to them first and more familiarly. Whence the Apostle: *What is,* saith he, *the dispensation of the sacrament hidden from ages in God, that the manifold wisdom of God may be made known to the princes and powers in the heavenly places by the Church [n: (Ephes. III)]*. [var: Vulg. Eph. 3:10 *principatibus et potestatibus*, "to the Principalities and the Powers" — the angelic order; Migne prints *principibus*, "to the princes"] The wisdom of God, remaining uniform in itself but working outwardly many and divers things, deserved to be called manifold, which is made known as it were more manifoldly to the princes and to the angelic powers, when the secret mystery of the Word to be incarnate shineth out more clearly [0413A] upon them. But because to neither angel nor man doth understanding suffice enough unto merit, if a sweeter affection of loving apply not itself to the understanding, rightly after the eating are the friends also freely admonished, that both a learned making and a perfect refreshing may work a vital sufficiency. *Drink,* saith he, *and be inebriated, most dearly beloved.* If, by me, saith he. giving, ye take in the hidden sacraments by understanding, being not yet content therewith, be ye careful for advancement; and that ye may seem both to profit enough and as it were to perfect what ye have begun, eating, drink — that is, love what ye have perceived by understanding. For it profiteth nothing, or little, to understand what things have been great, what perfect, if we love not with a mightier grace the things understood: and as the people that understandeth not, by the testimony of Osee [n: (Osee. IV)], shall be beaten, so [0413B] the wicked servant, not loving the things understood, shall condemn himself as guilty of negligence. Rightly therefore are the companions or friends admonished not only to understand but also to love, that when they have joyfully perceived deep things they may marvel at a most sweet sweetness; and that they who a while since had as it were grieved over the wretched fall of the sinner may now for joy stand amazed at so marvellous a counsel of the Redeemer. Whose height, when by understanding and by loving they lay hold of it as it were with hands, being made drunken with amazement and joy they suspend themselves into so great an ecstasy as it were, that, forgetting the wounds which the serpent's fraud once brought upon men, they now think of nothing but the physician or the medicine at hand. They eat, when they understand that a life-giving mystery, that saving nuptials are celebrated; they drink, when they love that man is reformed unto his former, nay unto an ampler [0413C] grace; they are inebriated, when they stand amazed and cleave fast, and for joy suffice not to marvel that manhood, taken up into God, deserveth to be exalted above the angels. Them that were privy to this secret the bridegroom in speaking named friends, but them that were drunken with love and joy he heaped with the name of most dearly beloved: signifying both that they are pleasing to him who apply a spiritual understanding to the knowing of subtle things, and that the same are most pleasing when they come and attain unto the advancement of loving. These being refreshed with food and drunken with a more gracious draught, the bride, reclining her head in a sweet conscience or love, forgetting things visible, suspendeth herself among things invisible; and what she tasteth, what she perceiveth, she grudgeth not to us, but showeth.



## CHAPTER V.

[0413D] *I sleep, and my heart watcheth.* When the companions and friends that stand by a work so divine give heed and marvel, made drunken with the amazement of a deep greatness and not with wine: the bride reclineth herself within the chamber in a softer reclining, to whom the bridegroom now serveth the desirable cup of a marvellous savour. The friends watching, and striving as it were to lay hold, and standing amazed at the manner or the measure of a thing so deep: the Virgin, judging whatsoever applaudeth not in deep silence to be a market and a thing of the market-place, resteth in the nuptial bridal chamber and closeth her eyes even for a little with [sic: *sommo*]. For the business, or the solicitude of a clamorous business, being driven away, the noise being shut out abroad, the door of a pure mind being closed as it were: amid the bridegroom's embraces she falleth asleep the more eagerly as it is the sweeter, and, failing into [0414A] him, and by failing advancing, she desireth things insensible alone. Abiding in the body, a stranger to the things that are of the body, forgetting her cares, her serene mind is caught up into ecstasy: borne up by a calm rapture, she rejoiceth to forget whatsoever is beneath, sleeping and resting in the things which she chiefly loveth to obtain. But lest her sleeping should seem to strike in negligence or torpor, and to afford confidence to the ambushes of the enemy, to open a looser entrance: the virgin setteth a watchman who may keep the watches unwearied, who may foresee from afar whatsoever maketh an unlawful noise. For while she sleepeth, and is loosened into the tender embraces of the bridegroom, and hath forgotten the things behind and is loosed from the cares of temporal things, her own heart watcheth, driving far from sleep the clouds of phantasms, the empty phantasies, the heavy noises of the world, [0414B] the seducing melodies of sirens. Her own heart watcheth, acting with a circumspect solicitude lest a mass of forensic acts cast upon her should trouble the sweetness of sleep that she hath found; lest any molestation should enter, even secretly, the secret of her chamber, which, being entered, might rage and violently shake off her sleep. Lastly her own heart watcheth, that when with a careful hand it hath driven away every adversary, it may hearken and hear the bridegroom whispering with a slender murmur: and, the door being as it were shut against whosoever maketh a harder noise, it may lend an ear to the bridegroom that more sweetly and more subtly *239* speaketh. For the more closely she loveth to be joined to him, the more eagerly to cleave to him, so much the more gratefully doth she will to hear, and for the bridegroom's voice to rejoice with joy: and giving her ear to the hearing, she counteth herself the more grievously hurt if for his voice she refuse not whatsoever else hath sounded. For he, [0414C] cherishing her sleep and favouring the desire of her that sleepeth, when he shall so have given her milk, speaketh to the heart of her that loveth: and to her, as to her leisure so to her business, he setteth what bound he will, as he is read of old to have promised by the prophet: *I will give her milk,* saith he, *and I will speak to her heart [n: (Osee. II)]*. I will give her milk, saith he, when she shall lay herself down in my bosom with her head bowed, and shall put nothing between with mutual embraces; when, greedy of silence, she shall be delighted to fall asleep under my shadow, and, thirsting, to draw in the sweetness she hath found, and, drawing it in, to thirst. But I will speak to her heart, when I shall admonish her to awake, when I shall restrain her from her own profits out of regard for her neighbours, that, the draught of the foretasted sweetness being laid aside for a little, she may go forth to work abroad, watching [0414D] with brotherly charity. The bridegroom therefore giveth the Virgin milk, when he leadeth her in to the secrets of his breast: he speaketh to her heart, when he calleth and bringeth the same back watchful unto us; when, the sweetness of sleep being tasted, wherein she loveth to forget temporal things, he biddeth her awake unto the love and the care of her neighbours. And she, while she sleepeth and tasteth what sweetness there is in resting, and her heart watcheth with a solicitude of serving more diligently: lo, of a sudden a certain interruption of the sweetness now perceived, a hand as it were knocketh at the door, the voice of her beloved shaketh her ear. By which shaking the Virgin, perceiving herself challenged (for she knoweth the voice again, because she hath now heard it often), seemeth to answer to herself alone, or to the maidens standing by her, and to recount with a mindful word both whose and what voice she had heard.

## CHAPTER VI.

[0415A]

*The voice of my beloved knocking.* When in my chosen reclining, saith she, I am held by the gift of sleep, and with a heart watchful enough am nonetheless intent upon the Bridegroom's good pleasure: out of a hidden place a certain voice, as I perceive, breaketh forth as it were into the open, which the more carefully interrupteth my advancement as I sleep, lest it come, as I will, unto perfection. Whose importunity beateth the more harshly upon my ears, and driveth me back from that which I was burning more firmly to lay hold of: and a repulse so strong, that I may confess the truth, I should bear ill, if I did not worthily set his good pleasure before my own will. For I know that it pleaseth his will not a little, that the door of a holy mind be found not to stand open to strangers; that whosoever shall have passed by through the by-ways of worldly [0415B] pandering may find it shut, and not lying open after the fashion of a brothel. The bridegroom himself also, when he willeth to come to that same door, loveth to find it shut rather than open, and to prove its seal so tenacious, so indissoluble, that it should altogether never know how to be opened save when he himself hath knocked. For a holy mind, restraining itself within a spiritual workshop, ought so to embrace the zeal of contemplating, so the discipline of leisure or of silence, that it open not its cloister to itself, that it break not forth to the office of preaching, unless it have been knocked upon and have drunk in the voice of him that commandeth. Therefore the Virgin sleeping, and soothed with a delightful sleep, rejoicing to be shut in by her cloister as one entangled in softer meshes: hasteneth to open not only not to any man, but not even to the bridegroom, until at last, being knocked upon, she is commanded [0415C] and by the commandment is compelled to obey. Who indeed requireth not the commander to command, but the more quickly knoweth again the voice, even a slender voice, of him that knocketh: and as she heareth not, nor giveth ear, to open at any admonitions of a deceiver, so she stoppeth not her ear when the voice of the commander soundeth. And it soundeth and knocketh at the door, or the leisure, of her that resteth, when by the benefit of one that teacheth he willeth to counsel them that are without; when, pitying the blindness and the neediness of the orphan that is ignorant, he willeth it to be wiped away by a virginal labour, and the merit of her that laboureth to be increased. But what that voice thundereth above, or what it saith, what it commandeth or showeth, soothing the bride as she sleepeth, the bridegroom himself willed not only that the bride should know it more secretly or more sacredly, but willed also that it should come, even slenderly, unto them that are without.



## CHAPTER VII.

[0415D]

*Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my undefiled, for my head is full of dew, and my locks of the drops of the nights.* Thou, saith he, that hast barred the chamber of thy mind against the malevolent robber, that hast made firm the virginal enclosure, that hast made firm the watchful guard against all things whatsoever: to me, who am not envious of thee but desirous of thee and of thine advancement and of thy crown, unbar the doors, lay aside now for a little while thy leisure or thy silence. Rising, awake; hear more healthfully the voice of him that knocketh; shake the lock from the doorpost — to me indeed nothing at all ought to be shut; and that which thou shuttest worthily against the enemy, against the world, against any stranger whatsoever, try thou more surely that it is worthy of merit or of praise to open to me alone. When I suffer thee to be at leisure *240* and [0416A] to give thyself more quietly to sleep, to take care of thyself, to give thy hands to leisure or to be silent — I confess it — the bridal chamber ought to be shut, the door barred, the virginal secret not to be unbarred by vice nor by outward business. For with the door shut that Father of spirits willeth to be prayed to, willeth his face to be sought, willeth the kiss of him that seeketh to be made serene: he willeth so fruitful a leisure not to be troubled by the crowds of businesses, but to be prospered by a gentler breeze and by a most effectual course. But when I stand by and knock more diligently at the fastening, when my voice soundeth and asketh that an opening be given it, it is not of counsel that thou lie hid longer under the shadow of silence, but that thou stand to the commandment and show thyself subject to him. Open therefore to me, the sweetness of sleep being interrupted a little, not cast away, that what thou hast received in the chamber thou mayest preach upon the housetops; and, as it were forgetful of thyself, that thou be mindful for me of them that [0416B] stand by me, and be not grieved to speak for the sake of thy brethren and thy neighbours the peace thou hast foretasted. For neither oughtest thou to indulge thy own desires only, nor to milk out the sweetness of the heavenly milk unto thine own lips alone, but also, when the time requireth, to provide for the profit of others, lest thou seem to envy them that cannot what thou hast been able to draw sooner or more abundantly. In short, there is no cause wherefore a sister ought to shut against a brother, who as heirs, yea rather as co-heirs, war together for the most high Father; whom kinship of flesh, whom the most powerful force of nature joineth, whom one love, one concord maketh of one mind by a just right. As therefore thou shuttest, and rightly shuttest, against the enemy with the bar of anxiety, so, as a friend, draw back the bar, shake off the lock for thy brother and thy friend alike — thou that art made a friend by the diligence of thy mind, by the bond of charity, [0416C] a faithful keeper of secrets, privy to my truth. And because thou dost not, like the peacock, rejoice or swell with a blind beauty of eyes, but growest gentle in the spirit of innocence by my irradiating grace, thou that art sister and friend art rightly called my dove also, cheerful in the hope of things to come, groaning for those same things because they are not yet fully present. In these and in other such things, well enough furnished about by my gift, thou art worthily called an undefiled Virgin and perfect; perfect, I say, not that nothing at all is wanting to thy present life, but because thou art so wholly beautiful that now there is no spot in thee. Thou therefore, that art marked with names of this sort — nay rather with the very substance of the names — that findest me so favourable in the bounty of these gifts: hear the voice of him that knocketh, open the shut doors; and lest thou think the instancy of him that knocketh idle, behold the causes. For my head [0416D] is full of dew: and my locks of the drops of the nights. The head of Christ, Paul bearing witness, is God. But the dew, which the icy night poureth over the earth, and which the sun dissolveth as a mist when with the morning radiance it poureth itself into things, is the cold of unbelievers, and the subtle malice of the perfidious whereby the nations are held fast, and the iniquity of the Jews is chilled [n: (I Cor. II)]. Who, while they understand not, confess not, that Christ the man is God, the Son of God, what do they but fear not to burden and to offend his head, and to fill it with so great burdens and vexations that he can as it were not bear so full a labour? Whence God by Isaias: « *I am full, saith he [n: (Isa. I)]*. And again: *I have laboured with bearing (ibid)*. » With so great a dew, saith he, with so nightly a cold do you burden me, [0417A] that I seem to myself stricken and full with the weariness of your depravity; and I, who, knowing not to be troubled, do tranquilly judge the world that groweth worse, do labour hard in bearing the loads of you that are unjust. The Jewish dew indeed, and the cold malice of him that believeth not, speaking in the Gospel uttereth the words of one that oppresseth more harshly; who, seeing Christ to be that man, understandeth not nor loveth aught else, offending herein most of all, that he truly proclaimeth himself God. *For a good,* say they, *work we stone thee not, but for blasphemy; and because that thou, being a man, makest thyself God [n: (Joan. X)]*. And above: *Therefore did the Jews the more seek to kill him, because he said God was his Father, making himself equal to God [n: (Joan. V)]*. You see the head of Christ pressed down with dew cold enough, and Christ worthily complaining of a malice [0417B] more wicked, whose not only head but locks also are weighed down with the like cold, while unbelievers persecute them with hatred and with reproaches.
