Locks is the name given to the balls or heaps of hairs which, cleaving to the head by the root, are outwardly leagued together by a certain covenant of nearness; which, while each keepeth its due place or course, do themselves afford to the head both covering and honour alike. By whom, as I see, the saints are not unfitly figured, who are called together unto the faith out of divers places or nations; whom the firmness of the same faith maketh to cleave the more tenaciously to the head, and whom a brotherly nearness maketh outwardly to cohere one to another after the manner of bees. Such do I judge them to have been in the primitive Church who are read to have come together to Christ with a devout spirit; who either, few in number, followed him before his passion when he was about to suffer, [0417C] or, when he was raised up, obtained more largely the faith of the resurrection. Of whom Mark: *He called,* saith he, *unto himself whom he would himself, and he made that there should be twelve with him [n: (Marc. III)]*. And Luke in the Acts of the apostles: *There was,* saith he, *a company of men together, about an hundred and twenty [n: (Act. I)]*, *and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with divers tongues, according as the Holy Ghost gave them to speak [n: (Act. II)]*. And below: *They were baptized,* saith he, *and there were added in that day about three thousand souls [n: (ibid.)]*. And a little after: *The number of the men was made five thousand [n: (Act. IV)]*. And far below, Paul preaching: *they were baptized,* saith he, *in the name of the Lord Jesus; and all the men were about twelve [n: (Act. XIX)]*. These are the locks of the Bridegroom, for whom he hath no mean [0417D] care, *241* and whose advancement loving, he hardly beareth their oppression: for the most part the nights grow heavy with drops that water, or rather that rush in, which, the sun being put far off, grow dull with colder darknesses. But as every just man is by merit called a day of life, so the ungodly man and the sinner, living in ruin, is called night; upon whom, because the light hath not risen and the sun of justice hath not shone, he hath drawn over himself a horrid cold and the darknesses of ignorance. Which sort of night, and the dark conversation of sinners, hateth justice, condemneth the innocence of the better sort; and forbiddeth her to go forth with a clean step as under the naked air, while with more frequent vexations, as with rainy drops, it disquieteth her. Doth not that night seem to you to have stood forth the more importunate, which rejoiced to have oppressed the apostolic choir the more harshly; which, although [0418A] it plucked not away utterly the whole lock from the head to which it had once cleaved, yet, shaking out one hair, brought it into the pit of perdition? For when the princes of the Jews would take and kill Christ, with many wiles and with many contrivings they laboured to seduce and to lead on Judas Iscariot, whom they had perceived beforehand to labour the more maliciously with avarice, that he should sell for a vile price his own Salvation. But all the rest were indeed grievously shaken by the wind of fear, yet were not shaken off from the base set under them nor from the root implanted in them; whom the hand of the spouse, calling them back, willed to restrain under a rule, that thenceforth they might bear with a more even mind both the threats of princes and the drops of the nights. Whence, when after the resurrection the princes of the priests thundered with threats and prisons, with words and stripes, that by fear they might call back the disciples [0418B] from their purpose of preaching, they: *If it be just,* say they, *to hear you rather than God, judge ye; for we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard [n: (Act. IV)]*. And below: *We ought to obey God rather than men [n: (Act. V)]*. Locks of this sort, whom charity knitteth, whom a fellowly love coupleth, whom an inward faith and a spiritual devotion maketh to cleave to God — these the nights assail from without, and the darksome hands of unbelievers, burdensome with colder drops and with more frequent malices. For as, the prophet bearing witness, a cistern maketh water cold [n: (Jer. VI)], so hath she made her malice cold. That therefore the locks of the faithful may be fortified against the enemies and against the enemies' burdens, and may not be wickedly oppressed either by ignorance or by voluntary consent, the spouse admonisheth the Virgin that [0418C] she open to him the gate of secrets, and, expounding what she knoweth, instruct the minds of her neighbours. For although the unction of the spirit is read to teach the just concerning all things [n: (I Joan. II)], yet not in vain is the Virgin bidden to apply diligence, because it hindereth not, nay rather it profiteth unto an effectual increase of spiritual grace, if by planting and by watering a fitting foundation be laid beforehand. But because it is sweeter to be at leisure and to see how sweet is the leisure and the pleasantness of contemplating, than to labour with the word and with the anxiety of preaching: the Virgin, choosing to be shut in and diligent not to be torn from her purpose, answereth as though she grieved to be driven forth to businesses.



## CHAPTER VIII.

[0418D] *I have put off my garment, how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them?* Adam was made naked, set under the naked air, wrapped neither in the enclosure of a chamber nor in swaddling clothes, that he might look up to heaven with a countenance hindered by no covering, that unto the seeing of God he might pass with an unhindered step. But because, being uxorious, he condescended to the will of the seduced woman, and, the Creator being offended, stretched himself out to that which was forbidden: guilty of death, he entangled himself and his own in troubles and in labours, and, his nakedness being lost, clothed them with a wretched mortality. Whence also after his disobedience he was clothed with skins, that, being destitute of a simple life and of a naked justice, he might know the loss of a miserable punishment to hang over him, the form whereof a garment made of dead animals representeth. To a punishment of this sort there seemeth, [0419A] as I see, to pertain that anxious labour whereby we desire to be taught or to teach; and, until we see that which is perfect with the eye of a sound mind more fully unveiled, in the sweat of our countenance we eat our own bread. From which heat or sweat we take breath a little, when, the burden of cares being removed, we breathe again unto things invisible; and we are stripped by a sweet leisure of the ragged garment of labour, when with the door of the mind shut we behold the sweetness of an inward quiet. Which sweetness, because the spouse now foretasteth it with a greedy taste, she consenteth not to open the sooner to the spouse that disquieteth her, but, fleeing, rejoiceth to behold the naked truth, her linen cloth left behind, fearing to be twisted back from so happy a leisure unto business. After that, saith she, the anxiety being laid aside wherein I sweated the more laboriously, I have stripped myself of the entangled garment of outward things by the beholding of peace, [0419B] how shall I break off the sweetness of the delightfulness I have found, and send myself back to outward cares, which I love not? I refuse not the commandment, I abjure not obedience, but I fear to be subjected again to a burden that will weigh me down: inward things being tasted, I care not now to revisit outward things; and yet against him that commandeth I stop not mine ear after the manner of the asp. I had indeed laid down the spoils of an old heaviness, and had found for myself the joys of a pure nakedness; I rejoiced that I was no longer where *242* I had been, nay rather that I was no longer what I had been; and by an advance pleasing enough I seemed, naked, to be present among the naked angels. Forgetful of things visible, I beheld things invisible the more gratefully; I knew not vexations, I was not pressed by narrow bars; nothing withstood me in this breadth of mind; what I love, what I desire, stood by me the more largely. Whence if mine own will [0419C] hath drawn me back, I am worthy to be accused; if necessity hath pressed my will, I seem to be weighed down; and thus a kind of peril as it were hangeth over on either side, since it is hard to do anything unwillingly or unjustly. Being free therefore from a ragged anxiety, how shall I be entangled again? Being stripped of temporal things, with what patience shall I be clothed anew? How shall I carry back my washed feet to the mire of the streets, that I may defile them with the vexations either of faults or of cares? For although in speaking to my neighbours and in anxiously bringing forth the things I now know I have not moved my foot from the just path, as very many are wont to do, yet I seem to myself to have incurred certain defilements, feeling that the vexations of cares have run against my heart. For whatsoever meeteth and withstandeth, even for [0419D] a little, one that contemplateth the divine cleanness, or standeth not by that same contemplator with a favouring compliance — if it be compared by a fitting consideration to that cleanness itself, then, although holy in its own kind, it shall yet rightly be judged defiled. How therefore, having tasted that sweetness, shall I bear this bitterness again, and twist back the steps of so great advances unto the defilements of failings? By what fruit of another shall I put myself under a burden of my own, when I desire henceforth to approach not the contest but the crown? But while I hesitate, while I doubt, as it were not knowing how to find a way whereby I may now be willing or able to return to that which I had broken off; while, rejoicing in silence, I defer to return to the accustomed [0420A] burden — behold, I feel the hand of my beloved put in through the hole.

## CHAPTER IX.

*My beloved put his hand through the hole, and my belly trembled at his touch.* He suffereth me not, admonished by his voice, to stick fast any longer; but the beloved, boring through the fastening, putteth his hand through the slender hole; to a shut mind he openeth a subtle understanding after the likeness of a hole, and, it being opened, he inserteth what he knew profitable for me unto advancement. The hand of the spouse is not unfitly named that grace of his which openeth the understanding, and, it being opened, worketh effectually; which poureth in and inspireth the more subtly to the opened understanding by what manner or order a man tendeth and aspireth the more perfectly to the pleasing of the spouse. By the help therefore and the working of this hand a subtler [0420B] understanding perceiveth that without the good pleasure of the spouse there is no advancement of them that are at leisure, none of them that labour; and that leisure is to be pursued when his good will inviteth us to it, and that he who, being bidden, shall have willed to desist from this escapeth not his wrath and judgment. For a man may both displease, being stubborn in leisure, and, being humble, obtain merit in business; and neither state is found profitable enough, if he be not, as one obedient, prevented by the good will of Christ. This being subtly understood, she striveth no more to resist violently, but that which in her had as it were hardened is rendered soft, like a belly; and her heart, softened by the gracious hand, is shaken strongly and trembleth; and, fearing lest she offend, she now desireth nothing but the good pleasure of the spouse. Good is the hand of grace, which mightily boreth through the things that are somewhat dark, giving light [0420C] to the understanding that it may the more clear-sightedly see the things that shall profit: at whose [sic: *sublilem*] touch, if aught had been hard, it groweth soft; and, being made soft, the trembling groweth strong unto obedience. Who will grant that he put his hand to us through the straits of the hole, and, the understanding being opened, suffer not anything to grow hard, but, when he hath given a subtle intelligence for the seeing, may consequently pour in a nimble diligence for the fulfilling? Happy therefore is the Virgin who is touched by the sent hand of him that worketh, whose soft heart trembleth at the touch or the efficacy of him that commandeth; who, the command being heard, withdraweth not into the lodging of negligence, is not darkened in understanding, halteth not in affection, but obeyeth. Whence she addeth: *I arose,* etc.

## CHAPTER X.

[0420D] *I arose to open to my beloved.* She who a little above shuddereth to take up again the garment she had laid down, and as it were knoweth not how she should defile her washed feet anew, now perceiving more fully in what and to whom she ought to obey, riseth and hasteneth to open to him whom she loveth. She was held indeed with herself in a pleasing seat or chamber, and rejoiced as in an inner room in a sweet leisure: rejoicing in a soft reclining, with her head laid back she rested, and knew not the wakeful tumults and whatsoever maketh noise without. Out of a rest of this sort, leisured, or out of a peaceful sitting, the Virgin, rising, is shaken out and is girded for the contest; and what the spouse's uttered voice obtained not with her, his hand put in [0421A] prevaileth to do with a fuller effect. For the voice that is heard teacheth to do, but giveth not also to do; and the ear which is rendered ready for hearing is not straightway rendered ready for effect also; but that which *243* the voice of him that commandeth speaketh out to us for the knowing, the touch of him that worketh followeth up with grace for the fulfilling. Whence Isaias: *Lord,* saith he, *who hath believed our hearing [n: (Isa. LXIII)]*? [var: Vulg. Isa 53:1 *Quis credidit auditui nostro?* — without *Domine*; the vocative belongs to the New Testament citations of the verse, Rom 10:16 and John 12:38.] The words of prophecy sound everywhere in the ears of all, but, the hand of the spouse being withdrawn, they give not faith to Isaias; because the word, whereby the ears of unbelievers are struck from without, becometh like a tinkling cymbal [n: (I Cor. XIII)], if their minds be not touched by grace. After the voice therefore whereby the spouse admonished the Virgin to open, because she deferred to obey the admonitions of him that admonished, he set himself by an operative grace to soften her heart, and by the touch of his hand to make her ready [0421B] to fulfil what he had commanded. Whence elsewhere also Solomon is found to commend the same Lord, showing that what he speaketh out with his mouth he consummateth with his hands, giving to understand that it is not sufficient enough that he be prompt to speak, unless with a more gracious good will he have set his hands also to the fulfilling. *With thy mouth,* saith he, *thou hast spoken: and with thy hands thou hast performed [n: (III Reg. VIII)]*. With his mouth therefore the Bridegroom admonished the Bride unto labour, but by the touch of his sent hand he rendered her the prompter: her that rested in sleep or in leisure he rendered watchful with his mouth, that she might hear, but nimble with his hand, that rising she might open the more watchfully. *I arose,* saith she, *to open to my beloved.* She who, lying, could not, or perhaps would not, open, being made to tremble by the touch of the hand riseth and hasteneth to obey; she riseth, I say, lest by deferring she seem to hinder him that knocketh, accounting profitable to herself [0421C] whatsoever at last she perceiveth to please him. Her silence therefore being broken off, she riseth and prepareth herself for doctrine, that she may set a moral discipline within the hearts of her hearers; she rendereth her hands active, that she may give to the rest a form of living, and, as well by word as by work, may open to the spouse a path for his coming. For then indeed is the way effectually opened to Christ, when in the teacher's word truth, and in his act severity, is found; when preaching or doctrine so instructeth the minds of the hearers that the discipline of the virtue shown beforehand edifieth them the more. Which the Virgin showing addeth: *My hands,* etc.



## CHAPTER XI.

*My hands dropped down myrrh, and my fingers are full of the most approved myrrh.* When the Virgin was rising, and [0421D] as it were going on to open, hoping that Christ would enter in the more fully when the gate was opened: in the going she felt that the gate itself would not easily lie open, unless she took care to apply strong hands to the lifting of the bolt. For the gate was not opened straightway, as she declareth herself to have risen, nor doth she assert that it lay open straightway when she rose; because, although she confesseth beyond doubt that she rose in order to open, yet the efficacy of opening is not straightway afforded. For she saith not: I arose and opened, but she saith: *I arose to open.* But because a certain difficulty perchance set itself against her as she rose, the Virgin advisedly applied her hands to the removing of it — hands, I say, not torpid with leisure, not dry, not deceitful, but strong with a nimble virtue, effectual to fulfil worthily what was purposed. *Hands,* saith she, *mine dropped down myrrh.* [0422A] Hands are actions; but by myrrh she seemeth to name the strictness of judgment, because whatsoever the Virgin did she willed to judge the more strictly, knowing that he deservedly feareth not the judgment to come who by a humble will hath chosen to bear the present one. The hands therefore of the virgin dropped the bitterness of myrrh, when all her acts held the rule of discipline, when whatsoever she took care to work in this laborious flesh she restrained the more diligently, lest it should presume to wander the more negligently. For myrrh is said to strengthen soft and flowing flesh, and to preserve it lest by a natural law it lie subject to rottenness; and the works of our hands, lest perchance they come to a natural failing, a regular strictness maketh firm and leadeth unto perfection. And because it sufficeth not for the virgin if by living strictly [0422B] she advance much in virtue, unless she both instruct the rest and draw them along with her unto salvation: she saith that her hands do not hold or have myrrh, but rather drop it down, that she may show the advance of her works to be derived unto them that are without. Ah, for to this she riseth, that her instruction stick not fast nor waver anywhere, and that whatsoever she knoweth profitable for the rest she hold not shut up but drop down, that she may profit them that stand by [sic: *assitentibus*] her not by the desire of her will alone, but by a form of justice shown forth and by the example of a strict holiness. To the opening therefore the anxious virgin stretcheth forth her hands; to the instructing of her neighbours she showeth beforehand a dropping of myrrh, holding it settled that then she instructeth the more effectually, when the strictness of manners hath hastened to go before the instruction of words. But because a severe strictness of living is not held sufficient to the full [0422C] if in it a discreet moderation, or a moderate discretion, be not held: after the hands dropping down the unction of a commendable myrrh, she consequently applieth herself to make mention of fingers. *Fingers,* saith she, *mine are full of the most approved myrrh.* Fingers, although beneath they cleave to one another as by one root or joining, yet come forth outwardly discrete with an unequal measure or proportion; and their discretion is fashioned by so prudent a craft of nature that, serving the hand, it is held as profitable as it is fitting. By the fingers therefore is rightly understood the discretive virtue, which, if it be joined undivided as a companion to our works, then whatsoever in them she affecteth not the more strictly, paineth the more severely or straiteneth, *244* that same discretion by her fellowship rendereth the more perfect and adorneth. Which doubtless, [0422D] although now more briefly, now more profusely she extendeth herself, according as she seeth through and attendeth what is expedient for the business set before her, yet, as she striveth not to pass beyond the due bounds, so she findeth it indiscreet and, injurious to stand short of them. Whence she herself, who is not denied to be called one and the same discretion, is applied so manifoldly to many, and to divers businesses, that it is not out of tune if she be figured not so much by the name of a finger as of fingers, in that she worketh very many things, dividing to each as she will. But willing to commend fingers of this sort, the most prudent Virgin asserteth that they abound with the most approved myrrh; because as strictness, being indiscreet, profiteth nothing or little, so discretion shineth not forth unless it be accustomed to hard burdens. But discretion shineth and is adorned with a rosy comeliness when the strictness joined to it is not straitened [0423A] by a niggard boundary, when myrrh is poured into the fingers not from an empty horn but rather from a full one, and the fulness thereof is worthily approvable, not confounded. But that may fittingly be called approvable or approved whereto the conversation of us that labour striveth so to be given over, that whatsoever miry thing the interruption of the present workshop draweth to itself, the severity of discipline brought over it may diligently boil away. But the Virgin named the myrrh wherewith she intimated her fingers to be full not approved, but rather, most approved: intimating perchance that the myrrh which is approved may be given with grace to the rest that labour, but that the most approved is truly, is specially, assigned to herself. Approved is that which chastiseth the restless body and subjecteth the chastised body to servitude, lest the law engrafted in the members withstand life and salvation utterly; which represseth the disordered motions [0423B] and the enkindling passions of the body as they sprout, and suffereth them not to be made oppressive. But most approved is that which utterly denieth entrance to all vices, which so banisheth the craftiness of enemies with the door of the mind barred, that not only doth she not permit a conceived wickedness to be led unto effect, but by a stronger advance doth not now even loosen the gate unto its conception. It is most approved when not only the hand committeth not an unlawful work, but the mind, far purer, admitteth nothing reprehensible; when not only the stronger spirit consenteth not to the law of the flesh, but both flesh and spirit have now felt nothing worthy of pardon. Which sort of myrrh, although it seem to be far from our borders, yet it is certain that it is not wanting to this so great virgin, but that by an excellent gift it is so at hand to her fingers that [0423C] she asserteth them to be not needy but rather full. For she it is whose discretion the more fully embraceth the bitterness of strictness, whose strictness is governed by a discreet moderation; who, being mighty in both, both rejoiceth with the doors shut to find the pleasing sweetness of silence, and utterly refuseth not, when she is touched by the hand of the spouse, to open. Whence she subjoineth: *The bolt of the door,* etc.



## CHAPTER XII.

*The bolt of my door I opened to my beloved: but he had turned aside, and was gone by.* After the Virgin had shown her hands and her fingers commendable with myrrh, and had prepared herself for the opening by a discreet exercise, she unbarred the door that was shut before, the bolt being removed, and what she had as it were hidden within she [0423D] declared at the command of him that knocked. For she who before rejoiced in a sweet silence now, the spouse knocking at the gate, judgeth it worthy that she speak, feeling that she pleaseth him none the less in speaking, whose grace she had rejoiced to obtain in silence. To him therefore whom she loveth she consenteth to open the door — that is, she looseth her silence and setteth about to instruct her neighbours: in the new and the raw laying a foundation of faith, in the advanced and the great heaping up a firmament of a loftier justice. Not for herself indeed but for her beloved doth she open the door and unbar the fastening; not for herself but for him that knocketh doth she loose the doors and set forth an opening, because when she layeth out the Lord's talent to the rest for usury, she taketh care not for her own glory or name but for his. For the charity wherewith the mother embraceth the spouse and the Virgin the son seeketh not the things that are her own, nor [0424A] catcheth after anything of her own, but whether she seem to give her pains to the leisure of contemplating or to the business of preaching, she serveth with a devout and whole spirit him alone whom she loveth. Who, although she affecteth leisure more than business, yet, cleaving to that, she utterly refuseth not this; but in business, when she now applieth herself to it, it more evidently becometh known by what cause she is held when she the more diligently cleaveth to leisure. For leisure indeed is not held worthy enough of the greatest praise if the sweetness of it be not held by a commendable cause; nor doth that highest judge will that leisure be held out to him as a merit, but that a commendable cause be shown beforehand in the face of it. Which the holy Virgin understanding, confesseth that she opened not the door but the bolt of the door, that not the bolt may be commended by the door but the door by the bolt; because that invisible [0424B] and most keen searcher of things invisible is an eager lover not so much of the study that proceedeth as of the cause that goeth before. *The bolt,* saith she, *of my door I opened to my beloved.* According to the letter, when any man is found knocking at the gate, it is not the bolt, as you know, but rather the door that is opened; and he indeed thrusteth back the bolt *245* who willeth to afford entrance to him that knocketh, which he had thrust in when he willed to keep the door shut. But here not the door but the door's bolt is said to be opened, wherein not the letter but a spiritual understanding willeth to be sought; because as the bridal chamber is not to be built of wood or of stone, so neither door nor bolt admitteth the grossness of a literal understanding. By the name of the door therefore silence is not unfitly figured, under the covering whereof the Virgin lieth hid and rejoiceth in her hiding-place; [0424C] but the bolt which is set to the door lest it be turned is the love of the Bridegroom, for whose sake the Virgin embraceth silence. Outward things indeed being put behind her, when the Virgin lieth hid shut up under silence, the love of the Bridegroom is in the cause, stronger than any bar; and, the cause and the effect running together in her, the Virgin, the home-born handmaid of quiet, rejoiceth unspeakably in her advancement. But if the beloved knock and ask the Bride to open, assuredly he willeth to find his own love in that very silence; and he proveth that love to be the cause of the silence she hath taken up, if for his sake for whom she rejoiceth in silence the Virgin endureth to be present at outward things also. Otherwise, if, the beloved knocking, the Virgin withstand with a stubborn mind, there is no doubt that she is instant upon silence with a desire that is not truthful; because she that truly loveth, not knowing how not to hear him whom [0424D] she loveth, rejoiceth to open her love to him whom she loveth, that she may be loved the more. The Bridegroom therefore knocking, the Bride taketh not away but bringeth forth the bolt evidently — that is, she diligently openeth the cause wherefore she rejoiceth in leisure — while for the Bridegroom's love she layeth aside and banisheth leisure, and for him for whose sake she was at leisure she now refuseth not to be instant upon business also. For whose sake, accustomed to the titles of victory, she willed to be shut in within; for his sake, now going forth without, she becometh an athlete again, showing in business by what cause she was held in leisure, singing that prophetic word which is briefly contained in the verse of the Psalm: *If I have remembered thee upon my bed, in the mornings I will meditate on thee [n: (Psal. LXII)]*. He calleth the bed that quiet wherein she is delighted in the chamber, when, the door being as it were shut, she is sequestered from the tumult of outward things; [0425A] but those morning things which return after the quiet silence of the night may rightly enough be called the action and the doctrine of temporal things. He therefore who for Christ's sake truly lieth hid under a pleasing silence, for the same Christ's sake acquiesceth also to give his pains to outward things; and he showeth what memory or what love of him he holdeth upon his bed when he shall have been called in the morning to labour. So also the Virgin, when, morning being as it were made, she receiveth commandment to speak, openeth to the Bridegroom the bolt wherewith her door was made fast, and showeth with what love, with what spirit she was held under silence, while she refuseth not to obey when she is asked to go forth into public. She openeth, I say, that to him who had knocked and had first moved her to open she may make satisfaction by answering, and may rejoice to find him without; that him whom in silence she could not yet sufficiently overcome, being called into [0425B] public, she may avail to ensnare by the merits of obeying. *But he had turned aside and was gone by.* The beloved knocketh at the Bride's door and asketh that it be opened to him, and, the bolt being opened, he cannot be found; and in a wondrous manner he inclineth himself to her presence, and when he is now thought to be as it were held, fleeing back to his own he straightway turneth aside. For the excellence of his nature is so incomprehensible that, when he hath poured himself with a large benefit into a mortal creature, he as it were offereth himself wholly and conferreth upon her that loveth a hope of holding him; and, her desire being stretched out, his immensity cannot be comprehended. He kindleth and stretcheth out the sweet desire of her that burneth; he provoketh her that burneth, he promiseth the presence of him that provoketh; and when he is now thought present amid the veins of her that more tenderly embraceth him, he fleeth her greedy hands and is withdrawn from the throat that gapeth for him. He fleeth, I say, [0425C] the Virgin, pressed not by a blameworthy offence but by corruptible flesh; and he turneth away from her eyes a face not granted her, and, not taking the thing away but rather deferring it, he rendereth her hope untired, maketh firm her faith, dwelling in light inaccessible. Who, turning away from his mother's gaze the face she most desireth, passeth to the bosom of the Father and to the light revealed to no mortal; whose immortality, although it will to be loved by mortals, yet willeth to be presented to none of them unto sufficiency. For although he will to be at hand for the helping of some and others abundantly, and more abundantly, yet he willeth always that something be wanting to all, so long as either guilt tendeth toward its remedy, or the weaker disease toward its medicine, or this corruptible thing busieth itself to lay aside its natural corruption. For not only [0425D] guilt but corruption also darkeneth us and conformeth us to the world wherein we live; and lest we fly forth from it more freely, it bindeth us with a knot not easily to be unravelled, by which thong our eye is not indeed utterly overwhelmed, but is dimmed. The beloved therefore, seeing the Virgin still subject to this binding, and held by the wrapping of a flesh that is not of vice but of nature, he presenteth himself to her the more frequently in what manner or order he will, but his immortal excellence quickly absenteth itself from a mortal. For the immortal, although he promise that he may in some sort be known and felt, yet admitteth not a mortal eye to see him more fully; but when he shall have come and shall have asked the Virgin to open, he straightway turneth aside and hasteneth to pass over to things invisible. He cometh indeed, when he poureth himself the more gratefully and sweetly into a pure mind; he passeth by, when [0426A] he hideth himself from the same lest he be seen face to face: he cometh, when he leadeth her into a true and sincere hope of the best vision; he passeth by, when he withdraweth himself from a desire that still hopeth and hasteneth. He cometh, I say, when he giveth the Virgin to thirst for the clear fountain of good; he passeth by, when to her that thirsteth he giveth not to find more fully *246* that which she seeketh. He cometh, when he granteth the Virgin's faith to attain to the highest merit; he passeth by, when he suffereth not yet that faith pass over into the thing, and hope into sight. He cometh, lastly, when by commanding or by knocking he carrieth the Virgin over unto the advancement of obedience; he passeth by, when she, not arriving, is as it were dissolved into a certain failing: he cometh, when the Virgin stretcheth herself forth with a prosperous course unto the things before her; he passeth by, when she, running, hath not yet laid hold of the prize. From whom withdrawing her hand [0426B] rather than her mind, she addeth: *My soul,* etc.



## CHAPTER XIII.

*My soul melted as the beloved spoke. I sought him, and found him not; I called, and he answered me not.* The Virgin marvelleth, and beyond what can be told is astonished, and within herself pineth away with an exceeding stupor, while she the more diligently acquiesceth in the commands or the admonitions of him whom she tenderly loveth, and yet as yet groweth strong by no powers, by no merits, unto the obtaining of him. He indeed speaketh and admonisheth the Virgin to open; she riseth and hasteneth the more diligently to obey him that speaketh; nay, the word being heard, she is so brought down into an affectionate tenderness that she seemeth to herself melted as by a mighty burning. That Spirit being present who vehemently loveth to stand by, [0426C] the word of the Bridegroom, mightily glowing as fire in a furnace, parcheth the whole Virgin, and putteth every dross far from her, and melteth her into his own love as a fusible material. Being melted, she seemeth to retain nothing of her own, nothing proper to herself, but to offer herself apt and tractable unto every form whatsoever: so that whether she be suffered to lie hid within and to be present at spiritual things, or be bidden to go forth without, to speak to her neighbours and to profit them, her heart be not troubled, nor bring forth a complaint about the precept, but rejoice to stand by him that commandeth and to persist in what she hath begun. Since therefore she rejoiceth to be intent upon none but spiritual things, whether in leisures or in businesses, and, the things that are behind being put after her, to be stretched out only unto the things before; she as it were complaineth that he whom she seeketh with so great [0426D] study, whom she seeketh with an eye so purged, is not yet found, nor doth she come to him with unveiled face. Him, saith she, I love with my whole heart, him with my whole soul, with all my powers; I cease not to call, I join prayers to prayers, vows to vows: and being sought he straightway slippeth away, and doth not yet more fully give what he promiseth; being called, although he heareth, yet he answereth not sufficiently to my desire. What is it therefore that, when he speaketh — that is, when his sweetness becometh known to me — my soul, tasting it, now melteth wholly with a fiery love; and when I seek the more greedily, he, as though envious, absenteth himself, and answereth not her that calleth — that is, presenteth not the face that is sought? Who nevertheless, considering me set in so great a desire, suffereth me not to be destitute of all solace whatsoever; but lest, that which I asked being deferred, I should seem to myself too much circumvented, [0427A] while I seek, I am sought; while I find not, I am found.

## CHAPTER XIV.

*The watchmen who go about the city found me: they struck me, and wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my cloak.* [var: Vulg. Cant 5:7 *Invenerunt me **custodes** qui circumeunt civitatem… tulerunt pallium meum **mihi** custodes murorum*. Migne's *vigiles* is the word the Vulgate uses at Cant 3:3 instead, and it makes the verse's two parties two different words; the exposition below turns on the distinction.] Far back the same Virgin is said to have been found by the watchmen [n: (sup. l. III, c. 22)], and the Virgin to have the more diligently accosted them that found her; who study the more anxiously to go about the city of the faithful, and, the reprobate being neglected, to impart their due care to the elect. Whereon I remember that I said in that place the things which occurred at that time — I know not whether they deserved to please or to suffice the reader; and lest perchance a repeated exposition of the same things be a burden, I pass over to expounding those things only which have lately been heard. *They struck me,* saith she, *and [0427B] wounded me.* The companions of the Bridegroom, to whom the care of the faithful is committed, who watch over their flock with an unremitted anxiety, go about Jerusalem, praising the name of the Lord upon the walls, and they cherish and promote those whom they shall have seen about to come to him. Nor doth it suffice them to visit once, but they are not grieved to visit again, and they rejoice to inspect and to perfect the affections of them that go forward; and those whom they shall have known to pass over from virtue to virtue more strongly and more freely, these they love to find, being sought the more frequently, in their purpose. They are therefore reported to find again the Virgin found before, and they follow up her fervid love with a due favour; and they whose care it is to arouse and to kindle them that love, that he may be loved the more, lift up and commend him that is loved. But while commending [0427C] the unspeakable magnificence of the Creator, they bring in upon the Virgin's mind a fuller force of love; who, while they desire to relate, and yet suffice not, how great is the excellence of him that is loved, the Virgin, strongly struck, is wounded with a sharper dart. For the praise of the beloved is a certain dart or arrow, wherewith when the mind of this Virgin *247* hath been worthily sought after, she rejoiceth not so much to be grievously pricked as to be sweetly pricked to compunction; nor is she accounted so much pierced through with a dart as soothed with a healing draught. By which dart or draught being the more sweetly dissolved into love, she seemeth to herself the more gratefully destitute of the things that are of the body; and, the sense of bodily things being unnerved wherein she was the more hardly wrapped, she loveth the more tenderly by how much the more freely she is set in mind among the heavenly things. So doubtless [0427D] the Virgin rejoiceth that her cloak is taken from her, when with a mind as it were naked she feeleth herself lifted up among the heavenly things; when she feeleth the exceeding praises of the Bridegroom preached by the watchmen, and feeleth herself stripped by the kindling of those praises from the care of bodily things. For she who is set among bodily things, either by the law of mortals or by the love of carnal men, is covered the more laboriously with a certain cloak as it were; whence it cometh to pass that if she be drawn out of it, either utterly in effect or in the affection of a devout spirit, she rejoiceth to open to the Bridegroom, and to cleave to him the more openly with an uncovered face. Whereunto when the watchmen exhort the Virgin with admonitions or with praises, they are said to wound her when she is struck and to take away her cloak; and while her mind is intent upon their presence or their converse, forgetful of her own flesh she stretcheth herself wholly into the love of the spirit. For to this end are the ministering spirits sent to men, to this end do they strive with much anxiety [0428A] when they have been sent, that they may instruct [sic: *informen t*] any lesser ones whatsoever unto lawful things, lest they transgress, but may urge the greater ones to forsake even lawful things with a stronger desire. Who, when they find the Virgin glowing with the torches of love, lay wound upon wound and study to inflame her the more, and take from her the cloak wherewith she is naturally clad — that is, the care wherewith all mortality is found to care for itself. For so do they cry out that he who is loved is admirable, so do they preach him unapproachable, that they may snatch the virgin mind wholly into an ecstasy; that, forgetful of the body with whose heavy presence she for the most part grieveth to be wrapped about, she may reckon herself for a little while loosed from the burden of it. Nevertheless the watchmen show not themselves for long to the Virgin either, but are quickly withdrawn from her to whom they sometimes condescend; not [0428B] utterly deferring to her will, but rather with a subtle prudence to her sanctity, and betaking themselves back to the care of the rest, to the guarding of the walls. But by the name of the walls I judge the apostles to be figured, by whose anxiety the Church rejoiceth to be defended; who, raised up and carried up not, as is wont, with stone or with mortar, but with a heap of virtues and with the indissoluble firmament of charity, go about the city, strongly equipped for its guarding — if yet they have been worthily guarded by the watchmen. Whom the most devout Virgin, considering them to be carried up unto advancement, because she cannot yet fully attain unto her beloved, turneth herself to them, willing to use a brotherly solace, not envying but rejoicing together with their grace or their salvation.



## CHAPTER XV.

[0428C] *I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you announce to him that I languish with love.* The Virgin, after she had been prevented, as hath been said above, by the admonitions of her Beloved, and, he turning aside, had been found by the watchmen; these also withdrawing themselves, willeth to return to the daughters of Jerusalem — that is, to the apostles — and to accost these also concerning him whom she loveth with so great a desire. You, saith she, who after the likeness of daughters burn the more vehemently with the tenderness of love, who prepare the inward chamber of the mind for the invisible Bridegroom; you I admonish — nay, lest the admonition be held insufficient, you I adjure, willing that none pass over what is so firmly adjured. If therefore by any manner or order it shall have been granted you to find the invisible, to touch [0428D] the unapproachable: announce ye, preach ye, that I am burdened with a tender love, that by your intervention I may deserve to be commended to him whom I love. If a purified delay hath held you in suspense, if it hath led you to the Bridegroom with a prompt desire, with an eye made clean: tell him of my heats, of my untiring love, of my mighty languor; ask him that he attend, calling to mind a wounded charity. But if the day most desired shall have led any of you out of the body, if you shall have come thither first, the linen cloth of the flesh being cast off, with a face utterly unveiled — because both the last for the most part rejoice to be made first, and they who seemed the first complain to be made the slower — if divine grace shall have given you an unhindered way, and you shall have found him first, whom we seek together, being sought for: I will that, when you have found him, you announce with what heat I am held, with what love, with what failing [0429A] I languish, with what desire or with what languor I faint away. If you, I say, the king's table shall have received; if the light that is found shall have poured itself over you before, while I remain in darkness, being still with Joseph kept in the prison: remember me who am held, and let a fresh prosperity not lead you into forgetfulness, but ask the mighty Lord that he lead me out also the sooner. And, that he who is mighty may be moved with a swifter mercy, say ye that I languish, and that my languor is intolerably weighed down; and, lest he laugh at my pains and at a heavier impatience, announce ye that this languor is begotten not of hatred of him but of love. It is an immoderate languor, which warmeth mine own soul with a more vehement fever, nay rather, being stronger than fire, melteth it like wax; which soul, being melted with heat, groweth utterly torpid toward the transitory things of the world, [0429B] *248* and, now knowing not to speak save of the Bridegroom, groweth the more languidly dumb toward all else. Which the daughters of Jerusalem weighing, they answer: *What manner of one is,* etc.

## CHAPTER XVI.

*What manner of one is thy beloved of the beloved, O thou most beautiful among women: what manner of one is thy beloved, that thou hast so adjured us?* [var: Vulg. Cant 5:9 repeats *ex dilecto* in the second question — *qualis est dilectus tuus **ex dilecto**, quia sic adiurasti nos?* Philip expounds the omission at 0430B–C and reports that most of the codices he could find carry the phrase twice.] The daughters of Jerusalem, hearing themselves the more diligently adjured by the Virgin that, if they find the Beloved, they should announce to him that she is sick even unto languor, seem to be the more inflamed unto the finding of him, and set about to inquire the more studiously what manner of one he is who is sought. Thou, say they, who hast already known the beloved by a wondrous privilege of love, out of whom by a new fashion thou hast known thyself Bride, mother, Virgin: hereby thou already seemest to us worthily most beautiful among all [0429C] women, thou who art not held by the blindness of us all, nor by a lot equal with ours. Because in no ages past hath the divine bounty granted this, and no woman hath so come near to the pleasing of him of whom the speech is: we know that none shall be better able to instruct our ignorance, and to impart to us some knowledge, such as it may be, of that same one who is sought. For this cause perchance hath he not yet utterly sent thee forth from the present world, and hath not yet admitted thy desire into full rest, but hath left thee among us, though against thy will, that thou mayest teach who he is that revisiteth thee the more frequently. For by how much the oftener and the more lovingly thou beholdest him, though through a glass, by so much the more dost thou deserve to obtain a fuller knowledge of him; and [0429D] by his visiting and his knocking thou art beyond doubt admonished to open for this end, that thou be not slothful to pour back upon the lesser ones the knowledge thou hast received. Say therefore what manner of one is he whom thou wilt have sought by us also, unto whom thou allegest us as messengers, if he shall have given himself to be found? Say what manner of one he is, lest in seeking we be rashly seduced, and, darkened with error, be brought in upon one instead of another. For because thou hast adjured us so firmly, so lovingly, we will not to despise but rather to attend to what thou hast asked; and we truly account the word of the oath as a precept: only say what manner of one is that beloved of thine of the beloved. We know indeed that thou lovest the Father, whose Son thou so affectest, and that thou failest not to join the begetter to the begotten in loving; but because none hath seen the Father save the Son, and none save through the Son, whereas to thee the same Son [0430A] hath not at all begrudged himself: tell us, if thou hast aught, of the quality of that same Son, of whose quantity we either hear or understand nothing, or but little. And because we too rejoice in no mean measure to love him whom thou lovest, we inquire for the grace of love not once only but again, that when thou hearest the inquiry of this attentive one repeated, thou mayest prudently understand with what affection it is asked by them that love. Let therefore the inquiry pointedly repeated move thee, that thou defer not to answer to the things inquired by them that love; and say what manner of one that beloved of thine ought to be reckoned, how God man may be firmly believed and loved. He indeed is God of God, light of light, and of flesh flesh, man of a virgin: and we will to be taught by thee what we owe, and to whom, since to each substance that which is its own [0430B] and proper ought to be rendered. For which cause also the aforesaid inquiry is fittingly repeated, wherein a twofold love of a twofold substance is unfolded; the knowledge whereof, because it is folded up in a certain volume as it were, a diligent inquiry is instantly applied to the loosing of its seal. She asketh therefore once, and asketh again, that it be more manifestly declared to her in what manner that giant of a twin substance willeth to be loved; what he willeth to be thought of himself according as he is called *beloved* *of the beloved,* and what according as he is called *beloved* and *of the beloved* is not added. For the first inquiry, when it had said *Beloved,* straightway setteth under it *of the beloved;* the second, repeating *beloved,* addeth not *of the beloved* according to certain codices: giving thereby to understand that God is none the less worthy to be loved [0430C] out of the Father by loving; but that man, although he be loved, is yet not worthy to be embraced equally out of man. For the deity of the Son is loved equally in the Father also; but his humanity, not knowing a father, is not so loved in his mother also — which that twofold inquiry seemeth subtly to admonish, whereof the first set down *of the beloved,* and the second willed to keep silence. But if any shall say that both the first set it down and the second kept it not silent, I will not to contend overmuch, nor stubbornly to strive against it, because I have found many codices to support this testimony. For, although not all the codices I could find, yet very many of them, as in the first inquiry, so in the second also have *beloved of the beloved;* nor have I sufficiently ascertained whether *of the beloved* was repeated by the author, or rather written by a fault [0430D] or an error. But *beloved of the beloved* may be said, man of man, because the Virgin both loveth the son in that he is man, and loveth that of which he is; for she loveth her own flesh, *for no man hated his own flesh [n: (Ephes. V)]*. We indeed love him because, being made man, he is partaker of our nature, and the creator of us all took upon him the lowly things of the creature; but the Virgin loveth him not only as made man, but as made man out of *249* herself, and out of that whereof he was made man she rather loveth herself for his sake. Whose becoming man, although it deserve worthily to be loved by angel or by man, yet it more befitteth him to be loved by her in whose womb, being the Virgin's, he becometh man; and what the obedience of all creation of necessity rendereth to him made man, the virgin, richer in grace, doth by a certain voluntary force of nature. Which [0431A] the daughters of Jerusalem seem to intimate in their inquiring, when they say not: What manner of one is *our* beloved, but: *What manner of one is thy beloved,* giving thereby to understand that that beloved is rightly assigned to the Virgin as it were specially, whose love nature together with grace mightily worketh. Of which beloved being inquired of, the Virgin deferreth not to answer, nor seemeth to envy the knowledge of him to them that seek it: understanding that, though she desire to be dissolved, she must yet for this end remain, that she may study to teach upon the housetops what she hath drawn in the chamber.



## CHAPTER XVII.

*My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands.* My beloved, saith she, whose acquaintance you have not yet (as it seemeth) acquired, but which by a zeal of acquiring you have already carefully sought out, is conspicuous not with one splendour only, but with a twofold [0431B] splendour, whose inestimable whiteness joineth to itself a pleasing redness. Now whiteness is a light unfailing, unapproachable to them that are dim of sight, a day that knoweth no evening, not pressed down by any darkness that followeth after: a light shining white eternally, and none the less the whiteness of eternal light, enlightening angels as well as men, present alike to the abiding and to the perishing. It is, I say, the whiteness of light, a light present to all yet not shown to all, shining indeed in the darkness, and not comprehended by the darkness [n: (Joan. I)]; a whiteness brighter than the sun, a light that hath gone beyond whiteness, snow, taking on a red garment, yet suffering no stain upon the garment. For God, the Word of God, the Only-begotten of the Father, the image of the begetter, putting on a servile body, the tunic of misery [0431C] and of toil, and conversing as man among men, liveth a life so modest that to them which look worthily he offereth as it were a ruddy countenance. For taking true flesh of others, he was so made like unto men that in the eyes of the dim-sighted there remaineth to him neither comeliness nor look: and being needy and weak, and, according to Zacharias [n: (cap. III)], wearing filthy garments, he sickeneth with foulness, he waxeth pale with a miry face. But I, the mother, whose mind is not darkened, whose understanding is not dull, to whom above all others my own child-bearing hath been made known and my conceiving made clear — I know my son's flesh to be utterly alien from every vice, and that he taketh nature, and of guilt taketh upon him nothing save the penalty. He therefore, as it were a fugitive, blusheth at every vice whatsoever, and sustaining its penalty alone, he is beyond doubt not befouled but reddened: [0431D] nor is it the hurt of guilt, but rather a flight from hurt, when his cheeks are suffused with the blood-red ruddiness of the passion. Nor the cheeks only, but the whole garment of the body is red; the passion maketh the whole comely, and empurpleth it with a penal adornment: and that which to any sinner is ignominy and an intolerable loss, is to him nothing but grace and a commendable increase of glory. Lastly, fire also is red and is found of one colour with blood, whose heat guilt endureth not, if it be not prevented by mercy; and he whose wood, hay, stubble maketh trial not of light but of burning — that fire, saving gold, silver, stone, measureth back to each the like [n: (I Cor. III)]. My beloved therefore is a fire burning up [0432A] the chaff, parching the mire, bringing the reprobate to nothing, mercifully chastening the dissolute: a fire shut up in an earthen vessel, red with a judicial power, shaking round about in judgment with a red power. For God, whom as Son he willed to be substantially united to himself before the ages, him in the end of times he willed to be found in the habit of a man, whose becoming man cannot easily be known by any, save by him to whom he hath willed to impart his grace thereunto. Which grace assuredly he willeth to be sought by the desire of the studious and the study of them that desire, and to you, as I understand, who worthily seek it, he willeth to grant it; and I envy you not, since I myself seem to be prevented by that same grace, but I teach them that seek, and I rejoice that you are effectually instructed. He is therefore the brightness of glory, the figure of the substance, the image of the paternal Godhead, the whiteness of eternal [0432B] light, the mirror of the divine majesty [n: (Hebr. I)]; he is white in the white Father, sprinkled with no stain, ever clean; and enduring to have a mother, he willed to become ruddy. Shining white, I say, as the light of light, he sought withal to be red; but being red that he might take counsel for us, he ceaseth not to shine white in himself eternally: among the choirs of angels and the crowds or assemblies of men, no giant is mightier, none is found like unto him. Wherefore out of thousands the Father, the more solicitous for us, chose this one, whom, sent by his own will, no hard law or necessity constrained; but being made priest and victim, he offered himself in sacrifice by his will, laying down the soul he had taken, and by a like power taking again the soul he had laid down. And it is excellently defined by the aforesaid [0432C] number, when this finite number is put for every infinite, that out of all, angels as well as men, who can be comprehended in no number, he alone should be the chosen for the ministry of offering. For no other, whether man or angel, was able so to offer, and no man's oblation could effectually confer this; and therefore out of thousands, that is, out of the infinite number of them all, he is singularly chosen, *250* who more perfectly effecteth that for which the imperfect sufficeth not. And that he is worthy to be chosen through whom this benefit is conferred, a worthy sequence of praises is subjoined in the testimony that followeth.



## CHAPTER XVIII.

*His head is the finest gold, his locks as the raised boughs of palm trees, black as a raven.* This beloved of the Virgin, [0432D] even as he is not of one begetting, so is he believed not to be of one substance or nature; because both from the Father alone he is believed to have that which he is as God, and from the mother alone that which he is as man: and thus, being of a twofold substance or nature, Christ abideth alike God and man. In which juncture, wherein a twofold nature have to come together into one person, there is one thing principal and another secondary to be found; and that indeed may by the privilege of dignity be named the head, but this other, whatsoever it be, may — if nevertheless it so seem — be fitted to it by some likeness. The head of Christ therefore is that principal nature in him which, begotten of the Father, is believed coequal to him that begetteth; according to which, as he is not greater than the Father, [0433A] so neither is he less than him; but greater, as than every man, so truly than himself also. Now this head is not unfitly compared to gold — to gold, I say, the finest, which is approved above the rest, which by the worth of its own price holdeth the primacy over all metals, and which, though it lie perchance in the mire, is not disfigured by any miry nature. For the Godhead of Christ, which he is known to have coeternal and common with the Father, taking our flesh, kept itself immune from carnal faults: and being mercifully bowed down by a deep counsel toward our mire, as it were, it lay hid under the shadow of the flesh, defiled by none of its filth. By this mystery therefore, wherein God bowed himself down, remaining in his own nature, and by the voluntary right of his power was wondrously made a creature — these natures running together, and neither complaining [0433B] of loss — Christ, God and man, was given to us out of such a juncture. In which juncture God, or the Godhead, is borne above after the manner of a head, and man, or the manhood, is brought in beneath after the manner of the feet or of the body. And the head, like gold, is more precious than all bronze, forasmuch as the creator is believed to be preeminent over all creatures. But the feet, or the body, are a vessel of clay or of earth, which, taken out of a hurt matter, is rendered alien from all vices; over which, as a head, he standeth eminent who taketh it up, who advanceth what he hath taken, enlighteneth what he hath advanced, and consumeth it not. Such a head in Christ usurpeth not to itself the primacy undeservedly — a head which foulness maketh not bald, which no unseemly baldness disfigureth; but, all foulness being put far off, being fortified with an inborn beauty, it is adorned for the showing of itself with befitting [0433C] locks. Now his locks are beyond doubt the virtues of the heavens, the worthier creatures, the preeminent choir of angels, who, while others flowed away and fell irrevocably into hell, cleaving more firmly to the head, remain fixed for ever. Who by the privilege of excellence and by the merit of the dignity they have obtained are like not to any trees soever, but to the raised boughs of palms, which warriors carry in their hand when their enemies are overcome, when on a festal day, all resplendent, they desire to show themselves conquerors. And those raised boughs of the palms are said to be the little branches which are advanced on high above the rest by a tall uprightness, which, when being advanced they have stood more firmly with their top on high, remain in all seasons alike unbending both in stiffness and in comeliness. So the virtues of the heavens are raised on high [0433D] above the rest, when they rejoice to enjoy him by whom, while the others fell, they were saved; to behold whose face they hasten ever to lift themselves up, and persisting in desire, they turn not aside through any languishing weariness. Whence as men triumphing they are glad to bear the raised bough of the palm, when, now secure concerning themselves, they glory in the titles of victory, when, fear being put far away, they keep now a festal day, carrying in their hand the branch that showeth forth the gift they have obtained. They indeed hold themselves forth to them that seek to see God, and they show not the bare head of Christ everywhere to any that will: and the splendour of the gold admitteth not the eyes of them that strain toward it, but that it may in some measure be borne, the hair goeth before them to meet them. [0434A] Which hair assuredly taketh not away the presence of that same head, but promiseth it, and by a fitting progress admitteth us afterward unto it; wherein, although it hangeth first and nearer by a certain glue of love, yet to us that follow far off it condescendeth by a certain likeness. For cleaving to the head the beauty of the locks shineth out, but condescending to us their foulness appeareth: the locks are white as a lily when they present themselves to the golden head, but when they are at hand to us, they represent the blackness of a raven. Considering the head of Christ, who with God the Father hath naturally one being, they rejoice to be like to the tall and glowing raised boughs of the palms. But considering whatsoever they understand to have been made, compared with the white maker, they see it to be as it were black. The angels therefore, lifted up [0434B] by the strivings of contemplation toward their maker, see that the Creator far excelleth all creatures; and that he indeed is white, or is somewhat that may be reckoned brighter still, while these grow as it were torpid and are made like unto blackening ravens. For by how much the more they hang upon loving him *251* with a greater desire, by so much the more do the angels perceive not only men, but themselves also, to be black; and to whom the excellence of the head shineth out brighter than gold, to those same their own humble consideration groweth black. So assuredly the locks of Christ are like, as hath already been said, to the raised boughs of palms, when they attentively consider the height of his Godhead; and yet they are not unfitly said to grow black after the manner of a raven, when by their own cry they confess themselves far unlike to him. For when they strongly and singularly love his eternal beauty, [0434C] they cry out with a humble voice that they are black and abject: considering that that which hath its beginning from another, and lacketh not an end save through another, is not compared to him who through himself abideth without beginning and without end. But this consideration, whereby the angels extol the head of Christ and humble themselves in the contest, derogateth not, detracteth not from their merits, nor from their crown; but they the more confidently seek out or obtain the branch of victory, by how much the more evidently they cry aloud that they are black and humble, like a raven.



## CHAPTER XIX.

*His eyes as doves upon the brooks of waters, which have been made washed, and sit beside the fullest streams.* [var: Vulg. *super rivulos aquarum, quae lacte sunt lotae* — "upon the little brooks of waters, which are washed with milk." Philip's exposition requires the milk, and glosses it four times below.] The Bridegroom hath eyes also, wherewith he goeth about and surveyeth all things, and with a mighty compassing advanceth [0434D] and illumineth what he hath seen; which eyes he loveth to open for the bestowing of his gifts upon us, and, lest he condemn, he hasteneth to cover us because of our deserts. Whence also these eyes are said to have not the eagle's severity, but with a more gracious affection they hold the dove's simplicity, because assuredly the eagle seeth far more severely and more keenly for the prey, but the dove more innocently, signifying a mild and simple discipline. And since eyes of this sort are likened to doves rather than to eagles, I deem it not unfitting if they be called grace and truth, because in grace and truth God made all things, and saw all that he had made to be very good, and vouchsafeth to angels as well as to men that are good a reward or a crown. For he who gave being to the angels, who [0435A] had not been, willed, when some of them fell, not to be wanting to the others that remained; and those whom he saw with grace, lest they should fall by a proud wickedness, he rendered fixed and stable by truth, so that now they could not fall. But that angel whom God looked not upon with the eye of grace turned himself aside from the uprightness wherein he had been made; and not being prevented by grace, he received no stable footing in truth, and being turned away from either eye, the wretch irreparably deceived himself. Happy therefore is that man whom the divine goodness beholdeth with the eye of grace, when, guilt requiring it, he is already held beneath the tree, when, his wife's false counsel being preferred to the rule of truth, he feareth the voice he hath heard, because of the fresh ignominy of his nakedness. For him whom, darkened beneath the fig tree, he mercifully enlightened with the look of grace, he consequently [0435B] recalled by an order gracious enough to the light of truth: and him that was worn down with labours, that he might render a requital for the wickedness he had presumed, grace instructed, that it might render him fixed unto truth. But that he might confer this benefit upon the whole human race, and, its origin being hurt, might set mercy above judgment, when the world was now pressing on toward evening there arose a light of sudden newness, whereby the Word was made flesh, full of grace and full of truth. Whose brighter rising, when it poured itself into us that were dim of sight, poured over us these two luminaries; and being made man he vouchsafed to see us with a twofold eye, that is, to join to grace, which seeth beforehand, truth as an undivided companion. For those whom he saw with grace, that he might endow us undeserving with deserts, he saw also with truth, that he might now heap rewards upon the deserving; who assuredly giveth the first deserts to none but the undeserving, [0435C] and again crowneth none with the rewards of deserts but the deserving Therefore he saw us with grace, when he called us undeserving, and them that were called he provoked unto justice and to the deserts of justice; he saw us also with truth, when, as we yielded our assent, he bestowed himself as a helper, who before had bestowed himself only freely as a promiser. Grace indeed was the calling and the promise of him that strengtheneth, but truth was the exhibiting or the benefit of him that helpeth: nor is it profitable enough if grace promise us any good thing with a liberal hand, if truth its companion answer not to that promise. Rightly therefore is the Bridegroom said to have eyes, wherewith he innocently and simply beholdeth all the elect; whereof the one going before envieth not, but freely seeth the undeserving, [0435D] and the other followeth them as now deserving, and dischargeth the office of truth. And since they look not upon us too severely, but regard us with a harmless simplicity, and meditate no prey, but stretch themselves out unto the salvation of us all, rightly doth the holy Virgin say that they are like doves, which their own nature maketh to be simple and harmless. Which doves haunt the brooks of waters and the fullest streams, that they may foresee the ravening birds which wickedly set themselves against the simpler sort — as they say who search more curiously into the natures of birds, and prove by certain conjectures that the matter standeth so. But that the doves are said to be washed not with waters but rather with milk intimateth that they are far removed from material doves; and because neither use nor reason admitteth *252* that doves be washed so, [0436A] this saying plainly sendeth us back to a spiritual understanding. The eyes therefore of the Bridegroom, as hath already been said, being like unto doves, are not only over the waters but over the little brooks of waters, when his grace and truth teach us the content of the Scriptures, showing whence, and by what way, and whither the doctrine of the prophets floweth as it passeth by. For they, drawing in joy out of the fountains of the Saviour, bring down even unto us the manifold promises of the Creator, which cease not to come upon us and to pass us by with a promising murmur, until the thirst of them that wait be refreshed with a fulfilling gift. Lastly, to this end are the Bridegroom's eyes said to be over the flowing abundance of the waters, and they set us in that same place, and grace and truth behold us so set, that they may teach us that nothing that is begotten [0436B] standeth fast, after the manner of a little brook, but by a natural flowing and by its own motion hasteneth to destruction. For over this — that the fashion of this world passeth away, and is rolled onward in the course of things, and that the inconstancy of times and days suffereth nothing to stand — there is need of a cleaner and simpler understanding, that in these transitory things the profit may be firmer and more solid. Therefore perchance the doves to which the aforesaid eyes are compared are reported to be washed not with waters but rather with milk, because to milk a snowy whiteness is naturally assigned, wherein the clean simplicity of the dovelike grace is designated. Which grace assuredly so seeth us, and so also giveth us to see, that it both harm us not and will have us not to harm another: and in our sight it willeth the mirror of the Scriptures to shine, that we may be able to foresee the hurtful assaults of others. Which [0436C] cleanness of seeing the prophet Habacuc commendeth in the Lord himself: *Thy eyes are clean,* saith he, *that thou mayest not behold evil, and thou canst not look upon iniquity [n: (Habac. I)]*. Good eyes indeed, which are known to shine again with so great a cleanness that they mercifully choose not to see our malice, which cannot turn back their gaze upon our iniquity, but rejoice to advance their glance toward our profit. Whence also they are consequently said to sit beside the fullest streams, forasmuch as they enlighten us and make us to sit beside those same streams, when they teach us to approach the Scriptures of the Gospel, which flow with a fuller doctrine, and to embrace them with a more gracious affection. For after the manner of waters the prophetic Scriptures make us fruitful, but the Scriptures of the Gospel [0436D] flow far more plentifully and abound, because in the former the spiritual understandings are wrapped up in figures and dark sayings, but in the latter they shine fully and are unfolded in plainer words. The bright fountain of good poured itself into us of old with an abiding little brook, but afterward more largely overflowed us with the great rush of a river, because both by the old Scriptures it gave us a profitable watering to drink, and afterward by the Scriptures of the Gospel it more fully satisfied our thirst. Who would not commend these eyes of the Bridegroom, like unto doves, which mingle for us the brooks and the fullest streams of the Scriptures, whose sight, knowing not our evils, advanceth and maketh fruitful our good things, and with a prosperous profit cleanseth us as with a milky whiteness? For that the eyes, or the doves to which the eyes are likened, are recorded either to sit beside the waters or to use a milky [0437A] washing, ought to be reckoned not frivolous but profitable, not superfluous but rather mystical, wherein the Bridegroom loveth to work our salvation by grace and truth. Whereof it is subjoined: *The cheeks,* etc.



## CHAPTER XX.

*His cheeks are as beds of spices, set by the perfumers.* After the praises of the eyes, the Virgin maketh a passage to the cheeks also, which she judgeth in no wise alien from the merit of praise; wherein, as was said long since [n: (supra l. I, c. 2)], the beauty of the face shineth out, and the face is worthy to be praised for the merit of its fairness. The Virgin therefore praiseth the Bridegroom's face, that is, the beauty of the Godhead, which flowereth with a certain laughter and gloweth with the flower of honourableness, which appeareth cheerful and delightsome to them that behold it dutifully, and is found [0437B] profitable and fruitful by them that worship it devoutly. He indeed is *in form fair above the sons of men [n: (Psal. XLIV)]*, whose comeliness is inestimable and, beyond what can be told, fruitful; to whom, although she judged that nothing at all was properly to be compared, yet the Virgin compared him to beds of spices, by a certain licence of speech. Now beds are little gardens, rich not in gold, not in silver, nor indeed in things of this sort, but in aromatic trees and in manifold spices, out of which by the skilled hand of the perfumer a medicinal ointment is made, whereby wounds are healed and a soothing is given to pains. So also is the Bridegroom's, that is, his divine beauty, wherein is nothing defiled, no unseemly foulness: adorned indeed with a flower, not with a transitory colour, not too fraudulently sought out by art, but [0437C] with an inborn splendour and with a form of worthy virtues. In which beauty eternity knoweth no beginning, immortality no end; an unwearied light shineth, change is fixed, peace resteth: power hath power, wisdom is wise, the presence of charity burneth, and there flourisheth a certain commonwealth, leagued together not of citizens but of virtues. Whose league is found not weak, not unprofitable, but whosoever loveth it findeth it mighty and profitable, while its aromatic ointment, while its confection or its fatness, is made unto us that are sick a mighty and sufficient medicine. For no *253* bed is set by a hand so prudent as to grow rich with spices so great, with a medicine so mighty; no perfumer hath adorned his little garden with plantings so effectual, nor pounded such [0437D] herbs or spices in his little mortar. Or certainly the cheeks of the bridegroom are his two substances or natures, for the Creator willed to be united personally to the creature; and a twofold substance was found to come together into one and the same bridegroom, and by a wondrous coming together to adorn as it were one face. Whose coming together made one God and man, long before divided, and, loosing the wall set between, joined heavenly things to earthly; condescending to men, it brought them an example and a doctrine, poured in the gift of grace, and afforded a salutary medicine. Whence also these cheeks are compared to beds, that is, to little gardens, out of which herbs and spices are fitly brought forth for aromatic uses, which assuredly the perfumers till with a carefulness that shall profit — perfumers whom, being taught in the healing art, the [0438A] care of the languishing that are to be made whole holdeth fast. For when God suffered the world to perish by sin through many thousands of years, and neither man nor angel prevailed to root it out, at length the perfumers prudently chose certain beds for themselves, out of which they gathered medicinal spices and the spices of salvation. For they joined together alike the divine nature and the human, and by a deep counsel laid upon them as it were a certain traffic of healing; and when these were joined into one person, as cheeks into one face, they compounded a spice, and refreshed the languishing world with the grace of health. Nor do the perfumers seem to me to be any other than the Father and the Son and their Spirit, who are said to take part in the aforesaid traffic by a common counsel; of whom, although none but the Son is rightly to be believed to be incarnate, yet the Father together with the Spirit are said to work [0438B] the incarnation. The cheeks therefore of the bridegroom, that is, the two natures which wondrously came together into one person, as beds set by the perfumers, brought forth aromatic spices, whose confection and the showing forth of a strange art conferred upon us the wished-for benefit of a salutary medicine. Worthily therefore, and for the cheeks' sake, doth the bridegroom deserve to be loved, in whose union the fruitful height of the mystery is contained, which the same perfumer turneth into an ointment for us that are sick, but for them that make progress, the Father together with the Spirit working with him, into a pigment. Whence it is subjoined: *The lips,* etc.

## CHAPTER XXI.

*His lips are lilies dropping the first myrrh.* [0438C]Whosoever is a teacher and lacketh not understanding knoweth, as I judge, that sometimes in the Scriptures the efficient is put for the effect; and because we come not to the effect of speaking save by the mouth and the lips, we find the mouth and the lips for the most part put for speech. By the lips therefore of the Bridegroom the Virgin willed to figure his words, which also she set herself, by a new manner of speech, to liken to lilies, because lilies, when looked upon, more simply signify innocence by their whiteness, and when bruised, more prudently confer a more liberal medicine. For the words of the Bridegroom know no guile, no deceit, and assuredly no falsehood, but being more diligently discussed they bring forth a firm truth; being more graciously understood they teach benevolence, innocence, chastity; being more perfectly loved they confer true holiness upon them that love. Which words, or [0438D] lips, are therefore said to drop the first or the chief myrrh, that is, to preach a doctrine effectual and necessary to all, because, although the wise men of the world willed both by writings and by words to condemn vices and to commend virtues, yet, *as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal [n: (I Cor. XIII)]*, they lacked spiritual efficacy.
