But the lips of the Bridegroom, bringing forth both the Old and the New Testament, confer in either a salutary lesson upon their hearers; because, although that which went before is perchance said to be in somewhat imperfect, since it found not yet the time of grace nor fitting hearers, this latter, which came upon it in the accepted time, brought a supplement, when the sun looked back upon the darkness and light came to them that sat in the shadow. And assuredly to the lips, whereof the one is necessarily [0439A] added upon the other that we may speak, the two Testaments agree, by whose admonitions we are rightly instructed; whereof the Old seemeth of itself to lie beneath as weak and insufficient, and the New, coming upon it, to fill up its insufficiency. In which Testaments, since they were brought forth by the two lips of the bridegroom and framed with a prudent craft unto the doctrine and salvation of us all, the same bridegroom alike provoketh his hearers to a twofold profit — such of them, at least, as by his gift have obtained a spiritual understanding. For he inviteth them both to love God and to have care of their neighbours, that, dispensing temporal things, they be not unmindful of eternal ones that every just man so put his hand to a temporal study or business that at fitting seasons he may the more eagerly apply himself to spiritual leisure. Because therefore the bridegroom's [0439B] lessons instruct us in these two pursuits, rightly are his lips two, and none the less are the Testaments two; that things which no discord soever of matters or of acts gnaweth at should in these also, by a like form, not disagree in the very number. For which cause also the lilies come in by grace of a seemly likeness, which in form or in colour exceed not the aforesaid pair, in the midst whereof somewhat *254* a little red is found, which is compassed about with leaves bent back and gleaming with whiteness. That middle redness indicateth a laborious action, which, while it is lived in this life, bringeth in much suffering; nor is any man so happy as to be able utterly to avoid the presence, the burning, some coming even to the shedding of their own [0439C] blood. But the whiteness in the leaves prefigureth that blessedness wherein the Bridegroom configureth our bodies to his own body, when, whiteness being drawn over — which befalleth us by merits together with grace — hiding, nay swallowing up what was mortal, he girdeth us about with immortal glory. So assuredly the lilies, agreeing with the lips in a twofold form or colour, signify present things in the short and red part, and the glory to come in the whiteness; whose kind droppeth the first myrrh, that is, a right profitable doctrine, at that time when the understanding of it wavereth not among us that are capable thereof.



## CHAPTER XXII.

*His hands are turned, golden, full of hyacinths.* The hands of the Bridegroom, as I judge, the Virgin named his works, which both when he was not yet born and when he was already born of the Virgin [0439D] he wrought; wherein so incomparable a praise of him that wrought them is held, that what he willeth is proved by an easy efficacy to be also what he can do. For which cause she saith also that these same hands are turned, intimating that nothing standeth in the way of the will of him that worketh, because a carpenter is found to do nothing more easily than with the lathe, and what hath been wrought with the lathe is found wholly round. In the lathe therefore the ease of him that worketh is understood, but the roundness holdeth the praise of him that consummateth, because he bringeth to effect whatsoever he willeth as soon as he willeth it, and what he willingly effecteth he also mightily perfecteth, knowing not how to slip back into defect. Which perfection assuredly, of an easy and rolling turning, is not of an angel, not of a man, not [0440A] of any simple creature whatsoever, but is of him alone who alone willed to be born of the Virgin, man and God; who was able to do whatsoever he willed, not simply as man, but as God also. To whom it rightly agreeth that the Virgin called these same hands golden, who in the gold, as it seemeth, figured the divine power, because as gold is said to prevail over the other metals, so in the Bridegroom's works the divine power is preeminent. For, to be silent of other things, that the Creator was made a creature by his own work, God willed to use his own power, not nature; and that, doing wonderful things in man, he endured grievous ones also — in the bringing of them forward it was not, as it seemed, a defect of strength, but a power. *Power,* saith he, *I have to lay down my soul [n: (Joan. X)]*. And the prophet: *He was offered,* saith he, *because [0440B] he himself willed it [n: (Isa. LIII)]*. In all things therefore which God willed to work in man, it is believed that neither lead nor tin, as it hath seemed to some, holdeth the primacy, but to them that rightly behold gold is conspicuous, gold shineth; and though it be not comprehended by the darkness, yet in the darkness the light shineth again. For the divine power, brighter and more precious than all gold, not appearing to blind men, flourisheth as it were more secretly in a treasury; and that which hideth itself from the eyes of the unbelieving, the cloud of the flesh being set between, spreadeth itself abroad (though unknown) into the branches of its works. But they who deserve worthily to understand that same power are not held by the love of visible works alone, but are rather kindled by the hope of invisible goods, and in them are held suspended by love and desire. Therefore the Virgin not only called the turned hands golden, [0440C] but with an equal testimony declared them full of hyacinths also, signifying in the hyacinths, which are stones like to the air in colour, the supernal goods which are commanded to be sought after out of love. Those very works indeed which God made man was seen to accomplish are known to abound in heavenly goods for them that behold worthily, while by a manifold doctrine they lead us in to a true understanding of them, and by sure promises bring us on to hope for them. For the dispensation of the incarnate Word containeth nothing else than hyacinths, to the buying of which it inviteth all that are nimble and girded, because the temporal working of Christ, which tendeth to nothing but heavenly goods, purposeth to lead us prompt and watchful to purchase the same by the merit of faith. Whose [0440D] praise is subjoined: *His belly,* etc.

## CHAPTER XXIII.

*His belly is of ivory, distinguished with sapphires.* Because the belly is held to be the softer and tenderer part in the body, by it the Bridegroom's flesh or manhood is rightly said to be signified, because, whereas he was God long before, he at length willed to be made weak for us, and to be made like to other men in nature, not in the vice of nature. But because *the Word made flesh [n: (Joan. I)]* was utterly ignorant of the faults of the flesh, the Virgin markedly called his belly not fleshly, because the softness of our custom or nature had not hurt the manner and the order of that begetting, such as she had known it. For that vice [0441A] which cleaved forthwith to the first men when they sinned hath by their desert so hurt the begetting of us all, that no man who begetteth can utterly *255* free himself from it, but maketh the guilt to pass over, as it were naturally, into the very child begotten. Which vice, which passing over, which now as it were a second nature, compelling both begetters and begotten to complain of the hurt, weakeneth the belly of all, that is, the flesh so begotten, and unnerveth and softeneth it, whose vicious softness no man's labour or industry taketh away from him. Which law, harshly implanted. The Virgin alone in conceiving is believed not to have felt, forasmuch as it is certain that she, knowing not a man, conceived of the Holy Spirit; and the guilt which after the manner of us all went not before her that bare came not to the Son, begotten without a father, of a mother. Whose conception brought [0441B] to his flesh not only no loss, but, the Spirit working, brought it no small strengthening; because as our begetting struck into us a nature worthy of wrath, so his flesh, conceived of the Spirit, is made stronger and more solid by nature. For from this, that both man and guilt were wanting to the conception against custom, and that moreover the Holy Spirit gave it a purer efficacy, he himself who was conceived — flesh indeed in substance, not carnal in vice — obtained a new strength of a certain natural eminence. Endowed with which nature he was utterly ignorant of the enkindling passions of the body, which generally oppress the rest of men living in this flesh; but those which are penal not by guilt but by the desert of guilt, he made subject to himself by a strength as of ivory. For unto hunger, thirst, sleep, [0441C] weariness, and such things as Scripture hath recorded him to have borne, he inclined not by any defect of strength, by the law necessary to us all, but, having by a certain inborn force powerfully surpassed the law implanted in us, he suffered none of these things save because, and when, and as much as he willed. Necessity therefore being a delay generally compulsive among us, he used his own will, powerfully effective; and he who, conceived man of the Spirit, could have not suffered human troubles nor been hurt, yet willed to bear hurts, that he might be able — which was that whereunto he had come — to be believed a man by men. For to this end had he come, that, the substance of flesh being assumed, he might truly be believed man, and by suffering willingly might heal the necessary sufferings of them that believe; that *the ivory belly,* [0441D] that is, the hidden and inborn strength of the manhood shown forth beforehand, might be turned into a remedy whereby our sickness, who truly languish, might be healed. Such a belly is not only clothed and girded with an ivory strength, but with *sapphires,* precious stones, is also *distinguished,* because the true flesh, which a singular conception strengthened with a wondrous fortitude, the Godhead joined to it beautified with an excellence of miracles. The sapphire stone is like the sky, when it is serene, when with a face as it were wiped clean it is seen alien from dark clouds; by which stone those works of the Bridegroom are rightly figured which, far above man, are specially assigned to the Godhead. For it is granted to man that he is flesh and yet [0442A] knoweth not the disordered motions of the flesh, that against soft heats he is found harder and groweth cold, bearing the part of ivory, since, if it be laid under a linen cloth, that same cloth is not burned though a coal be laid upon it. It is granted also to man that all the troubles which we are penally constrained to endure, he was able to keep off from his own body as well as his mind, as by a natural privilege, and none the less to apply the same to himself when he willed and as he willed, and, when applied, to restrain them, lest they avail more or less than the dispensation requireth. But it is granted to God that amid these things he changed water into wine by a wondrous mystery, that with scanty bread he satisfied many thousands of men, that he comforted all the sick with a wished-for remedy, and that at the last he raised the dead by the sole command of his voice. Therefore the ivory belly, [0442B] that is, the robust series of human works, is distinguished with sapphires, that is, with the beauty of divine ones, when amid those things which as man he was able, as he willed, strongly to endure, the heavenly excellence rejoiceth now and again to shine out in miracles. For he loveth neither always to work human things nor continually divine ones, but that the series of his working should be adorned by grace of distinction; and thus he so commendeth himself a man by an ivory strength, greater than Jonas or Solomon, that even in the man he showeth himself, to them that rightly believe, the beauty of the sapphire, that is, God.



## CHAPTER XXIV.

*His legs are pillars of marble, which are founded upon bases of gold. The legs* of the Bridegroom she nameth the ways or journeys whereby he came visibly unto us, when [0442C] he found us weak and torpid and knowing not how to travel, when, invisible in himself and by nature far unlike to man, condescending to men, he was made a creature, and appeared, and became known. Whose one leg was whatsoever belongeth to the incarnation and to a conversation that should pass away in time, and the other leg was that which pertaineth to his death and to his burial; so that his whole action and his whole passion were as it were two legs, whereby there came to us a salvation that should abide, while they passed away. Which are therefore not unfitly compared to pillars of marble, because these his journeys are proved straight and strong, since in willing what he was able there was a just straightness, and in fulfilling what he willed an equal and sufficient strength. And because it is doubtful to none that [0442D] the whole heap of works is confounded if *256* that which seemeth well heaped up be not founded upon a solid base, *the pillars of marble founded upon bases of gold* are recorded, which being set beneath them, those pillars are not denied to be stable and commendable. For whatsoever God, made man, willed to do or to suffer, he is believed to have done or borne unconstrained; but he was seen to lean upon that twin charity which, more precious than gold, assigneth all things set upon it unto firmness. For he loved God, whose commandment he willed to obey, and he loved men, to whom he knew his obedience would be profitable; in the one of which he understood the first and greatest commandment to be held, and in the other he neglected not the second and like unto it. The Son loved [0443A] the Father, because the Father also loved the Son; he loved men, whom together with the Father he alike disposed to save; whose twofold love he held as certain causes lying beforehand, whereby he endured to be made man, and in man to do and to suffer so many things.

## CHAPTER XXV.

*His fairness is as of Libanus, chosen as the cedars.* Because the Virgin above commended the bridegroom as it were by parts, and from the head even to the legs set forth his praises one by one, now with a shortened speech she comprehendeth as it were the whole alike, and highly esteemeth his fairness by comparison with Libanus. Among the other mountains by which the land of the Jews is said to be occupied — whose level plain complaineth that it is straitened by the frequency of the mountains — as they say [0443B] who know it, Libanus shineth out higher, more fruitful in trees, and groweth white with continual snows. Which is well said to hold the type of the bridegroom, forasmuch as the excellence of this mountain is compared to none of the saints; who, made fruitful with the plantings of virtues and with the density of works, knoweth not to be burned with vices, being whitened by the native frost of the flesh. Whom assuredly God the Father chose, unto the salvation of us all, that through him every just man might be advanced from virtue to virtue, and that by his examples, manners and doctrine the workshop of the Church might be built, as with beams that cannot rot. The cedar, of a nature that cannot rot, knowing no sudden failures, by its odour more largely scattered driveth off the assaults of serpents; which cedar Solomon with prudent counsel willed to employ, when he was zealous to set up [0443C] either a house for himself or the temple promised to the Lord. So also the Virgin's bridegroom is of a nature that cannot rot, knowing not to be hurt by guilt from the beginning of his begetting; whose odour of works, whose repute of virtues, whose praise of doctrine drive all hurtful things far from the thresholds of discipline. For which cause he is chosen that he may be placed in the building, that through him the house of God may be strengthened with a worthy strength, that no man may work anything at all worthy of praise which is not commended by his benevolence, as by the strong presence of cedars. For whatsoever is found to be raised up by the zeal of them that build cannot stand if it be not fortified with his cedarn strength; and the incautious workman, who measureth not himself with a worthy judgment, findeth whatsoever he doth without cedars to be liable to ruin. But he who chooseth the bridegroom for the safeguard of all his work findeth no ruin, [0443D] suffereth no loss, because his benevolence both giveth to them that build a welcome patience in their labours, and conferreth upon the building the far more welcome strength of cedars. Whereof also it is added: *His throat,* etc.

## CHAPTER XXVI.

*His throat is most sweet, and he is all desirable.* Because taste is contained in the throat, and holdeth the nearer place, wherein also it judgeth of all savoury things and of savour, by the name of the throat I reckon that taste is figured, by that manner of speech whereby the container is wont to be named for the thing contained. The taste therefore of the bridegroom is called not so much sweeter as most sweet, lest, if aught were said too little, somewhat should be reckoned wanting to him; because than that which proceedeth out of him, if it be tasted with a sound throat, no delightfulness is sweeter, no sweetness more delightful. For whether [0444A] a man attend distinctly to that which he is as God, or to that which he is as man, and stretch himself with a devout zeal to see what is proper to each, he seeth nothing subtler than this distinction, nothing more wondrous than this union, and tasteth nothing sweeter than a vision so subtle, so conspicuous. For he seeth that the Godhead, taking man, was in no wise consumed; nor did the manhood fail, but it profited, when it was wondrously taken up into God, where there is no confusion, no conversion of the one nature into the other, but a personal union, in the mystery of a virginal begetting. For the contemplating whereof, if a heavy rheum straiten not the eye, if the mind with open throat taste the delightfulness of this secret, what can be found sweeter than this taste, what happier than this throat, to which it is now granted to experience that which the angels desire? [0444B] But if the angels desire God, whom they contemplate unceasingly, and venerate him made man with an unfillable wonder, worthily do men also both desire and marvel at the same whole, and with their whole desire embrace him who is wholly desirable. For he is God, and there is none other beside him; he is man, clothed with the form of man for his own sake: worthy to be loved, not only because he is God, not only *257* because he is man, but because by a salutary mystery one and the same is alike God and man. He is man, I say, not such as any other man soever, but one through whom every man may be able to be made safe; that as a man was the fall or ruin of men, so, nay far more, this man may be the medicine of men. Who therefore would not desire such a one wholly, would not [0444C] wholly love him, would not wholly admire him? who would not rejoice to embrace him with his whole desire, as God and as neighbour? who would not seek such a one more zealously, would not hold him more eagerly if it fell to him to find him, and would not be zealous to instruct others with fitting admonitions to seek him? Therefore the prudent Virgin, who in love knoweth no rival, nor feareth a concubine, everywhere preacheth him whom she loveth, that he may be loved; and him whom she deserved to see such as he is, she willeth not to grudge to the rest, but rejoiceth with a solicitous affection to provide for them that stand by her. For which cause she thus concludeth: *Such is,* etc.

## CHAPTER XXVII.

*Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem.* Such, I say, is he by whose tender love I am held fast, and (as I seem to see) I am not [0444D] deceitfully beguiled; nor hath an intemperate love, as sometimes it useth, defrauded me, because a transitory speech hath not yet worthily praised him. Although many things have been said whereby it is clear that he is proclaimed commendable, yet must this proclamation still be judged insufficient, because such as I rejoice to perceive him to be, I am not yet able utterly to pour out in transitory words. And to this end have I set about to follow out his praises, so manifold — although the things which ought to have been said are not yet fittingly enough expressed — that he whom I love may in some measure become known to you, and that your mind also may grow warm toward the love of him. For he cannot be loved if he have not been understood, nor doth he seem to be understood if he have not also been loved; for this very cause I desire that he be understood and be loved of all, whom [0445A] I have loved, and whom I have understood to become a friend also to them that truly love. You therefore, daughters of Jerusalem, labour with all your strength to love him and to be loved by him, because nothing is holier than to love one so benevolent, so mighty, and nothing more blessed than to be loved by him who knoweth not how not to love him that loveth. *I,* saith he, *love them that love me [n: (Prov. VIII)]*. The praises of the Bridegroom being unfolded in so diverse a kind of figures, the Virgin is silent for a little while, and awaiteth [0446A] the answers of the daughters, considering whether perchance by this hearing they have received a fuller grace, whereby they may be more vehemently carried away into the love of him whom she preacheth. But before their answer be brought forth into the midst, I have thought it fitting that our pen be a little withdrawn from its toil; and that, where the Virgin was silent, the pen also choose to be silent, that this fifth book may at last rejoice to obtain its end.

## BOOK SIX.




## CHAPTER THE FIRST.

[0445A]

[0445B] *Whither is thy beloved gone, O thou most beautiful among women, whither is thy beloved turned aside, and we will seek him with thee.* The praise of the Bridegroom being heard, the daughters of Jerusalem are stirred up, and are provoked with a greater desire into the love of him; rejoicing that the Virgin hath spoken so many things beforehand concerning him, and hath followed out that quality of his after which she had inquired above. For above they had said: *What manner of one is the beloved of the beloved,* and now, rejoicing, they rejoice in him understood by mystical similitudes; but because he suffereth not himself as yet to be seen clearly even by them that understand and after a sort love him, they ask whither he is gone, that he may be sought by them more certainly. To whom, when the Virgin above [n: (l. IV, c. 10-12)] made haste to open the bolt of her door, hoping to find him nearer, whose voice knocking she had heard in the doors: *He,* saith she, *had turned aside and was gone by,* [0445C] and offered not himself to be seen of the Virgin — perchance that, the sight being withdrawn, he might render her more solicitous to seek. Since therefore the Virgin is found to have commended the Bridegroom in manifold wise, and it is certain that such a one, as hath been said already before, turned aside, the daughters of Jerusalem ask, and will be taught more diligently, to whom, as it were to a place, he that went away and turned aside willed to show himself. Such a one, say they, whose praises so manifold thou hast woven, unto whom thou hast so solicitously admonished us that thy love, nay thy languishing, should be told — how shall we either seek him, or, being sought, be able to find him, since we know not the place whereunto, when he escapeth us, he chooseth to come? Say therefore whether he hastened to the left, or rather to the right; say, if thou knowest, unto what desert, or unto whose, [0445D] he turned aside, that we, seeking, *258* be not carried away by a wandering error, and that we may follow after him, unto whom he came, by the imitation of desert. For when, thou teaching us, the place or the desert of the place shall become known, our mind shall the more burn to hasten thither; and we shall be carried away to seek the Bridegroom with a desire with thee, if not equal, at least like; of whose finding we shall not have the fruition unless thy benevolence accompany us. For we know that whosoever shall have sought him, thee being neglected, such an inquiry shall be proved utterly imperfect; nor willeth the Bridegroom to be found by us, or by the rest that seek, if he see not them that seek to be prevented by the fellowship of thy favour. With thee therefore, that is, thy patronage favouring us, we will seek him whom without thee, without thy benevolence, we are not able to find; by thy benefit our devotion shall follow after him: [0446A] being taught beforehand in what place, or in what desert of place, he tarrieth. [0446B] And in very truth none other shall be able to teach us better whither the Bridegroom is gone, or where he hath chosen to show himself present, than thou, who by the gift of grace hast entered into his sanctuary, and hast better known the secrets of spiritual understanding. To these things the Virgin answereth: *The beloved,* etc.

## CHAPTER II.

*[CAP. VI.] My beloved is gone down into his garden, to the bed of spice, that he may feed in the gardens, and gather lilies.* You desire to know whither he goeth or turneth aside whom I love, since he inclineth not himself as yet utterly unto your desire, since he setteth not before you, as it were hungering, a full refreshment; in what places meanwhile he layeth himself open more fully and more abundantly. He hath indeed deferred your hope, and hath not [0446C] cast away your desire, choosing to go down into a garden which by the gift of grace he hath made his own, that he may vouchsafe a prosperous sight unto the bed of spice, and, the lilies being found, may rejoice in the ripe reaping of them. Who, when he heareth not the apostles more fully according to their pleasure, and applaudeth not their prayers with a fulfilling effect, cometh down perchance unto the deacons as unto a pleasing garden, wherein above the rest he findeth Stephen worthy to be reaped. For he, as a bed diligently tilled, humble in the contest, bruised like spice with a manifold passion, both representeth lilies by the whiteness of an innocent soul, and, the sickle coming, showeth himself meet for the reaping. For attending what the Saviour in his pity set about for them that were to be saved, what breasts, what death at last [0446D] he endured, he glows, nay he burns, to imitate that which the other showed beforehand, accounting it too grievous if he be not the first to repay the debt that is due. Therefore in the enduring of martyrdom, fearing to be prevented by another, impatient of delay, he is zealous to be found the readier, esteeming that he hath somewhat the more glory in the martyrdom itself if, the time being shortened, he shall be able to obtain it first. Unto such a one and unto them that are like him the beloved loveth to turn aside, when he willeth to carry them over from the threshing-floor into the barn; who, withdrawing himself as it were from them whom he willeth to tarry longer in this life, hasteneth to be presented unto the untimely and unto them that shall depart hence more quickly. Of whom she addeth: *I to the beloved,* etc.

## CHAPTER III.

*I to my beloved, and my beloved to me, who feedeth among the lilies.* I know, saith she, that my beloved [0447A] layeth himself open as it were more nearly and more manifestly unto those whom, white as lilies, he now disposeth to gather unto the harvest; whom, threshed on the floor and stripped of the ragged covering of the chaff, he willeth to carry over into the barns and the full rest of souls. Therefore do I strive with all my strength to please him, to show myself a garden, myself a bed, myself a shining lily, that when he shall have come and found me flowering with the tillage that is due, taking me out of the midst, he may make me cleave unto him for ever. I, I say, prepare for my beloved a welcome pasture, that he may feed and suffer no hurt of bitterness; for him, fed and refreshed, I prepare a mansion in myself, that, being held by the mansion, he may thenceforth make no mention of flight. And the beloved, as I perceive, prepareth himself for me, that he may love and gather me, and draw me unto himself: [0447B] being about to give nothing better unto her that is gathered and drawn than himself, that I may sleep and rest in the selfsame, my cares being driven far away. He, I say, lifteth me up, though yet set upon the earth, into the love of heavenly things, and, lest I cleave long unto the earth, whetteth as it were the reaping-hook; he rejoiceth to be fed with my lilies, not only while they are yet fixed by the root in the earth, but if, already reaped in ripe season, they be set upon the table. I therefore am zealous to prepare myself for him unto this, and I will purchase by deserts the joy that I hope for; he rejoiceth to render me the like, nay to add over and above, whose benevolence delighteth in conferring benefits. *259*



## CHAPTER IV.

*Thou art fair, my friend, sweet and beautiful as Jerusalem, terrible as an army of camps set in array.* The Bridegroom, attending [0447C] that the Virgin is ready in his praises, that she willeth to be dissolved more quickly and rather to be always with him, although he hasteneth not yet to fulfil her desire wholly, yet inclineth himself with a benevolent affection to console her. Thou, saith he, who burnest with so great a desire to see me, and art fed with my praise, while thou art not yet able to obtain that which thou hopest: by this affection or zeal thou formest for thyself a wondrous fairness, and conformest thyself by a fair likeness unto him whom thou lovest. Being therefore like unto the fair one, thou canst fitly enough be called fair, who by the zeal of likening rejoicest and art busy so to be devoted, that, solicitously spitting out all the dregs of the enemy, thou mayest as a friend rejoice in those things which are wholesome, which are delightful, of thy friend. In which affection and profiting thou knowest not to envy the rest, [0447D] but by form and by doctrine thou lovest to advance all unto better things: rival of none, detracting from none, grievous to none, but solicitous for all, drawing all, and sweet unto all. For nothing is sweeter than, in loving God, so to embrace one's neighbour that he who loveth rightly should choose not to be turned aside from either alike; so to love God and to embrace him with the tenderer arms, that he in no wise envy, nay that he even rejoice that he is loved by any neighbours whatsoever. But the Virgin, rightly loving the Bridegroom, knoweth not to envy — than which not even the Sicilians, according to a certain heathen, found a greater torment: she feareth no rival, she is not racked by the suspicion of a concubine, nay she gathereth together all those women whom she beholdeth to love him whom she loveth. She flourisheth assuredly with a spirit so sweet, [0448A] so peaceable, that she rejoiceth that the Bridegroom is loved of all, and grieveth when he is not loved; nor doth she judge her spirit to be burdened in any other way whatsoever than when he whom she so greatly desireth to be loved is not loved. And so, seeing that he is loved by the daughters of Jerusalem, she, knowing nothing of spite, rather chooseth to rejoice, and with a glad spirit is zealous to work whatsoever she is able, that they which behold may rejoice to imitate the beauty of her works. She is sweet, when she willeth that the daughters of Jerusalem should please the Bridegroom; beautiful, when she is zealous to show forth in words and in works the form of pleasing; sweet indeed, when she willeth that the same glory which is hers should be present unto them, save perchance that she willeth herself to be the only mother of an only Son. Although she envieth not unto them the dignity of mothers, knowing that whoso shall have worthily done the will of the Bridegroom, or of the Son, he shall deserve to be called his brother, [0448B] and sister, and mother, even as the same is found to testify in the Gospel [n: (Matth. XII)]. But because she among mothers hath deserved to obtain an excellent primacy, who by a singular grace begat God incarnate of herself: although unto others no small loftiness of deserts is granted, hers above the rest is the beauty, the sweetness, the fairness that is commended. She is fair, while she burneth toward him who *in form is beautiful above the sons of men [n: (Psal. XLIV)]*, in whose manners sweetness, in whose works beauty shineth again; and, to be compared to none of men, she is likened unto that Jerusalem which, set in the heavens, contemplateth God unceasingly. For that holy multitude of angels, consonant with itself, which an indissoluble strength fortifieth after the manner of a city, is conspicuous with so great beauty that in it nothing seemeth worthy to be reproved, [0448C] burning with a wondrous zeal that man also may deserve to come unto this very thing. Whereunto, because the Virgin is believed to have come by the grace of the Bridegroom, and, set in the flesh, to have found a desert above the flesh, she is rightly proclaimed comely, like Jerusalem, whose beauty the enemy beholding marvelleth with terror. For seeing her to be fortified with so many and so great virtues, and that, as in an army of a camp set in array, no entrance is anywhere found, he is astonished that the firmness of angels is strong in a human being, and that in one Virgin there is the order of an army, the force of a camp. For in the angels so great an order, so great a firmness of array is strong, that the enemy leapeth back at the meeting of the first face, and, shaken with a mighty terror, presumeth to pursue nothing against them, to dare nothing, whom, relying upon a singular order, he seeth to prevail by a strong prudence. [0448D] Whom when Jacob had once seen, he said: *These are the camps of God [n: (Gen. XXXII)]*. And Eliseus to his servant: *Fear not,* saith he, *for there are more with us than with them [n: (IV Reg. VI)]*. Eliseus feareth not, and the assault of the enemy shaketh him not, whom the array of angels set in order beateth far back, whose stronger order admitteth not the onsets of the enemies that run against it, and permitteth not the threatening sword to enter the compass of the camps. With a like terror the enemy fleeth back from the Virgin when he hath assailed her, marvelling in her both at the order of virtues and at an ordered fortitude: and considering that a human being holdeth the likeness of the heavenly camps, he faileth at the first encounter, and, leaping back further off, sufficeth not to shudder. And rightly [0449A] is the holy Virgin compared both to camps and to angels, forasmuch as in both the excellence of chastity is commended; because the flesh, or the coupling of the flesh, never hurteth the angels, and chastity gave its name unto the *castra*, the camps that are removed from the household embrace. As an army of camps, therefore, is the Virgin found terrible, who, begetting God in the flesh, experienceth not the coupling of the flesh; whom when the enemy heareth proclaimed chaste in conceiving, he is terrified and fleeth back, nor perceiveth he such a mystery with his understanding. *260*

## CHAPTER V.

*Turn away thy eyes from me, for they have made me fly away.* Although by my judgment thou art proclaimed fair, sweet and beautiful, yet I will that thou search not out things higher than thyself and unsearchable, nor think, while thou livest here, to obtain more fully those things which I will to show unto no mortals [0449B] save after this life. Those eyes therefore wherewith thou hangest thyself toward things invisible, call them back as it were, restrain them as it were, while thou now perceivest that thou canst not reach thither; and while thou stretchest thyself with hope and desire unto the things that are before, know that thou dost not yet fully or effectually apprehend them. Thus assuredly shalt thou seem to remove thine eyes from me, when thou shalt be constrained humbly to turn them back upon thyself; and when, living still mortally, thou shalt turn thee unto thine own ineffectualness, thou shalt turn thyself away, as it were from my excellence, suffering not a repulse but a delay. In fine, by Moses, a most truthful seer, I spake long time above, that no man living hath attained unto the sight of me, but that whosoever is mortally wrapped about with the girdle of the flesh is darkened and groweth dim, until he shall have been loosed. *Not me,* I say, *shall [0449C] man see, and live [n: (Exod. XXXIII)]*. So long as man is bound by the stains of the present life, he is darkened as it were by a certain cloud, though not damnably, yet penally; nor shall he be able to behold my Godhead as it is, if he cease not to live and to be confined by the fellowship of the flesh. The more attentively therefore thou fixest thine eyes upon the light inaccessible, the more dost thou perceive it to be ungranted unto thee; and when thou strivest to see, and yet art constrained to call back thine eyes, those same eyes being beaten back, I seem unto thee to fly away. For because they stretch themselves with all their efforts to see, and yet do not as yet fully apprehend that which they aim at, I fly away from them, while they find themselves dim and weak, or even when, being clear-sighted, they find me to be incomprehensible. That which I solicitously say unto thee concerning the turning away [0449D] of these is not a repulse, not a command, but I foretell it, that thou mayest know that the sight of me can be given more fully unto no man, unless he first rejoice to be stripped of the burden of the flesh.

## CHAPTER VI.

*Thy hair is as a flock of goats, which have appeared from Galaad. Thy teeth as a flock of sheep, which came up from the washing. All with twin young, and there is none barren among them. As the bark of a pomegranate, so are thy cheeks, beside thy hidden things.* Lest it should as it were trouble the Virgin that she is not yet able to behold the face of the Bridegroom, that he swiftly flieth away when he is truly believed to be already held, the Bridegroom hasteneth to soothe her with repeated praises, that she may bear the delay more patiently, her ears being soothed. Which praises, because they are set down above [n: (l. IV, c. 8)] in wellnigh the same words, [0450A] and, when we came thither, were expounded as God gave; I forbear at present to repeat the exposition, lest I should seem to apply delay unto the reading and weariness unto the reader. Yet when the Bridegroom repeateth those praises, when he bringeth them so often into the midst, he doth not act idly, nor speaketh he negligently; but it is proper to a lover (if indeed he burn vehemently) to make mention of that which he loveth, nay and to repeat it diligently.



## CHAPTER VII.

*There are threescore queens and fourscore concubines, and of maidens there is no number.* The Bridegroom attendeth unto those who by the gift of grace attain unto the Catholic faith, and follow after the firmness of the same faith either in deed or in show: whose divers deserts, willing to designate them figuratively, he seemeth mystically [0450B] to assign unto them divers names. By the name of queens are they not unfitly figured who, hedged about with a kingly defence, are overcome neither by the fraud of the adversary nor by his violence; who, while they keep their ways, that they offend not in word and in work, draw nigh unto the bed of the eternal King by the profiting of spiritual things. Where both they are filled with a lofty knowledge and are gladdened with a lowly conscience, and, gladly resting in the embrace of the Bridegroom, are made fruitful by his benefit; and with the fruitful seed-plot of doctrine they beget unto him spiritual sons, by whose fertile begetting the nuptial chambers are enriched and made glad. Who are rightly said to be comprehended in the number of sixty, because it is certain that in the ten and in the six the perfection of the law and of works is commended, the one of which being multiplied by the other, the number sixty cometh [0450C] to be completed. For as six times ten, *261* so ten times six, make sixty. He therefore who rejoiceth to fulfil in works the ten precepts of the law, or who ordereth according to the form of the law whatsoever he worketh in time. he assuredly is worthily contained in the number sixty, whose fruitful dignity is said to please the highest King. It is also possible to find in this number the five and the twelve, whose multiplication seemeth to come unto sixty; because if twelve be taken five times, or five twelve times, it is doubtful to none but that they are brought unto the sum of the number sixty. And he is rightly said to take five twelve times who governeth the five senses of the body in that manner or order which the form or the institution of the apostles hath prudently ordained, whose perfection [0450D] the number twelve hath commended. *And fourscore,* saith he, *concubines.* As they who chastely love the Bridegroom and beget sons unto him are queens, so also they who love not sincerely and yet preach are concubines, whose knowledge and preaching doth indeed beget spiritual sons, but, their conscience being wounded, they themselves that beget remain animal. Who are not unfitly reported to be fourscore, because they are known to hold the ten of the law in word and in knowledge, but, lacking the twofold love, they slip back into the eight, while they embrace in life and in manners the things that are of the world. For four are the seasons of the year, four the elements of the world, four the climes of the globe, four in fine the affections wherewith any man is carnally affected and travaileth, and, if he know aught rightly, he discoloureth it by a lost will. Which [0451A] affections that prudent philosopher biddeth and exhorteth to be driven back, knowing that he erreth over whom a carnal passion beareth rule; which passion, naturally implanted, although he pluck it not up by the root, yet he erreth if he drive not the same back with a fitting chastisement. *Joys,* saith he, *drive away,*
*Drive away fear,*
*And put hope to flight,*
*Nor let grief be present.*


Whosoever, being lost in sense, is found to double the aforesaid four, that is, to strengthen the carnal affections with an affection added over and above, against the philosopher's prohibition: he assuredly, filling up the eight, is not yet granted to come unto the ten, because in the evils which he accomplisheth it is not possible to find the twofold form of love. *And [0451B] of maidens there is no number.* When queens and concubines preach and sow the spiritual word, although the desire of the former be just and of the latter carnal: a new offspring is assuredly begotten by their zeal or labour, which receiveth the Bridegroom by faith and followeth him with a readier affection. For whether they that preach the word be held just or unjust, by their word many are begotten in faith and in knowledge: and as from the good, so from the evil, a copious offspring is born, numerous indeed unto no man, but rather unto God alone. Of whom he saith: *I will number them, and they shall be multiplied above the sand [n: (Psal. CXXXVIII)]*. They who yield assent unto the teachers that preach the faith are fully known unto him who numbereth the multitude of the stars; but unto us that attend unto them gathered together of every kind of fishes in a net, [0451C] their multitude is utterly innumerable as the sand. Who, because they have already received the rudiments of the faith they have heard, but have not yet profited so far as to announce unto others the instructions of the same faith: by reason of their newness or of their imperfection are named [sic: *a dolescentulae*], and are unknown of the man whose knowledge is yet dull, whose eye is dim. Not whether they be good, who are afterward chosen into vessels, or evil, who, being sent out, are spewed forth without, so long as they are contained in the net as it were in a confused order, are they held numerable by any man.



## CHAPTER VIII.

*One is my dove, my perfect one; one is she unto her mother, the chosen of her that bore her.* [var: Vulg. *matris suae*, genitive — "she is the one of her mother"; the dative Migne prints here is repeated three times in the exposition below] It is certain that many cleave unto me with a lawful [0451D] love, that many, it being renounced, obtain only the appearance of truth; but by the word and doctrine of them that preach so many are everywhere begotten in the faith, that unto any man attending solicitously they seem utterly innumerable. But the Virgin above the rest, pleasing unto me [n: (II Tim. II)], useful, seasonable, knoweth not the plural number, but is one: burning with the desire of me alone, she is held by a religious unity, one is joined unto one, with a singular or a unique dignity. She is one, I say, forasmuch as she is not carried away into divers and perverse desires; forasmuch as she is never, not even for a little, taken away from him whom, being the one, she uniquely loveth; forasmuch as she is not straitened by the allurements of earthly things or by the bonds of many affections from beholding the Bridegroom [0452A] more fully, and is retarded by nothing save only the burden of the flesh. Rejoicing in the hope of things to come, groaning amid the transitory things that are present, the present things being loathed, she groaneth as a dove for the eternal things that are still absent; while she is held by the flesh, she seemeth to herself harshly to wander; nothing sufficeth her, until, rejoicing, she see the Bridegroom more fully. She is one, while, cleaving unto him, she loveth nothing beside him; and if perchance she seem to love aught, she loveth it not save for his sake; and so, if she do aught, she referreth it unto nothing other than unto him, one, watching unto him alone, until at last she sleep in peace in the selfsame. And because she is thus gathered by a watchful effect into the love of the One, by the desert of this unity she hath already deserved to be called my perfect one, seeing that unto her no holiness is lacking, so far as the present life suffereth, *262* in whom, I dwelling therein, dwelleth the [0452B] fulness of the whole Godhead. For neither is there another unto whom I would promise so great a gift of grace, so long as she yet complaineth that she is held in the prison-house of the flesh; who, to wit, if she should apply care to behold herself, might dare, while she liveth mortally, to confess herself perfect. *Not that I have already received,* saith a certain one, *or am perfect [n: (Philip. III)]*. And another: *My imperfect being,* saith he, *thine eyes did see [n: (Psal. CXXXVIII)]*. But if Paul and David acknowledge themselves truly imperfect, though in thine eyes, O God, deservedly not despised, unto whom, whether of the new or of the old, is so great, or so singular, a praise rendered, save perchance unto the Virgin, who is rightly set before all the rest? She therefore is one unto her mother, and in this excellence singular, at whose singularity the remaining throng and the common converse are astonished; every man marvelleth at a Virgin so [0452C] uplifted, so perfect, and her mother rejoiceth for a daughter such as this, so unique, so singular. But the mother who willed to nourish such a daughter for herself, who cherished and advanced her, and gave her to come unto so great an excellence — who is so worthily, who is so rightly proclaimed as grace herself, of which the angel Gabriel testifieth that the Virgin is full by gift? *Hail,* saith he, *full of grace [n: (Luc. I)]*. For grace herself, who by the goodness which is her own hath abolished the stains of our faults, so filled the aforesaid Virgin with an excellent benefit, that, one bearing one, she yet remained an unbroken Virgin, and, remaining a Virgin, answered the fructifying grace with a new and singular offspring. She is therefore one unto her mother, because grace her mother is seen to have neither a first like unto her [0452D] nor a second, who in a like form should show herself alike a Virgin and fruitful: no other did she honour with so great titles of virtues, this one and only one she adorned with a singular privilege. But lest any think that she deserved a privilege of this kind, and that she was not first chosen, but rather that she chose, as she is one unto her mother, so also is she reported the chosen of her that bore her, that not only her perfection, but also the election that went before it, may together be commended. Her assuredly did grace choose, and as it were beget her when she was not; the same received and nourished her, advanced and helped her, when now she was: in choosing or in begetting holding the part of her that beareth, in nourishing and advancing discharging the office of a mother or of a nurse. For she [0453A] who by a provident knowledge chose the Virgin beforehand, the same mercifully received and gathered her with a motherly affection: there as one that beareth, when in secret she foresaw that she should come; here a mother, or a nurse, when more evidently she advanced her unto an incomparable profiting. For she advanced her, and formed her in her own workshop; formed her by desire, by manners, by discipline; formed her also by letters, by ripe counsel, by the prudence of the serpent; and when she was formed, the simplicity and perfection of the dove completed her. Therefore perchance is she alike named *my dove* and *my perfect one*, that the perfection of the dove may be known to be at hand in her, that those seven virtues, as it were, which are naturally bestowed upon doves, may be known in her to be spiritually completed in a like number. As they say who have more diligently searched out the natures of birds, [0453B] setting their mind not upon a wandering report, but rather upon a truth known beforehand: the dove is naturally marked with a certain seven of virtues, wherein the perfection of our Virgin is found to be spiritually figured. Whereof, because I am found to have deferred speaking long above [n: (l. II, c. 13)], when in the second book this epithalamium seemeth first to have brought doves into the midst, that which I there had promised I will after a sort follow out at present, since now no mention of doves is set down in what followeth.

The dove lacketh gall. Our Virgin also, from the time when the angel Gabriel saluted her, from the time when the Holy Spirit coming upon her overshadowed her, hath given unto God to drink no bitterness either of acts or of affections, but [0453C] hath dropped down the honeyed sweetness of her manners more sweetly than the honeycomb.

The dove teareth not with her beak. And the Virgin repayeth not the deserved requital unto any that do her wrong, but in every grievance so showeth an unbending patience, that even when she saw her only Son betrayed, and, being betrayed, crucified, she had rather that the wicked should be converted than that they should be so afflicted according to their desert.

The dove nourisheth another's young The Virgin indeed keepeth in the surge of this life a mind so serene, that she thinketh it not foreign to succour clemently even them that are without and unworthy: nay unto all that are in need, as to the Jews, so to the Gentiles, she both giveth by her discourses a profitable doctrine, and with an equal benevolence showeth by her manners a discipline.

[0453D]The dove gladly dwelleth beside the streams. So also the Virgin diligently leaneth upon the streams of the Scriptures: she embraceth the books, she liveth according to the admonitions of the prophets, she is assiduously intent upon divine readings, she is at leisure for spiritual study, not detained by outward cares.

The dove chooseth the better grains. The Virgin nevertheless, while she applieth care or study in the Scriptures, doth not only set whatsoever things are profitable before all that shall be hurtful, but with a clear-sighted eye chooseth among good things the better, embracing the more eagerly whatsoever she hath known to be more pleasing unto the Bridegroom.

The dove gladly buildeth her nest in the rock. The Virgin also worketh in a firm faith whatsoever she is able, whose working is made solid by the rocky defence of faith; a faith that overtoppeth all is not troubled by the flood of waves, groweth not weary by a windy rage, is not shaken by the hammer of fear.

[0454A]The dove groaneth instead of singing. The Virgin, although she modestly rejoiceth in the aforesaid six of virtues, yet, because him whom she loveth she contemplateth not yet with a revealed *263* face, although in these as it were six days she busieth herself to work all things very good, yet, because it is not yet granted her to keep holy day more fully in the seventh, still, as one in need and expressing the nature of the dove, she groaneth, while she prevaileth not in that which she desireth, while she is held, and longeth to be dismissed more quickly. By which groaning the Virgin detracteth nothing from her deserts, nothing from her holiness; nothing from it, from that unity which above we commended as we were able, doth the groaning of the dove take away, but that for the place and the time she is perfect; nay, if for the present she groaned not, she would the more rightly be called, and would be, imperfect. Of whom it is added: *They saw her,* etc.



## CHAPTER IX.

[0454B]

*The daughters of Sion saw her, and proclaimed her most blessed: the queens and the concubines, and they praised her.* [var: Vulg. *Viderunt eam filiae*, with no place-name; Migne prints *illam* for *eam* and adds *Sion*, the word Philip's next sentence expounds] The daughters of Sion are above called the daughters of Jerusalem, who, as hath been said before, accompany the Virgin in this epithalamium, who truly behold with faith the nuptials that are present, and, while the rest are dim of sight, are not held by a wandering error or by ignorance. Who, attending unto the Virgin marked with so great virtues, so perfectly, so incomparably polished by labour together with grace, are astonished, they marvel, and they proclaim her not blessed (which they see to be common to very many), but rather most blessed, that is, the most excellent of all the rest. For whereas many others may not undeservedly be called blessed, both the Angel and Elizabeth affirm that this one is blessed among all, that is, above [0454C] all women, who against the custom of the flesh, against the interdict of mighty nature, alone remaining a Virgin brought forth the blessed fruit of a fruitful womb. Which when they see, and are not able sufficiently enough to open so great a mystery, nor can they find any like thing among women, the daughters of Sion extol her, and confidently proclaim her most blessed, and with a speech that envieth not they evidently announce her excellence. For the apostles, seeing through with a lynx-like understanding that Christ was born of a Virgin, and envying that same benefit neither to the Jews nor to the Gentiles, affirmed not only the Son but also the mother to be most blessed; by which kind of sight they also, according to their own little measure, deserved blessedness. [0454D] *Blessed,* saith he, *are the eyes that see the things which you see [n: (Luc. X)]*. Not only the apostles, but other teachers also, their successors in place and in time, are made in the Church the praisers of this so great Virgin; of whom some, by the fruitful desert of a chaste desire, are queens, others, not loving but feigning love, are more rightly called concubines. For in these days wherein the faith, bringing forth fruit in the whole world, increaseth, but among not a few, malice abounding, charity waxeth cold, both many praise the Virgin, provoked by a most devout love, and many, denying virtue, are coloured with the show of piety. For the honour of the Virgin hath so grown unto this present time, and her fame or knowledge hath so filled the whole world, that not only true but also false believers seem to exult in her praises, and whom devotion doth not, them [0455A] at the least occasion maketh to praise her withal. Therefore may this Virgin be called wondrous, and enough to be wondered at, whom the Angel and the prophet affirm to be blessed above all; whom, being blessed, they that love to exalt with praises rightly rejoice, and they that neglect to love her yet dare not now to cease from her praises. In whose praise it is added: *Who is she,* etc.

## CHAPTER X.

*Who is she that cometh forth as the morning rising, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army of camps set in array?* The Bridegroom provoketh his devout hearers unto wonder, that they may deservedly be rendered the readier unto the praise of the Virgin; and that, when they shall have heard the question asked: *Who is she that cometh forth as the morning,* being admonished [0455B] of her going forward, they may be the more astonished at the things that went before. The morning rising, the darkness is affrighted, the night groweth thin, the obscurity is scattered, the grosser shadow vanisheth away: a new light springeth up, a certain face of the world shineth out, colour is restored unto things, the surface of the earth groweth glad. Our Virgin therefore is like unto this morning, who visiteth us that are oppressed with a deeper darkness and a denser shadow; upon which, while with the majesty of her hand she striketh as it were a sudden terror, they disappearing, she bringeth in unto us the morning radiance. But the moon, as they say, shineth not with her own light, but rather with another's, and what she receiveth from the sun she poureth back upon the rest with a full horn: assigned indeed especially to give light unto the night, less than the sun alone in such wise that she is set before the remaining stars. So also the Virgin knoweth that whatsoever of light she holdeth, whatsoever [0455C] of grace or of honour, is from Christ, who is of a mightier excellence; less than whom alone, she herself hath the primacy over the other saints, putteth our darkness to flight, and rejoiceth to render light. Fair therefore is she unto us, nay fairer than *264* the moon, who refresheth at last with a seasonable light them that are pressed by a long night, who with a torch going before bringeth us back unto the way when we wander and grope, and with a watchful care leadeth us in unto the longed-for presence of the sun. She is also chosen as the sun. The sun was made that it might appear a greater luminary than both the stars and the planets, and, whithersoever it shall have turned itself, might be seen to flash overtopping them all: that it should know not the shadow of night, should not grow dim at the onset of the mighty, should go about the world with a firm course, should not chastise its falls with penitence. But from the time when the Virgin entered the sanctuary of a fuller grace, having gone beyond not only any saints whatsoever, [0455D] but even the apostles that went before, burning with an exceeding love, glowing red with an unwearied holiness, she taketh the care of us all, having suffered nothing destructive in herself. She rejoiceth to go about with a watchful care the world that is pressed with darkness, to repair the cooling ruins with a most fervent affection, to drive away the clouds of our faults by a shining intervention, to make fruitful the earth of our minds by a most kindly regard. In this she abideth and remaineth, unto this she is divinely chosen, that in affection and in effect she may be perfect among the remaining saints: after the manner of the sun, marked with a steadfast splendour by the rays of virtues, never negligent of her own, not forgetful of us that are set far beneath. Who, because, bearing the part of the morning, she is found [0456A] to shine out unto us that are dim of sight, and knoweth that she hath the fairness of the moon from none other than another, and is seen, like the sun, to remain with a steadfast step in that which she hath begun; even as she is profitable and welcome unto them that rightly behold her, so is she terrible unto her enemies as an army of camps set in array. Which array or terror, because you can remember that it was set down and expounded above, it is not necessary that the exposition of the foregoing be repeated.



## CHAPTER XI.

*I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys, and to look if the vineyard had flourished, and the pomegranates had budded.* Whence this cometh to the Virgin, that she should be likened, as hath been said before, unto the moon and the sun, that, set before the rest, she should be adorned with so great an excellence of virtues, is not hidden, since the Bridegroom confesseth that he goeth down unto her, [0456B] showing that out of his own presence this is mercifully given unto her. In fine, he showed himself to confer a benefit upon the children of Israel in Egypt, when at last he came down from the highest throne of heaven unto them that were oppressed with clay and brick, when he visited with the regard of his mercy them that were afflicted with misery, and, having visited them, delivered them from a hard servitude with a most mighty hand: *Seeing I have seen,* saith he, *the affliction of my people, and I am come down to deliver them [n: (Exod. III)]*. [var: Vulg. Exod. 3:7–8 gives *Vidi* and *descendi ut liberarem eum*, "I have seen… I am come down that I might deliver him"; the doubled verb and the plural object printed here are the wording of Acts 7:34, under a note naming Exodus] In the Gospel also he is reported to come down not in vain [n: (Luc. VI)], but that he might console the multitudes set in a plain place; whom, when he understood them to be [sic: *invados*] and poor in spiritual things, and yet by the counsel that he knew carried them not up unto the mountains, he despised not to visit them where they stood in the plain, and, out of the fulness of his treasure of blessings, [0456C] neglected not to bring forth gifts. But if his going down into Egypt, or into the plain, is found to have been fruitful, much more rightly shall his going down unto the Bride not be esteemed idle — who is like neither unto darksome Egypt nor unto a turbulent plain, but unto a garden of delight rich in fruits and in nuts. The garden of nuts is the Virgin, into which the Bridegroom saith that he goeth down, forasmuch as no difficulty in any wise, no importunity gainsayeth him as he goeth down; unto whom, although the heaven of heaven and the habitation of angels be pleasing, yet neither the nuts of the garden, nor the flowers of the vineyard, nor the buds of the pomegranates displease. In a nut the outer rind is bitter, and that not in a middling degree; beneath the rind a shell hard yet brittle lieth hid; but the kernel shut up beneath the shell groweth the more sweetly pleasant unto him that eateth. And so the Virgin is a garden of nuts, [0456D] when she is troubled with the bitterness of sufferings and of temptations, when the malice of them that persecute her wickedly withstandeth her repose, when whatsoever this world either flattereth or thundereth groweth utterly bitter unto her, when all that shineth out unto them that savour ill is filthy in her sight. She is a garden, when, as a harder shell, she is fortified with a wondrous strength, when she is found unfailing in watchings, in fastings, in prayers, when she is in no wise softened by the reproaches of the Jews, by the swords of the Gentiles, when in every strait, with an unwearied rigour, she is found to stand strongly. Who, although she be found to remain fixed and stable unto all things, yet desireth to be broken and dissolved, and to appear more manifestly unto Christ, knowing that he is delighted not with the shell, not with the rind, [0457A] not with any bitterness whatsoever, but that, the kernel being offered, the sweeter it is the more festively he feasteth thereon. But the hidden kernel is the inward sweetness of the loving soul, which lieth hid from the eyes of the persecutor that are seduced by malice, which, the shell being broken, is not taken away, but is borne as it were in the hands of her that offereth it, and is presented unto the Bridegroom, and unto him that presideth at the same table or banquet. Into this garden of nuts the loving Bridegroom then goeth down, when he stretcheth himself near and propitious unto his beloved that laboureth, when he is solicitous to advance her from virtue unto virtue [n: (Psal. LXXXIII)], and willeth with a gracious regard to see the fruits of the valleys in her. For what humble virtues busy themselves to work in the Virgin, what out of their own labour or desert they love to await with a sure faith, the Bridegroom seeth, and approveth, *265* and maketh all things to prosper, and with a prosperous favour, [0457B] as with a west wind blowing, to ripen. For the fruits of the valleys are the labours of humble virtues, they are solicitous endeavours, hands the readier unto works: they are fruitful acts, the more welcome in a well-planted garden, which, although they be not yet fully ripe for reaping or for storing, yet please the sight, and shall pass the sooner unto the eating. But the fruits of the valleys being seen, the bridegroom loveth nevertheless to see through whether the vineyard, worthily flowering, hasteneth to answer the husbandman; whether the ordered series of virtues is found to shine again with a fragrant beauty; whether with a flowery odour to forbid all hurtful venom from her borders. For lest a venomous spite should hurt the tender Virgin, a seemly fame fortified her, a flowery beauty exalted her; who, when with a new kind she brought forth unto us the swelling of the womb, yet far off brought forth the stain of unlawful suspicion and the [0457C] serpent's venom. Whose conscience not only did the presence of faults not confound, but neither did a sinister rumour suffuse her face with a blush; with so great a flower did the vineyard, with so great an odour did the flower flourish, that her integrity lacketh both fault and blush. In a garden of this kind the bridegroom seeth also that pomegranates are not lacking, but that in the hidden place of the will the mind is ready unto patience: that she willeth to endure not only death but even the threatening sword, and that, if not yet in effect, yet already in affection, the shedding of blood is ruddy beneath. The pomegranates indeed do not yet present themselves more manifestly, but unto him that beholdeth more diligently they show themselves as it were in the bud: the passion is not yet red, because the executioner draweth not the sword, but the will, more firmly rooted, already putteth forth a bud upon [0457D] the shoot. To look upon this the bridegroom sent no messenger before him, but with a lowly benevolence he himself comforteth the Virgin and visiteth her again: with a gracious descent he cherisheth the garden, he rejoiceth to ripen the fruits of the valleys, he giveth the vineyard to flower, and the pomegranates to bud.

## CHAPTER XII.

*I knew not: my soul was troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab.* [var: Vulg. *anima mea conturbavit me*, "my soul troubled me" — the active, with the soul as the agent of the trouble; Migne prints the passive, which Philip glosses both ways at 0458A–B] The Virgin, seeing that the bridegroom hath wondrously come down into her garden, and by a wondrous descent hath brought a grace equally wondrous, cannot sufficiently utter that which she spiritually beholdeth in herself; and, rejoicing in her present knowledge, she confesseth her former ignorance. *I knew not,* saith she, before the Angel announced me full [0458A] of grace, and the Holy Spirit overshadowed me with a cloud bright enough, before the Son of God made me fruitful with his kiss, and a new fruitfulness honoured a virginal conscience: I knew not that so much of grace, so much of gift, was imparted unto me, that a lowly handmaid could experience things so unexperienced by the rest. Before he enclosed his garden — yet not with a hedge, not with a wall, nor with a rampart — before he sealed the fountain — yet not with an iron bar, not with a bolt, not with metal — before he came down into the same garden, and looked upon it with the large gift of his goodness, I knew not that he was so mighty, so kindly, so rich in so great bounty. When therefore he came down unto me, and showed himself unto me after a sort, I was troubled, I was afraid, I was astonished, marvelling at so great a benefit: my soul laboured toward its salvation [0458B] with a prosperous fainting, and, fainting with a healthful labour — or rather profiting — it troubled me. For seeing [sic: *Videos*] that the bridegroom had come down not poor, not needy, not as any one of the people, but had arrived upon horses or in chariots after the manner of the mighty, I had no more spirit in me, considering that he both worketh salvation mightily, and that in that very might religion is worthily preserved: *Thou that ridest,* saith he, *upon thy horses, and thy chariots are salvation [n: (Habac. III)]*. You know that the men of Azotus, who held the ark of the Lord some days after they had taken it, being constrained by the wounding of their hinder parts, at last restored it free; which, set upon a new cart, was carried back into the house of Aminadab, where both a more reverent worship and a more fitting religion was rendered unto it. Aminadab is interpreted [0458C] *spontaneous*, signifying him who of his own accord willed to come from the bosom of the Father, and to unite unto himself in the womb of the Virgin the nature of man; who presideth over the angelic powers after the manner of a king or of a charioteer, and with an agile concord all serve him as chariots. Which kind of empire or of obedience when the Virgin more diligently beholdeth, she confesseth that she, aforetime unknowing of them, is after a manner troubled at this knowledge: recalling that at the marriages of them of old festal assemblies of men were wont to be employed, and that angelic chariots and invisible timbrel-players were not seen. Who therefore perchance hold in this epithalamium the name or the appearance of chariots, because this solemnity of the nuptials runneth together with and succoureth a fourfold world: and those four living creatures which are described in the prophecy of John or of Ezechiel [0458D] are subscribed unto the same business as heralds or as yoke-fellows. Because of the chariots of Aminadab therefore the Virgin, before unknowing, is troubled, when, being brought into his sanctuary, she marvelleth at the thousands of thousands that minister unto him, when, as one delivered from the borders of the enemies or from the men of Azotus, both the mighty excellence of a king and the religion of a priest receiveth her. To whom Aminadab, speaking, addeth: *Return,* etc. *266*



## CHAPTER XIII.

*Return, return, Sunamite: return, return, that we may behold thee.* [var: Vulg. *Sulamitis*, the Sulamitess; the name Migne prints is the one whose etymology — captive, despised, scarlet — the whole chapter expounds] Lest the Virgin should seem to return into the house of Aminadab by her own merits (for she herself is the ark of God, which for some time is held captive by the law of us all), Aminadab sheweth that it is not the efficacy [0459A] of her that returneth, but rather the compassion and the mighty benevolence of him that recalleth her. The bridegroom therefore recalleth her who is called Sunamite, that being loosed from her bonds she may return with unhindered steps, lest she tarry among the men of Azotus and the allurements of carnal senses, but be carried back of her own accord, upon the wain of a foursquare newness, into the house of him that loveth her. Sunamite is interpreted *a captive* or *despised,* or *scarlet*. But the Virgin, like the rest, was by nature a daughter of wrath, from whose stains her manner of life could not wholly free her; wherein, although there was present in her a virtue expulsive of damnable faults, yet she is still weighed down by the bond, and by the laws of nature is a captive. And since she was by nature conceived in sins, her manner of life was infected with faults, even light ones; by the desert of that infection she is [0459B] despised in the purer eyes of God, but her humility was at length regarded through grace. For he regarded the humility of his handmaid, and recalled her once and again, and by a twofold recalling delivered her both from captivity and from contempt; that her whom the law of wrath, the law inborn, had held guilty, the divine law might afterward keep wholly free from fault. Therefore the bridegroom also addeth to recall the same once and again, and with a repeated word more diligently to invite her to return; and her whom the first recalling led forth from the harder sentence, he maketh firm the second time by a more bountiful estate or grace. For having first said, *Return, return, Sunamite,* he added, *return, return that we may behold thee.* Whom I would have return, saith he, that she be no longer held a captive and despised; I would have her return, that she may be held more pleasing to me also, that she may love him that recalleth her, and may burn, [0459C] not with a burning, but with love, and be worthy to be named scarlet by desert, not by colour. Scarlet holdeth the appearance of fire, signifying love; for he that loveth burneth. But because that fire, or the love of the Virgin, is of necessity doubled, while in the bridegroom, as I recall was said already, she embraceth God and man: her whom the bridegroom enricheth beyond the rest with so great a gift, that the scarlet may be twice dyed, he twice inviteth to this twofold love. Her therefore whom the first doubling recalleth captive and despised, the second far more firmly maketh loving and beloved; and both he himself and the companions whom he willeth to be present and privy to this mystery love to see and to behold her, such and so scarlet. Whom the angels, marking her both free from fault against the wonted [0459D] right of nature, and scarlet with love, above the efficacy of any visible creature, are not able enough to wonder at so great an excellency of the thing; and rejoicing with the Bridegroom, they love to enquire concerning the Bride.

## CHAPTER XIV.

*[CAP. VII.] What wilt thou see, say they, in the Sunamite, but the choirs of camps?* Thou invitest, say they, the Virgin, and so often and so often wilt thou have her return, and with a marvellous advancement [0460A] wilt have her wholly turned to thy good pleasure, that fault may avail to obtain nothing in her of its own right, and that by the privilege of love she may be worthy to please us that behold her. In this Sunamite therefore, who so often returneth, what wilt thou see, and of her, when she shall have been presented to thy sight, what wilt thou judge — in whom, as we consider, there meeteth us so great a perfection of manners that not men, but rather the camps of angels, accord with her? For the divine reading is found to name the angels camps, in that the violence of enemies cannot pierce their squadrons, and the presiding emperor giveth them so great confidence that every assailant, beaten far back, taketh flight. Of whom Jacob: *These are the camps of God [n: (Gen. XXXII)]*. Who also may not unfitly be called choirs, in that they are both concordant in affections and tuneful with unwearied [0460B] praises, whose melody soundeth so great in the ears of him that presideth that neither the harmony of the heavens, nor of the stars, nor even of the planets can compare itself thereto. And by what virtues the angels consider themselves to flourish, by those same they both see the Virgin to be pre-eminent and envy it not; and since they recognize in her the angelic life with a marvellous newness, they wonder, and now demand of the bridegroom whether he know aught further. What wilt thou see, say they, in this Sunamite whom thou recallest, but a marvellous concord of praise and of exquisite fortitude, but praiseworthy choirs and the ancient armies of the angels, but concordant virtues and a strength unfailing as of camps! These things assuredly we already see in the virgin whom thou lovest so greatly, and if aught yet lieth hid, we would see it with a desire pleasing enough; [0460C] and both these things and the rest which we rejoice to behold in her, we would have recounted by thyself, who art known to know them better. To these the Bridegroom: *How fair,* etc. *267*

## CHAPTER XV

*How beautiful are thy steps in shoes, prince's daughter.* The Bridegroom deferreth not to answer benignly to the things enquired, but in answering he loveth to turn back his speech to the virgin; not deeming that he in any wise displeaseth the aforesaid companions, if to them that enquire he chooseth to shew himself affable to her. To them therefore that ask he cutteth not off hope by silence, but turneth himself to her to whom he is not weary to speak the more often; and when he undertaketh to accost her with new praises, he willeth the bridesmen standing by to hear whatsoever he speaketh. But now [0460D] he beginneth to set forth his praises from the steps, who above [n: (l. IV, c. 7 et 22)], when he praised her, chose to begin from the eyes; perchance that, if the repetition of praises admonish the drowsy to weary, another order and a varied colouring may render them watchful and attentive. Finally above [n: (l. IV, c. 23)], when he many times sought to praise the virgin as it were part by part, if I recall well, he passed not beyond her breasts or paps, but beginning from the upper parts, his praise so turneth about them [0461A] that from the breasts downward he speaketh not of the remaining members. But the Virgin herself in the preceding book [n: (l. V a c. 18 ad 27)], praising him as it were particularly or member by member, descended in order from the head to the legs and their bases; to whom the Bridegroom, rendering the like, ordered herein the series of her praises, but for variety's sake changed that very order. The steps of the virgin I deem to name her acts, which he willed to be hidden from us that are far more remote; through which he willed her to come into our knowledge, whose sanctity would lie hid from us if she chose a slothful or a continual sitting. Which steps assuredly no halting limp disfigured, no girlish levity accused of being wandering and unstable; no dry disease twisted them back to the weak and needy elements of this world, nor did any wicked [0461B] exactor wring from them anything by way of tribute. Of so fair a soundness, of so strong a beauty were they, and in this beauty they stood fast with so great a constancy, that wonder rather than narration befitteth the praiser, since not only the full expression, but even a foretaste, may suffice the hearer.
