And that it may be plain that nothing necessary is excluded from those same steps, walking through the unevennesses of this life they are not bare; but lest either the dryness of the sun or the harshness of winter bring in aught of grievousness, a certain mortification of pleasure shoeth them as it were. If therefore aught threateneth, whether delightful or troublesome, which would overturn in them anything useful or honest, a certain patient insensibility putteth itself forward to repel it, [0461C] which permitteth nothing pestilent to come to the tender foot. In shoes of this kind the beauty of the steps lieth hid, which, not open enough to us, is better known to the bridegroom, who loveth to be at hand for that same virgin in all things, and maketh her to be like himself as a daughter. For this cause perchance in the present place — that nowhere above did he name her daughter, that after his own fashion he shod her more especially, and made her in the shoes to accord with him more expressly and more like, while, set in the flesh, he granted her not to feel the laws of carnal men. Who is rightly said to hold the princedom of the prerogative of that gift, who, when he was made flesh, would not be bound to carnal things, who willed to keep the manhood he assumed unharmed by vices, and to conform the chosen virgin to himself as a daughter. Taking away therefore from the midst the privilege [0461D] of stubborn wrath, he is rightly called by Isaias' testimony the prince of peace [n: (Isa. IX)], whose peace whosoever is granted truly to experience in himself (for many say peace, peace, in whom peace cannot be found); whosoever, I say, is found partaker of this peace by the gift of grace, is rightly marked with the filial name because of the likeness.



## CHAPTER XVI.

*The joint of thy thighs is like necklaces, which are wrought by the hand of a craftsman.* With a fair manner of speech he hath commended the integrity of the virgin, while he compared the joint of the thighs to wrought necklaces, because in the thighs is most often figured carnal begetting, [0462A] but in the joint of the thighs the denial of begetting and barrenness. Finally the sinful soul which embittereth God with carnal allurements, as the prophet [n: (Isa. LI)] recordeth, spreadeth her feet apart to all that pass by, and not content with the lawful, being loosed from law taketh other men — nay, adulterers; she beareth not the straitness of the marriage-bed, but, her couch widened, is prostituted to panderings. But the Virgin, who in conceiving feeleth no man at all, who by an ancient privilege of nature consenteth not in body any more than in mind, her thighs being coupled with an indissoluble joint, holdeth from thenceforth and thereafter the firm covenant of perfect chastity. For such as she is read to have been at the conception, the Angel preaching it [n: (Luc. I)], such by a pious faith not straying from the truth is she believed to have continued; and neither was the body divided from the mind, nor afterward [0462B] the mind from the body, but undivided by a continual consent and by unharmed affections. Which joint ought rightly to be compared to necklaces, which are known to be wrought by a learned hand out of gold and stones, which not only by their own worthy *268* price bring the comeliness of an ornament, but to fortify the virgin bosom clasp together the upper edges of the garment. So the joint of the thighs, more precious than gold or stone, keeping flesh and spirit, and busy for the acquiring of merit, fortifieth indeed the virgin, that no seducing corrupter be admitted, and admonisheth her also to love him by whose benefit she is thus adorned. For from fortifying or from admonishing, as some say, are necklaces named, in that whatsoever things are fortified are by such a gift admonished, that by such a guard they may drive far off [0462C] the envious corrupter, and with a mutual affection benignly love the giver. For the learned craftsman with his own hand wrought these necklaces, which, denied to many, he denied not to the Virgin Mother; which Paul with a wondrous desire asketh to be given him — I know not, while he lived here, whether perchance he deserved so to be blessed.

## CHAPTER XVII.

*Thy navel is a turned bowl, never wanting cups.* The navel coupleth and fasteneth together the parts of the belly set round about it, and lest by their native softness they flow down or perchance flow away, calleth them back and restraineth them; wherein the woman also is said to have the seed-bed of begetting, which nevertheless among men is chiefly contained in the loins. The navel therefore of the virgin is her stable doctrine, which, when the apostles were flowing away with a fleshly fear [0462D] and a womanish softness; standeth firm by a [sic: *virita*] faith, and floweth not away with the like levity, but by a certain firmness of her own calleth back those that are light and wandering more than is just. For the men, seeing that they had too lightly fallen away from the purpose of faith, and that she, though shaken with exceeding grief, had yet stood the more firmly — when the resurrection accomplished was shewn by sundry visions, and the Virgin was held suspended in the zeal of contemplation and in devout prayers — being called back to her, humbly blush for the things past; and thenceforth cleave to her hearing more believingly and more constantly. For than a turned bowl her turning is fuller and more perfect, to whom the begetting of the rising Christ had been more fully made known; and all things which are read of him in Scripture through the long series of times, [0463A] these she drew more abundantly, and poured back to her hearers with measure. Whose turned bowl, or ready perfection of discoursing, drieth not with want, is not straitened by narrowness of understanding, but filled with cups and inebriated with the wine of wisdom, both sufficeth for all peoples far off and, being poured out, never faileth.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

*Thy belly is like a heap of wheat, set about with lilies.* The belly is humanity, weakness, or temporal manner of life, which needeth the fostering of raiment and of bodily nourishment, whose softness, as it were, so demandeth the care of natural fostering that in it there may be heaped up spiritual advancement and eminence. For although the Virgin hath not her own flesh in hatred, but preserveth it, yet in the care of it she enervateth not the powers of the spirit, but while she of necessity cherisheth [0463B] it, she reserveth herself for hard labours, in which she heapeth up a store of merits after the manner of wheat. Which store, while it lifteth itself on high as by a certain point, yet raiseth not itself with the windy multitude of chaff; and is held gracious to the husbandman for the making of bread, and no less fruitful for the casting of seed. For not only is the Virgin's manner of life proved to please the Bridegroom, but in these also that stand by it worketh as it were a seminal force, while it instructeth them and provoketh them to all better things, and admonisheth them, not by word but by example, to grow and to stretch forth unto the things that are before. Whose merits, so great, lest robbers presume to carry them off violently, lest thieves plunder them, lest even mice seek fraudulently to drag them away, are set about indeed not with stakes, [0463C] not with stones, not with mortar, but with lilies, that is, with the allurement of cleanness and of inviolable grace.

## CHAPTER XIX.

*Thy two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe: thy neck like a tower of ivory.* The force of love maketh these same words said above to be repeated, but they are not to be expounded again, for the sake of a briefer delay; yet that which can be reckoned changed and as it were different may be enquired into — what it meaneth, what ought therein to be figured. For above it was said [n: (l. IV, c. 12)]: *Thy neck is like the tower of David;* but here, *like a tower of ivory.* In the tower is figured a certain fortitude of the virgin, in the ivory the chaste and sincere beauty of that same fortitude; because her whom the tower setteth against the enemies fore-armed with virtues, the coldness inborn [0463D] in ivory sheweth to be polished from fiery passions. A tower therefore is the Virgin, when she bravely *269* defendeth herself from enemies, but a tower of ivory when she sheweth herself free from the heat of the flesh; a tower, I say, when the onset of the malignant shuddereth at the mass of her virtues, of ivory when with a cold rigour she whiteneth as with the frost of winter.

## CHAPTER XX.

*Thine eyes are like the fishpools in Hesebon, which are in the gate of the daughter of the multitude.* Of the eyes also I deem enough was said in the second book [n: (sup. l. IV, c. 7, et alibi)], nor do I think it necessary that what was said be repeated but because a new comparison seemeth here to be added, that very newness demandeth to be here expounded. Hesebon is a city which a multitude of peoples inhabiteth [0464A] the fishpools are fountains, or lakes and a fitting fulness of waters, which, set in the gate of the city — the truth of the matter being so — refresh the dwellers of that city with a manifold bounty. The eyes therefore of the Bride, not infected with serpentine dregs, but, as the second book explaineth, conformed to the manners of doves, are for this cause perchance in the present place like unto fishpools, because they steep the washed, or wash the steeped, with saving disciplines. For those whom the Virgin vouchsafeth to behold with gracious eyes, on whom she worthily chooseth to have mercy by a regard of benevolence, calling them back from wandering in the open field, she leadeth us to a profitable gate, through which she bringeth us in to the citizens and the household and the throng of them that worthily deserve. Hesebon is interpreted *the girdle of sorrow.* By her regard indeed the Virgin restraineth us from an outward licence, and when we have entered the straits of the gate a necessary sorrow [0464B] girdeth us; and she no longer suffereth us to be glad from all the things that clamour without, but willeth us to be afflicted with misery and worthy of mercy. And when the Virgin in pity beholdeth us such, she guardeth us as citizens and household of the daughter of the multitude; which daughter, that is, the city, admitteth indeed many comers unto herself, but, by a law strange enough, admitteth none save the mournful and the wretched. This refuge they have, this guard they use for the present, that the Virgin cherisheth them with the fitting benefit of her eyes, [sic: *qnod*] she visiteth the mourning with a diligent solicitude, so kindly refreshing them for the present that she promiseth far better in what followeth. I have experienced what I say. When, by the divine judgment urging it, the sons of my mother fought against me, when, while strangers spared me, they whom I believed to be mine own bowels wounded me, [0464C] the ash of this Hesebon, mine own sadness, would have compelled me to perish, had not the Virgin vouchsafed with outstretched hand the sooner to succour me. She stood by me, and cast not away the care of me any further, but interposed herself in the midst of the tongues of the malignant; and marking that they raged not with zeal of justice but with a hostile faction, with the strong hand of mercy she stopped the mouth of them that spoke things so unjust. To whom that which followeth rightly agreeth: *Thy nose,* etc



## CHAPTER XXI.

*Thy nose is like the tower of Libanus, which looketh toward Damascus.* Pestilent men, who are the champions and athletes of the devil, like unto him by whom they are sent, stir up quarrels without discretion; and blinded by malice they know not the reason of judgment, and if perchance they have known it, rancour [0464D] and envy corrupt their knowledge. But the Virgin, seeing that some have need of a greater patronage, knoweth not how to fail those whom she hath known to suffer wrong, shewing to them that rightly consider that she hath a strong nose, not flattened after the manner of an ape, not unnerved with softness, not shorn away. For although as it were in silence she sometimes permitteth her own to be afflicted, perchance so far as it is expedient that they be amended by tribulations, yet when the malignity of the envious groweth up more violently and assaileth, the discretion of this strong one, as the tower of Libanus, standeth forth and fighteth back. And so much the more doth she prevail and more effectually withstand the malignant, as she is solidly confirmed in Christ, who is the mount of Libanus, upon whom set and built up she looketh and gazeth toward Damascus, that with a solicitous gaze she may call it back and turn it from its purpose. Damascus is interpreted *thirsting for blood.* [0465A] But the city of the lost ever thirsteth for our blood; yet lest it drink it all, the Virgin forbiddeth by the regard of her eyes, which both confer a saving defence upon us that piously ask, and mightily bring loss upon her that evilly thirsteth. For her discretion knoweth when and how she may console those that suffer unjust things, and with what penalty she may strike back, or with what patience await, them that inflict them; she knoweth whom, humble and abject, she may regard with a pitying countenance, and whom on the contrary, Damascenes, she may despise, their malice so deserving. In all which things she attendeth not to her own good pleasure alone, but greatly esteemeth the will of the Bridegroom, whom she desireth to please; loving whose friends, she groweth glad at their advancement, and over whose enemies, as with a perfect hatred, she pineth away. To whom is well subjoined: *Thy head,* etc. *270*

## CHAPTER XXII.

[0465B]

*Thy head is as Carmel, and the hairs of thy head as the purple of the king joined to channels.* [var: Vulg. *vincta canalibus*, "bound in channels"; Philip's own gloss keeps the Vulgate's word, saying that the purple is *alligari* — bound — in the channels] The head of the Virgin may not unfitly be called her mind or intention, to which the remaining works, as subject members, seem so to be assigned that they deserve neither to be directed unto [sic: *proficiendnm*] nor to be raised up unto pleasing, if they be not governed by the intention going before as by a head. Which intention, because iniquity presseth it not down, weakness softeneth it not, but it raiseth itself to the things above with a sound desire of pleasing, hath deserved to obtain the eminence and the name of a mountain, whose interpretation is found not to lack the fruit of a mystery. Carmel is interpreted *the knowledge of circumcision,* or, *knowing circumcision.* Circumcision, as the Jews have known, is a cutting of the flesh, cutting away the foreskin, that is, carnal desire [0465C] in a figure; which, given by Moses, the Jews held literally, but they spiritually who studied to lay aside what the flesh suggesteth. The Virgin therefore, whose intention is known to stand above desire, is rightly called Carmel, not knowing how to lie under carnal things — she who, spiritually circumcised in heart and ears and all her senses, in bearing a son pleased, undivided, not a man but God alone. That new mother indeed saw in herself the wondrous excellency of the mountain, when, coupling herself to the Bridegroom, she circumcised the desires of carnal men; when the Spirit so overshadoweth her, a spiritual circumcision so cleanseth her, that she who beareth transmitteth not to the born the hereditary fault of the flesh. Whose hairs of the head, that is, her holy and most subtle thoughts, [0465D] by which there cometh to the head no mean comeliness or ornament, are likened to the purple of the king joined to channels, while by faith and love of the passion of Christ they are empurpled as with a certain blood. Among those who are said to be skilled in this craft, the purple is wont to be bound in little bundles in narrow channels, and upon it so bound water is poured, in due manner and measure, by which pouring the dye may be serviceable for empurpling the wool. Or, according to some, at Tyre and Sidon, where this craft is chiefly practised, fine and white wool is straitened in channels, which by the blood of the shellfish poured over it is changed into a purple colour, and thenceforth is called purple — nay, is called the purple. Which is therefore said to be the purple of the king, because from of old it was wont to be as it were proper to kings that they should be clothed [0466A] with a purple garment by special privilege, and that by this sign, marked off from the rest, they should without doubt be shewn to be kings. Whence in the Gospel [n: (Matth. XXVII; Joan. XIX)], because Christ had as it were presumed to attest himself a king, the persecuting Jews were seen to be intolerably indignant; and before they slew him whom they would not have reign over them, they in mockery clothed him with a [sic: *pnrpuream*] chlamys. But the hairs of the head are laid in narrow channels, when the Virgin's thoughts are put under spiritual exercises, when the faith of Christ's passion prepareth for itself a cleaner place, when the rain descending upon the fleece turneth the whole of it into love. The blood of the sea-fish is the very love of the Redeemer, who was made man in the world by the precept of the eternal begetter; upon the Virgin, whom he marketh to be shut in the frying-pan of discipline, [0466B] he poureth over and poureth in the love of his own blood by the grace of a medicine. Whereby she is said to become purple — nay, the purple — and thenceforth is exhibited to the highest king so properly, so specially, that she is fitted no longer to human but to divine use only; and is proved to know and to love not a man that is man, but God and man. Which God-man also is not unfitly called the head of the Virgin, who by a princely excellency is proclaimed the mountain of the house of the Lord above the top of the mountains, to whom perchance the name of no other but of Carmel is assigned, because as knowingly as mightily he taketh away the foreskin from the true Israel. But the hairs, which are known to cleave to the head by the root, and yet to stray further abroad unless discipline study to restrain them, are all the acts of the Virgin which she hath more firmly established from the root in Christ, and hath called back from [0466C] excessive going forth by a judicial strictness. Which she willed to be brought into channels, that is, into low and humble straits, and the joy of the passion to be drawn over them as a purple dye — whose whole manner of life knoweth not to be highminded, but to fear, and to shine forth with a reddening martyrdom as a living victim.

## CHAPTER XXIII.

*How fair art thou, and how comely, most dear one, in delights? Thy stature is likened to a palm tree, and thy breasts to clusters of grapes.* Because the praises begun from the steps have come in a straight series to the head or the hairs, and have found nothing in all the aforesaid that is not praiseworthy, he comprehendeth the beauty of the Virgin in a kind of little summary, calling her most dear, in whom he findeth [0466D] nothing reprehensible. How fair art thou, saith he, with a will *271* that knoweth not torpor, but is lively; how comely, pursuing a just willing with an effectual hand; and that the praises may be strengthened by an end more worthily heaped up, most dear amid so many delights to me who am delicate. In one such, so praiseworthy, I complain of no loss, because thy stature is like a commendable palm tree, which is narrower in its lowest parts, spacious in the upper: thou rejoicest in a good beginning, fruitful with a better end. Finally, as the palm is set before the girded warrior, so assuredly it is delivered to the ungirded victor also; and that which had led on to labour and roused the mind of the fighter is raised up unto praise when it is borne in the hand of the triumpher. Thy stature therefore is found like unto this palm, when persevering labour is marked with such titles of praise, when, beginning from [0467A] the lowest, thou art enlarged with a fruitful advance, when, the world's champion being conquered, thou rejoicest in a reward now certain. Thy stature is said not undeservedly to be likened to a palm, which is known rather to stand in an upright purpose than to be bowed; and because her standing is granted to go forward unbending unto perfection, she deserveth to obtain the palm, that is, a worthy title of victory. And thy breasts, wherewith thou givest suck, or feedest abundantly them that stand about — that is, the form of thy life whereby thou instructest the ignorant both morally and spiritually — is like, not to useless herbs, not to barren trees, but to fertile clusters, joyous with [sic: *recundito*] wine. For they that attentively behold thee perfect both in moral and in spiritual things, and so carried up from the bosom of the earth to the lofty likeness of a palm, wonder, are amazed, and are not held within their own [0467B] bounds, while among all women they behold none like unto thee. Pressing therefore thy breasts with certain hands of consideration, and foreseeing more fully that the perfection of both lives floweth from them, they seem to have pressed out for themselves as it were certain clusters, and to have brought forth an inebriating wine of amazement and wonder.



## CHAPTER XXIV.

*I said: I will go up into the palm tree, and will take hold of its fruits; and thy breasts shall be as the clusters of the vine; and the odour of thy mouth as the odour of apples.* Whence so great a grace beyond the rest is conferred upon the Virgin, that her breasts are held like to clusters and her stature like to a palm, the Bridegroom evidently intimateth in the following verse, shewing what he had foretold, and that he hath consequently fulfilled what was foretold. *I said,* saith he: [0467C] *I will go up, and thy breasts shall be clusters.* His saying is the purpose which from eternity he willed to be ordained, which, remaining fixed with himself, he willed for a very long while to be hidden; but at length, when the happy fulness of times shone forth, there was given to this Virgin an evident certainty of this saying. For he who had long been hidden with himself or in the Father, an Angel indeed being sent, yet himself going before the Angel, was presented to the Virgin; and he willed that wonderful saying to be exhibited as it were visibly, while, invisible by nature, he granted himself by grace to be seen. *I said,* saith he, and what I said I will no longer keep silent, but *I will go up into the palm tree,* that is, I will appear visible: I will go up into the Virgin, through her I will shew myself to the rest, through the flesh assumed of her I will triumph over the prince of the world. For the depth [0467D] of my divinity was inaccessible to men, by love of whom being led I will go up on high, that when from the deep and hidden invisible I shall have been visibly exalted, I may draw all things to me, not defrauded of the efficacy of drawing. The Virgin therefore is a palm, lofty by the privilege of her merits, into whom the Bridegroom willed to go up as into a sycamore tree, whose ascent, that is, the assumption of flesh, is reckoned by every faithful one a foolish fig, but to him that worthily looketh up and humbly receiveth it, worketh a saving fruit. Which fruit the Bridegroom himself thankfully taketh hold of, when he findeth in it nothing at all to displease him, when he accepteth, when he approveth, when he rejoiceth that it accordeth with his good pleasure, that the fruitfulness of the palm is granted to bring forth the salvation of the faithful. He taketh hold, I say, when a keeper [0468A] most faithful draweth near to it, when he fore-armeth it and taketh heed that he leave nothing of it to be exposed to the birds, when he cherisheth the palm itself and advanceth it into so great a power that whatsoever befitteth the world unto salvation hangeth from it. And there hangeth from it the flesh of Christ, the passion of the flesh, the wood of the cross: the abolishing of faults, the flight of night, the return of the true light, the reconciliation of the world, the constancy of virtues, the confidence of rewards — all which things he thankfully taketh hold of, who is the author and disposer of them. Which being taken hold of, the breasts of the Bride are likened to the clusters of the vine, because by her benefits the minds of them that worthily consider are made drunken; and her odours, or the odour of her mouth, is made as of apples, because her fame and her teaching hath a good savour in the nostrils of her hearers. To which is subjoined: *The throat,* etc.

## CHAPTER XXV.

[0468B]

*Thy throat like the best wine.* If the things that are borne to them without by a faithful messenger are as clusters, as apples, what and how great things *272* may be believed to be those which are felt by the Virgin herself, which she, pouring out with a bountiful hand, offereth timely to the jaws of the hungry — who but a blind man would deem that she is fasting from things so great and such? She indeed above the rest rejoiceth to feel things so many, so excellent; she chiefly draweth in what sweetness is had in the Bridegroom, and how great; and what others scarce foretaste, whom so great an excellency of merits adorneth not, she with an eager draught feeleth more fully and tasteth. Whose taste the Bridegroom figured by the name of the throat, and willing to commend it, compared it to the best wine, because to whomsoever the taste or the throat of the Virgin becometh known, he seemeth [0468C] to himself to have drunk, in that he groweth unspeakably glad. For to whom the Virgin, not envious, maketh her taste known, his heart she gladdeneth as though it had drunk wine; and so much is she granted to know and to feel in the secret of her heart that he to whom it shall be given to consent is not able not to rejoice. And well did the Bridegroom proclaim that wine to be the best, whereof whosoever hath drunk hath deemed none better: the vineyard of Naboth gave not the like to drink, nor perchance the vineyard of Sorec; nor did Noe drink better of the first vineyard that he planted. But because that taste, or the throat of the Virgin, is more fully made known to none, nor doth any other rejoice more over what he hath received, than the Bridegroom, who needeth not to be taught by a transitory word (for he seeth and approveth whatsoever useful thing is thought); the Virgin, knowing that wine [0468D] to please more worthily the herald of it, catching the word as it were from his mouth, hasteneth to answer.

## CHAPTER XXVI.

*Worthy for my Beloved to drink, and for his lips and his teeth to ruminate upon.* He commendeth, saith she, my throat — nay, that which now groweth sweet in the throat, which whosoever is dull and stupid in palate approveth not enough; but he himself, by whose gift so great a grace shineth clear to me, drinketh with a full draught, and his bowl drieth not with want. I indeed have experienced the wondrous sweetness of this wine, and, the Bridegroom proclaiming it to be the best, am not uncertain of it; whereof, lest by keeping silence I be reproved, I have confidently spoken, and what he rightly began I have followed up with a worthy heralding. He, a discerning judge, saith that wine to be the best; and relying on that saying [0469A] I consequently assert it to be worthy — worthy, I say, that it be offered him to drink in a pleasing cup, to whom assuredly whatsoever shall be unworthy is not owed. But all the best things ought to be given to none more worthily than to him who ought to be deemed the best of all, who, as he in no wise willeth to be given drink in a dreggy cup, so requireth of me that unmixed wine, and that only, be presented to him. My throat therefore, which he named the best wine — that is, the affection of my heart, which hath tasted of him things so great, so unspeakable — I judge it worthy that I diligently present it to his sight, and fill up his thirst, offering a fitting draught. For he thirsteth, and thirsteth for the good of us all, who nevertheless admitteth not the gall of dragons and the wine of asps [n: (Deut. XXXII)]; he drinketh not the vinegar of the Jews, nor the bitterness offered him, [0469B] but refuseth it; and he putteth far off the wicked, whom in the Gospel he thus accuseth: *Go,* saith he, *you cursed; for I thirsted, and you gave me not to drink [n: (Matth. XXV)]*. [var: Vulg. Matt. 25:41 has *Discedite a me*, "Depart from me," where Migne prints *Ite*, "Go"; and Vulg. 25:42 has *potum*, "drink," where Migne prints *bibere*, "to drink." Migne also joins the two verses and inserts *enim*] And so I judge it worthy that I offer the best wine to him that thirsteth, which may please not only at the first taste but no less at the repeating; that drinking it eagerly, and holding what he hath drunk pleasing, he may suffer no weariness, but rather love it ruminated. The lips and the teeth, wherewith clean animals are known to ruminate, I deem to figure a re-handling, and in the re-handling a strictness, wherewith that benevolent and most keen judge, to see whatsoever he loveth in the Bride, handleth it again and strictly examineth it unto pleasing. He drinketh indeed when he thankfully embraceth her understanding or her affection; he ruminateth when he handleth again and strictly examineth [0469C] what is loved; and the more he perceiveth that nothing unfitting appeareth before, nothing after, so much the more he loveth to rejoice in things exquisite and well-pleasing. And as the law willed that the animal which ruminateth not be proclaimed unclean, so that understanding or affection is not clean enough which endureth not to be handled again; but whatsoever lieth hid in the Virgin feareth not a repeated judgment, and the subtle ruminator findeth nothing in her that he should cut away. Therefore she addeth: *I,* etc.

## CHAPTER XXVII.

*I to my beloved, and his turning is toward me.* I, I say, rejoice to be found serving and obeying my Beloved, to cleave to him more gratefully, to experience his pleasing sweetness; [0469D] whatsoever I feel in myself feareth not to be laid open to him more openly, my conscience shrinketh not from being met by his scrutiny. I indeed, not distended with womanish levity through the vain and various windings of the world, am intent with a ripe gravity upon him whom alone I love; from him I am turned away neither in act nor in affection, not even for a little, but am turned to his face with a devout desire. And my beloved himself slumbereth not while he keepeth me *273*, nor doth he snore, but is at hand; when I shall have cried out, he sheweth himself benevolent to her that crieth; he turneth not away his face from my prayers, nor even from my affections, but turneth himself to my desire with a cheerful countenance. And since between us there is proclaimed not an aversion but a mutual conversion, it pleaseth that my speech also be turned again unto him, that my face, which in seeking out beholdeth his face [0470A] sought out, may address that very face familiarly as it were mouth to mouth.



## CHAPTER XXVIII.

*Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field, let us abide in the villages.* Thou saith she, whom I love, who above didst not refuse, being called, to come; whom coming I have known to impart to me a more bountiful grace — come yet again, if thou lovest to find me prompt and prepared, that I may both will and be able to consent to thy commandment. Above indeed I had as it were feared that my washed feet should be defiled, and that, rejoicing in a pleasing little bed, I should again be called forth to outward things; but because I now understand that this is expedient for the needs of many, I refuse not whatsoever I shall see to accord with thy good pleasure. Come therefore, my Beloved, and let us hasten to go forth together into the field, that we may announce thy name to the world and thy [0470B] grace; that the things which thou hast long since hidden and now disposest no longer to lie hid may become known to all who shall nevertheless be worthy to obtain this benefit. Not only in Judea, which is called as it were our city, where our fellow-citizens are and the generation of our flesh is propagated, but in the villages also, that is, without, among the Gentiles, let us cause the knowledge of us to be spread abroad; and that it may be spread the more effectually, let it not irk us to abide there the longer. And the beloved and the beloved one are then seen to go forth into the field, and are not held in the secret of the bridechamber with the door shut, when the world loveth to embrace by faith the Word made flesh, and venerateth the mother of whom the Word willed to be incarnate. But to those the mother and the son are not yet gone forth who, by a rustic dulness not having professed the catholic faith, adore not God [0470C] and man together, being struck with scandal, and abhorring the fruitful Virgin honour her not with a worthy reverence. Therefore the Virgin, seeing that this ought no longer to be deferred, willeth the knowledge of hidden things at length to be brought forth into the midst, and a sure faith to be carried over in the apostles to the Jews, and that the Idumeans be not made outcasts from the grace of the same gift. For into Idumea Christ refused not to stretch forth his shoe, and changed enemies into friends and strangers into household folk, when by teaching and grace he made known to the distant nations that his immortality had shod itself with our mortality. In which nations the Virgin admonisheth him to make a stay, and he, being admonished, refuseth not; wherein she secretly reproveth and accuseth the hardness of the Jews, who, deserting the faith of Christ all too soon after the apostles, [0470D] so remain, deferring their conversion even to the end of the world. But into the villages, that is, the nations which were foolish far from the citizens, which, rude and untilled, had not yet known the prophetic teaching, the mother and the son come, and make a lingering dwelling among them, while they so cleave to the son that they hold also a grateful mention of the mother; at whose advancement the Virgin, loving to rejoice, and understanding that this same thing pleaseth the son no less, yet urgeth and taketh it upon her confidently to admonish him that he persist in promoting unto better what hath been well begun.

## CHAPTER XXIX.

*Let us get up early to the vineyards, let us see if the vineyard hath flourished, if the flowers bring forth fruits, if the pomegranates [0471A] have flourished. There will I give thee my breasts.* Because all the faithful have found our benevolence profitable to themselves, and are not uncertain of their own advancement if grace shall have continued, let us get up early, when night is now compelled to be turned into light, and let us render them watchful with a labour and a zeal not slothful. In the morning indeed the solicitous husbandman willeth to go out to the vineyards, to provide them what is useful, to free them from what is useless, to cut away superfluities, to apply diligence to necessary things, rejoicing if he shall have weighed that they answer him with a fitting increase. And so let us also get up early, that is, let us hasten to take away the evening horror, to give the dawn to the vineyards, to pour in the morning sun: let our visitation drive far off and beat back the darkness of ignorance, and pour over the Churches of the Gentiles the new light of grace. Let the nations know that the Lord is thy name; [0471B] let them know and go forth and begin their work; and let those which before, barren and dry, were weighed down with a nightly dulness, advance and flourish in the morning, and be held as fertile vineyards. Let our visitation, our vision, confer increase upon them, and let it not permit them to be afflicted more than is just, but with the tribulation make also an issue: let us press upon the work, thou going before mightily and mercifully, and I diligently and faithfully interceding for the Churches. Let us see if it hath flourished — that is, let us hold it pleasing that the vineyard seemeth to have flourished; already *274* it sheweth beforehand that it hath received our grace; already it hath grown green, already it hath flowered, already it rejoiceth to have given hope to the solicitous husbandman, and with a flowering appearance to have given forth sure signs of advancement. And because the flower sufficeth not, if it be not granted to come to fruit, let us see, let us approve [0471C] that the flowers seem to bring forth fruits, because the nations which are taught to come together into the hearing of faith delay not to mark that faith itself with worthy works. Let us see also if the pomegranates have flourished; let us weigh that in them many have been strong with so great a fortitude that, fervent with love, they expose themselves to the enduring of martyrdom, even though the executioners set no material sword against them without. But that the syllabic conjunction, that is *If,* is so often repeated, is no doubting, but the speech is confirmed; because what she foretelleth is by no means doubtful, but certain to the virgin, nor doth the outcome of the matter contradict such a saying of hers. For many among the Gentiles, upon whom the mother and the son conferred their benevolence, after the manner of a vineyard have by labour and zeal brought forth a flowering [0471D] appearance, and by the advance of grace have led their flowering affections into fruitful effects, and by their form as well as their teaching have brought others to fruit. But some who burn with the torches of a greater desire flower as pomegranates, they redden with tribulations, they endure in their purpose so many and so great troubles in the contest that they differ from the fruit of martyrdom only by the suffering of death. For the Spirit which resteth not from envy and from lying oftentimes so burneth against certain men with unbridled malice that with the utmost zeal it busieth itself either to weaken their life, or at least to defile their good name with sinister rumours. It goeth forth therefore, and infecteth those whom it findeth more prone to malice; it armeth with shamelessness elders that are such not by mastership but by presbytery, who, when they are not able [0472A] to fulfil their concupiscence at their pleasure, determine to turn back the whole weight of the crime upon Susanna. A sinister report flieth, and shaketh the whole city; they are amazed and wonder at the unseemly novelty; and the innocent woman would have utterly perished by a false judgment, had not the divine mercy at length come to her aid, Daniel being sent. Who is there that would not praise her, that would not praise Marina and Eugenia and others of that kind — who would presume to defraud them of the reward from martyrdom, whom the guile of accusers and a shameless falsehood assailed, and whose souls the sword, not of iron but of trouble, pierced through? Finally God, sometimes suffering some to be deceived and to perish, permitteth the spirit of lying to rage in their ears; and the prophets, who deserve not to see true and useful things, prophesy by their own spirit whatsoever they know to please the king. [0472B] Being seduced therefore, they seduce Achab, itching in his ears, and with false soothsayings assert an imminent victory; but Micheas, who alone with a free voice testifieth the truth, first smitten with a buffet, is straightway made over to prison. There are some who, loving to speak vain things and to divine lies, in no wise will that any truthful man meet them; and both the prophet and he to whom it is prophesied smoothly and wickedly, not foreseeing his own case well enough, rejoiceth over a brother's trouble. A disease or pestilence of which kind creepeth widely even to-day and rangeth further; this stain occupieth many and is spread over a broad space; and very many are found who, bearing before them the appearance of love in countenance and habit, maliciously detract, and curiously hear them that detract. For being darkened with malice they deem that more is conferred upon their own praises if [0472C] they shall have weighed that the honour due is not paid to their brethren; if they have known the fame of others to be weakened by any reproach whatsoever, they think their own either to stand more firmly or to be more copiously heaped up. And so, hating Micheas, they follow not his truthful soothsaying, and lying to the king they comply with his desires; and while both king and ministers are seduced by a flattering lie, those are not deserted whom they unjustly and wickedly persecute. For the Virgin is at hand, and vouchsafeth them her own vision, whom she prudently understandeth to be pressed down by an unjust wounding; and lest, being wounded, they fail, but rather that, being tempted, they may rejoice in the issue, delivering them from present things she promoteth them to better by her intervention. Therefore she addeth to the Bridegroom: *There will I give,* etc



## CHAPTER XXX.

[0472D]

*There will I give thee my breasts.* When I shall have seen, saith she, the vineyard marked with new flowers, when I shall have seen the following fruits brought forth by the foregoing comeliness of the flowers, when I shall have seen any oppressed man afflicted more than is just, and coloured in our sight with a Punic beauty: *There,* that is, then — at an opportune hour, to wit, at a fitting time — I will pour in my breasts, I will give my help to him that is in need. And well doth the Virgin promise that she will give, not a breast, but breasts, because very many will, whose action answereth not their will; for many seem to have compassion when they mark us wretched, but labouring under want or avarice they stretch not forth the hand of help. Of such men a certain heathen: All men, saith he, pardon, no man succoureth. But the Virgin both pitieth our [0473A] miseries with an affection of benevolence, and with a most powerful hand worketh whatsoever she shall have seen necessary for us; and lest under a hard burden faith had languished and hope should waver, she is quickly at hand, so to refresh us with both breasts. But because her benignity hath mercy on none of us save for the sake of the son, *275* whom she beholdeth most merciful toward us, lest she should seem to refer the cause of the benefit to us rather than to him — whom assuredly she loveth not for our sake, but us for his — therefore she said not: *I will give* them *my breasts,* but, *I will give thee.* Whatsoever, saith she, I shall have bestowed on them who so need to be helped, I will attribute the whole to thee, whose good pleasure I see to work in these things; nor will I have this favourably assigned either to them or to myself, but rather that both they and I myself more justly glory in thee alone. Whatsoever [0473B] therefore I be found mercifully to impart to thine — whom I shall see to flourish as vineyards, whom to bring forth good works, whom finally, suffering unjust things, I shall have weighed to be like unto pomegranates, sighing only unto us, awaiting our patronage — whatsoever help, I say, I shall confer upon such, I will give to thee, because through thee and for thee, and referring the whole to thee, I will help them.

## CHAPTER XXXI

*The mandrakes have given a smell in our gates.* [var: Vulg. divides otherwise — *Mandragorae dederunt odorem. In portis nostris omnia poma…* — attaching the gates to the apples, not to the mandrakes; Migne's division gives the gates to the mandrakes, which is what this whole chapter expounds] Because the Virgin before named the villages and the vineyards and the pomegranates, in which she figured the Churches of the Gentiles and their various advancements, making a passage to the Jews, under a riddle nevertheless and a figure, she foretelleth that their conversion shall one day be. Whose conversion [0473C] a prophetic nostril, most sagacious in perceiving, smelleth out, and she rejoiceth with a most certain hope of their converting, knowing and foreknowing the conversion of the people of the Jews, which, though it must be deferred, shall yet come at the end of the ages. Signifying which beforehand: *A smell,* saith she, *in our gates the mandrakes* now *have given;* our nostrils, not blunted with ignorance, have perceived beforehand that, after the fulness of the Gentiles shall be granted to enter in, then the remnant of the Jews, then all Israel shall be converted. Mandrakes, as they say, are herbs suited to the uses of medicine, bearing before them a human likeness, save for the head; by which the Jews, prudent and erring, are figured fitly enough, who are formed to the divine worship by a written law, as being men. But because they know not Christ the head of the faithful, nor [0473D] adore him, being truncated and disfigured they discolour all the remaining body; and they who by the knowledge of the Scriptures and by the legal commandments are conformed to the faithful are deformed by the absence of the head and by an unbelieving ignorance. Who also confer no mean medicine upon the sick, when they read the law to us, when they bring forth a discipline of living, when they keep for us the codices, as a furnace of moral things, as a workshop of spiritual, and bring to us for teaching those whom they hold as severe judges. And these indeed bring forth no fuller fruit as yet in the houses, as yet in the bridechamber, but in the gates, that is, in spiritual senses, they give a pleasing smell to the virgin, because what the divine goodness disposeth to impart to them in the last days is already granted to the virgin, smelling it from afar, to perceive beforehand; for she perceiveth that after the fulness [0474A] of the Gentiles shall have entered in, Judea, which now, wandering, is gone forth from the borders of the Church, which, labouring with famine, receiveth not even the crumbs from the table of the masters, shall then be converted to the faith, and shall feed on the bread of the children.

## CHAPTER XXXII.

*All the apples, new and old, my Beloved, I have kept for thee.* That the Gentiles, called together to the faith by the gift of a new grace, bring forth worthy fruits and works agreeable to holiness — this is my desire, this assuredly my zeal, my care, who diligently care for whatsoever I shall have known will please thee. Likewise that the Jews, who now stray abroad as with bonds broken, are called back in the last days to the ancient binding of faith — my solicitude no less desireth this, demandeth this, which affectionately grieveth with them that go astray, and pardoneth them. And so, my Beloved, [0474B] I keep for thee apples new and old, when I more studiously heap up the merits of both peoples, when I permit not the good beginnings of the Gentile and of the Jew to perish, but study to make firm the purpose of the one and to repair the hurt of the other. Which merits, or fruits, or works the Virgin perchance willed for this cause to name apples, because she rejoiceth to present gifts of this kind to the bridegroom for his eating: that he may both be taken with their delightful appearance, and, lest he start back as one defrauded, be held by the useful and commendable substance. She keepeth the apples of the Gentiles, when she cherisheth and embraceth their newness, when she rejoiceth that they are grafted in and that a richer fatness of the olive is given to them so grafted, when she presenteth herself powerful and benevolent to them as they labour, and with a pious devotion presenteth their fruitful labours to the son. But she is seen no less to preserve the apples [0474C] of the Jews, when, at length pitying them, she willeth them not to err any longer, when she busieth herself to restore the household of her own race to their ancient state, and, giving her hand, turneth the people long an enemy of the faith into a friend. She keepeth new things and old, when she so helpeth the Gentiles to be now converted to the newness of faith that she willeth them not to be wholly turned away from the older Jews; when she loveth the Jews so to return to a faith now lost, or rather *276* interrupted, that yet she grudgeth not that the Gentiles were grafted in before. These things I have kept, saith she, not seeking, to wit, a nearer glory for myself, but all of them utterly for thee, that is, unto thine honour; because, when the Virgin, solicitous, rejoiceth concerning them or for them, she glorieth not in herself but in the Bridegroom, as was said a little before.



## CHAPTER XXXIII.

[0474D]

*[CAP. VIII.] Who shall give thee to me for my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother, that I may find thee without, and thoroughly kiss thee, and now no man shall despise me?* [var: Vulg. *et iam me nemo despiciat*, "and now let no man despise me" — a present subjunctive, and with the pronoun before *nemo*; Migne prints the future indicative *despiciet*, which is the tense Philip's own gloss below carries throughout (*deferetur… tolletur… erit*).] The Virgin desireth that the things which, touching the Gentiles and the Jews, she already foreknoweth while they are yet absent, may become known without to a world that knoweth nothing save what is evident; and that the knowledge of the Bridegroom, which already lieth open to her as it were within the bridal chamber, may go forth abroad into the field, where the sun dawneth more largely. Who shall give thee to me, saith she — that is, who shall bless me with so great a gift of his own, who shall so enlarge my desire, pressed down with straits, that I may be able to find thee without for my brother, and to set forth to the rest, who know them not, the things that are known to me? Thee indeed the begetting of flesh maketh my brother, nay, the brother of all; thee a mother feedeth in time, and that not of necessity, but of nature: [0475A] thou suckest her breasts, thou refusest not to take from her the nourishment of little ones, when thou usest food, drink, raiment, sleep, whereby thou excusest not thyself from being man. Him whom my mother proclaimeth to be such a one, so very little, who shall give me to find without in the street — to find, I say, not man only, which is not denied to the eyes of unbelievers, but God made man, which is imparted to none save the faithful? I will, saith she, that the Gentiles and the Jews, who are wont to be knowers of nothing but things visible, may see thee, understand thee, love thee to be God; and that thou, who art proclaimed a hidden God by prophetic foretelling, mayest be seen by these with a sure faith, the eye of the heart being unveiled. And if it be granted me to find thee there, I shall rejoice, and shall thankfully kiss him whom I have found among men; that is, I shall be delighted with the love and the honour of thy name, [0475B] namely when I shall behold thee loved and praised of men. Yet the Virgin willeth not to kiss him when found, but rather to kiss him thoroughly, and the composition of the word betokeneth nothing less, but an increase; and we are affirmed thoroughly to kiss, as it hath seemed to some, in that we kiss through very many places, expressing thereby a greater desire. The Virgin therefore willeth, if it may be, to find him among men, that she may thoroughly kiss him whole, and be compelled to pass over nothing without joy; that she may see him honoured by them as God and man, and, thoroughly kissing him who is marked with a twofold honour, may rejoice to be delighted. And when such honour shall be worthily paid to the Son, the reverence due to the Virgin herself also shall not be taken away, and she shall not be despised in the eyes of them that rightly seek, who before all women was chosen to bring forth such a one. For whosoever shall rejoice that he understandeth and loveth him as at once God and [0475C] man will not hold her, of whom he was born, contemptible, nor shall he be smitten with the scandal of the Jews nor with the folly of the Gentiles, when by the just heralding of the truth the wondrous integrity of the mother shall be established. Whosoever, I say, willeth to pay honour to the Son according to his good pleasure, setteth himself also not to take away from the mother the honour due to her, because a good son accepteth the homage of no man who seeketh not consequently to pay honour to the Virgin Mother.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.

*I will take hold of thee, and lead thee into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that bore me: there thou shalt teach me.* [var: Vulg. Cant. 8:2 has no *et in cubiculum genitricis meae*, "and into the chamber of her that bore me"; the phrase is Cant. 3:4's, printed as the lemma at 0349D. LXX and Vet. Lat. carry it at 8:2 (*καὶ εἰς ταμιεῖον τῆς συλλαβούσης με*), and Philip expounds the added chamber through this chapter and the four that follow.] When I shall perceive thee prudently understood and lately loved, favouring them that love, I will take hold of my beloved as it were with hands; [0475D] and holding him whom I have taken, I will not suffer thee to be led back from the purpose, but will cause thee to be brought in more largely into my mother's house. For far be it that I should fail them that love, that I, who am not despised, should despise; but I will cherish the imperfect more diligently, even unto the perfect. I will love them that love, and will advance them that they may love more; and thee, O Beloved, I will admonish with unwearied prayers, that thou help them. Thus will I take care to lead or to bring thee into my mother's house, when with dutiful solicitude I shall make her ready for thine entering in, when thou shalt solicitously obey me as a son his mother, and shalt follow not their ancient deserts, but my desire. The Virgin's mother, as was said before, is the very nature of mortals, which bringeth us all forth into this light by a not unlike begetting; which, that it may have for itself a house wherein it shall abide unto the [0476A] end of the world, bringeth forth men for itself by a succession that shall at no time cease. Into this house, that is, into men, the Virgin promiseth to lead the Bridegroom, that in them he may mercifully work their own salvation, that he may walk about in them, and rejoice to come to the chamber, where he may lie down, where he may rest, and may be able to find the reclining of quiet. Into the house *277* of her mother, and into the chamber, the solicitous virgin leadeth the bridegroom, when, dutifully pitying us, she leadeth him with devout prayers unto this: that he dwell in us, that he walk about in us for his goodness' sake, that he tarry in us, and be not called away thence by the desert of our depravity. *There,* saith she, *thou shalt teach me.* When it shall have come to this, that I rejoice thou art brought in to all the elect, and art not led back from the accomplishing of their salvation by the desert of their faults, then thou shalt teach me, [0476B] and shalt make me certain of hidden things; then shall I know both that they are elect, and that I am solicitous for the elect. Thou shalt teach me, I say, when the hope which before thou hadst given me by promise thou shalt with a larger grace translate into a thing fulfilled; when of that glory, whereof thou givest the longing to them that wait, the promissory term ceasing, thou givest the effect by a better.

## CHAPTER XXXV.

*And I will give thee a cup of spiced wine, and the new wine of my pomegranates.* When thou shalt make me taught, the effect of a fuller grace being known, I also will give thee the gifts of a mightier abundance: I will offer thee a cup most sweet in taste and in savour, wine indeed spiced, a love compounded out of labour. For the deserts [0476C] of them whom I shall have known to please thee — their loves, that is, and their labours — I will heap together as it were in a mixing-bowl, and will pledge them to thy sight, or rather to thy drinking; and, that thou mayest receive them the more thankfully, I will commend them with devoted benevolence. For if aromatic kinds bestow a seasoning upon wine, a skilled hand being applied it is turned into a spiced draught; and if to love there be added tribulation and the straitness of suffering, that love, being offered to the Bridegroom, obtaineth the place of a welcome draught. Which urging home, she saith: *And the new wine of pomegranates.* New wine boileth and bubbleth up, raging with tumult and with turbulence, casting all filth from itself with a stronger onset, and so betokeneth that love which careth not to be soothed with the quiet of this life, but, running to martyrdom, burneth to be polished by pressures and by beatings. But by pomegranates he willed those to be figured in whom, like [0476D] seeds, very many virtues are gathered together, whom the inward collecting of virtues maketh precious, and the ruddy face of their sufferings maketh beautiful in the eyes of them that rightly see. But "my own" the Virgin saith perchance for this cause: that whosoever, loving Christ, giveth himself over to the Passion and to martyrdom, she rejoiceth to bestow help and care upon him, and whatsoever he profiteth she reckoneth all her own. The new wine therefore of pomegranates is the unrestrained fervour, or the fervid love, of them that show themselves ready to suffer patiently all things which the world either horribly threateneth or rejoiceth violently to inflict. The cup of this wine or new wine the virgin loveth to pledge, when she rejoiceth that men fervent in spirit flash with virtues, and, taken away out of the midst, pass over at last to the table or the unfailing banquet of the Bridegroom, [0477A] and soothe the taste of him that feasteth with the sweet excellence of their deserts. And lest she be reckoned to ascribe this to herself more than is just, nay rather, that she may testify that whatsoever she rejoiceth over in them is of the divine gift, turning to the maidens that stand by she saith: *His left hand,* etc.



## CHAPTER XXXVI.

*His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.* That I lead the bridegroom, saith she, into my mother's house and into all the elect, that I serve the cup and heap gifts upon gifts, is his benefit, his left hand, his temporal consolation, which receiveth me as I lean back far more softly than the feathery tenderness of a pillow. For with this solace he cherisheth my insufficiency, and sustaineth it in the present, who with a more bountiful right hand shall embrace me in that which followeth; and he who now [0477B] so ruleth me that he forsaketh me not at all, shall one day so rule me that he shall set all sufficiency round about. In the fruit of that thing, and in the shadow of this hope, I now sweetly lie hid; much from things present, more largely from things to come, do I grow glad [sic: *nilaresco*]; which assuredly for this cause I make known to you that stand by, that you also may love him by whose so great gifts I am now enriched. Now this little verse is found set down and expounded before, and there another goeth before it which betokeneth the virgin's languor, because, when the virgin languishing asketh to be compassed about with apples and stayed up with flowers, straightway mention is made of the left hand, which is understood to sustain her as she lieth down. But here, where salvation is in the doorway, and no mention is made of languor, where the age is more advanced, and the advancement is of a stronger desert, she, [0477C] now secure of her own things, is solicitous for the profitings of others, and, forgetting as it were herself, rejoiceth in the perfected deserts of the elect. She seeth that they are to be compared, by the sweetness of love, to wine, to new wine, to the fervour of the spirit, and that they are the more worthily to be offered to the royal table and to the divine taste; whose oblation she desireth so ardently to be fulfilled, that in regard of it she patiently beareth her own to be deferred. For considering with what fruit her conceiving and the integrity of her childbearing become known to the hearts of the faithful, and to what end many in the process of time grow hot to love the bridegroom, she cannot but rejoice over such things, as well to come as present; and, their *278* glory being foreseen, she seemeth more gladly and more quietly to await her own. Beholding which, the bridegroom saith: *I adjure you,* etc.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.

[0477D]

*I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, that you stir not up, nor make the beloved to awake, till she herself will.* You, saith he, ye apostles, you teachers of the Church, go, teach all nations; and as touching them whom the Virgin foreseeth by a prophetic understanding to be saved, see that your negligence draw not back from advancement him that was foreseen; lest, if perchance you watch too little over the keeping of them, you stir up the desire of her from the quiet she hath already found. Now this adjuration, whereby the vigilance of teachers is so solicitously called upon, is found none the less in the second and third book of this work, where it hath been worn down enough by expounding — if at least it please the reader — nor, being repeated in this last one, hath it now need to be expounded. [0478A] Yet this may be said: that in the first place, taking care of her own self, she rejoiceth in spiritual leisure, from which she is forbidden to be called away by temporal business or unquietness, lest, while she loveth to be at leisure and contemplateth spiritual things, she be compelled to return, until she will, to the solicitude of her neighbours. But in the second place she taketh care lest Judaea, her heart being hardened, be seduced, but that the knowledge of the bridegroom be brought into her house or chamber; nor doth it suffice her enough that she be made thankfully an attendant to the bridegroom or to the son, if she should know that her own mother is utterly forsaken of grace. From this also the bridegroom forbiddeth her to be called away, as well in affection as in effect: namely, lest the apostolic teachers be found by their negligence to thwart it, but let them take care and be zealous to employ a watchful diligence, that the Virgin cease not to rejoice at the advancement of her own nation. [0478B] But in the third place she taketh care either only for the Gentiles, or alike for Jews and Gentiles, naming her mother the infirmity or the nature of men, into whose house — that is, into all flesh — she willeth the knowledge of the bridegroom to be brought in; and the bridegroom willeth that she be not drawn away from this desire by any trouble whatsoever. That that may be fulfilled which is written: *And all flesh shall see the Salvation of God [n: (Luc. III)]*

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.

*Who is this that cometh up from the desert, flowing with delights, leaning upon her Beloved?* The angelic spirits, standing by the bridegroom and the bride as they talk together, privy to the secrets of the espousals, beholding the deep mysteries, are held fast, nor are they able enough to be astonished [0478C] or to marvel what, or how great, the Virgin is, whose nuptials they see celebrated. They weigh indeed that she, endowed with a wondrous understanding, rejoiceth at the present advancement of others and is solicitous for that to come; that she burneth on this side with desire of the bridegroom, on that with solicitude for her neighbours; marked with virtues, comely with the eminence of her deserts. They consider also that the Bridegroom so rejoiceth in her leisure or quiet that he utterly keepeth off every approach of any indiscreet person, that he admitteth no importunate one within the cloisters of quiet, and suffereth her not, as she resteth, to be stirred up until she herself shall will it. But when they perceive the virgin to excel in these and other such things, when they scarce comprehend so great a grace of hers, so great deserts of hers, they speak one to another and inquire in mutual discourse what or how great is she [0478D] whose eminence they contemplate.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.

*Who is this that cometh up from the desert,* etc. The earthly habitation was already, through a long series of times gone by, a desert, and, sins requiring it, untried in heavenly goods; which Astraea forsook, being fuller of nettles, of thorns, of briers, and, bearing herself back to the stars, held a more pleasing place there. In which solitude the nature of mortals lay down oppressed with languor, while, the vigour of the spirit being corrupted, it leaned upon the allurements of carnal things; and, sunk under a heavy flood, it knew no way of coming up, it was sorely weighed down with mire, nor was there any possibility of wiping it away. Thence, by a new kind, by a newness [0479A] incomparably to be admired, by a portentous miracle as it were, by a thing to be compared with none in all the ages gone by, a virgin riseth and standeth forth, infected now with no filth of vices, and by a wondrous ascent is carried up to the excellence of deserts. What therefore, or how great, is she? Who worthily weigheth her eminence, who so ascendeth out of the ancient horror, out of the vast solitude, that, abiding there in body, in mind she holdeth a higher degree, and now floweth not away with the vices of manners, but, against custom, floweth with the delights of deserts? And in very truth we see her flowing with exceeding delights, and leaning, after the manner of delicate women, upon him whom she loveth; who, walking upon the earth, scarce attempteth to touch the earth, whose delights the beloved beareth up on high and sustaineth. Who shall worthily consider her, who shall not [0479B] marvel at her height, seeing that neither before nor afterward is she compared to any *279* of women, who, leaning and specially trusting in him whom she loveth, needeth nothing of ours, not distrustful of the advancement of perseverance? But that it is so solicitously asked by the angels who she is — if you will call it to mind, you shall find it thrice repeated; and whosoever be brought in to make such a question, the question itself maketh mention of the Virgin's advancement. First it is asked: Who is this that, made slender after the manner of a little rod by manifold disciplines, and compared to the smoke of spices and to all the powder of the perfumer, while yet living in the flesh so stretcheth herself on high by desire that whosoever more diligently attendeth to this is delighted by her odour or her example? Secondly it is asked: Who is this that, going forward, is like the dawn, while, the things behind being left [0479C] as it were a thicker shadow of the nights, she obtaineth the beauty of the moon, nay, and the likeness of the sun or of the day, and, striking terror into her enemies, is comparable to an army of camps set in array? Thirdly it is asked: Who is this that, delicate after the manner of noble matrons, forgetful of all things, delighted in him alone whom she loveth, so faileth from her own things that she willeth not to stand in them even a little, and so profiteth in him that she loveth to lean her whole self upon him? And that she may know and call to mind whence and whither she hath come, she heareth the Bridegroom saying: *Under the apple tree,* etc.



## CHAPTER XL.

*Under the apple tree I raised thee up: there thy mother was corrupted, there she that bore thee was violated.* Thou, saith he, who so leanest upon thy beloved with a delicate tenderness, who, hunger being driven far off, now reclinest at the banquet upon my breast, [0479D] to whom thou owest whatsoever thou hast — who raised thee up to this desert, save he who raised thee when thou wast languishing and lying under the tree? That first woman, who, ill containing herself, coveted the forbidden apple, and by an unlawful eating ensnared a husband ill uxorious, was straightway under the tree given over to languor, or rather to death; and the same death was left to them that came after as it were by hereditary right. Under this tree therefore, which is made comely by a mystical fruit, all posterity lieth and is laden with the laws of death, while in the fault which the tree brought in every creature languisheth and groaneth which a like begetting bringeth forth from those parents. Under the same tree the Virgin was held by a like bond, when the divine goodness (a thing that was covered with itself through many ages gone by) [0480A] looked more kindly, and chose her before all women, that through her he might redeem them whom hereditary death compelled to be damned. From the tree therefore to the tree he carried over the chosen Virgin, when, leading her out of fault, he raised her to the height of a greater grace; when, being free from the blemish of the fatherly and hereditary hurt, he translated her to the faith and the love of his passion to come. For the Virgin, receiving God out of herself, flesh being taken, to be born as man, acknowledged consequently that the same should die according to the flesh; in which death, because she understood the life and salvation of us all, she loved, if not the death, yet assuredly the gift of grace which it brought. When therefore she was snatched from under the apple tree which brought in death, she was none the less carried over under the apple tree which brought the fruit of life; [0480B] under whose shadow she was borne up to so great a summit that in grace and in desert she was made perfect before all women. But that which is said, *There thy mother was corrupted,* if it be referred to the first tree which brought in death, human nature is not unfitly called the Virgin's mother, which under that tree bore so great a hurt and loss that, being corrupted, it corrupted, and turned vice into nature for us. But if under the tree of the cross the bride's mother is believed to have been violated, Judaea is rightly understood to be called her mother, who, where the Bridegroom raised the Virgin to a singular grace by the desert of faith, there the mother, demanding that the Bridegroom be slain, violated her heart by obstinacy. Under the wood of the cross therefore both the bride's faith is strong and Judaea's chastity is violated, who, denying the true Bridegroom, is obstinately joined [0480C] to a corrupter; and him to whom she ought to have cleaved familiarly and been fastened, him, with a corrupted mind, with repeated voices she demandeth to be crucified. Where the Virgin, being raised up, heareth the bridegroom consequently saying: *Put me,* etc.

## CHAPTER XLI.

*Put me as a seal upon thy heart, as a seal upon thy arm; for love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell.* Because thy mother, by a ruinous error, cast me forth out of her heart, she also put far from the chamber of that same heart the salvation that was nigh; but thou, my Beloved, who in that same place art raised up by an incomparable grace, love him that raiseth thee, that loving thou mayest be the more diligently loved. But because in loving [0480D] thou appearest vehement enough, and not weak, I see that this must be added: what thou doest, do it more perseveringly, and confirm it; and thy heart, wherein my love seemeth in a large fulness *280* to be contained, close thou with a seal set upon it, which by no craft whatsoever can be done away. Now this seal, which I admonish to be set upon thy heart as it were a cover, is subject to no craft, to no hurt; because that which a subtler art doth not newly devise, nor a more learned hand fasten together, craft doth not unbar, violence doth not break. Me therefore, whom it is plain that no contrivance at all can hurt or corrupt — me, I say, myself set thou upon thy heart as a seal; and it sealing thee, no entrance nor going forth that bringeth loss shall lie open, and, that lying not open, love shall abide constant and unfailing. The same [0481A] seal also I will that thou set upon thine arm, namely that thou set not thyself to work anything save out of me, save through me; and that, when thou shalt have rightly sealed whatsoever thou doest with such a defence, thou mayest know that thine arm lieth open to no detriment at all. And for this cause I admonish that what thou doest, what thou lovest, be sealed by the setting of me upon it, because thy heart or thine arm, relying upon such a seal, shall not be hurt, but shall prevail against all things with an incomparable strength, and, being to be compared with death itself, shall not fear whatsoever cometh upon it. For as death standeth by all men indifferently, strong and undaunted, and no power or industry whatsoever withstandeth it as it standeth by, so love, if it be truly fortified beforehand with the aforesaid seal, is found strongly to prevail against all hurtful things. Again, as hell, when it [0481B] rejoiceth to rage more hardly against the wretched, and neither labour nor the groaning of the wretched can soften its hard cruelty, so the jealousy wherewith the virgin, loving, burneth to imitate God willeth not to be called back from her purpose, neither by prayer, nor by price, nor by softness. It is expedient therefore that this love, this jealousy, be held in thee strong and unbending, that the memory of me be not taken away from heart and from arm, from love and from work; because whosoever lacketh that seal is easily violated, and a vessel lacking a cover is judged unclean by the testimony of the law [n: (Num. XIX)]. But the vessel that burneth with the fire of love, and is covered with the hand of my solicitude — the heart, that is, of him that strongly loveth, which is guarded by me set upon it as a seal — is a commendable vessel, knowing not to be emptied, copious; the heart is [sic: *incibile*] [ *f.* lucibile], the heart is like unto a lamp, [0481C] not shadowy. Whence it is subjoined: *The lamps thereof,* etc.

## CHAPTER XLII.

*The lamps thereof are lamps of fire and of flames; many waters shall not be able to quench charity, neither shall the floods overwhelm it.* [var: Vulg. Cant. 8:7 *aquae multae non **potuerunt** extinguere caritatem*, a perfect — "many waters have not been able to quench"; Migne prints the future *poterunt*, and *neque* for the Vulgate's *nec*.] Not thou alone, saith he, O Virgin, who art commended with a worthy title of praise, in that thou art chief both in the grace of deserts and in the excellence of love, but whosoever loveth is called a lamp of fire and of flames, withstanding indeed a fall, yet not fleeing from pressures. For the lamp which stretcheth itself with open mouth to obtain love, and among the ill-hearted rich holdeth itself forth outwardly contemptible, is shown to them that worthily consider, and is understood to be [0481D] a lamp of fire, hiding its fire from them that are ill-darkened and unworthy. For it burneth and delightfully kindleth with an inward heat, and toward those things that are without it seemeth not to glow, but groweth cold, while it now careth not for whatsoever is of this life, as for a barren frost, and by an inward desire conformeth itself to the burning seraphim. Nevertheless, that it may be plain that the same lamp is not uselessly kindled, nor that a neighbour complain that nothing useful is bestowed upon him out of it, that which is first a lamp of fire is consequently said to be also a lamp of flames, that to them who diligently weigh it it may appear not to be wanting, not only to itself, but the neighbour also. For he that loveth, and is strongly burned up with the fire of love, is not torpid with languor, nor with leisure, but worketh the more watchfully; and with eyes not blear [0482A] he poureth out a welcome light with a bountiful gift, and offereth himself as a pattern to them that work, as a guide to them that walk. Him, burning and shining, the multitude of waters quencheth not; the lover, or his strength, yieldeth not to threats, not to blandishments; nor at last shall floods, nor the inundation of greater pressures, nor famine, nor the sword overwhelm the exuberance of the fire or of the flames. For charity is strong with so great violence or vigour that it cannot be overwhelmed by a small onset of tribulations nor by a greater, so that for love of the spiritual reward it beareth the multitude of waters, and the little drops of rainy dew, and the greater assaults of floods. To this charity therefore nothing perfunctory is rightly compared; nay rather, charity is worthily set before whatsoever can be had here: and from whomsoever a sound head and the truth of judgment is not taken away, he [0482B] chooseth her and loveth her above all that is offered here as transitory. Whence he addeth: *If a man shall give,* etc.



## CHAPTER XLIII.

*If a man shall give all the substance of his house for love, he shall despise it as nothing.* Whosoever rejoiceth not in the portion of things senseless or irrational alone, but, obtaining a human shape, useth a prevailing *281* reason — if he shall have given whatsoever he hath in regard of the charity that is to be gotten, he shall seem to have given nothing, if he be made master of this will. Substance is the name of whatsoever our necessity or our cupidity heapeth up in the present, and of whatsoever management either spendeth or keepeth for temporal uses; substance, I say, not that whereby we essentially subsist for living, but that which is said to stand under us or to subsist [0482C] for us that live, for our using. Which for this cause is not unfitly called the substance of a man's house, because his necessity is sustained by such supports, and with them every solicitous man enricheth and honoureth his house — he, that is, who laboureth either, being provident, to keep off poverty, or, being covetous, to increase riches. Such substance he more largely squandereth and scattereth who plungeth himself into a deep desire of getting love; who, when he shall have given the one and shall have perceived that he hath received the other, comparing what was given with what was received, shall seem to himself, as he looketh the more diligently, to have given nothing. For with so great eagerness he loveth and embraceth this that he hath received, that, accounting for nothing whatsoever he had given, thus despised, there seemeth to be no comparison [0482D] of that which passeth away with that which perisheth not; but that is held as nothing and falling, and this as abiding, as somewhat great and chief. Nor is it beside the purpose if a man's body be in this place named substance, since man is proved to subsist in it or out of it; and for this cause Scripture addeth to make mention *of his house*, because there the treasure of the soul hath its dwelling as in a fruitful vessel. If therefore this body, wherewith it is plain that the soul is so tenaciously mingled that it cannot easily be restrained from affection toward it (for there is none to be found who would be despoiled of this house or body, since Paul also chooseth rather to be clothed upon than to be stripped; and love drew not Peter, who loved thrice, utterly back from that law of the flesh, but, Christ foretelling it, another led him whither he would not) — if, I say, a man of heart shall have given this body, to which [0483A] the soul is bound with clamps so tenacious, it is fitly judged that he hath given nothing [n: (Rom. VIII)]. For the sufferings of this time are not worthy.
