Which love the Bridegroom for this cause so manifoldly extolleth and commendeth, that the loving Virgin may greatly esteem what is so greatly commended, and that, when she shall have weighed that by the Bridegroom's gift she hath attained no small height of that which is commended, she may understand that she is not despised in his eyes. Concerning whom the companions subjoin: *Our sister,* etc.

## CHAPTER XLIV.

*Our sister is a little one, and she hath no breasts. What shall we do to our sister in the day when she is to be spoken to?* We see, say they, that the Virgin hath advanced not slightly in the grace of love, yet that she hath not yet [0483B] more fully attained to that which she desireth; because, although in regard of love she is already come to a contempt of the aforesaid substance, yet she hath not yet found him whom she so loveth in his own comeliness. And because she is our sister by most lofty deserts indeed, and not by nature, being afterward to receive with us the inheritance of the one God the Father, let us, speaking one to another, confer a little concerning her; and if perchance she needeth aught of ours, let us bring it, not now singly, but all alike. So far as it hath seemed to us, this our sister, who, as was said above, hath already deserved to be brought into the chamber, doth not yet rejoice that she is brought in from chamber to chamber; and this indeed is the cause: that she is not yet sufficient enough, nor grown up, but labouring under littleness, and not brought on to years as it were [0483C] marriageable. A dishonest love, which intemperance or lust forerunneth, which a Venus or a Cupid ill-persuasive usurpeth and defileth — such a love, I say, is wont to snatch away a Virgin at an unripe age, obeying pleasure rather than making ready things that shall profit the Virgin. But since this love which we have in hand, though it be more vehement, yet loveth to be more prudent, and the lover willeth this love to profit not so much himself as the Virgin, the same Bridegroom waiteth, and waiteth again, and hath patience in love, so long as the Virgin advanceth in deserts and in an ampler grace. Still therefore she is little, and we see that she hath no breasts, although it was shown above that the same lacketh not breasts; but because they seem not yet to have obtained a full sufficiency, we are said not to have those things which are willing indeed to appear to the bridegroom, [0483D] but are not yet strong enough to appear. Not fit for nuptials are virgins, while they are yet in childhood, while the age is little, while the breasts do not yet swell — which, though they stand out a little and put forth a token of the age that shall be, yet still keep the old tenderness of one still unripe. Since therefore she is thus little, and it is thus plain that she hath no breasts, what shall we do to her? what further shall we now be able to employ? what that belongeth to us can now further be bestowed, that she may at last rejoice that the day of the nuptials is not deferred? *282* She is indeed to be spoken to, and to be brought into a more secret bridal chamber, but first she must be led forth from things present and not yet sufficient; and that she may be led forth hence, what more is to be done by us, that may avail, namely, toward obtaining a day so desirable? In that day, that [0484A] is, in respect and in furtherance of that day, what can we bestow upon this sister? with what zeal or love of ours shall we prepare her more amply, that she may come to the day for which she is now held as it were impatient and so solicitous, when the noble lover, the law of the espousals being consummated, shall speak to her? For although above he hath spoken with her, or of her, in many parts and in very many ways, yet he hath followed not a completing gift, but a meritorious zeal; now it remaineth that she follow him within the chamber of the chamber, and that he, in that manner which he knoweth, ineffably speak to her when she hath followed. Under the word "to speak to" a spiritual mystery is covered, because this nuptial epithalamium familiarly useth figures; and this speaking-to, whereby we desire and foretell that the bridegroom shall come together with the bride, is itself that [0484B] conjunction whereby the face of the seeker is granted to find the face of him that is sought. It is a speaking-to when he, being present to her that is presented, shall hide nothing fitting to be said, but shall reveal his face to her that lacketh corruption; and, with none mediating, the one shall be joined to the other in secret, and the Virgin, seeing the Word, shall be satisfied with a love now fulfilled.



## CHAPTER XLV.

*If she be a wall, let us build upon it bulwarks of silver. If she be a door, let us join it together with boards of cedar.* When the companions ask what they may do that shall be fitting for that day whereon the Virgin is to see the long-desired glory of the divine beauty, they themselves delay not to answer as it were with an answering speech, and they determine to provide for the Virgin [0484C] with a solicitous benevolence. *If she be a wall,* say they, compacted of stones and mortar — nay rather, of virtues coupled by the binding of a charity set between — it remaineth that we fashion upon it bulwarks of silver, and that we confirm the strength of the wall by a defence added above. Jerusalem is the city of the Holy One, the numerous gathering of the faithful, given over in the present to fruitful labours, glorious with a hope that cannot be confounded, which one Lord, one faith coupleth and bindeth into one sheaf as it were; and the same the holy Virgin girdeth about with example and doctrine, with deserts and intercessions. If therefore she be a wall — nay rather, because she is, rejoicing to be set about the citizens — it is expedient that some defence be set above her that is thus set about, that namely our solicitude, our exhortation may watch and be intent from above, lest [0484D] the enemy stretch himself even a little to pierce it. For although we cannot yet carry the labouring Virgin hence, as she desireth, this at least we owe and will now bestow upon her that laboureth: that our defence may render her fortified against whatsoever cometh upon her, and our frequent speaking-to may render her instructed to bear it patiently. Thus we prepare for the wall bulwarks not of stone, but of silver, when we strengthen the virgin with solicitous defences and with speakings-to, when we strongly forbid the malice of assaulting enemies from approach, and cry out to them that the virgin is secure of the issue. But lest this city seem so shut in by the wall set about her that through it she be shut out from those benefits which she hath not from herself, but as it were from without, she who is the wall is none the less [0485A] called a door, through which whatsoever is necessary for the city is ministered. For through the Virgin the Bridegroom loveth to enter in to the gathering of the faithful, and through her also to succour all that trust in her; she, closed to every man, is unbarred to God alone by the little key of faith, that through her the Word made flesh may be visibly brought in to men. If therefore she be a door, let us join it together with boards of cedar, that is, let us add to this aforesaid grace an unconquered strength, that an odoriferous breadth may meet whosoever detracteth, and an unfailing strength withstand him that presseth on perchance more hardly. Meanwhile, while the noble Virgin laboureth and sweateth in the contest, let us prepare and strengthen her patience with the hope of the crown; and in very truth that which she hopeth and asketh to be given her is not far off: as we perceive, she shall now see and rejoice that the Bridegroom is revealed with unveiled [0485B] face.

## CHAPTER XLVI.

*I am a wall, and my breasts are as a tower, since I am become in his presence as one finding peace.* The Virgin, hearing that the angels are not held negligent and slothful toward her, but, being solicitous for her, promise their patronage or their ministry, showeth in a short discourse what she rejoiceth to be already bestowed upon her, hoping that the things which remain be not deferred by a longer delay. I, saith she, grace giving it and the industry of the hand working it, am now a wall not about to fall, charity binding in the midst the heap of living stones, *283* over which my breasts rise up, as a tower, affording honour to the wall, striking terror into the enemies that shall approach. As the wall betokeneth the heap of virtues and the bond of inward charity, so the breasts betoken the form of life [0485C] and the doctrine of truth, which come forth and hasten to appear without unto all, that they may instruct them that love, and compel adversaries to shrink away. In which, although she is not yet perfected for the completing of the present nuptials, yet she hath obtained them very many years since, namely since she deserved to find as it were peace in his presence, whose other peace she desireth and looketh to find right soon. For since the Holy Spirit overshadowed her for conceiving, the Son that was to be born brought her not peace, but as it were peace: peace, that is, from vices, peace in grace, from the din of a carnal begetting — not the peace of vision, not the peace of a dwelling that shall abide in eternal glory. Neither doth she show that she rejoiceth in her own advancement alone, but she showeth that the rest also obtain no slight advancement, who [0485D] through her, grace giving it, have so far advanced that they have deserved to become a vineyard rich not in vine-shoots, but in peoples. Whereof she subjoineth: *There was a vineyard,* etc.

## CHAPTER XLVII.

*There was a vineyard to the peaceable, in that which hath peoples. He delivered it to keepers: a man bringeth for the fruit thereof a thousand pieces of silver.* Since, the Spirit working, I found as it were peace in his presence, the vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth hath had an effectual advancement; and that which before was held within the narrow bounds of Judaea is now found more broadly and more fruitfully in that which hath peoples. That which hath peoples may be called faith, or unity, or love, to which it is plain that divers peoples are so given over with one mind that, the apostles preaching, not only did many [0486A] thousands of the Jews believe, but their sound also went forth into all the earth, and their preaching was heard. Such a vineyard he committed to the apostles and to apostolic men to be kept, whose preaching propagated it not only in Judaea, but among the nations also; and Paul, when he beheld Judaea hardening and being perverted, from that time and thenceforward declareth that he turneth himself to the Gentiles. Which vineyard, grace prospering it, so grew up in a little time, so did away the newness of infancy and its tender ineffectualness, that a man — that is, one mighty not so much in strength as in virtue — should give for the fruit thereof a thousand pieces of silver, that is, all his own things for salvation. The flower of the vineyard is the conversion of life; the fruit is the perfection that shall follow, for whose hundredfold whosoever desireth to be a man casteth away things transitory; the fruit, lastly, is the very repaying of the spiritual reward, [0486B] which a man procureth for himself by the contempt of a temporal price. For he who is found to act not womanishly, but manfully, measureth not what he can give for the fruit of that vineyard, but, greedy of the spiritual reward, that he may receive it with usury, prodigal of the temporal price, bringeth it without weight, number or measure. For the thousand pieces of silver — that is, whatsoever he possessed either infinite in number or great in price, which deceitfully smiled upon his eyes and favourably rang in his ears — he bringeth to the apostles' feet and casteth down, and holdeth in contempt in the stead of dung, that he may receive the eternal fruit by the intervention of temporal things despised. But when the Virgin hath related both her own advancements and those of others, and the vineyard hath been commended which flourisheth more in peoples than in a multitude of vine-branches, she heareth not now [0486C] the angels answering, but with ears erect the bridegroom, who both favoureth and applaudeth the praises of the Virgin and of the vineyard.

## CHAPTER XLVIII.

*My vineyard is before me: thy thousand are the peaceable, and two hundred they that keep the fruits thereof.* [var: Vulg. Cant. 8:12 *et ducenti **his** qui custodiunt fructus eius*, "and two hundred for them that keep the fruits thereof." Migne's text drops *his*, so that the two hundred are the keepers themselves rather than a payment made to them — which is the construction Philip's exposition follows.] The Bridegroom showeth that the vineyard which followeth him, and giveth temporal things for his sake, walketh not in darkness, but is in the light before him; to which, favouring and approving that, its own things being given, it now abideth in him, he repayeth not like for like, but double, or a hundredfold, together with himself. He, saith he, who for my sake holdeth temporal substance in contempt, that he may be the more comforted, let him know that he is in my sight; and let it be made known to whatsoever inexperienced man readeth or heareth, that, loving him that loveth, I turn not away thence [0486D] my gracious face. For those thousand pieces of silver, which, according to thy word, a man loveth to bring — he who after thy pattern loveth to set things invisible before things visible — shall be peaceable, that is, they shall earn the rewards of peace: he shall bestow peace upon them that lavish their own for things eternal. Nor shall they be able to be called peaceable only, but two hundred, that is, they shall confer a double peace upon him that lavisheth; because the peace or perfection which the distribution of goods earneth is both great in the present, and shall follow greatest in the time to come. As perfection is understood in a thousand, so is it understood also in a hundred, which are assuredly doubled when the vineyard is brought to so effectual an increase that, superfluous things being cast away, he may deserve to find a double *284* peace, whosoever loveth to keep the fruits thereof with watchful care. For he who willeth to preside by his form and to profit by a commendable doctrine, [0487A] and loveth to be a solicitous keeper of the aforesaid fruit, he by the thousand pieces of silver bringeth in the first peace, but not the chief; and, changing the hundred into two hundred, he afterward bringeth over the second and better. But having briefly shown what belongeth to all the perfect by a general grace, he straightway returneth to the virgin with a special love and solicitude; and having care of her above all the branches of the aforesaid vineyard, he willeth her to pass over more quickly from a transitory peace to one that shall abide.



## CHAPTER XLIX.

*Thou that dwellest in the gardens, the friends hearken: make me hear thy voice.* Although, saith he, I still defer both them that bring and them that defer to bring the thousand pieces of silver for the two hundred, and suffer them not to be led on to the desired [0487B] reward that followeth, yet thee, whom I love before all, I will not restrain any longer from thy desire; but, the choice being given, I will that thou shortly have whatsoever thou shalt have chosen. Thou therefore, whom I led forth out of the dwelling-place of darkness, out of the shade of hard death, and who by an excellent grace dwellest not in a dry place, but in the gardens — choose a pleasing word, put forth thy voice, speak thou thyself: the companions stand by, the friends hearken, they desire to hear from thee thyself. I myself, who know better whatsoever thou art now purposing to say, will to hear thy voice, and the good pleasure of thine inward choice, that the manner of thy saying may become known, not to me, but to the rest, from whom thy choice lieth hid, if it shine not forth in words. With thee the love of things vainly passing away and the fear of things coming on do not wither, but faith, hope, love, like [0487C] gardens, grow bright with a flowering dew; and so wondrous a grace of these things so delighteth thy desire that no shaking bendeth thee toward the things that are beneath. Thou desirest indeed to go forth, or to pass over straightway to things above; loathing whatsoever is of time, thou wilt the more quickly lay hold on things eternal; whatsoever I have bestowed for the present, thou wilt exchange for the desire of things to come, and, the cloak of the flesh being cast off, to greet in presence my face, the face of thy beloved. And she: *Flee,* etc,

## CHAPTER L.

*Flee, my beloved, be like to the roe and to the young hart upon the mountains of spices.* In many places or times above the loving Virgin hath invited her beloved, and hath asked in many ways that he come; and in the very head of the Canticle she more diligently longed for his kiss, [0487D] and through this whole epithalamium hath shown that she willeth and seeketh this. What then meaneth it that she now driveth him away, with desire of whom she above crieth out that she languisheth? what cause shall we say there is that she biddeth him flee whom she so loveth, unless perchance this, that lovers have their angers in hope of a more pleasing concord, because, as a certain man declareth: *The angers of lovers are the renewal of love?*

But, as I seem to see, the Virgin's love knoweth no angers, but burneth to see the more quickly him whom she so loveth; and because she knoweth that he is not seen in this place or body, she desireth to go thither with him, where she may be able to behold him. *Flee,* saith she, *my beloved,* to the secret sanctuary of the Father; [0488A] return quickly, call me thither with thee, where I may be hurt by no troubles any more; strip me the more quickly of the corruption of this body, and where it is lawful, as much as is lawful, reveal thyself visible to me. And because above thou wast wont to be likened to the roe and to the young hart, be now also in this business swift, nimble and discerning; let thy consideration worthily discern what beseemeth a bride and a mother, and let it set me apart, by a more excellent privilege, from all that are purely men. The mountains of spices are the supernal and angelic powers, which bring to us that labour divers and necessary healings, by whose ministry useful spices are procured for us — he nevertheless disposing it by whose perfumer's art they are tempered. Below these angelic mountains I will not that thou speak with me any further, but flee above them, that thou mayest be held far more excellent; [0488B] hold thy seat at the Father's right hand, unapproachable to angels as to men, and already granted, as I see, to me with thee, to the mother with the son. Hold therefore my right hand, and lead me forth in thy will: I will follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth [n: (Apoc. XIV)], halting with no slowness. Flee quickly, that I may flee, because I also am ready to flee; fleeing, exalted above the angels, I shall see thee going before. But after that the virgin Bride, the mother, hath been more gloriously received by the Son, and hath obtained a glorious seat with the Bridegroom above the angels — with what honour she rejoiceth, with what joy she seeth herself honoured, I judge that silence is rather to be kept than that I should dare to be wordy of such things. For that which my understanding, or the understanding of one like me, taketh not in — what manner or effect of uttering can there be, [0488C] since even that which the understanding somehow reckoneth that it contemplateth cannot easily be unfolded in fitting words? This surely may be said: that where the Son is, who set the flesh he had taken at the Father's right hand (whatsoever that truly is which Scripture hath called the right hand), there is his mother, who ministered to him her own flesh, who out of her womb, her integrity safe, brought forth God as man. *285* There, I say, she is, and is crowned with a glorious honour or with an honourable glory, and of him, and in him, and with him whom she bore, having her desire, she glorieth; and to him as Bridegroom the Bride so cleaveth with true and sincere embraces that, love being satisfied, an unremitted desire of love endureth. The mother therefore is with the Son not only in spirit, whereof not even a slight doubt is held, [0488D] but in body also, which assuredly seemeth not incredible; because although canonical Scripture crieth not this out with evident proofs, yet dutiful faith is led to it by likely arguments — which, though one hasty in word and in knowledge prove it not sufficiently, yet that Augustine of ours affirmeth it worthy to be believed. Nor is it grievous to the angels if they see the Bride with the Bridegroom, the mother with the Son, obtain the royal throne, and hold now upon the heavenly seat him whom before she held in her lap; if they see human flesh gloriously honoured above themselves in the mother and in the Son, and the nuptials happily begun among us there more happily consummated.

Of which things, because I have spoken [0489A] as I was able, though not as I would, and with a foot slow enough have reached the end of speaking: I beseech thee, O holy Virgin, that, since thou now standest by thy Son in the heavens, thou cease not from care and solicitude for him who is thine. Thine indeed am I, if not by a sufficiently worthy desert, yet at least by an affection a little readier; thine, serving thee, though as yet not knowing whether I be worthy of hatred or of love [n: (Eccle. IX)]; thine, desiring to please thee with services and with gifts, if only thou shalt grant me effectually to prevail in my purpose. Do thou therefore, O holy Virgin, receive from my hand a little gift. It is not gold, not silver, not a stone fit for the offerings of kings, but an unpolished libation of words, brought forth with a grosser understanding, an offering small enough, yet full of watchings and of toil. After I betook myself [0489B] to the exercise of it as to a rough training-school, I was smitten with many troubles, and by the onset of the malignant was heavily beaten back as it were in the face; and the work begun I many times laid aside under harder pressures, [0490A] yet, thy more gracious remembrance calling me back and helping me, I let it not go. Do thou therefore, by whose help I failed not in the furnace of pressures under a heavy hammer, but, breathing again as best I might, have now finished in thy name the work begun — do thou now receive it offered, correct mercifully him that offereth it and amend him, love him amended, and commend me, being loved, to thy Son. For I know that, if I shall have been commended to him by thy benevolence, either the venomous serpent shall not bite me at all, or by his biting he shall not hurt me; and that Son of thine shall either call back the tongues of detractors to a modest silence, or shall change their poisonous rumours into a health-bearing antidote. So assuredly I hope, by thine intervention and by thy grace, to be delivered from all things hurtful, and, being delivered, to be heaped through grace with mightier gifts; and to me thus heaped thou wilt now [0490B] grant to rejoice through thee in the Son, and — that I may set an end to the book — thou wilt grant me, freed at last from evils, to glory with you in the heavens.

*Joannes GALLEMART, Doctor of Sacred Theology, and professor of catechesis in the University of Douai, this 7 Feb. 1618.*
